Read: The Evolution of Honey Bees How did bees evolve? Before bees ☆ Key Points existed, there were several species of wasps. These wasps, just like wasps today, hunted prey to feed their young. Evidence suggests that millions of years ago, one species of wasp started feeding their young pollen from Honey bees evolved from carnivorous, solitary wasps Bees first evolved about 130 million years ago, shortly after flowering plants first evolved flowers. These wasps were the ancestors to modern bees, who feed on nectar and pollen. In a way, you can say that bees are vegetarian wasps. Over time, they evolved hairs on their bodies and special pollentransporting apparatuses that allow them to collect pollen efficiently. All species of bees within the family Apidae carry pollen on their legs. Other species carry pollen inside their bodies or on the undersides of their abdomens. (Photo credit: Jennifer Tsuruda) Fossil records of bees preserved in amber indicate that bees have existed for at least 100 million years, but they are estimated to have first evolved around 130 million years ago, shortly after flowering plants first appeared on Earth. Plants evolved colors, odors, shapes, and food rewards that attract bees, while bees evolved mechanisms to collect pollen, which help plants reproduce through pollination. This period is known as the Cretaceous period, and was a time when dinosaurs roamed the earth. Humans did not evolve for another many million years. While bees have been around for roughly 130 million years, the oldest fossils of honey bees (the bees in the genus Apis) date back to around 60 million years ago. They occupied the so-called Old World: what is now Asia, Africa, and Europe. There is still debate over where precisely honey bees arose within the Old World. Recent genetic analyses suggest that all honey bees (genus Apis) actually originated in Asia, and Apis mellifera later diversified into Europe and Africa. They were introduced to the New World for the first time in the 1600s by European settlers. Now, they have been introduced to all continents except Antarctica.

The native habitat for Apis mellifera included rainforest, savannah, desert and other relatively warm climates in Africa, Asia, and southern Europe. These broad geographical ranges and differing climates allowed for several subspecies (races) of honey bees to evolve adaptations specific to their region. Honey bees have adapted to a variety of climates, including the colder temperate regions of North America. Some subspecies are better able to withstand cooler climates and store food for their year-round needs; others are better able to avoid or combat pests and diseases that are more prevalent in warmer climates. (Photo credit: Ben Rulison). Back to Table of Contents

Eusociality: How Honey Bees Are Truly Social You may look at your hive and wonder ☆ Key Points how this bustling honey bee society of tens of thousands of individuals working together evolved from a solitary wasp-like organism. Honey bee colonies are examples of the most Honey bees are eusocial, meaning that individuals depend on societal organization to survive and cannot live on their own advanced form of social living on the planet. This level of organization is called eusociality. "Eu-" means true or genuine. Individuals fully depend on a societal organization to survive and cannot live on their own. There are three defining characteristics of a eusocial organism: Overlapping generations: More than one generation is living together. For honey bees, there are, for the most part, two generations present in one colony: a mother (the queen) and her offspring (workers and drones). Cooperative brood care: Individuals share the duty of raising young that is not theirs. Cooperative brood care is rare in the animal kingdom. Only a few species care for their young, and the work is usually done by the mother. In the case of honey bees, the queen lays the eggs, but the larvae, pupae, and young adults are cared for by their older sisters. Reproductive division of labor: In honey bees, reproduction is divided among the members of a colony. The queen is the sole egg layer under normal conditions, and workers do not usually reproduce. The workers are not fully sterile, for they can still lay unfertilized eggs that can develop into males, but they normally do so only if they lose their queen. The three members of a bee colony (queens, workers, and drones) are divided by their reproductive ability and sex.
Honey bee colonies exhibit all three characteristics of eusociality. Photo Credit: Bee Informed Partnership Back to Table of Contents

Watch: How Did Eusocial Societies With Distinct Castes Evolve? Having multiple distinct forms of the same sex — like the queen and worker castes in honey bee females — is very rare in the animal kingdom. Evolutionary biologists have spent a lot of time studying other close relatives of honey bees to find out how such a caste system evolved in the first place. This video explores the prevailing theory. Video Transcript So how did these honey bee colonies get to have such distinct castes between queens and workers? The main theory is that the ancestor to honey bees, the solitary wasp-like organism, actually did all of the jobs that she needed to do in life by herself. She collected her own food, she built her own nest, she mated and laid her eggs and then provisioned all of those eggs with food, similar to how solitary bees live today. The resources that were available to her determined how much time and energy she was going to allocate to these different tasks. So it's not like she could be collecting food and laying eggs at the same time. There was only a short period of time where she could do each of these tasks. Importantly, once her offspring actually emerged from those eggs they left the nest. They didn't stay and hang around for any period of time to help the mother. So at some point in the honey bee's evolution, tens of millions of years ago, there was a mutation or a genetic change that occurred. And likely, it was probably more than one. And this genetic change allowed the offspring to remain at the nest with her mother after emerging instead of flying away and starting her own nest. And this was the first time that we start to see overlapping generations present in the nest, the mother generation and the daughter generation. And we also start to see cooperative brood care, as the daughters would cooperate in rearing the brood, or their younger sisters. This change and other genetic changes were favored by natural selection and persistent in the population, allowing these family groups to start to develop, with a mother bee and helper daughter bees evolving. So over time the mother was sort of allowed to start specializing in reproduction and laying eggs, while the daughters, this kind of frees up time for them to start specializing in other helping strategies. Over time natural selection sort of continued to favor this and then these rigid castes were finally in place. Their evolved, there's reproductive division of labor between the queen and reproduction and the workers in other tasks. In the case of

honey bees, these castes have become so rigid that female bees must function either as a queen or as a worker. It's not like a queen bee can revert back to being a worker and vice versa. A worker can't psychologically change to become a queen. Some other species of bees like bumble bees aren't quite as distinct and rigid. They still have queens and workers, but if a queen suddenly dies, a large worker can actually start to dominate her sisters and it is physiologically possible for her to mate and lay eggs. Where as it is not physiologically possible for workers to mate. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Kin Selection The evolution of a non-reproducing worker caste is one of the most extreme examples of altruism in nature, and has fascinated biologists for centuries. The term 'altruism' refers to the fact that the majority of female bees in a colony suppress their own reproduction and instead invest energy into helping another individual (their mother, the queen) reproduce. On the surface, this appears to go against nature. Reproducing to pass its genes on to the next generation is, biologically speaking, the most important thing an organism can do – it is usually the measure of success for living things. Charles Darwin, who first proposed the theory of evolution, wondered how individuals who refrain from reproducing could evolve. If an organism does not have any offspring, how do its genes persist in the world? And why would some bees refrain from reproducing in order to raise another bee’s young instead? In The Origin of Species (1859), he describes the non-reproducing caste of honey bees as “one special difficulty, which at first appeared to me insuperable, and actually fatal to my theory”. It was not until the 1960s that a clear explanation arose: kin selection. Watch the video below to learn about kin selection: Video Transcript Workers inhibit their own reproduction in order to help the queen reproduce. And it's really costly for them to invest so much energy into rearing the queen's offspring. It's costly for them to go out and collect pollen from flowers, and risky because they might come in contact with predators. It's costly for them to produce royal jelly in their glands and to feed that to the offspring and to keep the brood warm. It's also costly for them to keep on checking on the brood and making sure that they're developing okay and that they're not getting any diseases. And most of all, one of the biggest costs is that they sacrifice their own lives to sting intruders to protect the colony. So all these things are really energetically expensive. So why are workers behaving so selfless? The answer is kin selection. Even in humans, the want to help is more likely with kin or your relatives than non-kin. Think of how protective you feel if someone wants to fight one of your siblings. Or a time when you might put yourself in danger or in a risky situation to try to save one of your relatives. Another good example of family helping is when there's a new baby in the family and aunts and nieces and other relatives will come together and help raise the baby.

Kin selection is a strategy where individuals reduce their own reproductive success or survival in order to increase the reproductive success of someone else. And in the honey bee colony it's the worker who's reducing their reproduction to help their mom, the queen, reproduce. On the surface this appears really selfless, but at the genetic level you can start to see why it's advantageous and why this behavior likely evolved. Being related means you share genes with someone and the amount of genes that you share influences your helping behavior. And humans and bees are different. They differ in how they inherit their genes and how related they are with their kin. So let's start with humans. Individuals inherit genes from their parents, so you have genes in common with all your relatives: your parents, your grandparents, your siblings and your own children. And the closer you are related, the more genes you're actually sharing. So you share more genes with your mom than you would with your great, great grandmother, for example. Humans are diploid organisms. This means that they have two sets of each chromosome in all of their cells. So their skin cells, their bone cells, their muscle cells, they all have two sets of chromosomes. One set is inherited from your mom, and one set is inherited from your dad. The exception is when you're looking at your gametes. Your egg cells or sperm cells only have one set of chromosomes. So because you're inheriting one set from your dad, and one set from your mom, this means that 50% of your genes are shared with your mom, and 50% of your genes are shared with your dad. And also as a result, 50% of your genes are shared with your sibling. Looking at a family tree, we can see the average degree of genetic relatedness. And this just goes to show again how many genes you're sharing. So, mothers and daughters share 50%, fathers and daughters share 50%. And same with your brother, they share 50% with their mom and 50% with their dad. Honey bees have a slightly different genetic system and it's called haplodiploidy. The females are similar to humans where they come from a fertilized egg so a sperm and an egg come together and they have two set of chromosomes. So they're also diploid. But, the males are different. Instead, males come from unfertilized eggs. They only inherit one set of chromosomes. That from their mother. So they are called haploid. They have half the number of chromosomes than the females in the colony do. So drones are haploids and all the females, workers and queens are diploid. A haplodiploid system actually makes bees more related than 50%. So this is where we see the difference from humans. In fact, if a queen only mates with one male, workers will share 75% of their genes. So how does that even work? Well, both drones and queens are passing on one copy of their DNA to create diploid daughters. And since the drones only have one set of chromosomes to begin with, all the copies that he's passing on to each daughter are going to be identical.

So, sisters are sharing 100% of genes that they receive from their father. But with the queen she's diploid. She has two sets of each copy of each gene in her DNA. And she gives one copy to each of her daughters. So one sister might inherit the same set of chromosomes or some of the same genes as the other sister. But sometimes they receive different copies. Across the thousands of genes that they're inheriting the amount of times they end up sharing the same copies averages out to about 50%. It's similar to tossing a coin. There's two options. You can have heads or you can have tails. If you and your sister are each flipping the coin over time, over thousands of tries, the average amount of time that you are going to get the same copies is about 50%. So sisters share about 50% of their genes that they receive from their mother. So a daughter of a singly mated queen who has the same dad will share on average 75% of their genes; 100% from the dad side and 50% from the mom side averages out to 75%. Okay, so what if a worker were to lay her own eggs? If a worker were to lay her own egg she would pass on 50% of her DNA. Workers can't mate or store any sperm so they're producing unfertilized haploid drones. They're always drones. So if we're thinking about it, what is the better avenue to get the most genes to persist in the population? Is it to have your own offspring, where you're passing on 50% of your genes? Or is it to help rear your sisters, who are going to be sharing 75% of your genes? It's to help raise your sisters. And if we are looking at a honey bee colony, we see that the queen is able to lay many many eggs a day, up to a thousand eggs a day, so it is a really good way to pass on your genetic information even though you yourself aren't reproducing or the workers themselves are not reproducing. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Polyandry When honey bees first evolved, queens ☆ Key Points were monogamous, meaning they mated with just one male. This meant that all of her daughter bees were highly related to one another and had 75% of their genes in common. This high level of relatedness helped drive the evolution of eusociality. Once eusociality was established, however, other colony traits also evolved. One such trait is polyandry. Polyandry is the practice of females mating with multiple (poly) males (andry). Queen honey bees are promiscuous, typically mating with between 12 and 50 males. By mating Queen honey bees usually mate with between 12 and 50 males, which helps to increase genetic diversity among her offspring, the colony's workers. Genetic diversity improves colony health and productivity. Relatedness among sisters decreases with polyandry, but it is still more advantageous for workers to rear the queen's offspring (their brothers and sisters) rather than their fellow sisters' offspring (their nephews). with multiple males, a queen greatly increases the genetic diversity among her daughters, the workers in the colony, thus improving the colony's health and productivity.

Queens mate with multiple drones. The Impact of Polyandry on Relatedness When queens mate with multiple males, the relatedness between sisters decreases. While they share 75% of their genes when they have the same father, daughter bees only share 25% of their genes when they have unrelated fathers. Under these circumstances, one might expect workers would produce their own offspring instead of helping rear their sisters. Yet workers still refrain from reproducing, despite the fact that they would now be more related to their offspring than their half-sisters. How come? One possible reason has to do with the high reproductive output of the queen. The queen can lay 1,000 to 1,500 eggs per day, while a laying worker lays only a few eggs per day. Even though workers are less related to the queen's offspring than their own, they can still effectively pass on more of their genes by helping the queen. Another possible reason has to do with the relatedness between a worker and her sisters' offspring. Although it would be advantageous for a worker to rear her own offspring, it would not be advantageous for her to rear her sisters' offspring. If several workers began laying eggs in the colony, one worker would invest energy in rearing many of her nephews as well. In this situation, it is more advantageous for sisters to invest energy and resources into rearing their mother's offspring (with whom they share 25% of their genes) than their sisters' offspring — their nephews — with whom they only share 12.5% of their genes.

A specific social behavior has evolved to discourage workers from reproducing. This behavior is called worker policing, and it refers to workers consuming the eggs that are laid by their sisters. In the rare instances where workers do lay eggs, their sisters will eat them so that they never develop. We've talked about the genetic relatedness among several family members in a honey bee colony, and it is possible to calculate these values for all their relatives. It is, however, beyond the scope of this course to have you calculate genetic relatedness among family members. The take-home message is this: Understanding genetic relatedness among family members in a bee colony can help us learn how and why honey bees evolved such a social living strategy. Watch: The Importance of Wild Bees There is incredible diversity in bees and ☆ Key Points striking differences in the way they look, behave, build their nests, and live alone or together. Although honey There are 20,000 species of wild bees in the world bees are the species most commonly used for pollination in agriculture, many species of bees also have important roles in pollinating food crops and wildflowers. Across the world, there are over 20,000 documented species of bees! Watch this video to hear Bryan Danforth discuss the many other bees (besides honey bees) that are found in the world. Video Transcript So honey bees are not the only bees in the world. In fact, there are over 20,000 described species of bees in the world. In North America, we estimate about 4,000 described bees. California hosts over 1,000 species of bees and French-speaking Europe, hosts nearly a 1,000 species of bees as well. In New York state, we have recently tallied up the numbers and come up with a total 420 species. So, while these are extraordinarily diverse, and if you compare the species richness of wild bees to other familiar large vertebrate groups, bees are comparable to fishes in the vertebrates with about 20,000 species. There are about five times as many bees as there are mammals and there are about three times as many bees as there are birds. So bees are an enormously diverse group. They're a group that arose over 120 million years ago. That's well before the extinction of the dinosaurs and it's a period when the earliest flowering plants were just evolving on earth. I'll use two terms throughout this presentation. One is native bee to describe bees that are native to a region or of the world. And wild bee to describe all the non-managed bees that we'll be covering in today's presentation. Bees occur on all continents except Antarctica and they're particularly diverse in desert habitats such as the circa Mediterranean region, western Australia, Southern Africa, and western North America. By comparison, honey bees encompass only eight species in the genus Apis. And one of those, the managed honey bee, is Apis mellifera. Now it turns out wild bees are actually very important agricultural pollinators and we've learned this fairly recently, from studies in crops like apples, peaches, cherries, blueberries, cranberries, strawberries, squashes and pumpkins. Wild bees are a large component of the fauna in these agricultural habitats. And in New York, for example, we have 120 species of wild bees visiting apple trees, just alone. Apple

growers, for example, in New York and other agricultural producers are well aware of the role of these wild bees. And they do a very good job of trying to maintain a diverse wild bee fauna in and around their cultural habitats. Native bees and the wild bees we're talking about today have coevolved with many different host plants. And one of the interesting things about native wild bees is that they are often narrow host plant specialists, unlike the honey bee, which is a very broad generalist visiting many different host plant families. So what do we know about these other wild bee species? First of all, they are extraordinarily diverse in anatomy and behavior. There are a tiny species the size of a fruit fly in arid regions of western North America and there are enormous carpenter bees the size of a bird that one can see flying in, more or less, tropical habitats. Bees come in a range of colors and in different amounts of hairiness. But they're quite diverse anatomically and behaviorally. The vast majority of bees are solitary. So our estimate is that about 77% of the bee species on earth are solitary. A single female constructs her own nest. She guards that nest against parasites and predators. She gathers pollen and nectar for her offspring, and she lays eggs. She's usually active for a very short period of time. Somewhere between two to three weeks. In contrast to a honey bee colony which is active for months throughout the summer. And again, many of these solitary wild bees are narrow host plants specialists, visiting just a few host plant genera or even species. Now these wild bees build nests in a variety of substrates, including soil, hollow stems, wood, snail shells, some of them build above ground nests, and some of them build nests in solid wood, those are the carpenter bees. So let's start with the soil nesters which are the largest proportion of wild bees on earth. These are bees that burrow into the soil. They can build nests from just a few inches deep to up to nine feet deep. There are records of these bees building nests that go down nine feet into the soil. At the bottom of their nest, they will construct a series of underground brood chambers which they provision with pollen and they'll waterproof these brood chambers with glandular secretions or floral oils. And then they'll provision that brood chamber by making many trips, usually five to ten foraging trips. They'll lay an egg on that collected pollen and then they'll close that brew chamber and start the whole cycle again. A typical solitary bee produces about one offspring per day, but some very rapid foragers can do five to even six offspring per day. And an average wild bee doesn't live for very long. She might produce 10, 12, 15 offspring over the course of her entire life.

Another group of solitary bees are the cavity and stem nesters. These include the mason bees, the leaf cutter bees, and the wool carder bees. And we call these renters because they occupy cavities that were created by another organism or just cavities available in the environment. And what they do is they construct their brood cells within these cavities by modifying the cavity slightly with mud, leaves, plant fibers, even flower petals and once they've constructed their brood chamber with those materials they then provision the brood chamber with pollen and nectar just like the ground nesting bee would do. They lay an egg and then they close the brood chamber and carry on with another brood cell the next day. Another group of wild bees are the wooden pith-nesters. And these include the large carpenter bees as well as the small carpenter bees. These are bees that construct a burrow in solid wood or in pithy stems. And carpenter bees have an enormous head with stout mandibles for burrowing into solid wood and constructing a series of burrows. and then from within those burrows they construct their brood cells. They provision their brood cells again with pollen and nectar, they lay an egg and they close the brood cell. And they will construct multiple brood cells throughout their lives. And finally, the last group of wild bees are the resin bees and these are bees that actually construct above-ground nests from resins combined with pieces of stone or chewed up leaves. Again, they use a variety of floral products, but they actually construct their nest above-ground, and they attach it to a plant or a stone, almost like a little flower pot. And then they forage out from that nest collecting pollen and nectar, and they bring those floral resources back to their nest, they provision their brood cells, they lay an egg, and they close that brood cell off. So those are the resin bees in the family megachilidae. And again these are all solitary, like most of the bees I've told you about so far. Now one of the really fascinating groups of bees are the kleptoparasites. These are bees that very few people know about. They comprise 13% of wild bee species, and almost 25% of the family Apidae which is the group that includes the honey bee. These are bees that don't construct a nest. They don't gather pollen and nectar. They sneak into the nest of other bees. And they lay an egg discretely in the brood cell of that host and then they leave the nest as quickly as possible so as not to alert the host to their presence. Their egg hatches and the first instar larva usually seeks out the host egg or early instar larva and they kill it with greatly enlarged mandibles. And, then the klepto parasite larva consumes the pollen provisions gathered by the host female. So these are really similar to the cuckoo birds that some of you might be familiar with that are known for birds where the cockoo lays eggs in another birds nest and then flies away and hopes that that bird will take care of its offspring. So these are called cuckoo bees or kleptoparasites or brood parasites. And

you can often see them if you look around bee nesting sites, if you look near the ground, you'll see what look like wasps almost flying near the ground and looking for nests of their hosts and then entering those nests to lay their eggs. So, we don't know whether these are good pollinators but they're certainly fascinating bees that have adopted a very unusual lifestyle. And then the last category of bees are the Social Bees, which of course would include the honey bee. In this group only includes 9% of the bees in the world. Social bees other than honey bee would include bumble bees, sweat bees and stingless bees in the tropical parts of the world. Stingless bees are comparable to honey bees in terms of social complexity. They build enormous colonies with thousands of workers. They are aggressive defenders of their nest. They communicate about the location of resources. They've actually been managed in various parts of the world for honey production, just like we manage honey bees today in North America. It's a little more difficult to manage a stainless bee colony for honey production, so they're not as widely managed as the honey bee. So while honey bees are fascinating and extremely effective pollinators in all kinds of crop systems, we shouldn't forget that wild bees are important pollinators, but also fascinating from a biological perspective. And what we're discovering with our work on wild bees of apples is that conserving wild bees is an important approach for agricultural producers who want to maximize the pollination of their crops. It's also important for environmental conservation and for carrying on sustainable agricultural practices. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Conserving Wild Bees There is a lot of interest today in bee ☆ Key Points conservation. Honey bees are not alone in facing impacts from parasites, diseases, nutrition, and pesticides; some wild bee populations are also facing challenges from these factors. Some wild bee species are experiencing population declines, and several have been added to the Endangered Species List Their conservation is equally important for maintaining natural ecosystems and sustainable agriculture. Wild bees contribute to overall ecosystem health and the biodiversity of native flowers, and as beekeepers, we are regarded as stewards of all pollinators and advocates for healthy environments. Although honey bees comprise only 9% of bee species (and aren't native to North America), they have become the face of pollinator declines in the media. Master Beekeepers can use this opportunity to help educate the wider public about all kinds of bees and pollinators. The beekeeper's voice is an important one. In the Northeast U.S., there are 53 species of wild bees whose populations are currently in decline. In 2016, several species of bees were added to the Endangered Species list for the first time in history. These bees were seven species of yellow-faced bees that nest in small cavities and stems in Hawaii. In early 2017, the rusty patched bumble bee, native to eastern North America, was also added to the list. With most research focused on the factors affecting the health of honey bees, we are only recently identifying how wild bees are impacted by some of the same factors. Wild bees, for instance, are more susceptible to habitat loss than are honey bees. While wildflowers generally only provide food for honey bees in the U.S., they also provide nesting sites for some native bees. Habitat loss in the form of agricultural intensification and urbanization has been identified as one of the main driving factors for reducing some wild bee populations. The impact of various pesticides on wild bees is only beginning to be investigated. We are learning that pesticides affect different bee species differently — some are much more sensitive to certain chemicals than honey bees. We are also starting to better understand the role of certain parasites and pathogens in wild bee health. At least two are shared between honey bees and bumble bees; Nosema ceranae and Deformed Wing Virus can

infect both genera ('genera' is the plural of genus). Research on how pesticides and pathogens are impacting native bee populations is currently underway at Cornell and other institutions. Back to Table of Contents

Module Wrap-up: The Evolution of the Honey Bee Colony as a Superorganism In this module, you explored the remarkable evolution of honey bees from solitary wasps to one of nature's most sophisticated social organisms. Understanding how individual bees function as part of a larger, interconnected colony helps beekeepers appreciate the complex adaptations that make honey bees such successful and fascinating creatures. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Honey Bee Reproduction Reproduction in honey bee colonies occurs at two levels: The entire colony can reproduce through swarming. Individuals within a colony can reproduce by mating and having offspring. This module focuses on individual reproduction and covers everything you need to know about the biology and behaviors involved. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Passing on Your Genes Through reproduction, bees pass on their genetic material to their offspring. This course uses a variety of terms when talking about genetic material: genome, chromosome, gene, and DNA. These words are all related, but mean slightly different things. Let's get familiar with these terms so that we can better understand honey bee reproduction and genetic characteristics. Basic Genetics ☆ Key Points DNA is the name of the molecule that carries genetic material. An organism's DNA is coiled up into chromosomes Genes are sections of DNA that code for particular proteins. Genes are passed down to offspring through reproduction Beekeepers can selectively breed for the characteristics they desire A genome is an organism’s complete Many honey bee behaviors are set of genetic material. governed by multiple genes Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is the name of the molecule that carries this genetic material. The honey bee genome is different from the human genome and the genomes of all other organisms because each species has differences in their DNA that make them unique. The genome includes information for a variety of elements, the most important being genes. The honey bee genome was sequenced in 2006 and is one-tenth of the size of the human genome. An organism's DNA strands are incredibly long. For instance, if a human's DNA was stretched out it would be three meters in length! In order to fit all the DNA into each cell of an organism's body, it is tightly coiled up into molecules called chromosomes. Honey bee DNA is distributed across 16 different chromosomes: Queens and workers. Diploid females carry two sets of chromosomes, so each cell (except their egg cells) contains 32 chromosomes total. Drones. Haploid males carry only one set of chromosomes, so each cell (including their sperm cells) contains 16 chromosomes total. An organism's DNA serves as the blueprint for its body. Different regions of the DNA strands are the written instructions for different genes. The honey bee genome contains

around 10,000 different genes, so each chromosome contains the instructions for many hundreds of different genes. Small particles within cells read the gene instructions and build their corresponding proteins. For example, a gene with instructions to build an eye cell would get translated into an eye cell protein. Like most other animals, honey bees reproduce by creating egg cells and sperm cells. These cells contain the parents' chromosomes, so all offspring that are produced inherit their parents' genes. How would a beekeeper breed for the trait they desire? Many of the traits we observe in honey bees are due at least in part to genes, so beekeepers can selectively breed for characteristics they desire. For example, there are many genes involved in nectar collecting, in temperament, and in hygienic behavior. Bee breeders can try to improve their operation's honey production, gentleness, or colony health by breeding queens from colonies that have these traits. Honey bee behaviors are complex because they tend to be governed by multiple genes and the environment also influences their behaviors, but nonetheless beekeepers have been breeding for traits like these for decades - long before we knew about DNA. All honey bees are recognizably honey bees, but no two are identical. While they all contain 10,000 or so genes in their chromosomes, the versions of those genes can be different. To illustrate this point, let's think of an example in humans: eye color. Everyone has a gene that codes for eye color located on the same position on one of their chromosomes, but people can have different colors of eyes: some have brown, while others have blue or green. This is due to different versions of the eye color gene. Individuals inherit their specific gene versions from their parents. Scientists refer to different gene versions as "alleles". Now let's look at an example with honey bees: temperament. Let's imagine that we have a bee yard with many hives in it, and the colonies vary greatly in their temperament. Some colonies are very gentle, while others are much more prone to sting. In the honey bee genome, there is one gene that codes for temperament (in reality temperament is governed by many different genes, but we will keep this example simple). Some colonies carry a version of this gene that makes them more aggressive, while other colonies carry a version of this gene that makes them gentle. Over the years, we can improve the temperament of our entire bee yard by selecting which gene versions are going to be passed down to subsequent generations. We can allow the queens from gentle colonies to reproduce, and can prevent the queens from aggressive colonies from reproducing (by

replacing them with queens raised from our gentle colonies). Over a few bee generations, we can have a yard of entirely gentle colonies, as that gene version becomes predominant over the other version in the population. By understanding honey bee reproduction in this way, beekeepers can start to breed for characteristics they desire - whether their goal is to increase honey production or to help improve honey bee health in an effort to be a better steward to the environment. ▶ Read: The Molecules of Bee Life DNA and chromosomes are important molecules of bee life, but there are others to consider as well. We don't often think of tiny microscopic molecules when we think of honey bee reproduction, development, and growth, but in order to understand how these processes occur we need to take a step deeper than what we see with the naked eye. It's interesting to know that honey bees reproduce and develop in unique ways as animals, but it is even more valuable to understand how they do it. Chemical compounds in the form of molecules are key players in development and reproduction of all living organisms, for they enable communication among the cells inside a body and among the individuals within a honey bee colony. The molecules important to honey bee reproduction, development, and sociality that we will cover in this course are proteins, neurotransmitters, hormones, and pheromones. Proteins Proteins form the building blocks of life (human, honey bee, and every other living thing) because they are involved in so many functions. For example, many organs and tissues (e.g. hearts and muscles) are made primarily of different types of proteins. Even the immune system relies on proteins to function. Proteins also play a big role in development and reproduction. The instructions for building proteins are written in DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid), found in most cells within an organism. Neurotransmitters Neurotransmitters are chemicals released by neurons in the brain to send very fast signals to other neurons. They are the important messenger molecules of the nervous system and are involved in many functions ranging from muscle movements to learning and memory in the bee. Many neurotransmitters in honey bees are also present in humans, such as dopamine, octopamine, and serotonin. ▶

▶ ▶ Hormones Hormones are chemicals produced in special glands that are secreted into the blood (called the hemolymph, in bees) to be carried to specific organs and tissues to influence how these structures function. Hormones travel within the body and do not exit it. In the honey bee, as in humans, hormones are involved in reproduction, development, and the general functioning of the body (e.g., stress hormones). Pheromones Pheromones, like hormones, are also chemicals created by specialized glands, but they are secreted outside of the body to elicit a behavioral or physiological response by another individual of the same species. Insects, vertebrates (including humans), plants, and even yeast commonly use pheromones as a means of communication. Some pheromones function as airborne molecules (odors) that are detected through the sense of smell, while others function as surface-borne molecules that are secreted onto the outside of the body where they can be detected through taste or closerange smell. Some honey bee pheromones are even transmitted throughout the colony by worker bees engaging in trophallaxis (transferring or exchanging fluids or food mouth-to-mouth). Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Mating In order to pass their genes on to their offspring, honey bees mate. Queens and drones are the only colony members that mate. Mating activity in honey bee populations typically follows a seasonal cycle that coincides with swarm season. When colonies swarm, they leave behind new virgin queens. Drones are produced amply in spring and summer to mate with these queens. In northeast North America, this mating activity peaks in the spring and early summer but continues to occur to a lesser degree throughout the summer as queens are superseded and late swarms occur. Watch this video for details of where and how mating happens. Video Transcript So when a virgin queen is sexually mature, she's ready to take a mating flight and she'll take between one and three mating flights where she leaves the hive and flies to the specific geographical location called the drone congregation area. And this is an area high in the sky. It's between 50 to 250 feet up and it's just essentially a cloud with hundreds of drones that are waiting for a queen to arrive. So queens will fly up to nine miles to get to these drone congregation areas. Even if there's one near her own hive, she wants to fly far. And this is so that she reduces the chances of mating with her brothers and other relatives. And it's actually quite effective. Only a very small percentage of queens are mating with drones from the same apiary. So drones actually get a little bit of a bad rep. People often say that drones are lazy and they don't do too much, and the word drone is literally synonymous with the word lazy. But when it comes to reproduction, drones are anything but lazy. What they do is they leave their colony many times a day to fly to this drone congregation area, where they hang around for about half an hour waiting for a queen to show up. After about a half an hour, they're very hungry, so they have to return to the hive refuel, and they set out again. So they do this several times, just hopelessly waiting for a queen and seeing if they're going to get lucky. So a really cool thing about drone congregation areas is that queens and drones from colonies in a given region actually return to the same drone congregation area year after year. In fact, right here next to Dyce, we have a drone congregation area that people have observed for decades. But we really have no idea what attracts drones and queens to these congregation areas to begin with, or how they

become established, or how they know to continue going to these spots year after year. We do know that there are some traits that make drone congregation areas more attractive. So for instance, open areas are more attractive than areas that are near dense forests or urban areas and congregation areas that are above slopes that are facing southward are more attractive than slopes facing any other direction. But beyond that, really a lot more research needs to be done and drone congregation areas still have a lot of mystery to us. Okay, so let's talk about the act of mating. We have hundreds of drones in these drone congregation areas and suddenly a queen arrives, this is the moment they've been waiting for. And the drones can detect the queen with two ways. First is sight, they have very large eyes. They have to be able to distinguish one queen in a cloud of hundreds of drones. And the second is smell. So queens are continuously producing a combination of pheromones that are collectively called queen substance or queen pheromone. And it acts as a sex pheromone to males. It's very attractive, and it makes them want to mate with her. So once they see her or smell her, the race is on. And they are trying to get to the queen. And out of hundreds of drones in a drone congregation area she only mates with between 10 and 20 other males. So the competition is fierce. The actual endeavor of mating is very quick, it lasts less than five seconds. Normally the drone's penis is tucked underneath its body, but it gets everted when it's ready to mate, and inserted in the queen's vagina. Less than five seconds later, he ejaculates, and this actually ruptures his penis. His body falls away and he dies, and the tip of the penis remains in the queen. The next drone to meet with the queen will remove the tip with this specialized structure on his own penis, and then he will mate with her. So consecutively she'll mate with 10 to 20 drones and then when she's finally finished mating with all the drones she's going to, she returns to the hive and the last tip remains. And some beekeepers actually witness this and they can see this, and it's called the mating sign. And it says to them that they have a mated queen. So it's actually a good thing if you happen to see this. The workers in the colony will remove the last tip. So after the queen returns to the hive from her one to three mating flights she'll never mate again. All the sperm that's stored inside of her is the sperm she's going to use to fertilize all of her eggs. And it's going to be stored inside of her for several years. You can tell that she's mated because her abdomen is larger, it's more full of sperm. She's actually moving slower in the colony because she's heavier, and she won't fly again unless she's going to swarm. After she's returned from a mating flight, two to four days later she'll begin laying eggs, and this is what she continues to do for the rest of her life.

Most mating flights take place in the afternoon, usually between 2:00 and 5:00 p.m. While queens can fly quite far to drone congregation areas (DCAs), on average they will typically fly 1.2 to 3 miles (2 to 5 km). Drones, on the other hand, will visit much closer DCAs that average 0.3 to 1.2 miles (0.5 to 2 km). If drones do not get to mate with a virgin queen on the first flight they take, they will continue to take up to six 30-minute flights each day as the weather permits. In between flights, they return to the hive to refuel on carbohydrates. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Reproductive Systems The physiology of reproduction varies by sex and by caste. Review the information on each tab below to understand the reproductive physiology of the drone, the queen, and the worker bee, as well as the role each plays in the process of reproduction. ☆ Key Points Queens have a very high reproductive output and signal their fertility to the colony through queen pheromone Worker honey bees have similar reproductive systems to queens, but they have fewer ovarioles and are not able to mate Drone The Reproductive System of a Drone Drones become sexually mature and ready to mate after nine to 12 days of adult life. The drone’s penis (called an endophallus) only everts when he latches onto a queen to mate; it is normally tucked inside the drone’s abdomen and is not visible. Because the bees are mating while flying, the drone’s endophallus also contains a pair of claspers for gripping onto the queen. In a successful mating, 6 to 12 million sperm travel through the endophallus and into the queen's vagina. Many fewer sperm than this make it to a queen’s sperm storage sac (the spermatheca); the rest exit her body. Queen

The Reproductive System of the Queen The queen bee is an egg-laying machine for nearly her entire lifetime: In the right conditions, she lays about one egg every minute, which translates to 1,000 to 1,500 eggs a day and about a half-million eggs in her two- to three-year lifespan, although this can vary enormously. Some sources have stated that some queens can lay over 2,000 eggs a day! When the quality or quantity of her egg laying declines and signs of her fertility weaken, the workers supersede her with a new queen. Queen eggs laid in cells. Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership. The ovaries in queen bees are two large, tube-like organs that are comprised of 150 to 180 ovarioles each. All of the queen’s eggs are produced in these ovarioles. When an egg is released, it leaves an ovariole, slides down an oviduct, passes by the spermatheca, moves through the vagina, and exits the queen’s body from her vagina. The spermatheca is a large sac that stores sperm from all the drones a queen has mated with; about 5 to 6 million sperm total. To fertilize an egg, a small duct at the entrance of the spermatheca opens as the egg is passing by to allow sperm to exit and fertilize the egg. In this way, queens are able to control whether they lay fertilized eggs that will develop into workers or unfertilized eggs that will develop into drones. There is generally enough sperm in a spermatheca to last for a few years of egg laying; only a few sperm are released to fertilize each egg. Note that a queen who has just mated may, for a time, lay multiple eggs into a cell, but

within a couple of weeks, she should settle into a productive and sustainable pattern of egg laying. The queen (marked) signals her fertility by producing a blend of pheromones, collectively called "queen pheromone." Workers pass along this information about her fertility to other bees in the colony by transmitting the pheromone to them. Workers near the queen brush this pheromone blend off the queen’s body with their antennae and lick it off with their tongues, then walk through the hive spreading it to one another by making antennal contacts and via trophallaxis. In this way, they can constantly assess and communicate the presence and fertility of the queen. As the queen ages and her fertility wanes, she produces less queen pheromone. Once worker bees can no longer detect queen pheromone at a minimum threshold, they start to construct supersedure cells to replace her. If the queen dies or is removed from the hive by a beekeeper, the workers come to realize she is gone because of the lack of queen pheromone being passed among the bees. In response, they begin constructing emergency queen cells to rear a new queen.

(Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership) Worker The Reproductive System of the Worker While queens and workers have the same basic biological equipment for reproduction, they differ vastly in their ability to lay eggs. Under normal circumstances, when the hive is queenright, worker bees are effectively sterile. They have two ovaries just as queens do, but these ovaries are small, with only two to 12 ovarioles each, in striking contrast to the 150 to 180 ovarioles in each ovary of a queen. Similarly, a worker's spermatheca is tiny and cannot store sperm. Because of this, workers cannot mate and do not tend to lay eggs. In circumstances when they do lay eggs, their eggs are unfertilized and develop into haploid drones. There can be a few laying workers even in a queenright hive, but rarely do they make up more than 1% of the worker population, and the eggs that they lay are usually eaten by other workers. If the queen dies, workers can detect the absence of queen mandibular pheromone in as little as 20 minutes. If the colony is not successful in rearing a new queen from emergency queen cells, some of the workers' ovaries may activate, and they can start laying eggs, becoming what are called "laying workers." The young workers (nurse bees) in particular are affected by shifts in this pheromone, as they are much more likely than the foragers to be in the hive and in

contact with the queen. It is these young house bees that can become reproductive. In the absence of queen pheromone, up to 30% of young workers in the colony may start to produce and lay eggs! The reproductive output of laying workers is very different from queens. Laying workers only lay a few eggs here and there — not nearly the 1,000 or so per day that a queen is able to lay. Because workers have short abdomens that cannot reach the bottom of a cell, their eggs tend to be on the sides of cells rather than at the bottom. Also, there is often more than one egg per cell. Beekeepers often look for the eggs to confirm the presence of the queen — but Master Beekeepers must be able to inspect the egg pattern and identify whether the eggs were laid by workers or by a queen. Workers will often lay eggs in worker cells, but because they cannot mate, all the eggs they lay will develop into drones. The drones' larger bodies will cause the cell cappings to extend outward and become bullet-shaped. These bullet-shaped cells, in combination with multiple eggs on the side of cells, is a good indicator that there are laying workers present in the colony. Worker eggs in cells look like several small white eggs crowded together.

Worker eggs laid in worker cells develop into drones. Because drones are larger, they form "bullet"-shaped cells when they are capped. Photo Credit: Bee Informed Partnership Finally, an important part of reproductive anatomy that is different in honey bees compared to most other insects is the ovipositor, or the egg-laying organ. In most other insects, the ovipositor is used to lay eggs; in honey bees, however, it has adapted to become a stinger. This is why only female bees can sting: Their stinger is a modified egglaying organ! Instead of laying eggs from the ovipositor, honey bees lay eggs from the vagina. Back to Table of Contents

Module Wrap-up: Honey Bee Reproduction In this module, you examined the dual nature of honey bee reproduction, exploring in detail how individual bees mate and produce offspring within the colony. Understanding these fundamental biological processes and behaviors is essential for successful colony management and provides crucial insight into the complex reproductive dynamics of honey bee societies. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Honey Bee Development All bees begin life as an egg. From there, some become workers, others queens, and others drones. As adults, bees continue to change in response to the social and physical environment of the colony and the natural world. In this module, you will learn all about how bees develop and how their physiology and behavior change throughout their lives. Photo credit: Lucinda VanVleck Back to Table of Contents

Watch: The Stages of Development Honey bees go through an ordered pathway of development as they transition from egg, to larva, to pupa, to adult. Although there is slight variation in development time from bee to bee, one is able to generally track how many days it takes queens, workers, and drones to mature through the various phases. Being able to identify the different stages of development, knowing how long each stage lasts, and predicting the emergence of the different castes will come in handy for you as a beekeeper. Such knowledge is directly applicable, for instance, to queen rearing and to management practices that reduce Varroa mite loads. Watch this video for more about how honey bees develop from egg to adult. Video Transcript So by now, as a beekeeper, you're probably familiar with the basic development of honey bees. Honey bees begin life as an egg that hatches into a larva that becomes a pupa, and then undergoes metamorphosis to form an adult. But it's really important, as a master beekeeper, to know how the developmental timing differs among the castes. So for all three castes, they all take three days as an egg and six days as larva. The amount of time as a pupa is what is different. Drones take 15 days to pupate, workers takes 12 and queens only take seven days despite the quality and quantity of resources that goes into creating them. So why would this be? There's actually a few reasons why natural selection would favor a quick development time in queens. So think about a time when a colony is producing lots of queen cells, like when they're swarming. The first queen to emerge is going to be the queen for that colony, and as soon as she emerges she's going to kill all the other rival queens. So it's actually advantageous to develop as quickly as possible. Also developing quick as a queen gives you a little bit of a headstart to start growing your colony, collecting food and gets you better prepared to survive winter. And even though this might be a difference of a day or two, this can make an impact if it's perfectly timed with a nectar flow. And lastly, if a colony finds itself suddenly queenless, if the queen dies or something else happens to her, then they need to produce a new queen quickly. And if you have a quick development time for queens, this ensures that the colony isn't queenless for very long.

Okay, so what is exactly happening during development? Three days after the egg is laid it hatches and a small larva crawls out. And a one-day-old larva is actually really tiny. It's about the same size as an egg, but you can detect it with your eye. The main function of a larva is to eat. In fact, its stomach is almost the entire length of its body. And it's fed many meals a day by nurse bees. Workers are first fed royal jelly and then they're fed bee bread, which is pollen mixed with honey and some saliva and fermented by microorganisms. After it's eating, it's growing, and it needs to shed its skin to accommodate its bigger body. So after six days of eating, growing, molting, eating, growing and molting, it's finally ready to pupate. And during this time, workers are going to cap the cell with wax, the larva spins a cocoon around its body, and it doesn't eat anymore until it becomes an adult. While it's a pupa, it starts to develop features that make it look more like a honey bee and less like a grub. Its three body segments — the head, thorax, and abdomen, are becoming distinct. And you can start to see its mouth parts, its eyes, its legs and antennae. And the eyes will start to take on color. Instead of being white they start to turn purple, which is referred to as the purple-eyed stage of development, and then they'll eventually become black. And after seven to 15 days, depending on if it's going to be a queen, a worker or a drone, it has its final molt and it chews its way out of its cell. It actually leaves its cocoon behind in the cell, and it's ready to begin life as an adult bee. And you can actually identify these one-day-old bees that have freshly emerged in the colony, because they have really fuzzy heads and thoraces, and they're actually not able to sting at this stage. So they're pretty cute. To witness and understand the full process of bee development (including under the pupal cappings!), watch this video by Anand Varma. It shows the 21 days of a worker's development from egg to emergence, condensed into one minute. Back to Table of Contents

Tool: The Stages of Development Timeline Take a look at the developmental timeline tool to get a better sense of the stages of development for all honey bees.  Download the Tool Use this chart as a developmental timeline reference for honey bees. Understanding developmental timing can give you information about the queen’s fertility, which is more valuable than actually seeing her in the hive. The presence of queen-laid eggs is a sign that the colony's queen has been there in the past one to three days, so she is most likely in the hive. If there are no eggs or young larvae during a time when you would expect the queen to be laying, but you see older larvae, you can infer that it has been six to nine days since she has laid any eggs. You should then do a thorough check to see whether she is in the colony and anything else you can learn. Similarly, understanding the timing for queen emergence is critical if you are selling queen cells or introducing them into queenless colonies. You want to make sure that emergence is timed for a day or two after they have been introduced to a colony, rather than before! You’ll notice in this course that we simplify the amount of time it takes the different colony members to pupate. Scientific observations find queens take an average of five to six days, workers take six days, and drones take six to seven days. In this tool, we report all colony members take approximately six days to pupate, but just know there can be some variation. Back to Table of Contents

Read: How Sex Is Determined What determines whether a bee develops into a male or a female? Honey bees, as well as the other insects in the order Hymenoptera, have a different sex determination system than humans. ☆ Key Points The ratio of females (workers) to males (drones) in the colony is dynamic, depending on colony size, comb architecture, and queen fertility. In humans, both males and females inherit two sets of each of their chromosomes in their cells, one set from each parent. One particular pair of chromosomes is the sex Inbreeding can result in high numbers of diploid males because of the sex determination system in honey bees. chromosomes, and these are what determine a person's sex. A person inheriting an X chromosome from its mother and a Y chromosome from its father develops into a boy, while a person inheriting an X chromosome from both its mother and its father develops into a girl. In honey bees, chromosomes also play a role, but there are interesting differences. Before we describe the role chromosomes play, let's talk about the ratio of male to female brood produced in a colony. The queen has control over which eggs she fertilizes by opening her spermathecal duct to release sperm or keeping it closed so no sperm is released. So what makes her fertilize an egg or not? It is actually the worker bees that build comb that affect the ratio of worker offspring to drone offspring in the colony. They build large cells (approximately 6.4 mm wide) to accommodate drones and small cells (approximately 5.2 mm wide) to accommodate workers.

Drone cells (bottom) are slightly larger in diameter than worker cells (top) The ratio of workers to drones depends largely on the population of the colony. Once the colony has at least 4,000 or so workers, it can begin investing in drone production, and comb builders will begin constructing larger cells for drones. The queen walks along the combs and assesses which type of egg she should lay in each cell based on its size. She sticks her head and thorax into empty cells and measures their size using her front legs. Small cells stimulate her to lay a fertilized egg, whereas large cells stimulate her to lay an unfertilized egg. Honey bee sex determination is usually explained simply in this way: Fertilized eggs yield offspring that inherit two sets of chromosomes (so are diploid organisms) and develop into females, while unfertilized eggs yield offspring that inherit only one set of chromosomes (so are haploid organisms) and develop into males. However, it actually goes one step beyond this. Let’s explore the Complementary Sex Determination gene next. Back to Table of Contents

Read: The Complementary Sex Determination Gene It is not the number of sets of chromosomes a bee inherits that determines their sex; rather, it has to do with the gene version (also called an allele) they possess at a specific gene position on a certain chromosome. The special gene is the Complementary Sex Determination (CSD) gene, and this is what ultimately determines sex in honey bees. If a bee receives just one copy of this gene (from the mother’s egg), then a male is created. Yet if a bee receives two copies of this gene (one copy from their mother’s egg and one copy from their father’s sperm), then it generally means a female is created. Here is the key, however: A female’s two copies must be different versions. If a bee receives two different versions of the gene, then she develops normally as a female, but if the two versions happen to be identical, the bee will develop as a male — even though it has two sets of chromosomes. We call these "diploid males," but you rarely see diploid male adults walking around the colony because they usually get detected and cannibalized by their sisters while they are still larvae.

Sex determination in honey bees depends on the CSD gene (horizontal yellow, green, and gray rectangles) located on a specific chromosome. A colony formed from a queen that mated with two drones yields six potential offspring. The number and version of the gene inherited determines each offspring's sex. There are several implications this has for the colony. If many larvae receive the same two versions of this gene and get removed, the brood pattern will end up looking spotty. Populations with largely unrelated honey bees usually have higher genetic diversity. In these instances, there are many versions of the CSD gene in the population, and the chances of a bee inheriting two identical versions are low, so diploid males are rare. Yet in populations that are heavily inbred, with low genetic diversity, the likelihood of inheriting the same version of the CSD gene is much higher. These highly inbred bees will likely produce a spotty brood pattern because the workers are removing so many diploid males. For this reason, it is important that honey bee breeding programs do not result in inbreeding. Spotty brood pattern can be the result of inbreeding. Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership Back to Table of Contents

Read: Diploid Male Occurrences If spotty brood can indicate health issues in your hive, how many larvae can we normally expect will receive two copies of the same gene in a normal, healthy population? The number of different versions of the CSD gene varies in normal populations, but studies have found it tends to range between six and 17. Let’s imagine one population has 10 different versions of the CSD gene. Each of the colored circles in the above illustration represents different CSD gene versions. Our queen has two of these 10 possible versions, one on a specific chromosome she inherited from her mother and the other from her father. So let’s say our queen mates with 10 males, and each male has a unique version of this gene. We can draw all the potential fertilized offspring this queen can have. In this scenario, there are 20 different combinations that are possible, and of all these combinations, there are two cases where the offspring inherits identical gene versions. These two offspring — representing 10% of all the offspring the queen lays on average — would be the ones that are removed and cannibalized. This goes to show that in normal populations, we can always expect to see some spotty brood due to the sex determination system in honey bees. It would be rare to find an absolute perfect brood pattern on a frame. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: How Caste Is Determined For generations, people have wondered what determines whether a bee will become a queen or a worker. How is the decision made? What factors are involved? There are still some mysteries surrounding the exact molecular changes that occur during the process of caste determination, but scientists are getting close to piecing together the whole picture. This video addresses our current understanding of honey bee caste determination. Video Transcript Interestingly, caste determination in honey bees is due to environmental factors instead of genetic factors. This means that a young, female larva can become either a worker or a queen. Think about that for a moment. They differ vastly in their appearances and in their behavioral repertoires and an order of magnitude of a difference between their lifespan. Workers only live for a few weeks and queens live for a few years. Yet they arise from an identical DNA blueprint. The key is that there is a short time period during which a larva determines to either become a queen or a worker. And this time period is between 12 and 36 hours, from when it hatches as an egg. So anything beyond 36 hours the larva has already been destined to develop the way that it was meant to whether it's a worker or a queen, there is no switching. And this has implications for a colony if it suddenly finds itself queenless. If the queen dies, workers need to try and rear emergency queens out of larvae that is already existing in the colony. And they could only do this from larvae that are less than 36 hours old. So if there aren't any young larvae in the colony it's considered hopelessly queenless unless a beekeeper intervenes and introduces a new one or a frame with young brood on it. So what determines this developmental pathway of a larva? What is that environmental factor? It's actually royal jelly. And royal jelly is a food that's secreted from the hypopharyngeal glands and the mandibular glands of nurse bees. It's milky in its consistency and it contains water, sugars, salts, fatty acids, other lipids, vitamins, free amino acids, and proteins. So basically it's highly nutritious. And queens and workers actually receive different amounts of royal jelly, and this contributes to why they are different castes. So queens receive royal jelly for their entire period as a larva, all six days. But workers are fed royal jelly only for the first two to three

days as a larva, and then they transition to eating bee bread. Also, queens are fed approximately ten times more often than worker larvae are fed. About 1,500 times, versus 150 times. So, essentially, some components of royal jelly are starting a cascade of reactions in the bee's cells that begin to drive this differential development. And it turns out that there are hundreds of genes that are involved. Hundreds of genes are being turned off and turned on, and worker larvae, and queen larvae as they're developing. And although queens and workers have the same DNA blueprint to begin with, the take-home message is that genes of this blueprint are turned on and off differently. And these can be genes that are involved in life span or body size or other factors as well, like reproduction, and there's just many that are involved and it's a very cool and complex process. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Molecules and Food Involved in Caste Determination There are slight differences in the jelly fed to workers and queens. The popular name for all milky brood food, whether it’s fed to queen or worker larvae, is “royal jelly.” It’s worth noting, however, that scientists have determined that, while the substances are largely the same, there are slight differences between the jelly fed to workers and the jelly fed to queens. You may sometimes hear the terms “worker jelly” and “royal jelly” used to differentiate between the two. Royal jelly has a lower moisture content and a higher sugar content than worker jelly. It also contains higher amounts of a fatty acid called 0-hydroxy-2-decenoic acid. The jelly fed to different-aged brood changes slightly over time as well; e.g., the moisture content, sugar content, and mineral content in the jelly are different depending on whether it’s fed to a larva that is one day old, two days old, three days old, and so forth. The consumption of royal jelly triggers responses in hundreds of genes and proteins; many hormones are also involved. Caste determination is complex and dynamic, with scientific research still unfolding. For the purposes of this course, we will cover only two components that are well studied for their role in caste determination. Juvenile hormone is a hormone found in all insects, but it plays an important role in honey bee caste determination. The hormone is high in emerging queens and low in emerging workers. Eating lots of royal jelly as a larva stimulates a high production of juvenile hormone, which in turn contributes to the development of a queen with large ovaries comprised of many ovarioles, as well as a long lifespan. Vitellogenin is a protein that is produced by the fat body in the honey bee and found in the ovaries, among other tissues. In the ovaries, it functions to help make eggs. Larvae with high vitellogenin levels in their hemolymph develop into queens. Consuming royal jelly as a larva increases the level of vitellogenin in the developing queen, ensuring that she can create many eggs throughout her lifetime. Vitellogenin levels in queens remain high as adults, which likely plays a role in contributing to their long lifespans. On the other hand, larvae with low vitellogenin levels in their hemolymph develop into workers. As adults, this protein remains at low levels in their ovaries, contributing to their reduced fertility.
The quantity of royal jelly a larva consumes initiates cellular reactions that lead to the development of either a queen or a worker bee. Photo Credit: Eleanor Andrews Back to Table of Contents

Read: Intercastes A queen is successfully reared from a female larva under three conditions: When the larva is exclusively fed royal jelly When it is fed copious amounts of royal jelly When the larva is selected at a young age to start receiving this special queen diet If even one of these three conditions isn’t met, the resulting queen that develops is an “intercaste." Intercastes can develop when they are fed small amounts of royal jelly as larvae, when their diet is altered to differ in the ratio of sugars or other nutrients that are naturally occurring in royal jelly, or when the larva that starts receiving a queen diet is older. Intercastes can develop from larvae that are as old as four days! Intercastes have characteristics of both queens and workers. The length of their abdomen, the size of their spermatheca, and the number of ovarioles for intercastes are between those of a worker and a queen. Some intercastes develop corbicula on their legs for pollen storage, while others develop with a shriveled spermatheca and are therefore incapable of storing sperm. If an intercaste develops with more queen-like features than worker-like features, they can act as a queen for at least a short period of time in the hive — mating, laying eggs, and attracting a retinue of workers — but they tend to be superseded by workers in the same season. Naturally occurring intercastes are rare in a colony and only result if workers are forced to rear an emergency queen from older larvae. They can occur, however, if beekeepers are grafting older larvae when they are queen rearing. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: How the Worker's Role Transitions Throughout Its Life The tasks that workers specialize in allow the colony to perform many functions at once. The nest can be constructed and cleaned, food can be collected and stored, brood can be fed, and the colony can be guarded - all at the same time! This is made possible because workers specialize in different tasks at different times. As a worker ages, she learns and performs different roles. Watch this video to learn how tasks change over a worker's life. Video Transcript The queen and worker castes represent a division of labor and reproduction. But this isn't the only division of labor we see in a colony. Labor is also divided up among workers who transition through many tasks or duties as they age. And this transitioning and specializing in different tasks at a time is called polyethism. And the tasks that they perform depend on the age of the bee and also the needs of the colony. So roughly speaking, workers begin their first half of their life as house bees, performing tasks inside the nest and then they spend their second half of their lives as field bees, performing tasks outside the nest. The very first thing that a bee does when she emerges from her cell is she cleans her cell and cleans the other cells around her. Then she transitions into capping brood and tending to the brood where she's called a nurse bee or attending to the queen where she's called the retinue, or makes up the retinue. Then she transitions into receiving nectar that's coming into the colony, cleaning debris in the colony, packing pollen and comb building. So just general hive maintenance. When she's finally ready to start transitioning outside of the hive, they will perform tasks that are right in the intermediate, right at the hive entrance. So they can participate in ventilation at the entrance or guarding the entrance against intruders. And then when they're finally ready they take their first foraging flight. And as foragers they can collect a variety of different things. They can forage for nectar, pollen, water, resin or even new nest sites if a colony swarms. And they usually remain as forages until they die of natural causes. A really neat thing is that foragers specialize in what they're collecting. So they may be specialize as water collectors or as propolis collectors, although they can be flexible if the need arises. It's really interesting to note that there is a variation as to when a worker is beginning a new task. So, a worker that's finally becoming a forager might do that after 14

days, whereas another worker might do that after 19 days. It's not so rigid or set in stone. It's flexible. And the really interesting thing to know as a master beekeeper, and where it's relevant, is that workers with different duties are found in different parts of the nest. So nurse bees are usually found on the brood comb, because they're tending to the brood. And that's usually toward the bottom or center of the hive. Guards are usually found at the entrance of the hive. And comb builders are found wherever there's new comb being built, which could basically be anywhere within the colony. And when home, foragers can also be found throughout the colony. but they're most often clustered below the brood area, so that they can easily enter and exit the hive. And this is important to know because it might impact your decisions when you’re inspecting colonies, when you’re monitoring for certain parasites or diseases and also for swarm control.
