Read: Molecules Involved in Worker Polyethism The structures and chemicals in honey bee brains change as they age and as they adopt new behavioral repertoires. The shifts in worker duties are regulated by hormones, proteins, and neurotransmitters within the bee’s hemolymph and neurons. Some of these molecules may be familiar to you, as they are also involved in caste determination. It is not uncommon in biology for molecules to be involved in more than one function. Changes in worker duties are caused by subtle changes in the levels of these and other hormones and proteins, which are in turn regulated by the social environment of the colony. The presence and fertility of the queen, the population level, the amount of brood present, and the amount of food coming in, can all influence what task a worker is going to perform. Here we will touch upon four molecules involved in worker polyethism: Juvenile Hormone JH (Juvenile hormone) influence the transition from in-hive tasks (like nursing) to outside tasks (like foraging). Newly emerged worker bees have low levels of this hormone in their bodies, but the level increases steadily throughout the first 15 days or so of a worker’s life. At this point, juvenile hormone assists in the shift from tasks inside the hive to tasks outside, thus promoting the shift to foraging. You may be wondering why this hormone is called 'juvenile' hormone if it is actually highest in bees. It turns out, the progression of juvenile hormone levels are actually opposite in honey bees compared to other insects. In other insects, this hormone is highest in juveniles and decreases as the insect ages into adulthood. Vitellogenin In addition to facilitating egg production in the ovaries, vitellogenin is present in the hypopharyngeal glands, the fat body, and the hemolymph. In the hypopharyngeal

glands of nurses, vitellogenin helps create royal jelly to feed to brood. Nurse bees have high levels of vitellogenin in their hemolymph and their hypopharyngeal glands, and the levels decrease as bees age and become foragers. This makes sense because it is nurses that feed larvae, while foragers do not tend to the brood. It is this rapid decrease in vitellogenin, combined with the increase in juvenile hormone, that is associated with the behavioral switch from nurse to forager. Dopamine Dopamine is a neurotransmitter that is present in many organisms, including humans. Neurotransmitters are chemicals released by neurons in the brain to send fast signals to other neurons. In honey bees, low levels of dopamine stimulate nurses to care for brood. So which bees in the hive likely have low levels of dopamine? You guessed it – younger nurse bees. Their levels are much lower than those found in foragers. It is the presence of the queen (and her pheromones) that regulates dopamine production in worker bees’ brains. Nurse bees (rather than foragers) come in contact with queen pheromone, which sets off a molecular pathway in the nurse bee brain to reduce the production of dopamine and thereby stimulate nursing behavior. Pheromones Several pheromones are know to play a role in the regulation of workers's role transitions throughout their life. For example, the foraging pheromone and especially one of its component, ethyl oleate, is emitted by returning foragers and it suppresses a premature switch to foraging roles in young bees. Here is another example: the brood pheromone emitted by the developing larvae signals the need for nursing. This pheromone can delay the onset of foraging behavior in worker bees, ensuring that the brood is well-cared for by young bees. These, and other

pheromones, assist workers in their assessment of the needs of the colonies (more foragers? more nurses? etc.) and they contribute to the remarkable flexibility exhibited by honey bees when it comes to role allocation in the colony. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Social Environment Influence on Worker Tasks How does the social environment influence worker tasks? Although the molecules involved in worker polyethism change as a bee ages, and this influences the transition to different tasks, age is not the only factor that determines when workers will be house bees and when they will be field bees. If that were the case, colonies wouldn't be able to respond to changes in their environment. So, in addition to age, there are also strong effects of the social environment. Honey bees are able to detect what is going on inside the nest and alter their behavior accordingly. For example, although house bees transition to become field bees at around 15 days of age, the exact age at which this happens is adjustable. If a high percentage of the foragers are removed from a colony (e.g., through a pesticide poisoning event), their sisters will recognize that the colony no longer has enough bees to bring in pollen and nectar. Some nurse bees will transition to becoming foragers earlier than they would otherwise. In the reverse, if the nurse bee population suddenly declines, some foragers will revert to being nurses. More broadly, worker bee behavior is flexible enough to take on tasks that are needed to help the colony run smoothly. Worker bees spend a considerable amount of time performing tasks, but they actually spend most of their time being inactive and walking around the nest. It is likely that they are assessing their colony's state at this time, sensing social and environmental cues of the colony condition. This ability to read the colony's situation and then respond accordingly makes these honey bee societies flexible and resilient. For example, during a nectar flow, foragers will recruit more bees to help receive the food through a tremble dance, and brood rearing increases. When there is not enough storage space for holding the incoming nectar, more bees will engage in comb building. A remarkable example of this ability to detect and respond to a colony’s needs is the work of heater bees. Heater bees are workers found in the brood nest that generate heat through shivering as a way to incubate pupae at the proper temperature. While brood needs to develop at a certain temperature (91°F to 97°F) to become healthy adults, they can tolerate slight variations. Interestingly, these small variations can impact the behaviors of these bees after they emerge. For instance, bees that develop at the highest end of the range (closer to 97°F) transition to become foragers at an earlier age, are more likely to

perform undertaking tasks, are better learners, and perform more dances than bees that develop at the lowest end of the range (closer to 91°F). Beyond this range, however, pupae fail to develop properly or die. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Bee Lifespan While healthy queen bees live on average two to three years (a very long time for an insect!), worker lifespans are a lot shorter. Their lifespan depends on a number of factors, including their genetics, the activities performed throughout their lives, and the season. During spring and fall, workers typically live for one to two months. In the summer, they live much shorter lives, typically two to five weeks. Bees that live throughout the winter are the longest living bees. These bees are called winter bees, and can live for four to five months! They are needed to survive over winter so they can regulate the temperature in the brood nest and help rear the first brood at the end of winter. Winter bees are generated within the colony in autumn from the end of August through November and they differ in their physiology compared to summer bees. Winter bees have lower levels of juvenile hormone (analogous to nurse bees who spend their time performing in-hive tasks) than summer bees, and they have much larger hypopharyngeal glands and larger and more numerous fat body cells than summer bees. The fat body is a collection of tissues comprised of many fat body cells that store fat and glycogen (stored sugar) to release for energy production in times of food shortage. It is located mostly in the abdomen, but also spans the thorax and head. Drones that do not mate with queens will live an average of three to four weeks. Their lifespans may be shortened as winter approaches because workers usually evict drones from the hive prior to winter. The colony does not expend precious food stores on feeding drones that do not aid in survival over the winter Drones usually get evicted by their sisters in the fall. Back to Table of Contents

Module Wrap-up: Honey Bee Development In this module, you examined the remarkable journey of honey bee development, from egg to adult. You learned how environmental and social factors determine whether eggs develop into workers, queens, or drones, and how adult bees continue to adapt and change their roles throughout their lives. This knowledge of bee development and physiology reveals the dynamic nature of colony life and the impressive adaptability of honey bee behavior. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: How Honey Bees Communicate If you think about it, you’ll realize that all living things need to communicate. Birds sing, wolves howl, and even fish use body language. We typically think communication is all about our own uniquely complicated use of the voice, but most forms of life use other sensory modalities to communicate. It is really no surprise that eusocial insects like honey bees are elaborate, multi-sensory communicators. Even though we only understand a fraction of their language, that tiny part is fascinating! Bees live together in the dark. It is reasonable to assume that vision is not a sense they rely heavily on for communication. Instead, bees mostly use the senses of “hearing” (vibration detection), taste, smell (pheromones), and touch to “speak” with each other. The famous biologist Karl von Frisch first described a type of bee communication that he called a “dance” in the 1940s, work for which he won a Nobel Prize. Subsequent studies of different forms of physical bee communication — all called “dances” — were conducted by a number of his students and others, such as Martin Lindauer, Jürgen Tautz, and Tom Seeley. In 1960, the communication signal “Queen Mandibular Pheromone” was discovered, opening the doorway to the captivating world of bee pheromones. In the years since this discovery, over 28 uniquely different honey bee pheromones have been described. In this module, you will learn some of the ways honey bees communicate important information through pheromones and dances, and you will learn how to recognize different communication behaviors in your own colonies. Photo Credit: Lucinda VanVleck Back to Table of Contents

Read: Pheromone Communication Honey bees have evolved one of the ☆ Key Points most complex systems of pheromone communication known in nature. This communication regulates functions ranging from reproduction to foraging, enables communication among the colony members within a hive, and occasionally permits communication between colonies. The The honey bee colony is a chemically busy environment, with pheromones secreted by the queen, brood, and workers. Pheromones elicit behavioral changes in members of the same species. pheromones emitted by an individual bee can change over the course of its lifetime or as a function of its reproductive status. Of the many chemical signals that bees are known to emit, only a small fraction of them are well understood. ▶ Queen-Produced Pheromones Let us start with the most important pheromones, the ones produced by the queen. Why are those the most important? First, it is known that when the queen is old or sick (low pheromonal signal) or it dies (no pheromonal signal), workers are driven to rear new queens from young brood within 12–24 hours. Second, the removal of the queen in absence of young brood soon leads to the decline of the colony: the workers stop performing their activities and start to lay unfertilized eggs that develop into male adults (drones); the colony becomes disorganized, unfit, dirty, susceptible to diseases and prey of predators; it rapidly depopulates and goes toward a certain death. The queen signal includes 40-100 compounds produced from multiple glands: the mandibular gland, tergal glands, Dufour's gland, Koshevnikov gland and tarsal glands. Those chemicals attract drones during mating flights. They stimulate foraging and brood rearing, while inhibiting queen rearing and

suppressing ovary development in workers. They stabilize swarms (along with the Nasonov pheromone produced by workers), and much more. How can ONE individual affect the physiology and behavior of thousand of individuals dispersed in the hive? The answer is that the queen signal attracts workers to surround and tend to the queen. This retinue of workers that are constantly touching and licking her pass along the pheromone to the rest of the colony through body contact, antennating (touching antennae), and trophallaxis. The transfer of these pheromones enables the bees in the hive to know that the queen is alive and fertile, thus providing social cohesion to the colony. Five of the dozen components of the queen signal are secreted by the mandibular gland; these are collectively known as queen mandibular pheromone (QMP). This is the best-understood, behaviorally and chemically, pheromone in honey bees. A strong signal indicates that the queen is healthy and productive, which inhibits the development of Workers detect queen pheromone by licking and antennating the queen. Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership. workers’ ovaries. It also attracts workers to surround her in the hive or in a swarm and stimulates them to tend to her. Queen mandibular pheromone also helps regulate the transition for nurse bees becoming forager bees by delaying the onset of foraging. What about the other compounds emitted from other glands? They are less well known, behaviorally and chemically. We know about the queen’s Dufour’s gland which is located near the egg laying device of the queen, aka the ovipositor. As the queen lays an egg, she secretes a unique waxy, non-volatile, mix of ~ 20 compounds that ends up covering her eggs. This unique chemical signature allows nurse worker bees who inspect the eggs later using antennal contact/mouthpart contact to identify queen-laid eggs. Why is that important? Because this allows nurse workers to identify worker-laid eggs, since those do not have the same chemical signature. As you know, workers are not supposed to lay eggs, and there are many pheromones present in the

▶ hive to deter them from having functional ovaries, yet every now and then, and more under some situations, workers lay a few eggs. Those eggs do not bear the queen's chemical signature thus workers destroy them. This is called worker policing. Another portion of the queen signal that has been characterized is what oozes from the queen’s tarsal glands in the last segment of her legs. The footprint queen’s secretion is oily, colorless and composed of ~ 12 non-volatile substances that are extruded through openings on the tarsi when the queen is walking onto the comb, as she explores the hive for empty cells she can use to lay her eggs. Those secretions deposited as the queen walks throughout the hive signal to the colony that there is a functional queen present and that she is active. This in turns maintains colony stability, contributes to the inhibition of queen cup construction by workers and also to the inhibition of worker reproduction. Brood-Produced Pheromones While larvae do not seem to do much other than eat and grow, they actually influence the behavior of nurses and help ensure their own care through brood pheromone. This pheromone is released by the larvae and detected by the nurse bees. It gives the nurses information about a specific larva’s sex, caste, and age, which in turn influences the nurses to provision them different amounts and types of food. It also Larvae release pheromones to provide nurses with information. inhibits worker ovary development and can affect the onset of foraging in nurse bees. Young nurse bees that detect brood pheromone delay their transition time to becoming foragers, while older nurse bees that detect the pheromone are stimulated to “speed up” their transition to foraging.

▶ Worker-Produced Pheromones The Nasonov pheromone is the primary means of aggregation and orientation for honey bees. The pheromone is released from the Nasonov gland, located near the end of the abdomen in workers. There are three primary behavioral contexts where the Nasonov pheromone is used: marking the nest entry to assist returning bees, aggregation during swarming, and marking a water source. The ability of adult workers to release this pheromone increases with age; peak production occurs when the bee is about 28 days old. This pheromone is unique to workers, as queens and drones do not contain a Nasonov gland. Synthetic Nasonov pheromone has been manufactured into a lure that can be used by beekeepers to attract swarming bees to unoccupied hives. Some of the same compounds in Nasonov pheromone are also found in lemongrass oil, so beekeepers can also use lemongrass oil to increase the chances of catching a swarm. The forager pheromone is derived from fermented nectar, which foragers regularly consume when they are out collecting resources. They process a chemical in the nectar and exude it through their exoskeleton. Bees inside the hive smell this chemical when the foragers return. This pheromone delays the onset of foraging in nurse bees: When there are numerous foragers and therefore high levels of the pheromone, the transition is Worker bee exposing her Nasonov gland. delayed. By contrast, when there are Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership few foragers, the level of this pheromone is low, and some nurse bees are stimulated to transition into foragers to help maintain the field force.

▶ Alarm Pheromone When a worker bee is disturbed by a predator or threat to the colony, she emits alarm pheromone to mark the location of the potential threat and to rally others to aid in defense. She releases alarm pheromone from her mandibular gland and a gland beside the stinger. When stinging, the gland near the stinger produces the pheromone and it coats the sting shaft. When the bee stings the enemy, the alarm pheromone "marks" the sting position so other bees can quickly locate it. Promptly Alarm pheromone coating the sting shaft removing the stinger and smoking the area helps to mask the smell of helps mark intruders for easy identification by other bees. this pheromone to prevent future attacks. Note that dark colors, erratic movements, and certain odors, such as leather, can elicit an attack response prior to alarm pheromone being released. Alarm pheromone is one of the honey bee pheromones that is easily smelled by humans. If you've smelled it before, you may have thought it smells a bit like bananas. Interestingly, one of the main components in alarm pheromone, isoamyl acetate, is the same compound that gives bananas their sweet smell. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Honey Bee Dances — The Waggle Dance The various forms of physical (touch) communication among honey bees are called “dances.” Karl von Frisch described what has become known as the“waggle dance,” a behavior used by a successful forager to share information about the location and scent of a rich food source with other foragers. In this video, Dr. Tom Seeley, the Cornell professor who has dedicated much of his career to studying honey bee communication and behavior, describes this fascinating behavior. Video Transcript Okay, hello. What I want to share with you now is the waggle dance of the honey bee. This is a very special communication signal. And what makes it special is that it's a signal that honey bees produce that shows other individuals the location of a rich food source and there's only one other species that has that ability with the honey bee. That's ourselves, human beings. We do that when we give somebody directions to find a good grocery store, for example. And the honey bees are doing that to show their hivemates the locations of rich food sources, flower patches. Now, one thing I'd find helpful in explaining the waggle dance is to understand that you can think of this as the bee performing a miniaturized reenactment of her flight out to the flower patch. And when I say a miniaturized reenactment of the flight, that's actually realistic because as the bee goes through the movement of the waggle dance which consists of her doing the waggle motion in the center of the formation of the dance and then she circles back and does another waggle run. She's also buzzing her wings. And she is pointing you in the direction that indicates the direction to the food source and the length of that waggle run, the duration of it, how long each waggle run lasts, whether it's a half a second or several seconds, indicates the distance. So it's a lot like the bee making a miniature flight out to the food source. Let's look at this waggle dance. Okay. You can see that as this bee walks forward she's waggling her body back and forth. In this case she's pointing. Well I should explain that this is a bee doing the dance on the side of a swarm. So it's a vertical surface. And the bee is dancing. As she walks forward doing the waggle motion, she's pointed 90 degrees to

left of straight up. And again, this is on a vertical surface, the side of a swarm of bees. So she's telling other bees the direction and as we'll see in a second, 90 degrees to the left of straight up means the direction of the flowers is 90 degrees to the left of the direction of the sun. We'll come back to that in another diagram. The other thing I want you to notice now is that she's consistent in the direction she faces, as she does the waggling, and she's consistent in how long each waggle run lasts. In this example, each waggle run lasts about eight tenths of a second. And so that indicates a food source about 800 yards away. Okay, let's take a look at how this information is encoded. As I mentioned, the direction is indicated by the angle of the waggle run. And here we've got an example where the bee is, as she does her waggle runs, you can see that she would be walking upward on the comb but 40 degrees to the right of straight up. And what she's telling the other bees following her dance is that when they go outside of the hive, the flowers are 40 degrees to the right of the direction of the sun. So inside the hive, up is the reference direction. Outside the hive, the sun's direction is the reference direction. So it's a very simple translation from what the bee experiences in the hive to what direction she should fly outside the hive. And then the distance is indicated by the duration of the waggle run. You can see that in the chart. So our little bee that was dancing eight-tenths of a second you can see that corresponds to a distance of about, well I see, 500 meters really. And it's just like doing a long flight. If the food source is a long ways away, each waggle run lasts for longer and longer amounts of time. So, that's how the waggle dance works. And you might sometimes hear about two types of dances being done in the hive, a round dance and a waggle dance. That's what people used to think but we now understand that these round dances are just waggle dances where the waggle portion of the dance is very very short. It's the same signal, it just looked different before people had means of video recording the dances and studying them closely. A waggle dancer uses scents, vibrations, and repetition to enhance her communication. A successful forager performing a waggle dance will carry on her body the scent of the flowers she has found; this helps other bees find the exact flowers to which she is guiding them. The number of waggle circuits communicates the quality of a food source. A dancing bee produces only a dozen or so circuits if the food source that she has found is good but not great, but she produces hundreds of circuits if it is a great food source or if the colony is desperate for what she has found (nectar, pollen, water, or even propolis). Her
excitement about the food source is also communicated by how rapidly she conducts her dance. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Honey Bee Dances — The Shaking Signal Like most animals, bees need sleep. Foragers that aren’t busy foraging can be found fast asleep on the margins of the cluster or up in the honey supers. You can tell a bee is sleeping because she is very still on the comb. If you poke at her with your finger, she doesn’t react. Researchers have found that the brain activity of sleeping bees is reduced, just as it is for people. During a honey flow, most foragers are at work bringing in nectar and pollen all day, and they only sleep at night. When nectar sources are scarce, however, or when the weather is bad, foragers have little to do. It is then that you find sleeping foragers while doing a daytime hive inspection. During this time there are also many foragers inside the hive that are awake but aren't participating in any tasks. When a bee finds nectar-laden flowers early in the morning, after a dearth, or following a period of bad weather, she wants to recruit sister foragers, many of whom may be asleep or are not already occupied with tasks inside the hive. She must therefore motivate some of them to get a waggle dance audience, which she does by grabbing inactive bees with her forelegs and shaking them. This shaking motion is accomplished by the bee vibrating her abdomen. Dr. Tom Seeley calls this behavior the “shake and wake.” The foraging bee will first unload her nectar, shake a few inactive foragers, and then fly back out to collect another load of nectar. She repeats this routine a number of times before she has enough of an audience to perform her waggle dance. After the waggle dances begin, it is only a very short time — about an hour — until many foragers may be found at the food source. Most often, the shaking signal is performed on the waggle dance floor. The signal “activates foraging preparations,” so the earliest foragers motivate others to receive information from dancers. The shaking signal doesn’t only occur during foraging; for instance, workers shake the queen during swarm preparation, inducing her to stop egg laying and to become more active on the comb. It is thought that the shake signal is a general one used to alter what bees are doing. In this way, the shake signal means "Switch tasks!" In the context of foraging, the shaking signal tells sleeping or inactive bees to get ready to “watch” a dancer and then go forage as well. In this video, a bee performs the shaking signal.

Watch: Honey Bee Dances — The Tremble Dance and “Stop” Signal As increasing numbers of foragers bring their bounty back to the hive during the start of a honey flow (abundant nectar supply), they deliver their harvest to receiver bees. If a forager cannot find a receiver bee, she must recruit one using the “tremble dance." Another dance performed by foragers, specifically nectar foragers, the tremble dance is used to recruit additional receiver bees to unload nectar from incoming foragers at the start of a honey flow. If a forager that has found an excellent nectar source has a hard time finding a receiver bee to unload her when she returns to the hive, then she will perform a tremble dance instead of a waggle dance. She trembles her body and walks throughout the hive so that middle-aged bees (ones older than nurse bees but younger than foragers) can pick up on this communication signal and learn of the need for more bees to function as nectar receivers. Once more bees are engaged in nectar receiving, the nectar foragers will get unloaded promptly when they get home, enabling them to more efficiently exploit the richly flowing nectar sources that they have found. The average duration of a tremble dance is around 30 minutes! Over time, there will be a rise in the number of nectar receivers, so the colony gradually adjusts to handle the rich nectar sources that the foragers have discovered. Witness a forager performing a tremble dance in this video. A worker bee (located slightly right of center in the clip) performs a tremble dance. The "stop" signal Eventually, as a food site is failing or too crowded with bees, returning foragers convey this information to other foragers in the hive. They will press themselves up against others and give a short, high-toned beeping noise. This beeping sound has the effect of stopping waggle dances if the dancer has been “beeped.” In this way, waggle dances, shaking signals, tremble dances, and beeping help to stabilize and coordinate the flow of nectar and its processing in the colony, and form the basis of the ways in which bees "talk" to one another to regulate food gathering and storage. Back to Table of Contents

Read: How Are Dances Perceived in the Dark? Dance followers stand still during the dance and “listen” with their antennae stretched out stiffly at an angle of between 90 to 120 degrees to each other. The dancer’s rhythmically moving abdomen displaces each follower’s antennae. Because followers use their own gravity detectors to determine where they are on the comb, they can calculate the position of the dancer and thus the direction to the resource that the dancer is advertising. Bees choose particular places on the comb to conduct their waggle dances. Most dances occur on areas of empty cells about 10 cm square — quite a small area considering a hive typically has an overall comb area of five square meters! Motivated foragers congregate at the dance floor to learn from dancers where the best forage might be. It has been discovered that the wax on their “dance floor” has unique vibrational properties that help to transmit dance vibrations to the maximum number of “listeners”! One experiment showed that bees dancing over empty cells recruited three to four times as many foragers as those dancing on sealed cells. Normally, a dancing bee creates strong vibrations using her uncoupled flight muscles, which are synchronized with the left and right movements of her abdomen during the dance. However, when the dancer first “calls” for attention but does not yet have a following of interested foragers, she does not use her flight muscles. During this early phase of dancing, she is signaling to distant recruits only through vibrations she introduces to the comb with her legs. Every waggle generates a pull on the edges of the cell she is standing on, and that pull sets up a vibration through the wax. Bees looking for dancers can feel comb vibrations at some distance away and, in response, come looking for the dancer. The comb dance floor can be “tuned” by changes in temperature and by the addition of propolis to the rims of the cells. Vibrational properties of the comb are slightly dampened by the beekeeper’s four-sided frame. On combs where bees dance, the bees often improve the vibrational property of the comb by constructing large gaps between the edge of the comb and the sides or bottoms of the frames. The wax on the dance floor is also chemically marked by the bees, as has been shown by experiments in which the dance floor is cut out and put back into a different place in the hive. The bees search for

the relocated piece of comb before starting to dance again! They do not search for the “old dance floor” for more than a day, suggesting that its chemical signature dissipates. Several versions of the waggle dance are variously referred to as the round dance, sickle dance, or transition dance. All are variations of the same dance, modified to indicate distance from the hive to the food source. It has been shown that the different races of bees (Carniolan, Italian, German, and Caucasian) have different “dialects” or “accents” of waggle dances that vary in the number of waggles per run. There is also some evidence that certain odors are released by dancers’ abdomens during the waggle dance to help motivate followers. When these substances were experimentally released into a hive, more foragers left to collect food. Back to Table of Contents

Module Wrap-up: How Honey Bees Communicate In this module, you explored honey bees' sophisticated communication systems, from their complex use of pheromones to their intricate dance languages. Learning to recognize these communication behaviors in your own colonies enhances your beekeeping skills and deepens your appreciation for these remarkable social insects.Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Honey Bee Biology Have you ever wondered how bees function as living organisms and navigate the world around them? In this module, you will explore the biological systems of honey bees that are needed for them to survive and succeed in their environments. Photo credit: Lucinda VanVleck Back to Table of Contents

Read: The Nervous System The honey bee nervous system is an ☆ Key Points intricate network of many nerve cells called neurons. A typical neuron is formed of a “body,” where most of the cell is found, and “processes,” thin filamentous projections that can be quite long (in some mammals, they can be several feet long!). These The central nervous system of the honey consists of the brain and ganglia. Honey bees have a capacity for learning and memory that surpasses all other insects. processes are called "dendrites" or "axons" depending on whether they receive input or convey output, respectively. The brain of the bee is where most of her neurons are located, and their processes, both axons and dendrites, extend along a “nerve cord” (analogous to our spinal cords) through the bee's thorax and abdomen, passing through a number of neuron cell body clusters called “ganglia”. The brain and the ganglia act as “control centers”, connected by nerve fibers to every part of the honey bee’s body, including wings, muscles, legs, and even cuticular hairs. Although the bee brain coordinates all the body’s functions including the activity of the ganglia, it is the ganglia that exert local control. This is why honey bees can continue to walk, flap their wings, and even sting for a short while after they are beheaded.

The brain of a worker bee is tiny, and yet it contains nearly one million neurons, so it is not surprising that a worker honey bee's capacity for learning surpasses that of all other insects! They are able to communicate with their nest mates, learn directions, and remember a vast array of smells, sights, and tastes. Honey bees also have impressive mathematical abilities. They are able to count up to four and can understand the concept of zero. After a long foraging trip visiting many flowers, they can determine how to "beeline" home. The bee brain is organized into clusters of neurons that are called lobes. Different lobes of the brain receive inputs from different sensory stimuli, and in turn, each lobe controls a different function or activity in the body. For example, the antennal lobe receives inputs from olfactory stimuli (smells) and the optical lobe receives inputs from visual stimuli. A very important lobe in the brain is the mushroom body (indicated in orange in the illustration), named so because it resembles the shape of a mushroom. The mushroom body is the center for learning and memory. Sensory information that is processed by different lobes in the brain (like smells and tastes) are interpreted in the mushroom body where it is

learned and remembered. This lobe takes up 20% of the bee brain in volume, while only 2% in a fruit fly. This gives an idea of the vast capabilities of honey bee learning and memory as an insect. It is useful to realize that the bee’s nervous system as a whole operates according to a very simple principle. Information (input) is perceived by sensory nerve cells (neurons) that convey the information to the brain, eliciting a chemical or motor reaction by other neurons (output). This very basic organization “input—(reaction)—output” is found in all animal nervous systems, including that of humans. The sensory input of the bee's nervous system includes the tactile senses (temperature, pressure, gravity), the olfactory system (smell), the gustatory system (taste), the auditory system (hearing), and the visual system. The neurons concerned with delivering output are either “motor” or “endocrine” and they govern muscle contractions and the secretion of chemicals, like hormones. On the following pages we will take a brief look at some of the inputs and outputs of the honey bee’s nervous system. Back to Table of Contents

▶ Read: Sensory Systems: Mechanoreception “Mechanoreception” is the ability of an animal to detect and respond to certain kinds of stimuli, such as touch, pressure, temperature, or vibration. Mechanoreception permits animals to navigate their world, react to mechanical stimuli, and even understand their place in space by perceiving gravity. Animals have evolved a clever way to discriminate among different sensory inputs by developing biological structures that are specifically attuned to certain physical stimuli. The most complex of these structures is the eye, whereas the simplest sensory input structure is merely a naked neuron that reacts to being touched or bent. For bees, sensory information is perceived by many small sensory organs or “mechanoreceptors” that are located on the periphery of their body, just below the cuticle, and on the tarsi (feet), mouthparts, wings, and antennae. These sensory organs are called sensilla (singular “sensillum”). They are small, hair-like structures that contain at least one neuron. Sensilla that perceive tactile information enable honey bees to recognize and learn the feeling of different objects, navigate different surfaces, land on flowers, and physically interact with their nestmates. Bees can perceive gravity Bees have groups of sensory hairs called “hairplates” that are essentially a hair attached to a neuron. Hairplates are found on antennal joints, in the neck joint between head and thorax, the waist joint between the thorax and the abdomen, and in joints of their legs. Deflection of these hairs is how sensory neurons attached to them detect gravity. Humans detect gravity in the same way. Hairs located in our inner ears bend when tiny crystals lying over them are pulled by gravity, triggering sensory neurons attached to the hairs. Bees use their sense of gravity to orient their waggle dance inside the nest so they can communicate resources to other bees. Bees also use gravity to build their combs straight down. This has implications for how level a hive body should be: if a hive is slanted to one side, bees may build comb across the frames, which can become a nuisance for you as a beekeeper trying to move frames. It is important that a beekeeper ensures hives are not slanted

downward to the left or right in the bee yard. Tipping your hive forward to enhance drainage out the entrance is fine, because the angle is parallel to the direction of the combs. The perception of gravity helps bees build their combs straight.

▶ Bees can hear When you hear a sound, your ear is detecting vibrations in the air. These vibrations are actually minute changes in pressure, like ripples on a pond, and just like the ripples they occur with different frequencies and amplitudes. Sometimes you may notice that you feel the floor vibrate when someone turns up the bass on their subwoofers. The power of the air’s vibrations can be transferred to other substrates. This fact is a key to understanding how hearing works in both bees and humans. Bees can hear both substrate vibrations (i.e. comb vibrations) and airborne vibrations (e.g. the sounds of dancing bees). They detect surface vibrations with pressure detectors in their legs (more specifically their tibia) called “subgenual organs”, and they discern airborne sounds using another type of sensory hair structure found on their antennae called a “Johnston’s organ”. The quality of the bee’s hearing differs from our human sense, but the basic neural mechanism is very similar. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Sensory Systems: Olfaction (Smell) The sense of smell is arguably the most important sense for honey bees. They rely on smell to help them find and learn important food sources, to communicate through pheromones to their other nest mates, and even to discriminate against non-nest mates that might be trying to enter their nest. Each honey bee colony develops a unique odor profile that is created by individuals secreting hydrocarbon molecules from their exoskeletons. By smelling these hydrocarbons, bees can determine who is a nest mate and who isn't. Watch this video clip to learn more about olfaction in honey bees. Video Transcript The sense of smell is called olfaction and honey bees have an incredible sense of smell. They have hundreds of olfactory receptors on their antennae that all bind to different odor molecules. An antenna can even determine the direction of an odor. So whether it's the right or left antenna that's sensing the odor more strongly, that tells them exactly which direction to fly to zone in on a flower. Olfactory receptors are found beneath these hairlike structures called sensilla located on the antennae. And odors bind to these receptors and stimulate a nerve signal to the brain, which can interpret exactly what they've smelled. When we sequenced the honey bee genome, we found that they have an expansive olfactory system with more olfactory receptor proteins than the other insects than we've sequenced so far. So the fruit fly and the mosquito. So for instance, the fruit fly has 62 olfactory receptor proteins, the mosquito has 79, and the honey bee has an impressive 170 olfactory receptor proteins. And this isn't surprising, given the importance of smell to honey bees. They need to be able to distinguish between their nest mates, and non-nest mates, to smell and interpret all of the different pheromones that are found in the colony, and even to recognize many different types of flowers that they are encountering in their everyday lives. And honey bees actually have a very good memory when it comes to smells. When the brain is processing the olfactory information from the antennae, they can send the nerve signal to other lobes that help them learn and remember this smell. And one of the major lobes that does this is the mushroom body. It's the center for learning and remembering in the bee's brain. So this is important because they want to be able to remember which flowers are really good nectar sources. So, for instance, maybe in the fall they can smell

that distinct smell of goldenrod and know that this is associated with a really good food reward. And actually, humans have sort of been taking advantage of this, in training honey bees using classical conditioning, similar to the Pavlov dog. And, what they do is that they expose honey bees to a certain smell, even if it is a smell they would never come in contact with in nature. And then after they expose them to the smell, they'll give them a reward, usually sugar syrup. And honey bees learn really quickly, often after just one or two presentations of this odor food reward system, to associate the odor with this reward. And researchers will actually use this technique to measure learning and memory in bees. And some people have even trained bees to sniff out landmines and illegal drugs using this technique. Though neither of these applications has really proven to be practical yet. Okay. So researchers can even look at this technique to look at how certain substances might impair learning and memory in bees. So for example, if honey bees are exposed to or consuming a particular pesticide, does this have an impact on their learning and memory? By doing this training, we can see whether or not bees are unable to learn an odor associated with a food reward, or if they learn it more slowly than normal, or if they forget it quickly than they normally would. And even though these sort of presentations for testing, learning, and memory and response to different factors are done in a lab, it actually has practical real world applications because learning and memory is so important for honey bees to navigate in their world, to collect food, and to cooperate socially. So it's just cool to know that by understanding the olfaction system in the honey bee, we're actually able to apply this technique to have broader implications in the bee's ability to function normally in the real world. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Sensory Systems: Gustation (Taste) The sense of taste is related to olfaction. In bees, as in humans, the sense of taste is less well-developed than the sense of smell. Bees have about 10 gustatory receptor sensilla types on their mouthparts, tips of their antennae, and tarsi that are specialized to taste a few chemicals, most of them sugars. Humans have around 10,000 taste buds that detect about six tastes. But the most impressive gustatory system that we know of is found in the catfish, which has an amazing 175,000 or more taste buds scattered all over its body! Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Sensory Systems: Vision Honey bee vision is well adapted to enable these insects to perform all the functions necessary to thrive. They are able to detect the movement of predators, fly safely, find flowers and other resources, navigate based on polarized light, and use visual cues to find their way back to the hive. Drones also use their eyes to find queens on their mating flights. However, inside the dark hive, bees rely more on their senses of smell, touch, and vibration detection than on their visual sense. Video Transcript Honey bee vision takes place in two types of eyes. The first type are the ocelli. These are three eyes that are formed in a triangular pattern near the top of the bee's head and here you can see the middle ocelli. The ocelli detect light intensity, they can't form an image. But detecting light intensity is needed for orientation during foraging, and also to regulate behavioral and hormonal changes that occur between daytime and nighttime. Each ocellus has a lens with retinal cells beneath it. The next type of eyes are the ones that we commonly refer to as bee eyes on the side of the head. And these are compound eyes and they're much more complex. They're actually comprised of thousands of individual, independent facets with lenses. And this doesn't mean that honey bees see thousands of repeated pictures. But the lenses each form a larger picture, kind of like pixels in a computer screen. The structure of these eyes means that honey bees actually have a low visual resolution. They can't really see great at distances the way that humans can. But that's okay, because they get really close to the things they need to see, like flowers, the nest entrance, intruders. So the effective resolution is quite high. But anything beyond about two yards is actually blurry for a honey bee. Drones have a bit better vision. They have twice the number of facets and lenses as worker bees. Why do you think that's the case? It's to find the queen in the drone congregation areas. So vision is really important for honey bees because it allows them to detect color, to detect light polarization and also to detect movement. Perception of color occurs with the compound eyes. This is what's detecting the color of light that's entering it. And the colors that bees see are a little bit different from the colors that humans see. Human eyes can detect combinations of red, green and blue. They can essentially see these colors on this

wavelength spectrum. But because bees have different pigments, they can see combinations of green, blue and ultraviolet. Ultraviolet being beyond violet or beyond purple on the color spectrum. So they can actually see these colors on the spectrum. And so you can tell that bees actually can't see red, and they interpret that as black. And their sensitivity to ultraviolet light helps them when they're orienting the sun as a compass, even when the sun is sometimes behind a cloud. Another neat thing is that because they're sensitive to ultraviolet light, they can also see flowers differently than humans can. So some flower petals actually reflect the ultraviolet light and they appear brighter to bees and they kind of have these really cool patterns on the petals that humans actually can't see. So when they're detecting polarized light, what happens is they're able to detect these bands of light polarization that are in the sky. And basically, air molecules actually scatter particles of light so that you can see this band that's at a 90 degree angle to the sun. And as the sun moves throughout the day so does this band. Always at a 90 degree angle. So as long as bees can see this band of polarized light they can tell where the sun is. And it's a special arrangement of the light sensitive molecules in the compound eyes that enables bees to see where this skylight overhead is polarized and where it isn't. And this is really important, obviously, because it helps bees detect the position of the sun even when it's hidden behind a cloud. But bees must still see some patches of blue sky in order to determine the sun's direction. So if it's completely cloudy, you won't find any foragers about, they'll all be inside the hive. And the sun serves as a really important visual reference for navigating during flight. They need to be able to tell exactly where the flowers are that they're going to, how to get back to their hive, and especially, how to communicate this important flower patch in relation to the sun to their other worker bees through the waggle dance. Another thing that they're able to perceive with vision is movement. And even though honey bee eyes lack detail, these can actually discriminate fast movements better than humans can. They can discriminate them out of 0.03 of a second, incredibly fast. And this is really important for detecting predators. They can sense any mammals that are moving in front of their colonies so they can have a really quick attack. They could also sense when bee keepers are moving sort of agitated or quickly in front of their colonies too. A cool thing about movement is that this helps them determine how fast they're flying. So, the speed that objects are moving past their eyes or the optic flow helps honey bees sense how fast they're traveling and the distance that they're actually traveling from the hive, which is also important not only so they can find their way back home, but also to

communicate it through the dance language to their sisters — the other worker bees. Vision is really important for learning and memory in bees. On the first journey from a hive, all bees whether they're drones, workers or queens, they perform an orientation flight. And they're trying to learn what their house looks like from the outside and how they can find their way back home. And they leave their hives and they sort of perform very short flights that are kind of hovering around the hive, and they're taking in what their hive looks like and other landmarks around them so that they won't get lost. And they have to be able to remember this. Honey bees will use the patterns of polarized UV light and the position of the sun to learn the patterns of the sun's movement during the day. And this is a really cool other thing about memory and it's something that you don't often think about. But for instance let's say that you are a worker bee and there's this really good patch of flowers directly east from your hive. So in the morning when you go and forage on those flowers, you know that you're going to fly directly toward the sun which is in the east. But let's say you come back to the hive and you're just hanging around until the afternoon when you're ready to go back out to that patch of flowers. This time the sun is in the west. So instead of flying directly toward the sun they have to know to fly directly away from the sun to get to those flowers. So bees are actually able to compensate for the change in the sun's position relative to the earth and remember how the sun is moving during the day. They're really good at using it as a directional reference even though it's changing which I find really fascinating. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: How Understanding Honey Bee Vision Can Make You a Better Beekeeper Studying an organism's biology is a great way to learn how we can maximize its health and success in the real world. By applying a few simple principles we learned about honey bee vision, we can reduce drift and confusion among our colonies in our own bee yards. These tips are applicable in a variety of beekeeping circumstances from colony arrangement in your yards to moving your colonies specific distances. Watch this video to learn some tips on what you can do. Video Transcript Another navigational technique that honey bees use is landmarks. This is really important to know as a master beekeeper because it impacts what you're doing with your colonies. So it's important to have landmarks that are sort of large, clear, and distinctive near the hives. This helps bees find out what their hive looks like and how they can get back home. It could be something as simple as putting the hive near a tree or painting your hive bodies different colors. Or at Dyce, we have sort of these unique symbols that are near the hives to help the bees. So the normal foraging radius or the average foraging radius of a honey bee is about two miles. So they're pretty good at learning a lot of the landmarks within that area. So if you're going to move your colonies you need to keep this in mind. If you're moving your colonies beyond two miles that's not a problem. A bee will leave her hive, she'll look around, not recognize anything and know that she has to relearn new landmarks and the landscape as she flies about because she's in an unfamiliar place. However, if you're moving your hive within two miles this is when confusion can arise. Now the hive position has changed, relative to familiar landmarks. A worker bee will leave the colony, she'll look around and she'll kind of remember some of the things that she's seeing and then she'll fly back to where the hive used to be. But now it's changed, so they're still recognizing their landmarks, but now they're not able to orient the same way that they did before. So we recommend to reduce confusion, move your hive small increments of a few feet at a time or move them over winter if you can when the bees are inside for many months and individual bees have to learn their surroundings again come spring. Another way where landmarks are good is in reducing drift. So honey bees drift from their home hive to

another hive, especially if these hives are close together because there's not enough landmarks or visual cues to distinguish among the hives. And this isn't necessarily good, especially with disease transmission or transmitting Varroa mites. So you'd like to reduce drift as much as possible. And you might think, well isn't that what guard bees are for? Are they going to keep out all of the non-nest mates? And they do keep out a lot of the non-nest mates. But it turns out that if a forager is coming into a neighboring hive full of pollen or nectar, they're more willing to be accepted into that colony. So it's almost like the guard is saying okay, you're bringing food to the party, you can come on in. And so it turns out that there's actually a fair bit of drift that's occurring between colonies. And especially if you have hives in a row, the hives at the end of those rows tend to be comprised of a lot of drifting bees. And when we think about how hives are actually or how nests are actually spread out in nature in tree kind cavities in these wild bee colonies, they're really spread out. And it's nothing like how humans actually keep honey bees really compact together in an apiary, sometimes with 10 or 20 hives really close together, or even on pallets. So just having extra landmarks so that they can distinguish which hive is theirs is going to help them out a lot. Back to Table of Contents

Read: The Muscular System: Flight The bee’s body has many dozens of muscles that help it move, but by far the largest muscles are those associated with flight, located in the thorax. Honey bees flap their wings incredibly fast (a whopping 240 times per second!) allowing them to reach speeds of 20 miles per hour! Although they appear to only have two wings while they are flying, they actually have four that hook together in pairs (with hamuli) so they can beat in synchrony and reduce drag and turbulence. Having wings hooked together by hamuli is a characteristic of Hymenopteran insects, as are membranous wings (hence the name of the order Hymenoptera). Veins in the wings add strength to the thin membranes. Honey bee hamuli The way bees and other insects effect flight is one of the most amazing marvels of bioengineering. Bees use both their cuticle and muscles to beat their wings. The cuticle has a tendency to retain its shape, yet it is also somewhat flexible. This allows it to act like a springboard when it is deformed - it has stored energy that is released when it regains its shape. Two massive sets of muscles in the thorax of the bee are attached to the inside of

the cuticle as shown in the diagram below. These sets of muscles squeeze the thorax to deform it alternately, either along the body axis, or side-to-side. This causes the wings, which are attached to hooklike wing-processes of the thoracic cuticle, to flap up and down. Thus the power stroke of the wings is aided by the natural recoil of the cuticle. Back to Table of Contents Photo credit: Christina Wahl

Read: The Respiratory System Instead of relying on lungs like humans, honey bees breathe through a series of tubes called tracheae (singular: trachea) throughout their bodies. Tracheae function much like lungs, carrying oxygen to muscles and organs and carrying carbon dioxide away from them. You can watch a bee breathe. She expands and contracts her abdomen like an accordion. This rhythmical movement brings the air in through the thorax and eventually, out through the abdomen. Air enters the tracheal system mainly through holes in the bee’s thorax called “spiracles”. From there, the air is drawn throughout the body via smaller and smaller tracheae, much like capillaries. These tiny tracheae come within just a few cells’ width of every living cell in the body of the bee, ensuring that adequate gas exchange can occur. After gas exchange occurs, the tracheae consolidate and enlarge again, then exit the body of the bee through several pairs of smaller abdominal spiracles, one pair per segment, for a total of 10 pairs (three thoracic pairs and seven abdominal pairs). Tracheal mites, a pest of honey bees, enter through the large thoracic spiracle and reside and reproduce in the tracheae, impairing honey bees’ ability to breathe. Bees suffering from tracheal mite infections are unable to fly, because the heavy congestion of mites in their tracheae means they cannot get enough air to supply their muscles with the oxygen needed to respire and provide the energy for flight.
Dissected honey bee tracheal tube full of various life stages of the tracheal mite. Photo by Christina Wahl Back to Table of Contents

Read: The Circulatory System The circulatory system of the honey bee is called “open” because it has no capillaries. In contrast, the circulatory system of humans, containing millions of capillaries, is called “closed”. This is because the blood is contained within the blood vessels of humans whereas in honey bees it leaves the arteries and circulates freely through the bees’ bodies. Humans have fluid moving freely around the body’s cells also, called “lymph”. Thus the blood in the bee is aptly named “hemolymph” since it functions both as blood and as lymph. Hemolymph is kept moving a few ways: 1) by the bee’s heart, located in its abdomen, 2) by the large blood vessels with their muscular walls, and 3) by general body muscle contractions as the bee moves. When bees are inactive for long periods of time – such as during the winter – they can stimulate circulation by contracting the muscles in their abdomens. Hemolymph that is in the abdomen of the bee enters the heart through the valves, where it gets pumped through the aorta and empties out of the aorta into the body cavity near the brain. As the bee moves, the hemolymph will make its way back to the abdomen. The cycle repeats. In this way, the hemolymph is able to move throughout the bee's body.

The circulatory system has five main functions: Transporting energy from digested food to the rest of the body cells to sustain function and life Bringing waste from cells to the excretory organs to be removed Lubricating body movements Conferring immunity through cells that attack pathogens Carrying hormones from the glands where they are produced to the organs and tissues they are intended to target Back to Table of Contents

Read: The Digestive System The digestive system of animals is like a “tube inside a tube": Food goes in one end, fecal material comes out the other, and the gut tube’s walls along the way not only function to absorb nutrition and eliminate waste but also to protect the body’s inner tissues from assault by foreign pathogens. Just like an animal's skin or cuticle (the outer “tube” in our “tube inside a tube” analogy), the gut tube functions as a barricade. It is divided into three parts: the foregut, midgut, and hindgut. ▶ Foregut The foregut is located in all three body segments — the head, thorax, and abdomen. Food (nectar, honey, water, and pollen) enters at the mouth, located in the head. Bees use their proboscis to bring liquids into their mouth. The proboscis is formed of several mouthparts that the bee brings together to form an airtight tube for drinking. The hairy middle part is what we think of as the bee’s “tongue.” The salivary glands of the bee, which are also part of the foregut, open on its upper surface. Photo credit: Christina Wahl Salivary glands are distributed in both the head and thorax. The salivary glands in the thorax are also called thoracic glands. When the proboscis is not in use, it is folded back under the bee’s “chin.” When she wants to feed, she swings the proboscis forward and brings its several parts together into a tube. The bee then rapidly moves her tongue back and forth, bringing the liquid up through the proboscis and back into her pharynx (throat). If you have a dissection scope at home, you can watch a bee drink. It helps to visualize the process if you give her a colored sugar syrup to drink. During drinking, the outer parts of the proboscis remain stationary, acting simply as the walls of the “straw” through which liquid is drawn in. To chew bee bread, a bee uses its mandibles to break it down into small pieces that it then places in its mouth.

Swallowed nectar, honey, and bee bread pass through the esophagus and enter the last part of the foregut called the crop (also called the honey stomach), located in the abdomen. The crop is a storage area for nectar, honey, or water. Bees can partially fill their crops with honey before leaving the hive on foraging rounds to use as an energy resource, or they can fill it with nectar or water while foraging to bring back to the hive. A valve called the proventriculus is located at the base of the crop; when shut, it prevents the nectar that a bee has collected from moving into the midgut and being digested. The crop can swell enormously from the collection of nectar, displacing other abdominal organs.

▶ A bee that has brought red syrup home in her crop. Photo credit: Christina Wahl Midgut While a bee collecting nectar shuts her proventricular valve to keep nectar in her crop, a bee that is eating and digesting honey or bee bread will open her valve so food can pass from the crop to the ventriculus, an organ somewhat analogous to both the human stomach and small intestine. Here, food is digested and nutrients are absorbed. The ventricular walls are only one cell thick. They are protected from the abrasive qualities of ingested pollen by an onion-like, noncellular membrane that wraps around and around the inner ventricular walls, called the peritrophic membrane. It is here in the ventriculus that pathogens such as Nosema and various viruses break through the peritrophic membranes and infect the ventricular cells. Hindgut ▶

At the rear end of the ventriculus is another valve, called the ventricular valve, which separates it from the hindgut. The hindgut begins with a short intestine, a narrow tube from which the 100 or more Malpighian tubules emerge. Malpighian tubules are bee versions of kidneys. They secrete nitrogenous waste from the hemolymph into the hindgut tube for elimination. Little is known of the function of the bee’s intestine. It is much shorter and anatomically more simplistic than the small intestines of animals that rely on the small intestine for nutrient absorption. The hindgut ends with the rectum, where solid waste materials are stored for eventual excretion. A wintering bee, unwilling to defecate inside the hive, will store fecal material in the rectum for many weeks. When she is eventually able to relieve herself, the rectum can be enormously engorged, displacing most of the other abdominal organs.

Photo credit: Christina Wahl Bee feces Bee feces contain undigested pollen fat and husks; dead cells from the midgut; undigested products from food supplements; some pesticide residues; and, in the case of a disease or parasitic infection, materials that might infect other bees. Bees, therefore, generally do not void waste inside the nest and instead take cleansing flights outside the nest to keep the colony clean and to reduce the potential for disease transmission. The bees' ability to avoid defecation within the nest is especially important in winter, for then they

can be confined inside for weeks or even months. Finding fecal deposits inside the hive or in abnormally high amounts on the hive exterior (dysentery) signals a problem, as dysentery is a symptom of nutritional issues and some diseases. Orange bee feces on snow from a winter cleansing flight. It is healthy and normal for bee feces to be evident outside the hive in winter, generally after a window of warmer weather when they were able to take cleansing flights en masse.
