Module Wrap-up: Honey Bee Biology In this module, you discovered the essential biological systems that enable honey bees to survive and thrive in their environments. This journey through their fundamental life processes showed you how honey bees function as living organisms and interact with the world around them.Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: How Honey Bees Construct and Maintain Their Nests To care for honey bees more effectively, we need to understand their uniquely constructed nests. In particular, the nests of wild honey bee colonies reveal a lot about the bees’ needs and preferences, despite regional and racial variations. Much of the information included in this module was derived from studies by Cornell University of wild colonies and swarms being installed in hives. In this module, you will investigate how bees construct and maintain their homes, what characteristics they prefer, and how they keep them livable and conducive to healthy development. Back to Table of Contents

Read: The Building Blocks of a Nest Honey bees are one of the few animals Nests are built from wax produced on Earth that are able to make by bees' bodies and plant resins architectural constructions from that are processed into propolis. materials produced by their bodies. The properties of wax enable it to be an ideal material for building comb, storing honey, and communicating. ▶ Wax Production Wax is composed of over 300 individual compounds and is considered energetically “expensive” for the bees to create. The book "The Hive and the Honey Bee" (2015) estimates that a colony must consume anywhere from five to 20 pounds of honey in order to produce one pound of wax. Wax production is stimulated by two things: excess nectar and a colony’s need for more storage space. Bees only build comb under these two conditions. Because comb building is so expensive for the colony, bees typically only produce wax when there is an excess amount of carbohydrates coming into the hive, like during a honey flow or when feeding on 1:1 syrup. Furthermore, the bees will only build comb when they have a need for more storage space; most of the current comb in the hive must be in use before the colony invests in constructing more. Some examples of conditions where bees need more space are during a honey flow, when they need more room to store the incoming nectar, or when the queen is laying plenty of eggs and the colony needs more room to accommodate the growing brood nest. Worker bees between 12 and 18 days old produce most of a colony's wax (making comb building one of the final roles of house bees before they transition to foraging). Their wax glands (four pairs) are located on the undersides of their abdomens, growing when wax is being produced and shrinking when it is not. If comb building is urgently needed after a bee has transitioned into another job, the bee can reactivate her glands to once again

▶ be a wax producer. Liquid wax is excreted from these glands and deposited onto plates called wax mirrors, where it hardens into wax scales or flakes as it dries. Every 12 hours, each bee's gland can form one new scale. The bees then scrape off the hardened wax scales, chew them, add saliva, and manipulate them Worker's wax glands secreting wax. Photo with their legs. Once the wax is the credit: Jennifer Tsuruda right consistency, the bees transfer it to the comb, where it is worked over by other bees to construct comb and cappings. Comb Comb-building workers determine how much comb will be built to accommodate worker brood and how much will be built for drone brood. They walk along the brood comb already constructed to evaluate the amount of drone comb that is present. If there is already sufficient drone comb available for the queen to lay in, they will produce worker comb; if not, they will build drone comb. Honey bees will rebuild or repair damaged comb as needed. One behavior that is associated with wax construction and repair is festooning. This is where inactive bees hang between combs, linking themselves together by holding legs with one another. Comb is often repaired beneath the bees that are festooning. In a hive, wax will darken over time, particularly in the brood nest, where it is littered with pollen, pupal cocoons, larval feces, and other debris. Wax also absorbs lipophilic (fat-loving) substances, which include pesticides, antibiotics, and other toxins. Because this litter and these contaminants accumulate in

beeswax combs, it is a good idea to replace them regularly. Our recommendation is to replace the two oldest frames (or the two with the darkest combs) in each hive body with fresh foundation every year. A good recordkeeping tip used by many beekeepers is to write the year on the top bars of each frame to easily identify which are the oldest to rotate out. You can work these combs toward the edges of the brood nest so they are not full of brood when you would like to remove them. Honeycomb is commonly referred to as an architectural marvel: Its shape uses a minimum amount of material for maximum strength and storage space. The combs themselves are generally parallel and upright in accordance with gravity, with the cells tipped upward slightly to help keep in their contents. Comb serves not only as a place for food storage and brood production but also as a medium for communication within the hive by transmitting vibrations. The nest interior is dark, so sound and vibrations are important for communication. Propolis Propolis is used to caulk and seal holes around the perimeter of the hive, protect the hive from moisture, and even cover/mummify intruders that cannot be removed (e.g., mice). Bees also add a thin layer of propolis to the ▶

surface of newly constructed combs to provide structural support. Notice this layer of orange propolis on the photo of the comb to the right. In the nests of wild colonies, a layer of propolis often covers all the inner walls of the nest cavity. Propolis even provides the colony with antimicrobial protection, and research has determined that creating a propolis envelope around the nest cavity can actually help protect the colony from some Propolis used to seal the hive inner cover to the top hive body. Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership pathogens. This is an important advance in understanding the function of what has long been considered just a sticky and unsightly annoyance! Propolis is collected by specialized foragers who carry home resin from a range of trees (poplar, aspen, cottonwood, pine, and others) in their pollen baskets. This resin is mixed with wax to create propolis. It can be sticky or stiff, depending on its origin and temperature. Back to Table of Contents

Read: How a Nest of a Honey Bee Colony Is Organized — Location and Foraging Area Honey bee colonies can and do thrive in many locations, including forests, cities, and agricultural areas, in part because honey bees fly so far from their homes to collect food. Estimates vary, but an individual forager may fly up to six miles from the nest, although they usually fly shorter distances when resources are available (one to two miles). Even with foraging trips extending out only two miles, the foraging area of a honey bee colony is more than 12 square miles, or over 8,000 acres. This flight range is important for management: It affects how beekeepers respond to pesticide applications, how many colonies they can place in one apiary, where and how far apart they locate multiple apiaries, whether they must feed closely packed colonies to supplement their forage, and so forth. Natural areas have long been recognized as prime locations to keep honey bees due to the variety of floral resources. Agricultural areas can also have excellent resources and yield bumper honey crops, but some can put the bees at risk for pesticide exposure. More recently, cities have proven to also be a good habitat for honey bees (and for many other wild bee species), although, of course, this can vary enormously. Cities tend to have high floral diversity from the presence of gardens, parks, green roofs, and community gardens; this and other factors have contributed to the rise in popularity of urban beekeeping. Beekeeping was legalized in New York City in 2010. Beekeepers in urban areas, however, need to be especially cognizant that their bees don’t bother neighbors and passersby. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: How a Nest of a Honey Bee Colony Is Organized — Bee Space We’ll start out small to understand the organization of a honey bee colony’s nest. Combs in wild honey bee nests and managed honey bee hives alike are built about 3/8” apart from one another, a dimension known as bee space. This leaves just enough room for bees to pass one another on opposite combs. If the open space between two combs is greater than 3/8”, then the bees will tend to build comb (commonly called burr comb) to fill this extra space. If there is a space less than 3/8”, bees will likely fill it in with propolis and won’t use this space at all. Bee space has implications for beekeeping equipment. It prevents the combs from getting stuck to each other and to the hive walls, and therefore allows the beekeeper to inspect a colony without needlessly ripping apart the combs. Indeed, the invention of a movable-frame hive by Reverend Lorenzo L. Langstroth depended on understanding bee space. Before designing hives that adhere to the dimensions of bee space, it was nearly impossible to remove the combs to evaluate the health and productivity of the colony without destroying the comb. Being able to pull out each comb one by one without greatly disturbing the colony caused a fundamental change in the way people kept bees. It just goes to show how much beekeepers can learn by studying the biology of honey bees. The patent for the Langstroth hive was filed in 1852, and the hive design spread throughout North America and Europe, ushering in the modern era of beekeeping. Watch this video to observe how nests and hives of honey bees are typically organized. Video Transcript Typically brood is raised in a spherical arrangement in the bottom and center of the nest surrounded by a thin layer of pollen and bee bread. Honey is stored around and above the

brood nest, hence the name of a honey super. Super means over or above. When you pull all frames from a broods nest in a time when there’s ample nutrition and ample brood production, you can expect to see ideal frames that have brood in the center with arcs of pollen surrounding the brood, and an arc of honey surrounding the pollen. Seeing frames like this always gives the beekeeper a good feeling that there's lots of resources coming in. Sometimes however, a colony can become honey bound. This is where a nectar flow is occurring, but there's not enough space for the colony to store it above the brood nest. In these cases, the bees who receive the nectar will deposit it in empty cells in the brood nest, thereby restricting the area where the queen can lay. The cells that are being filled with nectar are usually cells that the queen would lay eggs in. And this can reduce the amount of overall brood that's being produced and if there's not enough available space to continue rearing brood, the colony may swarm. Similarly, colonies can become pollen bound, if there's a very large pollen flow in your region. We'd recommend regularly checking in the amount of pollen or honey in your hives, and where they're being deposited, to make sure that bees have enough space. If your colony is pollen or honey bound, the beekeeper can make more space in the brood nest by switching out honey filled frames, with frames of drawn comb or foundation. The honey filled frames can then be moved to a higher box if those boxes hold the same size frames or they can be placed in a freezer and then thawed, and put back in the same colonies later in the season when food reserves are low. Reinserting them back into the same colony that they came from will help reduce the transmission of any disease spores that may be present. It's important to note that over time the organization of the hive changes. Bees move up vertically within their nest, so in summer and autumn the brood nest will be located in the bottom deep of the hive with honey stores above. But throughout the winter, the bee cluster moves upward to consume the honey stores. By springtime the clusters occupying the upper deep and there's virtually no stores or bees on the bottom deep. The colony will become congested if they've got no more room to grow vertically or to store honey. And this has implications for management. Bees tend not to store any honey below the brood nest so beekeepers will often switch the positions of the two deep boxes in spring to bring the brood nest back down to the bottom deep and giving them more storage space above. And this practice of rotating your deeps to ensure the brood nest is brought to the bottom is referred to as rotating hive bodies or reversing hive bodies. And it allows the bees to use their space in a continuous, seasonal cycle. It's really important that

you first check all the frames in the colony to make sure the brood nest isn't split between the two deeps. If that's the case, you can accidentally disrupt the brood nest when you're rotating hive bodies. And this will make it hard for the bees to keep all the brood warm and can result in chilling of the brood. The colony's vertical movement over time is also a consideration in winter. Honey stores should be located above the cluster going into winter and the beekeeper should remove the queen excluder so the queen isn't left behind as the cluster is moving upwards. The position of queen cups and queen larvae are also created in specific areas of the nest. So within the brood nest queen cups tend to be toward the bottom of the cones or frames and facing downward. Queen cups are present at most times during the year, but are most abundant in the spring swarm season. These special cups are called queen cells once eggs have been laid in them. Queen cells that are produced in preparation for swarming, called swarm cells, are often located at the bottom of the comb. The exceptions to this general rule are with supersedure cells and emergency queen cells. Supersedure cells are created while the original queen is still alive, but the workers would like to supersede her with a new queen. These cells are the most often found in the center of the comb although there are also exceptions to this as well. Emergency queen cells are built when workers abruptly find themselves without a queen and they must convey larvae that were originally intended to be workers into queens instead. And these cells can be located wherever there are worker larvae. The timing of the production of drone comb is just as important as its location. It's built only after the hive has become well established. The Cornell bee researcher Michael Smith calls drone comb construction a sign that the colony is undergoing puberty. That is, it's starting to invest in reproduction by beginning to produce drones. And these drones are helping the colony reproduce because they're passing on the colony's genes by mating with queens in the region. Back to Table of Contents

▶ Read: How a Nest of a Honey Bee Colony Is Organized — Nest Characteristics Understanding a honey bee nest characteristics is very helpful for beekeepers. Let’s explore the precise architectural elements that make up their homes. Size/Volume Wild honey bee colonies living in hollow trees occupy an average nest cavity size of about 10 gallons and range from five gallons to about 15 gallons. This is much smaller than a typical Langstroth hive, in which two deep brood chambers and one medium honey super amount to about 30 gallons. ▶ Entrance Bees in temperate climates tend to prefer the entrances to their homes to be small (an area only two to three square inches wide), south-facing, high (more than 15 feet off the ground), and positioned at the bottom of the nest cavity. These characteristics help the colony to defend its nest against predators and intruders, to regulate its nest temperature, and to store and ripen enough honey to survive winter in Honey bee nest entrance high in a tree. Photo credit: Thomas Seeley the cold climate of the northeastern U.S. Beekeepers can manipulate hive entrance size with simple tools like an entrance reducer. ▶ Previous Use One colony will often continuously occupy a cavity and can do so for decades. Swarms will preferentially occupy a previously used cavity, indicated in part by
the presence of comb. Bait hives with comb are more successful in luring swarms than those without. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Hive Styles The Langstroth hive (photo on left) is the style that we will be discussing throughout the course. There are many variants of the Langstroth hive, which are also popular in Europe, and you can order or build Langstroth hives that fit eight frames or ten. Some other hive styles that you may be familiar with include the top-bar hive (seen in the middle photo and sometimes called the Kenyan top-bar hive) and the Warré hive (in the photo at the right). The best hive style for your bees depends on factors such as climate, goals, and budget, but all hive styles and management regimes require regular inspections. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Temperature Control in the Nest Unlike most insects, honey bees are capable of generating heat by exercising their flight muscles, both during flight and when they are stationary inside their nests. Given the ability of individuals to generate heat, it is not surprising that a whole colony of honey bees is able to keep the center of its nest (the brood area) at a constant and elevated temperature, approximately 92°F to 97°F (33°C to 36°C). This ability to regulate the temperature of their environment is called thermoregulation. Thermoregulation helps the colony's brood to develop properly; temperatures outside of this range lead to developmental and behavioral abnormalities or failure to emerge as adults at all. This capacity for regulating the temperature of the nest has enabled Apis mellifera to thrive in a wide range of climates around the world, including the cold temperate regions of Europe and North America. Bees can regulate the temperature of their nests in two ways: passive regulation and active regulation. Passive thermoregulation refers to temperature control effected through the structure of the nest itself, while active thermoregulation is temperature control effected through behaviors performed by the bees. Bees expend energy performing active thermoregulation. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Temperature Control in the Nest — Heating Honey bee colonies use several techniques to keep the brood nest portions of their nests warm. This allows them to be active inside the nest and ready to fly in cool weather without first requiring the sun to heat the nest from the outside. This also allows them to survive and even rear brood when the outside temperature drops to frigid lows during winter. Passive strategies to maintain a warm brood nest include nesting in cavities whose walls act as insulation and shelter them from cold winds. The entrance is usually near the bottom of the nest cavity to keep in warm air (as hot air rises), and cracks are sealed with propolis to keep out cold drafts. Wax and honey that surround the brood nest also provide additional insulation. Active thermoregulation largely pertains to the incubating of brood. Heater bees cover the brood nest, and some may press their warm bodies against the capped brood, increasing the temperature much in the same way that a chicken incubates an egg. Others crawl into empty cells headfirst to heat adjacent brood from the side. In these ways, the brood is kept at approximately 92°F to 97°F. Beekeepers should take care not to open up the brood nest in cold weather, exposing and chilling the developing bees. We generally recommend not to expose brood to temperatures below 59°F, and to not expose brood to rain, which can cause them to become chilled and fail to develop. The most notable active thermoregulatory behavior that bees use to keep warm is the formation of a winter cluster. When ambient temperatures drop below 57°F, the colony clusters together as a group to stay warm. The brood nest is warmed, but the rest of the hive or tree cavity interior is not. While the winter cluster is not technically in hibernation, many other colony functions, such as foraging and water collection, cease when bees are clustering. Photo: The winter cluster. Bees on the inside of the cluster generate heat by shivering. They contract and relax their flight muscles without flapping their wings. At the center of the cluster, bees can move around, tend to brood (if there is any), and eat honey. Bees around the edges of the cluster act as insulation to prevent the heat from dissipating. Bees take different roles in the cluster at different times, moving from the center to the edge and back over hours or

days. If there is a respite in the cold, individual bees may leave the hive for brief cleansing flights, often their only opportunity to defecate for several months. The cluster as a whole will also move upward to the honey stores when the temperature is warm enough to give them access to food. If the temperature stays too cold for the bees to break the cluster and move, the bees can starve despite there being plentiful honey stores in the nest. Finally, an interesting note is that the heating behavior of bees can be lethal to predators. The Asian giant hornet is a predator of honey bees in Asia, and bee stings do not penetrate the hornet’s cuticle. Instead, bees will perform balling behavior as defense instead. They crowd around individual hornets and heat them to death! Honey bees will overheat the Asian Giant Hornet to kill it. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Temperature Control in the Nest — Cooling Honey bees have also adapted several techniques to help cool their nests on hot days. Watch the video to learn some of these strategies. Video Transcript On hot days, bees also need to be able to cool the hives so that it doesn't exceed a rough ceiling of 97 degrees. Above that point, the heat can kill the brood and adults and can soften beeswax combs. Most cooling of the colony is active, the main passive mechanism is the ventilation that's achieved through the entrance of the nest and any upper entrances provided by the beekeeper. Bees use a variety of active methods to reduce heat. First, just as clustering helps the bees keep themselves warm, dispersing helps them cool the colony. So on warm days bees will actually move away from the brood to other areas of the hive, to help dissipate the heat. Bees can also fan their wings to increase ventilation within the hive. They gather along the inner walls of the hive and along the entrance and fan their wings to expel warm air from inside. The motion of the wings is actually different from when they're flying. They are moving air horizontally, as opposed to vertically. Fanning bees face the hive entrance and point the tips of their abdomens downward, and then fan their wings. This is in contrast to when they're fanning the nasonov pheromone to orient other bees to the entrance. In this case, the abdomens are pointed upward. So fanning actually helps create air currents that bring in cool air to circulate through the hive. If fanning alone doesn't cool the nest adequately, forager bees collect water for evaporative cooling. They pass the water off to water receiver bees who place it on the cappings of brood cells or in open cells. Fanning with their wings then evaporates the water and cools the nest. If the temperature continues rising in the nest, more bees will turn to receiving, which signals to water foragers that they need to increase their water collecting and recruit even more bees to fetch water. Bees can only collect water during the daytime, so during especially hot nights it might be difficult for them to control the temperature inside the nest. Finally, the worker bees may beard on the outside of the hive, where they literally hang out on the front in a beard shape. Leaving the nest helps increase ventilation and also reduces the amount of heat that's generated by workers inside the hive. Bees may also

beard after miticides are applied or if a fume board is inserted as the bees are making an effort to escape the chemicals. But it's most commonly seen when the colony is overheating. Honey bees are resourceful organisms that have adapted a variety of behaviors to help them survive in temperatures that exceed the thermal range necessary for brood development and adult survival. Additionally, bees in the wild carefully select nest sites that will help with thermoregulation. These passive and active strategies have allowed them to be successfully managed nearly everywhere in the world. Back to Table of Contents

Glossary Master Beekeeping Part 1: Honey Bee Evolution, Biology and Behavior College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, Cornell University abdomen The abdomen is one of three main body segments of insects (which also include the head and thorax). The abdomen contains the digestive and reproductive systems. altruism Altruism, biologically speaking, is animal behavior that benefits another animal at the expense of the first, in terms of survival or reproduction. Worker bees that forgo their own reproduction in order to help the queen reproduce is one of the most extreme examples of altruism in nature. See kin selection. amino acid Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. They are a necessary part of bees’ (and humans’) diets, necessary to function and develop. Pollen is the source of amino acids in bee bread and royal jelly. anther The anther is the part of a flower that contains pollen. apiary An apiary is a collection of one or more hives, also called a bee yard. Most backyard beekeepers have only one apiary, but commercial beekeepers may manage dozens. Apidae Apidae is a family classification of bees. It is the largest family of bees and includes honey bees, bumble bees, carpenter bees, and many others. Apis Apis is a genus classification of bees. It includes all bees that produce and store honey. Apis mellifera Apis mellifera is the scientific name for the Western honey bee. Apis is the genus and mellifera is the species. Mellifera means “bearer or maker of honey” (melli means “honey” and fera means “bearer”). arthropods (Arthropoda) Arthropoda is one of the many phyla of the animal kingdom. Honey bees are in the phylum Arthropoda, and are therefore known as arthropods. All arthropods are invertebrates and have jointed bodies and paired jointed appendages. . All rights reserved. All other copyrights, trademarks, trade names, and logos are the sole property of their respective owners.

Master Beekeeping Part 1: Honey Bee Evolution, Biology and Behavior College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, Cornell University bee bread Bee bread is pollen that has been moistened by honey and honey bee glandular secretions and fermented by microorganisms such as yeast, bacteria, and fungi. Pollen in the form of bee bread is honey bees’ major source of protein, fats, and vitamins, and is an important nutrient source for the development of brood. bee space Bee space is 3/8”, which leaves enough room for bees to pass one another on opposite combs. If the space between combs is less than 3/8”, bees will likely fill it with propolis. It if is greater than 3/8”, the bees will tend to build burr comb to fill the space. bee yard See apiary. beeswax See wax. brood Brood is the name given to the egg, larvae, and pupae stages of insects. brood nest The brood nest is the part of the hive where the brood is developing, distinct from the area where honey is being processed and stored. Conditions such as temperature are more important here, for the healthy development of brood. brood pheromone Brood pheromone is released by larvae and indicates its sex, caste, and age. It influences development and behavior of other bees, most notably by inhibiting the development of ovaries in workers. burr comb Burr comb is comb built anywhere the beekeeper doesn’t want it, namely between frames or hive bodies. It is likely to be built in spaces with dimensions that exceed the width of bee space. carbohydrate Carbohydrates are the sugars in food that are a source of energy for organisms. caste A caste is one form within a species that may differ from other forms in terms of anatomy, physiology, and reproduction. The three honey bee castes are queens, workers, and drones. . All rights reserved. All other copyrights, trademarks, trade names, and logos are the sole property of their respective owners.

Master Beekeeping Part 1: Honey Bee Evolution, Biology and Behavior College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, Cornell University chromosome Chromosomes are the structures containing an organism’s genetic material in the form of DNA. class Class is a rank in the classification of life, below phylum and above order. Honey bees are members of the class Insecta (insects). cleansing flights A cleansing flight is the delicate name given to the act of leaving the hive to defecate. Bees can delay defecation for months during winter, but will leave the hive on a warm day to void their waste. Fecal staining may be evident around or on the outside of hives in winter and early spring. cluster (also winter cluster) Clustering is a thermoregulatory behavior where bees congregate on the comb to keep warm when environmental temperatures are below 64°F. Colony functions such as foraging and water collection cease when bees are clustering. cocoon A cocoon is a silky pupal casing spun by insect larvae to protect them during their pupal stage. colony The colony is the family community of honey bees that share a nest. There is usually a queen present, many workers, and fewer drones. comb see honeycomb Complementary Sex Determination gene The Complementary Sex Determination gene is responsible for sex determination in honey bees. compound eye The two large eyes found on either side of a bee’s head. Each compound eye consists of thousands of individual independent facets with lenses that collectively form a coherent image. cooperative brood care Cooperative brood care is the practice of sharing the work of raising young that is not one’s own. In the case of honey bees, the queen lays the eggs, but the larvae, pupae, and young adults are cooperatively cared for by their older sisters, nurse bees. Cooperative brood care is one of the three hallmarks of eusociality. . All rights reserved. All other copyrights, trademarks, trade names, and logos are the sole property of their respective owners.

Master Beekeeping Part 1: Honey Bee Evolution, Biology and Behavior College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, Cornell University corbicula (plural: corbiculae) See pollen basket. crop See honey crop. diploid organism Diploid organisms have paired sets of chromosomes in each cell (excluding sperm and egg cells). They inherit one set of chromosomes from their mother and one from their father. Female honey bees (both queens and workers) are diploid, because they develop from eggs that are fertilized (by sperm) and therefore contain two sets of chromosomes; in contrast, drones are haploid. See also haplodiploid. DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) DNA is the long molecule that carries an organism’s complete set of genetic information. drift Drift is the entering of bees into hives or nests that are not their homes. It is more likely when hives are close together and difficult to distinguish from one another. These bees tend to be gentle and calm on the comb. They overwinter well in cold climates, and rapidly build up in spring. They were originally found in Hungary, Austria, Romania, Bulgaria, Slovenia, Croatia, and Serbia. Apis mellifera ligustica is the most common subspecies in North America. It is often referred to as the “Italian” bee, as it was originally found in Italy and introduced to North America in the 1860s. This gentle bee has yellow, gold, and light brown coloration. Colonies are capable of rapid growth when there are floral resources available and decrease brood production in the fall more than other subspecies in the U.S. Apis mellifera anatoliaca Apis mellifera caucasica Apis mellifera meda Apis mellifera pomonella Apis mellifera syriaca Apis mellifera caucasica is known as the Caucasian bee, and is from the Caucasus Mountains in Russia, Georgia, Armenia, and Turkey. The worker bees have gray hairs, while drones have characteristic black hairs on their thoraces. In general, these bees are gentle; they build up slowly in the spring and are less likely to swarm. They are also tolerant of cold temperatures. Apis mellifera jemenitica “Y” is for yemenitica, an alternative name to jemenitica Madagascar (U) Apis mellifera unicolor “U” is for unicolor Egypt (L) Apis mellifera lamarckii “L” is for lamarckii . Homepage Video Transcript This course is going to be a really fun learning experience, because we’re going to cover some of the practical aspects of beekeeping, the science and art of beekeeping, and how you can achieve some of the outcomes that you’re desiring. So whether it’s just managing colony growth, or being able to predict exactly what to expect in your colony at different times of the year, we’re going to cover all those basics. Also, if you’re starting to get excited about getting a little bit larger, or starting a small breeding program, or rearing your own queens, these are skills that we’re going to talk about as well. It’s important not just to see this as a how-to protocol, but to understand why you’re doing these things. This is the difference between a beekeeper and a master beekeeper. You’re going to gain confidence in your ability to analyze a situation, and to make informed management decisions, based on the principles that we cover. What you'll do Identify seasonal needs and management practices to support honey bee health Understand how to conduct an effective hive inspection Identify how to meet your colonies’ nutritional needs Explore swarming: preventing, catching, and baiting Identify when you want to requeen your colony Manage colony growth: when and how to split and merge colonies Understand how to breed bees and rear queens for the traits you desire Explore how to keep records to learn more about your colonies Identify robbing and learn how to intervene Course Description Supporting your colonies’ ability to thrive and achieving your desired outcomes requires a systematic approach and the application of practical techniques and knowledge. In this course, you will learn how to predict what to expect in your colony season by season. You’ll gain confidence in your ability to analyze different situations and make informed management decisions based on the scientific principles you learn here. Apply the hands-on techniques used by experienced, expert beekeepers, honey bee biologists, and the Cornell University Honey Bee Extension team to keep your colonies healthy and to produce your desired outcomes year after year.

Module Introduction: Safety and Biosecurity in the Bee Yard Keeping yourself and your visitors safe in the bee yard is a top priority. Honey bee stings can cause a wide range of reactions, some of which can be life-threatening, and learning how to prevent or respond to them will help you enjoy beekeeping for many years to come. The safety of your bees is also a priority. Following biosecurity practices minimizes the spread of infections, parasites, and predators, helping keep your colonies healthy. In this module, we will learn how to keep both you and your bees safe in the bee yard. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Preventing Stings Beekeepers are liable to get stung at least occasionally. By now, you probably have a few pictures of your swollen hands or face! If it weren’t for their stingers, most bee colonies wouldn’t get to keep so much of their honey from predators and intruders, and they could starve to death. As best you can, let those stings tell you something. Colonies that sting a lot relative to other colonies may be experiencing extra pest pressure, or need to be moved, requeened, or even culled outright. If all your colonies sting a lot, you may need to retool your inspection style: how you do it, when you do it, or even what you wear. ☆ Key Points Accept that some stings are inevitable. Protective equipment is a personal choice requiring a balance of risk and ease of movement. Communicate with potential visitors that there are honey bees in the area and provide visitors with appropriate protective equipment. Stinging is something to be avoided, but not beyond reasonable measures. If you don’t let yourself accept that some stings are likely inevitable, then you probably won’t get comfortable enough to really know and understand your bees. Protective equipment to prevent stings in your own bee yard is a matter of personal choice. It’s a balancing act. On the one hand, you should not endanger yourself or others just to prove that you’re capable of handling thousands of stinging insects without protection. On the other hand, you shouldn’t insulate yourself so much that you are clumsy or immune to any ill effects that you are having on your bees. Different veil styles offer different levels of convenience and protection. It’s important to have a veil handy even if you don’t use it, for the rare occasion that a hive suddenly becomes too defensive to handle easily. Gloves are a matter of personal choice- some, like nitrile gloves, are thin enough to permit more tactile sensation; others, like kidskin or rubber gloves, will protect you better, but at the cost of your dexterity. Cost and waste are also factors.

Other, low-tech protective clothing measures abound. Some beekeepers tuck their pants into their socks or stretch rubber bands around their pant legs to prevent bees from crawling up into their clothing. As a Master Beekeeper, you may be bringing new beekeepers or members of the public to your bee yard. Many people unfamiliar with honey bees are afraid, and some may have unexpected reactions to stings if they have not been stung before. Even if you do not generally use it, you must always have protective clothing available for visitors — a veil, gloves, a suit, or clothing with long sleeves and pant legs — and use your best judgment about your visitors’ tolerance and comfort around bees. You should also exercise safety precautions — again, more than you might generally — to reduce the chance of stings. Avoid inspections in poor weather, when a hive is shaded, or during a nectar dearth. Use adequate smoke and instruct your visitors not to block the hive entrance. Pay attention to warning signs from your bees, such as pinging your veil or louder buzzing, and close your colony for another day if you see any of these signs. Lastly, post a sign at your bee yard(s) informing readers that live honey bees are in the area; this should include a contact phone number for the public to be able to contact you. Many beekeepers keep their bee yards out of sight, especially from roadways, to limit their view from the public. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Bee Sting Reactions There are two general types of reactions to bee stings. Local Reactions Local reactions at the sting site will usually hurt for a few minutes, with milder pain for about one day. The area may be swollen, red, and itchy for two to three days, with the swelling increasing after the first day before it decreases. Taking oral antihistamines, such as Benadryl, and applying ice to the sting site will help reduce swelling. In rare cases, numbness at the sting site can occur, even for an extended period. Be careful about restricting blood flow to the site of the sting; if you are stung on the hand, you may want to remove any rings on your fingers immediately afterward. ☆ Key Points Be careful about restricting blood flow to the site of the sting. Systemic reactions occur within 10 minutes to an hour of being stung and affect the body well beyond the site of the sting. Age is an important factor for bee sting allergies. Systemic Reactions Systemic reactions occur within 10 minutes to an hour after being stung and affect the body well beyond the sting site. A variety of reactions can occur, either on their own or in combination: a large rash, hives, swelling at sites other than the sting site, dizziness, fainting, wheezing, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Anaphylactic shock, or anaphylaxis, is the most severe reaction, where the tongue swells, and the throat begins to close, making breathing difficult and possibly leading to a loss of consciousness and respiratory failure. Call 911 for immediate medical attention if you see or experience any of these reactions. Emergency responders can provide epinephrine (adrenaline) to the patient. At the hospital, other treatments may include steroids to reduce inflammation and inhalers to open the airways. Anaphylaxis is caused by a chemical overreaction in the body’s immune system in response to an allergy. A person typically does not have an allergic reaction the first time they are stung; the first sting stimulates the immune system to produce specific antibodies for an allergen in the venom. After the second sting, these antibodies recognize the venom allergen and bind to it. This, in turn,

stimulates white blood cells to release histamine and other chemicals, which then cause anaphylaxis and associated symptoms, such as swelling and an inability to breathe. Bee sting allergies can be unpredictable. Many people with a history of systemic bee sting reactions do not experience severe reactions the next time they are stung; however, they may again in the future. One important factor is age: bee sting allergies are more common in adults than in children, 1% of children and 3% of adults. Adults over 40 years old are more likely to experience life-threatening reactions and die than children. Bee clubs or universities with apiculture programs generally do not carry epinephrine auto-injectors, such as EpiPens®, or generic alternatives, in case visitors are stung and have a systemic reaction. This is because EpiPens® require individual prescriptions. The wrong dose — e.g., an adult dose for a child — or an unnecessary injection can cause serious harm. As a beekeeper, it's a good idea to talk to your doctor about getting your own EpiPen®. Even if you don't have a history of systemic bee sting reactions, an anaphylactic allergy can develop at any time. It's a good safety measure to keep an EpiPen® on hand when you are beekeeping, for the rare instance you may need it. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Hygienic Management Practices As a Master Beekeeper, you should follow hygienic management practices that reduce the risk of disease transmission and pests in your operation. The social nature of bees usually helps them thrive, but some characteristics of social living may also make them more vulnerable. Bees may drift from one colony to another, or rob honey from a weak colony, putting them at risk of catching whatever illnesses are present in that colony of bees. Robbing or drifting can spread parasites and pathogens, including Varroa mites, viruses, Nosema, and American foulbrood. Spacing apart your colonies and placing them near landmarks so bees can easily identify them will help reduce drifting. If you keep your hives on pallets, having each face a separate direction can help as well. Wash your hands and sterilize your hive tool between bee yards to prevent pathogen transmission. If a colony is visibly infected with disease, clean your hands and hive tool before moving on to the next one. To clean your tool, scrape off propolis and wax, then immerse it in a disinfectant — alcohol, bleach, or a stillburning smoker (be careful not to burn yourself when you take it out!). Colonies infected with American foulbrood require immediate attention, and your first line of defense is preventing the spread of disease. Any hive tools used in infected hives need to be scraped clean and disinfected thoroughly with alcohol or bleach — though these solutions do not kill American foulbrood spores, they can dilute them. These hive tools should then be inserted into a still-hot burning smoker or fired with a blow torch. Keep your bee yards clean. Leaving burr comb, exposed frames, or equipment in the yard can attract other pests and stimulate honey bees to rob. Clean your protective clothing regularly as well by throwing your suits and jackets into the washing machine. Some veils need to be removed from the suit and hand-washed separately. If you are visiting someone else’s bee yard, do not bring your hive tool or other equipment; use theirs instead. The same logic goes for when you have visitors in your yard. If you have staff or helpers in your operation, train them on safety, hygiene, and emergency procedures. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Robbing Robbing is the name for honey bees collecting — or stealing — honey or nectar from another colony instead of from flowers. It most commonly occurs when flowers are not producing much nectar. It is especially pronounced in late summer or early fall when colony populations have grown, and there are lots of foragers out looking for food. The smell of honey, particularly from an open hive, attracts foragers. Weak colonies are a relatively easy target to get some sweet food. Robbers will sneak in the entrance, or fight the guard bees to get in, quickly rip the cappings off the stored honey, slurp up honey, and fly back to their colonies. They will communicate to their sisters the location of the great food source they found, and their sisters will come to check it out themselves. In a short period of time, you can get a lot of robbers from nearby hives targeting the weak colony. Robbing can happen gradually over a few days, or it can escalate within a few minutes or hours to kill an entire weak colony. Watch this video to learn how to identify robbing behavior. Video Transcript When your colonies are getting robbed, this is something that must be dealt with immediately. Because there's negative outcomes for both colonies; the weak colony that's getting robbed, and the stronger colony that's doing the robbing. So the weak colony that's getting robbed is going to lose their food stores, and part if not all of their adult bee population. An extensive robbing can actually wipe out an entire colony altogether. The stronger colony that's doing the robbing is also going to be at risk for developing certain infections. And this is because robbers have to walk across the brood nest in order to get to the honey stores. And when they're walking across a brood nest, they might come in contact with spores, bacteria, mites and other infectious agents that they're bringing back to their own hives. And the reason why this is likely a problem with robbing is because weak colonies might be weak because they have certain parasites and pathogens. So how do you know if a colony is getting robbed? What are the signs and symptoms? Robbing bees actually have a very characteristic behavior to them. There is usually frenzied activity at the front of the entrance, and also the robbers have this kind of exploratory behavior where they're hovering around the entrance, swaying to and fro, looking for a place to enter and sneak past the guards. And they won't just be hovering around the front entrance, but they'll also be hovering around any cracks or any outer cover, anywhere where they're attracted to the smell of honey that's being exuded from the colony and looking for additional entrances to access it. So once a robber lands at the entrance of a hive, ideally, they're going to be detected and attacked by guard bees. So

the guard bees are the ones that are patrolling the front entrance looking to see if the intruders are coming in. And they can tell when a honey bee is not a nest mate because they have unfamiliar odor and usually strong colonies can do The more populated the colony the more guard bees are present and the better protected they are against robbers. But, weak colonies that don't have a very big population also don't have many guards to patrol the entrance. So, when a guard bee detects a robber, they release an alarm pheromone, which stimulates the older forager bees to exit the hive and sting the intruders. And this fighting at the entrance is noticeable. This is a major symptom of hives that are being robbed. You'll see bees grappling and stinging each other. Also within an hour or maybe a few hours, you'll start to see the buildup of wax cappings on the bottom board of the hive and also on the ground in front of the entrance. You'll also start to see dead bees that are accumulating on the ground, the bees that are dying in fight essentially, and also in front of the entrance. Another thing that you might notice on your colonies are dirty light brown footprints. And these are the footprints of the robbers that are landing on the entrance of the hive and also on the front entrance as they're tracking out honey. And these footprints are noticeably different than bee fecal matter, which is more of an orangey or dark brown color, and more in a drip shape than an actual footprint shape. But these footprints are really noticeable. They're more the color of honey because they're literally honey that's being trailed out of the colony. So the reason why robbers are leaving cappings and dirty foot prints behind is because they're in a hurry to escape with their honey. If you go into a colony that has been robbed, you might be able to tell, because you'll notice that the cappings are ripped off of the honeycomb. And you may also notice a reduction in population size from the last time you went and inspected the colony. But it's important to note that not all robbing isn't this frantic, escalating war that ends in colony death. Sometime robbers are just gradually taking honey from another hive and the can go undetected by the bees in that hive and also by the bee keeper. And the way that this works is that the robber bee will sneak past the guards the first couple of times that they go in the hive, they manage to get pass them and the more they're entering the colony, the more they're starting to acquire the colony odors, and the less the guards are detecting them. And over time, they eventually come to smell as nest mates, they're not attacked by the guards at all. And they become these chronic robbers, stealing a little bit of honey here and there. So let's take a look right now at this film clip, where we can see one of my poor colonies that got robbed at the end of summer and start to identify what these symptoms are. Okay, so while we're looking at this hive we see that there's a lot of frenzied activity. And if you're just walking past you might think there's just a strong honey flow going on, there's nothing too serious happening. But, when we look closer we'll start to notice that we are seeing fighting at the entrance. Look closely and you'll see a few groups of bees that are actually grappling. They're biting each other. They're stinging each other. And here we get a closeup where we can really tell. There's a couple bees totally fighting it out right now. And you can even see this yellow jacket who is a little opportunistic

in thinking, there seems to be a lot of distractions going on and this colony is weak. Maybe I can sneak in and steal a little honey for myself. On the front of the hive entrance, here, you'll notice some of the fecal matter that I talked about. You can see the characteristic drip, but I want you to differentiate that from the dirty footprints that you're seeing on the entrance here. This is after a few hours of robbing and actually this colony didn't end up making it. And after a few hours you'll notice there's a pile of dead bees on the ground and these are the bees that essentially died in combat while trying to fight off the robbers. So those are the characteristic symptoms of a colony that's really being robbed extensively. Back to Table of Contents

Read: How to Prevent Robbing Robbing behavior can increase a colony's susceptibility to parasites and diseases. Robbing is a relatively common occurrence during a dearth, but beekeepers should try to minimize their colonies' susceptibility to robbing. Colonies that get robbed are usually weak to start with, with fewer guard bees to defend the entrance than strong colonies. Apiaries with many colonies or where colonies are kept close together are more susceptible to robbing behavior. Robbers can quickly smell honey and access weak colonies more readily than they would in their nests that are spread out in the wild. Keeping the colony population strong and healthy is best achieved by ensuring there is a fertile queen present, providing bees with adequate nutrition, and maintaining low parasite levels. When providing sugar syrup, be mindful of how you are doing so. Having open feeding areas close to hives or Boardman feeders can attract other bees to the colonies being fed and promote robbing behavior. We generally recommend an inside feeder, especially when feeding bees during a dearth. If you prefer open barrel feeding, place your feeding barrels a couple of hundred yards away from your bee yard to divert robbers away from your colonies and to the feeding station instead. If you need to inspect colonies during a dearth to do necessary management, keep your inspections brief. While in the hive, try not to open capped honey with your hive tool or as you pull out a frame. In addition to the risks to the colony, bees that have experienced robbing can be more aggressive in the following days or weeks. Reducing the potential for robbing will help keep both your bees and you safer. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: How to Stop Robbing What if, despite your efforts, some of your colonies end up getting robbed? It is important to act fast. If the robbed colony is quite weak or if you don’t intervene within a few hours, it can die in as little as one day because of the loss of life to fighting. Colonies that have survived being robbed are more likely to be defensive in the following weeks. Use caution when opening up these hives. Watch this video to learn what measures you can take to stop robbing once it has started. Video Transcript So how do we go about stopping robbing? What do we do if we are witnessing these symptoms in our own colonies? There's a few things that we can do. So to deal with robbing the main thing that we want to do right away is to reduce the entrance to the colony to the size of one or two bee bodies. So this is about half an inch in width. And the idea is that this opening is big enough for the colony's foragers to be able to enter and exit. But small enough so that the guards can easily defend it. And using a wooden entrance reducer is fine but ideally it would best if you could use a mesh screen. So if you could staple a mesh screen across the front entrance leaving just this tiny opening in the middle for the guards to defend, this is still going to allow ventilation to happen through the hive. And, also, it's not directing robbers directly to that small entrance where they're able to smell the honey odors. Instead, they can smell the honey odors throughout the entire entrance and they are more distracted. And this gives the opportunity for the foragers to be able to enter and exit out of that small hole that they can easily learn. Alternatively you can purchase a robbing screen from your local bee supply company to use, and these screens can be left in place for the entire period of a nectar dearth to prevent robbing and they have a similar idea. They distract the robbers from finding the true entrance to the colony. It might also be beneficial to place a wet sheet over the colony, something like a bed sheet, and to do this for one to two days. And you want to completely cover the entrance and drape the sheet all the way down to the ground. So here, the resident bees are still able to find their way underneath the sheet back into the colony, but the robbers are directed away from the colony entrance, and they're directed away from any cracks that may be exuding honey odors in hopes that in a day or two they'll move onto another food source. The main consideration with this is that having a bed sheet over the hive can put the colony at risk for overheating. So we recommend that you use a light colored sheet instead of a dark sheet and that you re-wet the sheet if it dries out so the colony doesn't get too hot. And don't leave the sheet on for more than a day or two. And finally, if these two measures using an entrance reducer and using a sheet don't stop the robbing behavior, then you might just want to move the hive entirely to a new location, away from the apiary at least two miles away if you can, and if you have the land to do so. And this is

something that you might want to consider from the get go if you already know that the colony is weak and will most likely die from being robbed. Sometimes, having the entrance reducer and the wet sheet just still proves futile and moving the colon is the only way to save it. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Minimizing Competition Between Your Hives and Native Bee Species The Western honey bee (Apis mellifera) was introduced to North America in the 1600s, and it is now considered livestock, like cows and sheep. In contrast, native bees are wildlife. There are ~4,000 described bee species in the USA, and ~450 bee species in New York State alone. When you place managed honey bees in a landscape, you’re adding a large, social, efficient, high-density foraging organism into the environment that includes thousands of foragers per colony. What are the impacts on the native bee fauna? Several studies in the last 10 years, conducted in the USA, have looked at the possible competition between managed and native bees for flower resources (nectar/pollen). While some studies found evidence of such competition, others did not. Another impact explored focused on disease spillover, the sharing of honey bee pathogens/parasites with native bees. While many native bees were shown to acquire honey bee pathogens when visiting flowers previously visited by honey bees, there is no conclusive evidence that those pathogens/parasites are detrimental to those native bees. Even though no clear detrimental impact has been reported from having hives next to native bee populations, most experts agree that these effects are difficult to study and document; thus, the possibility of negative interactions between managed honey bees and native bees remains a concern. Here are practical actions to reduce competition for flower resources and disease spillover. 1. Place your apiaries in agricultural or human-dominated landscapes such as orchards, mixed farmland, suburban gardens, and roadside plantings. 2. Provide or enhance forage by planting high-nectar, high-pollen patches near the apiary to absorb some foraging pressure. You could also include native wildflowers, so native bees also benefit. 3. Reduce the likelihood of disease spillover by maintaining strong colony health because healthy bees shed fewer pathogens. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Inspecting the Colony Colony inspections are key to managing healthy colonies. Regularly monitoring colonies gives you information about their population dynamics, the condition of the queen, whether and when to treat for pests and diseases, and when to add supers for honey production. In this module, you will learn how to perform a colony inspection with all this information and more. Back to Table of Contents

▶ Read: Preparing to Inspect Your Hives Your motivations for keeping bees will directly impact how often you inspect your colony. If you are interested in learning about and observing bees, you may want to inspect more often, but remember that frequent disturbance to the colony may unnecessarily disturb the bees or set back their productivity. We recommend inspecting your colonies and recording your observations and management activities every 10 days to two weeks in the spring and summer, less in the fall and winter. This cycle of inspection can allow you to spot and remove swarm cells and identify any disease issues in an early state. This inspection frequency allows you to monitor population dynamics, including swarming; identify disease or pest issues in an early state; evaluate your colonies’ nutrition; and more. This schedule is more frequent than in the past because honey bees face more intense parasites and other pressures today. If you have too many colonies to inspect that often (over 50 or so), aim to inspect a representation of the colonies in each yard every time to get a snapshot of your operation. For instance, if you run 1,000 colonies, aim to inspect 100 colonies (10%), randomly selected. In this case, make sure to at least inspect the entrances of all the hives in the yard to see if anything is obviously wrong that requires further investigation. Have an objective For each inspection, you should have a clear objective before you open your hives: Are you monitoring for diseases? Checking whether you should add supers? Evaluating the colony's nutrition? Having a specific purpose will help you plan which equipment to bring, prepare you for how long you will need to keep the hive open, and help you stay on top of your management tasks. Stock your toolkit Keep a stocked toolkit so that you are prepared anytime you see something unfamiliar, unusual, or worth documenting. Some items worth keeping in your toolkit — beyond your smoker, fuel, matches/lighter, hive tool, and protective gear — are the following: Notebook or record-keeping binder Pen or pencil Queen cage and marking pen ▶

▶ Disease ID handbook, such as Penn State’s Field Guide to Honey Bees and their Maladies Disease sampling equipment: quart-sized ziplock bags, Sharpie® marker, toothpicks, a bottle of rubbing alcohol, at least 70% Vita® American foulbrood or European foulbrood test kits Camera or a camera phone to record interesting things There are many other useful tools you can implement in your inspections that you may decide to use throughout your beekeeping endeavors. Beekeeping catalogs are full of products that promise to make inspections easier: by easing the weight of heavy supers, holding frames, etc. Some are very useful; some aren’t. Ask around before purchasing anything expensive or that you haven’t used yet. Check the weather Before going into the apiary, check the weather to make sure it is conducive to working bees. Consider checking several days in advance so you don’t miss a crucial weather window to get something done in the hive. By now, you should be familiar with the best weather conditions to inspect a colony: sunny skies, little wind, and temperatures above 59°F (15°C). Opening the colony in cooler temperatures can chill the brood. In cloudy weather, more foragers stay inside the hive since they are unable to use the sun to orient themselves while flying. Foraging bees are more likely to sting than their nurse bee sisters. You’ll likely notice their increased defensiveness when inspecting your colonies while more of them are home. Read: What to Look For When Inspecting A colony inspection should be a quick procedure, taking about five to ten minutes. Click on the tabs to get an overview of the factors to consider in assessing the health and productivity of the colony. Population Management 1. Population: How many adult bees are in the colony? Is the number appropriate for the season? 2. Queen status: Is the queen laying worker eggs? Is there evidence that the bees are intending to supersede her or swarm? Is there evidence of laying workers? 3. Brood quality and quantity: Is the brood solid or spotty? Is it sufficiently abundant for the time of year? Is brood of all ages present — eggs, larvae, and capped brood? 4. Population dynamics: If you compare the apparent brood rearing activity with the natural attrition rates of foragers at this time of year, does the population seem to be increasing or decreasing? 5. Drone population: Is drone production seasonally appropriate? Are there a disproportionate number of drones? Nutrition 1. Floral sources: What flowers are blooming in your area at the moment, and what pollen sources are your bees bringing in? Are there environmental conditions that may be impacting the bees’ nutrition, e.g., prolonged bad weather or a drought? 2. Foraging behavior: Are there sufficient numbers of bees foraging? Seeing 10 to 20 bees entering with full pollen baskets per minute is an indication that lots of resources are coming into the colony. Are bees bringing in pollen or propolis in their pollen baskets or nectar/water in their honey stomachs? 3. Food stores in the colony: How much pollen/bee bread and nectar/honey is stored? Is this amount appropriate for the season? 4. Larval nutrition: Are the young larvae floating in abundant pools of royal jelly? Pests, Parasites, and Diseases

1. Do you see any symptoms of brood disease in the colony? Not all problems will be visible, but brood that is discolored, twisted, melted-looking, partially cannibalized, or has punctured cappings may indicate a problem. 2. Do you see any adult bees with deformities or behavioral abnormalities? Do you see any Varroa mites or pests such as hive beetles, wax moths, or the larvae of beetles and moths? It is important to note that for Varroa, without sampling procedures that follow specific protocols, such observations alone do not necessarily provide a full picture of the mite pressure within a colony. 3. Do you see other pests — or evidence of such pests — present in the honey supers or other areas of the hive? 4. Are the bees acting more defensively than usual? Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Walk Through a Hive Inspection To illustrate a colony inspection, the well-known California beekeeper and bee researcher Randy Oliver from ScientificBeekeeping.com will take us through the steps. He will start by inspecting the outside of the hive and then pull out a few frames from each box to get an idea of the status of the general categories we outlined. We recommend pulling two to three frames from each honey super and at least four frames from each brood box to gauge the health and productivity of the hive. For a quick inspection, start with the highest box and work your way down. Starting at the top, quickly checking some of the frames, then working your way downward, helps reduce aggression because you are not opening and moving all the boxes from the start. Working this way can help minimize overall disturbance to the colony and the number of bees flying about. While you are working through the hive, you will inevitably squish some bees. Try to squish as few as possible, and always try to be mindful of the queen's presence to avoid accidentally hurting her. Move slowly and quietly to reduce defensiveness, as bees can react to quick, jerky movements. Watch this video to see Randy Oliver conduct a colony inspection. ▶ Read: Outside the Hive Before even opening the hive, you can learn a lot from observing the exterior of the hive and the activity of bees at the entrance. Predator Evidence — Skunks, Bears, Raccoons Skunks have been scratching the ground in front of this hive. Check the outside of the hive for damage or signs of predators. Skunks often scratch the ground in front of a hive or at the entrance to lure out curious bees. Bees that come to check out the sound get eaten. In this way, skunks can hasten the depopulation of weak colonies. If you see scratch marks on the ground or your hives, elevate your hive on a stand so the skunks can no longer reach the entrance. You can also put small mammal fencing around your apiary to keep them out. Bear damage is much more obvious: knocked-over hives and ripped-up supers. In their search for brood and honey, they can kill colonies entirely. If there are bears in your area, you will probably need to install an electric fence around your apiary.

Photo Credit: Jon Ryan Another often overlooked predator is the raccoon. Raccoons are very intelligent animals that, like skunks, eat bees at the entrance of the hive. However, they go one step beyond skunks and remove the covers from hives and pull out frames. They can eat everything on the frames, right down to the foundation, and leave the frames strewn about in the bee yard. Unlike bears, however, they do not shatter boxes or frames. Raccoons will keep coming back night after night unless you install an electric fence that is low enough to the ground that they can't crawl underneath it. Photo credit: Kimberly Carpenter Fecal Matter Look at the exterior of the hive for bee fecal matter. Bees defecate outside the colony to maintain a clean home and reduce the spread of infection to their nestmates. A little bit of fecal matter on the outside of the hive is normal; in fact, some fecal matter visible on snow in winter is a good sign, since it means that the bees found a mild day to ▶

▶ defecate outside after a long period of confinement. But excessive drips of orange or brown stains on the front of a hive are a signal that something is wrong. Guard Bees The last thing to look for before you open the colony is guard bees. They stand at the entrance, often holding their front legs up. They check out bees entering the hive — and may even be checking you out. Wave your hand slowly in front of the entrance. If a guard bee follows your hand, she is watching you. You’ll need to use smoke to break her attention. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: What Can We Learn From Bees at the Entrance? Observing bees at the hive entrance can give us several indicators of the colony's health. There’s so much information you can get from just looking at the outside of the colony! Now, when you open the colony, you are better prepared for what you might find. Video Transcript So we're still standing at the outside of the hive, but after we've checked the exterior of the hive to look for any evidence of predator damage or fecal matter, now let's turn our attention to the bees. So let's focus on the bees that are flying around the hive. Are they gentle, are they unusually aggressive, what is their temperament like? If they are more aggressive than normal, then it can be a sign that did experience some predator attack or something like extreme heat in the summer might be bothering them. And if the hive is unusually aggressive, it's up to the bee keeper to figure out what the cause is and determine the stressor that's causing this behavior. So keep that in mind as you're inspecting your colony. Now let's look at any indication of adult bees that are found on the ground, or at the entrance of a hive. Are you noticing dead bees? Are you noticing just a few dead bees or is there a big pile of dead bees? Do you see any bees that have deformed wings, or any other deformities? Are there bees that are slowly crawling or twitching? A few dead bees are a normal sight to see but piles of them can be a sign of either intense robbing or a pesticide poisoning event. It's important as a master bee keeper to learn that there are normal seasonal fluctuations for dead bees. Bees are naturally dying over winter and early spring and their sisters are cleaning out their dead bodies on warmer days whenever they get the occasion to. You may even expect to see a few dead bees scattered in the snow, which is a sign that they were performing their cleansing flights, but it may have been too cold for them to make it back to the hive. Bees that are twitching or extending their proboscises, clumped in a big pile, or scattered across the ground near the hive, in the times of year that I just described, are indicative of a pesticide poisoning event. If you're witnessing this, take photos or videos and report it as soon as you can. It's even helpful to take a sample of these bees and put it in a ziplock bag, or a jar and freeze it.
