So, they could be pointing their abdomens downward, flapping their wings to circulate air and increase ventilation in the hive, that's what fanning looks like. And on hot summer days you can actually help the bees by providing them with a good source of water and improving their ventilation. So you can increase ventilation by giving them a screen bottom board or drilling in an upper entrance in the top hive body or even by propping open the outer cover above the inner cover with a stick or a shim just to try and release some of that hot air and moisture out of the hive, much like the way that hot air is released out of the chimney in a house. Another behavior that you might witness and that I actually got a lot of questions about is wash boarding behavior, and this is where bees are taking one step forward and one step backward repetitively and they're licking the surface beneath them. And they do this behaviour for hours without stopping. And bees will washboard at any time during the day, they'll do it past dark, they'll do it when it's hot out, they'll do it all the time. And it's actually a common behaviour, and it doesn't signal that anything is wrong. But we don't fully understand why bees perform washboard behaviour. We think that it may help smooth the entrance of the hive. Or it could just be a sign they're performing general maintenance activities, because bees who are washboarding also tend to engage in other nest maintenance activities such as building comb. And the last thing that you might see with activity on the outside of the hive is bearding. And bees may hear on the outside of the hive for two different reasons; either they're too hot or the hive is too crowded. So they can beard, just like wash boarding, at any time of the day or even after dark.

And on really hot summer evenings, you'll see bearding after dark because all the foragers are home, but it's really hot and it's not sunny, so they can't go out and collect water to cool off. And bearding isn't a behavior to be too concerned about if it is hot outside, it's a natural thing that they do. But the bees will be gentlest if they're not hot and bothered, so you might want to manage your colonies to help the bees regulate the hive temperature, or provide them with adequate space if they need it. So for temperature regulation you can do the same things to improve ventilation I mentioned before, giving them a screen bottom board, an upper entrance or improving heat release from the top of the hive by propping up the outer cover and by giving them some water. Now colonies that beard may also do so because they're really crowded. So either they're out of space to grow, or just out of space to distribute themselves to help keep the brood cool on hot days. So to increase the space for a bustling population, you can either add honey supers or you can expand your brood nest to two boxes if it's currently one. It's important first to do a colony inspection and look for swarm cells that may have started getting constructed before you add a super. If they are confined and there's no more space for them to grow, then they could have started thinking about swarming and building these swarm cells. So you don't want to get to the point where you're giving them more space just to find a few days later that a lot of the bees leave in a swarm. So make sure that you check and rule out the fact that they're swarming before you give them additional space. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Inspecting During Less-Than-Perfect Conditions You might not always be able to inspect, ☆ Key Points manage, or treat your colonies on beautifully sunny days; however, if something needs to be done to keep a colony alive (for example, feeding during cold weather), then you should do it — just be quick. If you need to open the hives when the bees are stressed or when their behavior has higher stakes — e.g., when you are demonstrating a hive inspection to visitors — the usual precautions apply, but even more so. Extra smoke will help calm the bees, especially If you need to open the hives in less-than-perfect conditions, the usual precautions apply, but even more so. Different amounts of smoke are required depending on your goals, the bees’ disposition, and the amount of time you plan to spend with the hive open. if you smoke for a few minutes before opening the hive. You might apply a few puffs of smoke to the entrance and under the outer cover quickly, wait a minute, and then open the hive. In the same way, you might puff smoke During a nectar dearth, only inspect your colonies when you absolutely must, and do it as quickly and efficiently as possible. between hive bodies before lifting off the topmost one. Depending on your goals, the bees’ disposition, and the amount of time you plan to spend with the hive open, different amounts of smoke are necessary. Inspecting During a Nectar Dearth

If your area is experiencing a mid-summer nectar dearth, robbing may start during an inspection. In severe instances, robber bees try to enter your colony as soon as you stick your hive tool in to separate the boxes! Only inspect your colonies when you absolutely must, and do it as quickly and efficiently as possible. Do not smoke the entrance before opening the colony, as you want the guard bees present to fend off intruders. Stack the boxes squarely as you remove them so there aren’t any open cracks for robbers to enter, and keep an extra outer cover or sheet on top of them until you are finished. The goal is to limit the areas robbers can access a hive. If severe robbing starts, close the hive and try again another day. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Inspecting Honey Supers The reason to inspect honey supers is to make sure that bees are filling them and that you are adding them at the right pace throughout the season (not so slowly that the bees run out of room to store honey, and not so quickly that the bees cannot defend the far corners of their hive). If honey production is your goal, add supers as needed during a nectar flow to maximize the nectar your bees take in and allow you to separate different honey varietals. ☆ Key Points Inspect honey supers to ensure bees are filling them and that you are adding them at the right pace throughout the season. Assess honey supers for signs of pests and moisture issues. Become familiar with the nectar flows in your region. Lift off the outer and inner cover and peer into the honey supers. If you see bees poking their heads between frames, watching you, give them some smoke to divert and disorient them so they won’t be defensive. Adding Honey Supers Pull out a few frames from your honey supers to see how they are being filled. If most of the comb has been drawn, bees are working on the comb, and the frames are being filled, there is probably a nectar flow on, and you’ll need to add another super soon. Seeing fresh lightcolored wax on the top bars of the frames is also indicative of a nectar flow. Some beekeepers remove and extract supers throughout the season; others continue adding supers and extract only once or twice a year. This choice depends on how much time and hive equipment you have. If supering during a nectar flow, we typically recommend placing a new super underneath the top super to draw the bees into it, a practice called bottom supering. If you add a super on top of one that is already full, the bees may not use it as readily. If you don’t use a queen excluder, it's a good idea to leave one super full of capped honey between the brood nest and the next super you are adding. The super of capped honey can act as a barrier to dissuade the queen from moving up into the supers. Instead of adding a super of drawn comb or foundation below a honey-filled super, some beekeepers choose to checkboard their supers instead. With this practice, honey frames from the full super and foundation or drawn comb from the empty super are rearranged so

that they create an alternating pattern in both supers. The bottom super contains frames in this pattern: honey, foundation, honey, foundation, etc., while the top super contains frames in this pattern: foundation, honey, foundation, honey, etc. Checkerboarding supers is done to encourage bees to draw out frames of foundation. It also helps prolong or prevent swarming if done before the brood nest begins to be backfilled with honey. It does so by interrupting the full super's solid band of honey above the brood nest, freeing up more storage space for honey above and for brood below. Fresh white wax on the top bars of the frames indicates nectar flow. Supering usually begins here in the Northeast around mid-May. Once a super is half full of nectar, you can add one to the colony. Don't wait until all the honey in the super is fully capped before adding another one. If a super is three-quarters full or nearly full with nectar, some beekeepers may add an additional two or even three supers to their colonies during a strong nectar flow to minimize the number of trips they need to take to the bee yard. We would suggest adding multiple supers only if you have a large bee population that can defend that much space. If you add a honey super that only contains frames of foundation and no drawn comb, don’t immediately separate it from the rest of the hive with a queen excluder. You can add an excluder later, once the bees have drawn out comb on some of the frames. The reason for doing this is that bees can sometimes be reluctant to build comb in a new super with undrawn foundation if the excluder is put on at the same time. But if the excluder is left off initially, the bees readily draw out the foundation when there is a honey flow, and since they have begun working on it, they will continue building and using that super once you put the excluder on. Otherwise, the beekeeper who adds both the excluder and undrawn foundation super on at the same time may come back to find the super empty, the brood boxes completely full of honey, and the colony ready to swarm or has already swarmed. If the colony has a vigorous young queen, the super may end up with a few eggs, but usually it

doesn’t. Just make sure to check that your queen isn't in the super before adding the excluder! Looking For Signs of Pests You may see pests or their signs in the honey supers since they congregate where there are fewer bees. Pests in the honey supers are not usually an issue during the active season, particularly if the bee populations are strong enough to defend the space, and if colonies are not weak from other issues. In great numbers, however, small hive beetle larvae can cause the honey to ferment and look slimy in appearance.

Wax moth on a honey frame Assessing Moisture Look at the inside of the inner and outer covers, the hive walls, and the tops of the frames. Do you see any moisture problems? Moisture promotes the growth of mold, which can appear as black, blue, or gray streaks or spots in the woodenware or on the honey cappings. If any of the wood has condensation or looks moldy, improve ventilation at the top (either by creating an upper entrance or propping up the outer cover with a shim), tip the hive slightly downward to allow water to flow out the entrance of the hive, and make sure your covers are free of holes or cracks. Replace any moldy frames. If the moisture problem persists, consider relocating your hives to a new location with dry ground and ample sunlight. Hives sitting in standing water or soggy ground are more likely to experience moisture problems, as are hives with tall grass or weeds at the entrance. Another moisture issue specific to honey is fermentation. Normally, after bees collect nectar, they evaporate the water until the moisture content is below 18%, before capping it. But in very humid climates or during heavy nectar flows, bees may cap honey before the moisture level is low enough. In this case, the natural yeast population of the honey rises and ferments the honey (converting the sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide). Fermented honey looks bubbly or foamy, due to the carbon dioxide, and often smells yeasty. You can remove the affected frames and rinse out the fermented honey with water. The combs are fine to reuse after they are dry. Understanding Nectar Flows It’s important to familiarize yourself with the nectar flows in your region. Depending on the nectar flows in your area, you will see variations in the color of the honey, from water white to chocolatey brown. There will also be variations in smell, taste, and texture. If there is a strong nectar flow from one source in your area (which changes from year to year), most of the honey in a given super will likely come from that source, and you may be able to market it as monofloral honey, such as basswood, clover, Japanese knotweed, or goldenrod honey. Keeping track of the starting and ending points of major honey flows in your area over the years will help you plan for supering and extraction.

You may also notice variations in honey cappings. Sometimes bees will leave air between the honey and the wax capping, giving the wax a convex, white appearance. Other times, the cappings lay flat against the honey and appear darker. No one knows the reason behind the difference, although there appear to be genetic predispositions; it does not affect the quality or taste of the honey. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Starting Your Inspection of the Brood Nest During your inspections, you should carefully inspect at least four frames from each brood box. It is important to base your understanding of the quality and health of the queen on multiple frames, as early stages of a disease might only affect a few cells that can be easily missed by only inspecting one frame — but this aim for thoroughness should always be balanced by the imperative not to disturb your colony for too long, for their sake and yours! Throughout this course, we will refer to the following numerical positions of specific frames in a hive. ⌃ Long description There are ten frames in the hive. The frames in the hive are numbered one through ten, with one being the first frame on the left, and ten being the last frame on the right. Start your inspection by removing one frame first and setting it aside to make room to manipulate the others. We usually try to remove the #2 frame first so that we remember its position later when we are ready to close up the colony, but you can choose to remove whatever frame is most

convenient for you. We recommend against removing the #1 frame first, as this can roll any bees, including the queen, between the hive wall and the first frame, possibly damaging them. Carefully set aside the first frame you've removed to make space and reduce the risk of crushing bees as you inspect a few other frames. Aim to only keep two frames out of the hive at all times — the first one you set aside and the one you are looking at. This helps you keep all frames in the right orientation and reduces the risk of squishing bees. Also, try to inspect your frames while holding them above the brood nest. If the queen falls off a frame, she will likely fall back into the hive instead of on the ground. Back to Table of Contents

▶ Read: What to Look For When Inspecting the Brood Nest Click the accordions to explore what to look for as you are examining the brood frames. Adult Bees First, look at the adult bees on the frames. Is the population strong? If there are sufficient numbers of bees to nearly cover both sides of each frame in the brood nest, the colony has a strong population. In contrast, if there are not enough bees to cover the brood, it may signal a problem and cause other issues. For instance, the brood is at risk of being chilled in a colony with a low population. Next, look for indications of diseases on the adult bees, such as hairlessness, greasiness, deformed wings, or twitching movements. Estimate the proportion of drones in the adult population: too many may indicate you have a drone-laying queen or laying workers. During peak drone production in late spring and early summer, about 5% of the adult population in a hive will be drones. As you inspect the frames, scan for the queen to see if she has a retinue of bees responding to her pheromones. Work to make sure she doesn’t get harmed during the inspection. If you plan on pulling more frames or doing anything that might stress or harm her (e.g., sampling bees for mites), you can ensure her safety by gently caging her and placing her in a shady spot while you work, and reintroducing her to the top brood chamber at the end of the inspection. If you cage her, be careful not to forget about her!

▶ Brood Health If you have a strong population with many adults covering the frames, it may be difficult to assess the brood pattern beneath the bees. In these cases, you can gently blow on them or place your hand over them so that they move out of the way, or shake the bees off into the hive body you are working in. When inspecting brood frames, hold the frame with the sun at your back and angle it so the sun shines directly into the cells. A healthy brood frame has a solid pattern of brood (with few open cells), with arcs of pollen and then honey surrounding the brood. The frame will resemble a rainbow, with brood in the center, pollen arcing around it, and honey as the topmost layer. Some empty cells are normal: 6% to 17% of larvae are generally removed in a healthy colony (those that inherit identical same sex determination gene versions), but a higher percentage than that can indicate that the queen is poorly mated, inbred, or failing from age, or that the brood may be diseased or afflicted by parasites. Diseased brood can take on a variety of symptoms depending on the parasite or pathogen in question. Instead of pearly white larvae, diseased larvae may be coffeecolored, brown, gray, black, or appear chalk-like. Their position may also change from being curled up nicely in their cells to being twisted, pointy, melted, or mummified. Infected pupae show other symptoms: perforated or concave pupal cappings are indicative of diseases, as are pupae that have been uncapped and chewed down by nurse bees. Lastly, bees that die upon emergence with their proboscises extended are indicative of some diseases and pesticide poisonings. Always be on the lookout for any signs of brood disease, even if symptoms are seen in only one cell. Take photographs and notes of any issues. If the disease is unfamiliar to you or resembles American Foulbrood, send samples for free analysis to the Beltsville Bee Lab in Maryland, and label the affected colony so you can identify it later. Lastly, check for deposits in empty cells in the brood frame. Take note of any black scale that does not scrape off with a toothpick (indicative of American Foulbrood) or small patches of white crystals on the ceilings of brood cells called guanine; these crystals are indicative of high Varroa mite levels.

▶ Brood Pattern and Sex The queen's pattern of laying is important. A healthy hive has brood of all ages: eggs, larvae, and capped pupae. A good fertile queen will usually begin laying eggs near the center of the frame, and work her way outward in concentric circles. The result is brood aging in a “step down” pattern: larvae the same age sit next to each other, and moving outward from the center, the larvae are one day younger, then two days younger, and so on. As the fully developed bees emerge, the queen should fill those newly open cells with eggs. If you cannot find any eggs after a thorough inspection, you should take measures to replace the queen or introduce a frame with eggs on it so the bees can rear their own queen. The sex of the brood is important. The colony starts investing in drone production once its population reaches around 4,000 individuals. For colonies of this size or bigger, drones are most plentiful during swarm season, when males are needed to mate with the newly emerging queens. Here in the Northeast, swarm season peaks from about mid-May to mid-July. Drone production ceases toward the end of summer as the colony begins to invest most of its energy into preparing for winter by building up its honey stores. On average, about 17% to 20% of comb in a colony is drone comb (about two full frames' worth in a 10-frame hive body). This is the “natural” average in wild colonies and in foundationless hives, but beekeepers will likely find less drone comb in their hives if they are using frames of worker cell foundation. Drone comb will usually be built along the bottom or sides of the frames, not usually in the center of the brood nest. Drone comb can also be found in the burr comb on the tops of the frames or in other areas. If you see a high number of capped drone cells late in the summer (representing well over 5% of the drone population) or in colonies with weak

▶ populations, those colonies may have a drone-laying queen. A drone-laying queen will still lay only one egg per cell, while laying workers will lay multiple eggs in the cells. This brood pattern is not great. There are many empty cells, and larvae of different ages are next to each other. Queen Cups and Queen Cells Examine the frames for queen cups and cells. Queen cups are, by definition, small wax cups that are empty. It is normal to find a few of these throughout the year, as the colony keeps them on hand in case it needs to raise a new queen or swarm. a couple queen cups do not signal any impending changes in the colony. This is true even if you find them in different places in the nest, as they may be torn down and rebuilt several times throughout a season. However, colonies will ramp up the production of queen cups in preparation of swarming. In this case, you can see many queen cups, usually close to a dozen, usually located along the lower edge of the brood nest. If you see an egg or larva in the cup, it is now a queen cell, indicating that the bees are seeking to raise a new queen. The placement of the cell can indicate why. Generally, many queen cells along the bottom of a frame signal that the colony is preparing to swarm, and are known as swarm cells. In contrast, a few queen cells near the center of the frame are usually either queen supersedure cells or emergency queen cells. These can be used to replace an existing queen that may be failing, or to make up for the loss of a queen. The presence of queen supersedure cells is usually a sign that there is an issue with the queen and the workers are naturally replacing her.

▶ A swarm cell placed near the bottom of the brood nest. Brood Nutrition Take note of the brood nutrition. One to two frames’ worth of pollen/bee bread in each brood box is ideal for brood rearing. However, some colonies may not always have that much on hand because they are using it up relatively quickly after they collect it. Observe the diversity of pollen in the colony. Does it appear that bees are foraging on pollen from a single source, or are there multiple sources of pollen (evident by various colors) present in the hive? Document any observations of entombed pollen, where bees cover a cell containing pollen with propolis and wax. Entombed pollen has been found to contain high levels of certain pesticides. Besides looking at bee bread, you can get a good idea of a colony’s nutritional levels based on the amount of royal jelly surrounding young larvae. Abundant white pools of royal jelly signal that there is a lot of protein available for nurses to synthesize into royal jelly, whereas colonies with little or no jelly visible around the larvae may benefit from receiving a protein supplement.

▶ A young larva with a good-sized pool of royal jelly. Pollen is present in the cell beside it. Condition of the Frames Lastly, examine the condition of the comb. Is the comb old and/or dark? An old comb can harbor old pupal cocoons, disease spores, and pesticides, with the latter two posing a risk to colony health. Each year, aim to replace your two oldest frames in each hive body to keep your hives in optimum health. However, do not remove more than four frames from a hive at once, as the Bee Informed Partnership found this can have negative effects on the colony's population. Removing more than four frames from a hive at once will divert the bees’ resources to building comb rather than raising brood or producing honey. There is a tradeoff between reducing the risks to the hive by discarding old, possibly contaminated, comb and requiring the bees to expend more of their energy.

This brood frame is five years old and should soon be replaced with a newer frame. To make all the cells visible so you can identify potential diseases or issues, or to make later inspections easier, you may want to remove any burr comb (comb anywhere other than on the faces of the frames) from the bottom of frames or the sides of the hive as you go, placing any scrapings into a bucket to take with you. Leaving comb in the bee yard attracts other bees and pests. Keep the frames in each hive body tightly squeezed together or spaced in accordance with bee space to prevent the bees from building more burr comb. Once the Colony Inspection Is Complete As you finish inspecting frames, place them back in the boxes in the same orientation and order that they were in to ensure that the brood nest is intact — again, this is easily accomplished if you only take one to two frames out at a time. The inspection is complete when you have accomplished everything you set out to do. After the inspection, consider what sort of management the colony needs: do the bees need more room to store honey, or do you need to take steps to prevent or manage swarming? Take note of when you need to return to your colonies for the next routine inspection or to follow up on anything you saw or did today. Back to Table of Contents

Tool: Beekeeping Calendar Timing is critical for good hive management. By  Download the Tool now, you should have some familiarity with the seasonal cycles of a honey bee colony. You have seen the exciting activity in spring and summer, as well as the quiet periods of overwintering. Use this Sample Beekeeping Calendar to help track hive conditions throughout the year. Beyond that, knowing bee biology, predicting cycles of pests and diseases, monitoring the succession of flowering forage, and staying attuned to other seasonal changes helps beekeepers to keep their hives alive and healthy. These biological and phenological observations tell beekeepers when they need to supplement a dearth of good forage, help the bees take advantage of a good honey flow, or ensure that a hive is prepared for winter. Developing this environmental awareness is also one of the great pleasures of keeping bees. Here we present a sample beekeeping calendar that describes the goings-on in a hive and environmental conditions more broadly during different months of the year, and the associated management practices that support colony health and productivity throughout the year. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: A Year in the Bee Yard Timing, location, and local conditions make all the difference between a successful honey harvest and a disappointing season. Watch this video to learn more about the beekeeping calendar and why it matters. Video Transcript Our calendar has a focus on the northeast, in part because that's where we are here in Dyce Lab, Ithaca New York, And you have to pick somewhere. But every area is a little different. It’s wellknown saying that all bee keeping is local, that's what keeps it interesting, keeps it fun from year to year. The calendar is also geared toward small scale honey production. That's not what all beekeeping is anymore and especially not for a master beekeeper. And so we have included information about producing nucs, rearing queens, providing pollination services. But those are more specialized and you'll want to create your own calendars according to your own schedule and your own business goals for that. Here in the northeast the active season is short but it tends to be more predictable than other areas. For example, the orange blossom honey flow in Florida can vary by as much as two months but here in New York State the blooming of the American basswood trees, the linden, doesn't usually vary by more than a week or two around July 4th. But the northeast is a big area with lots of variation. They include the US hardiness zones, the regional hardiness zones from all the way from the 3 to 7. And things continue to change. Climate change means that there are new crops here and new flowering dates. The apple bloom here in New York is about two weeks earlier than it was a hundred years ago. And even the nutritional value of some plants is changing because of climate change. One study found that goldenrod has less protein when there's a higher concentration of carbon dioxide in the air. And so, the flowering plants that we have listed, are the ones that are most abundant here in the Northeast, not necessarily the most nutritious. For example, dandelion is an incomplete protein source that's missing some amino acids that are key for your bees. But, because of when it blooms, and relative to other plants, it's pretty likely to be foraged by your bees at that time of year. So as you embark on your beekeeping, pay attention to what's in bloom. That includes more unusual stuff, like a late flowering broccoli in your garden. I've got hives at a friend's place with broccoli that goes all the way until October or November. And witch hazel, on the other end of the calendar, as early as February or March. You'll want to keep records of blooms and other seasonal changes. And because that season, our season is short, the weather conditions actually play an outsized role for honey production. Because if the weather, say is bad and keeps the bees in the hive for all around July 4th, they're going to miss that basswood flow even if it was abundant. So your record will be a great source of information for your calendar in years to come.

Watch: Colony Assessments At different points during the season, you may want to conduct a colony assessment, which is more detailed than an inspection. An assessment helps you to quantify the growth and productivity of the colony by pulling out every frame to estimate and log the following: 1. Number of frames of adult bees. 2. Number of frames of brood and proportion of eggs, larvae, and capped brood. 3. Number of frames of honey. 4. Number of frames of pollen. 5. Number of frames of drawn comb and foundation. Watch this video to learn more about the process of conducting colony assessments and the circumstances where it could be beneficial to you and your bees. Video Transcript Assessments have several uses for experienced beekeepers. And I find that as I'm getting to know my bees more and get more confident in my colonies I'm starting to ask more questions, and want to do more testing with my bees to find the answers to those questions that I have. So with assessments you can actually quantify how productive your colonies are. You're quantifying the number of frames of bees, the amount of pollen you have in your hive, the amount of brood that you have, or the amount of honey that you have. And so, you can sort of engage in a small research project with your colony to figure out some of these questions. So, for instance, you might want to know if a new pollen substitute on the market is worth trying, and if it's actually going to help build your brood production or build your adult population. And for this you can feed some of your colonies as pollen substitute and leave some of your others colonies without it which will be your control group and after a certain amount of time, you can assess the amount of pollen and the amount of, sorry, the amount of bee bread that they would be converting it into. The amount of brood and also the amount of adults in your colony to see whether or not it's worth spending the money to invest in this pollen substitute. You might also wonder whether or not the crops that your bees are pollinating with pollination services. if it's negatively affecting brood production. And you can get to learn which crops are more healthy for your bees and which ones might not be and may need some additional management to make sure that they remain healthy when they're in those landscapes. So for instance you can be measuring the amount of brood that's produced before they go into this crop and afterward to get an idea of how that's being quantified. And lastly if you're interested in breeding some queens assessments will let you know which colonies have queens that are laying

early, which ones are building up quickly and which are heading colonies that produce a lot of honey. So in your beginning days of bee keeping you might not start asking these questions. But certainly after a few years you start to think about these things and assessments can help you find those answers. We generally recommend to conduct two full colony assessments during the year anyways, regardless of whether or not your testing a question you might have. And we recommend that you do an assessment in the spring, right after the bees have come out of winter, to see what tape of shape there in, whether or not they're strong enough to split or whether or not they have a good viable queen. And then also to conduct an assessment in late summer, before the weather turns cooler, to make sure that your queen is still viable and has a good laying pattern. And if not, then this is the time that you can re-queen her with enough time before fall to ensure that she gets accepted and that the colony survives winter. So these types of assessments and quantifying everything that's in your hive is time consuming. It's much more time consuming than conducting an inspection. But they do provide very valuable information to the master beekeeper. Okay, so when you are accessing a colony, you are basically pulling out all of the frames and quantifying these different factors on it: bees, brood, pollen, honey. You can just do the ones you are interested in or you can do all of them. And the way that it helps me to do it when am conducting an assessment, is to picture the frame being broken down into quarters or sixths, so that you can actually estimate the fraction. And then we quickly record the fractions for each frame. We just write it down on our record sheet and then we can add it up in the margin at the end and figure out the quantity of all the brood and all the pollen and all the bees in one hive. So to assess frames of bees, sometimes it's tricky to actually be looking at a frame if your bees aren't very still on the frame. And if they are still then it's fine. You can break them up into fractions and continue doing it that way. But if they are moving around or more flighty, than an easy way to assess the frames of bees is just to tip up each hive box and lay it on its side to quickly estimate how many frames are covered by bees from the bottom. And it's a simple as it sounds. One frame of bees will be completely covered with bees on both sides. So, estimating these frames of bees and other materials is also subjective. And even when I'm in the field sometimes what I interpret as being three quarters of a frame of pollen someone else may interpret as a slightly different fraction. So for the sake of consistency, it's best that the same person conduct each assessment for the colony. And since assessments take more time than inspections, it usually takes us on average about 15 minutes to do an assessment versus just a few minutes to quickly go through and inspect your colonies. The bees might become more defensive and they're a bit more disoriented. So we recommend wearing more protective clothing than you normally would. And you need to be watching to make sure that you're colonies aren't getting robbed. When you're having the boxes totally separated, it can be easy for robbers to get in. So it's also helpful to stack your boxes squarely and put an outer cover on the outside, just so that there aren't any options or room for robbers to sneak in. And it's really handy to have your record keeping

materials ready with you, when you go out and do your assessments. Having a check off list. Being able to quickly write down fractions will help you in your efficiency much more than if you're writing everything word for word. Okay so let's go back to assessing the number of frames of bees. Because this is actually the most difficult part of an assessment I find. So when you're assessing your frames of bees we usually work the colonies a little bit differently before inspecting our colony. When we conduct an inspection, we are usually starting at the top and working our way down. But when we're assessing our frames of bees, we usually start from the bottom and work our way up. And the reason why we start from the bottom is because if we started from the top, as we're smoking the bees down, we're driving them down into that bottom box. And by the time you get down to the bottom box, it's literally overflowing with bees. So you can't really get an accurate response or accurate estimate. However, some people still prefer to work form the top down just to reduce aggression and disorientation and it is possible to still conduct assessments working from the top down. In these cases, the key is in the amount of smoke you're using. So smoke the hive very lightly so that you are not driving the bees down to the bottom. Again, wear extra protective gear if need to. But you just want to make sure that you're able to get the accurate quantification of frames of bees. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Keeping Good Records Whether you are a hobbyist or a large-scale beekeeper, record keeping is a crucial component of beekeeping. Monitoring your colonies and documenting the dates of your inspections and manipulations helps you predict and meet your colonies’ needs, but it can also be a source of learning and enjoyment in its own right. Record keeping has a range of applications and is particularly useful for managing honey production, pest and disease outbreaks and progression, queen health/productivity, and swarming and population dynamics. With written or photographed information, you can track a colony’s population, health, behavior, and production over the course of a season. From year to year as well, records can help you compare the same colony's performance across years and predict what to expect at different times of the year. In short, good record-keeping allows you to manage your colonies more precisely for your goals. Watch these videos to learn how record-keeping can benefit your operation. Video Transcript Record keeping is important no matter your goals and motivations, whether you have 3 hives or you do migratory pollination contracts every year. There's a ton you can track and a ton you can learn from just one metric. For example a lot of people track their hives weights over the years or within a given year and that helps you see honey flows, maybe a swarm event and making sure they're putting on enough weight for winter. But even simple records can help you see your problem, for example, monitoring how defensive or gentle a hive is and whether that changes suddenly. In the short-term, records could help you plan for your next inspection. Do you need to return sooner rather than later to check on a new queen or to resample after a mite treatment? Do you need to bring equipment that you don't normally bring and you don't have available in the bee yard? I think most importantly for us though it's pest and diseases, is what record keeping kind of helps you keep a handle on. Which of my treatments are working? When is an apparent disease, when is the outbreak cyclical or when does it just follow bad weather or a period of confinement? If you lose a colony your records will tell you if anything was off in the previous weeks or months even, or whether you're not seeing something that you really ought to and you need to go ask somebody else. And finally, of course, records help you compare colonies in the same year. Colonies naturally vary, that's why we tell novice beekeepers to have at least two when they start. It depends, each one varies on how fast they build up, how much honey and pollen they're storing, their temperament, and much more. And records will help you determine when a hive seems to have a problem or

whether it's always lagging behind one of its neighbors. Finally, if you do want to do breeding, record keeping will help you learn which colonies have the traits you're most interested in, whether there's one that's more productive or more gentle or even more hygienic. As a lot of people are trying to breed for hygienic bees these days. But without records, you'd never be able to breed successfully. With your records, you might be able to do small experiments or tests in your area. You probably can't do thoroughly scientific experiments. But you can certainly test out different types of equipment for your own use. On a bigger scale, you might coordinate with people in your club or even a local citizen science project and record the data that they need for their own data sets. So we've got a few tips. Some of them are pretty obvious but we still think they bear mentioning. First of all, stay consistent with your abbreviations in the type of data you're taking. Of course your own system is going to evolve over time, but you can't compare say 15 frames of bees, that looks crowded, to a lot of activity, to 2 deeps. Those are all different ways of measuring more or less the same thing - population dynamics. And so using a data sheet will prompt you to record the same things every time and to count them in the same way. Plus they also make records more legible to others so you can share them with your club or maybe your local extension associate. We have got a few sample data sheets we are sharing with you. But there are lots of others out there and you can of course create your own. As you record data you want to stick to the facts. If you can see if something is wrong but you can't tell why, don't jump to conclusions. Just write down everything you can about the symptoms clearly so you can ask somebody else. If you have a guess mark it as such but it's not helpful to write down that you have AFB and then go back later and realize of course you didn't. Finally, there's a lot of other helpful tools and supplements you can use. You can take photos, make drawings, take samples, even do a voice recording that you transcribe later. As always, you'll want to include the date, the hive you found it in, and any other relevant information. And you can send that to your honey bee extension associate or just a local club member. And of course you have to make sure you don't mind getting your camera or camera phone a little bit sticky. Video Transcript Be aware that there's a learning curve to beekeeping and the learning curve never ends. You will be learning until the day you die. The question is whether you want to actually learn something. There's a lot of first year beekeepers 20 years in a row. First year beekeepers who never really know what they're doing. One of the things about learning is keeping records. What we use is just a simple Excel spreadsheet, a yard log, where we can fill in a list of all of our yards. And we can put the date down and what we did on that date. What the mite counts were on that date, whether we fed them, did a mite treatment, and observations on bloom. Your first several years, just a little spiral bound logbook for each yard to talk about what was blooming and put down the date and what the bees were doing. That could be extremely valuable

in later years then because then you can look back for patterns and see what to expect in those yards. You just can't trust your memory at all. Our memory just does not work for that. And we often, like last year we had a problem with Varroa, late this season and my sons, one my sons, the accusatory son said, "well dad it's because you did this and this and because we didn't get the mite treatment on." So I just calmly say, get the yard log, let's take a look. And he grabs that, he looks at it. I could tell by how long that he looked at it that he realized he was wrong about that. Anyway, we have a documented record of when we did mite treatments and what we did and what the mite counts were. And then I can say, "ah, now that we got that straight let's have a tailgate meeting, a learning experience, and see what we can learn and what we're going to do differently next year. So I very much encourage everybody to keep some kind of simple record keeping. Make it simple enough that you will actually do it. If you make it too complicated that you're not going to do it, then don't do it. Make it a simple record keeping. Back to Table of Contents

Tool: Record Sheets You might be wondering — what kind of  Download the Tool records should you keep? The answer to this question depends on your operation, as the importance of certain types of records will vary with different beekeepers’ goals. But at a minimum, you should keep basic information on your individual hives and apiary organization, records of ongoing inspections, Record keeping sheets: • Colony Inspection sheet • Varroa Mite sheet • Apiary Information sheet • Hive Information sheet • Contact Information sheet and logs of monitoring for Varroa mites and management regimes. You might also choose to track nectar and pollen flows, particularly if you are producing varietal honey. For rearing queens, you can keep colony breeding record cards. Businesses of course need to keep financial records, inventory, and many other logs. We have developed several record keeping guides that we use here at the Dyce Lab, available for download. We have tried to find a middle ground between small- and large-scale beekeepers, which is to say by leaving room for enough detail to learn from the colonies year after year, but not so much detail that such record keeping is impossibly time consuming. On the inspection sheet, in particular, we have left room for different sorts of information. On your record sheets, you can also note the temperature and weather, as this will help with evaluating the bees' temperament during inspections. Your record sheets should not be limited to those provided here. Make your own sheets as necessary. As the season ends, consider preparing an archive with all the data sheets combined, or entering them into a computer database such as Excel for easy analysis. ▶ Colony Inspection Sheet If you do no other record keeping, the colony inspection form, or a variation of it, should be a standard part of your beekeeping routine. You will update it continually throughout the active season, taking note of the population, nutrition, queen status, and indications of disease. There is room to briefly describe the quality of the brood pattern (whether it is spotty, large/small — and relatedly, whether the brood nest needs to be expanded — whether there are signs of a laying worker, etc.). From there, you should make comments on the state of the queen and her laying, note if you see her or her eggs, whether she is marked or not (only relevant if she was marked and does not now appear to be, which

means that the old queen was likely superseded), and whether there are queen cups or cells. You might also note if they are supersedure cells or emergency cells. You should also estimate the stores available to the bees in the form of honey and pollen, and whether there is extra room available/unused in the hive. These will, of course, fluctuate over the season, but knowing their storage levels (past) and needs (present and future) will help you keep them nourished and healthy throughout the year. Finally, there is room to take notes on a range of indicators. Population management refers to any actions you have taken to split or merge a colony, requeen it, move frames to another hive, etc. Pests and diseases refer to any signs you may see in the hive and notation of any treatments or equipment, e.g., a screened bottom board. There is admittedly some overlap with the Varroa monitoring sheet, but in part, because Varroa needs to be monitored consistently, and in part because we recommend that Varroa be an apiary-level consideration (rather than just at the level of the colony). The nutrition and hive products category refers to whether you need to or have already added supers, fed sugar syrup, extracted honey, installed a pollen trap or a queen excluder, or other relevant actions. The general notes category captures anything else of interest, e.g., who performed the inspection (if multiple people are working in the same apiary), the bees’ temperament, activity in and around the hive (e.g., bees bringing in lots of pollen), whether you added any equipment, or took any actions like cleaning the bottom board or reversing the brood chambers. You can include notes if samples from the colony were taken. Indicate what type of samples you took and where you sent them for analyses (e.g., brood comb sample sent to USDA Beltsville Bee Lab). Varroa Mite Monitoring and Treatment Sheet Varroa mites are behind much of the recent concern over bee health, directly and indirectly. Controlling Varroa is key to healthy and productive colonies and requires ongoing monitoring of mite levels. Use the Varroa mite record-keeping sheet to aid your monitoring. Our monitoring sheet includes a column for mite counts. Common monitoring techniques involve sampling a ½ cup of bees, which is about 300 bees. But many treatment thresholds are specified at the number of mites per 100 bees, or a percentage of mites. To avoid confusion, we have included both ratios here. There are a variety of different monitoring methods (powdered sugar rolls, alcohol washes, etc.), which is why you should indicate which method you are using. You can compare your methods and mite counts to neighboring beekeepers. ▶

▶ ▶ The sheet then includes room to describe your treatment method(s). Note that this can include chemical treatments as well as cultural management practices for those practicing treatment-free beekeeping or Integrated Pest Management. Timing is critical for both chemical and cultural treatments (anyone who has ever left drone comb in a frame too long knows this well!). Notes might include information about the conditions (e.g., temperature, since temperature affects the efficacy of some chemical methods, or the presence of a lot of brood since many treatments only work on mites present outside of brood cells). Finally, any good monitoring and treatment regime also needs follow-up to see whether a given treatment was effective, which can be filled out in the next line below. Apiary Information Sheet The apiary information record-keeping sheet only occasionally needs to be filled out and can be left at the front of a binder. It includes information about multiple apiaries (name or code for hive IDs, location, contact information for landowners, the number of hives in that location, and the dates they are moved in and out, and whether the yard requires any ongoing maintenance. There is room for other notes about nearby bee yards, forage and honey production, and any other measures you might want to track. Hive Information Sheet Like the apiary information sheet, the hive information record-keeping sheet should be updated once a year or as necessary. It tracks individual colonies, with information about their origins (split, nuc, package, swarm, other), the colony’s longevity, the origins of the queen(s) (supersedure, swarm, purchased — from where), and the queens’ stock and/or subspecies. Contact Information Sheet It is handy to keep a contact information sheet in the bee yard in case you need to quickly make a call to diagnose a problem or ask a landowner about changes in the site. We have included the information for the USDA Beltsville Bee Lab in Maryland; most other contacts will vary from state to state and beekeeper to beekeeper. Back to Table of Contents ▶

▶ Read: Record Keeping Tips To help you record your colony inspections, we've included some tips that can make your records meaningful for future reference. Make Record Keeping Convenient A key to accurate record keeping is to label all your colonies and yards with an identification system that clearly distinguishes them from one another. If you anticipate moving hives between apiaries, be sure to use a system that can account for that. You may want to label individual hive bodies (at least the brood chambers). You can paint it on, write it with a permanent marker, burn it on, or scratch/etch it in. If you do not anticipate moving any hive bodies between hives, you can put a waterproof label on the hive lid or make a map of your apiary with the hive IDs clearly labeled. Some beekeepers label frames within a colony with the year they were made using different colors, markers, notches, etc. This can be useful in allowing you to discard the oldest frames in each hive body every year, to reduce contaminants in your hives. Photo credit: Jon Ryan Make Record Keeping Consistent Don’t wait until after you’ve returned from the bee yard to take notes because you could forget important information. To make record keeping a consistent and immediate habit, keep your record sheets in the bee yard or with your smoker and ▶

▶ other equipment. They can be stored in a weatherproof container in a nearby shed, or even beneath your hive(s) in a zip-lock bag. This not only ensures that you have them, but also that you are using the same notebook every time. Keep writing implements handy — try tying one onto a clipboard or binder with a string. Finally, having extras of everything — writing implements, paper, clips, etc. — will undoubtedly come in handy. Use Technology There are also an increasing number of digitized forms and apps such as 'Hive Tracks' or 'Beetight'. If you want to input information directly to a smartphone or other device, you need to consider the conditions in your bee yard. You will need connectivity or a system that doesn’t need to be online, or can be uploaded later. You may want to avoid a lot of typing, particularly if you have sticky fingers! Back to Table of Contents

Read: Tech-Enhanced Beekeeping Tech-enhanced beekeeping, also known as precision apiculture or smart beekeeping, is one of the fastestgrowing areas of apiculture research and commercial innovation. It uses sensors, AI robotics, and data analytics to monitor hive health (temperature, humidity, sounds, weight) in real time and provide early warning for pests or disease. These technologies aim to shift management from reactive to proactive to improve yields and bee survival. Those expensive tools can be useful, yet it is important to note that they detect indirect signals that are claimed by the companies that sell them to be correlated with various colony conditions. Some of those correlations are clear, e.g., an increase in hive weight and nectar flow/abundance of honey in the hive. Others are less clear; e.g., some sensors claim to reliably measure Varroa infestation levels. Current tech-enhanced beekeeping should be best seen as an early-warning and triage system, not as a diagnostic or decision-maker. Those tools might reduce unnecessary hive inspections, but they should be complemented with direct observation of brood, disease, or mites. Below is an overview of some useful technologies and how they are used by some beekeepers right now. Hive Scales and Weight Sensors These measure nectar flow and honey harvest readiness (gain), absconding or colony loss or swarming (sudden weight drop). This helps detect nectar flows without opening the hive, alerts beekeepers to feed during dearth, and helps commercial operations know when to move hives. Temperature and Humidity Sensors hose are placed inside the brood nest or upper super and can reveal the brood presence (brood nest stays ~34 to 35°C), queen failure (temperature fluctuations), colony stress or starvation (temperature decreases). Honey bees maintain humidity and temperature remarkably tightly, so changes recorded by those sensors indicate biological problems days to weeks earlier than visual inspection. ▶ ▶

▶ ▶ Acoustic/Vibration Monitoring (AI-Powered) Microphones or accelerometers can be used to listen to colony sounds. They can detect queenlessness (distinct acoustic signature), swarming preparation (piping, quacking, wing-beating patterns), and colony collapse signals (reduction of sounds altogether). Those devices must be coupled with machine-learning models that were trained to evaluate the "acoustic fingerprint" of hive states. RFID Tagging for Individual Bee Tracking Individual bees can be equipped with Radio-frequency identification (RFID) tags. Those tags are tiny, passive chips that can be attached to individual bees (usually on the thorax) and record their movements and behaviors through automatic tracking. Useful information includes the forager lifespan, the homing success rates, the sublethal pesticide effects, and the orientation drift. Back to Table of Contents

▶ ▶ Read: AI for Beekeepers Besides assisting tech-enhanced beekeeping, AI offers all beekeepers equipped with a computer and Internet a wide range of capabilities for complex, high-powered situations and personal use. Beekeepers can tap into AI tools to help understand science and to bring that knowledge into the public sphere. You likely have access to free AI tools. As of 2025, the capabilities and rapid evolution of AI threaten to make any recommended tools outdated by 2026, so ask your classmates or facilitator for suggestions on which tool to try first. Below are some ways AI can be useful to you as a beekeeper. Understand Science Reading scientific papers is hard, unless you do it all the time (and sometimes even then). If you want to understand the context of some academic research, upload the document to an AI chat (or give it a link to a publicly available paper) and ask it questions about it. Jumpstart Your Thinking If you can’t seem to get started on a document, citizen science idea, or presentation, you can use an AI chatbot as a sounding board or to set your thoughts off in a new direction. The AI tool will present ideas for you to explore further or reject outright. Either way, you will have external input to push you to think in different directions. Polish Your Writing Not everyone can put together sentences with ease, avoid grammatical errors, or argue about the Oxford comma. Use AI as your copyeditor. Note that the suggestion here says “copyeditor,” not “writer.” Use your own voice and your own thoughts first, and then the AI as the polish. Make Global Connections ▶ ▶

Query an AI tool for non-English sources, and then ask it to translate it for you. You can even use AI translation services to conduct a conversation with someone in another language. You can also make your own documents and presentations available in other languages at different reading levels. Back to Table of Contents

Discussion: Module 2 Discussion and Questions This course provides the opportunity to discuss content with fellow beekeepers, as well as with the course facilitator. You are welcome to participate in all course discussions, but you are only required to participate in this discussion. Your participation in it counts toward your final grade. Hive inspection is not a one-size-fits-all task. What you inspect, how often you inspect, and even whether opening the hive is encouraged at all depend strongly on the beekeeping philosophy and operational scale. For example, commercial beekeepers tend to inspect their hives frequently but quickly, typically looking for queen rightness (presence of eggs, visual evaluation of the brood pattern), brood diseases (AFB/EFB, chalkbrood), and Varroa levels (sampling routines). In contrast, natural/treatment-free/Darwinian beekeepers tend to inspect their hives infrequently and use observations such as the flight activity of workers outside the hive and the amount of debris on bottom boards. Those two examples represent two extremes in a continuum of ways to keep bees. As a Master beekeeper, it is important that you are aware of the many different beekeeping practices available to Humans. Research the many ways humans keep bees (make sure to find information about natural/treatment-free/Darwinian beekeeping), then answer the following questions about Module 2. What’s the most interesting thing you learned from this module that you’d like to keep in mind when inspecting your colonies this upcoming season? Module Introduction: Honey Bee Nutrition Bees use the nectar and pollen from many kinds of flowers to fulfill their nutritional needs. Foragers from just one colony can visit over 200 different plant species in one year! A Master Beekeeper learns the important floral resources in his or her region, understands the nutritional needs of the colony, and knows when and how to supplement this natural forage through feeding when necessary. In this module, we will help you make sure you are meeting the nutritional needs of your colonies. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Honey Bee Nutrition Overview Nutrition is intricately tied to proper brood development and honey bee health. Colonies with adequate nutrition can rear healthy brood, have well-functioning immune systems, and store food for times of shortage. Unlike solitary organisms, honey bee foragers are tasked with the duty to fulfill all the nutritional requirements for themselves and for their nestmates. They must ensure they gather food that contains sufficient carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins, minerals, and lipids so the colony can thrive. Furthermore, nutritional requirements vary depending on the age of the bees and the season. Brood and young bees require a protein-rich diet, while older bees feed mainly on carbohydrates. Honey bee colony nutrition is a dynamic process, and one arena in which beekeepers can sometimes intervene to improve health and productivity. What happens if the colony has inadequate nutrition? Honey bees' nutritional needs may not always be provided for with ever-increasing reductions in natural habitat, growing agricultural monocultures, and changes in climate. Management practices also affect nutrition, e.g., when bees are used for pollination services of specific crops. Inadequate nutrition can have several physiological and behavioral impacts on bee health. Bees that receive inadequate pollen during development live shorter lives as adults, transition to become foragers much earlier in life, and forage less often than bees that receive adequate pollen. These bees also perform fewer waggle dances to communicate good food sources to their nestmates, and when they dance, the information they convey is not always accurate. Insufficient protein during winter bee development results in reduced fat bodies, which shorten their lifespan. Colony survival can be in jeopardy if too few bees survive the winter. A colony will react to food shortages by rearing fewer brood and sometimes cannibalizing brood to acquire their nutrients. The multitude of stressors affecting bees today can also interact with nutrition. Poor nutrition can reduce bees' resistance to stress: they are less resistant to Nosema apis infections, Varroa mite infestations, and pesticides. In the same way, honey bees infected with Nosema ceranae live longer if they have more pollen available. Photo credit: Jennifer Tsuruda

Watch: Nutritional Requirements — The How and Why of Bee Food Although natural forage (pollen and nectar) is almost always better than substitutes, beekeepers can help reduce nutritional stress by supplementing bees in times of need. At the Master Beekeeper level, we are delving deeper than how to feed your colonies to focus on the why. Why is it important to feed during certain periods? Why should you sometimes use 1:1 sugar syrup and sometimes 2:1? Is honey always better than sugar syrup? Why do your colonies need pollen from a variety of floral sources? Understanding the principles behind nutrition and feeding will help you anticipate your colony’s needs. Video Transcript Honey bees consume carbohydrates in the form of honey and sugar syrup. And they need carbohydrates all year long to maintain the adult population and to fuel their day-to-day activities. And even before a bee is about to take her energetically expensive foraging trip, she'll consume a little bit of honey to get some carbohydrates to fuel her. And, she'll store this honey in her crop, and digest it during the duration of her trip. And you can even tell which bees are about to take a foraging trip by looking at the hive entrance. And those that are taking foraging trips actually don't fly straight out of the entrance, but instead they sort of dip down before flying upward because they are weighed down by their food. So carbohydrates fuels everything for the way that adults are living, but it can also affect the behavior of adult bees too. So if you're having steady or increasing amounts of nectar, so a nectar flow, this can actually stimulate the colony to build comb and to start rearing brood. And the idea is that they're perceiving that there's a lot of nutrition in their environment, so this is a good time to start having larvae and boosting their population size. So, if you want to encourage comb building, or brood rearing, when there's limited nectar in the environment, then you can supplement your colonies with light sugar syrup to stimulate them the same way. So how much honey does a colony need? Well here in the Northeast, to fuel all their activities, colonies here, on average, consume about 95 pounds of honey during the summer. And during the winter, in order to stay warm and to begin rearing brood and melt in winter, colonies will consume on average another 50 to 90 pounds of honey. And there's a lot of variation on how much they're eating in the winter. This depends on the strength of the colony, the environmental temperatures and the amount of brood rearing that they're actually doing. So I often get asked how many pounds of honey do I need to make sure that my colonies have over winter? And I usually recommend to aim to provide them with 100 pounds of honey. So you wanna go on the safe side of things. So, while 50 pounds might be okay for some winters, it's often not going to cut it. So, aim to have 100 pounds of honey on your hive. Anything that's left over can be given to splits in the spring or can be extracted.

Video Transcript Protein is a really important nutrient for reproduction in the colony. Protein is needed for brood production because brood is eating protein in the form of royal jelly and in the form of bee bread. And it's also needed for the development in young adult bees. So these are usually the nurse bees. And they need to consume bee bread in order to complete developing their hypopharyngeal glands, which are producing royal jelly to feed to the brood. So the building blocks of proteins are amino acids, and there's 20 amino acids that are needed to build all the proteins necessary for bee life. 10 of these amino acids are manufactured in the bees' bodies. But the remaining ten must be acquired through protein either by pollen ideally or through pollen substitute, which bees are going to then convert into bee bread and consume. So how much protein does a larvae need anyways to develop properly? It turns out that one larva needs about one cell of bee bread to develop. And a typical colony will consume about 50 pounds of pollen in total, in the form of bee bread, each year. So if you're the type of person that likes to calculate exactly how much pollen you need to be feeding your bees based on the number of cells that brood then go around ahead. But if you just want a general rule of thumb, then you can ensure that every deep hive body that has brood in it, has at least one to two frames worth of pollen or bee bread. So this includes full frames of pollen, but also pollen that's making up that rainbow arch around the brood. But sometimes, it's not always easy to base your colony's nutrition on the amount of pollen that you're seeing in the colony, alone. And a really good way to tell if brood has enough protein is by checking the amount of royal jelly in each brood cell that has larva. So, when you're looking in the cells that have young larva, you want to make sure that you're seeing a small pool of glistening white jelly, with a larva floating on top. And when pollen is especially plentiful, when there's a pollen flow on, you may see larvae with tons of royal jelly surrounding it. And this is what we call wet brood, and these larvae have ample amounts of nutrition to develop into really good, healthy bees. But if pollen stores are low, you'll see very little jelly or the cell will be completely dry. And in this case we recommend supplementing your colonies with a pollen substitute just to make sure that they do have those nutrients to develop okay. Video Transcript The requirements and rules of vitamins and minerals for honey bees is not well understood. We do know, however, that several vitamins and minerals are necessary for insect life. And vitamins appear to be especially important for brood production and for the development of nurse bees hypopharyngeal glands. So, where do bees get these vitamins and minerals from? They mostly get them from pollen. And there's only trace amounts that they're getting from nectar. And there's starting to be this interest in supplementing your colonies with vitamins or minerals or even probiotics. And research is beginning to investigate whether there's positive effects of doing so.

But right now the nutritional science is not yet developed enough for us to make clear-cut recommendations for using any of these supplements to promote colony health. Video Transcript Honey bees acquire their fats through the pollen, they don't actually get any fats from nectar in their diets. And fat content of pollen depends largely on the flower species just as sugar content in nectar depends on the flower species. And fats are stored in the bee's fat body which is a collection of tissues comprised of many fat body cells that are mostly found in the abdomen of the bee, surrounding the reproductive and digestive organs. But they're also distributed across the abdomen or sorry, they're also distributed across the thorax and the head. And here these tissues are storing fat and glycogen, which is stored sugar, to release for energy during periods of food shortage. And the biggest time here in the northeast that this is critical for is over winter. So fat nutrition is very important for wintering bees. And you want to make sure that bees who are reared in late summer and early fall have adequate fats in their diet. Because these bees are going to be the hive's winter bees. So you want to make sure that their fat bodies are large enough to provide energy throughout the entire winter. If they don't have large enough fat bodies to sustain them, then these winter bees can die before the winter is even over. So, it's critical that bees have access to adequate pollen from August to November in order to help them build their fat bodies. And they're building these fat bodies starting as larvae and continuing until they're young adults. So, if there isn't ample pollen at this time of year, then we would advise you to provide them with a pollen substitute in late summer or early fall. And sometimes, in your area, at least here in the northeast, we get a really big pollen flow of goldenrod. And this supplies a lot of pollen to bees right in that late summer period of when winter bees are starting to grow or develop. But this isn't predictable every single year. Sometimes, if you're not having that guaranteed pollen flow, then these are the times that you want to intervene as a beekeeper. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Natural Forage The flowering plants in nature provide bees with the nutrients they require in the form of nectar and pollen. Nectar Nectar is mostly sugar and water, but not all nectars are created equal. Plants vary in the amount of nectar they produce, the time of day it is produced, and the concentration of sugar in that nectar. Environmental conditions (such as drought) can also affect the quality and quantity of nectar available in a plant or across a landscape. Indeed, the concentration of sugar in the nectars of different species of flowering plants varies from 5% to 92%. Honey bees largely use the sugar concentration of nectar to guide their foraging decisions - nectars with high sugar concentrations are perceived as high quality to bees. The main sugars found in nectar are sucrose, glucose, and fructose. Nectar also has small amounts of minerals, vitamins, fats, and enzymes. Because of this, honey is more nutritious for bees than syrup from cane or beet sugar, which only has trace amounts of minerals. Darker honeys, like buckwheat, contain more minerals than lighter honeys. However, these mineral-rich (darker) honeys tend to make bees produce more fecal solids, which can be a problem in winter or other periods of confinement when they cannot take cleansing flights. That is one reason some beekeepers choose to harvest all honey from the hive and heavily feed their colonies sugar syrup in the fall. Some nectar can also be poisonous to bees — and humans — due to very small amounts of naturally-occurring toxins. The most famous are rhododendron and azalea nectar, but despite their widespread presence in North America, poisoning incidents are rare. This field of red dead nettle makes great forage for honey bees. Photo credit: Jon Ryan

Pollen Like nectar, not all pollen is created equal. Protein amounts in the pollen of different species can vary from 5% to 40%. Pollen must contain at least 20% protein to fulfill the nutritional requirements for bees. Pollens containing at least 25% are considered excellent protein sources. Only a few forage plants have been analyzed to determine their protein contents, as the costs for these analyses are quite high. Examples of poor protein pollens are cypress (2.5%), blueberry (13.9%), and sunflower (12.9%), in contrast to the good and excellent protein pollens of vetch (24%), white clover (25.9%), viper's bugloss (34.9%), and the Californian flower Padre's Shooting Star (61.7%). Pollens also vary in their amino acid content. Some, like canola, have sufficient amounts of all of the 10 essential amino acids that bees are not able to produce. In contrast, others may have low amounts or not have certain amino acids altogether. For example, pine pollen is deficient in four essential amino acids, dandelion pollen is deficient in two, and weeping willow and corn pollen are deficient in one. Because of this, honey bees cannot rear larvae on any of these pollens alone, no matter how much they consume. So, a colony collects pollen from a variety of flowers, and the amino acids from the different sources complement each other. Table 1. Amino acid requirements for honey bee nutrition (based on DeGroot (1953)).

Read: Learn the Blooms in Your Area As beekeepers grow to better understand bees, ☆ Key Points they also become more connected to the environment around them. Through simple observations, beekeepers can learn the important honey plants and pollen plants that their bees are visiting. Each year, the foraging Through simple observations, beekeepers can learn the important honey plants and pollen plants that their bees are visiting. patterns of colonies vary, based on weather and how it affects the availability of different floral resources over the course of the year. Some years, plants bloom successively, and bees can be observed bringing in pollen from many different species. In other years, periods of poor weather can delay the bloom of early flowering plants until their bloom times correspond with later flowering plants. In these times, bees may visit the early flowering plants less than normal. The observations of when and what is blooming year to year are integral to being a successful beekeeper. We encourage you to identify the flowering plants that contribute to your honey crops. The colors and flavors give you clues about which plants they come from. There is a great variety in honey colors here in the Northeast and in other parts of the world. For instance, basswood honey and fireweed honey are water white, alfalfa honey and orange blossom honey are white to light amber, blueberry honey is light amber to amber, tulip poplar honey is dark amber, and buckwheat honey is dark brown.

Clockwise from top: basswood, Japanese knotwood, and clover honey Flavors range from caramel and marshmallow to mint and even bitterness. Honey flavor is determined by a synergistic interplay between the chemistry of the nectar source, enzymatic and ripening processes by bees, environmental conditions, and post-harvest handling by humans, all of which collectively create honey’s extraordinary diversity of tastes and aromas. It is important to recognize that, despite of the many factors involved in determining the flavor/aroma of honey, the primary determinant of honey flavor is the chemical composition of the nectar from which bees collect sugars, namely the ratio of different sugars present in the nectar (ex: sucrose, fructose, glucose) as well as the presence of allelochemicals (ex: terpenes, phenolic compounds). Plants vary widely in that respect, both at the species level, but also within plant species, since the particular profile of these sugars/allelochemicals will change based on the environment these plants experience as they grow, for example, soil type, temperature, and rainfall. Master Beekeepers should also become familiar with the plants from which their bees are collecting pollen. Different plants produce a variety of different colored pollens, and there is even variation in the colors of pollen from the same species of plant. This can depend on how long ago the pollen was released by the plant, the amount of dust or other particles incorporated in it, and the amount and color of the nectar/honey the bee uses to moisten the pollen to pack it in her pollen baskets. We encourage you to observe bees collecting pollen and take note of the color of their pollen loads and the type of flower they are on. There are many field guides for identifying wildflowers. In the same way, as you inspect your colonies, notice the colors of pollen stored in the comb.
