Read: When to Feed Carbohydrates Because natural forage is not available or sufficient all year round, you may find that you need to feed your bees, particularly in the following situations: In winter, if stores are low. In early spring, before much is in bloom, to provide food if their winter stores are low and to grow the population by stimulating brood rearing. In spring or summer, after installing a nuc, package, or swarm into a hive. In spring or summer, if there is a local dearth of flowering plants and little nectar/honey in the hive. In late summer and fall, to ensure sufficient winter stores, particularly if you have taken off honey. When rearing queens, for cell builders and mating nucs (if you do not have honey frames to spare). During and after requeening, to encourage acceptance of the new queen (if there is no nectar flow). When you want the bees to draw out foundation, and there is no nectar flow. When administering certain treatments to colonies. For example, Terramycin to help control European foulbrood is mixed with powdered sugar, Fumagillin for Nosema control is dissolved in sugar syrup, and oxalic acid for Varroa control is dissolved in syrup when applied using the dribble method. Back to Table of Contents

▶ Read: How to Feed Carbohydrates There are several ways to feed your bees carbohydrates. Explore the options below to learn more. Frames of Honey The easiest way to feed bees is with frames of honey that you have saved from earlier in the season (that you froze) or took from another hive after making sure that they are pest- and disease-free. It is important to only feed bees honey from your own diseasefree colonies; do not feed them honey purchased from a grocery store or from another beekeeper, as there could be disease spores present (American Foulbrood or Nosema). In the early 1990s, Dr. Roger Morse and K. Steinkraus screened 82 random samples of Canadian and American honey from honey producers and found 8.5% of those samples contained spores. It is hard to know how comparable those levels are to those of honey produced today, but it certainly demonstrates that there is some risk to this practice. If you do not have extra honey frames on hand, sugar syrup helps meet bees’ carbohydrate needs. Additionally, bees eating sugar syrup produce less fecal matter than when they eat honey, especially the dark, mineral-rich honeys. This is most important in winter when the bees must go long stretches without a chance to defecate outside the hive. Therefore, feeding your colonies a heavy sugar syrup in autumn (usually until the end of October in the Northeast) is a fine practice. Types of Sugar and Syrup Only feed your bees refined cane or beet sugar (both are sucrose), liquid sucrose, or high fructose corn syrup (fructose). Never feed bees mannose, raffinose, galactose, or lactose sugars; these sugars are toxic to them. Other sugars, such as brown sugar, molasses, powdered sugar, maple syrup, or raw sugar, contain impurities that are indigestible to bees. Powdered sugar contains cornstarch to prevent clumping, which can pose problems with bee digestion, so it should not be used as the main method of bee feed (although in small quantities, like when using it to monitor Varroa mites, it does not appear to have detrimental effects on the colony). Refined sugar, because it is refined of all other components, is the best. ▶

▶ Even refined sugar can be problematic if it is overheated. Overheated sugar syrup may caramelize if the water is boiling when you mix in the sugar, or if the mixture cooks too high and for too long. The bees cannot digest the caramel and may kill them. Syrup Concentration You probably know that you should feed your bees a syrup of one part sugar to one part water in the spring, and two parts sugar to one part water in the fall. But why? Light sugar syrup — one part granulated sugar (cane or beet) to one part water — supplements bees’ natural forage in the spring and stimulates them to draw comb. Its sugar level is similar to that of rich nectar, so colonies respond as if there is a nectar flow coming in: workers draw comb and the queen lays eggs. When feeding light syrup at the end of winter or early spring, feed continuously until the bees begin bringing in nectar. This ensures the colony is adequately fed and is well prepared for when the nectar flow starts without any interruption: honeycomb is being constructed, and the queen continues to lay eggs. Stop feeding as soon as the nectar flow starts and the bees begin bringing in more than they are consuming. Otherwise, the bees may store the syrup in supers that you later extract. Such honey is considered adulterated by law. If bees have a surplus of sugar syrup in their brood nest, they may move some of it upward to be stored in supers if they need to create more room for the queen to lay. In late winter/early spring, you can also consider putting a solid feed (dry sugar, fondant, or a candy board) in the hive. They will consume this solid sugar and not store it; however, it does not stimulate brood rearing in the way that syrup does. In the fall, the beekeeper should instead use heavy syrup (two parts sugar to one part water). Syrup with a lower ratio of water to sugar is easier for the honey bees to evaporate the water from and cap for their winter stores; they may not have time to evaporate a lighter syrup before the cold weather hits, and their efforts may raise moisture levels inside the hive. Excess moisture can condense on the inner cover above the cluster and drip down onto the bees, potentially killing your colony mid-winter, so the less moisture in the hive when temperatures are cold, the better. The extra water in unripe honey can also bulk up the honey bee hindgut quicker, so bees consuming this honey may need to take a cleansing flight sooner. If the weather isn't conducive, this can lead to dysentery in the hive. High Fructose Corn Syrup ▶

▶ ▶ Some beekeepers feed their bees high fructose corn syrup instead of sugar syrup. On a large scale, this option is cheaper and more convenient than sugar syrup, as it is already in liquid form. Nor, despite concerns, does it have detectable quantities of neonicotinoids, an insecticide applied to virtually all corn in the United States. But bees fed high fructose corn syrup produce less wax and have a smaller body mass than those fed sugar syrup, and their colonies have smaller populations compared to bees fed sugar syrup. Additionally, if high fructose corn syrup is stored improperly (above 105°F), the sugars inside can dehydrate, producing hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF), which is toxic to bees even at relatively low doses. Adding Stimulants Some beekeepers add essential oils to their sugar syrup. For instance, lemongrass oil is very attractive to honey bees and can stimulate them to consume sugar syrup when it is mixed in, as it contains some of the same components as Nasonov pheromone: citral and geraniol. Honey B Healthy is the most common feeding stimulant on the market. It contains lemongrass and spearmint oil. Adding this stimulant to the syrup also helps delay the growth of mold. But there is not enough scientific evidence to suggest that adding other essential oils is beneficial to colony health. Feeders There is a variety of equipment that you can use as feeders for sugar syrup. What type is right for you depends on your colonies’ needs, your management goals, the size of your operation, the equipment you have available, the costs, and logistical concerns such as how often you can refill the feeder. Feeders can be placed inside or outside the hive. Top feeders and bucket feeders placed upside down on top of colonies (above the inner cover and below the telescoping or outer cover) are the easiest way to feed. They can hold several gallons at a time and can be refilled without opening the hive beyond lifting off the outer cover. A Boardman feeder is also convenient, but its location outside the hive can encourage robbing and make it susceptible to freezing in cold temperatures and to moldy growth in the summer heat. It is also small. Inside the hive, frame feeders (which are the size and shape of frames) are popular. They can hold one or two gallons of syrup at a time and may need to be refilled often, which requires opening the colony. With some practice, you can learn to refill these feeders without fully opening the hive. Frame feeders also require a sort of ladder (a screen or textured surface) for the bees so that they do not fall in and drown.

While top feeders require no extra equipment and can simply be placed on top of the hive, a bucket feeder usually requires the beekeeper to have an additional empty deep hive body on top of the colony to set the bucket feeder into. Others may cut a hole in the top cover to set the bucket over, and when the bucket is not in use, insert a plug into the hole. Methods vary depending on the operation size. One caution with bucket feeders: the feeder should be level and sealed properly; otherwise, the liquid feed may immediately drain out of the feeder and could drown your bees. Feeding in open barrels is common for commercial beekeepers in North America. In this feeding practice, a barrel is filled with sugar syrup, straw is placed inside the barrel to act as a flotation device for the bees to stand on without drowning, and it is left in a yard for all the colonies to feed on. The open barrels or buckets are usually placed out of the line of sight of any colonies a few hundred yards away so that the bees have to actively forage to find the site initially like any other nectar source. This method is less time-consuming for the beekeeper. In addition, if barrels are located outside the bee yard, it can help direct robbers and wasps away from weak colonies that are susceptible to robbing. Some provinces in Canada have banned open barrel feeding, with the concern that it could facilitate disease spread, encourage robbing behavior if the barrels are placed close to hives, and concern for the public should they observe the frenzied bee activity that barrel feeding incites. There is also concern that populated colonies collect more syrup than the weaker colonies that need it most, leading to the strong getting stronger while the weak get weaker. To offset this, weak colonies can be fed directly with frame feeders at the same time that open barrels are available. Since the strong colonies are feeding at the barrel, robbing should not pose an issue. To date, there is no evidence to support these concerns, as, to our knowledge, no scientific studies have compared barrel feeding with other feeding regimes. Finally, the barrels may also attract mammal pests or be blown over. You may need to experiment with a few different feeders to find what works best for you. Regardless of which model you choose, you need to monitor the system carefully, especially to detect and prevent robbing at individual hives and at the feeders, to check whether they need to be refilled or dumped, and to remove dead bees and pests. Sugar syrup can become moldy or ferment after a few days in warm weather, so if the bees are not actively taking up the syrup, you should remove it and clean the feeder with hot soapy water and rinse thoroughly. If the feeder is not properly washed out, it can contaminate any syrup you add to that feeder again. Different feeder styles are shown below.

Read: Dry Feeding Carbohydrates in the Winter When feeding bees during winter (when they ingest it directly rather than storing it), do not use sugar syrup; solid sugar is better. Bees can hold in their feces for a long time — but only up to a certain point. The water in the syrup is the problem: as the solids already in the digestive tract absorb it, they expand and may push the bees past their limit. Bees also need to consume a greater volume of diluted syrup to receive the same amount of carbohydrates as they would if they consumed a small volume of pure dry sugar. Dry sugar also does not stimulate brood rearing, as it does not resemble nectar. This is good for winter feeding since you do not want to stimulate brood rearing until mid- to late winter. In the Northeast, beekeepers usually resume syrup feeding in March, as the occasional warm days will offer bees opportunities to take cleansing flights. Several options for dry feeding include using dry granulated sugar, candy boards, fondant, or winter patties with a small amount of protein added. Granulated Sugar The first method of using dry sugar, usually referred to as the “Mountain Camp Method,” is simply to pour a few pounds of dry granulated sugar onto a sheet of newspaper or wax paper on the top bars of the frames beneath the inner cover. A rim or spacer is added below the inner cover to accommodate the large lump of sugar. The dry sugar can also be placed on top of the inner cover, but the bees may not be able to break their cluster to retrieve it there, whereas if it were on the top bars, the bees would have easy access to it. The dry sugar has the additional benefit of absorbing moisture moving up through the hive, and as it does so, the sugar hardens on the newspaper. This helps reduce moisture problems in the hive. Dry sugar is not used during the warmer months of the year when bees are actively flying outside the hive, as they tend to carry the sugar granules out of the hive. You will then notice piles of sugar on the landing board or in front of the hive, which may attract other pests and predators. Candy Boards

A candy board looks like an inner cover with a deep (1" to 2”) rim into which you pour hot bee candy. Let it cool and harden before placing it on top of the hive, in place of the inner cover. Recipes for candy boards vary, but the basics (sugar + water) are the same. You can order pre-filled candy boards from most bee supply companies, or you can make them at home. Fondant Alternatively, you can feed your bees fondant, which can be found at some bakeries or purchased from bee supply companies. Be sure to buy fondant that only contains water, sugar, and corn syrup. Do not purchase any with food coloring or other additives. Place thick patties of fondant on wax paper on the top bars for bees to reach directly; they will chew through the paper and carry it out of the hive. Without the wax paper, the fondant could drip down onto the cluster, so it should always be placed on wax paper. Winter Patties Lastly, winter patties (such as Pro Winter Patties®) are similar to fondant. They are comprised of water, sugar, corn syrup, a very small amount of pollen substitute, and sometimes essential oils used as a feeding stimulant. These are usually purchased in onepound patties in waxed paper and should be placed right on the top bars of the frames in late winter. The sugar provides energy to sustain them throughout the winter. In contrast, the small amount of pollen substitute provides them with some protein, so they can rear some brood in late winter without building up as fast as they would with a regular pollen patty. Any time you feed your bees in winter, be sure to do it on a warm day or as quickly as possible to avoid chilling the bees. There usually is no perfect time of day to open a hive in the winter, but try to feed on days when the sun is shining, temperatures are mild, and there is little to no wind. Read: Feeding Protein In the Northeast, pollen is available from early March, sometimes late February, through the beginning of October. Depending on the weather variations year to year, and the species of flowering plants in your region, there can be periods during the bee season when there is a pollen dearth — a period of very low pollen availability. If your bees do not have enough pollen, you will see lots of dry larvae with little jelly and little pollen stored in the hive. In this case, you may decide to feed them bee bread, pollen, pollen supplements, or pollen substitutes. Timing is important: Supplementing brood rearing with pollen substitute in late winter and early spring can help a colony build up its population before spring nectar flows, allowing more bees to forage for nectar and produce more honey. Many beekeepers feed pollen substitute in late winter, usually starting in mid-February and continuing until mid-March if their goal is to produce strong colonies for making splits or spring pollination. In autumn, however, bees use the reduction in natural pollen as a cue to increase their production of winter bees. If fed pollen substitute to prolong the protein coming into the hive, a colony continues rearing summer bees until that incoming protein slows down. For this reason, it is not necessary to feed pollen substitute in September or October, as it continues to promote the production of short-lived summer bees; however, it is not harmful to the colony either. It is best if colonies have three to five frames of bee bread stored in the hive at the beginning of November, entering winter. If honey production is your goal, you want to time the growth of the forager population with the nectar flows in your region. Keeping in mind that it takes a worker bee 21 days to develop from an egg, and an additional 20 days or so until she has transitioned to become a forager, a mid-May nectar flow requires ample brood to develop by the beginning of April at the latest. It is advisable to start even earlier. Many beekeepers in the Northeast begin feeding pollen supplements or substitutes as early as February, when the colony starts building its population. Similarly, if you manage your bees for pollination services, you also may plan to supplement your colonies’ protein to stimulate brood rearing and guarantee the growers a minimum number of frames of bees. This should begin a minimum of 45 days before the crop in question is blooming if there is not a lot of brood already present. Again, it is advisable to start earlier if the crop your bees are pollinating blooms at a time when colonies may not be at their peak strength, such as apples in May. On the other hand, feeding may not be necessary if your bees are going to pollinate crops that bloom when colonies normally have strong forager populations, such as pumpkins in mid-July.

Lastly, if you are keeping honey bees for minimal pollination in your garden, modest honey production, and just the joy of working with bees, then you may not wish to feed protein in the spring to build strong colonies. Colonies naturally adjust their brood production in accordance with what pollen is available in the environment. We do, however, recommend feeding sugar syrup in spring, when the colony needs it, to keep it alive until regular nectar is coming in, and feeding protein if there is a strong summer pollen dearth in your region. In summary, feeding protein is recommended in the following situations, depending on your goals: In early spring, to kick-start brood production, if you want to build the strength of your colonies for summer. Beekeepers typically begin feeding pollen substitute five to six weeks before natural pollen is available. In spring or summer, if there is a local dearth of flowering plants, young larvae do not have adequate jelly in their cells. When rearing queens, for cell builders and mating nucs, if you do not have pollen frames to spare. Before, during, and after providing pollination services to ensure adequate nutrition, especially if the hives will be placed in an extensive monoculture field without much floral diversity. Preparing pollen supplement patties to feed colonies in early spring. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Protein Feeding Options There are several different options for supplementing your bees with protein. Stored Pollen As in feeding carbohydrates, the most straightforward way to feed bees protein is with frames of bee bread that you have saved from earlier in the season or taken from another colony (after making sure that they are pest- and disease-free). If you do not have extra frames on hand, pollen or pollen substitutes can help meet their protein, fat, vitamin, and mineral needs. Fresh pollen is the most nutritious of your options, and pollen substitutes the least. You can collect fresh pollen using a pollen trap during a pollen flow and then use it later during a dearth. There are a variety of models on the market, such as the Sundance™ pollen trap and the Superior Pollen Trap™. Most models have two settings, one to collect pollen “activated,” and one that allows foragers to bypass the trap and bring pollen into the hive, “inactivated.” In general, we recommend activating a trap only when you see many foragers returning with pollen baskets — 10 to 20 entering the hive per minute — and only for a few days at a time, with several days between uses. If you want to collect pollen for longer, you will need to provide the colony with a supplement or substitute to fulfill their protein requirements. Depriving the colony of too much pollen may slow their brood production or lead to malnourishment. Monitor your colonies regularly to ensure there is ample royal jelly around the larvae and that the colony is not under stress from the trap — perhaps overheating if the trap is blocking a screened bottom board or preventing adequate ventilation at the entrance. To store pollen to use later to feed your bees, dry and freeze it. Pollen can be lightly dried in a low-humidity room, spread out on a cookie sheet for a few days, placed in an open container in a frost-free freezer for a few weeks — the freezer draws out moisture — or dried in a food dehydrator. Pollen dried for too long in a food dehydrator can cause the pollen to become too dry and grainy, so care should be taken as to how long pollen is dried. Pollen is dry enough when it can be gently rubbed between your thumb and index finger without disintegrating into dust.

Once the pollen is dry, store it in sealed Ziploc bags in the freezer. Pollen stored at room temperature loses 76% of its nutritional value after one year, but dried and frozen, it can retain its nutritional properties for up to 11 years. We generally recommend keeping pollen trapped from each colony separate from each other, as pollen can contain disease spores and other contaminants. The easiest way to do this is to put all the pollen from one colony in a large Ziploc bag and label it. If you are harvesting pollen from many colonies and this practice is unrealistic, at the very least, make sure not to harvest pollen from colonies that are diseased or have experienced a pesticide poisoning event. To feed pollen to a colony, you can make a pollen patty by mixing the trapped or purchased pollen with sugar and water, two to three parts pollen to one part heavy sugar syrup, or enough to give it the consistency of dough), or you can pour pollen pellets into drawn comb and spray sugar water on the comb to make them stick in the cells. The bees will process it into bee bread. If you are purchasing pollen for feed, it is best to purchase irradiated pollen. This pollen has undergone a process to remove disease spores. Pollen Supplements Pure pollen is the most nutritious avenue to feed bees, but the second-best method is to provide them with a pollen supplement. Pollen supplements are a mixture of a pollen substitute — a product that contains no pollen — and natural pollen. The added pollen makes the supplement more attractive and nutritious to the bees, and they are more likely to consume it. To prepare a pollen supplement patty, mix pollen substitute purchased from a bee supply company with at least 10% pollen — preferably more — that you have trapped or purchased.

A pollen supplement patty placed on top of the brood box. Pollen Substitute Lastly, if you do not have pollen, you can feed bees the pollen substitute alone. There are a variety of protein substitutes available from bee equipment companies. Some examples include Bee Pro®, FeedBee®, MegaBee®, UltraBee®, and Pro Winter Patties® — this last one contains only a small amount of protein and is fed in late winter; see the previous section. Beekeepers have long made their own pollen substitutes — the most common ingredients being soy flour, skim milk powder, and dried brewer’s yeast — but this must be done with care, and we generally recommend purchasing substitutes from bee supply companies. Some ingredients must be quite specific to be safe for honey bees: for example, skim milk powder must be lactose-free since lactose is toxic to honey bees. Others must be processed in a specific way: for example, soy flour must be processed using the expeller method and heated to remove certain enzyme inhibitors that can be unhealthy to bees. Manufactured pollen substitutes are analyzed and tested to ensure that they contain the necessary amino acids and vitamins, minerals, and fats needed for optimal honey bee nutrition. These products can be fed to the bees in many ways, but they are most commonly

fed in a dry pollen feeder outside the hive (that the foragers find) or placed directly into the colony as a patty sandwiched between pieces of wax paper to retain its moisture. Honey bees collecting dry pollen substitute. Photo credit: Jennifer Tsuruda Protein Feeding Considerations When you are feeding bees protein in the colony, location is important. Place pollen patties directly above the brood nest so that they are accessible by nurse bees. If you are inserting pollen frames, the type of brood you place them beside matters. Bees are more likely to use protein that is adjacent to open larvae than protein next to capped brood. This stands to reason, as foragers usually deposit their pollen loads in cells adjacent to open larvae. Finally, feeding sugar syrup at the same time can also stimulate bees to eat the pollen. When feeding protein in late winter and early spring to promote early spring brood rearing, supply the bees continuously until they are regularly bringing in natural pollen to allow for the maintenance of brood that is already developing. Activity: Langstroth Hives: Not the Only Hive Design Available As a Master Beekeeper, it is important to be aware of the variety of hive designs available. The Langstroth hive is ubiquitous in North America and Europe, yet it is not the only hive design that supports healthy honey bee colonies worldwide. In this activity, you will be invited to explore various hive designs: top bar hive, flow hive, and more. As you explore different hive designs, you might discover one that works better for your beekeeping practice than the one you are currently using, most probably based on Langstroth hives. Alternatively, you will be introduced to the wide variety of hive designs throughout the world, and that variety often reflects geographical constraints. For example, most hives in Eastern Africa must be small because the Eastern Africa subspecies of Apis mellifera tend to swarm and abscond easily, and they are often hung from a tree because of the ravenous honey badgers that roam those lands. Instructions Take some time to investigate the origin of the Langstroth hive, the most popular hive design in North America and Europe, as well as the many other hive designs that humans across the world developed — make sure to look at the top-bar hives and the flow hives. Then, choose a hive design, grab a pen and paper, or open a Word document, and answer the following prompts: Describe the history of the design you chose to focus on. Compare the advantages/disadvantages of that design for a beekeeper. This activity is not graded. However, completing it will prepare you to complete and submit assignments later in the course. Module Introduction: Techniques in Managing Colony Population A colony's population changes throughout the season. Maximizing a colony's health and achieving your beekeeping goals requires understanding the needs of its changing population. In this module, we will provide an overview of managing colony population dynamics. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Annual Population Cycle of a Honey Bee Colony Successful beekeeping is fundamentally based on understanding the annual cycle of a honey bee colony. The population ebbs and flows with the seasons, and the division of young and old, male and female, summer and winter bees, changes over time. The following illustration demonstrates the population of a healthy honey bee colony in the Northeast that does not swarm. ⌃ Long description The graphic shows the rise and decline of the adult honey bee population throughout the winter. In January, the population is around 5,000, which steadily grows until it peaks in midJune at 40,000 to 50,000 bees. It then slowly declines until mid-August. After that, it takes a sharp decline, and once again reaches around 5,000 bees in December. In winter, the colony has a population of around 10,000 workers, which is steadily dropping. They are clustered in a ball about the size of a basketball, keeping the small brood nest warm. In mid to late January in the Northeast, the queen begins laying the first eggs of the new season. Around the first of March, the colony reaches its lowest population as the winter-bee cohort that emerged last fall dies off. But the brood increases steadily, tended to by these overwintered bees. The colony can consume up to one frame of pollen per week to sustain this brood rearing — all this before anything outside the hive is blooming.

With the first early blooms of the season and incoming nectar comes a rapid increase in brood rearing. The newly-emerged adults boost first the nurse, and then the forager population, and the colony grows very quickly, quadrupling or more by the end of June. This degree of growth requires favorable conditions. In some years, the availability of forage is delayed by poor weather, and colonies exit winter with a weak population. If resources are not available to support early colony growth, old winter bees can die off faster than new bees can replace them, and the colony population drops. This is referred to as “spring dwindling”, and it can imperil the survival of the colony. In this case, the beekeeper must intervene by feeding the colony until good forage is available and the bees are numerous enough to take advantage of it. As healthy colonies with plentiful resources grow rapidly in the spring, congestion in the nest can initiate swarming behavior. Thus, the period of most swarms here in the Northeast is from midMay to mid-July. As July winds down, the population begins to decline. It is not uncommon for there to be a dearth of nectar and pollen at this point in the summer. Brood rearing slows, and foragers born during the earlier “baby boom” die off. In some areas, there is a final fall flow with incoming nectar and pollen in August and September. This nectar can be critical for colonies to store for winter. The pollen helps provide a small increase in brood rearing, and the population experiences one final, small boost. At this point in time, from mid-August to mid-September, there is a second swarm season in this area. When incoming pollen starts to lessen, it is a signal for the colony to begin rearing winter bees. The summer bees die off, and brood rearing ceases around November. Winter weather typically arrives — and stays — in the middle of this month, with the colony again forming a cluster, and slowly decreasing in size until next January, when the cycle repeats itself. Back to Table of Contents

▶ ▶ Read: Reasons for Splitting Colonies In times of population increase or peaks, you may wish to split your colonies. Taking a strong colony and dividing it into two smaller colonies is a very simple practice, though there are steps to ensure that both resulting colonies (the splits) are healthy and productive. Once you are confident in making splits in your operation, you can become a much more self-sufficient beekeeper. There are a few reasons why you may want to split colonies: Replace Your Winter Losses Some degree of colony loss, especially over winter, is expected. In the U.S., beekeepers report that winter losses of around 17% are acceptable. These losses can be made up by purchasing more packages or nucs, but the most affordable option is splitting strong survival colonies. Beekeepers who replace their losses through splitting and manage these splits to become strong colonies that earn them acceptable profits are practicing sustainable beekeeping. Grow Your Operation Growing your operation through splitting colonies is a slower process than simply ordering many packages; however, it is arguably the best way to expand. Increasing slowly allows you to learn more about beekeeping, become comfortable adjusting to managing more colonies, and evaluate whether and when you need to hire help. Colonies can typically be split once a year if they are strong enough, but more than once a year may result in colonies that are too small or have too few resources to survive over winter. Prevent Swarming Splitting a colony is essentially an artificial swarm — taking around half of the bees and placing them in a new home. Splitting a colony can reduce the instinct for colonies to swarm, although it cannot always prevent it. If your colony has already produced many swarm cells, or if they are very genetically predisposed to swarm, they may swarm regardless. Splitting a colony to prevent swarming only helps if it has not yet begun swarm preparation, that is, before the queen has laid eggs in the swarm cells. ▶

▶ Reduce Varroa Mite Levels Performing splits to reduce Varroa mite levels has become increasingly popular in recent years. It is a treatment-free method that can be used on its own or in combination with other cultural or chemical treatments. Performing a split can be effective at reducing mite levels because it creates a break in the brood cycle in the part of the split that does not receive the queen. When the colony is broodless, Varroa mites are unable to reproduce, and their population decreases. The most effective way to use splitting to reduce Varroa levels is by removing the queen altogether and leaving both resulting colonies to rear their own queens. In this case, both colonies reap the benefits of an interruption in the brood cycle. Back to Table of Contents

Read: How To Make a Proper Split Making a split is simple. Splits should only be performed on strong colonies: crowded with bees and at least six frames of brood of any age and four frames of mixed food stores. Remove four to five frames and all the bees they contain from the original hive and insert them into a new hive body. Aim to move over two to three frames of brood (all stages) and two frames of food (honey and bee bread). Check each frame for the queen so you can make sure she remains in the original hive, or so you can remove her altogether if you want both colonies to rear their own queens. If you do not have at least one frame of pollen, cumulative from the food frames and the brood frames, for each of the two resulting colonies, you can supplement your colonies with pollen, pollen supplement, or pollen substitute. Insert a caged queen or a queen cell into the new colony, or let the colony rear a new queen. For the latter, there must be nurse bees, pollen, and eggs, to guarantee that there are larvae sufficiently young to still develop into queens; less than 36 hours. The easiest way to ensure there are young enough larvae is to have eggs present. Replace the now missing frames in your original colony with drawn comb or foundation. Put these in the end positions of the hive bodies regardless of where you pulled the other frames out from. It is best not to divide the remaining brood nest or to separate the brood nest from other frames of food stores. Similarly, add drawn comb frames or foundation to fill up the rest of the split. Drawn comb gives them a head start to fill them with stores and brood, but if you are uncertain about your comb sanitation, or do not have any on hand, you can use foundation. Feed your split, and add an entrance reducer for at least the first few weeks, just as you would for a newly established colony. Finally, shake three frames of nurse bees from the original colony into the split. It is important to have enough bees to keep that brood warm. Nurses congregate in the brood nest to accomplish this. The original colony was strong, so it should be able to tolerate the loss of these bees. If you are keeping this colony in the same bee yard, shake an additional frame of bees into your split. Any foragers in the split are going to fly back to the original colony, and you need to make sure enough bees will remain. The colony with fewer foragers will adjust as well as it can. Some nurse bees become early-onset foragers and start collecting pollen and nectar. The colony may build up its honey stores more slowly and needs to be fed before winter. If your goal is honey production and you have the land, we recommend moving splits into a separate bee yard at least two miles from the original colony. Any foragers in the split will learn their new surroundings and not travel back to their original colony. These foragers can start collecting nectar immediately. Should you transport your colonies that rear their own queens,

make sure you do it before the colony has begun rearing queen cells, as queens are very fragile during their development and may be injured during transportation. Return to the split two weeks later to see if the colony is getting established and whether the queen is laying. A strong colony (top) can be split into two smaller colonies (bottom). ⌃ Long description The graphic shows how a strong colony can be split into two smaller colonies. The top of the strong colony has frames one through three filled with honey, frame four filled with pollen, frames five and six filled with open or capped brood, frames seven and eight are filled with pollen, and frames nine and ten are filled with honey. The bottom of the strong colony has

frame one filled with honey, frame two filled with honey, frame three filled with pollen, frames four through seven filled with open and capped brood, frame eight filled with pollen, and frames nine and ten filled with honey. The two split hives have one stack of frames. Each has frame one as a syrup feeder frame, frame two is drawn comb/foundation, frame three is pollen, frames four through six are filled with open/capped brood, frame seven is pollen, frames eight and nine are drawn comb/foundation, and frame ten is honey. Ours is comprised of two deep hive bodies but you can certainly split a strong colony in one deep hive body as well. The first thing we do is separate the hive bodies and look for the queen. Once we find her, we're going to put her in a cage for safekeeping. And we can't forget to put her back into the original colony at the end. Our goal here is to move over the following frames from our parent colony. Two to three frames of brood, one frame of honey, two frames of pollen and then fill the remaining spaces with drawn comb. So here is a good brood frame. We got capped brood on top, larvae on the bottom, some eggs. In here is a really good honey frame. We got capped honey on the top with some open nectar on the bottom. And here is an example of our pollen frame. So we can see some pollen in here. Okay so let's assemble our split. First we're going to put a feeder frame in the number one position and we're going to fill this with light sugar syrup. After that, we're going to put in a frame of drawn comb, followed by a pollen frame. After this one, we're going to put in three frames of capped brood. And even though you can't see it in this video I continue to fill up this box to make sure that we have another pollen frame, two more frames of drawn comb and then a final frame of honey in the number ten position. And we're going to shake about four frames of additional bees in it to help keep all that brood warm that we just transferred over. You can introduce a clean cell or clean cage between the two frames of brood but we're going to let this colony rear its own queen. Because it's a small colony, we're going to add an entrance reducer and we're going to move it into another yard over two miles away. So, Eleanor is going to take this box after it has been stapled to the bottom board and move it. Regardless of whether the colony is rearing its own queen or if you're introducing one we recommend leaving the colony for a bed of week without opening it. So the bees have some time to adjust and not be disturbed. After one week, it's good practice to come back and check on it to make sure that all is well in your split. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Alternate Ways to Split a Colony There are many alternate ways to split a colony, but the method that we describe in this course is the easiest, requires the least equipment, and is the least time-consuming. Other methods may not require you to find the queen in advance, but require multiple trips to the bee yard. We encourage you to try different variations and see what works best for you in your operation. All splits are based on the same few principles: The new “mini” colony must have all the necessary resources: brood, honey, bee bread, nurses, and foragers. The original colony needs to retain these resources, too — you do not want to deplete it as you want to end up with two functioning colonies. The colony with fewer resources and foragers may need to be fed. Foragers that are moved into the split will likely return to the original colony if the split is not moved at least two miles away. Nurse bees are required to tend to the brood in the split. The split needs to be provided with a new queen or rear its own. To rear one, eggs need to be present in the new colony. The best time to perform splits is early in the beekeeping season, around the same time as swarm season. In the Northeast, this is April through June. Splitting early allows bees to have time to build their population and collect food for several months, which increases their chances of overwintering successfully. If you wish to split later in the season, monitor the new colony closely and feed them as needed so they can build sufficient stores and a large population for winter. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Nucleus Colonies Nucleus colonies (nucs) are small colonies contained in small hive bodies with only two to five frames. They are created by pulling frames and bees from larger colonies. Nucleus colonies are good to have on hand for extra resources — brood, eggs, nurse bees, honey, bee bread, or queens — and we encourage beekeepers to keep a few "resource nucs" for this purpose throughout the beekeeping season. Nucs can also be used for mating queens that you have reared or sold for profit. Lastly, they can be very useful for queen introductions. If you have a failing queen in one of your colonies and plan to replace her, it is good practice to place her in a nuc rather than killing her. This way, if the colony rejects your new queen, you can temporarily place the failing queen back into the colony until you are ready to order a new one or try again. While there are many benefits to making nucs, they do require maintenance. If bees and resources are not taken from a nucleus colony and its population continues to grow, it may swarm. Swarming preparations usually begin once the nuc has reached a strength of four to five frames of bees. To delay swarming, a frame of brood can be swapped with drawn comb from another hive. Some beekeepers use their nucs to establish new full-size colonies. This has a double benefit of preventing swarming and of growing their operation. Nucs are ready to be inserted into an 8 to 10 frame hive body once they have reached four to five frames of bees. After the colony has grown for three to four weeks in a full-sized hive under favorable conditions in spring and early summer, you can pull another nuc out of it. In this way, you can continually grow your operation and have nucleus colonies on hand. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: How to Make a Nuc Watch this video to learn the proper procedure and considerations for making a nucleus colony. Video Transcript Let's go through the process of making a nucleus colony. We're going to start out with a very strong colony that's at least in one deep hive body. And, in this example, ours is actually very strong, it's across three deep hive bodies. We start out with an empty nucleus colony, and we're going to separate the hive bodies of our strong colony, so that we can see what resources we have to work with. And here we have Eleanor in the bee yard helping us assemble this nuc. So we first put in one frame of honey right at the edge of nuc box. And we're going to follow this up with a frame of drawn comb. The drawn comb is going to give the queen more space to lay, or for the colony to fill it with food stores. It'll take time to fill up this frame, so the colony won't swarm in the very near future. After this the next frame we are going to add is a frame of brood. And this frame contains mixed brood, there is capped brood, open larvae and eggs. The frame after that is going to be another brood frame. In this case this one has much more capped brood to contribute to the colonies population once it emerges. The last frame we're going to add is a frame of pollen. In this case, this frame is only partially filled with pollen, and the rest is simply drawn comb. Again, giving the bees a bit more space to work with. And some beekeepers will forego the frame of pollen altogether, in favor of a full frame of drawn comb or foundation. Having more drawn comb gives the colony more room to grow and can prolong the time it takes for a bee keeper to perform more management. And we here are providing a frame of pollen because we want the nuc to rear its own queen and it needs protein to do so. With a nuc, we don't shake additional bees into the box, we want them to grow their own mini colony slowly. So we put on the lid and we'll be moving it to another bee yard to minimize the amount of bees that will fly back to the parent colony. Back to Table of Contents

Read: The Composition of Constructed Nucs Your constructed nuc should have the following frames in these positions: ⌃ Long description The graphic shows the orientation you should have your frames in for a constructed nuc. There are five frames. Frame one is honey, frame two is drawn comb, frames three and four are mixed brood, and frame five is pollen. While we give this formula for making nucs, the formula can vary depending on the resources you have available and the amount of time you can afford to spend managing your nucs. For instance, some beekeepers do not provide a frame of pollen but will instead provide a frame of foundation to slow the growth of the colony before they need to conduct swarm prevention measures. Bees are quite resilient animals and can tolerate variations in nuc arrangements, so follow this procedure as a guide, but don't feel obligated to always follow it to a tee. Double Nucleus Colony A double nucleus colony is the size of a standard deep Langstroth hive body but can house two four-frame nucs separated by a solid divider board. The double nucleus box has two entrances, on opposite sides from each other, so that each colony has an entrance. Having entrances on opposite sides reduces the chance of bees drifting from one nuc colony to the other.

Double nucleus colonies made up in spring or early summer can be supered once they have nearly filled their frames of drawn comb and have drawn out and partially filled any frames of foundation. Before adding a super, add a queen excluder. Workers from both nucleus colonies contribute to honey production in the shared super above. Supers are usually removed in early fall, and the two nucleus colonies overwintered in the double nuc box. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Wintering Nucs Many beekeepers also make up nucs in mid to late summer, overwinter them, and use the surviving ones the following spring to replace any full-sized colonies that perished over the winter. This is a good way to be more self-sufficient and potentially save money. Creating nucs in mid to late summer has the added advantage of breaking the brood cycle and reducing Varroa mite levels. In general, nucleus colonies do not winter quite as well as full-sized colonies because they do not form as big a cluster. Nevertheless, it is possible to overwinter many nucs and have them available for next spring. The most success in overwintering nucs is to make sure they have a strong population of four or five frames of bees entering winter. The cluster should be about the size of a football, compared to a basketball-sized cluster for full-sized colonies. Nucs also require two full frames of honey to consume during winter. In mid-September, feed a heavy syrup to build up these carbohydrate stores if they are low. The colony's final weight should be close to 50 pounds. There are three common ways to overwinter nucs in North America. We encourage you to try one or more methods and find the style that works best for you. 1. A double nucleus colony can be placed on top of a strong full-sized colony in early November. In the southern U.S., where winters are milder, nucs are often separated from the full-sized colony by a double screen board or a screened inner cover to prevent bees from mingling between the two colonies. Heat generated by the bottom colony can pass through the screen and help warm the cluster in the nucleus colonies. However, moisture from the bottom colony may also rise upward into the nuc, so this practice is less common in the Northeast and Canada, where lower temperatures generate more moisture. In the Northeast, double nucleus colonies are often placed on top of a strong full-sized colony, separated by a regular bottom board. Some heat can still transfer to the top colony. It is important that the bottom colony has an upper entrance to provide ventilation and to allow bees to perform their cleansing flights in the event the bottom entrance gets plugged with bees. It is also important that upper ventilation be provided to the nucleus colonies, usually in the form of a small hole drilled into the top half of the box and covered with mesh wire. The nucleus colonies are usually provided with insulation board placed on top of their covers and along the two longest sides, and are wrapped in tar paper. 2. A nucleus colony can overwinter on its own or can be placed adjacent to or stacked on top of other nucleus colonies to share some heat. It is usually provided with insulation and wrapped in the same manner as a full-sized colony, and is left outside, sheltered from the wind.

3. Nucleus colonies can be overwintered indoors, where they are less susceptible to temperature fluctuations and cold and do not require wrapping or colony insulation. Indoor wintering facilities are more common in the Canadian prairies, but some U.S. beekeepers will use them as well. Indoor wintering facilities should be maintained at 39°F to 41°F, dark, and ventilated to remove excess water vapor and carbon dioxide produced by the colonies. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Merging Colonies Overview If you find that one of your colonies has a small population in late summer or early fall, fewer than eight frames of bees per brood chamber hive body, you may wish to merge this colony with another to give those bees a better chance of surviving. Before merging colonies, you need to ask why the colony is weak in the first place. Rule out the possibility of disease as best you can with a thorough inspection. The last thing you want to do is introduce a disease from your weak colony into your strong, healthy one. Look for brood diseases and any other indication that your bees may be sick. Know your levels of Nosema and Varroa, which cannot be interpreted by a visual inspection alone. If you are unsure how to measure disease levels yourself, you can send a sample to the USDA Beltsville Bee Lab in Maryland for a free analysis. The colony may have been weak due to a failing queen, poor nutrition, predation, etc.; just be sure it was nothing contagious. Now you can get to the main event. You can merge two weak colonies, a weak colony with a strong colony, a nuc with another full-sized hive, or a newly caught swarm with another colony. Indeed, if you catch a swarm anytime from mid-July to September in the Northeast, we recommend merging it with another colony, as it likely will not have time to prepare for winter on its own. Merging is most often done in late summer or early fall when beekeepers are starting to prepare their colonies for winter. By this time, you should know which colonies are strong and which ones should be merged to boost their chances of survival. Merging can also be done in spring if you have one or more colonies that are weak coming out of winter, often from spring dwindling, when the population of winter bees is dying at a higher rate than new bees are emerging. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Merging Colonies — The Newspaper Method The easiest way to merge colonies is the newspaper method. If two colonies are merged and the bees from those colonies interact with each other immediately, they are likely to attack each other and the queen(s). The colonies need to meet gradually and become accustomed to each other’s odors to accept each other as nest mates. To prolong their introduction, separate the colonies with newspaper. ⌃ Long description

The graphic shows a stacked hive with two boxes containing a strong colony at the bottom and one box with a weak colony at the top. They are separated by a red line, which indicates a newspaper. Frame ten in the weak colony is a honey or a syrup feeder. It will take the bees a few days to chew through. By the time they do, their odors will have mingled, and they will be more likely to accept each other. Remove the queen from one colony. Consider making a nuc colony with her, to keep a nuc on hand, or in case the other queen is killed in the merge. If you are uniting two weak colonies, you can choose which queen you want to keep or let them fight it out. Remove the outer and inner covers from the other hive, the one you will add bees to. This colony usually has the queen you want to keep in it if it is the stronger colony. Place one or two layers of newspaper on top of the open colony. Do not let newspaper hang over the edge; in the event of rain, it can bring moisture into the colony. If the week’s forecast calls for hot weather, cut a slit in the newspaper with a razor or scissors to improve ventilation. Do not use a hive tool, as the slit it creates is too large and allows bees from the two colonies to mingle too quickly. Rearrange the frames in the queenless hive so that they are consolidated to one deep — or two mediums if you use only mediums in your operation — with brood, honey, and bee bread. Shake all the bees into this single box. Place this hive on top of the newspaper. If you do not have at least one frame of honey in this hive, add one from another healthy colony or supplement it with sugar syrup. This colony will not be able to fly freely for a few days, so you need to supply it with food. Make sure there are no other entrances for the bees to use. If there are, seal them up. Leave the combined colony alone for one full week. The bees will begin to chew through the newspaper and begin mingling in one to two days. At the end of the week, check on the colony to make sure the bees have chewed through the newspaper and are mingling in harmony. Confirm that the queen is alive and laying. Foragers from the merged colony will continue to gather at the location the hive used to be. If they are gentle, they will find their way into other colonies on their own. If they are defensive, you can collect them by placing an empty super or hive body in the old location, returning at night when the bees are inside, and killing them with soapy water. Continue to catch them this way every day until they cease to be a problem. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Merging Colonies Watch this video to see a merge being performed between two colonies. Video Transcript Alright. So we're going to merge a weak colony with a strong one. The weak colony was originally in two hive bodies. But we actually consolidated it into one hive body by rearranging some frames and shaking all the bees inside. Because it's much easier to merge a colony that's in one hive body compared to two. But before we even started thinking about merging these colonies, we gave the weak colony a very thorough inspection to make sure it didn't have any disease symptoms. And we determined that the colony was weak because the queen was failing. So here the weak colony is on the right and the strong colony is on the left. We want the queen from the strong colony to remain, so we're going to remove the queen from the weak colony, before we get started. Eleanor found it here in the frame and we're going to put it in a cage. And I like to transfer here temporarily into a nuc in case the queen from the strong colony gets injured or killed during the merge, I have a backup queen. Next, we're going to lay a single sheet of newspaper on top of the strong colony and cut a small slit in it to give the bees a head start at chewing through the paper and to allow the colony's odors to begin mixing. Then we place the weak colony on top of the newspaper. We have ensured that this hive body has at least one full frame of honey in it. Because the bees won't be able to exit the hive for a couple of days, they need to have food available to tide them over until they have successfully merged. The last step is to trim the edges of the newspapers so that there isn't any paper sticking out between the colonies. We do this because, if it happens to rain, the newspaper will actually absorb the water and bring it into the colony. And we don't want excess moisture getting into these hives. After one week, we're going to open up the weak colony and peer down to verify that the newspaper has been chewed through, and that the two colonies are successfully mingling as one. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Merging a Nuc With an 8 to 10 Frame Colony This can be accomplished in two ways: 1. Take all the frames out of a nuc and place them in a deep. Fill up the rest of the frames with drawn comb, making sure that they have at least one frame of honey for food to tide them over until they have merged. Proceed with the newspaper method. If you are performing this merge in spring, simply allow the colony to grow into those additional combs. If you are performing the merge later in the year, such as late summer, feed heavily to encourage the bees to fill the additional combs with food in preparation for winter. 2. Take the frames out of the nuc and place them in a full-sized deep without adding any additional frames. Proceed with the newspaper method. After the bees chew through the newspaper, you will need to consolidate the best frames from the nuc and the uniting colony so that they fit in a standard-sized hive. Four or five frames will be left over. They can be stored or used for other colony management. Back to Table of Contents
