Module Wrap-up: Techniques in Managing Colony Population In this module, you examined how colony populations shift throughout the seasons and how these changes influence colony health. Understanding these population dynamics will help you to better manage your colonies and achieve your beekeeping objectives. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Swarming Swarming is the subject of books, debates, folklore, and more. Most beekeepers today try to prevent swarms and keep their bees where they want them, with strong populations making lots of honey. Swarming can cost beekeepers a honey crop, inadvertently spread pests or disease, cause fear and consternation among the public, and risk the survival of the parent colony if the new queen does not develop and mate properly. Furthermore, it can be difficult to prevent if early signs or triggers are not recognized. On the other hand, with careful management and a little bit of luck, swarming can also be a way to expand your colony count, provide a brood break for managing Varroa mites or other maladies, requeen with a minimum of fuss, and/or spread the genes of relatively fit colonies around in the local environment. Swarms may also present an opportunity to you as a Master Beekeeper to educate the public. In this module, we will take a comprehensive look at swarming. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Colony-Level Reproduction — Swarming Swarming is colony-level reproduction, when one- to two-thirds of a colony’s population — up to tens of thousands of bees — leave to found a new colony. The swarm consists of worker bees of all ages and a small percentage of drones, and it includes the colony’s queen. It leaves behind developing queen cells for the original colony to requeen itself. The original colony experiences a long break in the brood cycle as a new queen emerges, reaches sexual maturity, takes her mating flight(s), and begins laying eggs. It takes about six weeks for new bees to emerge in the original colony. In this video, Tom Seeley discusses the process of swarming. Video Transcript What I want to share with you now is some information about swarming. And one thing I want to emphasize right at the get go, is that swarming is completely natural and it's good for a honey bee colony. It actually helps them with their disease control but even more importantly it's a natural part of a colony's reproductive process, colonies reproduce by swarming. So even though in your beekeeping classes you may have been taught that you want to prevent swarming - you want to take on this measure or that measure to stop swarming, you don't have to do that and you can let colonies swarm and your colonies will actually be a little better for them. They may not make as much honey but they'll be healthier. How does swarming work? Well the starting point is when a colony becomes strong enough to divide and reproduce itself. When it does, and that's usually in May or June. The nurse bees in the colony start rearing additional queens and they also interestingly put the mother queen on a diet. She will need to lose 30% of her body weight so that she can fly when the swarm leaves the hive. At the same time as the nurse bees are doing their thing, some of the foragers, some of the oldest foragers, start going out of the hive and no longer going to flowers but looking in the woods for potential nest sites and these are the nest-site scouts. And then a week or so later after those things have started on a day of good weather, the nest-site scouts who are outside, sensing that the weather conditions are good, trigger the bees that will be in the swarm to leave the nest and they fly out en mass and form the swarm cluster. From here, the nest-site scouts continue their process of choosing the home site. And once they finish choosing that home site, that can take a day or two, the nest-site scouts then organize the movement of the swarm to launch into flight and fly to its new home. And, that's the end of that swarming process. Meanwhile, back in the original nest of course, the young queens are emerging and if the colony is still strong because a lot of brood has emerged, the colony can emit an after swarm. But if the colony is actually weak at that point, the workers just let the new queens fight it out among themselves to see who will inherit the old nest. One thing I want to stress about the activity of the scout bees is that as they choose the swarms new home to set up the new colony, this is a life or

death decision. Because they have to find a home site that gives their new colony good protection. Now a dream home for honey bees has a couple of key features. One is that the cavity that they move into is sufficiently spacious. It has to be 1 to 1.5 cubic feet of volume to give the bees enough room for their combs, for having a good brood nest, enough space to store up the 40 or 50 pounds of honey the colony needs to get through the winter. So, cavity volume is critical. What they are seeking is about the size of one deep hive body. The other thing that also matters is the entrance. And the entrance has to be ideally for the bees. It's high off the ground. At least ten or 15 feet up off the ground. And this means that it's well above the snow level in the winter. It may make it less vulnerable to predators like bears. They also like the entrance to be small, so it's not a drafty home site, and it can be defended easily against things like yellow jackets, wasps. And they like the entrance to face south. Probably, I'm not sure, but probably because that helps the bees do their cleansing flights in the winter, if the entrance is sunny and southerly. I'll say a little bit about how the scouts actually make their decision, how they make the choice of their new home. It's a competition among scout bees that have found different sites. And it's a competition that's done by the bees adjusting the strength of the dances that they produce to advertise the site that they're visiting. I want to stress this is a friendly competition. All of these scout bees, have the shared interest of finding the best site for the colony's new home, for the swarm's new home. But it is a competition. And, the way it works is the bees adjust their dancing. That is, to say, how long a bee will perform a dance to advertise the site is adjusted to the goodness of the site. The better the site, the longer the dance. And, this means that, the discussion or the debate might start out with two bees coming back from two sites. One better, one poorer The bee coming back, the scout coming back from the better site will do a dance that lasts three minutes. And the bee coming back from the poor site, a dance that lasts only one minute. Well if you came back a few hours later, you would find that there are many more bees dancing for the better site than the poor site, because there were many more bees that were able to attend the dance of the Bee from the better site. And the process then snowballs in favor of the better site because of the positive feedback of the buildup of the bees, the scouts for the better site. And all of those bees are still dancing three times as stronger, more strongly from the poor site. And finally, the process ends when one of the sites attracts enough, has reached what we call the quorum. One of the sites has accumulated enough scout bees visiting it, that the scout at that site can sense, they look around, they see there's lots of scout bees here, that means this site has had a lot of interest, sufficient interest to tell them that that site is going to should be chosen for their new home. Once the quorum has been reached, the swarm flies as a group to the new nest site. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Swarming Timing and Initiation The timing of swarms follows a seasonal pattern. Mid-May is the beginning of the major swarm season for the Northeast and Ithaca, NY, more specifically. Nearly 80% of swarms issue between mid-May and mid-July. Warm, clear, and calm days tend to be especially “swarmy”; even more so if they follow a few days of bad weather. A modest number of swarms issue during a smaller, second swarm season from mid-August to mid-September. These later swarms, if captured, require much feeding and care to store enough food and grow in population to overwinter successfully. Because so many factors contribute to population buildup and floral resources, some years see more swarms than others. Swarming is stimulated by crowding of adult bees in the entire hive or crowding by brood in the brood nest. In other words, swarming is initiated when there are high numbers of bees relative to the size of the hive. Bees can perceive this crowding in several ways, including a lack of ventilation or raised temperatures within the hive. Their perception of crowding is also related to a decline in the concentration of queen mandibular pheromone (QMP), the pheromone that signals that the colony is queenright. This decline may be due to its dilution across a large population or because the brood nest is plugged with bee bread and nectar and the queen is restricted from laying (laying affects the amount of pheromone she produces). Abundant food resources coming in, whether through a nectar flow or through feeding, may also prompt swarming. As in many of the relationships among population, communication, and resources within a hive, this one is redundant: If resources are so abundant as to fill up the brood nest, thereby restricting laying, causing the amount of queen pheromone to decrease, and stimulating swarming, they are also abundant enough to support a colony that will lose a significant proportion of its workers and the honey they load up on before they leave the hive. Crowding and an abundance of resources are common conditions, particularly as colony populations build in spring. Because they are not managed to prevent it, feral colonies are estimated to swarm nine years out of ten. This may also be the case because of the smaller cavity size of most feral colonies. Finally, some subspecies and stocks swarm more than others. Africanized honey bees swarm more often than their European counterparts, although often with smaller numbers of bees. This is partly because their populations tend to grow faster. They also migrate by way of swarming, often for long distances, which partly explains how quickly they moved north after their initial release in Brazil. Russian bees are known for swarming as well. German and Buckfast bees generally swarm the least. Back to Table of Contents

Read: The Preparation and Process of Swarming Since ancient times, beekeepers have recognized that the process of swarming is the way honey bee colonies propagate themselves. Before the invention of moveable-frame hives that allow beekeepers to do splits and utilize other techniques for increasing their operation size, apiaries were increased chiefly by collecting and/or managing swarms. There are benefits to keeping bees in this way. When it swarms, a colony accomplishes more than just reproduction: Swarming requeens the mother colony (since the old queen is the one that leaves with the swarm), and requeening is an act known to reduce symptoms associated with several bee diseases. It promotes a brood break in both the mother colony and the swarm (daughter colony) that can help reduce mite loads in both. The swarm leaves behind toxins and pathogens that may have accumulated in the mother hive. It provides an opportunity for the swarm to settle in a more suitable location. Every swarm after the first one — and there may be three or four afterswarms, depending on the weather and strength of the colony — is headed by a young queen, ready to work hard to grow her new colony. In northeastern North America, some swarms start to issue in mid-May, but the swarm season really begins in earnest during June. To learn which colonies will be likely to swarm, inspections should begin during April or May, as soon as the weather becomes favorable and dandelions are in bloom. Signals that stimulate the swarm impulse Colonies begin reproducing when environmental conditions are favorable to support the new “daughter” colony’s rapid growth and ample food storage before winter comes. This period typically begins in spring. The strength of a colony’s swarm impulse, as we currently understand it, might be described as the sum of several trigger signals. Assuming that the weather has become favorable, meaning that nectar and pollen are abundantly entering the hive, the chief signals appear to be: The rapid growth in the number of workers and amount of comb The resulting abundance of young adult bees Congestion in the brood nest The reduced transmission of queen pheromone When these signals collectively reach some as-yet-undefined threshold, the colony begins its swarm preparations. We don’t yet understand how the different signals combine in different ways to trigger these swarm preparations. For example, a colony ▶

▶ under a young queen might grow vigorously in plenty of space and then swarm, while a neighboring colony that appears to be very similar in these same respects does not swarm. Why? Less-visible signals caused one colony to prepare to swarm but not the other. These differences could include faster transition from nurse to worker bee in the non-swarming colony (resulting in less abundant nurses; i.e., “young adult bees”) or a better laying pattern conducive to less brood nest congestion. These less-obvious changes have caused many experienced beekeepers to fail to recognize when certain colonies are about to begin swarm preparations. Drone brood is produced A strong colony with many workers and worker brood in May will be building abundant drone brood, while a weak one will have little, if any, drone brood. Queens will not be raised and swarming will not occur in the absence of mature drones. Also, as soon as virgin queens reach sexual maturity, they need drones to mate in their environment so that they can begin laying worker brood as soon as possible. Although virgins do not mate with drones from their own colony, bee colonies are all depending on drones to mate with their virgins that other colonies provide. Therefore, the timing for drone production must precede that of queen production. An immature drone develops, pupates, and emerges in 24 days, but that newly emerged drone is still immature and unable to fly or mate. At about nine to 12 days of age, drones are sexually mature and are ready to mate. Thus, the time taken from when the first drone eggs are laid until those drones are able to mate with a virgin queen is, at a minimum, 33 to 36 days. However, it only takes 16 days for a queen to fully develop and emerge, and she sexually matures and is ready to leave the hive on her mating flight about one week later. So we expect to start seeing the colony produce drone brood at least 10 to 13 days before the earliest queen cells appear.

▶ ▶ The hive becomes congested Congested hive conditions that initiate swarm cell production include: Worker volume (the space worker bees occupy) is greater than the free volume of the hive (there are more than 2.3 workers per mL of hive space). The volume of workers can be so high that bees will congregate outside the hive at night in these conditions. More than 90% of the brood comb is in use (unavailable for egg-laying). There is a large proportion of young (nurse) bees in the colony. Colonies preparing to swarm are often seen to have workers crowded into the brood area, even when there is room for them elsewhere in the nest. Not all congested colonies build swarm cells, and some colonies with plenty of space do build swarm cells! It turns out that all three of the above conditions must meet some as-yet-undefined threshold before swarm cells are built and other preparations for swarming commence. Queen cells are produced The next swarm preparation is the most obvious one for the beekeeper to recognize: the production of many queen cells! Workers construct plenty of queen cups in response to the perceived decline in QMP and to the other triggers we mentioned earlier. The queens also perceive the decline in QMP (as it returns to them after it has been distributed throughout the colony), and this stimulates them to lay eggs in queen cups, which then become queen cells. Empty queen cups are generally present whether or not a colony is preparing to swarm; their presence along the lower third of the frames, including between hive bodies, is part of the normal “architecture” of a hive. But bees ramp up the production of these cups during the preparation of the swarming process. However, the presence of cups on their own is not a signal of an imminent preparation to swarm; what matters is whether there is an egg or larva inside one or more. Queen cells for swarming can be very numerous (there are usually at least 10), and are referred to as “swarm cells” due to the time of their appearance, their location along the lower edges of the brood nest, and their generally — though not always — large size. The stronger the colony, the more swarm cells are constructed. The colony often does not wait for a new virgin to emerge before it swarms; in fact, they usually swarm shortly after at least one of the new queen cells has been capped and before a virgin has emerged. If the larva in a queen cell is two days old, for example, the colony could

swarm as early as one week later. If one or more of the queen cells are capped, the colony has probably swarmed already. This fact makes it very important for the beekeeper to locate a mature queen in the hive before cutting out all of the swarm cells! It is unclear why swarm cells are often produced in large numbers, when at best only three or four queens from that number may eventually head up a colony. It is often said among beekeepers that workers will “select the best queen from a number of queen cells," and this may, in a sense, be true, as the first queen to emerge will kill all her sisters if she finds them. Queens about to emerge will pipe (make a chirping sound) in their cells, and these shrill calls may provoke any emerged queens to find and kill the singer. This murderous phenomenon favors the genetics of early maturation among queens: she who emerges first has the best chance of surviving. Selection over many generations thus favors queens that emerge in less and less time. This is a desirable feature if a queenless colony must rear an emergency replacement! But if that first queen kills her unemerged sisters, how can there be afterswarms? Afterswarms only occur in very large and strong colonies. Perhaps the sheer size of a large colony containing many swarm cells reduces the likelihood that the first virgin queen to emerge will be able to locate and destroy all her competition, thereby leaving enough cells for subsequent afterswarms. Another possibility is that the workers may control the behavior of their queens in ways we as yet have not observed and do not understand. Meanwhile, the drones continue to develop their flight ability until they are able to congregate at drone congregation areas, at which point they are competent to mate with virgin queens. Scout bees begin to look for nest sites In addition to raising queens and drones, scout bees begin to search for suitable nesting sites well in advance of the swarming event. Scout bees are almost all foragers, ▶

▶ but instead of looking for bright flowers that offer food, they start seeking out dark crevices that could be good nest sites. How scouts are recruited and which workers assume the job of scouting is unknown. The queen prepares to leave To produce all those additional workers needed for a colony to swarm, the old queen must be in full production mode. This means that she is devoting most of her body’s energy to egg production and egg-laying, and it means that her abdomen is heavy with eggs. To be ready to fly with the swarm, the queen must make physical changes. A few days before the swarm is cast, the queen reduces or sometimes even stops laying eggs. Her physiology alters: New eggs do not mature in her ovaries or descend the oviducts, and she becomes thinner and more restless on the combs, preparing herself for flight. The queen’s retinue of attendant workers assists in her weight-loss process. One way in which they do this is to decrease feeding the queen. Another way is to “vibrate” the queen by hanging onto her forelegs while rapidly moving their abdomens up and down — a “shake” that alerts her to change activity — over a period of about two weeks. Workers will also vibrate each other in this way prior to swarming. Back to Table of Contents

▶ Read: The Swarm Event Bees prefer to swarm when the day is sunny and calm, and when temperatures are between 75 and 85° F (24 to 29° C). A beekeeper observing a strong colony with little activity at the entrance on the chosen day when nearby colonies are busily at work could reasonably expect that colony is about to swarm. As the swarming impulse reaches its peak, with ample pollen and nectar coming in, plenty of worker bees and brood, and both drones and queen cells in the hive, the bees will be inside on the combs, engorging themselves with honey in preparation for their journey. The old queen’s restlessness is communicated to the whole colony by her rapid movements over the combs. The workers also cause some commotion, piping and performing “buzz-runs” where they briefly dash through a crowd of bees, vibrating their wings. Such a colony becomes noisy. The bees flying outside face the entrance, where some are seen flying in and out. Generally, between the hours of 11 AM and 3 PM, they depart in a mass exodus that is awesome to observe. As the swarm issues from the hive, you can stand beside the flurry of activity and the bees will simply ignore you. Forming a temporary cluster The emerging swarm has not yet decided where their new “home” will be. During the time needed to choose a permanent nesting site, the swarming bees cluster temporarily with their queen, usually on a tree branch not too far from where they emerged. Bees mark this location with Nasonov pheromone to help the members of the cluster orient to it. This temporary cluster is called a bivouac. In apiaries that have existed in the same location for many years, beekeepers report that emerging swarms use these same temporary cluster sites over and over again — a useful tip for the apiculturist who hopes to collect swarms! Because the temporary cluster site is not protected, the bees must hurry to find a suitable place to set up their new colony. If they are unable to find a good shelter, they will build their combs in the open. Such colonies do not survive Northeastern winters. In the wild (absence of beekeepers and buildings), the places bees choose are often

▶ hollow trees, but they also consider other locations such as crevasses in rock outcroppings. With knowledge of the type of shelter bees are seeking, beekeepers can lure swarms into “bait boxes.” Scout bees are looking for specific features in their new home. We will cover these details further along in this module. Evaluating potential nest sites There are about 200 to 300 scouts in each swarm. They fly from the temporary cluster to search in all directions. Although scouts begin searching for new nesting sites before the swarm emerges, the final decision is made after the swarm has formed its temporary cluster. The scout bees spend time examining each site very thoroughly. They fly around the interior of the cavity, inspecting every nook and cranny. When a scout locates a place she is enthusiastic about, she returns to the cluster and performs a waggle dance on its surface. Without the vibratory properties of a brood comb, this dance message doesn’t penetrate the swarm very well. It is no small matter to communicate with up to 20,000 clustered bees! The ones in the middle of the cluster will have no idea that dances are happening at the surface and won’t get any messages. Compounding this problem is that other scouts may also come back with information about other good sites. They also convey their information through dance on the swarm’s surface. How does the colony learn which spot is the best one? How do they know to leave their bivouac and go to that place? To convince the colony that she has located a good home, a scout must recruit some of her sisters to return to the potential nest site with her. By flying to and fro, and by dancing to recruit more bees to visit, she can eventually persuade as many as 5% of her sisters to become enthused about that new place. They return to advertise the same site through dance. The more recruits that dance, the more bees are persuaded to check out that place the dance tells them about. A less desirable spot will produce lackluster recruitment and fewer dancers. Some of the new recruits remain at the location and spend their time marking it with Nasonov pheromone. Departing for their new home ▶

Eventually, all the dancers stop dancing and force their way into the cluster of bees, piping or “quacking” as they go. This high-pitched sound is made by wing muscles, and it is transmitted to all the bees the piping scout comes into contact with. Each bee that is contacted in this way begins to raise her body temperature, as hanging in an exposed bivouac for a while can cause them to get a bit cool. Within about 10 minutes, the entire colony has heated up and is ready to fly. When the swarm reaches an internal temperature of about 95° F (35° C), the bees leave, suddenly, with a tremendous buzzing roar. They form a large, loose cloud that becomes organized by the scouts, who fly back and forth in a straight line through it. The axis of their flight path indicates the direction the swarm will take. As more and more bees recognize the flight path, the swarm shapes itself into a thick cigar, and off they go to their new address! A swarm may only take a few hours to find a suitable nesting site or it may be hanging onto a branch for several days before flying off to its new home. The scouts’ process of evaluating, describing, and deciding on a site is beautifully described in Tom Seeley’s book, "Honeybee Democracy."1 1. Seeley, Thomas D. Honeybee Democracy. Princeton University Press, 2010. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Swarming or Not? Several behaviors might look like swarming to the uninitiated. The most common and the most easily confused are orientation flights and robbing. When the population is growing rapidly, and hundreds or even thousands of new bees are emerging every day during the active season, orientation flights may look like swarming, because of the sheer number of bees looping around in front of the hive. In contrast to swarming, however, they are simply returning to the hive entrance; the hive entrance is not flooded with bees trying to join the swarm. Robbing may also look like swarming, except bees are trying to enter the hive, not leave it (including through cracks between supers), and it is accompanied by fighting at the entrance. Other behaviors that may look like swarming include bearding, a common phenomenon in the summer months where the bees cluster on the outside of the hive to cool off or vent fumes; cleansing flights after a period of confinement (look closely and you can see the bees' defecate); and absconding. Absconding is a mass exodus from a hive, when all or most of the population leaves — not to reproduce or to alleviate crowding but as a survival mechanism in the face of various threats and pressures (from pests and diseases or something threatening the bodily integrity of the hive). Look carefully at the bees’ behavior to identify whether, in fact, you are watching a swarm. Remember also that each of these easily confused behaviors is likely to take place more often during one time of the year: orientation any time of the year, but most impressively during the times of greatest population growth; robbing during a nectar dearth or the end of summer; and bearding on the hottest days of the summer, evenings, or immediately following a mite treatment where fumes are being released in the hive. In the same way, swarming is a specific seasonal phenomenon.
While checking out heightened activity at a hive entrance, this beekeeper found himself become the gathering spot for a swarm! Photo credit: Scott McArt. Back to Table of Contents

▶ Read: Swarm Prevention Preventing swarms is difficult because the act of swarming is fundamental to the instinct for survival in the honey bee. It is, after all, the urge to reproduce. When conditions are right, the swarm impulse can become so strong that bees will overcome almost any obstacle a beekeeper can contrive to prevent it. Basically, a good swarm prevention technique is aimed at reducing the future (not imminent!) impact of one or more of the signals that the colony uses to begin its preparations for swarming. The method you choose will also depend on your beekeeping plan. Are you trying to produce as much honey as possible? Do you want to limit the number of colonies you are managing or grow your operation? Are you interested in producing nucs for yourself or to sell to others? The answers to these questions will help determine the best method for swarm prevention in your apiary. You know that swarm season is coming, so be prepared and take steps before queen cells appear. The classic way this is done in the Northeast begins at the first colony inspection, when the hive bodies in strong colonies are often reversed to reduce brood nest congestion and bottom boards are cleaned. After that, inspect colonies every week or 10 days. When you see drone brood appear, add honey supers as necessary and consider requeening or making splits, depending on your management goals. Let's cover a few more details for these practices. Lower the Colony Population Shake some nurses into weaker colonies Shake a couple frames of nurse bees (not including the queen) into other colonies that would benefit from a population boost. This method equalizes the colonies in your yard without increasing the number of colonies. Before doing this, confirm to the extent possible that you are not inadvertently spreading disease or pests by moving around these adult bees. Because of this, it is advisable to confine this method to colonies in the same bee yard. Make splits or nucs To reduce the population of bees in a colony, you might make a split or pull a nuc out of it. This method allows you to increase the number of colonies you manage, but reduction in the season’s total honey yield may result, depending on the weather and how aggressively you split. Provide More Space ▶

▶ ▶ If there is unused space beneath the brood nest, you can reverse the two bottommost hive bodies, which is routine for many beekeepers in spring. After that, timely supering allows bees to store most honey in supers boxes instead of plugging the brood nest. In some cases, just adding a super on top may not be enough, although it certainly helps, provided that the foundation on the frames is already drawn out. Sometimes colonies temporarily ignore frames of foundation, as they do not offer immediate comb for queen laying and food storage. If the brood nest is still getting congested with honey, move some frames of honey out of the brood nest and into a super. Replace the removed frames with drawn comb to make space more immediately available in the brood nest for the queen to lay. Lastly, you can try expanding the brood nest, where you place frames of drawn comb between the existing frames of the brood nest. Be careful about doing this and chilling the brood nest when there are cooler temperatures. Increase the Bees' Perception of QMP Increase the amount of perceived QMP in the colony by requeening with a young queen with pheromones stronger than those of her predecessor. This method results in no increase in operation size; you start with one colony and end with one colony. Adjust the Bees’ Perception of Crowdedness Finally, the perception of crowdedness is due in part to sensory signals of rising temperatures, limited ventilation, and a decline in the concentration of QMP. You can add more room, an upper entrance, or a screened bottom board to increase ventilation and lower the temperature. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Swarm Control Once you see swarm cells, the bees are motivated and will attempt to swarm. If you are not able to prevent these conditions from arising, you may need to try to prevent the act of swarming itself. Swarm control is trying to stop the process once the colony has already constructed swarm cells. There are a few strategies you can employ to try to stop the colony from swarming. Whichever method you choose should be accompanied by practices that help to reduce the swarm preparation instinct (e.g., providing more space) so that the colony does not continue to try to swarm several times. What you can do at this point that might help reduce the chance your colony swarms: 1. Remove the old queen and cut out all but a couple of swarm cells. Removing the old queen may not stop a swarm, but it does increase the likelihood that your colony will not swarm. You have induced a period of “queenlessness” in the colony. The brood nest congestion is relieved as sealed brood hatches, and removing the old queen simulates conditions in a post-swarm colony. Be prepared to check the colony in about two weeks to determine that there is a newly mated queen there. You can relax when you see fresh eggs and young brood. 2. You can cut out all queen cells if you do not find any that have been capped. Even a single capped cell could indicate the colony has already swarmed. If any cells are capped, you must first confirm the queen is still in the colony before cutting the cells. Seeing eggs is not enough, as the queen can continue laying some eggs up until the day she leaves. You must physically see her. This is a laborious way to prevent increase and maintain a single colony, but it may be your best option if you missed the early appearance of queen cells and it is too late to requeen, or if you did requeen and they are trying to swarm anyway. Make certain that you have found and isolated the queen by putting the frame she is on in a nuc box or by caging her temporarily as you ransack the brood nest. Some beekeepers use the cells they cut out in their newly made nucs and splits. You must find every last queen cell. They can be in any nook or cranny among the combs, so be sure to smoke or brush away the bees as you look, or breathe on them to get them to clear the combs, because a layer of bees can easily conceal queen cells. Return to the colony every five days to continue cutting cells throughout the swarm season until the impulse has passed. Each time you must isolate the old queen to protect her. (Yes, this is very labor intensive!)
This colony will swarm any day now, if it hasn't already. The two swarm cells in this photo are already capped. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Ineffective Practices for Swarm Control Clipping the queen's wing Some beekeepers clip the queen’s wing to prevent her from leaving with a swarm. Yet this does not always prevent the colony from swarming and, as the swarm leaves the colony, the queen remains in the hive or gets lost in the grass. The swarm usually returns to the hive, only to leave again as soon as a virgin queen emerges from a swarm cell. Note: Clipping a queen’s wing can help inform a beekeeper of her age. The left wing is usually clipped in years that end in odd numbers, and the right wing is usually clipped in years that end in even numbers. This serves as a backup identifier if her paint dot fades. Placing an excluder below the brood nest Some beekeepers place a queen excluder between the bottom board and a lowest hive body in an effort to prevent the swarm from leaving. The idea is that the queen won't be able to fit through the excluder to exit, so perhaps the bees will stay inside. Unfortunately, this method does not work. The swarm instead leaves with the first virgin that emerges and can fit through the excluder. An excluder in this location can also reduce ventilation and cause the colony to overheat. Neither of these practices works, and neither mitigate the triggers that lead to a colony initiating the swarm process. Back to Table of Contents

Read: My Colony Swarmed! Now What? If you see no new eggs or young brood when inspecting your colony that has swarm cells, or if you find a queen cell that has been opened, your colony has probably swarmed. There will also be fewer bees in a post-swarm hive, but that is not always evident to the beekeeper. Of course, you will want to know if there is a queen in the post-swarm colony, but in such a situation, the best thing to do is close up the hive and wait. If a virgin is present, doing an inspection can increase the chance that you injure her, that she gets lost, or that the bees fail to accept her. In two to four weeks, return to check for new brood. If you are especially anxious to ensure that the colony becomes queenright quickly, you can transfer a frame with eggs and very young brood to the colony. If there is no virgin present, the bees will immediately build emergency queen cells using the brood in the frame you’ve transferred to them. If there is a queen present, the bees will simply rear the brood in the frame you’ve given them. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Should I Let My Colonies Swarm? A good beekeeper is a good neighbor to other beekeepers and the public and is motivated to help protect the health of native pollinators as much as possible. Our philosophy at the Dyce Lab is to prevent swarms from becoming loose in the wild to the best of our ability. In suburban or urban areas, it can be stressful to the public and your neighbors to have bees take up residence in buildings or in trees close to public walkways. More than that, feral colonies that are unmanaged can introduce viruses and other diseases to your neighboring beekeepers' colonies as well as to wild bees. Uncontrolled swarms (those that leave without being caught and hived) cannot be managed for diseases and mites. Therefore, we do not recommend allowing colonies to swarm naturally and consider it an essential beekeeping skill to take steps to prevent swarming and to recognize when a colony is preparing to swarm then take appropriate counteractive measures. As Tom Seeley1 says, swarming is indeed a healthy, natural behavior for honey bees. This act of reproduction can reduce Varroa mite loads, as 20% to 35% of adult mites leave with the swarm. Swarming also provides one to three weeks of a brood break (a period where there is no sealed brood), which can further reduce mites. The process results in a young queen in the colony, and queens produced during swarming are often high quality because they developed from good nutrition. Luckily, there are ways that beekeepers can simulate these phenomena without allowing swarms to get loose in the wild. Through creating intentional brood breaks, producing splits, and requeening, colonies can reap these same rewards without the risks. 1. Seeley, Thomas D. Honeybee Democracy. Princeton University Press, 2010. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Catching and Baiting Swarms Catching and baiting swarms is a fun and free way to obtain bees, although, of course, it’s not foolproof. Catching swarms in a bait hive is the easiest method. Such hives should be set up in advance of the full-on swarming season since the scouts are already looking for new nest sites a week or more before the swarm issues from the parent colony. During swarm season, you can check on your bait hives every week or so to see if you need to rehome any bees. As in all facets of beekeeping, there are many styles of bait hives that you can build or buy, but most derive from the same principles. Watch this video to learn what characteristics bees prefer in bait hives and how you can set some up. Video Transcript Now, what we've learned about how swarms choose a home is not only fascinating in terms of its basic biology but it's also very useful information for the beekeeper. Because it means that we now know how to put out bait hives that fulfill the bee's home site preferences so that these bait hives are very attractive to swarms, and so the beekeeper can catch swarms. And this is a way to get free bees, freebies. Let's review what matters to the bees. There's six things that they're seeking, at least six things that matter. They want the cavity to be sufficiently spacious. We mentioned already, about one cubic foot which is about 40 liters. And with respect to the entrance: they want the entrance small, they want it high off the ground, they want it near the bottom of the cavities so that it keeps the heat in the nest during the winter, and they want it to face south. And there's one more thing that matters to the bees. If they can find a cavity that comes preequipped with combs from another colony that already lived there, but died out, then that is very attractive to the bees as well, because that gives them a tremendous economy in their comb building. They can move right in, it's like moving into a furnished apartment. Okay, so with that knowledge, what do we do? How do we make a bait hive? Well, one way to do it is to use an old hive body and put in some old combs. But if you do that, you'll need to make sure it has only a small entrance. Only about two or three square inches is needed. You can do that by drilling a hole in the side with bait hive, or use a bottom board an just put block of word to reduce the size of the entrance. The small entrance is very important to the bees. Another thing that's really important is you want to get that bait hive above the ground, 10 or 15 feet will make it much more attractive than leaving it at the ground level. You want to have it face south. And you may want to, make sure that it's visible. And what I mean by visible is, when I put up my bait hives, I put them on the edges of woods, rather than deep in the woods. And why is that? It's because, when you think about what is a scout bee doing when she's looking for a home site? She's going from one tree to the next, to the next, looking for knot-holes. And I think the scout bees find these dark knot-holes, or dark openings more easily If it's on the edge of the woods and

not deep in the woods. I also put my bait high in places that are shaded. I don't have real strong evidence about this but I do think the bait hive is more attractive if it's not overheated by sitting in the full sun. You might wonder, should you be putting something inside? Well, I mentioned the combs, putting in frames of old combs to give it the aroma and the attraction of a site filled with combs, so that's one thing. Another thing that's good is to put in the pheromones, the bee lures. These are not essential but they're helpful and the reason they're helpful, I know from my experiments, is that they make the site, your bait hive, much more conspicuous to the scout bees if you've put in one of these swarm lures. Some bee keepers have asked me can I just put in frames as foundation? I would say yes you can, because that will still have the aroma of beeswax, especially if it's beeswax foundation. But also put in a comb or two of, a frame or two with old combs, to give it their full odor. And one thing I want to stress about this whole process of trapping swarms with bait hives is that, in my experiences, the swarms that you get are excellent bees. Why is that? It's because only good strong colonies with good queens are able to become strong enough to swarm. You might be worried you may have heard the wild swarms you'll catch are going to be too stingy. Well in my experience that's extremely rare, but if it happens big deal, you just requeen your colony. And I do want to stress, I've had really beautiful bees with my bait hives, really, really beautiful bees. But I do want to caution you, the trapping success varies from year to year. Last summer, I put up ten bait hives and I caught ten swarms, so 100% success. The year before, I had 0% success. There just weren't many swarms produced. So it's profitable in the sense you get free bees. But it's also a lot of fun, it's kind of like magic, you put up this box and you can check it on your way home from work or something like that. And one day, sooner or later, you're going to find that a swarm of bees has moved into it, it has come to life, so you can have a lot of fun. There's one other way I'll mention too that you can have fun with the bees. You're all beekeepers, some of you will become bee trappers. If you want to become a thorough, complete bee enthusiast I encourage you to also consider becoming a bee hunter. Bee hunters go out and track down wild colonies of bees living in hollow trees. And that's a lot of fun — doesn't involve cutting down the tree, the thrill is in the chase, not in the kill. There's no killing of the bees or the colony, or collecting honey, taking honey out of these trees. You're just taking yourself on a natural treasure hunt. If you're intrigued by this possibility, I can steer you to a nice little book that's been written on this and published recently called Following the Wild Bees. Catching swarms that have settled on an object Every swarm is different, but all are probably a little further out of reach than they look! There is no way to provide specific directions; just remember basic safety guidelines (stings to you and onlookers, heights, tools), common sense, and patience. Some useful swarm-catching equipment

includes the usual protective gear (veil and gloves), smoker, fuel, phone, and hive tool, plus pruners, extension-pole pruners or limb loppers, a long rope, a bucket or nuc box (ventilated to allow for transportation), bee brush, spray bottle with sugar water, ladder, drop cloth, extra frames and foundation, and duct tape. Some beekeepers use vacuum cleaners adapted to safely suck up bees. In many cases, you can shake or sharply rap the bees off a branch and into a box or bucket. If you manage to secure most of the bees in the swarm and particularly the queen, the rest of the bees should simply walk over in time. You can set them up in a new hive or combine them with an existing colony. A newly settled swarm builds comb very quickly, so you might use them to help draw out foundation in a hive that needs it. Be careful in handling a swarm, especially if you do not know its origins, whether it has been disturbed, or how long ago it left its parent colony. While swarms are typically gentle (with full stomachs and no resources to defend), a dry swarm that has been clustered for a few days and digested the honey it brought with it may be defensive. A swarm that has been sprayed with insecticide but not killed may also be defensive. Furthermore, since the window to catch swarms can be quite limited, you may need to work in weather conditions that are less than ideal. If you are using a swarm as an opportunity to educate curious onlookers, it will be a much more positive learning experience for everyone if you handle them safely. There are several ways to catch swarms, and every situation will require your analysis to decide how to proceed. Shown below, from left to right: Bees can be shaken off a branch into a hive body, they can be brushed gently off a surface into a hive body (made easier if the queen is first found and placed in the hive body), or, if the object can be moved, it can be placed in front of a hive body with a frame of comb. The odor of the comb will draw bees into the hive as their new home. Photo credit for middle and right photos: Jon Ryan

Get your name on a swarm list! To get your name on a swarm list in your area, talk to your local beekeeping club, nearby extension offices, emergency responders, and pest control companies. Note that layman's language is often imprecise around swarms. If someone calls you to pick up a swarm, try to confirm whether it is indeed a swarm of honey bees or if it is an established feral colony of honey bees, a wasp’s nest, or something else (asking for a photo may help). Your first opportunity to educate the public may be on the difference between honey bees and wasps. In New York State, the Dyce Lab maintains a swarm catcher directory. If you would like to be added to the directory, email dycebees@cornell.edu. Keeping a swarm in its new hive

If you have captured a swarm from its bivouac and re-housed it, you’ll be anxious to prevent that swarm from abandoning the home you have just put them in. Sometimes swarms do abscond from their new hives. You should give them several frames of drawn foundation and several frames of plain foundation (for room to draw comb, which they are primed to do once they have a new home). The queen will take a few days to begin laying eggs. Try not to disturb the colony while it is becoming settled. If you are really anxious to know all is well, some beekeepers recommend listening with an ear against the hive body. If you hear gnawing and knocking sounds, they are building wax, and all is well! Perhaps the easiest way to ensure that the bees don’t abscond is to provide them with a frame of unsealed brood from another colony at the time you establish them in their new hive. Bees almost never abandon brood, so they should stay put. Back to Table of Contents
