Module Wrap-up: Swarming In this module, you studied swarming from multiple perspectives — both its challenges and opportunities. You learned how swarms can impact honey production, colony health, and public relations, while also discovering their potential benefits for colony expansion, pest management, and genetic diversity. This comprehensive look at swarming will help you manage this natural process and educate others about this fascinating aspect of honey bee biology. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Queen Management The queen bee is the sole female reproducer and the mother of all the other bees in the colony. The health and productivity of a honey bee colony is inherently linked to the queen. A healthy queen lays over a thousand eggs a day in a solid brood pattern, giving rise to a strong population of 40,000 or more workers by early summer. A strong population also helps protect colonies from some pests and diseases that can take advantage of low honey bee populations. Beekeepers must always be aware of the queen's status and quality as they inspect their colonies, since failing or lost queens can put the colony at risk of dying. In this module, we will go over important concepts and management practices to make sure that your colony has a healthy, fertile queen. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Queen Status Since you first began to keep bees, you have known that the queen is the most important member of the colony. The queen is intricately tied to colony performance. Her health and fertility are responsible for the colony’s population as well as the proportion of workers and drones in the colony. This workforce, in turn, influences nearly all aspects of colony performance: the amount of nectar and pollen coming into the colony, its likelihood of overwintering successfully as a strong population, its susceptibility to pests, and whether it will be able to reproduce through swarming. The importance of a healthy, productive queen cannot be emphasized enough. Yet queens have been failing at high rates in recent years. Historically, beekeepers would replace queens every two or so years. Now, Bee Informed Partnership surveys show that as many as 50% of beekeepers are replacing failing queens every six months, and commercial beekeepers report queen failure as the most common cause of overwintering mortality. The reason behind the widespread queen failure in the U.S. is largely unknown but thought to be the result of multiple interacting stress factors, including pathogens, reduced sperm viability of the drones a queen mates with, and pesticides. Failing queens pose a big risk to the colony. Colonies that experience a queen event, where a queen fails or dies, are 3.1 times more likely to die within two months than a colony without such a problem. It is therefore very important — and even more so today — that a beekeeper is always aware of the queen status in a colony. If queen failure is detected early, intervention can help save the colony. At the height of the season, regular inspections every 10 days to two weeks should include observations of the brood quantity and quality, which gives you an indication of queen fertility. A poor or failing queen lays a spotty brood pattern or has brood of different ages adjacent to one another. Interpret what the brood pattern tells you about the queen with regard to the time of year. There may not be eggs in mid-autumn as the colony winds down in preparation for winter or

in periods of a dearth when there is not enough nutrition to support brood development. With knowledge and practice, beekeepers will be able to identify, analyze, and respond to queen issues in their colony in a timely manner, allowing them to maintain healthy colonies year after year. How can I test the health of my queens? If you are interested in knowing how healthy your queens are, you can have them tested through the North Carolina State Queen and Disease Clinic. You can have queens screened for Nosema, seven different viruses, and insemination quality. The fees for each service, as well as more information on submitting samples, can be found at the NCSU Queen and Disease Clinic. Back to Table of Contents

▶ ▶ Read: Signs of Queenlessness Queens can die for a variety of reasons: predators, old age, getting lost on a mating flight, pesticide exposure (including some miticides), pests or disease, or mishandling by a beekeeper. Recognizing when a colony is queenless and taking steps so that the queen is quickly replaced is an important skill to have as a Master Beekeeper. Roaring In less than an hour, bees recognize that their queen is gone because queen mandibular pheromone (QMP) is no longer being passed throughout the colony. They become very agitated and fan their wings. A beekeeper can detect this within an hour if the colony is small, such as a nuc, or within a few hours if it is a full-strength colony at peak population. This fanning is more pronounced than the usual fanning to cool the hive and is characterized as “roaring” because of how loud it is. At this initial time, the bees are more defensive and more likely to sting. Emergency Cells The bees then begin to create emergency queen cells. Nurses enlarge the cells of several larvae that are less than 36 hours old to the shape and size of a queen cup and feed them copious amounts of royal jelly. However, if the queen died without leaving behind young worker larvae in the hive — perhaps in late fall after brood production had ceased for the year or another interruption — the colony will become hopelessly queenless unless the beekeeper intervenes by introducing a new queen or a frame of eggs/very young larvae.

▶ Laying Workers After three to four weeks of queenlessness, some of the nurse bees may activate their ovaries and lay eggs, becoming known as laying workers. Again, this is because QMP is no longer detected. In queenright colonies, workers’ ovaries are inactivated. The presence of this pheromone signals to them that there is a fertile queen that is laying eggs and passing on the colony's genes. Without this pheromone, up to 30% of workers may begin laying their own eggs. While healthy queens lay a single egg neatly at the bottom of the cell, workers often lay eggs on the side of the cell — their abdomens are not long enough to reach down to the bottom — and several different workers will lay eggs in the same cell, so you will see multiple eggs in one cell. Their eggs are scattered in cells haphazardly throughout the brood frames. All bees that develop from worker-laid eggs are drones because workers do not mate and therefore cannot fertilize their eggs. This cohort of drones is a final biological attempt by the colony to reproduce, as these drones can then pass on the colony's genes by mating with other queens in the area. Without intervention, such a colony eventually dies out. Since these are drone brood, further evidence that a colony has laying workers is the presence of scattered, capped drone cells throughout the worker brood area, that take the appearance of “bullets” because larger drones are developing in small worker-sized cells. Once they hatch, these drones tend to be smaller than their queen-mothered brothers for this same reason. Laying workers, however, are not necessarily a sign of queenlessness: Sometimes workers lay eggs even in the presence of the queen (about 0.01% of them), so one or two cells with multiple eggs are not a concern. Often, other nurse bees consume those eggs before they can hatch into larvae, but this "policing" behavior breaks down in advanced stages of queenlessness.

It is important to note that sometimes newly mated queens lay multiple eggs in a cell in the first few days of egg-laying as she gets into the swing of things. The pattern of these eggs differs from worker-laid eggs in that queen-laid eggs are at the bottom of the cell and often parallel to each other. After a couple of days, the queen should begin laying one egg per cell. A worker-laid egg. When To Expect You’ll Observe These Symptoms During every colony inspection, you should be verifying the presence of a laying queen. If you are inspecting all of your colonies every 10 to 14 days, you can identify a queenless colony before laying workers become an issue. If you are inspecting only a proportion of your colonies during each inspection, check all colony entrances for signs of reduced pollen coming in or fewer bees foraging, and listen for roaring. Inspect colonies that exhibit any of these symptoms. If, upon inspecting the colony, you cannot find the queen or eggs, or if you see multiple eggs in a cell during a regular inspection, here are the clues that your colony may be queenless: ▶

Signs of Queenlessness and Time Characteristic Time Observed Roaring bees In the following hours/days Increased defensiveness In the following days In the following Emergency queen cells days to three weeks Multiple eggs per cell After three to four weeks Bullet-shaped drone cells After about one month A high number of drones After about two months Drones that are smaller After about two than normal months Dwindling adult After about two population months Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Considerations for Requeening a Queenless Colony As a beekeeper, you already know by now how to introduce eggs, young larvae, a queen cell, or a caged queen into a colony to address queenlessness. As a Master Beekeeper, it is important to understand timing. Sometimes not enough time has passed for a colony to rear its own queen from an existing egg or young larva. Sometimes too much time has passed and a population of laying workers has become established, making the introduction of a new queen difficult if not impossible. Watch this video to learn how to critically analyze a queenless colony so that you can make an informed decision on how best to manage it. Video Transcript So requeening a queenless colony isn't just putting in a queen cell or a queen in a cage, closing up the colony, and walking away. As a master beekeeper, we want to look at the other considerations that we need to take when we're requeening a queenless colony. So for instance, knowing the developmental time of bees, knowing that they begin life as an egg for three days, and as a larvae for about six days, before they're capped brood. We can actually estimate the last time the queen was present. And knowing the last time the queen was present can let us weigh our options of how we are going to deal with requeening this colony. So now examine the age of larvae or brood the you are able to see. If you're seeing absolutely no capped brood then you know that it has been a few weeks the queen has been in there. If you are seeing larvae, for instance, then you know that it's been between nine days and maybe four days since the queen has been in there. And if you are seeing the eggs then you are okay the queen is in there and you don't need to continue with anything. So if you are seeing young larvae, larvae that look like they're less than 36 hours old, so about the size of an egg, and you're positive that there's no queen, then you know that you've caught this really early. The queen has been there as little as four days ago, and we actually have these young larvae that the bees can develop into a queen. So, if you want to have the colony requeen itself, you can close up the hive and walk away, return in one week to make sure that they have started building those emergency queen cells, and return two weeks after that to make sure that there is a new queen in your colony. The thing is, is that every time you're getting a colony to rear queens from young larva, you need to make sure that they have enough nutrition and especially protein. So make sure that the colony has ample pollen or provide them with a pollen substitute so that the nurses can rear some healthy queens with enough nutrition. Okay so in this case though, you might wonder why the queen died in the first place, why she failed, and you might be skeptical to have the colony rear a queen from her own young larva, in case there was a genetic issue. So, in this case, you might want to introduce your own queen of a specific genetic line or stock that you're interested in. And here you can insert a queen cage using the method that works for you and go back every few days to

destroy any emergency queen cells that the colony is producing, and make sure that you go back and see that she's been released and accepted by the colony. Okay, so lastly if the queen hasn't been around for a few days or a few weeks even, but you're not seeing any laying workers, you can also introduce a frame of healthy young brood from a different colony. And with these young larvae that are less than 36 hours, again the queenless colony can rear a queen from those. So the frame that you're choosing should have eggs and young larva and lots of nurse bees on it. And the main thing is you want to make sure that this is healthy. You don't want to be introducing any sort of disease into the queenless colony. So here are the considerations for moving over a frame from one colony into your queenless colony. You want to make sure that you're moving the frame over as quickly as possible so that you're not leaving open brood out in the colony for more than a few minutes. If you need to go more than an hour or if you need to drive between apiaries with this frame, then put it into a new colony with bees to keep it warm and protected. And with bees developing around 95 degrees Fahrenheit, any deviation of a few degrees can cause developmental problems or death. So you want to make sure that they're not deviating in temperature for any given amount of time beyond a couple minutes. Now, also it's important that you're not just introducing a frame with eggs and brood on it, but that you're introducing nurse bees too. So your colony might have been queenless long enough to the point where any nurse bees that used to be in that colony have now developed into foragers. And now, there really isn't any bees that can care for and help rear a queen from this young larva that you're about to introduce. So, the nurse bees that you're going to introduce are typically bees that are found on any brood frame. So, when you're moving over the frame of bees, keep the bees that are on it into that new queenless colony. You can also shake nurse bees off from other colonies, just to make sure you have enough in there. And again, supply them with pollen or pollen substitute if the reserves are low in the colony. Okay. So what if you're in a situation where the colony has been queenless for a long time? There isn't any capped brood in there and it's now at the point where you're seeing laying workers. And in this case, you can't simply introduce a new queen. The laying workers are likely to kill the new queen that you're going to introduce. So here you need to make sure that every laying worker is gone. And since laying workers are the young bees, usually nurses, since young bees can activate their ovaries but foragers can't, then you just need to make sure that all of the young bees are out of the hive. And this is fairly easy to do it because young bees don't usually fly and they haven't yet taken their orientation flight to locate their way back to the colony. So the procedure that you do is to remove every single frame from the hive and shake and brush all of the bees off, the nurses and the foragers, all of the bees off from the frames and do this about 20 feet away from your colonies. And you're going to also do this to the hive boxes for any bees that are standing on the side of the hive boxes. Then reassemble everything, put the frames back in the colony, and wait until the next day for all the forager bees to return and then introduce your queen. So the forager bees will fly back and all the young bees that have activated their ovaries, all those laying workers are actually

going die outside because they can't find their way back to the colony. And in this case, some of the forgers will revert back to being nurse bees to care for any of the eggs and larvae that the new queen is laying. But it might be helpful to shake some additional nurse bees into the colony just to make sure you do have some of those present. And then, keep an eye on the colony over the next few weeks to make sure that the new queen is establishing herself and that brood is being tended to. An alternative method to requeening a colony with laying workers requires a bit more equipment and time but is also quite effective: Introduce one frame of open brood with nurse bees into the laying worker colony every few days. The open brood releases brood pheromone, which helps suppress worker ovary development. It takes time to suppress the workers' ovaries and for them to be willing to accept a new queen; sometimes up to three weeks. As new open brood frames are added, the beekeeper can check for the construction of supersedure cells. This indicates the colony is ready for a queen. The beekeeper can now either 1) allow the supersedure cells to develop — the most popular option, 2) destroy them and introduce a queen of their choice, or 3) merge the colony with a queenright colony using the newspaper method. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Tip for Introducing a New Queen In recent years, nearly 30% of newly introduced queens die within six months in the United States. Either they are immediately rejected or they are superseded after a few weeks. Queen acceptance can be particularly challenging when installing packages because the queen in the cage is not related to the bees in the package. To improve queen acceptance, introduce a frame of young brood and eggs at the same time you are introducing a new caged queen. Research from North Carolina State University finds this practice increases queen acceptance by 200%. In a 2021 study, researchers tracked queen acceptance in colonies for 12 weeks after introducing them. They compared queen acceptance rates among colonies that received 1) a frame of young brood and eggs, 2) brood ester pheromone, and 3) no brood or pheromone in the control group. They found 86.7% of queens that were introduced along with brood were accepted, compared to 53.3% of queens that were introduced with brood pheromone, and compared to only 33.3% of queens that were introduced in the conventional way without any brood or pheromone. Back to Table of Contents

▶ Read: Requeening to Improve Health and Productivity It is common practice among some beekeepers, especially commercial beekeepers, to routinely requeen colonies to improve health and productivity. Requeening in response to a problem can occur at any time of the year, but routine requeening is generally done in early spring or at the end of summer/beginning of fall. Requeening in the spring can be easier than requeening in late summer or early fall, as colony populations are lower and it is easier to find the old queen. Also, because a new queen is most easily accepted when there is food coming into the hive, it can be easier to requeen during a spring nectar flow or to feed the colony at the same time. Spring is also the time when colonies are most inclined to swarm and produce new queens. Requeening in fall, however, is gaining in popularity as a way to interrupt the brood cycle and therefore reduce Varroa mite levels. The colony also enters winter with a young, vigorous queen. Here, we do not cover how to requeen a colony, but rather when and why a beekeeper may want to requeen. Reduce Impacts From Pests and Disease Chalkbrood, sacbrood, small hive beetles, wax moths, and robbing from other honey bees can be overcome or handled better by colonies with strong populations. In fact, wax moths and small hive beetles tend to be secondary symptoms of an underlying issue and are not normally problems on their own. For chalkbrood, requeening is a recommended course of action if the colony does not clear the fungal infection on its own in a few weeks or months. A new queen that is freshly mated should start laying eggs and building up the population to overcome these issues. Requeening in summer to reduce Varroa mites works because it creates a break in the brood cycle. As mites reproduce in honey bee brood, this break means that mites cannot breed for this time. This has the effect of driving down their numbers and making them more vulnerable to mite treatments that target them while they are in their phoretic stage (outside of the brood cells, on the bodies of the bees). Letting the bees requeen themselves guarantees the largest break in the brood cycle since it takes many days before a new queen develops, hatches, mates, and starts laying eggs. You can also requeen with a queen cell or a mated queen in late summer. This won't cause a break in the brood cycle but may provide other advantages, such as more control over the genetics; e.g. if you introduce a queen of hygienic stock. Requeening in

▶ summer to reduce Varroa can be accompanied by a mite treatment that works best in broodless periods. Maintain High Levels of Brood Production Beekeepers can also requeen their colonies routinely to ensure sustained high levels of brood production. The queen stores the sperm from her mating flight(s) in her spermatheca for her entire life and never again mates. Her ability to lay fertilized eggs, therefore, declines as she ages, and after a couple of years, it will decrease to the point that she will naturally be superseded by the colony. Queens are the most productive egg layers in their first season, and for this reason, many beekeepers replace the queen annually to maintain high brood production levels. A downside to this method is that it removes selection pressures on queens to be good layers for beyond one year. If queens are replaced every year, it does not matter whether they continue to be any good in Year 2 or Year 3, so we do not seek out queens that can remain fertile for many years. Instead, we may be selecting for queens that are good layers during the first year but dwindle quickly after that. Purchasing new queens is expensive, and rearing your own is time-consuming, so queens that perform well for multiple years are desirable. If you can afford to experiment, consider letting your queens age to see how many years they remain productive. You can then try breeding from your long-lived productive queens and, in time, help create a stock of hearty queens that have strong brood patterns year after year. Of course, this long-term fertility also depends on the quality and quantity of sperm that she stores upon mating; breeding for a desired trait is never that simple! Improve Weak Population or Spotty Brood Pattern You might consider replacing the queen if brood is spotty or there is not the expected amount of brood in the brood chamber at the right time of year (in the Northeast, high in early spring and summer, low during nectar and pollen dearths, and slightly higher again in early fall). This is especially critical if the number of adults being produced is not enough to replace the adults dying from old age or other causes. Be sure to first rule out the possibility of pests, disease, or pesticides in causing irregular brood or a reduced adult population. Keeping notes of brood, pollen, nectar, and population levels in your inspection records help you see if these issues have been occurring gradually and could be associated with poor genetic stock or an old queen, or if they have occurred suddenly and are likely due to some other environmental agent. ▶

▶ Sometimes reduced egg-laying is a result of the colony being honey bound. Check to see what the empty cells in the brood nest are filled with: If they are filled with nectar instead of brood, this can be a sign that your colony is honey bound and the queen simply does not have room to lay. This can happen with infrequent supering or during a strong nectar flow if bees are bringing in nectar faster than the queen fills cells with eggs. If there are no empty cells for them to deposit their nectar in supers, they will do it in the brood nest. If the queen does not have room to expand the brood nest because honey is taking up too much space, rearrange some frames or introduce drawn comb to make sure there is enough room for the queen to lay eggs and check back in a couple of days to verify she is laying. The colony may have already begun preparing to swarm; check for swarm cells. Note: Colonies can become honey bound relatively quickly in the spring, especially if you are feeding them. Keep an eye on the brood chamber to make sure there is still sufficient room for the queen to lay. Reduce Defensiveness Ongoing defensive behavior has a genetic basis, so requeening with a gentler stock can mitigate it. For example, Italians are known for being docile bees. Many beekeepers may tolerate defensive bees that may have other desirable traits; e.g., hygienic behavior. In this case, the benefits of the stock may outweigh the cons of being stung regularly. It is usually up to the beekeeper what kind of bees they prefer to work with; however, there are two exceptions where very defensive behavior is not tolerated. The first is if you find you have Africanized bees. If you suspect that you have Africanized bees, contact your state apiculturist or local extension associate immediately. Depending on the state, you may be required to requeen or destroy colonies that are confirmed to be Africanized. Africanized bees are rare in the Northeast. The second instance where defensiveness is not tolerated is in urban beekeeping. While many cities, like New York City, are embracing beekeeping, there are often rules about the temperament of your bees because these areas have high human populations and neighbors are near. Requeening with gentle stock can be mandatory upon public complaint, and keeping the colony specified distances from property lines and public areas is also often required or recommended. As a Master Beekeeper, you need to be sensitive to the fears of the public and the reputation of bees and beekeepers at large. Reduce Swarming ▶

Requeening with a young queen can help reduce the swarming impulse in a colony if that is something that you wish to prevent. The urge to swarm increases when the ability to detect queen pheromone decreases and young queens produce more pheromones than older queens. To be effective, requeening must happen in early spring before the colony has begun preparing to swarm and should be complemented with other methods, such as providing more space for the bees. Certain stocks of bees are genetically more likely to swarm, such as Russians, so requeening with stock less prone to swarming behavior may also be helpful. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Managing a Two-Queen Colony Sometimes beekeepers may run a colony with two queens to maximize honey production. In theory, two queens are producing twice as many bees and, therefore, more honey and other hive products can be made. The major trade-off is that managing a two-queen colony can be time consuming to set up and manage properly, so it is more popular among sideliner and hobby beekeepers than commercial beekeepers. What happens when two queens are present in the same colony? In nature, there is sometimes more than one queen present in the colony during supersedure or swarming, but it is usually only temporary. Under normal circumstances, when a queen finds another queen in the hive, she grabs onto her with her mandibles, climbs on top of her, and stings her to death. Workers can also reject a second queen through balling behavior or withholding food from her. Because of this behavior, free-roaming double queen colonies have only yielded mixed levels of success. Physically removing the queens’ mandibles so they cannot position themselves on another queen to sting her and removing older workers, which tend to ball and kill queens the most, make the colony more stable, but it is unlikely for beekeepers to undergo such measures. By far the easiest way for beekeepers to maintain a two-queen colony is by keeping them separated. In this way, a two-queen system is essentially created by performing a split, adding a queen to it, placing the split on top of the parent colony, and separating the two with a queen excluder. How productive are two-queen colonies at producing honey? Little research exists that compares honey production between two-queen systems and singlequeen systems. The most extensive study is from a USDA report that compared annual honey yields of the two types of colonies. It found that two-queen colonies averaged 112 pounds more than single-queen colonies each year. However, it also found that two-queen systems require 50% more time to maintain than single-queen systems. They are difficult to inspect with brood boxes between several heavy honey supers, can become quite tall, and are prone to becoming honey bound. Additionally, using this system to maximize honey production requires extensive planning ahead to set up — around two months before a honey flow — to maximize the number of foragers available to collect nectar. Back to Table of Contents

Read: How To Make a Two-Queen Colony Here, we outline the steps for making a vertical two-queen system, the most popular kind. Other people have experimented with other designs of two-queen colonies. Start with a colony housed in two deep hive bodies that have at least eight frames of brood. Separate the hive bodies and place the queen in the bottom deep. Manipulate the frames in the colony so that there are approximately five frames of mixed brood flanked by approximately five frames of honey and pollen. ⌃ Long description Two deep hive bodies with eight frames of brood. The top body has the frames in the fourth, fifth, and sixth position. The bottom body has them in the third through seventh position. The queen is in the bottom frame among the mixed brood. Place a new deep hive body on top of this bottom deep. To this new hive body, add approximately four frames of honey flanked by approximately six frames of drawn comb. Place a Snelgrove board, also known as a division screen or double screen board, above this newly added hive body. A Snelgrove board has two screens of mesh that bees cannot pass through and a notch in the top for bees to enter and exit. Place it on the colony such that bees can enter and exit the uppermost brood chamber, the third hive body that you are about to add. Add the top hive body from the first step on top of the Snelgrove screen — this is acting as your split. Place three frames of capped brood — with the nurse bees on it — in this hive body and flank

it with two or three frames of honey and pollen. Fill the rest of the hive body with foundation or drawn comb. Replace any frames you removed from the bottom colony with foundation or drawn comb at the periphery. A Snelgrove board. Photo credit: Betterbee Introduce a mated queen to the top hive body. The screen on the Snelgrove board prevents the two queens from stinging each other and allows heat from the colony below to rise and help keep the brood warm until it emerges. It also allows the colonies’ odors to mix so they become accustomed to each other’s scents. Bees cannot pass through the screens to venture into the other colony. ⌃ Long description

A three deep hive body. The top body is separated by a Snelgrove board. This hive body has drawn comb in the first, second, ninth and tenth frame positions, honey/pollen in the third, seventh, and eighth positions, and capped brood in the fourth through sixth position. One queen is among the capped brood in the top body. Another queen is in the body hive body. There are two hive entrances. One above the Snelgrove board, and one below. Timing is important for this to work if you want the honey flow to coincide with both colonies having a strong forager population. Setup should therefore happen around two months prior to the flow beginning; they are at their strongest production eight to nine weeks after being assembled. In the Northeast, setting it up in late April or early May is best if the weather permits. Remember that it can take around three weeks for emerged adults to become foragers. Having a surplus of foragers is the key to this system yielding lots of honey production. When the honey flow begins and both colonies are populated with bees of all ages, remove the Snelgrove board and replace it with a queen excluder. Bees should begin filling the middle hive body with honey and drawing out any foundation and filling drawn comb. Start supering both colonies for honey production — super above the queen excluder on top of the bottom hive and above the top hive.

⌃ Long description A hive with multiple honey supers. There is one hive body on the bottom with three honey supers on top, then a queen excluder, then another hive body, then two more honey supers. There is one queen in each of the individual hive bodies — two queens in total. You may need to manipulate frames or reverse hive bodies below the excluder again in the summer if you find the lowest brood nest has moved upward. Try to keep the queen as low in the first colony as possible so that she does not encounter the new queen through the excluder. This system is not maintained over winter. In the fall, after removing the supers for honey extraction, either combine the colonies into one strong colony (remove one queen) or separate them into two individual queenright colonies.

Read: Using Local Queens There is much discussion today about the benefits of locally adapted bees. The term “locally adapted” refers to bees that are well-suited to their specific environment, although this is not a strict definition, and often advertisements for “local stock” or “locally adapted stock” simply refer to bees that have thrived in a specific region for at least two years with minimal intervention. Likewise, queens from colonies that have survived at least two winters are sometimes termed “survivor stock,” although this does not specify what sort of mite management regime has been used. Because of the advantages of locally adapted bees, we recommend that you try rearing some queens from your best colonies or consider buying local queens over ones originating from long distances. However, it can be difficult to produce large numbers of queens in the Northeastern U.S. by this time of the year. Many commercial beekeepers here need their colonies to be strong by spring for pollination of early crops or to take advantage of the first nectar flows, so they often depend on queens bred in the South. Indeed, most large-scale queen and package producers are concentrated in the warmer regions of the U.S., like South Carolina, Hawaii, Georgia, California, and Florida. Because winters are mild or nonexistent in these areas, queens can be produced, mated, and available to ship in April or May, when many beekeepers are looking to requeen or install packages. Furthermore, as stocks of Varroa-tolerant and Varroa-resistant bees are being developed, queens with those genetics may not yet be available in your local area. Back to Table of Contents

▶ ▶ Read: What Are The Benefits of Using Local Bees? There are many benefits to using local bees. They can thrive in your climate. Environmental adaptation is important. In general, many beekeepers like to purchase queens, packages, and nucs from the same region they wish to keep them in because the bees may be well suited to that climate, especially if the populations have been persisting without the introduction of outside genetics. Honey bee populations that have lived in cold, northern climates for many generations have adapted to prepare for winters that stretch from November to April by building up large food reserves and ceasing brood production in mid- to late autumn. The most locally adapted bees in a region are often the wild bee populations that have been residing in tree cavities for many generations without human intervention. In the United States, there has been a lot of genetic mixture within the bee population over time, so sourcing bees that are truly adapted to your local climate can prove difficult. They can be more productive. Locally adapted colonies tend to be more productive than non-local colonies. While research is needed to investigate this relationship in the U.S., several large-scale studies in Europe have compared locally adapted bees to bees that are not locally adapted in the same region. Collectively, these studies have found that worker population levels, overwintering success, honey production, queen lifespan, and overall colony lifespan are found to be greater in the locally adapted colonies. It can reduce transportation stress. Purchasing local bees can help reduce shipping stress. Queens can be exposed to fluctuating temperature spikes during long-distance shipments, and these spikes may reduce their reproductive output by killing some of the sperm stored in their spermatheca. It may help reduce the spread of pathogens. ▶ ▶

▶ The prevalence of many pathogens and parasites impacting bees today is due to the global and national network of honey bee markets and transportation. Small hive beetles, Nosema ceranae, and Varroa mites all originated outside the U.S., entered at specific sites, and are now prevalent throughout the country as bees are transported for pollination in different states, and queens and other bees are shipped in the mail to new regions. Rearing your own certainly does not mean that they will be free of infection, as these pathogens are quite widespread, but it may help reduce the introduction of further infections or strains. It supports beekeepers in your community. Purchasing bees from local beekeepers enriches your agricultural economy and supports your beekeeping community. In addition, local producers that are selecting for specific traits can help contribute good bee genetics to their environment. Back to Table of Contents

In the September 2016 issue of Bee Culture, Clarence Collision wrote, “In the U.S. in recent years, queens have been failing at a high rate, with 50% or greater of queens replaced in colonies within six months when historically a queen might live one to two years or even longer.” Queen failure refers to queens that die, get superseded, or become drone layers. Module Introduction: Variation Within Apis Mellifera Throughout your experience beekeeping, you may have come across many different kinds of honey bees. Some are gentler than others, some swarm more than others, and some may be better equipped to survive year-round in your climate. Honey bees even exhibit variation in their coloration, from golden Italian bees to dark German bees. In this module, we will explore these variations and their causes, introducing you to the different kinds of honey bees, Apis mellifera, in the U.S. and around the world. Back to Table of Contents

Tool: Honey Bee Subspecies and Lineages After honey bees first evolved in Asia, they  Download the Tool dispersed throughout Africa, Asia, and Europe. Seven genetically distinct populations, called lineages, arose in the Old World: African (A), Western and Northern European (M), Eastern Check out this Honey Bee Subspecies Table to learn more about subspecies and lineages. European (C), Eastern and Central Asian (O), Western Asian (Y), Madagascar (U), and Egypt (L). Lineages differ in their geographical range, their behaviors, and their morphology (size, shape, color, etc.). Each lineage contains one or more subspecies; indeed, all modern subspecies and stocks of bees have descended from these lineages. Subspecies are often referred to as races of honey bees; we will stick to the term “subspecies." Genetic differences in morphology and behavior among different subspecies arose through natural selection after populations were geographically isolated and unable to mate freely with other populations for a period. Note that subspecies names are an extension of species names. Each subspecies belongs to the species Apis mellifera, but they have an additional name afterward. While different species cannot mate to produce viable offspring, different subspecies can. For instance, Apis mellifera and Apis cerana cannot produce offspring together, but Apis mellifera mellifera and Apis mellifera ligustica can. Their offspring would be a hybrid of the two subspecies and possess a mix of genes and characteristics from each of the parent subspecies. There are at least 27 recognized subspecies of honey bees in the world, shown in the Honey Bee Subspecies Table. Some scientific debate exists about the actual number of subspecies, and as genetic analytic tools improve over time, additional subspecies may surface. For this course, you only need to familiarize yourself with the subspecies highlighted in orange in the middle column of this table. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Apis Mellifera in North America Apis mellifera mellifera (M) (“German bees” or “German black bees”) was the first honey bee introduced to North America, in 1622. It was the only honey bee kept here for almost 250 years, until Apis mellifera ligustica (C) (“Italians”) was introduced in 1859, followed by Apis mellifera carnica (C) (“Carniolans”), Apis mellifera caucasica (O) (“Caucasians”), and many other subspecies depending on the origin of immigrants. The map below shows when seven subspecies were introduced to the mainland United States between 1859 and 1922: A. m. ligustica (1859), A. m. lamarckii (1866), A. m. carnica (1877), A. m. cypria (1880), A. m. syriaca (1880), A. m. caucasica (1882), and A. m. intermissa (1891). ⌃ Long description This image shows a historical map depicting the introduction of different Apis mellifera (honey bee) subspecies to North America. The map focuses on the central and eastern United States, with state boundaries visible and coastal areas shown in gray. The legend identifies three distinct lineages of honey bees. The map includes dates ranging from 1860 to 1910, showing when different subspecies were introduced to specific locations. Various introduction points are marked across the map, with dates such as:

1866, 1868, and 1865-1868 in the central region 1880-1882 in some areas 1902-1910 and 1905-1910 in other locations The distribution pattern suggests a gradual introduction of different honey bee subspecies across multiple decades, with various entry points throughout the eastern and central United States. The dates and locations demonstrate the systematic introduction and spread of honey bee populations during the latter half of the 19th century and early 20th century. Although several subspecies of the Western honey bee were brought to the U.S. since the 1600s, a 2023 study showed that approximately 93% of all current U.S. honey bees are from lineages primarily found along the northern Mediterranean coast and mostly from TWO subspecies: A. mellifera ligustica (Italian honey bee) and A. mellifera carnica (Carnolian honey bee). This means that current U.S. honey bees are not very genetically diverse; this is potentially making them less able to fend off threats from new enemies and pesticides. Efforts to increase the genetic diversity of U.S. honey bees have been particularly thwarted by the ban on live honey bee imports from all countries in 1922 when tracheal mites were discovered in Europe. Honey bees are no longer allowed to be imported from Europe, with an exception of the importation of Russian queens for a few years in the late 1990s for a USDA Varroa-resistant breeding program. Until 2019, queens and packages could still be easily imported from Canada, yet imports from Canada (or any other country, in fact) are now allowed only under conditions defined by U.S.-based federal regulatory authorities (USDA/APHIS). For example, certain life stages (queen bees, package bees, drone semen) may be permitted, depending on their health (absence of notifiable diseases like AFB-American foulbrood), physical inspection, and documentation criteria (several export/import permits needed from both Canada and the USA). Even though humans have been hunting honey and keeping honey bees for thousands of years, bee breeding is a relatively recent practice. Honey bee reproduction was not well understood until 1845, and the practice of mating specific queens and drones did not begin to occur in a controlled fashion for another hundred years. Beekeepers bred the different subspecies available to them together, combining gene pools through artificial or natural insemination of queens with selected drones/sperm over multiple generations to produce bees with traits they desired. In North America, we call these bees that were intentionally bred stocks. They represent a small amount of the large genetic variation found

in the bee lineages. Many have been so thoroughly bred with each other that they differ greatly from the original subspecies brought over hundreds of years ago. While most bees in North America today are descended from Italians, they are not the same pure Italian bees first introduced in 1859. They have been bred with other subspecies and have genes associated with these other subspecies, although they are called Italians since they resemble Apis mellifera ligustica most closely, with regard to their coloration and other traits. Other stocks, like Buckfast bees, are a hybrid of Apis mellifera ligustica and Apis mellifera mellifera and contain a mixture of genetic traits from each. Anyone who breeds bees to maintain specific traits is essentially creating a stock of honey bees. There are many stocks available for purchase in the U.S. from bee breeders, with new ones constantly in development. Italian bees (Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership)

Carniolan bees (Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership) Traits Associated With Subspecies and Stocks Different subspecies and stocks are known for different traits. The Honey Bee Subspecies and Stock Traits Table includes the most common past and present stocks in the U.S. It outlines the general traits of each stock. We have also included notes on their origin, rarity, other behavioral traits, and appearance. Keep in mind that there can be a lot of variation in traits within a stock, so this table serves as a general guide, not a guarantee. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Africanized Honey Bees The Africanized honey bee (AHB), colloquially called “the killer bee,” is a hybrid of Apis mellifera scutellata (A) and Apis mellifera mellifera (M). Note that “Africanized” refers to hybrid bees and “African” refers to pure Apis mellifera scutellata (or other African subspecies) in their home region. These bees are known for their highly defensive nature. In 1956, A. m. scutellata were introduced to an experimental apiary in Brazil for a program meant to breed bees adapted to a tropical climate. Within a year, however, 26 queens, along with several swarms of A. m. mellifera, were accidentally released from their enclosure. They mated with other Apis mellifera subspecies in the vicinity and moved both south and north, sometimes hundreds of miles a year, reaching California in 1985 and Texas in 1990. They occupy several Southern and Southwestern states of the continental U.S. (Arizona, New Mexico, California, Nevada, Utah, and Oklahoma) and, more recently, Southeastern states (Louisiana, Arkansas, Florida, and North Carolina). They are therefore not a major concern of Northeastern beekeepers, except for the occasional hot hive that is traced to a Southern queen or package. The rapid spread of Africanized bees is due to the relative success of their genes. More than half of the genome in most Africanized honey bees (AHB) is of A. m. scutellata descent. Traits from European bees have tended to be lost or less expressed over time due to several factors. AHB colonies tend to be smaller, but they grow faster and swarm more. They also produce more and faster drones, meaning that queens of all subspecies mate disproportionately with AHB drones. Queens fathered by AHB drones also emerge earlier and can kill their rivals within their queen cells. AHB swarms sometimes practice “nest usurpation,” meaning they invade other colonies and replace the queen with their own. Africanized bee swarm.

The name “killer bee” comes from their tendency to sting with less provocation and in greater numbers than other subspecies. Their nest sizes are often smaller than European bees, but they defend a larger area around that nest. The nests are also more likely to be in ground cavities, less visible, and therefore less easily avoided. The bees can pursue intruders well beyond the vicinity of their hives; up to a quarter mile. An estimated thousand humans and more animals have died from a large quantity of stings. These have generally been in situations where they could not run away (because of young or old age, or confinement; e.g., a dog being chained). The stings of individual AHB are no more painful or venomous than those of other honey bees, but they are generally greater in number. The same precautions and reactions apply: Leave the area, cover your face/head, do not swat at the bees. Because Africanized bees do pursue and persist, jumping in water to hide is not recommended; they may wait until you emerge for air and continue to sting. Identifying AHB can be difficult: In short, any colony that is excessively defensive needs to be kept away from humans and animals and may need to be destroyed. In this case, there is no need to identify whether the colony is Africanized or not; it is simply unsuitable in an area inhabited by humans or livestock. If the colony needs to be identified, however, some behavioral and morphological traits distinguish European bees from AHB: AHB workers tend to be smaller in body size than European bees — although hybrids may be just as big — and their wings have different vein patterns. Behaviorally, in addition to those traits already discussed, individuals tend to transition to foraging earlier in their lives and have a lower threshold of sugar concentration for foraging, meaning that they bring back more watered-down nectar/resources. Finally, they are more resistant to some pests; e.g., Varroa mites. This may be in part to their relatively high use of propolis, their tendency to swarm, or other factors. In general, however, this is not a surefire route to identification. Genetic testing is the most reliable method to determine whether your bees are indeed Africanized. Watch this video to learn more about Africanized honey bees and how to approach a colony you suspect may be Africanized. Module Introduction: Queen Rearing With the Doolittle Method The ability to rear queens is a key skill to begin breeding bees or simply to raise queens for your own colonies without needing to purchase them every year. Whether your goal is to rear queens on a large scale for profit or on a small scale to keep bees sustainably in your backyard, the Doolittle method is our recommended route. This module outlines the steps and considerations you should take with this method to be able to successfully rear queens. Rearing queens can benefit your beekeeping operation because it allows you to have queens on hand to replace failing or missing queens in your colonies. If you like to requeen your colonies annually to improve their productivity, you can have your own source of queens to do so. Being able to rear your own queens instead of relying on purchasing queens is a great way to become a more self-sufficient beekeeper. Back to Table of Contents

Read: The Doolittle Method There are many ways to rear queens depending on the number of colonies you manage, the number of queens you need, and the amount of time, money, and effort you want to invest. If you are a hobbyist who only wants to have a couple of extra queens on hand, you can simply pull nucs from your strong hives and allow those nucs to rear their own queens — make sure to include frames with eggs in the nuc. This practice becomes even more convenient if your strong colonies have begun building swarm cells. Move some young swarm cells into a nuc and allow the bees in the nuc to finish raising those queens. If you are only looking to rear a few queens and can do it in this way, it's a great approach! A paper published in 2019 found when queens lay eggs directly in queen cups, the daughter queens have a larger body mass and more ovarioles than queens grafted from eggs laid in worker cells. In this course, however, we cover a more advanced method of queen rearing called the Doolittle method, based on grafting larvae that develop into queens. This method is used most often by beekeepers who require more than a few queens at one time. This method scales well; you can rear several queens or hundreds at once. It also allows you to select larvae from your best colonies and ensure that they have abundant resources to develop into strong and healthy queens. Rearing queens by grafting entails carefully moving young larvae from a regular worker brood frame into manmade queen cups. Grafting lets you be in control of the timing: You know exactly how old the cells are at each stage and when they are ready to be inserted into new colonies or sold as is. Yet it requires some specific tools, fine motor skills, and much practice. Injuring the young larvae in any way, drying them out, or placing them in the wrong position in the queen cup will result in failure. You shouldn’t expect a 100% success rate, although with practice you might get close. Although this course focuses on grafting, there are many methods to rear queens that do not involve grafting. Your knowledge of these methods will not be tested here, but if you are interested, you can read up on them in "Queen Rearing and Bee Breeding," the comprehensive book by Harry Laidlaw and Robert Page (1997). These methods include but are not limited to the Miller method, the Alley method, and the Smith method.

The Doolittle method of queen rearing. Overview of the Doolittle Method 1. Very young larvae are selected from a queen mother colony and are placed (grafted) into manmade queen cups. 2. These new queen cells are inserted into a cell starter for 24 hours, where nurse bees feed them with abundant royal jelly. 3. After 24 hours, the larvae have doubled in size. The larvae are then transferred to a cell finisher, where workers continue feeding them and eventually cap the cell. 4. After nine to ten days, the queen cells are nearly finished developing and can be harvested one to two days before they will emerge. 5. The capped, nearly mature queen cells can be placed into new hives as is, but most are placed in small hives called mating nucs. Mating nucs permit queens to emerge from their cells to sexually mature, take mating flights, and begin laying eggs. 6. After queens have mated, beekeepers locate the queen in the mating nuc; if she is mated and laying a good pattern, she is removed to be sold or placed in a full-size colony. Back to Table of Contents

▶ Read: Biological Considerations Honey bee biology is key to queen rearing. You need to think about timing, resources, and bees’ instincts to requeen themselves, and be aware of other instincts that might stymie your efforts! Timing A female larva develops into a worker or a queen based on the nutrition she receives in the first 12 to 36 hours after hatching from the egg. Queen rearing, therefore, requires specific timing. Whether you leave it up to the bees or graft larvae yourself, the process starts with eggs or larvae less than 36 hours old. Seasonal considerations are important, too. While it is possible to rear queens from late April to the end of September, swarm season is the easiest time to rear queens. It is during this period that there are abundant food resources in the colony, rising colony populations, and drones to mate with in the area. When you start to observe drones being produced in your colonies, you have the green light to get started! In the Northeast, swarm season generally starts in mid-May and ends in mid-July. Queen rearing is also easier during a honey flow. Before and after swarm season or during a dearth, you may need to supplement your queen rearing operation with more food and you may not rear as many queens. Resources Colonies require resources to make new queens. There need to be sufficient nurse bees to care for and feed royal jelly to developing larvae. To create royal jelly, the nurse bees need to have access to adequate pollen and nectar, which, in most queen rearing operations, requires feeding. In short, developing healthy queens requires lots of nurse bees and lots of food. Instinct to Create Queens Honey bees will create queens under three conditions. First, if the current queen is aging or otherwise failing, they will create a new queen to supersede her. The old queen’s pheromones signify her age since the amount she produces diminishes over time. It is also thought that workers can detect a reduced rate of egg-laying by their queen. This prompts them to build supersedure queen cups. Second, if the queen is accidentally killed or lost, the colony will undertake emergency queen replacement. ▶ ▶

When a queen is removed, workers can begin to detect that she is missing after as little as 15 minutes. If there are eggs or larvae less than 36 hours old in the colony, they will mold a worker cell with an egg or young larva in it into a larger queen cell. If there are no larvae young enough, the colony will not be able to rear a new queen and it will die as its bees age and are not replaced. Finally, when the colony population grows bigger than the space available to it in the hive, it prepares to swarm and creates several highquality swarm cells. Colonies will usually produce many more swarm cells than supersedure cells. They can create a few swarm cells every day for a week or so leading up to swarming. To stimulate bees to produce queens, the beekeeper needs to create these conditions. The easiest to do are the latter two: causing a queen emergency and simulating swarming conditions. This colony was crowded and produced multiple swarm cells; the cell on the left is capped. The cell on the right will be capped within a few days. Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership Instinct to Kill Queens When bees need a new queen, they generally produce many queen cells as insurance that at least one of those cells will successfully rear a queen. The first queen to emerge kills the other queens still developing in their cells, and if multiple queens emerge, they fight to the death until one queen remains. So, if you want to rear multiple queens, the nearly mature cells must be separated to permit the queens to emerge from their cells without competition. Back to Table of Contents ▶

▶ Read: Queen Grafting Queen grafting entails choosing larvae of a selected age and placing them in manmade queen cups. It takes fine motor skills, practice — around 50 tries — as well as a few tools. Rearing queens through grafting lets you be in control: You know exactly how old the cells are at each stage and when they are ready to be inserted into new colonies or sold as is. Once you have the practice down, you can expect a success rate of around 80% to 85%. Picking up the young larvae incorrectly, injuring them in any way, drying them out, or placing them in the wrong position in the queen cup will result in failure. Nurse bees check all the larvae once they are inserted into cell building starters, and nurses will avoid feeding the larvae that have any of these issues. Any problems will be visible within a day because they won't feed the larva or draw out the cell. Selecting and Preparing Larvae To Graft Pull out a frame of brood that contains the right age larvae to graft; 12 to 36 hours. These larvae will be around the same size as an egg, will be laying in a slight crescent shape, and will have a small amount of jelly in their cells. Choose frames from a colony that contain eggs and search in the cells close to those eggs to find the very young larvae. Some beekeepers make the process easier by confining the queen to a certain spot on empty comb with a "push in" cage so she is forced to lay eggs in that spot. After three days, the eggs hatch, and the beekeeper can confidently graft from these larvae knowing they are the right age. When you are ready to select the brood frame you are going to graft from, place the queen on another frame and gently brush the remaining bees off. Be very careful not to let the larvae dry out as you bring the frame indoors; otherwise, they will not develop properly. Ideally, your breeder colony will be located close to your grafting room so that the larvae are exposed to wind and dry conditions for the shortest time possible. If there is more than a minute or so of a walk, carefully wrap the brood frame in a damp towel to keep it moist and protected. Bring the frame into your grafting room. The Grafting Room Grafting should be done indoors as working with brood frames outdoors can attract pests and robbing if there is honey on the brood frame. The room conditions should be warm — ideally warmer than room temperature — and should be very bright to properly see the young larvae for grafting. Having a bright lamp to shine directly into ▶

▶ the brood cells is very handy. A damp cloth should be on hand to lay over the queen cups on the grafting frames as you insert larvae to prevent them from getting too dry. It is important to maintain a clean area for grafting. Surfaces should be disinfected ahead of time, and the grafting tool should be cleaned between colonies. Tools Needed Grafting tool — there are a variety on the market; try several to see which you prefer Grafting frame — a frame with three bars and 45 cups Lamp Something to elevate your frame to be at the appropriate angle and comfortable height Glass vial with previously collected royal jelly and dropper (optional) Headset with a magnifying glass (optional) Damp towel to lay over the part of the brood frame you are not working on The grafting tool used to pick up larvae.

▶ Queen cups attached to a bar. If you look closely in the cups, you will see larvae of the appropriate age settled on top of a small pool of royal jelly. Grafting Frame Assemble your cups on the bars. Modern equipment from bee suppliers allows you to slide plastic cups onto a bar, and you can choose how many cups to put on each bar and how many bars you will insert into your colonies. Grafting frames vary in the number of cups they can hold, but they generally have three frames that each hold 15 cups, allowing you to insert up to 45 grafted larvae into one cell building colony at one time. The maximum recommended cups to have on one frame is 45: 15 cups per bar, three bars per frame. If you want fewer queen cells than that, you can adjust it however you want. The nurse bees in the cell-builder colonies tend to accept the cups better if they are first placed in a colony for a day to be “conditioned” by the bees or if they are lightly painted with melted wax. Grafting With Royal Jelly ▶

Before placing the larvae in the queen cup, many beekeepers will add a small amount of royal jelly mixed with water in a 1:1 ratio to the bottom of the cup to prime the cell. This gives the larvae a gentler landing in the cell by floating it off into royal jelly. Royal jelly can be collected ahead of time by the beekeeper from swarm cells or other queen cells and stored in a glass jar in the freezer for a few months before being used. Royal jelly is collected from two- to three-day-old queen cells by scooping it out with a royal jelly spoon and discarding the queen larva. Dilute the jelly in a 1:1 ratio with warm water in a small vial or cup and use a dropper to prime each cup with a small amount of this solution — less than a full droplet — immediately before grafting. After you have primed your cell, use your grafting tool to carefully scoop out larvae that are 12 to 36 hours old. At first, you may find it easier to break down some of the cell walls to access the larvae until you get good at the scooping method. It is critical that the larvae enter the cups in the same orientation that they were in the cells. Larvae lay on their sides and breathe through the spiracles on the side facing upward. They should not be jarred on the side of their original cells as you remove them, as this can injure them. The scooping needs to be very gentle. Do not flip the larva over, do not submerge it in the royal jelly, and do not shake it. Flipping them over or submerging them in royal jelly blocks these spiracles and causes suffocation. Very carefully, place the larva into the center of the queen cup. Some grafting tools scoop up the royal jelly and the larva, while others scoop up mainly the larva. Some grafting tools, like the Chinese tool, have a small plunger to help release the larva. You will figure out what method and tool work best for you as you practice. If you suspect you injured a larva, discard that one and try it again with a new larva. Most commercial queen rearers dry-graft; that is, they do not prime the cell cups with royal jelly first. They carefully scoop up the desired larvae and some of the jelly it is floating in, and they place it into a dry queen cup gently. With this method, the cup contains the larva as well as a small amount of the royal jelly it was resting in. After you have completed one bar of grafting, place it upside down (the larvae will remain in the cups) on a damp towel while you finish grafting the other bars. This will prevent the young larvae from drying out. After you have completed grafting your frames, you are ready to insert it into your cell starter box. Back to Table of Contents

▶ Read: Considerations When Placing Your Graft in Cell Builders There are several things to take into consideration when placing your graft into cell builders. Placing Your Grafting Frame in the Cell Starter Immediately after you are finished filling your queen cups, add the bars to your grafting frame and carry it out to the bee yard covered in a damp towel. Slowly and carefully insert the frame into the middle position of your cell starter. One by one, quickly inspect the other frames in your cell starter to make sure there are no other young larvae present that will compete with your queen cells. Once the grafting frame is inserted, it is critical that you do not disturb or shake the colony. Developing queens are very sensitive and can easily be damaged or killed from rough handling. Handle grafting frames as little as possible and with extraordinary care. For the highest quality of queens, we recommend only inserting one grafting frame in a cell starter. Each grafting frame can contain up to 45 queen cells; three rows each with 15 cells. A very strong finisher, three to four deep hive bodies tall, can provide for two grafting frames, but too many queen cells may mean there are not enough nurse bees or resources to adequately feed them. Fewer healthy, strong queens are preferable to many poor queens. ▶ Placing Your Grafting Frame in the Cell Finisher

▶ After 24 hours have passed, carefully lift the grafting frame out of the cell starter. The queen cells will have more wax added to them and the larvae will be larger and provisioned with lots of jelly. The queen cells will be covered with nurse bees. Gently brush the nurses off with a bee brush. You can use a little smoke as well, but do not drive smoke directly into the open cells. Place the grafting frame into the cell finisher and, again, be very gentle when doing so. Removing Your Grafting Frame From the Cell Finisher Nine days after you introduce the queen cells to the cell finisher, the queen cells are ready to harvest. They will be ready to emerge from their cells in two days. Queen cells can either be inserted directly into mating nucs or can be placed into an incubator set to the proper temperature and humidity to keep them warm until you are ready to ship them to customers. If you are going to be away from the bee yard the day the queens are to be removed, place queen cell protectors over each cell on your grafting frame prior to inserting it into the cell finisher. Without a queen cell protector, the first queen to emerge will quickly destroy all the other queen cells in your cell finisher. Queen cell protectors can be bought from your local bee supplier. With them, the queens will emerge in their protectors and workers will feed them through the mesh/holes until you have time to return to the colonies and can harvest the queen cells.
Cells are removed from the cell finisher after nine days. They are then transported in a protective box or incubator. (Photo credit: Jon Ryan)
They are inserted in mating nucs. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Cell Builders — The Cell Starter Healthy queens can be reared by using cell builders, which are colonies used to build queen cells. Grafting frames containing larvae are inserted into cell-building colonies. The workers will provide them with royal jelly and draw out and cap the cells. These cell builders can be either cell starters or cell finishers, and each is prepared one day in advance of when they will receive larvae. Strong cell builders are overflowing with bees. Photo credit: Ben Rulison The Cell Starter The purpose of a cell starter is to provision the developing queen cells with ample early nutrition to get them off to a good start. Queen larvae are only placed in the cell starter for one day. When nurses are primed to raise queens, they produce a lot of royal jelly. Yet as they age, their ability to sustain an intense level of feeding this many queens decreases. For this reason, after 24 hours, queen cells are often transferred to a cell finisher. The cell starter colony can be a swarm box — a nuc with a screened bottom to allow ventilation and no entrance — or it can be a deep hive body on a bottom board with an open entrance. The advantage of using a swarm box is that fewer bees are needed. Remove the queen from the cell starter 24 hours before you introduce the grafting frame to simulate an emergency queen-rearing situation. The bees will be eager to quickly start rearing queens from the larvae you introduce. The cell starter should also have a large population of bees — especially nurse bees — packed to the point that they beard at the entrance. Provide it with frames of capped brood that will soon emerge and continue contributing to the population. There are no larvae (open brood) in the cell starter. This ensures that all of the nurse bees’ resources go toward the queen cells you introduce. It also prevents the colony from raising its own queens. Supply the cell starter with abundant bee bread. Frames of pollen/bee bread placed next to the queen rearing frames allow the nurse bees to use this protein to produce royal jelly to feed the

queen larvae. Protein supplement/substitute should be supplied if little pollen is naturally available, and sugar syrup (1:1) should be supplied to feed the adult bees. Lastly, if using a swarm box with no entrance, place a small sponge soaked with water inside the colony, and place the swarm box in a cool, dark space so the crowded colony can remain cool. If using a deep hive body, you may need to provide extra ventilation if the weather is quite warm. ⌃ Long description A hive box with ten frames. Frame 1 is a syrup feeder frame. Frame 2 is honey. Frames 3 and 4 are capped brood. Frame 5 is pollen. Where Frame 6 usually is, there is an open space for a grafting frame. Frame 7 is pollen. Frames 8 and 9 are capped brood. Frame 10 is honey. Mating nucs are small colonies so that it is easy to find the queen after she has returned from her mating flight. These colonies also do not require a lot of resources, which makes them easier for beekeepers to create and manage. The queen emerges from her cell on Day 16 (Day 1 is the day she was laid as an egg). She takes approximately one week to become sexually mature then takes her mating flight(s) if weather conditions are good. Two days after she returns from her mating flight, the queen should begin laying eggs. Initially, she may lay multiple, parallel eggs in some cells until she gets into a regular laying pattern. Module Introduction: Breeding for the Traits You Desire If you're interested in maintaining a few colonies that are better able to survive the winters in your region or thinking about starting a largescale breeding program to sell mite-resistant stock for profit, having a fundamental understanding of honey bee breeding is required. In this module, we begin to explore how to breed honey bees and what traits beekeepers can select for. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Breeding Bees Honey bee breeding is a powerful tool at the disposal of beekeepers. The goal of bee breeding is to increase desirable traits in a bee stock while removing undesirable traits. Just as horse breeders can breed the fastest horses and farmers can breed the juiciest tomatoes, beekeepers can breed bees for a variety of different traits. Let’s say you have 10 colonies. Two of them produce a lot of surplus honey for you to harvest, three of them produce very little surplus honey, and the remaining five produce a moderate amount. Breeding bees (queens and drones) from those two productive colonies may help you produce more colonies that express the same trait — good honey production — in the following generation. Of course, breeders can only select for traits that arise, at least in part, from genes. These traits include gentleness, a good laying pattern, a reduced tendency to swarm, fast spring buildup, good wax production, some elements of hardiness in cold winters, high honey production, hygienic behavior, grooming behavior, an instinct to bite or otherwise incapacitate Varroa mites, and more. It is more complicated than that, though. Some traits are easier to select for than others, depending on particular qualities of the genes. A complex trait like honey production is governed by many genes, and it can be difficult to select multiple genes at the same time. Furthermore, the environment plays a big role in behavioral traits. The forage available within its flying distance, the amount of precipitation, and the weather conditions during nectar flows all influence how much honey a colony stores. Lastly, we often want many beneficial traits in our bees. Not only do we want them to be good honey producers, but we also want them to grow quickly in the spring, be robust in the face of cold winters, and be resistant to major pests and diseases. Selecting for all these traits, which are governed by many different genes, while also considering how outside environmental factors are influencing the expression of those traits, is complicated and requires trade-offs. No one bee stock can excel in every single trait, so it is up to the breeder to decide what traits to prioritize. If you are new to bee breeding, try selecting one trait to begin with, then build up your experience over several years. There are many ways to approach breeding. Some methods include the inbred-hybrid breeding system, the circular mating system, and the mass selection system. These systems for extensive breeding efforts will not be covered here; what we will do instead is cover the primary principles behind breeding. From these principles, Master Beekeepers can develop their own approaches.
Variation in honey production among colonies. Photo credit: Jon Ryan Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Genetic Diversity While many breeders select for one or more traits in their honey bees, an emerging trend is to instead promote colonies that have high genetic diversity. This is important for organisms to adapt to environmental changes and other pressures within one generation or over time. Genetic diversity — having many different gene versions present in a colony — is a result of the queens mating with many different drones. Some breeders strive to promote genetic diversity in their colonies. Instead of removing undesirable gene versions in a population through selective breeding, they establish populations of bees with many different gene versions and, as a result, many different traits. Different workers carry these different gene versions, so the colony as a whole is mixed. Genetic diversity has been shown to improve a colony’s ability to survive disease, stabilize the nest temperature in changing environments, store more honey, and build comb faster. Colonies with queens that have mated with many different males have lower rates of American Foulbrood infection than colonies with monandrous queens (queens that have mated with only one drone). Genetic diversity also leads to more productive colonies. In one study, colonies with polyandrous queens produced more new workers and drones, and therefore had more foraging workers returning to the hive every minute, stored about 40% more food, and were more likely to survive the winter than colonies with monandrous queens. Swarms from colonies with polyandrous queens also found new nest sites faster. Watch this video to learn more about the benefits of genetic diversity.
