Read: Inbreeding Inbreeding, or the production of offspring from closely related individuals, leads to a loss of genetic diversity. Sometimes breeding efforts can lead to inbreeding, when breeders remove so many gene versions from a population that only a few remain. When inbreeding occurs at length, there are a limited number of gene versions in a given population. Select mutations may become more common. If colonies are faced with a new selection pressure (such as a drought or a bad infection), an inbred colony may have no workers with traits that can survive that event, and the colony could die out. Inbreeding also increases the likelihood of larvae inheriting two identical versions of the sex determination gene, which causes them to be cannibalized by their sisters. Less dramatically, if certain desirable traits are missing from the gene pool, a beekeeper using only an inbred population to select from for breeding purposes may find that none strongly display the trait of interest (for example, none may be especially gentle or especially good honey producers). No matter how carefully bees are bred, the desired traits cannot be produced unless the gene versions associated with those traits are present. You can avoid inbreeding by making sure that your queens come from genetically diverse lines and periodically requeening from different stock as well as by ensuring that virgins can access a large and diverse population of drones, whether through mating flights or artificial insemination. It is best to use unrelated drones from different colonies to mate with your queens to reduce possible inbreeding. To reduce the chances of inbreeding, it is ideal to use five to 10 colonies as your queen mother colonies and 10 to 15 colonies as your drone mother colonies. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Overview of Breeding Bees There are many methods to breeding bees, but they all boil down to mating the queens from your best colonies with drones from your other best colonies. You can allow them to mate naturally or you can use artificial insemination to insert semen from chosen drones into your chosen queen. Here are the main steps to bee breeding: Evaluate traits in your colonies to determine which colonies you will select as your queen mother colonies and drone mother colonies. To do this, set up an isolated apiary with the colonies you wish to evaluate. This apiary is called your testing apiary. The colonies that receive the highest evaluations will be your queen mother and drone mother colonies. Take careful notes on how your colonies perform with regard to your trait(s) of interest over time. Graft larvae from your queen mother colonies and place them into cell builders to mature. Place your drone mother colonies in yards one to three miles away from your mating nucs — this is the typical distance queens travel to drone congregation areas. If you can, have your drone mother apiaries spread out from one another in a circle, with your queen mother apiary located in the center of the circle, so no matter which way the virgins fly, they are likely to encounter a drone congregation area that contains your drones. If you do not live in a remote location, your queens will likely mate with other drones in the area — not just your drone mother colonies' drones. Make sure the timing aligns so that there will be sexually mature drones in your drone mother colonies when your virgin queens are ready to mate with them. The earliest you can time your first graft of the year is to coincide it with when much of the drone brood has reached the stage where they have developed purple eyes. Open a couple developing drones to check their eye color. Place mature queen cells into mating nucs one day before the queens are ready to emerge. Virgin queens will emerge and, within a week or so, they will mate with drones in the surrounding area. Once the queens are mated and laying, introduce them into full-sized hives or sell them. For any queens you keep, continue to evaluate their traits over time. Keep breeding in this way for several generations until the trait you are interested in is consistently expressed in your daughter queens.

Once a stock is established — say, one with good hygienic behavior that confers resistance to Varroa mites — it must be maintained through continued breeding. If it is not, this trait will eventually be weeded out as the queens carrying hygienic genes mate openly with drones carrying other genes. Some regions have cooperative breeding programs, where all beekeepers in the area maintain bees with certain traits, saturate the region with these drones, and perpetuate these traits in the population. Breeding bees with specific traits is a continuous effort. If you only want to breed bees for yourself, then you probably do not want to continuously maintain breeding lines. In this case, you can do small-scale breeding in your bee yard and, every few years, purchase a queen with the traits you desire from a reputable breeder. That way, if open mating has weeded out some of the traits you selected, you can reintroduce them. Back to Table of Contents

Read: The Role of Drones Female honey bees — both queens and workers — inherit half of their genes from their mother and half of their genes from their father. Therefore, selection of good quality drone mother colonies is equally as important as selection of the queen mother colonies. Add drone comb foundation to each of your drone mother colonies in your mating apiary well in advance — at least 35 to 40 days before drones are needed — to boost the number of drones in preparation for mating. Drones take 24 days to develop from egg to adult plus an additional nine to 12 days to sexually mature and be ready to mate. Remember that if you are inserting undrawn drone comb, the bees will need more time and resources to draw it out. Also, keep in mind colonies will only start investing in producing drones if they perceive they have the resources to begin investing in reproduction. These colonies should be healthy, strong, and have access to good nutrition. Under good conditions, you can expect up to 20% of comb to be built for drone rearing and about 5% of the bees to be drones. So in a strong colony in early June that may have around 20,000 bees, about 1,000 of them may be drones. Drone mother colonies may need to be fed honey/syrup and bee bread/pollen/pollen substitute in early spring to build the population. Simulating a nectar flow in a strong population encourages queens to lay drones, and good nutrition is critical for the first few days after emergence for drones to develop high-quality and abundant sperm. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Controlled Mating vs. Open Mating Controlled Mating Controlled mating is the surefire way to know the genealogy of your bees because you know exactly which drones the queen is mating with. Attempts at controlled mating began as early as the 1700s, when beekeepers confined queens and drones in glass dishes, hoping they would mate. As we know, queens and drones require specific conditions for mating and do not mate in confined spaces naturally. The past several hundred years have seen many advances in controlled mating, and now it can be accomplished in two ways: Isolated mating yards: Some beekeepers have isolated areas where they set up their breeding apiaries. These areas could be in mountain valleys or on islands, separated by at least nine miles — the maximum flight distance — from other wild and managed honey bee colonies. Only the colonies that they wish to breed are present in these areas; drone congregation areas only have drones from those colonies. Artificial queen insemination, also known as instrumental insemination: If you do not have access to an island or mountain valley, it will be difficult to ensure your queen is only mating with the desired drones. In this case, you can accomplish controlled mating using instrumental insemination. The first instruments for queen insemination were developed at Cornell University in 1927; the technique has been successfully implemented since the 1940s and refined over time. Open Mating You may not have access to an isolated island or mountain valley; you may instead live in an area with many colonies in your bees’ flight range. You may also not have the desire to learn artificial queen insemination and purchase the necessary equipment. In cases like this, your queens must mate openly. Open mating is the natural mating process, wherein queens mate with 10 to 20 adult drones in drone congregation areas. Most beekeepers rely on open mating, but there is no guarantee that their queens will mate with drones of their desired stock. To combat this, try to saturate your area with drones exhibiting the traits you desire by setting out many drone mother colonies and by putting drone comb frames in your drone mother colonies. If you contact surrounding beekeepers, you can collectively bring in colonies with desired traits and saturate the area with good drones.
An openly mated queen returns with her mating sign. Photo credit: Jennifer Tsuruda Back to Table of Contents

Read: Evaluating and Comparing Colonies' Traits Your inspection records may reveal which colonies exhibit traits that you like. Colonies that you like should be moved to a testing apiary to be evaluated for the traits of interest and considered for drone mother and queen mother colonies. If the traits are heritable, then the offspring colony should resemble the parental colonies. Selection of traits through a breeding program like this — and repeated every year for the continual improvement of colonies in your apiary — will, over time, generate your own desired stock of honey bees. Indeed, the colonies from your selected queens, and drones should also eventually be evaluated to ensure they have the trait(s) you want. In the testing apiary, reduce drifting as much as possible. Drifting bees from neighboring colonies can make up as much as 30% of the bees in a colony! We do not want to assess the traits of these adopted neighbors. Make sure the colonies are several yards apart and each colony has a unique landmark to help orient the bees. Do not arrange the colonies in rows or in a regular way. Do not interchange brood or bees between colonies, either. These practices ensure that the bees performing the behavior in a particular colony are from the same genetic line as the queen in the colony. Assessments A system for evaluating your colonies helps you choose which ones to breed from. The system will also evaluate your success to determine whether the new colonies did, in fact, inherit the traits you wanted. Assess all the colonies in your testing bee yard and keep detailed records of the scores they receive. For some traits, it takes two or more years to thoroughly assess a colony’s performance; e.g., queen longevity or winter survival. If possible, keep the colonies in the same apiary to reduce geographical factors, and treat them similarly: Feed them the same amount if supplementing in spring or fall and overwinter them using the same methods.

Next, develop a scale for assessing traits to help you keep records of how the colonies perform. These scales can vary as you see fit, but they traditionally look something like this. Scale for assessing traits Unacceptable Poor Satisfactory Good Excellent 0 1 2 3 4 For example, colonies with no frames of surplus honey might receive zero points, one to five frames receive 1 point, six to ten frames receive 2 points, 11 to 15 frames receive 3 points, and 16 or more frames receive 4 points. Assess your colonies yourself to reduce evaluation bias from other people and assess all of them during the same time period to reduce the influence of seasonal or other environmental factors. Since there is no North American standard for evaluating traits, there is a lot of variation in evaluations and record keeping. Here, we have provided some examples of assessment methods on a small selection of traits. Honey Production The most common way to assess honey production is by waiting until the end of the beekeeping season and weighing your honey supers after you have removed them. Record the weight of the honey supers for each colony, extract the honey, reweigh the empty supers, and subtract the second number from the first. This gives you the total weight of extracted honey. You can also count the number of frames of honey produced by their colonies. You can do this on a scale of 0 to 5, as shown above, or just use the total number of frames. Although these two ways are the most accurate, they require that you wait until the end of the season to compare colonies. Alternatively, you can keep track of hive weights during a honey flow. Honey production is directly correlated with short-term weight gain. Use a hive scale to weigh the colony gains at the beginning of an expected honey flow. Weigh all the colonies again after the honey flow is over and subtract the initial weight. Be sure to collect all colony weights on the same day and within a narrow time window. Evaluate each colony’s performance using the scale you have devised — either 0 to 5 or another scale. Gentleness

Gentleness is usually assessed with leather. Honey bees have an aversion to the smell of leather and are prone to sting it. You can attach a piece of leather to a stick and use it to provoke the bees. Wave it around the entrance of the colony and remove the inner and outer covers and wave it around the open hive. Do this for an equal amount of time for each colony — usually two minutes — and count the number of stings in each piece of leather. Score the colonies using the scale you have devised. Hygienic Behavior Hygienic behavior is the ability of adult bees to detect dead brood and their tendency to uncap the cells and remove/chew the dead brood quickly. Hygienic behavior lowers the likelihood of brood diseases like American foulbrood and chalkbrood because infection levels can be lowered if the affected brood is removed quickly. Hygienic behavior is also associated with Varroa resistance. Varroa mites reproduce in capped brood cells, so detecting and removing infested larvae can help reduce mite infestation levels. Testing for this hygienic behavior does not involve introducing any of these diseases into your colonies. Pull out a frame with capped brood from the colony you would like to assess. Kill a small section of the capped brood cells with liquid nitrogen or by pricking them with a pin. Replace the frame in the hive, and return to assess it after 48 hours. Bees with good hygienic behavior should remove all or almost all the brood that was killed. Bees with poor hygienic behavior leave the dead brood or are much slower to remove it. Score each colony’s performance using the scale you have devised. Swarming Historically, beekeepers tended to select against swarming tendency in colonies. Now that we know swarming is beneficial in reducing Varroa mite populations, more beekeepers are now more open to having their colonies swarm regularly. If you wish to select against swarming, it can easily be quantified by whether a colony swarmed and by the presence of swarm cells in the colony.

During each inspection, look for queen cups or queen cells. Colonies that initiated the swarming process despite having adequate room in the hive are not selected as breeding colonies, whereas colonies that do not initiate swarming are in the running. Make sure that the colonies being assessed have the same amount of room — number of hive bodies — available on the same dates. Brood Quantity The amount of brood a queen produces throughout the year can be assessed relatively easily. For example, a colony may have brood present on five frames. One frame is covered entirely with brood (100%), two frames contain 50% brood each, and two others contain only 25% brood each. The remaining five frames in the colony are honey, pollen/bee bread, drawn comb, or empty. This colony would therefore contain 100% + 50% + 50% + 25% + 25% = 250% or 2.5 frames of brood. You can also change these scores to values of 0 to 5, depending on the evaluation system you use. Brood Quality Good queens produce solid brood patterns. High-quality brood is continuous on the frame (not spotty) and arranged in concentric circles. This means that the queen begins laying in the center of the frame and continues in a circular fashion, moving outwards. You can rate brood quality on a scale of 0 to 5, based on the degree of spottiness and neighboring brood of mismatched ages. You may want to take into account the age of the queen. Additional Traits Additional traits that you might assess include early spring buildup, overwintering success, propolis production, pollen collection, and Varroa loads. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Evaluating Multiple Traits Across Multiple Yards Evaluating one trait at a time is straightforward. If you are interested in more than one trait, fill out assessments for each trait of interest and add up the total score of the colonies. Colonies with the highest scores will be the queen mother and drone mother colonies. Here is an example of an assessment sheet for three colonies: A7, A9, and A14. The beekeeper wants to select for honey production, gentleness, hygienic behavior, and reduced Varroa loads. Assessing Multiple Colonies for Multiple Traits Colony code A7 A9 A14 Date assessed 7/15/16 7/15/16 7/15/16 Honey production score 2 4 0 Gentleness score 1 4 3 Hygienic behavior score 4 0 3 Varroa score 22 1 Total 9 10 7 Honey production: No frames of surplus honey (0 points), one to five frames (1 point), six to ten frames (2 points), 11 to 15 frames (3 points), 16 or more frames (4 points). Gentleness: No stings in the leather patch (4 points), one sting (3 points), two stings (2 points), three stings (1 point), four or more stings (0 points). Hygienic behavior: Removed 80% to 100% of dead brood in 48 hours (4 points), removed 60% to 79% (3 points), removed 40% to 59% (2 points), removed 20% to 39% (1 point), removed 19% or less (0 points). Varroa: Mite loads exceeded 12% by the end of the season (0 points), mite loads reached 9% to 11% (1 point), mite loads reached 6% to 8% (2 points), mite loads reached levels between 3% and 5% (3

points), mite loads stayed below 3% (four points). These scores reflect mite loads as a trait the beekeeper wants to discourage. If you value these traits equally, your best colony would be Colony A9, which received an overall score of 10. You can also select for one trait above all else. If you estimate that you favor, say, hygienic behavior twice as much as any other trait, double the scores from that row and leave all the other scores the same. Your new table looks like this. Assessing Multiple Colonies for Multiple Traits Colony code A7 A9 A14 Date assessed 7/15/16 7/15/16 7/15/16 Honey production 2 4 0 Gentleness 1 43 Hygienic behavior* 8 0 6 Varroa score 22 1 Total 13 10 10 *Twice as important as other traits. Now the best colony is Colony A7, which received a score of 13. These are just examples of assessment and record keeping. You can alter these calculations to make your records work for you. As you begin to evaluate your colonies for multiple traits and assign different priorities to them, the math gets a bit more complicated. Evaluating Colonies From Multiple Testing Apiaries If your test colonies are set up in two apiaries, it might be difficult to evaluate and reliably compare traits. Take honey production as an example: If one apiary had much more forage surrounding it than the other apiary, the colonies in the first apiary would have a natural advantage in producing more honey. At the end of the season, you rate your colonies for honey production (using the scale described above), and these are your results:

Evaluating Colonies From Multiple Testing Apiaries Apiary A: Apiary B: Good honey flow Poor honey flow Colony code A1 A2 A3 A4 A5 B1 B2 B3 B4 Assessment 2 3 3 5 5 1 1 2 4 Apiary average 3.6 2 Standard deviation* 1.3 1.4 *The standard deviation calculates the variation among hives. In examinations, we will provide you with standard deviation values. Colonies in Apiary A produced more honey on average than colonies in Apiary B. Based only on the amount of surplus honey created, you might think that the best colonies are A4 and A5 (both creating 17 to 20 frames of honey and receiving a score of 5). However, they had an advantage because they were in an apiary that had particularly good forage and rainfall. If they were in a different apiary, would they have performed as well? We cannot know based on that score alone. To eliminate the apiary effect on honey production, you can calculate Z scores for each of your colonies. The colony with the highest Z score is the one you should choose as your breeder queen. Using Z scores is not the only way to compare colonies across several apiaries, but this method is fairly simple. Z scores synthesize the individual score of each colony, the apiary average score, and the standard deviation (which measures the variation among colonies). You do not need to know how to calculate standard deviation for this course, but you are required to plug in numbers to calculate a colony’s Z score. The formula is simple: Z = (individual score – average)/standard deviation Here are the Z scores for each colony.

Evaluating Colonies From Multiple Testing Apiaries Apiary A: Good honey flow Apiary B: Poor honey flow Colony code A1 A2 A3 A4 A5 B1 B2 B3 B4 Assessment 2 3 3 5 5 1 1 2 4 Apiary average 3.6 2 Standard deviation 1.3 1.4 Z score -1.23 -0.46 -0.46 1.07 1.07 -0.71 -0.71 0 1.42 Colonies with negative scores performed worse than average. Colonies with positive scores performed better than average. Colonies with scores equal to zero performed average. Based on these scores, we can clearly see that our best colony was Colony B4, with a score of 1.42. They produced more surplus honey than average given their location in the apiary with the poor honey flow. If you were wondering what colony to breed from, this is it! The worst colony for honey production was Colony A1, with a score of -1.23. Back to Table of Contents

Assignment: Course Project — Plan Your Upcoming Bee Year It’s early spring and the active beekeeping season is just beginning! Planning for the year ahead will help you focus on your goals and strategize how to achieve them. Based on the topics we covered in this course, create a calendar/schedule for the year ahead that is unique to your goals, operation, and region. Feel free to use the beekeeping calendar provided in the course as a guide. Include the following points: 1. Your region. 2. The number of colonies you manage and the number of yards in which they are located. 3. At least two specific beekeeping goals for the year. For example, "Improve colony wintering success by merging weak colonies in September and feeding dry granulated sugar to all my colonies in late February," "Learn how to better handle swarms by setting out two bait hives in May," etc. 4. At least two management practices and considerations for each month. 5. Bloom times for at least five important bee plants in your region. Consult books, reputable websites from scientific organizations or extension personnel, and/or beekeeping magazines as resources to help you. Include information that is directly applicable to your beekeeping activities and that will help you in the upcoming season. Your project will be graded Complete or Incomplete. A grade of Complete is required for you to pass the course. Your facilitator will provide feedback for your submission and is available to answer questions as you work on your calendar. If you receive a grade of Incomplete, you must resubmit your project after incorporating the feedback from the facilitator to pass the course. Only two assignment resubmissions are permitted. Before you begin: Before starting your work, please review the rubric (list of evaluative criteria) for this assignment and eCornell's policy regarding plagiarism (the presentation of someone else's work as your own without source credit).

Thank You and Farewell Congratulations on completing "Master Beekeeping Part II: The Science and Art of Beekeeping" I hope that you will apply the systematic approach, practical techniques, and knowledge you learned to achieve your desired outcomes. The material covered in this course is intended to help you gain confidence in your ability to analyze different situations and make informed management decisions. I hope it has met your expectations as you support your colonies' survival and success. In addition, I hope that your beekeeping journey is allowing you to enjoy the unique pleasure that comes from connecting with bees and nature. Emma Walters Honey Bee Extension Associate Dyce Lab of Honey Bee Studies Cornell University View how Randy Oliver describes what inspires him about beekeeping: Video Transcript It's not for the money, obviously. It's a tough job to do. It's for the lifestyle. You've gotta love it. And as a lifelong naturalist and biologist, I love being in touch with nature. You're very much, just like any other form of agriculture, you're very much in touch with the seasons, with the rainfall, the temperature, with the plants that are blooming. So it's a lifestyle in our modern age where you're living very, very close to the land, you're very much aware every single day what's happening in nature with the bees. One of the stories is my younger son, he was 16 and he was working with me out in the bee yard an April day, beautiful day, perfect conditions. And we're going through this bee yard and he says, "Dad I know this is going to sound kind of weird, but on a day like this when the bees are this happy, it's like I get high. It's just like, it's this weird feeling." And I put down my hive tool, walked over, I gave him a big hug and I said, Ian, "You just became a beekeeper. You've got the bee vibe!" You're feeling that vibe of the bees. And that's what beekeeping is, you get in touch with that vibe of the colony. It's almost like a sixth sense. And when you have that, and Ian's had that since then. Ian has just got the vibe of the bees. He can open a hive, take the lid off, he goes oh, there's something wrong with this hive, or this hive's doing great. You have that feeling of the hive. That's what a beekeeper can aspire to do, to really become one with a part of nature, the bees, which are so much involved with everything else out there. Enjoying working outdoors. Enjoying producing an honest, healthy food crop. Performing pollination services and leaving a very green footprint on the planet earth. Beekeeping leaves an incredibly green footprint on the planet. So it's a lifestyle that you can be very very much, very proud of.

Glossary PTRENT002: Master Beekeeping Part 2: The Science and Art of Beekeeping College of Agricultural Life and Sciences, Cornell University abdomen The abdomen is one of three main body segments of insects (which also include the head and thorax). The abdomen contains the digestive and reproductive systems. Africanized honey bee The Africanized honey bee, colloquially called the killer bee, is a hybrid of Apis mellifera scutellata (A), and Apis mellifera mellifera (M). These bees are known for their aggressive nature and sustained defense of their hives. afterswarm An afterswarm is a second, smaller swarm that can occur a few days following a colony’s first swarm. altruism Altruism, biologically speaking, is animal behavior that benefits another animal at the expense of the first, in terms of survival or reproduction. Worker bees that forgo their own reproduction in order to help the queen reproduce is one of the most extreme examples of altruism in nature. See kin selection. amino acid Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. They are a necessary part of bees’ (and humans’) diets, necessary to function and develop. Pollen is the source of amino acids in bee bread and royal jelly. anaphylactic shock Anaphylactic shock is an extreme, life-threatening allergic reaction. anther The anther is the part of a flower that contains pollen. apiary An apiary is a collection of one or more hives, also called a bee yard. Most backyard beekeepers have only one apiary, but commercial beekeepers may manage dozens. Apidae Apidae is a family classification of bees. It is the largest family of bees and includes honey bees, bumble bees, carpenter bees, and many others. . All rights reserved. All other copyrights, trademarks, trade names, and logos are the sole property of their respective owners.

PTRENT002: Master Beekeeping Part 2: The Science and Art of Beekeeping College of Agricultural Life and Sciences, Cornell University Apis Apis is a genus classification of bees. It includes all bees that produce and store honey. Apis mellifera Apis mellifera is the scientific name for the Western honey bee. Apis is the genus and mellifera is the species. Mellifera means “bearer or maker of honey” (melli means “honey” and fera means “bearer”). arthropods (Arthropoda) Arthropoda is one of the many phyla of the animal kingdom. Honey bees are in the phylum Arthropoda, and are therefore known as arthropods. All arthropods are invertebrates and have jointed bodies and paired jointed appendages. artificial queen insemination (also known as instrumental insemination) Artificial queen insemination is a method of controlled mating where semen from a drone is used to inseminate a queen. assessment See colony assessment. bait hive A hive body or other box used to catch swarms. bee bread Bee bread is pollen that has been moistened by honey and honey bee glandular secretions and fermented by microorganisms such as yeast, bacteria, and fungi. Pollen in the form of bee bread is honey bees’ major source of protein, fats, and vitamins, and is an important nutrient source for the development of brood. bee space Bee space is 3/8”, which leaves enough room for bees to pass one another on opposite combs. If the space between combs is less than 3/8”, bees will likely fill it with propolis. It if is greater than 3/8”, the bees will tend to build burr comb to fill the space. bee yard See apiary. beeswax See wax. biosecurity Biosecurity is the procedures and management practices one can take to reduce the spread of pests and pathogens. . All rights reserved. All other copyrights, trademarks, trade names, and logos are the sole property of their respective owners.

PTRENT002: Master Beekeeping Part 2: The Science and Art of Beekeeping College of Agricultural Life and Sciences, Cornell University brood Brood is the name given to the egg, larvae, and pupae stages of insects. brood nest The brood nest is the part of the hive where the brood is developing, distinct from the area where honey is being processed and stored. Conditions such as temperature are more important here, for the healthy development of brood. brood pheromone Brood pheromone is released by larvae and indicates its sex, caste, and age. It influences development and behavior of other bees, most notably by inhibiting the development of ovaries in workers. burr comb Burr comb is comb built anywhere the beekeeper doesn’t want it, namely between frames or hive bodies. It is likely to be built in spaces with dimensions that exceed the width of bee space. candy board A candy board is a piece of hive equipment used to supplement carbohydrates to honey bee colonies during the winter. They resemble an inner cover filled with a solid candy made of sugar and water. carbohydrate Carbohydrates are the sugars in food that are a source of energy for organisms. Honey bees acquire their carbohydrates from nectar, honey, or sugar syrups. cast swarm See afterswarm. caste A caste is one form within a species that may differ from other forms in terms of anatomy, physiology, and reproduction. The three honey bee castes are queens, workers, and drones. cell builder A cell builder is a colony used to rear queens. Cell builders can be either ‘cell starters’ or ‘cell finishers’. A cell builder consists of a strong population with many nurse bees, pollen, honey or sugar syrup, and can be queenright or queenless. cell finisher A cell finisher is the cell building colony used to finish queen cells when rearing queens. Nurses in the finisher colony continue to provision the queen cells with royal jelly and complete the construction of the queen cell. . All rights reserved. All other copyrights, trademarks, trade names, and logos are the sole property of their respective owners.

PTRENT002: Master Beekeeping Part 2: The Science and Art of Beekeeping College of Agricultural Life and Sciences, Cornell University cell starter A cell starter is the cell building colony used to start queen cells when rearing queens. Nurses in the starter colony provision the queen cells with ample royal jelly and begin building out the cell with wax. chalkbrood Chalkbrood is an infection in honey bee brood caused by the fungus Ascosphaera apis. It can affect both sealed and unsealed brood. Affected larvae often take the appearance of small white pieces of chalk and, in this stage, are referred to as ‘chalkbrood mummies’. checkerboarding Checkerboarding is the practice of alternating frames of drawn comb with frames that are already filled in the broodnest. This provides the colony more space to fill with brood and resources and, as a result, can help prevent swarming. chromosome Chromosomes are the structures containing an organism’s genetic material in the form of DNA. class Class is a rank in the classification of life, below phylum and above order. Honey bees are members of the class Insecta (insects). cleansing flights A cleansing flight is the delicate name given to the act of leaving the hive to defecate. Bees can delay defecation for months during winter, but will leave the hive on a warm day to void their waste. Fecal staining may be evident around or on the outside of hives in winter and early spring. cluster (also winter cluster) Clustering is a thermoregulatory behavior where bees congregate on the comb to keep warm when environmental temperatures are below 64°F. Colony functions such as foraging and water collection cease when bees are clustering. cocoon A cocoon is a silky pupal casing spun by insect larvae to protect them during their pupal stage. colony The colony is the family community of honey bees that share a nest. There is usually a queen present, many workers, and fewer drones. colony assessment . All rights reserved. All other copyrights, trademarks, trade names, and logos are the sole property of their respective owners.

PTRENT002: Master Beekeeping Part 2: The Science and Art of Beekeeping College of Agricultural Life and Sciences, Cornell University A detailed colony inspection that quantifies the amount of brood, adults, honey, pollen, and comb in an effort to assess the growth and productivity of the colony. comb See honeycomb Complementary Sex Determination gene The Complementary Sex Determination gene is responsible for sex determination in honey bees. compound eye The two large eyes found on either side of a bee’s head. Each compound eye consists of thousands of individual independent facets with lenses that collectively form a coherent image. cooperative brood care Cooperative brood care is the practice of sharing the work of raising young that is not one’s own. In the case of honey bees, the queen lays the eggs, but the larvae, pupae, and young adults are cooperatively cared for by their older sisters, nurse bees. Cooperative brood care is one of the three hallmarks of eusociality. corbicula (plural: corbiculae) See pollen basket. crop See honey crop. dearth A dearth is a period of time when flowers in a given region are not producing much nectar (in the case of a nectar dearth) or pollen (in the case of a pollen dearth). diploid organism Diploid organisms have paired sets of chromosomes in each cell (excluding sperm and egg cells). They inherit one set of chromosomes from their mother and one from their father. Female honey bees (both queens and workers) are diploid, because they develop from eggs that are fertilized (by sperm) and therefore contain two sets of chromosomes; in contrast, drones are haploid. See also haplodiploid. DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) DNA is the long molecule that carries an organism’s complete set of genetic information. Doolittle method . All rights reserved. All other copyrights, trademarks, trade names, and logos are the sole property of their respective owners.

PTRENT002: Master Beekeeping Part 2: The Science and Art of Beekeeping College of Agricultural Life and Sciences, Cornell University A method of queen rearing where larvae is grafted and placed into artificial cups. These cups are then inserted into colonies that have been prepared in advance to readily rear queens. drift Drift is the entering of bees into hives or nests that are not their homes. It is more likely when hives are close together and difficult to distinguish from one another. Hives at the end of a row of hives may contain a lot of drifting bees. drone A drone is a male honey bee. drone comb Drone comb is specialized brood cells where unfertilized eggs are laid and reared into drones. The cell size is slightly–but obviously–bigger than that of worker comb and it is often built on the margins of frames. drone congregation area A drone congregation area is where hundreds of drones congregate high in the air to wait for a virgin queen on her mating flight. drone mother colony A drone mother colony is the colony that contains the drones that will be used to inseminate queens for queen rearing. The drone mother colony is usually chosen based on specific criteria. Frames of drone comb foundation are often placed in these colonies to rear a maximum amount of drones to saturate a drone congregation area. Dufour’s gland The Dufour’s gland is located at the end of the abdomen in female bees and releases pheromones through the vagina. In the queen, these pheromones have a similar role to queen mandibular pheromone (QMP), serving as a signal of her fertility and promoting retinue behavior. When a colony loses its queen, laying workers may start producing their own queen-like fertility pheromones from their Dufour’s glands. dysentery Dysentery is honey bee diarrhea, which may be visible inside or outside of the hive. It is caused by the buildup of solids in the digestive tract, and can relate to infections. egg Eggs are the first stage of the bee’s life, and are laid by queens and sometimes workers into cells. The pattern of egg laying in the cells and across the comb can provide information about the health and trajectory of the colony. . All rights reserved. All other copyrights, trademarks, trade names, and logos are the sole property of their respective owners.

PTRENT002: Master Beekeeping Part 2: The Science and Art of Beekeeping College of Agricultural Life and Sciences, Cornell University emergency queen cells Emergency queen cells are built when workers abruptly find themselves without a queen and must convert larvae that had been destined to be workers into queens instead. EpiPen An EpiPen is a brand name for an epinephrine injector. Epinephrine is used to treat anaphylactic shock. eusociality (adjective: eusocial) Eusociality refers to the most advanced form of social living. Eusocial individuals fully depend on a societal organization to survive and cannot live on their own. The defining characteristics of a eusocial organism are more than one generation living together, cooperative brood care, and a reproductive division of labor. exoskeleton An exoskeleton is an organism’s outer body shell, made of tough, protective material. All invertebrates have an exoskeleton and do not develop a backbone. family Family is a rank in the classification of life, below order and above genus. Honey bees are members of the family Apidae. fat body The fat body is a collection of tissues distributed throughout an insect’s body. It mostly surrounds the gut and reproductive organs, but is also distributed throughout the thorax and head. Its main function is to store fat and glycogen to release energy for use in times of food shortage. It also produces vitellogenin. Winter bees have a larger fat body and more numerous fat body cells than summer bees. fermented honey Fermented honey is honey that has been fermented by yeast. It is often bubbly or foamy in appearance and has a yeasty aroma. Fermentation most likely occurs naturally when the moisture content in honey exceeds 18%. Under these conditions, yeast populations can rise. festooning Festooning is when inactive bees hang between combs, linking themselves together by their legs. It is associated with wax construction. field bees See foragers. . All rights reserved. All other copyrights, trademarks, trade names, and logos are the sole property of their respective owners.

PTRENT002: Master Beekeeping Part 2: The Science and Art of Beekeeping College of Agricultural Life and Sciences, Cornell University fondant Fondant is a thick frosting-textured food product that is used to supplement carbohydrates to honey bee colonies during the winter. It is made of sugar, water, and corn syrup. forage Foraging is the search for and collection of resources (nectar, pollen, water, and resin) for the colony. foragers Foragers (also known as field bees) are worker bees that take foraging trips for nectar, pollen, water, or resin. Typically, worker bees begin foraging halfway through their lives, and remain foragers until they die. Foragers specialize in collecting one kind of resource, but they can be flexible as needed. See also house bees and nurse bees. ganglia (singular: ganglion) Ganglia are nerve centers in the thorax and abdomen that constitute the nervous system. In the honey bee, ganglia control muscle movements more than the brain does. genome A genome is an organism’s complete set of genetic material carried by DNA. The genome includes information for a variety of elements, the most important being genes. genes Genes are the working subunits of DNA and are the basic unit of heredity, passed down to an individual’s offspring through reproduction. Genes act as instructions to make proteins and other molecules. genetic diversity Genetic diversity is the presence of many different gene versions in a population (in this course, a honey bee colony). High genetic diversity in a honey bee colony is the result of the queen mating with many different drones. High genetic diversity provides the colony with the ability to adapt to changing environments or pressures. genus Genus is a rank in the classification of life, below family and above species. Honey bees are members of the genus Apis. Genus names are always italicized. gland Glands are honey bees’ organs that secrete chemical substances. See Dufour’s gland, hypopharyngeal gland, mandibular gland, Nasonov gland, and wax gland. . All rights reserved. Homepage Video Transcript The most common questions that I get asked about are honey bee pests and diseases. And honeybees are susceptible to so many different diseases and problems. And it can be really difficult as a beekeeper to know how to diagnose these issues. Sometimes, a lot of the symptoms overlap. So, I'm really looking forward to providing you with the skills and tools to be able to keep your colonies as healthy as possible, and to be able to monitor and diagnose and treat different diseases, as they come up. You're going to learn how to take a proactive approach and take charge of the health of your whole bee operation. We're going to cover all known health issues affecting bees in North America and also some of the potential issues that we can expect to see in the future. What you'll do Examine how honey bees naturally combat infections through immune function and social behavior Apply the benefits of integrated pest management Identify, prevent, and control: Pests Parasites Viruses Bacterial infections Combination syndromes Explore what we can learn from and how we can protect native bees Understand the role of diseases and other factors in widespread colony declines Course Description The number one area in which beekeepers reach out to the Cornell University Honey Bee Research and Extension Program for support is managing pests and diseases. In this course, you will gain knowledge about honey bee immunity and apply integrated pest management (IPM) principles to prevent and control all known pests, parasites, and pathogens that interfere with honey

bee health and productivity. You'll feel confident in your ability to monitor, diagnose, and control specific problems in your colonies to be proactive and take charge of the health of your bee operation. This is the third in a series of courses that equip beekeepers (at the hobby, sideliner, and commercial levels) with the concepts, knowledge, and best management practices they need to sit for Cornell University's Master Beekeeper Certification examination (written, oral, and field components). Course Authors Emma Walters, MSc Honey Bee Extension Associate, Dyce Lab of Honey Bee Studies Cornell University Emma Kate Mullen is the Honey Bee Extension Associate at Cornell University. Emma works with beekeepers in New York State and beyond to understand factors affecting honey bee health, with a focus on pathogens, pesticides, and management practices. While studying honey bee social behavior for her Master's degree in Canada, Emma became fascinated with bees' interactions with each other, humans, and the environment. She is interested in pollinator conservation and has held advisory roles for the development of the Ontario Pollinator Health Action Plan and the New York State Pollinator Protection Plan. At Cornell University, Emma creates extension materials and hosts workshops to help educate beekeepers across the Northeast on various aspects of honey bee health and beekeeping. She is particularly interested in communicating research to beekeepers and working with them to improve the health of their colonies. Eleanor Andrews, MSc Honey Bee Extension Assistant, Dyce Lab of Honey Bee Studies Cornell University Eleanor Andrews is a Honey Bee Extension Assistant at Dyce Lab for Honey Bee Studies and a Ph.D. candidate in Development/Rural Sociology at Cornell University. Ellie is interested in strengthening beekeepers' abilities to evaluate sources of information about beekeeping, which is especially important now that honey bee health has moved into the political arena.

Ellie's research addresses how beekeepers learn to keep bees, how beekeeping clubs support different forms of sustainable beekeeping, and how educational resources for beekeepers have developed over time. She believes that the problems beekeepers face can only be addressed by combining physical science with social science. Ellie also brings a focus on pedagogy and organizational frameworks to support learning, based on her experiences teaching at Cornell, the Peace Corps, a Quaker boarding school, and prison. Katherine R. Urban-Mead Ph.D. Student in Entomology Cornell University Katherine Urban-Mead is a Ph.D. student at Cornell University in the Entomology Department. Kassie is broadly interested in the ecology of beneficial insects in agricultural landscapes. Her love of flower-filled meadows and commitment to sustainable agriculture both began during her childhood in the Hudson Valley, NY, where she raised 4-H dairy goats. Kassie's undergraduate research at Yale University was on the symbiotic microbial communities in honey bee guts, and her Master's thesis examined wild bee communities in old-field meadows across human impact gradients. For her Ph.D., Kassie is working with her co-advisors, Professors Danforth and McArt, on understanding early-season forage resources and factors affecting nest site availability for wild bee pollinators of New York apple orchards.

Module Introduction: Honey Bee Immunity When we talk about honey bee health, we often focus on the numerous—and increasing—diseases and pests that make bees sick. But bees have developed a variety of ways to protect themselves against invasions and infections, including internal defenses, individual protection strategies, and, most importantly, social behaviors that protect the entire colony. In this module, we will explore how honey bees resist pest and disease exposure, how they deal with infections, and how beekeepers can provide help when needed. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Individual-Level Defenses Bee colonies have persisted for ☆ Key Points thousands of years despite attacks from such diverse actors as bacterial and viral pathogens, insect pests, mice, bears, humans, and, more recently, chemical exposure. Many of their Stingers, grooming behavior, and special body layers are some of the individual defenses that protect bees from outside invaders. strategies are based in group defenses and cooperation, but let us first explore the simplest ways that each bee keeps itself safe and its body healthy. Preventing Invaders You have surely experienced a bee's most familiar form of defense: its sting! It might be strange to think of a bee's sting as immunity, but a bee uses its sting to keep out invaders. When the colony allows fewer external objects and organisms to enter the hive, it reduces the risk of damage and disease. To keep even smaller attackers out, the bee performs selfgrooming (called autogrooming), regularly removing foreign objects and pathogens from its body. Basic hygiene, like showering for humans, removes disease agents from the outside of the bee's body. This is important both for cleaning and for spreading cuticular hydrocarbon secretions (skin oils). Cuticular hydrocarbons are distinct for bees from the same colony and, as such, are used as cues for bees to distinguish their nestmates from unrelated bees trying to rob the hive. Grooming is so important that honey bees have evolved specialized grooming structures. One special groove on the inner forelegs has a dense row of comb-like spines that are perfectly fitted to run along an antenna. Bee “skin” itself is a successful blockade against the outside world. Called the cuticle, it separates the inside and outside of the bee, preventing the weather and physical abrasions from damaging the bee. The cuticular hydrocarbons form a thin wax coating on the bee's cuticle that protects it from water and keeps internal moisture from escaping. The cuticle is made of chitin and proteins; it does not break down in water nor is it

digestible by mammals. This makes it a reliable protective layer. The honey bee's cuticle provides a protective layer. Photo credit: Jennifer Tsuruda. Disease-causing viruses and bacteria (pathogens) can enter a bee's body through the food it eats or from contact with flowers, hive parts, nestmates, and the fecal matter of other bees. Once inside the body, the bee's gut plays a big role in preventing bacterial or viral infection. The physical barrier offered by the gut lining controls what can move between the gut and the insect's organs. Just as the gut lining can allow nutrients to enter the body, it can also prevent pathogens from entering. Further, having healthy, symbiotic bacterial communities in the gut can offer protection for the bees, and the acidic pH of some parts of the honey bee gut can help make it an inhospitable place for bacterial and fungal pathogens. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Attacking Pathogens Inside the Body: the Honey Bee Immune System Honey bees possess an efficient but ☆ Key Points simplified immune system compared to vertebrates. They lack an adaptive immune system (no antibodies or memory B/T cells) but have a robust innate immune system that is activated within minutes or hours. For example, some cells in honey bees' Unlike humans and other invertebrates, honey bees do not produce antibodies. Honey bees have fewer immunityrelated genes than do other insects. hemolymph have the role to destroy pathogens by physically surrounding (nodulation) and consuming them (phagocytosis). Also, bees facing bacterial pathogens can quickly produce antimicrobial compounds that kill or inhibit the growth of bacteria in the body (examples include abaecin, apidaecin, hymenoptaecin, and defensin). Honey bees can even defend themselves against viral intruders by activating RNA interference (RNAi), a widespread defense mechanism in animals that results in silencing of viral genes. Note that such responses are weakened when honey bees are faced with multiple stresses at once. For instance, innate immune responses are weaker when honey bees are under moderate levels of Varroa mite stress or when they are stressed with the bacterial pathogen that causes American foulbrood.

Part of the honey bee's immune system includes specific cells (purple) that consume and destroy bacteria (black). Although honey bees, unlike mammals, do not produce antibodies or have immunological “memory," it was recently shown that queens can still transmit a form of immune “memory” to their offspring. This phenomenon is called transgenerational immune priming (TGIP), and although its mechanisms are not fully understood at the moment, TGIP is currently leveraged in the first commercialized "vaccine" for honey bees (and insects!) that was approved by the USDA in 2023 for protection against American foulbrood. Killed bacteria are fed to worker bees, who then feed it to the queen. As a result, immune signals or fragments get passed into her eggs. The offspring exhibit a faster or stronger immune response as a result of having the pathogen previously encountered by their mother. Honey bees do not only rely on individual immunity; in fact, they have only one-third as many immunity-related genes as other insects. How do honey bees stay protected from attacks, with fewer genes dedicated to the job? The secret lies in social immunity: Honey bees have an advanced social life. Instead of investing in their individual defenses, like many solitary insects do, honey bees have evolved colony-level defenses that provide immune defenses to the group as a whole. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Colony-Level Defenses: Social Immunity When groups of organisms live ☆ Key Points together instead of alone, diseases spread more easily among individuals; just think about how quickly infections can spread in schools. It is not surprising, then, that many strategies Honey bees have evolved social behaviors that reduce the incidence and spread of pests, predators, and pathogens. for protection have developed at the colony level instead of at the individual level. Some social immunity practices are preventative; others are responsive to problems once they arise. Let's explore some of the behaviors that constitute social immunity. ▶ Grooming In addition to autogrooming, bees groom one another (“allogrooming”) to remove foreign objects and pathogens from their adult nestmates. Bees can remove items from hard-to-reach places on another bee's body. Grooming behavior has a genetic basis to it, so some colonies may have more grooming bees than other colonies. ▶ Undertaking Some bees clean up their hives to keep disease from spreading. “Undertaker” bees are a subset of middle-aged bees (two to three weeks old) tasked with removing corpses and debris to maintain low levels of dead, diseased, and unwanted materials in the hive. Also, because bees are fast learners and improve at repeated tasks, designated “undertakers” make hive management more efficient. ▶ Requeening Honey bees are unique from many other species in that they can control their genetic stock on relatively short time scales by replacing their queen. Remember, the queen is the primary egg-layer in the colony. If she is not

▶ ▶ laying sufficient brood, then there are not enough worker bees to keep up brood rearing, nursing, and cleaning. Furthermore, colonies that are under stress from parasites and pathogens may construct supersedure cells to replace the queen. The reasons are unknown, but it could be that the queen herself is sick or that the colony is attempting a "fresh start." Absconding Absconding is the act of an entire honey bee colony leaving their nest or hive completely. If mite levels or other disease or pest levels are too high, bees may leave their current location and search out another one. This can also be triggered by hive damage, repeated bear attacks, or other environmental problems. Siting the Nest The location of the nest site is a crucial decision made by bees; they become “immune” from bears and other attackers — including humans — when they select a nest site high off the ground, with only a small entrance hole to defend. This strategic decision in nest location makes them harder to detect, access, and destroy. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Propolizing the Nest You are already quite familiar with ☆ Key Points propolis. Bees make propolis by gathering plant resins and mixing them with wax. Propolis reduces drafts Propolis contains antimicrobial properties. and water damage. And just as it slows down your access to the hive, it also blocks or slows many small insects, pests, bacteria, fungus, and any number of other agents of disease and destruction. Bees can use propolis to “entomb” these pests and predators, which keeps the hive clean and minimizes the spread of disease — they'll even fully propolize mice or snakes that die in the hive. The presence of propolis has also been shown to reduce the expression of honey bee immune-related genes. This is not a problem; it means that the colony is healthier in general and the immune systems of honey bees are less stressed when propolis is present. Propolis also has antimicrobial properties, although its exact degree of antimicrobial activity varies based on the plant from which the resin came. There is some evidence that honey bees increase their resin collection following pathogen pressure. So even though as a beekeeper you may be tempted to think of propolis as a nuisance, it's actually a big help to your bees. Dr. Marla Spivak, Professor at the University of Minnesota, studies the beneficial properties of propolis. Watch this video to understand more about how propolis keeps colonies healthy. Video Transcript So, propolis is, or propolis, however you like to pronounce it, is composed of resins that bees collect from trees and other plants in their environment. And they collect the resins on their back legs and they bring them back to the nest, where they deposit them inside the nest. They sometimes mix the resin with wax. And once it's inside the nest, we call it propolis, or propolis. And the resins are produced by certain trees as a defensive compound. So, they protect the leaf buds, the new leaf buds, from infection, from UV light, and from herbivory. So, the bees are very good at cuing in on where these resins are, what trees produce the resins. And if they're available to them, then the bees go to them, they

scrape the resins off the tree, or off the leaf buds, mostly, stuff it on their hind legs, and return to the nest. In a feral, natural nest cavity, like in a tree log, they would put this propolis all around the inside of the tree, surrounding their brood nest and their honey. So, they would basically paint the walls, or varnish the walls, with propolis. In our Langstroth boxes, the inside of the box is very smooth. It's plain wood, and so they don't stick the propolis there as they would normally in a tree cavity. Instead, they put it between the boxes or under the frame rests, where it causes a lot of angst for beekeepers. Makes it very difficult to manage a bee colony when they stick everything together. It turns out these resins and propolis are highly medicinal. So, we've known of the medicinal qualities of propolis for humans since antiquity, but no one really, or very few researchers, looked at the properties of propolis for bee health. So, we began by looking at how the propolis envelope, if we could put one inside of modern bee boxes, Langstroth boxes, if we could give the bee colony a propolis envelope, how might it affect them. And the first thing we looked at is their immune function. So, we can measure antimicrobial peptide, gene expression for these peptides, and quantify what happens when a colony has a propolis envelope and when it does not. So, we started with healthy colonies and we give them propolis envelope. And the way we did it, to begin with, is we made a propolis extract. You take propolis scrapings, you dissolve them in ethanol, 70 percent ethanol, then you filter it and you have this propolis extract. Then we can make sure we know the concentration of the extract. We painted it on the inside of small, side frame nuc boxes. Put bees in there, and after seven days' exposure to the envelope, the propolis envelope, we removed those bees, now at seven days, and looked at their immune gene transcripts for these antimicrobial peptides. And what we found is that the propolis envelopes seemed to lower the microbe load in that nest cavity, which then helped the bees reduce the need to express their immune genes. So, the immune system is very costly for an organism to express. If you are constantly fighting allergies, for example, it's at a cost to your body. And so, for bees, it's the same way. So, having the immune system run quietly, or not having to be ramped up all the time, is a really good thing. So, we think that the propolis envelope for a healthy colony is just killing off microbes in the nest and helping the bees keep an efficient and quiet immune system. But if you make a colony sick, with chalkbrood or American foulbrood, the colonies with this propolis envelope are then able to really mount a strong immune response. And, somehow, the properties of the propolis reduce the infection load

in the colony. So, they don't eliminate the disease, they just reduce the amount of chalkbrood and American foulbrood that you see inside the colony. So, we don't know if the mode of action is by contact with the propolis, or if it's through the volatiles, or both. We do know that bees are not eating the propolis, so it's not per os, it's not through ingestion. So, there's lots of other questions we're asking. We know that if you challenge a colony with chalkbrood, in other words, infect a colony with chalkbrood, and you watch and count the number of resin foragers, after chalkbrood infection, the colony increases the number of resin foragers. But if you challenge them with American foulbrood, they do not increase the number of resin foragers. So, chalkbrood's fungal pathogen and American foulbrood's a bacterial pathogen. So, is there a difference? We really don't know. Most of the resins they're collecting are from cottonwood trees, or in the genus Populus. So hybrid poplar, balsam poplar. And then there's some other trees. The antimicrobial properties change depending on the species of resin, but it can also change within, for example, cottonwood, some trees that, the properties are higher than others. But, in general, it seems that the bees are collecting what's probably good for them, or at least what's accessible for them. One kind of mysterious thing is we know that white spruce, or some of the conifers, have really high antimicrobial value, but the bees are not collecting them, at least in our area. So, that opens a question, why not? Is it, like I said, just accessibility, or maybe, is it toxic? We don't, we really don't know. The take home message for beekeepers is that bees really need a propolis envelope. We don't know, our measurements of when they just stick it between the cracks in the boxes and the frame rests. Those were our control colonies, and we know that they still got chalkbrood and AFB infection at higher levels. So, it seems to be something about the whole propolis envelope within the nest, that has the best properties and is the most helpful. So, what we do is take propolis traps, the kind, they're black plastic traps, grids basically, that you put, normally, you put on top of the colony to collect propolis. We cut them up and staple them into the insides of the boxes. Or you could use unfinished lumber, but it has to have a lot of good cracks and crevices in it. You could take a router and make grooves in the boxes. Roughing it up with sandpaper is not enough. So, think about the interior of a tree log, and how rough that surface is. And that's what the bees like to attach the propolis to. The bees, the colony needs to have this whole lining around, especially, the brood nest. Back to Table of Contents

Read: The Microbiome Often when we think of bacteria, we ☆ Key Points think of the ones that cause problems. However, you may have also heard of beneficial bacteria that improve health, such as probiotics that help people digest food. Probiotics are the beneficial microorganisms that reside in our digestive systems, and consuming probiotics contributes The honey bee microbiome is the community of beneficial microorganisms found in the gut. Newly emerged honey bees acquire their gut bacteria from their hive environments and nestmates. healthy bacteria to these normal microbial communities. Scientists are only beginning to understand all of the different ways that these complicated, tiny communities help keep humans and other organisms healthy. Honey bees also have a distinctive community Healthy gut bacteria can outcompete harmful bacteria in the bee's body. Honey bee probiotics require more rigorous testing of their safety and efficacy. of beneficial microbes living in their gut that support their health, a small community referred to as their “microbiome.” Though larvae and pupae have some beneficial gut bacteria, they do not yet have the diverse community that adult bees do. However, once the pupa has developed into an adult and chewed its way through its cell capping, it quickly comes into contact with all sorts of bacteria. During the first four to six days of its life, it receives food from other nurse bees, interacts with other bees, and touches hive material and bits of feces. Interestingly, if an adult bee doesn't touch any fecal matter, it doesn't acquire its entire gut community. This may come as a surprise, since normally honey bees are thought to only defecate outside the hive. But there are some feces in the hive, at very low levels, and bees' contact with it is helpful in developing healthy gut bacteria.

Through trophylaxis and other means, the honey bee acquires bacteria to cultivate its microbiome. Photo credit: Jennifer Tsuruda. The Internal Team of Healthy Microbes There are several distinct groups of bacteria that are always present in the symbiotic honey bee community. We call them “symbiotic” because both the bacteria and the honey bees benefit from living together. Scientists think that because they are always present and are quite different from other bacteria, these species have been coevolving with honey bees for many years. Different bacteria live in different sections along the bee's gut, where they also perform different jobs. For instance, the healthy lactic acid bacteria in the bee's digestive tract can kill American foulbrood bacteria and other harmful bacteria sometimes present in nectar. When a healthy symbiotic community is thriving, there is not much space for “bad” bacteria to settle in. This is both because the healthy microbes physically use up space and resources, and because they fight against other bacteria that try to invade. Some species of gut bacteria can also help with detoxification in the gut and digesting food. For instance, specific microorganisms are needed to help them digest bee bread.

This understanding of beneficial honey bee gut bacteria is new. Despite the need for more research, commercial companies have already begun to create and sell probiotics to feed bees. Most of these products contain a mixture of lactic acid bacteria and yeasts, but they have not yet been rigorously tested in the field. Further scientific experiments are needed to test the long-term safety of these products and to ensure that they don't interact negatively with other products that beekeepers are putting in their colonies. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Beyond Immunity—Beekeeper Intervention Despite the impressive individual and ☆ Key Points group strategies that honey bees use against attackers, they still need help from beekeepers sometimes. When the pressures and challenges get too high, we can intervene to help. As a The most effective approach to managing pests and parasites is by using Integrated Pest Management. beekeeper, you are a caretaker of colony health. Photo Credit: Mary Kate Wheeler How do we know when the challenges are too high? That question is fundamental to the approach that you should be taking to help your bees. This approach, and the approach we will be taking for this entire course, is Integrated Pest Management (IPM). Integrated Pest Management uses a variety of different techniques, applied at different times depending on what the situation calls for. It can be broken down into three actions:

▶ ▶ Step 1: Support Honey Bee Immunity First, we want to help bees help themselves. For example, we provide them all of the conditions required for health, like access to flowers, supplemental nutrition if necessary, a clean and dry environment, protection from heat and cold, etc. These pre-conditions also include maintaining strong genetic stock (e.g. stock that is adapted to your local environment or stock that is more resistant to certain parasites or infections). Other strategies include cultural controls that are based on an understanding of pest/parasite and honey bee biology. Step 2: Track the Pest or Parasite Population Providing bees with this good head start is not enough. We have to be aware of the pest and parasite populations in the colony. IPM relies on careful monitoring to evaluate 1) whether pests or parasites are affecting the colony, 2) how those levels are changing over time, 3) whether or not the level is high enough to harm the colony and require intervention, and 4) whether or not a given intervention was effective. Step 3: Targeted Intervention by the Beekeeper Once pests or parasites reach a certain level or threshold predicted to cause harm to the colony, the beekeeper can intervene with a chemical treatment and/or additional cultural controls. It is important to note that chemicals and antibiotics are the last, not the first, resort of IPM. The method you use for any pest or parasite situation should be chosen to minimize the risk of harm to honey bee, human, and environmental health. Targeted intervention can be highly effective for managing certain parasites, such as the Varroa mite. Treating only when necessary and before the parasite population gets too high ensures that you are not treating before you need to, but that you aren't treating too late, either. This minimizes any side effects caused by treatments and minimizes natural and synthetic chemicals in the hive and environment. It ▶

also prevents the beekeeper from spending money and time on treatments that don't help. We will apply an IPM approach in treating different pests and parasites throughout this course, outlining specific monitoring and intervention strategies. Practicing IPM requires more careful planning, but in the long run it is better for both the bees and the broader environment. Back to Table of Contents
