Module Wrap-up: Honey Bee Immunity As we've seen, when it comes to honey bee health, the challenges from diseases and pests are numerous and growing. In this module, we've explored the various ways honey bees resist and combat pests and diseases. We've examined their natural defense mechanisms against exposure to threats, their methods for dealing with active infections, and the crucial ways beekeepers can intervene to support colony health. Understanding these aspects of honey bee health management is essential for successful beekeeping and maintaining strong, resilient colonies. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Insect Pests Honey bee hives can attract a variety of pests that feed on honey, detritus, and other hive materials. Their impact on colony health can range from being a small nuisance to total destruction of colonies and damage to hive equipment. In this module, we will explore four common insect pests: small hive beetles, wax moths, yellowjackets, and hornets. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Wax Moth Biology Wax moths have plagued hives for centuries and are a familiar pest to beekeepers around the world, especially in warmer regions. They are largely considered a secondary pest because they mostly affect stored equipment or unused/unprotected areas of a hive (including hives in an apiary that die over winter). In a strong colony, they will build up slowly (if at all) and keep to corners or small crevices that the bees cannot reach. In weakened colonies, particularly queenless ones, they can create a problematic infestation and destroy brood combs within weeks or months, although they are not usually the direct cause of eventual death. While other moths might make a home in your hives, especially if you are trapping pollen, wax moths are by far the most common and most destructive. Wax moth webbing damage to a frame. Wax moths aren’t all bad; the larvae (waxworms) are raised commercially for fish bait or feed for reptiles, birds, and small mammals because they are nutritious, easy to raise, and can survive at length without food. Recently, the greater wax moth has been discovered to

eat plastic bags, decomposing polyethylene plastic films into ethylene glycol, which is biodegradable. Life Cycle There are two species of wax moths: greater (Galleria mellonella) and lesser (Achroia grisella). The greater wax moth is more common and more destructive, although the lesser one can still damage stored equipment. Here we will discuss both species together. Greater wax moth adult. Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership Wax moths spend nearly all their lives inside hives. Eggs are laid in cracks and crevices or unprotected comb (e.g., in mostly empty honey supers or brood combs in weak colonies) within the hive. They usually hatch in three to eight days in warmer temperatures, leading to shorter development times, although they may require an entire month at colder temperatures. The larvae (also called caterpillars or waxworms) then feed on the nearby nectar, honey, pollen, bee bread, and wax, as well as cocoons/skins from molting larvae/pupae in brood comb. Indeed, bee bread, shed larval skins, and pupal cocoons in the brood comb are a good source of protein for the developing moths. During this feeding phase, which can last for up to five months (depending on temperature and other conditions), the larvae also spin silky webbing into tunnels across the comb. The bees have trouble removing them from the tunnels. The larvae burrow into the comb and chew up woodenware, eventually making little round depressions where they spin silk cocoons and

pupate. After a week or even two months, they emerge as adult moths and leave the hive for up to a few days to harden their wings and mate. The females then return to the hive to lay eggs, living for an average of 12 days, and the cycle begins again. Wax moth eggs deposited in a cell. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Wax Moth Identification in the Colony In hives or other unprotected equipment overwhelmed by wax moths, drawn frames are covered in grayish white webbing from the larvae, the drawn comb is tunneled through (under cappings), and woodenware is riddled with little depressions. Their feces (frass), small dark granules, may also litter the frames, caught in the webbing. Watch this video to learn how to identify when wax moths are present in your hives. Video Transcript Let's get familiar with diagnosing wax moth pests in our hives. Now, wax moths can be seen on the outside of our colony as we're approaching it to do a hive inspection, or they can also be found on the outer cover or inner covers of our hives. Greater wax moth adults are between half an inch and three quarters of an inch in size and are gray/brown in color. They have long, thin antennae. The larvae are three quarters of an inch long. Often, if you see larvae in your colony it'll either be a wax moth larvae or a small hive beetle larvae. Wax moth larvae are twice as big as small hive beetle larvae, and they can be differentiated from them by their prolegs. Looking at this wax moth larva here, we can see that it has three sets of legs on the front of its body, but it also has four prolegs along its abdomen. Prolegs are these small, stubby legs that help the larva grip onto surfaces. While small hive beetle larvae also have three sets of front legs, they do not have any prolegs. And lastly, they feel differently when you handle them. If you squeeze a small hive beetle larva, it'll feel rubbery and it won't be squishy. A wax moth larva, on the other hand, will squish very easily between your fingers, popping to release its internal contents. Wax moth larvae webbing is found most often on the surfaces of combs. As larvae walk along the combs, they can carry the webs along with them. And their fecal matter can be seen in their webbing. Cocoons can also be found on the surface of the frames or along the bottom of the frames where the wood is, where they can create marks and depressions in the woodenware, as seen here. This photo is a great example of a wax moth infestation. Here we can see four larvae webbing their fecal matter and a couple of cocoons.

Inside of a honey bee colony, wax moth larvae will actually tunnel beneath the cell cappings. And sometimes we can see a line of darkened, concave cell cappings that tells us where these moths are tunneling. We may also see uncapped pupa, also known as bald brood, in a line as a result from their tunneling. Bees can detect that there is a wax moth larva beneath those cells, so they uncap them as a form of hygienic behavior. Bald brood is a symptom of a variety of diseases, but when several occur in a path like this, it's quite indicative of wax moths. Try pulling out some of those pupae with your hive tool to see if there are wax moth larvae inside the cells. So, if you see any of these signs — the tunnels, or bald brood in a line, larvae, webbing, cocoons, or adult moths — this can tell you that there are wax moths in your colony. An opened wax moth cocoon to reveal a prepupa. Credit: Mary Kate Wheeler

Wax moth depressions in the bottom bar of a frame. Credit: Mary Kate Wheeler Eggs: Light-colored eggs are laid in masses of 50 to 150 eggs but are generally too small to be visible. Larvae: The larvae are usually 3/4 inches (2 cm) long, although their size depends in part on food availability and temperature. They are white with a dark head, but they darken as they age. They have three pairs of legs and multiple body segments with small “prolegs.” Pupae: When wax moths pupate, their tough off-white cocoons are 1/2 inches (1.27 cm) and 3/4 inches (2 cm) long and usually stuck into oval depressions in the woodenware, although they can sometimes be found in comb or in debris on the bottom board. The depressions are chewed out of the woodenware and therefore remain after the cocoon is hatched.

Adults: Greater wax moths are between 1/2 inches (1.27 cm) and 3/4 inches (2 cm) long, with a wingspan of 1 1/4 inches to 1 1/2 inches; lesser wax moths are a bit smaller. Both are mottled gray and fly mostly at night then hide in the dark during the day. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Wax Moth Prevention A strong honey bee colony will control ☆ Key Points the wax moth population within its hive by removing larvae and preventing adults from re-entering the hive. However, the bees are unable to prevent an infestation when they are weakened and spending their limited energy on collecting resources and raising brood. The best protection is, Keeping colonies strong and housed in the right-sized space prevent wax moth infestations. Before storing equipment, freeze or heat it to the appropriate temperature. Infested equipment can be treated with PDB crystals. therefore, keeping colonies strong and the hives right-sized (not bigger than the bees inhabiting it can protect), and only supering when the bees are bringing in nectar. To prevent an infestation in stored equipment, particularly brood frames, store it carefully; to the extent possible, avoid keeping equipment in dark and warm areas with little ventilation. Expose the boxes to light, tipped up so that light can shine between the frames. Freeze equipment before storing it to kill any wax moth adults, larvae, or eggs that may be present. The length of time varies with temperature; at lower temperatures (e.g., 5°F) you only need to freeze the equipment for two hours, whereas at higher temperatures (e.g., 20°F) you will need to freeze the equipment for four to five hours. After freezing your equipment, store it in hive body stacks flanked with telescoping covers, or keep them in airtight containers or bags to prevent reinfestation.

Freezing equipment before storage. You can also heat the frames, although temperatures above 120°F will weaken wax and above 140°F will melt it. At 115°F, you should heat for an hour and a half. Even though this temperature is below the wax-melting threshold, be sure that the heat is evenly distributed so that no smaller area is raised above the melting point of wax. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Wax Moth Treatment There are no chemical treatments approved to kill wax moths and waxworms in an occupied hive. To address an infestation in unoccupied equipment, you can freeze/heat it as previously described. This is preferable for a number of reasons, not least that it doesn't affect the honey. There are two chemical treatments available, if necessary. Honey supers can be fumigated with carbon dioxide (CO2), which does not affect the honey. Hive bodies (but not honey) can also be fumigated with paradichlorobenzene (PDB) crystals if the above options are not feasible. PDB is not effective against eggs, however, and needs to be used continuously. Additionally, it lingers in beeswax and may be carcinogenic. For these reasons, using PDB crystals should be a last resort for the beekeeper, and we don't personally recommend it. Any frames stored with PDB crystals should be aired out for at least 48 hours before being reused in a hive since the comb can absorb the odor. Even after equipment is sufficiently aired out, some beekeepers still report being able to smell PDB. PDB crystals work best above 70°F, off-gassing continuously. The gas is heavier than air, so you place it at the top of a stack of equipment. To use the crystals, stack the boxes tightly, sealing cracks with tape and closing the bottom entrances if necessary. Use six ounces of crystals for five deep boxes or ten medium/shallow honey supers, placing a small pile on newspaper or another support on top of the topmost frames. Check on the equipment every four to six weeks to see if more crystals need to be added. It does not kill eggs and will therefore need to be continuously replenished if ambient temperatures are high enough to support moth development.

Stacked hive bodies with PDB crystals. Photo credit: Betterbee Biological control of wax moths is still in development; a parasitic wasp, a bacterium, and at least one virus all show some promise. These control methods may be available in the future. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Small Hive Beetle Biology Aethina tumida, known as the small hive beetle (SHB), was first confirmed in Florida in 1998, although it may have arrived as early as 1996. It is widespread across the U.S., particularly in the Southeast, and has more recently appeared in some Canadian apiaries. In recent years, several honey bee pathogens were found in SHBs, including replicative forms of deformed wing virus (DWV), suggesting pathogen spillover between managed honey bees and SHBs. The epidemiological role that SHBs may play in pathogen transmission to honey bees and other insects, as a possible dead-end host or vector, is unclear. Photo credit: Jamie Ellis Life Cycle Understanding the life cycle of the SHB is important for effectively using cultural and chemical strategies to limit an infestation. The SHB spends only a portion of its life inside the hive. Eggs are laid in the hive (a single female may lay between 1,000 and 2,000 eggs total) and usually hatch within three to five days if they do not dry out and die. Once

hatched, the young larvae feed on the bees' resources (pollen, bee bread, pollen supplements and substitutes, honey, nectar, and brood) for 10 to 14 days, or longer if the food sources are poor. After this feeding period — when they can cause trouble for your bees — the larvae leave the hive to find soil in which to pupate. They tend to leave at night to avoid predators. They generally travel just a few feet from the hive and only 4 to 8 inches down into the soil, although there are records of greater distances. Sandy soil is more hospitable. In the soil, SHBs pupate in three to four weeks then emerge as adults, crawl out of the soil, and fly back into the hive, usually around dusk. Photo credit: Jamie Ellis Small hive beetles can locate bee hives by detecting the pheromones of adult bees and the smell of honey and pollen. They also introduce a yeast into the hive that mimics the smell of the honey bee alarm pheromone, attracting further SHB adults (low doses of alarm pheromone are common in the hive). In the hive, after about a week, SHBs are mature enough to mate. A female adult will then deposit eggs on pollen and brood cells or in masses in corners of the hive — her ovipositor is long and flexible, which allows her to leave tiny eggs in tiny cracks. In total, the entire SHB life cycle is only four to six weeks, with multiple generations in a year. Adults can live up to six months.

In the climate of the Northeastern U.S., the SHB does not reproduce during the winter months, although the adults can survive in the warm honey bee cluster. They may begin to reproduce quickly in the early spring when the honey bee colony is at its lowest population. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Small Hive Beetle Effects In the northeastern U.S., SHB are ☆ Key Points mostly tolerated by healthy colonies and build up slowly in such colonies; like wax moths, they are therefore often considered a secondary pest, as they cause the most damage in colonies that are already weak or queenless. Small colonies, including splits and nucs, or those with too much space to defend can sometimes become overwhelmed by them. Small hive beetles are mainly a problem when colonies are weak in population or are provided with too much space to adequately defend. Intense small hive beetle infestations ferment honey, causing it to take on a slimy, discolored, and frothy appearance. However, when an SHB infestation reaches high levels and larvae and adults are consuming honey and defecating in it, the honey ferments, becoming slimy and discolored and smelling of rotting oranges. Such honey may drip out of the cells and even out the bottom of the hive. It can no longer be eaten by humans and will be rejected by bees, although the combs and frames themselves are not affected. In extreme cases, larval feeding can also damage brood. Rarely is this observed in live colonies in the northeastern U.S., but it can be observed in colonies in year-round warm climates such as the southern U.S. African honey bees may abscond if SHB levels rise too high, but European honey bees will tolerate a much higher level of infestation before they reach the threshold for absconding.
Small hive beetle larvae in a frame feeder.

Small hive beetle larvae on a honey frame. Effects on honey The biggest issue with SHB in the Northeastern U.S. is when they infest honey supers. While in a live colony, honey bees are usually capable of deterring beetles to the point where larvae rarely slime up honey frames. But when beekeepers remove honey supers and temporarily store them before extracting, there are no longer bees to deter the beetles. If SHB are present in supers and the honey is not promptly extracted, beekeepers may see their honey become infested with larvae and lose part of their honey crop. Back to Table of Contents

▶ ▶ Watch: Small Hive Beetle Appearance and Identification There are several ways to identify if SHB are in your hive. Eggs SHB eggs are similar in shape and color to honey bee eggs but are smaller, at about 0.05 inches in length. They are usually laid in clusters, but sometimes a small puncture in the cap of a brood cell is visible from SHB oviposition. Larvae As larvae, SHB are whitish with brown heads and are much larger than the adult beetles. They closely resemble wax moth larvae, although the average wax moth larva is larger. Small hive beetle larvae grow to be 0.37 inches long by 0.06 inches wide. However, they can be distinguished by their number and behavior: A large, irregularly clustered heap in a corner is likely to be SHB. Even a single or small group of larvae can be distinguished by their legs. Both SHB and wax moth larvae have three pairs of legs next to their heads, but wax moth larvae have additional small prolegs. SHB larvae also have small spines and tougher outer bodies than the fragile wax moth larvae. If you squeeze one between your fingers it feels firm, whereas wax moth larvae are tender and squishy. In contrast to adult beetles, older beetle larvae are attracted to light.

▶ ▶ Small hive beetle larva. Note the spines along its back and the absence of prolegs. Photo credit: Jamie Ellis Pupae The pupae are underground and therefore not often apparent to beekeepers; they are pearly white and darken over the three to four weeks that they pupate. Adults SHB adults are about 0.2 inches long (females slightly longer than males) and 0.13 inches wide. They are dark brown, turning nearly black as they mature. They have six legs and small club-like antennae, with hard outer wings that protect them from bee stings, although their legs and antennae may not be visible if they have their heads tucked down. Adults prefer the dark and may stay near the tops of hives with screened bottom boards. Indeed, you may see them scatter across the inner cover or tops of the frames when you open up a hive. Watch this quick video clip to see small hive beetles scurry from the inner cover of a hive. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Small Hive Beetle Prevention SHB adults can fly up to eight miles in search of a hive, may be able to join honey bee swarms, and are further spread in the moving of hives for pollination services or returning north after wintering in the southern United States. Additionally, adults can survive for up to ten days without food. Keeping hives free of arriving adults is thus near impossible. ☆ Key Points Beekeepers should keep their apiaries and honey houses free of combs, cappings, and wet frames that can attract small hive beetles. Promptly replace any uneaten pollen patties and extract honey from harvested supers. Monitoring for SHB is generally based on a quick visual assessment when opening the hive. SHB will scatter to avoid the light, so looking immediately is key. Larvae are more likely to be found on unprotected frames and on the bottom board, or in pollen supplements or substitutes. There are no protocols for accurately measuring the level of an infestation, nor is there a threshold for treatment, since their ability to overwhelm a colony depends on many factors.

Uneaten pollen patties can attract small hive beetles. Maintaining general hive health and implementing other cultural controls are the most important tools for SHB management. As for many bee pests and diseases, the first line of defense is keeping strong colonies without extra hive bodies that the bees do not use and cannot patrol. The bees will also defend themselves, although European stocks of bees are poorly adapted to SHB, given its African origins. Honey bees in a healthy colony may confine and guard bees in “beetle jails,” or the small corners and crevices of the hive where they are already hiding. When a beekeeper opens a hive, they may be unwittingly disturbing the guards and releasing the SHB. Beekeepers should keep their yards and honey houses free of deadouts, combs, cappings, wet frames, and other attractive debris to discourage beetles as well as other pests. Locating hives on clay or rocky soil will help lower the number of successfully pupating beetles. Within the hive, removing pollen supplements and substitutes if they are infested or within two weeks if they remain uneaten is also advised. Hive bodies and supers should not be added unless there are sufficient numbers of bees to fill and patrol them. Equipment should be kept in good condition to reduce the number of cracks and crevices in which the beetles can hide, and debris should be removed from the bottom board if it accumulates enough to hide adult beetles or larvae — and especially if it is so deep that it allows for pupation. Honey supers harvested from a hive with even a mild SHB presence must be extracted immediately (within one or two days). Keeping the honey house humidity below 50% can delay eggs from hatching or kill them from desiccation outright. Infested equipment should be frozen for 48 hours at 30°F (-1°C), or a colder temperature (10°F or -12°C) for 24 hours. Combs with ruined honey can also be washed out and then frozen. Honey stored in hives over winter is not at risk of infestation; similarly, equipment can be safely stored in unheated spaces over the winter. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Small Hive Beetle Treatment Beetle traps can help keep SHB levels ☆ Key Points lower and should be the first mode of action to manage an infestation. Traps available from bee supply companies use apple cider vinegar and/or oil to bait and kill adult beetles. DIY traps Small hive beetles should first be controlled with beetle traps. If these prove ineffective, pesticides or ground drenches can be used. work on the same principle, using sugar, bananas, or other attractants to trap and kill SHB. The downside to these traps is it is easy to spill the oil when conducting hive inspections and tipping hive bodies. Beekeepers have also had success placing dry dustmop sheets (such as Swiffer pads) or Brawny Dine-A-Max towels on the top bars beneath the inner cover. As beetles run into the mop sheets/towels to escape bees, they get trapped. The beekeeper can replace the pads during the next inspection. Some species of nematodes that attack SHB while they pupate underground are commercially available, but research is still underway to determine where and when these are most effective.

▶ Beetle trap placed in a colony. Synthetic Chemicals Two synthetic chemical treatments are available: one that is applied in the hive (CheckMite+™) and another that is applied to the ground in front of the hive (GardStar™). Note: Using chemical treatments to control small hive beetles should be a last resort if the infestation is still out of control and you are still observing significant SHB larvae damage after using beetle traps. We do not personally recommend using CheckMite+™ at any time. The active ingredient in CheckMite+ (coumaphos) remains in comb for many years, contaminates hive products, and can reduce survivorship and fertility in queens. Checkmite+ should not be used in queen-rearing colonies. The active ingredient in GuardStar (permethrin) is toxic to honey bees. CheckMite+™ CheckMite+ can only be used when honey supers are not on the hive and will not be for another two weeks after the treatment has ended. Cut corrugated cardboard into 4"x4" squares and then peel off one side (taping the other side to smooth it and discourage bees from chewing it up). Cut a CheckMite+ strip in half and staple the two pieces to the cardboard squares. This creates small crevices between the cardboard and strips where the beetles can be trapped. In hives with solid bottom boards, place the squares near the bottom of the hive with the strip face down; in hives with screened bottom boards, place the squares above the inner cover. Beetles will try to hide under it. These can be left in the hive for 42 to 45 days; the treatment should not be repeated more than twice in one year. Take precautions when handling CheckMite+: Follow the label carefully, wear chemical-resistant gloves (not standard beekeeping gloves), and dispose of the strips according to the label. GardStar™ GardStar is a ground-drenching method that kills beetles pupating in the soil near the hive. Note that the active ingredient in GardStar, permethrin, is toxic to honey bees and other animals and cannot be applied near water sources or ▶

other sites where wildlife gather food. First, cut/mow any grass to ensure that GardStar reaches the soil, and then use a watering can to apply water mixed with GardStar to the soil. Drench the area for at least two feet around the hive (and under it if the hive has screened bottom boards). It may need to be reapplied after one or more months. Because GardStar is toxic to bees, the soil drench should be applied in the evening and care should be taken not to spray/drip any onto any part of the hive. Take necessary precautions when handling GardStar: Follow the label instructions carefully and wear eye protection. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Yellowjackets Yellowjackets can be a nuisance to ☆ Key Points colonies in late summer and early fall. They feed on honey and scavenge on dead adults and brood on the bottom board. Normally, strong colonies can defend themselves against Yellowjacket attacks can be prevented by taking measures to reduce colony robbing and by setting up wasp traps. yellowjacket intrusions, but weak colonies can be wiped out entirely. In some areas of the U.S., like the Pacific Northwest, yellowjackets can become an intense problem, even for strong colonies. Photo Credit: Bee Informed Partnership From mid-August until mid-October, if you begin to see yellowjackets attempting to rob your colonies, manage your colonies as you would to eliminate robbing behavior:

Place entrance reducers on the hive to reduce the size of the area to be defended, or install robber screens. Ensure your hive bodies do not have holes or cracks in them. Even if they are too small to be an entrance, wasps can be attracted to the odor of the honey. Refrain from feeding using open feeders, opening capped honey while working your hives, dripping uncured nectar, and keeping your colonies open for extended periods of time during inspections, as these odors can attract yellowjackets. For further protection, eliminate any yellowjacket nests that are in the vicinity of the apiary and hang yellowjacket traps at the edge of your apiaries. Environmentally friendly traps exist that rely on a pheromone lure instead of an insecticide. The wasps are attracted to the lure and are unable to escape. These traps can be quite specific to yellowjackets and avoid accidentally catching honey bees. Lastly, manage populous colonies that are better able to defend against intruders and threats — yellowjackets or otherwise. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Hornets Two invasive hornets with the potential to impact honey bees in North America have been detected in recent years. Their lifestyle consists of capturing and killing adult bees, often decapitating or dismembering them. These hornets can invade hives to consume brood or steal larvae/pupae as protein sources for their own brood. They use pheromones to recruit conspecifics to an identified hive target, magnifying damage. This increased predation risk may reduce honey bee foraging flights, reduce their efficiency, or force bees to avoid certain flight paths, which can be detrimental to pollination services. The loss of population, loss of brood, stress on defense, and resource drain can all increase the hive's vulnerability to other pests/diseases, thus weakening the bee colony. Vigilance, rapid response, trapping, and nest removal remain critical to prevent the establishment or re-establishment of highly damaging hornet species. All beekeepers should therefore be able to recognize these hornets and be ready to alert the USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service. The Northern giant hornet (Vespa mandarinia), aka ”Asian giant hornet" or “murder hornet,” has attracted a lot of attention because of its capacity for mass attack on honey bee hives. In its native range (temperate and tropical regions of Asia), it is known to decimate honey bee colonies. A few hornets can kill many bees per minute due to their large mandibles and strong predatory capacity. V. mandarinia was first confirmed in North America around 2019, with detections in British Columbia (Canada) and Washington state (USA). In recent official reports, authorities have claimed that the species has been eradicated from the U.S. since there were no confirmed sightings since around 2021. Despite the claimed eradication, vigilance continues (monitoring, traps) because reintroductions remain a risk. The yellow-legged hornet (Vespa velutina) is originally from Southeast Asia and became invasive in Europe in 2004. Workers prey on adult bees flying to and from hives or catch them near entrances (bee hawking). This hornet's voracious appetite can lead to severe losses in apiaries and diminish the effectiveness of pollination services, with considerable costs for beekeepers and agricultural yield. Native insects, including other wasps and flies, also suffer from predation and competition. The immediate impact is less extreme than V. mandarinia in terms of “slaughter phase” attacks on hive interiors, but cumulative

predation pressure is still concerning, especially for weaker colonies, and Europe has been struggling with this invasive hornet ever since it was introduced. V. velutina was first confirmed in the USA in 2023, when a live specimen was found in Georgia and later in South Carolina. The hornet's colony was destroyed in both instances. Vigilance remains essential because new introductions are possible. Vespa mandarinia attacking a bee

Module Wrap-up: Insect Pests We've now examined four significant insect pests that can threaten honey bee colonies: small hive beetles, wax moths, yellowjackets, and hornets. We've learned how each of these pests can affect colony health, from minor disturbances to potentially devastating colony losses and equipment damage. Understanding how to identify, prevent, and manage these common insect pests is crucial for maintaining healthy colonies and protecting valuable hive equipment. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Fungal Enemies — Nosema Nosema disease affects the digestive system of adult bees. It is a very common condition throughout the world, though in the U.S. it is not a major cause of honey bee colony losses. In this module, we will describe this disease in detail and discuss what beekeepers can do to keep their colonies healthy. Back to Table of Contents

Nosema Biology Nosema disease is one of the most ☆ Key Points prevalent infections in honey bees worldwide. It is caused by two species of fungal parasites in the honey bee, Nosema is a fungal gut parasite caused by two different species. Nosema apis and Nosema ceranae. Colonies can be infected with either species of Nosema or with both simultaneously, although the symptoms are different. However, both parasites can kill colonies that are unable to clear the infection. The New Nosema Nosema apis was first discovered in the early 1900s and was, for a long time, the only Nosema species infecting Apis mellifera. Yet in 1996, Nosema ceranae was discovered to be infecting the Asian honey bee, Apis cerana. Ten years later, the infection was observed in European honey bees, Apis mellifera, in Spain. Older museum samples confirmed Nosema ceranae switched hosts in the late 1970s. Since its first discovery in Apis mellifera, Nosema ceranae has increased in prevalence worldwide. It is now documented in North America, South America, Europe, Asia, Australia, and Africa. In the U.S. and Canada, Nosema ceranae has outcompeted Nosema apis almost entirely, perhaps because it produces more spores in the bees' guts than Nosema apis. In the United States, nearly 100% of cases of Nosema infection are now from Nosema ceranae. The most recent survey of species prevalence in New York state showed that only 1.3% of infections were Nosema apis in 2011 and only 0.7% in 2012. The vast majority of infections are Nosema ceranae, though in some circumstances, colonies can be infected with both species at the same time. While Nosema apis is specific to honey bees, Nosema ceranae can infect other species of bees, most notably bumble bees. In addition, a variety of other species of Nosema can infect many different insects. It should be noted that the names "Nosema apis" and "Nosema ceranae" have officially changed to "Vairimorpha apis" and "Vairimorpha ceranae," respectively. This name change occurred in early 2020 because a genetic analysis revealed these species are actually members of the genus Vairimorpha instead of Nosema. For now, we will continue to use the classic names in this course because they are well recognized by beekeepers,

but we will begin introducing the new names more often in our Cornell educational materials. How Does a Bee Become Infected? For bees to become infected, Nosema spores must enter the midgut epithelial cells and produce environmentally resistant spores. These spores are then shed in the bee’s feces, contaminating comb surfaces, hive walls, and water sources. Accordingly, Nosema can be spread through the fecal-oral route when bees ingest fecal matter that contains spores. Bees can also consume spores during trophallaxis (food exchange), through nestmate grooming, and by cleaning contaminated cells — all examples of within-hive transmission of the pathogen. The Nosema infection can also be transmitted from one hive to another. First, the pathogen can be sexually transmitted from spores present in drone sperm then transferred to a queen during mating. Second, bees moving between colonies (robbing/drifting) can introduce spores to other hives. Interestingly, the brood does not contract this infection. Once spores are consumed, they travel to the intestine where they become active and infectious. The active fungus feeds on the bee to acquire all the nutrients and energy it needs. It reproduces by producing spores, which then exit the bee's body in defecation. Infected bees can contain as many as 30 to 50 million spores in their midguts. The presence of spores does not cause symptoms in bees, but the active fungus can.
Photo credit: Jennifer Tsuruda Back to Table of Contents

Nosema Symptoms As the parasite uses up energy from the host bee, the bee has less energy available to perform its daily tasks; the parasite essentially starves her. Adult workers in this starved state consume more food, have reduced fat bodies, and have smaller hypopharyngeal glands. Smaller hypopharyngeal glands make them less able or unable to produce royal jelly and tend to the brood. ☆ Key Points Symptomatic Nosema infections present as colonies that are weak in population, slow to build up, and slow to produce brood and honey. Dysentery is not a symptom of Nosema ceranae. Infected worker bees usually begin foraging earlier in life, though the reason for this is not fully known. It could be that without the ability to tend to the brood, the bees transition to foraging. It could also be that infected bees take on the “riskier” role of foraging, leaving their healthy siblings to perform tasks inside the colony. It could also be that the infection alters hormones and neurotransmitters in the bee that are associated with worker polyethism. Inducing foraging behavior would help the parasite spread to other colonies and reproduce, as spores can be deposited on flowers to be picked up by other bees, and infected bees can drift into other colonies. Indeed, infected bees are less likely to return home compared to healthy bees, whether from disorientation or death. Although Nosema-infected bees begin foraging earlier in life, they are less efficient foragers, spending more time foraging but collecting less nectar and pollen compared to healthy adults. Infected bees usually die sooner than their non-infected nestmates — an average of nine days sooner — although this varies greatly with the number of spores present in the gut.

Photo credit: Jennifer Tsuruda Nosema disease is not restricted to workers; all castes can be infected. Both queens and drones have a shortened lifespan, and their reproduction is impacted. Infected queens may cease egg laying and die after a few weeks and/or be superseded. Infected drones' sperm lose viability faster than normal. Adults infected with Nosema apis may exhibit crawling behavior and their abdomens may appear swollen. These symptoms are not usually seen in bees infected with Nosema ceranae.

Worker bee crawling in the grass in front of the hive. Symptoms at the Colony Level Nosema infection is associated with reduced honey production, decreased adult population, and sometimes — though less commonly in the U.S. — colony death. As infected foragers die and nurse bees begin foraging rather than tending to the brood, there may be reduced brood production and the population may dwindle. To the beekeeper, this manifests as colonies that are slow to build up in spring and don't tend to produce much brood or honey, even if there is a queen present and a nectar flow. in some cases, the colony will create supersedure cells to replace the queen. These symptoms are most obvious to beekeepers when there are other colonies in the same apiary that are strong and producing honey, so they recognize when one or more colonies are doing poorly. Curiously, however, many colonies that have high Nosema spore counts are completely asymptotic and not negatively impacted by the disease. In colonies that do die from the disease, the majority of adults die far from the hive. Inside the hive, there may be a few dead bees on the bottom board and only some young bees and the queen remaining. If the dead bees have not decayed, it is worthwhile to test these bees to determine their Nosema spore loads. Interestingly, there are some countries and regions outside North America where Nosema infection is responsible for high colony losses. It could be that colonies respond differently depending on the species and subspecies of Nosema, the presence of pesticides or

nutritional stress, co-infection with viruses or other parasites, and the climate/environment surrounding the colony. Dysentery Beekeepers are often taught early on that the symptom of dysentery means a colony is infected with Nosema. While Nosema apis has for a long time been associated with dysentery, it's important to note that this symptom is not seen in Nosema ceranae. It is believed Nosema apis inhibits digestion and, as a result, bees become dysenteric — they defecate inside the hive or on the hive exterior instead of in flight. This dysentery has an advantage to the parasite, as it helps to spread spores to other nestmates in the colony. Yet this long-held belief that dysentery is a symptom of Nosema apis has recently been disputed, and further research is needed to illuminate this association. In North America, where Nosema apis is very rare, dysentery is often caused by nutrition issues. Honey bees can experience dysentery from consuming either fermented honey, dark honeys that have a high ash content, or unripened honey/sugar syrup with a high moisture content when they are confined in their hive for an extended period. These foods can fill the guts quickly and thus reduce the amount of time bees are able to "hold it" before needing to defecate. These periods are most often during winter or sometimes when bees are shipped in packages. Ensuring hives are dry inside and free of uncapped honey or sugar syrup during long periods of confinement is the best way to prevent dysentery from these causes.
Back to Table of Contents Dysentery in the hive.

Watch: How Can I Tell If My Colony Is Infected? The symptoms of Nosema are not unique to this disease. Reduced honey production, dwindling population, queen supersedure, and winter colony loss can also be symptoms of other colony diseases or problems. It is therefore difficult to tell from a simple inspection when a colony is infected with Nosema. The only ways to diagnose the disease are through microscopic examination or molecular analysis. Beekeepers can send samples to the USDA Beltsville Bee Lab in Maryland for a free diagnosis. Samples should include at least 100 bees that were collected alive. The lab provides the Nosema spore count per bee. The lab does not differentiate between Nosema species, but given that Nosema ceranae is so much more prevalent, distinguishing between the two species is largely unnecessary. Alternatively, beekeepers can count Nosema spores themselves by using a microscope. The most accurate method is to use a hemocytometer, a device usually used to count blood cells. Many bee clubs invest in purchasing a microscope for all their members to use. Many universities with apiculture extension programs also have microscopes for public use. The Dyce Lab for Honey Bee Studies, in Ithaca, New York, has microscopes available for beekeepers to diagnose Nosema for free. Contact the lab at dycebees@cornell.edu to set up a time. Diagnosing Nosema with a microscope just requires a couple of steps and is a quick and easy way to learn more about the health of bees. Watch this video to learn the procedure. Read: Prevalence and Seasonality Nosema is a common disease in the ☆ Key Points U.S., though most colonies do not exhibit infection rates high enough to negatively impact colony health. Since 2016, the NYS Beekeeper Tech Team facilitated by Cornell University has documented that approximately 86% of colonies in spring and 55% of colonies in autumn contain Nosema In the U.S., almost all infections are caused by Nosema ceranae and Nosema apis is now very rare. Nosema is most common in spring and less common in autumn. spores. The average infection rate in spring is 0.87 million spores per bee, while in autumn it is much lower at 0.23 million spores per bee. Although infections are less common and severe in autumn, colonies that have high spore loads at this time can sometimes die over winter. Nosema is highly seasonal in the Northeastern U.S. The graph below shows Nosema levels from hundreds of colonies sampled each spring and autumn between 2016 and 2019. Most infections occur in spring.

Read: The Interaction Between Nosema and Pesticides A combination of multiple stress ☆ Key Points factors is widely believed to be a driver for the increased rate of colony losses in recent years, and science is only beginning to uncover how different stress factors interact. As bees are Nosema infections and honey bees' vulnerability to them can be exacerbated by exposure to pesticides. often exposed to Nosema and pesticides together in the real world, investigations into their combined effects are valuable, and more are needed. Exposure to imidacloprid, a neonicotinoid, increases honey bees' susceptibility to Nosema infection. Furthermore, bees experiencing combined stress from imidacloprid exposure and Nosema infection die at higher rates than bees exposed to either one alone, suggesting these two stressors interact synergistically. It has also been found that bees reared from brood comb with a variety of pesticide residues (including insecticides, fungicides, and miticides) are significantly more likely to develop Nosema ceranae infections as adults than bees reared in clean comb, which suggests that the environment in which bees develop influences their susceptibility to infections as adults. Rotating out old brood comb and taking measures to reduce pesticide exposure (which may be difficult depending on the apiary locations) can help reduce pesticide buildup in combs and bees' susceptibility to Nosema infections.
Rotate out old combs to reduce the buildup of pesticide residues. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Nosema Prevention Nosema infections can be prevented ☆ Key Points in part by reducing the spread of spores and by keeping colonies otherwise healthy. Choose an apiary site with good drainage and sun during winter. Low moisture and adequate ventilation can Preventing the spread of Nosema requires properly caring for susceptible colonies and disinfecting contaminated hive equipment. help discourage fungi, including this fungal gut parasite, from proliferating. In spring, supplement colonies with syrup and pollen substitute if honey stores or larval jelly levels are low. If colonies do become infected, Nosema spores can remain in comb for several years and reinfect new bees that are installed onto that equipment. Regularly replacing old comb with frames of foundation can help prevent Nosema spore accumulation in your equipment over time. Combs from colonies that died from Nosema infections should be disinfected before being reused. There are several ways to accomplish this: Expose combs and hive bodies to freezing temperatures for at least four consecutive days. This is the easiest method for disinfecting combs. While freezing equipment does not kill Nosema apis spores, it does drastically reduce the viability of Nosema ceranae spores. Fumigate combs and hive bodies with acetic acid. Apply two cups of 80% acetic acid to an absorbent pad and lay one pad along the top bars of a hive body. Hive bodies should then be stacked and sealed, left alone for one week, and then aired for one week before being used. Expose combs and/or hive bodies to heat. Hive bodies should be heated to at least 120°F for 24 hours or to 140°F for at least 15 minutes (though this temperature melts wax). Expose combs and hive bodies to gamma radiation. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Nosema Management Symptomatic colonies with infection ☆ Key Points rates higher than 1 million spores per bee in spring should be moved to an isolated apiary to prevent Nosema spread. Once the weather improves, colonies start bringing in ample nutrition, and foragers are able to take regular cleansing flights, colonies tend to improve and treatments are not Nearly all colonies that have high spore counts in spring are able to naturally reduce or resolve their infections by autumn. At this time, there are no treatments registered for Nosema ceranae that are reliably effective. usually necessary. Long-term monitoring of 465 colonies in 2017 and 2018 by the NYS Beekeeper Tech Team found that almost all colonies were able to reduce or resolve Nosema infections on their own without any beekeeper intervention. Fully 90.6% of colonies with high Nosema infections in spring reduced their infections to levels below 1 million spores per bee by autumn. Of the colonies that had any detectable levels of Nosema in spring, 36% were able to completely eliminate the infection by autumn. To support symptomatic colonies (weak populations and low food stores), we recommend supplementing them with syrup and pollen substitute. Beekeepers can even introduce frames of healthy brood and nurse bees from other colonies in an effort to boost the colony population. Good nutrition, especially adequate protein, is necessary for a healthy immune system. While good nutrition cannot prevent or reverse Nosema infections in bees, it can help bees tolerate the infection. Infected bees fed high-protein diets live longer and have higher survivorship compared to infected bees on low-protein diets. Measure the spore levels in these affected colonies again in autumn. More often than not, the colonies will have resolved the infection and can be returned to their original apiary. If the colony continues to have a high spore count and is still symptomatic, then consider applying a treatment. If colonies that had high autumn spore counts die from this infection, disinfect equipment before installing new bees.

Good protein diets are important for a healthy immune system. Photo credit: Jennifer Tsuruda Naturally derived products are sometimes used to help resolve Nosema infections. One such product is called Nosevit and is made from oak bark extract. The mode of action is unknown, but Nosevit is commonly used in Europe. At this point in time, however, there is not enough scientific evidence to suggest Nosevit or essential oils are effective in controlling Nosema infections. It is not registered for Nosema treatment in the U.S., but U.S. beekeepers can purchase it online and are permitted to use it in their colonies. Another natural supplement that is gaining popularity is HiveAlive™. This product contains seaweed extracts, thymol, and lemongrass oil, and is also fed to colonies by mixing it with sugar syrup. One study tested its efficacy against Nosema ceranae infection. This study supplied infected colonies with HiveAlive™ in autumn (in syrup), winter (in candy), and spring (in syrup) for two years and found Nosema spores were significantly lower (about 50%) in spring of both years, compared to a control group. While these results are very promising, this product requires additional testing, particularly for long-term efficacy. Like Nosevit, it is not registered for Nosema treatment in the U.S., but beekeepers can purchase and use it. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Fumagillin Is Not a Reliably Effective Treatment Only one commercially available ☆ Key Points medication has been formally tested in the lab and in the field. This medication is fumagillin (product name Fumagilin-B®, formerly FumidilB®). Fumagillin is an antibiotic derived from the fungus Aspergillus fumigatus. Fumagillin was originally isolated to control Nosema apis in honey bees. In the U.S., fumagillin can The treatment threshold for treating Nosema ceranae is difficult to establish, but many institutions use 1 million spores per bee or greater. Long used to treat Nosema apis infections, Fumagillin may, in fact, exacerbate Nosema ceranae. be purchased through bee equipment companies without the need for a veterinary prescription. Fumagillin may have unwanted side effects on both honey bees and humans and must be used Is Fumagillin Effective? according to directions. The short answer to this question is that it depends on the species of Nosema you are treating. Fumagillin has been used since the 1950s as an effective treatment for Nosema apis infections. It works by inhibiting an enzyme in the Nosema parasite, MetAP2, that is important for tissue repair and protein production. However, it only targets the parasite in its active state and does not kill spores, so even if the active parasites are killed, remaining spores in the colony can reinfect bees. Treating colonies infected with Nosema apis in autumn has been found to significantly increase colony survival the following spring. Colonies infected with Nosema apis and treated with fumagillin have also been found to increase brood production, honey production, and adult bee lifespan following treatment. When Nosema ceranae appeared in Apis mellifera, beekeepers began using fumagillin to control it. They assumed it would work similarly, but they experienced variable efficacy. In some cases, fumagillin appeared to clear the infection, while in other cases it did not. Beekeepers began reporting that after a colony was treated with fumagillin, the Nosema ceranae infection returned within a few months.

A 2013 study investigated the efficacy of fumagillin on Nosema ceranae. The results of this study supported the observations from beekeepers in the field. After fumagillin was applied to colonies, the concentration of the antibiotic decreased as it naturally broke down over time. At high concentrations, the antibiotic was effective, but as the concentration of fumagillin decreased, the infection increased. In this study, the spore production in bees that had received fumagillin was 100% higher 20 days after they received the treatment compared to infected bees that did not receive any medication! This suggests fumagillin may actually exacerbate Nosema ceranae infections rather than reduce them. In the study, Nosema apis infection also increased as fumagillin broke down, but not nearly to the extent that Nosema ceranae does. Models estimate that following fumagillin treatment, Nosema ceranae spore counts may peak again two to five months later. Furthermore, a small-scale 2018 study by the Bee Informed Partnership found fumagillin was no more effective at reducing Nosema infections than giving colonies nothing at all. New Nosema treatment options are needed. What Is the Threshold for Treating Colonies? Despite there being no reliably effective registered treatment for Nosema, some beekeepers do wish to try some form of treatment in autumn if their colonies are still sick, whether it be Fumagillin, Nosevit, or Hive Alive. In these circumstances, we recommend taking an integrated pest management approach and apply a treatment only when the parasite reaches a treatment threshold. Many institutions in Canada and the U.S. (including the Bee Informed Partnership) recognize the treatment threshold for Nosema to be 1 million spores per bee. This treatment threshold suggests if the average spore count in a colony sample is 1 million spores per bee or greater, the beekeeper can apply a treatment. In reality, there is no well-established treatment threshold for Nosema. It is difficult to establish a threshold for a variety of reasons: Colonies can have many infected individuals without exhibiting any colony-level impacts (e.g., no reduced honey production, no decrease in adult population, no colony

death). Infection levels vary during the season and some colonies with high infections in early summer may resolve the disease on their own, without any treatment necessary. The seasonality of Nosema differs based on the geographic region. While the Northeast sees high levels in spring and low levels in autumn, other countries see different trends. Independent treatment thresholds would need to be established for different locations. Research suggests the number of infected bees in a colony might be a more important indicator of disease than the number of spores in a sample of bees. For the time being, beekeepers who wish to treat their colonies in autumn after seeing no improvement throughout summer can use the current threshold until further research can determine a more reliable figure. In other words, fumagillin can be applied in autumn if spore counts exceed 1 million spores per bee. Levels should be measured again following the treatment to evaluate efficacy. Fumagillin May Pose Risks to Honey Bees With the prevalence of Nosema and the unreliable treatment threshold, many beekeepers used to routinely give fumagillin to their colonies, regardless of the spore levels, as an insurance method to prevent Nosema infections. While this was a common practice in the past, we are now learning that prophylactic treatments can impact honey bee digestive health. This is because the MetAP2 enzyme targeted by fumagillin is not specific to Nosema but is actually present in all living organisms, including honey bees and humans. Low levels of fumagillin (lower than the amount needed to control Nosema) alter important proteins in the honey bee midgut. Because of these potential consequences to bee health, we do not recommend using fumagillin prophylactically. Residues in Honey and Human Health Impacts Fumagillin is toxic to humans and residues present in honey can pose a risk to human health. Fumagillin acts on the MetAP2 enzyme in humans as well and may induce abdominal cramping, diarrhea, and weight loss. For this reason, fumagillin cannot be applied while honey supers are present, although there currently is no maximum residue limit for fumagillin in honey. When fumagillin is present in honey, it usually degrades within a few days to a few weeks. The likelihood of finding fumagillin in honey is low when beekeepers apply it in accordance with the label.

Fumagilin-B, the trademarked product, contains dicyclohexylamine (DHC) in addition to fumagillin. DHC is five times more toxic than fumagillin to humans and can cause damage to chromosomes in humans. It is currently unknown how long DHC remains in honey. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Varroa Mites own colonies. Varroa is the most serious and destructive parasite for honey bee colonies. It began infesting Apis mellifera colonies in the 1960s in Asia and has since spread worldwide to be a leading cause of colony losses. In this module, we explore the origins and lifecycle of Varroa, the symptoms associated with a colony impacted by this parasite, and a range of treatment methods. Understanding Varroa biology can help beekeepers make informed decisions on how best to control mites in their Back to Table of Contents

Read: The Rise of Varroa Varroa mites are ectoparasites of the ☆ Key Points honey bee — “ecto” meaning “outside” — that latch their mouthparts onto the surface of a larva, pupa, or adult bees and feed primarily on the bees' fat bodies. Varroa mites are visible to the naked eye. They are about the size and shape of a sesame seed and reddish Varroa mites were originally parasites of the Asian honey bee. Varroa mites have since switched hosts to the Western honey bee and are now the most destructive parasite for this species. brown. They have eight legs (two of which are visible, protruding from one side of the body). These parasites depend entirely on honey bees to live; they acquire all their nutrients through feeding on the bee and reproduce exclusively inside honey bee brood. These mites can only parasitize honey bees and do not feed on other species of bees or other insects. There are two species of Varroa mites: Varroa jacobsoni and Varroa destructor. The two species differ slightly in appearance and can be differentiated by the naked eye: Varroa

destructor is larger and more ovular (less circular) in shape than Varroa jacobsoni. Both of these species parasitize the Asian honey bee, Apis cerana, and have likely done so for hundreds — if not thousands — of years. During this time, the mites have co-evolved with the Asian honey bee and therefore do not pose a significant threat to colony health. In the 1960s, however, one of the two mite species, Varroa destructor, switched hosts to parasitize Apis mellifera, when colonies of those Western honey bees were moved into an area in Asia where Asian honey bees resided. (Varroa jacobsoni did not switch and are unable to reproduce in Western honey bee colonies.) Varroa destructor has since spread across the globe through natural migration (swarming) and commercial transportation. From an evolutionary perspective, this mite is still a relatively new parasite to the Western honey bee. Until the development of widespread genetic resistance and adoption of resistant stock by beekeepers, Varroa destructor poses a severe threat to honey bee colonies. In North America alone, hundreds of thousands of colonies die each year from Varroa pressures and related infections. Microscopic image of Varroa destructor. Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Varroa's Entry Into the U.S. Varroa was first introduced into the ☆ Key Points U.S. in Florida in 1987, when hives transported to Wisconsin from Florida were found overrun with mites. That fall, colonies across twelve different Varroa mites are ubiquitous in nearly every country where honey bees are kept. states began dying. Varroa had rapidly spread across much of the country before beekeepers had taken notice, and beekeepers and researchers were unable to prevent their further distribution. By the mid-1990s, every contiguous state in the U.S. had Varroa mites, and by 2007, they were introduced to Hawaii. Migratory beekeeping played a large role in the spread of Varroa mites from Florida and beyond. Not only did Varroa mites take a toll on the honey bee industry, but it also decimated feral colonies (honey bees found in the wild). Within ten years, it was reported that feral colonies had largely disappeared across the country because of Varroa infestations. Varroa mites are now ubiquitous worldwide, with only a few islands remaining free of the mite (examples: Isle of Man, and some islands in the Azores archipelago). Australia was one of the few major beekeeping nations free of the mite until 2022. Unfortunately, V. destructor was detected in New South Wales in June 2022. Initially an emergency eradication response was launched, involving hive destruction, surveillance, and control efforts. However, by September 2023, authorities concluded that eradication was no longer feasible, and shifted to a “transition to management” strategy. This means that Australia’s Varroa-free status is now compromised in many areas; it may still have some zones under exclusion or surveillance, but not the entire country. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Life Cycle of Varroa There are two stages in the life cycle of the Varroa mite: the reproductive stage and the phoretic stage (though the phoretic stage may be renamed in the near future). ☆ Key Points Mites reproduce in honey bee brood cells. They prefer to reproduce in drone cells as compared to worker cells. Reproductive stage: During the reproductive stage, the mite is inside the honey bee brood cell, reproducing and feeding on honey bee pupae. Varroa mites feed primarily on the fat bodies of honey bee pupae and adults. They are found most commonly on nurse bees. Phoretic stage: During the phoretic stage, the mite is found on the outside of the bee's body, feeding on the bee. Mites are most often found on the underside of the bees' abdomens, tucked between body segments.
Reproductive mites found on a developing prepupa. Credit: Bee Informed Partnership

Phoretic mite on an adult bee. Credit: Jennifer Tsuruda Mites enter honey bee colonies by hitching a ride on a forager bee that drifts into or robs an uninfested colony. They can also be introduced to colonies from beekeepers exchanging frames with bees or brood between hives, or from nucs and packages. Once inside the colony, a mite generally gets off the robber/drifter and crawls into an open brood cell with older larvae that will soon be capped. Mites enter worker brood cells around 20 hours before they are capped, and they enter drone brood cells around 40 hours before they are capped. Mites are found in drone brood cells about nine times more often than they are found in worker brood cells; this is likely because drones take three days longer to pupate, allowing more mites to reach maturity before the bee emerges.

The mite hides inside the brood food until the cell is capped, and once the cell is sealed, it begins feeding on the pupa and transmitting viruses contained in its saliva through the open wounds from its bite. Three days after the cell is capped, the adult female mite (foundress) lays the first egg. This first egg is unfertilized and develops into a male (like bees, mites are haplodiploid). After the first (male) egg is laid, the foundress then lays subsequent eggs every 30 hours. Each of these subsequent eggs (usually one to six in total) are fertilized eggs that will develop into females. After the mites hatch, they all feed on the pupa. The male is white to light pink in color and smaller than a female; the females are nearly white after hatching but darken as they age. Photo of two immature mites (white) on a pupa. Photo credit: Mary Kate Wheeler It takes mites six days to reach sexual maturity, at which point the females and males mate. When the bee emerges, the mated females that survive exit the cell on the bee's body. The male mites and immature females quickly die inside the cells due to desiccation. Because most bees emerge 12 to 15 days after being capped (depending on whether they are workers or drones), most of the mites do not reach maturity before the bee emerges. In fact, only an average of 1.3 new mites are released from each worker brood cell with a foundress mite, and an average of 2.6 new mites are released from each drone brood cell

with a foundress mite. Some brood cells can contain multiple foundress mites, so more sexually mature daughter mites can emerge from these cells. During the phoretic phase, mites remain on adult bees feeding for up to 13 days (seven on average), moving from bee to bee, before they enter cells to reproduce. When the colony is broodless, they can remain on adult bees for much longer, and during the winter, they can survive five to six months in the bee cluster. They feed on nurse bees when given the choice between nurses and foragers. Nurse bees are not only in close contact with larvae (making it easy for mites to crawl into brood cells), but they also provide better nutrition to mites, allowing them to produce more offspring than if they were feeding on foragers. The life cycle of Varroa can differ depending on the species and race that is parasitized. Varroa mites are able to reproduce in both drone and worker brood in Apis mellifera colonies but reproduce exclusively in drone brood in Apis cerana colonies. In fact, any mites that enter worker brood cells in Apis cerana colonies remain infertile (they do not lay any eggs). This inability to reproduce in worker brood can really limit the population growth of Varroa in colonies and helps prevent them from reaching high infestation levels. In contrast, only 10 to 20% of mites entering worker brood cells are infertile in Apis mellifera colonies. The African honey bee, Apis mellifera scutellata, is in between, with 40% of mites entering worker brood cells remaining infertile. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Varroa's Impact on Honey Bee Health — Feeding Parasites feeding on their host can, of course, be taxing for the host. Scientists have recently discovered that Varroa mites feed predominantly on the bees' fat bodies. As a result, both pupae and adults parasitized by mites have reduced lipid levels. Lipids stored in the fat body are important for the development of winter bees and a colony's survival over winter. Indeed, bees parasitized by mites in autumn may not develop as winter bees and tend to live a shorter life. If infestation rates in a colony are high in late summer and early autumn, the colony can collapse in the following weeks or months as the population dwindles before or during winter. Unfortunately, Varroa population levels tend to peak at the same time that the colony is producing winter bees (from August to early October in the U.S.). Also, the fat body is much more than "fat storage"; it is a multifunctional tissue analogous to a combination of the liver, adipose tissue, and immune system in vertebrates. As a result, Varroa mites not only disrupt energy storage but also vital functions involved in immunity and detoxification. Infested bees then become immunocompromised and less able to detoxify the pesticides they encounter on a daily basis as they forage for nectar and pollen on flowers. Bees parasitized during their development also have smaller hypopharyngeal glands and lower protein levels in their hemolymph as adults. This may impact their ability to effectively feed larvae when they are nurse bees. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Varroa's Impact on Honey Bee Health — Transmitting Viruses Varroa is a vector for at least eight ☆ Key Points different bee viruses. In other words, a mite can carry and transmit viruses from one bee to another. When a virus enters the body, it can remain inactive or it can become activated and reproduce by making many copies of Varroa mites can transmit viruses to honey bees. The combination of viruses and mites is more deadly to bees than either pressure is alone. itself. Once it reaches a certain number of copies, the individual host can start to show symptoms. For instance, with one particular virus called deformed wing virus, the bee will develop the symptom of deformed wings once it has 10 billion copies of the virus in its body. Many of these viruses were present in honey bee colonies before Varroa mites were introduced, but they rarely caused symptoms. Varroa mites have been shown to activate some viruses in bees, meaning the viruses were present but not reproducing, but then begin to reproduce. In other words, where the viruses used to be harmless and asymptomatic, they begin to impair individual bee health and put stress on the colony as a whole. Now that Varroa mites are enhancing virus transmission, the combination of the mites and viruses has become a major issue for honey bee colonies. Indeed, a colony suffering from both is at a greater risk of death than if it were infected with a virus or mites alone. The next module explores these viruses in more detail and their effect on colony health. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Varroa's Impact on Honey Bee Health — Parasitic Mite Syndrome Parasitic mite syndrome (PMS) is the ☆ Key Points most advanced stage of a Varroa virus infestation. It has varied symptoms, but is most often characterized by high mite levels, diseased brood infected with one or more viruses, and adults with deformed wings (a symptom of deformed wing virus, transmitted by Varroa). Adult bees may also have mites visible on their bodies. There Advanced stages of Varroa mite infestations cause Parasitic Mite Syndrome. In the Northeast, Varroa populations peak in late summer and autumn. It is therefore critical to monitor mites in August through October. may be signs of hygienic behavior: spotty brood, perforated cappings (cappings that have been completely chewed off, revealing “bald brood”) and chewed down brood. Parasitic mite syndrome usually first becomes evident in late summer (August in the Northeast). Once the colony has developed Parasitic Mite Syndrome, it can quickly collapse within 1-4 weeks. Watch this video to learn how to recognize PMS in your colonies. Video Transcript Parasitic mite syndrome is the advanced stage of a Varroa mite infestation. At this point in time, colonies have very high mite levels, well above the treatment threshold. And they're also accompanied by high levels of viruses that are transmitted by the mite. Here in the Northeast, parasitic mite syndrome typically occurs around August or September. So, it's critical that you conduct a colony inspection at this point in time. However, PMS can also begin earlier in the year if Varroa mite levels were not well managed sooner. It's really strange because the colonies that tend to experience parasitic mite syndrome usually appear the healthiest and the strongest from the outside. They're often colonies that have lots of honey supers, have collected lots of honey, and also have a lot of activity at the entrance. And it's not until you start investigating the colony and inspecting the brood frames that you start to see symptoms.

Right off the bat, you might start to notice frames that have a spotty brood pattern. And it's really important that you look at any cells that have abnormalities. With parasitic mite syndrome, we tend to see lots of hygienic behavior, which is the effort for bees to clear up the virus infections, and also the mite infestations that are affecting those pupae. So, you can see various degrees of hygienic behavior. You can start to see cell perforations where they've begun chewing off the cappings, you can see bald brood, which are those white headed pupae that haven't developed any coloration or hair yet, and you can also see chew down brood, which is where the bees are consuming, partially, some of those pupae that are in there. And then lastly, just those empty cells where bees have been pulling out the pupae, and fully getting rid of them from a colony. Before you shake any bees off the frame, take a look at the adults. With parasitic mite syndrome, we tend to see a low nurse bee to brood ratio, or not enough nurse bees to fully cover the brood that's found on that frame. In healthy colonies, there's enough nurses to cover that brood so that they can keep it warm, and they can tend to it, and feed any larvae. But in sick colonies, a lot of this brood is dying. So, they're not replacing those adult bees, or there's not enough colony recruitment from brood to adults. Also on the adults, you might notice deformed wings from high levels of deformed wing virus, or you might actually see some mites that are visible on the adults. And remember, by the time that you're actually noticing mites on adults, you likely have high levels of mites, because usually, you don't come across many mites when you're looking; most of them are found in the brood. Like other diseases, supersedure cells might also be present. And with parasitic mite syndrome, larvae can die at any age. So, we might see larvae that are just slumped down, or laying flat at the bottom of the cells, or we might see larvae that are kind of twisted or contorted. We might see dead larvae or pupae that are white, or that are beginning to turn brown as they decay and decompose, and they can start to take on a foul odor at this point in time. Once a colony develops parasitic mite syndrome, it can actually collapse within one to four weeks. So, it's really important that the beekeeper acts fast and puts on an effective mite treatment. And even if they do this, it might still be too late to save the colony. So, let's take a look at some photos of parasitic mite syndrome a little bit closer so that you can familiarize yourself with some of these symptoms in your own colonies, if you happened to see it, and then, let's join Randy Oliver in the bee yard, where he inspects a colony that has parasitic mite syndrome. Alright. So, in this first photo, the symptoms that we can see right away are a spotty brood pattern. And we can also see various degrees of hygienic behavior. So, we have one cell here that has a perforated capping, and then we

have several cells with bald brood, which is the next level of hygienic behavior. And then, we even have a cell that shows chewed down brood, where this pupa has been chewed down partially, and only part of its body remains. Then we can also see some larvae that have died, and they're taking on sort of different shapes inside the cell. So, this larva here is slumped down in the cell. It's actually found at the top of the cell here. So, it's slumped and it's starting to change colors. In this next image, we can see a few adult bees that have Varroa mites on them. In this next image here, we can see a spotty brood pattern. Here we actually have the queen in this photo. But to the right of the queen, we can see an adult that has deformed wings. So, deformed wing virus. And the worker below the queen also has deformed wings. So, we have two adults here that show deformed wing virus. Again, we're seeing perforations in the cappings, we're seeing some chewed down brood, we're seeing some bald brood, and we're also seeing some larvae that are beginning to change colors in their cell and turning a little bit brown. At the beginning of June, the number of mites in the colony is not overwhelmingly high. In this example, there are around 1,000 mites and 39,000 bees, or 2.6 mites per 100 bees. Colony population peaks at the end of June. Once the July dearth hits, the queen begins to lay fewer eggs, less brood is produced, and the population begins to steadily decrease.
