As the bee population dwindles, the colony is also susceptible to robbing, especially during late summer or fall dearths. Robbers entering this collapsing colony can help spread Varroa to other hives in the area. This colony is likely to collapse, reaching critically low population levels in November, and dying before the coldest days of winter arrives. Symptoms at the Colony Level

Historically, many beekeepers only inspected colonies if they suspected something was wrong (limited activity at the entrance, a foul odor, dead bees outside the hive, etc.) During a peak Varroa infestation, there are few colony-level symptoms that would indicate the colony may soon collapse. Some spotty brood, chewed cappings, and chewed down brood may be evident. Bee populations remain strong until the colonies are extremely weakened by mite pressure, and Varroa infestations usually do not affect honey production until the point of extreme weakening. As the colony is growing in spring and summer, the mite population lags behind the honey bee population. During this time, the bees are likely still producing a normal honey crop. But this productivity can be deceiving! It is therefore critical that beekeepers' management practices include frequent inspections and mite monitoring. Remember, it is the strongest colonies that may harbor the most mites. Seeing a good honey crop might make the beekeeper think their mite levels are under control and the colony is healthy, but the colony must still be inspected and monitored for mites. Moreover, if nearby colonies have Varroa mites, robbing and drifting can significantly contribute to late summer and autumn mite levels and accelerate a colony's collapse. Back to Table of Contents

Read: A Leading Cause of Colony Losses Every winter, Varroa mites and their associated viruses kill hundreds of thousands of colonies around the world. Several studies conducted in North America and Europe have found that high mite levels in summer and/or autumn predict colony death over winter. One large-scale study in Ontario, Canada, determined how often colonies died from Varroa relative to other causes. Researchers monitored over 400 colonies and found that Varroa was the main culprit behind overwintering losses — the infestations accounted for over 85% of colony losses. This outweighed the contributions of other winter stressors, such as low population, lack of adequate food stores, or Nosema infections. Similarly, the NYS Beekeeper Tech Team, facilitated by Cornell University, has found that Varroa mites are the most significant predictor of winter colony loss for New York beekeepers. Our research in 2016 found that mites are extremely common and difficult to manage in autumn. Nearly every colony of the 300 we sampled in September had Varroa mites (90% of 309), and 78% of the 60 beekeepers we worked with had colonies with Varroa mite levels above the treatment threshold. There is a stigma surrounding Varroa mites. Some people feel that beekeepers whose colonies die from mite infestations must not be good beekeepers because they can't keep their mite levels under control. Because of this misconception, many beekeepers often don't want to admit that their colonies have high levels of or have died from Varroa mites. It is therefore important that, as Master Beekeepers, we foster an open and nonjudgmental environment when speaking with others about Varroa. We can help beekeepers and the general public understand how common — and increasingly harmful — Varroa mites are in modern beekeeping and teach beekeepers how best to manage them. Only by working collectively can the scientific and beekeeping communities combat Varroa mites.

Read: IPM for Varroa It is nearly impossible today to prevent Varroa mites from entering honey bee colonies. There are very few regions of the world that remain free of Varroa, and colony infestation is nearly unavoidable in areas where they are found. Instead of trying to eradicate Varroa completely, beekeepers are now focused on keeping their mite populations low all year long. The most effective strategy to combat Varroa mites is by taking an Integrative Pest Management approach. This is a proactive approach that allows beekeepers to manage their mites before they reach damaging levels. Central to this approach is being aware of colonies' mite levels throughout the year and using a variety of management options to keep levels low. This delays the need for treatments and reduces the amount of miticides introduced into the hive. It is helpful to develop a scheduling plan to incorporate regular monitoring and to have intervention tools and treatments on hand to apply as soon as they are needed. Over the next four pages, we discuss the steps of IPM for Varroa control in detail. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Monitoring Overview Monitoring should take place once a month from March to October in the Northeastern U.S. Accurately monitoring mites each month can help accomplish three things: 1. It informs you of the degree of infestation in your colony and allows you to track its progression, giving you information about the health of your colony. 2. It enables you to track the population growth of mites in your hives, allowing you to time your treatments when populations are at manageable levels, thus ensuring your treatments are most effective. It also helps you to time your intervention around other apiary tasks, such as removing honey supers and preparing your colonies for winter. 3. It allows you to observe mite levels before and after a treatment, which informs you as to whether or not that treatment was effective. Without regular monitoring, a beekeeper may assume a given treatment worked. If a treatment doesn't reduce the level of mites below the threshold, another treatment should be used promptly. How Many Colonies Should I Monitor? Monitoring mite levels in all of your colonies is ideal. But if your operation is large and this isn't realistic, randomly sample 10% of the colonies in each bee yard (for instance, if you have 30 colonies in a bee yard, sample at least three colonies). Maintain written records of your monitoring to track mite populations.

Powdered Sugar Shake A powdered sugar shake helps beekeepers estimate the number of varroa mites in a honey bee colony by coating a sample of bees in powdered sugar, which causes the mites to fall off. ▶ Read: Unreliable Techniques for Monitoring Mites There are several other techniques that beekeepers do to gauge whether or not their colonies are infested with mites. These methods include visually inspecting adult bees, uncapping drone brood, performing an ether roll, and using a sticky board to observe natural mite drops. While these methods can tell you whether or not mites are present in your colonies, they cannot reliably provide a mite number that you can use to gauge the infestation level. This means that it is difficult for beekeepers to make treatment decisions based on their observations with these methods. Click the accordions to read more about the unreliable methods of interpreting mite levels in a colony. Visual Observation Every now and then you may notice a mite on the body of an adult bee, usually on the thorax. Most often, however, they are not noticed on adult bees because they tuck themselves between the abdominal plates on the undersides of the bees to feed. In addition, about 80% of mites in a colony are inside the brood, while only 20% are phoretic. For these reasons, colonies can reach very high infestation levels before the beekeeper can spot mites on adult bees. Visual observations are therefore not a reliable indicator of the severity of a Varroa infestation. Indeed, the likelihood of observing mites increases as the infestation increases. In other words, by the time you see mites on bees, the infestation is likely severe. It is important to manage mites before the population is out of control.

▶ Uncapping Drone Brood Uncapping drone brood using either your hive tool or an uncapping fork can reveal mites. With 80% of the mites in a colony reproducing in the brood — and a disproportionate number of those in the drone brood — the likelihood of finding mites in brood is higher than visually observing them on adults. Uncapping several drone brood cells during your inspection can help determine if mites are present in your colony. It does not, however, give an indication of whether or not your colonies are above the treatment threshold. Bees tend to construct drone brood along the bottom edge of a brood frame. This location makes it very easy to slice off a section of drone brood with your hive tool and use your fingers to break apart the brood cells to look for mites inside. An uncapping fork is also used, as the fork can pierce through drones to remove several at once, allowing you to look for mites. Wash your hands and tools before you work in other colonies to reduce the spread of viruses.

▶ Sticky Board In this method, a sticky board purchased from a bee equipment supply company (or made at home using stiff paper and petroleum jelly) is used in conjunction with a screened bottom board to observe the natural mite drop of both dead and live mites in the colony. The sticky board is placed under the colony and examined 24 hours later, counting the number of mites stuck to it. The sticky glue or petroleum jelly prevents live mites from crawling back up to the colony after they have fallen down onto the board. Commercial sticky boards contain a grid to allow for easier counting of the mites. Many backyard beekeepers enjoy using the sticky board method because it does not kill any bees or require opening the colony. However, it is difficult to use the sticky board as an indicator of mite levels. For starters, scavengers such as ants can remove mites from the sticky board, interfering with your results. More importantly, the rate at which mites drop (without treatments) changes dramatically throughout the year. Many more mites drop when there is no brood compared to when there is brood present. Accurately estimating mite infestation levels requires you to know how much brood is in the colony and to make fairly advanced calculations to determine your mite levels.

▶ On top of the difficulty in interpreting mite drop values, the sticky board method is the most time-consuming one. It requires two trips to the bee yard (once to insert the sticky board, and again to remove it after 24 hours). It is also time consuming to count the mites, as they are mixed in with the other debris that collects on a sticky board. Ether Roll The ether roll method consists of collecting approximately 300 nurse bees in a mason jar and spraying them with two or three quick shots of ether (carstarter fluid). The bees quickly die. This amount of ether makes the bees and the inside of the jar sticky. The jar is shaken, removing mites from the bees' bodies that then get stuck to the sides of the jar. The number of mites stuck to the inside of the glass jar are then counted. This method is less reliable because it does not effectively remove all the mites from the bees, so typically it only allows the beekeeper to detect approximately 50-60% of the mites. This method is also riskier than others; ether makes bees defensive, and the highly flammable nature of ether makes it dangerous to use in close proximity to a smoker.

Read: Treatment Threshold A key part of integrated pest ☆ Key Points management is determining a treatment threshold. This threshold indicates the level at which the beekeeper makes decisions to control mites. If monitoring reveals that a colony's mite levels are at or above the Beekeepers should take action when mite levels meet or exceed two mites/100 bees April to July and three mites/100 bees August to October. threshold, it is likely to die within six months to two years unless the beekeeper intervenes with a treatment. It's important to note that treatment thresholds are not constant. They can change over years, within the year, across regions, and in accordance with a beekeeper's management goals. When Varroa mites were first introduced to the U.S. in the 1980s, colonies could tolerate much higher infestations than they can today before collapsing — upwards of 11,000 mites. The treatment threshold during this time was high, between 10 and 20%, and mites could be effectively controlled with one or two treatments each year. Since then, however, colonies have become less able to tolerate such high infestations. Today, colonies are considered to have a severe Varroa problem once populations reach over 3,000 mites per colony. As a result, the treatment threshold is much lower (2 to 3%, or two or three mites per 100 bees) and colonies often require several treatments each year. Scientists don't fully understand why bees' tolerance to mites has been reduced over the years. One possibility is that the viruses transmitted by mites have developed more virulent strains. Untangling the relationship between Varroa and viruses is an active area of research. The treatment thresholds in this course for the Northeastern U.S. combine recommendations from the Honey Bee Health Coalition and the Ontario Ministry of Food and Agriculture with evidence-based research from the NYS Beekeeper Tech Team. Varroa mite levels that exceed these thresholds require an immediate treatment; without one, they have been shown to predict colony death within six months to two years. From April to July, intervention is recommended when mites reach or exceed a 2% infestation (two mites per 100 bees). From August to October, intervention is recommended when mites reach or exceed a 3% infestation (three mites per 100 bees).

19 mites from monitoring a half-cup of bees. This example shows a 6.3% infestation. Autumn thresholds are set higher in the Northeast because Varroa mite populations are higher during this time than in spring. Also, more mites are phoretic in late summer and autumn because colony brood production is decreasing, which causes more mites to be observed when you monitor. Treatment thresholds can also vary regionally. Warmer states and countries may support brood rearing for longer periods during the year and so may have a lower threshold for mites. Similarly, a beekeeper's goals may influence their decision of when to treat. If a beekeeper has a very low tolerance for colony loss, they may apply a treatment at lower infestation rates than a beekeeper with a higher tolerance for colony loss. For instance, Randy Oliver is a proponent for treating colonies at a 1% infestation rate all year round. This takes into consideration his individual management goals as well as his yearlong warmer climate. Remember, however, that inadequately controlling your mite levels can not only cause colony losses in your operations but can also put your neighbors' colonies and wild honey bee colonies at risk. If your hives are located in an area outside of northeastern North America, consult your state/provincial apiculturist or extension personnel to discuss the treatment thresholds for your region. Read: The Importance of Hygienic Behavior Hygienic behavior is a trait where ☆ Key Points workers are able to detect and quickly remove infected or parasitized pupae. Worker bees are able to detect the parasitized or viral-infected pupa inside the capped cell based on odor and, as a result, chew open the cappings. First, a small hole is chewed in the capping, or the capping can be entirely chewed off. That bee or another one then drags Using Varroa-resistant stock is the best way to give colonies a head start in controlling mite levels. Hygienic behavior is a trait where bees chew cappings and remove pupae from infested cells. In doing so, mites inside the cells dry out and die. the pupae out of the colony or consumes it within the cell. Because Varroa can only reproduce in capped cells, hygienic behavior can disrupt their reproduction. Once cells are open, the immature mites die from desiccation. While the term "hygienic behavior" refers to the quick and complete removal of pupae, beekeepers can often observe the intermediate stages of hygienic bees' attempts to control disease and mite infestations. For instance, a beekeeper may observe (1) perforations (small chew holes) in the cell cappings; (2) “bald brood” (with the intact, white, hairless pupa visible inside); and (3) chewed-down brood (in which the bees have partially consumed the pupa in the cell). It is currently not fully understood how honey bees detect infested cells, but studies have found they can detect altered brood pheromone, other odors that are released by sick or dead brood, and odors released by reproducing mites. In many cases, the act of chewing holes in cappings alone, then resealing these holes later, is enough to significantly reduce Varroa mite reproduction within the cell. Several feral honey bee populations that persist with Varroa in the wild display an enhanced ability to uncap and recap parasitized cells.
Photo of perforated cell cappings alongside hygienic behavior (empty cells). Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership. Photo of bald brood. Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership.
Photo of chewed-down brood (blue arrow). Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership. Photo of chewed-down brood. Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership.

While conducting your regular inspections, look for evidence of hygienic behavior, uncapping, or chewed-down brood. If you see cells with perforations and you're not confident that the bees are merely capping a larva's cell, use your hive tool to open them up and see what's inside. Remove some cells with bald brood or chewed-down brood using a toothpick or small twig. You can sometimes find mites (both mature and immature) inside the cells during this process. Hygienic behavior allows bees to detect not only Varroa-infested brood but also other brood diseases, such as chalkbrood, sacbrood, viruses, and American foulbrood. For this reason, it's a good management practice to open cells with perforations. While hygienic behavior can be alarming to see in your colony, it is actually a good behavior. The bees are demonstrating that they are able to detect an issue and attempting to control mites by cleaning out parasitized brood. Seeing a couple cells of hygienic behavior on a frame signals to the beekeeper that they should monitor for mites if they aren't already doing so on a monthly basis. Seeing many cells with evidence of hygienic behavior, chewed-down brood, bald brood, or perforations often indicates there is a high Varroa mite population in the colony and should serve as a warning sign to beekeepers that the colony may have PMS. The beekeeper should monitor their colony and be prepared to add a treatment immediately if the monitoring results dictate that it's time. Uncap perforated cells with your hive tool to see any issues that could be affecting the brood. Back to Table of Contents

Read: How Is Hygienic Behavior Tested in Colonies? A classic test for hygienic behavior is the freeze-kill brood technique. It consists in freezing a portion of capped brood in a colony using liquid nitrogen. This kills the brood. The frame is reinserted in the colony and left for 24 hours for the bees to detect the dead brood and clean out the cells. After 24 hours, the frame is removed and the proportion of removed pupae is calculated as a percentage. Typically, colonies with greater than 90% of the dead brood removed are classified as hygienic. Liquid nitrogen is applied to a portion of capped brood. Some brood becomes "bald" in the process.

Twenty four hours later, Colony A did not do a great job of removing the freeze-killed brood. Although they uncapped many cells, this colony is not considered very hygienic. Photo: Bee Informed Partnership Twenty four hours later, Colony B detected and removed 100% of freezekilled brood. This colony is highly hygienic. Photo: Bee Informed Partnership If a beekeeper wishes to test his or her own colonies for free, the “pinprick” method can also be used. In this method, capped brood is pricked with a sharp pin to kill the pupae

inside. It is recommended that the beekeeper pricks at least 21 cells and that they apply a paint dot or smear to a few cells above the region they pricked to more easily identify that region later. After 24 hours, the beekeeper returns to the frame to count the proportion of pupae that were removed. If the beekeeper pricked 100 capped cells, and 24 hours later 92 of them were empty (had the pupae removed), that colony would display 92% hygienic behavior. Illustration of the pinprick method. In this example, the beekeeper pricked 30 cells (red dots) in two regions, for a total of 60 cells. Yellow paint lines mark the two regions that were pricked so they can quickly be identified later. Two other assays to measure hygienic behavior in honey bees have been developed recently. They provide a faster, more precise, and less destructive alternative to the traditional freeze-killed brood or pin-killed brood tests described above. The UBO assay (Uniform Brood Odor Assay) measures the olfactory detection stage of hygienic behavior, meaning how bees respond to chemical cues that mimic diseased or parasitized brood. It is based on the finding that hygienic bees respond to specific brood pheromones and decay volatiles released by unhealthy or parasitized larvae. These odors act as olfactory cues that trigger workers to uncap and remove affected brood. This is how beekeepers can implement this assay in their colonies. Synthetic disease-related "brood odor” compounds (like β-ocimene and oleic acid) can applied to healthy capped brood, and the hygienic response can be measured as the percentage of cells that worker bees uncap or remove 2–4 hours after application of the synthetic mix. That mix can be currently commercially obtained as "UbeeO" at https://opterabees.com/.

The second recent assay developed is known as the capping/uncapping assay, which measures how often and how effectively worker bees open (uncap) and sometimes re-seal (recap) brood cells that contain abnormal brood, usually Varroa-infested pupae. It is based on the finding that when a Varroa mite reproduces inside a capped cell, the developing pupa releases subtle olfactory and vibrational cues that differ from healthy brood. Some bees, in particular from hygienic lines, detect these cues through the cappings and open the cells to investigate. If the pupa is severely parasitized or dead, they proceed to remove it. If it seems viable, they proceed to recap the cell. This behavior interrupts the mite’s reproductive cycle, often killing or sterilizing the mites. These are the steps that beekeepers can use to implement this assay in their colonies. Step 1. Choose a frame with Varroa-infested sealed worker brood and mark a defined area of capped cells (~200–300 cells). Step 2. Reinsert the frame into the hive and leave it for 24–72 hours to allow worker bees to interact with it. Step 3. Examine the cells and record the following categories: capped cells (intact), uncapped cells (wax removed), recapped cells (new thin wax cap placed after reopening), removed brood. Step 4. Calculate the proportion of infested cells that were uncapped/removed versus those left intact. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Genetic Stocks for Varroa Resistance Soon after the Varroa mite jumped ☆ Key Points hosts to Apis mellifera, researchers began to breed for Varroa-resistant bees. Varroa-resistant stocks are the best non-chemical tool to help control mite populations. While several stocks have been imported and bred and are effective in lowering mite populations, surprisingly not many beekeepers use these stocks in their own operation. Share information about Varroa- Using Varroa-resistant stock is the best way to give colonies a head start in controlling mite levels. There are five different stocks that confer some degree of Varroa resistance: Varroa Sensitive Hygienic, Minnesota Hygienic, Russian, Purdue Ankle Biters, and Saskatraz. resistant stock and where to order it to help spread the word at your local bee club. If entire communities begin to adopt Varroa- resistant stock, the region will have a good head start in combating the Varroa virus epidemic. There are currently five different Varroa-resistant stocks that are commercially available in the U.S.: Varroa Sensitive Hygienic (the newest lines are called Pol-line), Minnesota Hygienic, Russian, Purdue Ankle Biters, and Saskatraz. Some of these stocks are effective at reducing Varroa infestation levels because they display hygienic behavior. Below you will learn more about the different Varroa-resistant stocks available in the U.S. Varroa Sensitive Hygienic This stock was developed by Dr. John Harbo and Dr. Jeffrey Harris at the USDA Bee Breeding Lab in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. Varroa Sensitive Hygienic bees kill and remove pupae from cells that contain reproductive mites. Immature mites die because they desiccate quickly once the cells are opened; in this way, mite reproduction is interrupted and the growth of the mite population is slowed. If there are many bees in a colony that perform hygienic behavior, this can significantly lower the mite population. This stock was originally called SMR stock (suppressed mite reproduction); with further research, however, it was realized that the impairment of mite reproduction was due to the bees' so-called hygienic behavior, so the stock was renamed Varroa Sensitive Hygienic (VSH).

The VSH stock was developed in 1997 and has had many generations to test and refine this trait. These tests show that VSH colonies have significantly slower mite population growth than non-VSH colonies. In one of these tests, VSH queens were exchanged for non-VSH queens in colonies. When VSH queens were introduced to colonies previously headed by non-VSH queens with high Varroa mites, the mite population decreased. When non-VSH queens were introduced to colonies previously headed by VSH queens with low Varroa mites, the mite population increased. “Pure VSH” queens refer to queens that have been mated with drones that also carry genetics for the VSH trait. Some commercial beekeepers purchase pure VSH queens and raise daughter queens from them, allowing these daughters to naturally mate with random drones in the area. These second-generation queens are often advertised as “VSH” queens, but the trait is more diluted than it is in colonies with pure VSH queens. Some beekeepers may purchase pure VSH queens and mate their daughters with drones that have other traits of interest, such as gentleness, winter hardiness, or high honey production. By doing this, stocks of bees can be bred that carry several traits of interest to beekeepers. How Do VSH Colonies Compare to Other Colonies in Beekeeping Operations? When VSH queens have been introduced to commercial colonies in the U.S., they have helped significantly reduce mite levels. One study found that colonies headed by pure VSH queens reduced mite infestation levels by 76% and daughter VSH queens (that mate openly with random drones) reduced mite infestations by 44%, compared to colonies headed by non-VSH queens, which reduced mite infestations by only 7%. Another study comparing VSH colonies and Italian colonies in U.S. commercial apiaries found VSH colonies required fewer mite treatments during the study period: Only 12% of VSH colonies required mite treatments, while 40% of Italian colonies required mite treatments. Furthermore, both stocks produced similar amounts of honey. Minnesota Hygienic Originally developed to help colonies resist and recover from American foulbrood and chalkbrood, the Minnesota Hygienic line of bees was developed by Dr. Marla Spivak in 1993. Colonies that display 95 to 100% hygienic behavior are used as breeder colonies. This stock is now also advertised as helping reduce Varroa mites. Tests show that this line is not quite as effective at lowering mite population as VSH lines are, but it is more effective than non-hygienic stocks.

In this video, Dr. Marla Spivak, Distinguished McKnight University Professor of Apiculture and Social Insects at the University of Minnesota, discusses the Minnesota Hygienic line that she developed. Video Transcript When I moved to the University of Minnesota in 1993, I started studying hygienic behavior of honey bees. This is the ability, it's a genetic trait, and it's the ability of some bees to detect and remove diseased and mite-infested brood. For a diseased brood, the bees do it very, very quickly. They're able to detect that the larva or the pupa is diseased. But they, when they're handling it, the larva or pupa has not become infectious yet. The disease didn't reach the spore stage, so they can handle it without transmitting the disease throughout the colony. For mites, the bees detect that there is a pupa infested with a mite when the mite is reproducing, starts laying eggs. And so, it's not the mite they're detecting, it's something wrong with the pupae. And so, they open up the cell, remove the pupa, and it interrupts the mites' reproductive cycle. And so it limits mite population growth in the colony. So, it's good for diseases, American foulbrood and chalkbrood, and for Varroa mites. It helps reduce the mite and disease loads in the colony. We started selecting hygienic behavior using the freeze-killed brood test. So, this was either you cut a section of comb of pupae, you stick it in your freezer for 24 hours, and you replace it back where you found it in the brood nest very carefully. And then you put it back in the colony. And after 24 hours, you come and check the amount of the freezekilled brood that was uncapped and removed. And colonies that remove the most diseased, the most freeze-killed brood in 24 hours, those that can do it the fastest, it's correlated with how quickly they would detect diseased brood and remove that from the nest. We moved from the sections of freeze-killed brood to using a liquid nitrogen assay. So, we freeze brood with liquid nitrogen, pouring the liquid nitrogen down a PVC tube. And it's easier for us, maybe not easier for small scale beekeepers, but we freeze-kill the brood that way, and check the amount uncapped and removed after 24 hours. The 24 hour test is much more accurate than a 48 hour test. That's important to know. So, based on this assay, we started selecting colonies for hygienic behavior. But our first criteria were that they produce honey, they winter well, they be very gentle, they build up very well in the spring, and they never, ever show signs of chalkbrood, ever, throughout the year. So, we would track colonies for a year and then test them for hygienic behavior. And if they had all of those characteristics and were highly hygienic, they would remove 95% of the freeze-killed brood in 24 hours, then I would raise daughter queens from them.

And after about 10, 7-10 years, I had at least a hundred colonies in the breeding program. And then I was maintaining the line through insemination. So, instrumental insemination. I distributed a lot of those queens to commercial beekeepers, who tested them in their stocks. We published a lot on the performance of those bees, and they started selling stock from the Minnesota hygienic line, is what we call it. Now, we're not breeding the line here at the university, but we're helping commercial beekeepers do the freeze-killed brood assay so they can be selecting for hygienic behavior from among many different stocks of bees, so that we can maintain genetic diversity. The Minnesota hygienic line that we bred using the freeze-killed brood assay is different than the Varroa-sensitive hygiene line, the VSH line. There's a lot of confusion and interchanging of words between VSH and the hygienic line. The VSH line is highly hygenic, but it also seems to have an additional trait where the mites don't reproduce as well on the worker brood in that line of bees. So, they're different. Purdue Ankle Biter Greg Hunt at Purdue University developed the Ankle Biter bee stock in 2007. While hygienic behavior bees target mites reproducing in the brood cells, Purdue Ankle Biter bees target phoretic mites. Purdue Ankle Biter bees injure mites by biting off parts of their body and removing their legs (hence the term “ankle biter”). Chewed mites either die from their injuries or are less able to crawl onto a worker bee or latch onto them to feed. To select for mite-biting behavior, breeder colonies are selected based on those with the largest proportion of mites with chewed legs and body parts on a sticky board. Over generations of selection, the breeding population has showed an increased response in chewing mites. At the start of the breeding program in 2007, only about 3% of mites on a sticky board were chewed. By 2015, 50% of mites on the sticky board were chewed. There is promise for using this line to help reduce the number of colonies that die from Varroa mites. Purdue University distributed 102 queens to 39 beekeepers in 2014. Half of the queens were Purdue Ankle Biters, while the other half were of other commercial stock. Beekeepers received one queen of each and were asked to keep records on colony survival and honey production. The beekeepers did not know which queen was an Ankle Biter and which was not — it was a “blind” experiment. The beekeepers introduced the new queens in the summer of 2014, and by March 2015, 55% of Ankle Biter colonies were still alive, while only 22% of the non-Ankle Biter colonies were. Honey production was higher in Ankle Biter colonies: Ankle Biters produced an average of 52 pounds per colony, while non-Ankle Biters produced 11 pounds per colony.

Varroa mite with missing legs. Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership Russian In 1997, the USDA-ARS program imported Russian bees and has continued breeding them for Varroa resistance. These bees have been naturally living with Varroa mites in eastern Russia for over 100 years and have developed some resistance through natural selection. USDA researchers studied the Russian bees in their own country before introducing them to the U.S. and found that they harbored lower levels of Varroa mites than U.S. colonies. In one study, untreated colonies in the U.S. had infestation rates of 33% and were collapsing from Parasitic Mite Syndrome, while untreated colonies of Russian bees in Russia only had infestation rates of 7% over the same time period. Trials in the U.S. echo these results: After three months without treatments, domestic colonies have a 17.3-fold increase in Varroa mite levels, while Russian colonies have only a 2.5-fold increase. Thus, Russian bees still exhibit a high degree of Varroa resistance, even when they are imported in the U.S. Furthermore, Russian bees in the U.S. produce equal or higher amounts of honey than domestic bees. Russian honey bees also demonstrate resistance to tracheal mites. Several traits of Russian bees better equip them to reduce Varroa mite levels. They have a high degree of VSH behavior, and they also cease brood production completely in times of

food shortage (such as a dearth in the summer). This cease in brood production reduces the availability of brood cells for mites to reproduce inside, so their population decreases. After years of continuous selection in the U.S., Russian bees were made available in 2000. Since 2007, the Russian Honey Bee Breeders Association has bred and evaluated Russian stock available for purchase. As of 2017, 12 beekeepers are involved in maintaining and distributing this stock. Grooming Behavior Grooming behavior is a type of social immunity that honey bees perform in the colony. Bees groom themselves or their nestmates to remove foreign debris, including Varroa mites. This behavior can help reduce Varroa mite levels in a colony. This effect can be more pronounced if the beekeeper also installs a screened bottom board with a sticky sheet beneath the colony. Mites that are groomed off the bees fall to the bottom of the hive and are unable to crawl back up to feed on other bees. The original host of the Varroa mite, Apis cerana, has more pronounced grooming behavior than Apis mellifera. It is thought that this behavior has contributed to Apis cerana's ability to resist mites. Apis cerana workers regularly groom mites off of themselves. They have also been observed performing “grooming invitation dances” to stimulate their sisters to groom them. During this dance, a bee stands in one spot and vibrates its abdomen while intermittently grooming its body. Dr. Jennifer Tsuruda of the University of Tennessee is working to produce a stock of honey bees with increased grooming behavior to help reduce Varroa mite levels. Watch the video below (from Jennifer) to view two bees with mites on their bodies. The bee in the top frame does not exhibit the grooming behavior trait, while the bee in the lower frame does. Saskatraz The Saskatraz breeding program started in Saskatchewan, Canada, in 2004. The goal was to develop a stock of bees that produced a lot of honey, overwintered well in cold climates, had a gentle temperament, resisted brood diseases and viruses, and exhibited hygienic behavior. Colonies in this breeding program are tested every year for these traits and breeder queens are selected from the top performers. The program began commercial queen production in 2012. Saskatraz stock is available as either queen cells or pure Saskatraz queens from Saskatchewan, Canada, or as Saskatraz hybrids from Olivarez Honey Bees, Inc., in Northern California.

For a list of reputable suppliers that sell pure VSH, Minnesota Hygienic, Ankle Biter, or Russian stock, click here. How Do I Introduce New Stock to My Operation? After reading about the advancements in Varroa-resistant stocks, you may be eager to order some resistant queens, nucs, or packages for your own operation. If you only order a few queens to try in some of your colonies, place those colonies in a new yard. Having a colony with a Varroa-resistant colony near a Varroa-susceptible colony can diminish the effects. Even a colony that is better able to resist mites can become overwhelmed if the colony next door is infested and continuously introduces mites to it. Compare the resistant colonies to your other colonies in terms of Varroa mite levels and other traits in which you are interested; this will help you determine whether this stock is right for your operation. Incorporating resistant stock is only one part of IPM, and having resistant bees does not mean that you’ll never need to treat your colonies again. Although these colonies generally have slower mite population growth, mites can still reach or surpass the treatment threshold over time. Always monitor your levels and intervene if necessary. Can I Select for Varroa Resistance in My Own Colonies? Yes! You can indeed begin selecting for more Varroa-resistant stock. Many beekeepers try to select for Varroa-resistant colonies by letting nature take its course. They don't treat their colonies, and every year lots of colonies die from mites. The few colonies that survive till spring may have some resistance. Queens can be raised from those survival colonies, and the process is repeated each year. The problem with this method is that your bees suffer, you risk spreading disease to your neighbors' colonies and the wild bees in the area, and you can waste a lot of money purchasing new bees to replace your losses.

To avoid heartache while still working toward developing a resistant stock, you can select for Varroa resistance right in your own backyard. Dr. Meghan Milbrath from Michigan State University has developed a great method. In order to breed for any trait, you need to have more than one hive so that you can compare colonies. With this method, you also need to have a source for new queens during your first year. They can be from a local supplier, or perhaps a commercial stock that already has some degree of Varroa resistance. Once you are set up with two or more colonies, you are ready to start. Keep in mind this method works best if your apiary is isolated from other colonies that could potentially reintroduce Varroa mites to your colonies. Here are six steps to begin your breeding program: 1. Spread your colonies out in your yard and give each colony a unique landmark to minimize drift. 2. Monitor your mite levels using a reliable method each month and keep records on these levels. 3. Record any other behaviors that could influence mite populations (performing splits, queen supersedure, swarming, a dearth, robbing, etc.) 4. When a colony exceeds the treatment threshold, treat that colony and requeen it. This is a key step. Allowing mite levels to build up without treatments can create a situation that favors virulent Varroa mites instead of Varroa-resistant bees. Treating and requeening these colonies enables you to remove those nonresistant genetics from your apiary and prevent mite bombs from spreading to your other healthy colonies. This program requires very diligent monitoring and record keeping. Continue

monitoring all colonies and treating individual colonies as needed. Prepare your colonies for winter at the end of the season. 5. The following spring, rear queens from the colonies with the lowest mite levels. In some cases, you may have colonies that always remained below the treatment threshold. In other cases, all colonies may have required at least one treatment. In this instance, rear queens from the colonies that required the fewest treatments and had the lowest mite levels. 6. Repeat this process again during the second year. If you choose to requeen colonies in this year and following years, raise queens from your colonies with the lowest mite counts. Over the subsequent generations, you can continue to refine your stock. Back to Table of Contents

Some beekeepers may purchase pure VSH queens and mate their daughters with drones that have other traits of interest, such as gentleness, winter hardiness, or high honey production. By doing this, stocks of bees can be bred that carry several traits of interest to beekeepers. How Do VSH Colonies Compare to Other Colonies in Beekeeping Operations? When VSH queens have been introduced to commercial colonies in the U.S., they have helped significantly reduce mite levels. One study found that colonies headed by pure VSH queens reduced mite infestation levels by 76% and daughter VSH queens (that mate openly with random drones) reduced mite infestations by 44%, compared to colonies

headed by non-VSH queens, which reduced mite infestations by only 7%. Another study comparing VSH colonies and Italian colonies in U.S. commercial apiaries found VSH colonies required fewer mite treatments during the study period: Only 12% of VSH colonies required mite treatments, while 40% of Italian colonies required mite treatments. Furthermore, both stocks produced similar amounts of honey. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Genetic Stocks for Varroa Resistance — Minnesota Hygienic Originally developed to help colonies resist and recover from American foulbrood and chalkbrood, the Minnesota Hygienic line of bees was developed by Dr. Marla Spivak in 1993. Colonies that display 95 to 100% hygienic behavior are used as breeder colonies. This stock is now also advertised as helping reduce Varroa mites. Tests show that this line is not quite as effective at lowering mite population as VSH lines are, but it is more effective than non-hygienic stocks. In this video, Dr. Marla Spivak, Distinguished McKnight University Professor of Apiculture and Social Insects at the University of Minnesota, discusses the Minnesota Hygienic line that she developed. Video Transcript When I moved to the University of Minnesota in 1993, I started studying hygienic behavior of honey bees. This is the ability, it's a genetic trait, and it's the ability of some bees to detect and remove diseased and mite-infested brood. For a diseased brood, the bees do it very, very quickly. They're able to detect that the larva or the pupa is diseased. But they, when they're handling it, the larva or pupa has not become infectious yet. The disease didn't reach the spore stage, so they can handle it without transmitting the disease throughout the colony. For mites, the bees detect that there is a pupa infested with a mite when the mite is reproducing, starts laying eggs. And so, it's not the mite they're detecting, it's something wrong with the pupae. And so, they open up the cell, remove the pupa, and it interrupts the mites' reproductive cycle. And so it limits mite population growth in the colony. So, it's good for diseases, American foulbrood and chalkbrood, and for Varroa mites. It helps reduce the mite and disease loads in the colony. We started selecting hygienic behavior using the freeze-killed brood test. So, this was either you cut a section of comb of pupae, you stick it in your freezer for 24 hours, and you replace it back where you found it in the brood nest very carefully. And then you put it back in the colony. And after 24 hours, you come and check the amount of the freezekilled brood that was uncapped and removed. And colonies that remove the most diseased, the most freeze-killed brood in 24 hours, those that can do it the fastest, it's correlated with how quickly they would detect diseased brood and remove that from the

nest. We moved from the sections of freeze-killed brood to using a liquid nitrogen assay. So, we freeze brood with liquid nitrogen, pouring the liquid nitrogen down a PVC tube. And it's easier for us, maybe not easier for small scale beekeepers, but we freeze-kill the brood that way, and check the amount uncapped and removed after 24 hours. The 24 hour test is much more accurate than a 48 hour test. That's important to know. So, based on this assay, we started selecting colonies for hygienic behavior. But our first criteria were that they produce honey, they winter well, they be very gentle, they build up very well in the spring, and they never, ever show signs of chalkbrood, ever, throughout the year. So, we would track colonies for a year and then test them for hygienic behavior. And if they had all of those characteristics and were highly hygienic, they would remove 95% of the freeze-killed brood in 24 hours, then I would raise daughter queens from them. And after about 10, 7-10 years, I had at least a hundred colonies in the breeding program. And then I was maintaining the line through insemination. So, instrumental insemination. I distributed a lot of those queens to commercial beekeepers, who tested them in their stocks. We published a lot on the performance of those bees, and they started selling stock from the Minnesota hygienic line, is what we call it. Now, we're not breeding the line here at the university, but we're helping commercial beekeepers do the freeze-killed brood assay so they can be selecting for hygienic behavior from among many different stocks of bees, so that we can maintain genetic diversity. The Minnesota hygienic line that we bred using the freeze-killed brood assay is different than the Varroa-sensitive hygiene line, the VSH line. There's a lot of confusion and interchanging of words between VSH and the hygienic line. The VSH line is highly hygenic, but it also seems to have an additional trait where the mites don't reproduce as well on the worker brood in that line of bees. So, they're different. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Genetic Stocks for Varroa Resistance Greg Hunt at Purdue University developed the Ankle Biter bee stock in 2007. While hygienic behavior bees target mites reproducing in the brood cells, Purdue Ankle Biter bees target phoretic mites. Purdue Ankle Biter bees injure mites by biting off parts of their body and removing their legs (hence the term “ankle biter”). Chewed mites either die from their injuries or are less able to crawl onto a worker bee or latch onto them to feed. To select for mite-biting behavior, breeder colonies are selected based on those with the largest proportion of mites with chewed legs and body parts on a sticky board. Over generations of selection, the breeding population has showed an increased response in chewing mites. At the start of the breeding program in 2007, only about 3% of mites on a sticky board were chewed. By 2015, 50% of mites on the sticky board were chewed. There is promise for using this line to help reduce the number of colonies that die from Varroa mites. Purdue University distributed 102 queens to 39 beekeepers in 2014. Half of the queens were Purdue Ankle Biters, while the other half were of other commercial stock. Beekeepers received one queen of each and were asked to keep records on colony survival and honey production. The beekeepers did not know which queen was an Ankle Biter and which was not — it was a “blind” experiment. The beekeepers introduced the new queens in the summer of 2014, and by March 2015, 55% of Ankle Biter colonies were still alive, while only 22% of the non-Ankle Biter colonies were. Honey production was higher in Ankle Biter colonies: Ankle Biters produced an average of 52 pounds per colony, while non-Ankle Biters produced 11 pounds per colony.
Varroa mite with missing legs. Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership Back to Table of Contents

Read: Genetic Stocks for Varroa Resistance — Russian In 1997, the USDA-ARS program imported Russian bees and has continued breeding them for Varroa resistance. These bees have been naturally living with Varroa mites in eastern Russia for over 100 years and have developed some resistance through natural selection. USDA researchers studied the Russian bees in their own country before introducing them to the U.S. and found that they harbored lower levels of Varroa mites than U.S. colonies. In one study, untreated colonies in the U.S. had infestation rates of 33% and were collapsing from Parasitic Mite Syndrome, while untreated colonies of Russian bees in Russia only had infestation rates of 7% over the same time period. Trials in the U.S. echo these results: After three months without treatments, domestic colonies have a 17.3-fold increase in Varroa mite levels, while Russian colonies have only a 2.5-fold increase. Thus, Russian bees still exhibit a high degree of Varroa resistance, even when they are imported in the U.S. Furthermore, Russian bees in the U.S. produce equal or higher amounts of honey than domestic bees. Russian honey bees also demonstrate resistance to tracheal mites. Several traits of Russian bees better equip them to reduce Varroa mite levels. They have a high degree of VSH behavior, and they also cease brood production completely in times of food shortage (such as a dearth in the summer). This cease in brood production reduces the availability of brood cells for mites to reproduce inside, so their population decreases. After years of continuous selection in the U.S., Russian bees were made available in 2000. Since 2007, the Russian Honey Bee Breeders Association has bred and evaluated Russian stock available for purchase. As of 2017, 12 beekeepers are involved in maintaining and distributing this stock. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Genetic Stocks for Varroa Resistance — Saskatraz The Saskatraz breeding program started in Saskatchewan, Canada, in 2004. The goal was to develop a stock of bees that produced a lot of honey, overwintered well in cold climates, had a gentle temperament, resisted brood diseases and viruses, and exhibited hygienic behavior. Colonies in this breeding program are tested every year for these traits and breeder queens are selected from the top performers. The program began commercial queen production in 2012. Saskatraz stock is available as either queen cells or pure Saskatraz queens from Saskatchewan, Canada, or as Saskatraz hybrids from Olivarez Honey Bees, Inc., in Northern California. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Genetic Stocks for Varroa Resistance — Grooming Behavior Grooming behavior is a type of social immunity that honey bees perform in the colony. Bees groom themselves or their nestmates to remove foreign debris, including Varroa mites. This behavior can help reduce Varroa mite levels in a colony. This effect can be more pronounced if the beekeeper also installs a screened bottom board with a sticky sheet beneath the colony. Mites that are groomed off the bees fall to the bottom of the hive and are unable to crawl back up to feed on other bees. The original host of the Varroa mite, Apis cerana, has more pronounced grooming behavior than Apis mellifera. It is thought that this behavior has contributed to Apis cerana's ability to resist mites. Apis cerana workers regularly groom mites off of themselves. They have also been observed performing “grooming invitation dances” to stimulate their sisters to groom them. During this dance, a bee stands in one spot and vibrates its abdomen while intermittently grooming its body. Dr. Jennifer Tsuruda of the University of Tennessee is working to produce a stock of honey bees with increased grooming behavior to help reduce Varroa mite levels. Watch the video below (from Jennifer) to view two bees with mites on their bodies. The bee in the top frame does not exhibit the grooming behavior trait, while the bee in the lower frame does. Back to Table of Contents

Read: How to Introduce New Stock and Select for Varroa Resistance After reading about the advancements in Varroa-resistant stocks, you may be eager to order some resistant queens, nucs, or packages for your own operation. If you only order a few queens to try in some of your colonies, place those colonies in a new yard. Having a colony with a Varroa-resistant colony near a Varroa-susceptible colony can diminish the effects. Even a colony that is better able to resist mites can become overwhelmed if the colony next door is infested and continuously introduces mites to it. Compare the resistant colonies to your other colonies in terms of Varroa mite levels and other traits in which you are interested; this will help you determine whether this stock is right for your operation. Incorporating resistant stock is only one part of IPM, and having resistant bees does not mean that you’ll never need to treat your colonies again. Although these colonies generally have slower mite population growth, mites can still reach or surpass the treatment threshold over time. Always monitor your levels and intervene if necessary. You can also begin selecting for more Varroa-resistant stock. Many beekeepers try to select for Varroa-resistant colonies by letting nature take its course. They don't treat their colonies, and every year lots of colonies die from mites. The few colonies that survive till spring may have some resistance. Queens can be raised from those survival colonies, and the process is repeated each year. The problem with this method is that your bees suffer, you risk spreading disease to your neighbors' colonies and the wild bees in the area, and you can waste a lot of money purchasing new bees to replace your losses.

To avoid heartache while still working toward developing a resistant stock, you can select for Varroa resistance right in your own backyard. Dr. Meghan Milbrath from Michigan State University has developed a great method. In order to breed for any trait, you need to have more than one hive so that you can compare colonies. With this method, you also need to have a source for new queens during your first year. They can be from a local supplier, or perhaps a commercial stock that already has some degree of Varroa resistance. Once you are set up with two or more colonies, you are ready to start. Keep in mind this method works best if your apiary is isolated from other colonies that could potentially reintroduce Varroa mites to your colonies. Here are six steps to begin your breeding program: 1. Spread your colonies out in your yard and give each colony a unique landmark to minimize drift. 2. Monitor your mite levels using a reliable method each month and keep records on these levels. 3. Record any other behaviors that could influence mite populations (performing splits, queen supersedure, swarming, a dearth, robbing, etc.) 4. When a colony exceeds the treatment threshold, treat that colony and requeen it. This is a key step. Allowing mite levels to build up without treatments can create a situation that favors virulent Varroa mites instead of Varroa-resistant bees. Treating and requeening these colonies enables you to remove those nonresistant genetics from your apiary and prevent mite bombs from spreading to your other healthy colonies. This program requires very diligent monitoring and record keeping. Continue monitoring all colonies and treating individual colonies as needed. Prepare your colonies for winter at the end of the season. 5. The following spring, rear queens from the colonies with the lowest mite levels. In some cases, you may have colonies that always remained below the treatment threshold. In other cases, all colonies may have required at least one treatment. In this instance, rear queens from the colonies that required the fewest treatments and had the lowest mite levels. 6. Repeat this process again during the second year. If you choose to requeen colonies in this year and following years, raise queens from your colonies with the lowest mite counts. Over the subsequent generations, you can continue to refine your stock. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Breeding for Resistance in Your Own Operation Some beekeepers really enjoy the stock they currently have but would like to incorporate some Varroa-resistant traits too. Great news - you can start selecting for Varroa resistance in your own operation. Many beekeepers try to select for Varroa-resistant colonies by letting nature take its course (a "survival of the fittest" philosophy). They don't treat their colonies, and every year lots of colonies die from mites. The few colonies that survive in spring may have some resistance. Queens can be raised from those survival colonies, and the process is repeated each year. There are many problems with this method: Your bees suffer You risk spreading mites to your neighbors' colonies and feral colonies in the area You risk spreading Varroa-transmitted viruses to wild bees in the area You can waste a lot of money purchasing new bees to replace your losses To avoid the heartache of losing bees and money, while still working toward developing a resistant stock, you can select for Varroa resistance right in your own backyard in a sustainable and responsible way. Dr. Meghan Milbrath from Michigan State University and Dr. Tom Seeley have both written about methods to select for mite resistance in a sustainable and responsible way. We'll outline a combination of their methods here. In order to breed for any trait, you need to have more than one hive so that you can compare colonies. The more colonies the better, as honey bee colonies can have a lot of natural variation to work with. With this method, you also need to have a source for new queens during your first year. They can be from swarms you caught in bait hives, a local supplier, or perhaps a commercial stock that already has some degree of Varroa resistance. Once you are set up with two or more colonies, you are ready to start. Keep in mind this method works best if your apiary is isolated from other colonies, as this limits the reintroduction of Varroa mites from nearby colonies.

Here are six steps to begin your breeding program: 1. Spread your colonies out in your yard and give each colony a unique landmark to minimize drift. 2. Monitor your mite levels using a reliable method each month. Keep records on these levels. 3. Record any other behaviors that could influence mite populations (performing splits, queen supersedure, swarming, a dearth, robbing, etc.) 4. When a colony exceeds the treatment threshold, treat that colony and requeen it. If you don't want to use any chemicals whatsoever, you can also cull the colony with soapy water. This is a key step! Allowing mite levels to build up without treating or culling highly infested colonies can create a situation that favors virulent Varroa mites instead of Varroa-resistant bees. Treating and requeening these colonies enables you to 1) remove those non-resistant genetics from your apiary and 2) prevent mite bombs from spreading to your other healthy colonies. This program requires very diligent monitoring and record keeping. 5. Continue monitoring all colonies every month, treating and requeening or culling individual colonies that develop high mite levels as needed. Prepare your colonies for winter at the end of the season. 6. The following spring, rear queens from the colonies with the lowest mite levels. In some cases, you may have colonies that always remained below the treatment threshold. These are excellent candidates for being breeders! In other cases, all colonies may have required at least one treatment. In this instance, rear queens from the colonies that required the fewest treatments and had the lowest mite levels.

7. Repeat this process again during the second year. If you choose to requeen colonies in this year and following years, raise queens from your colonies with the lowest mite counts. Over the subsequent generations, you can continue to refine your stock. If you continue this method for several years and your operation is isolated from other honey bee colonies, you will likely be able to have a sustainable treatment-free operation with colonies that convey some Varroa resistance. This more natural approach to beekeeping, sometimes called "Darwinian Beekeeping", is detailed nicely in Tom Seeley's Book "The Lives of Bees: The Untold Story of the Honey Bee in the Wild". Back to Table of Contents

Read: Cultural Methods for Varroa Management Overview Cultural methods are fairly simple non- ☆ Key Points chemical management practices that can be implemented to slow the population growth of Varroa mites. Cultural controls take advantage of understanding certain aspects of honey bee and Varroa mite biology. A Cultural methods are tools and behaviors beekeepers use that take advantage of understanding honey bee and Varroa mite biology. variety of different cultural methods have demonstrated varied success in reducing mite levels. None of these methods is effective at keeping levels below the economic threshold on their own, but combining multiple cultural methods as part of a greater Integrated Pest Management approach can be highly effective. We encourage beekeepers to incorporate as many cultural methods as they can, dictated by their beekeeping goals and their available time. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Cultural Methods for Varroa Management — Drone Frame How it works: One to two drone foundation frames are inserted into a hive at the edge of the brood nest (typically in the #2 or #3 position). The comb is built out and the queen lays drone eggs in the comb. After the eggs are laid, frames should then be removed between 10–24 days later, with an effort to remove the frame(s) with the maximum amount of capped cells on the frame. Frames should be frozen for 24 hours at 0°F (-18°C) to kill the drone brood and mites inside the cells. After freezing and thawing back to room temperature, the frames are reinserted into the colonies in the same locations. The bees clean out the cells and the process is repeated throughout spring and summer. After the first round, frames can easily be re-inserted and removed at approximately 24 day intervals, as it only takes a few days for the bees to clean the cells out and for the queen to start laying again. This method is most effective when the most drones are produced in colonies, from April until July in the Northeast US. Fewer drones are produced in late summer and autumn, making the drone frames an ineffective method later in the year. As drone production slows, the frames may be filled with honey instead. Simply scrape off the honey, rinse the frame, and use the frames again next spring. Colonies with low populations also do not produce many drones and may not use the drone frame. Watch this video to see how to use drone frames to help manage Varroa mite levels. Video Transcript This is a frame of drone comb foundation that I ordered from a bee supply company. And when you order these frames, they typically come in this bright green color, so it's very easy to pick out which one is the frame inside your colony. And they're a plastic foundation with just a thin layer of beeswax. And we're comparing it to worker foundation. You can see that the cell sizes are much different. So, the worker foundation is much smaller than the drone foundation. And it's the size difference that's actually going to stimulate the queen to lay eggs that will develop into drones. So, to lay unfertilized eggs. So, now, let's go out into the colony and actually put this frame in. And we'll go through the process of using this for Varroa control with an integrated pest management approach. Okay. So, once we have our foundation, we're actually going to insert it into the deep that contains the largest portion of the brood nest. And, in this case, it's this bottom deep. And we can either put it in the number two position, which is what I'm doing here,

or we can also put it in the number three position. You just like to have it on the periphery of the brood nest, if possible. So, when you first put in a frame of drone comb foundation, it might take a while for the colony to begin drawing it out with wax before the queen will lay an egg in there. And, remember, the timing starts from when the egg is laid. So, in the beginning, when you're just using foundation, you might need to check on it periodically to see when the queen begins laying an egg so that you can precisely time when you want to remove that frame. And once the egg is laid, it can be removed between 10 to 24 days, ideally more toward the end, just so that you're maximizing the amount of brood that's actually fully capped. When you're ready to remove your drone comb frame, it should look like this. This is ideal. Here, we have a frame that's just covered in drone pupa that are almost all capped. So, there's very few that have open larvae. And, in this way, we're actually maximizing the number of mites that we're killing. So, we're going to pop this frame directly into the freezer, leave it there overnight. The next day, let it thaw at room temperature. And we're ready to put it back in the hive and start over again. So, that's how to install drone comb foundation. It's a very quick, cost effective method to incorporate as part of your integrated pest management strategy for Varroa. Why it works: Mites are more likely to reproduce in drone brood, crawling into drone cells just before the cells are capped. Removing full frames of drone brood removes many reproducing mites, helping to drive down the population level. How effective is it? On their own, drone frames are not able to provide sufficient Varroa control for an entire season, but their use can delay the number of mite treatments needed. Several studies support drone frames as being an effective tool as part of an Integrated Pest Management approach for reducing mite levels. Research from Nicholas Calderone at the Dyce Lab at Cornell found that colonies from which drone frames are removed all season long have significantly lower levels of Varroa mites in autumn compared to colonies that do not receive any drone frame removal. Another study conducted by David Tarpy found similar results: drone frame removal kept Varroa mite populations below the treatment threshold until mid- to late summer, reducing the number of chemical treatments needed by the colonies. Throughout the entire study, the colonies from which drone frames were removed had significantly lower mites than colonies that did not. Studies in Europe find that using drone comb removal in combination with chemical treatments slows down the population growth of Varroa significantly more than colonies that received only chemical

treatments. These studies also report there is no negative impact on colony development, colony strength, and honey production. Who shouldn't use it? If you rear queens and have drone-rearing colonies established for mating, this is not a good practice to use in those colonies, as a surplus of drones is needed for mating. Also, if you do not have the time or organization to remove the drone frames on schedule, you may inadvertently increase mite levels in the colony. Other considerations: Many beekeepers remove drone comb that has been constructed elsewhere in the colony. To do this, you can simply scrape off drone brood with your hive tool while you are working your colonies. Colonies naturally tend to produce drone comb on the outside edges of the brood frames, making it easy to scrape off as you come across it. Unlike using drone frames, this method is opportunistic and is not timed to maximize the removal of mites. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Cultural Methods for Varroa Management — Screened Bottom Board How it works: A screened bottom board is installed below the lowest hive body, allowing it to sit beneath the hive in place of a solid bottom board. Screened bottom boards can be accompanied with a sticky board. If a sticky board is used, it must be cleaned or replaced regularly, as debris builds up. In the Northeast US, screened bottom boards are typically in place from May to October and then replaced with solid bottom boards for the winter months. In warmer regions, screened bottom boards may remain in place all year long. Screened bottom boards also help reduce debris build-up (which can host wax moth larvae, ants, and small hive beetles) and can also help reduce humidity and mold by improving ventilation. Watch this video to see how to use screened bottom boards. Video Transcript This is a screened bottom board that I purchased through a bee equipment supply company. I painted mine blue. This is going to sit directly underneath your hive. So, a hive body will sit on top of this, in place of a bottom board. As you can see, there's a screen on the top here that allows debris and mites to fall through. And, if you happen to have a sticky board attached underneath here, then it's going to stick to that sticky board so that the mites aren't able to crawl back up onto the bees. If we look underneath this board, we can see that it's not solid. So, I set mine on top of a regular bottom board, which I'll show you in a second, but you can also just put it directly on top of the stand, depending on what your highest stand is. On the back of the bottom board, we have this little tray that pulls out, and this is where you can attach your sticky board. So, you can purchase a sticky board from an equipment supply store or, if you are like me, you can make your own using card stock. And you simply draw a grid on there to make it easier for you when you're counting the mites. And you need to apply something that's going to make the mites stick to this. So, you can either use petroleum jelly or you can use cooking spray, and spray it on top of it. So, from there, you're going to put the sheet on top of your tray, and you want to make sure that you're using card stock that's long enough to take up most of the space on this tray. And

then, from there, you're going to be able to insert it into the screened bottom board pretty easily, so that you're not having to open your colony or disturb your colony in any way. So, let's take a look at this outside and get an idea of how to use a screened bottom board as part of your Varroa mite management plan. So, here we have a screened bottom board that's actually installed beneath a hive. It's this top board, here, that's painted blue, and it's actually sitting on top of a bottom board that's turned the other way, that's also painted blue. And I just needed to put it on top of a solid surface because it's sitting on a cinder block, and otherwise, the cinder block would directly touch the tray that's in the screened bottom board. So, right now it's directly beneath these hive bodies so that when bees are landing to enter the hive, they're landing on top of the screened bottom board. And then the tray with the sticky sheet on it, we're actually going to install it into the back. So, we're at the back of the hive now and we have our sticky sheet that's thoroughly coated in petroleum jelly so that it will trap any mites that happen to land on it. And we have it sitting on top of this tray, which we're now just going to insert into the back of the screened bottom board. Some beekeepers will leave these sticky trays in for about a month, and then after that, they'll swap them out for a new one. After a month, there's a lot of debris in there that might actually completely coat the surface, so that it's not really effectively capturing any other mites that are falling. But other beekeepers will actually use this to measure the number of mites that are dropping in a particular period of time, usually about 24 hours. And so what they'll do is they'll insert the tray, after 24 hours, they'll come back and just see how many mites have naturally dropped. Another way that you can use this is when you're putting on a mite treatment and you can insert the tray with a sticky sheet and you can get an idea of how many mites are actually dropping after you've put a treatment on. And while I can't really gauge quantitatively how effective that treatment is, it can give you an idea if lots of mites are dropping dead, then it could be working to some degree. But you definitely want to follow it up with a sugar shake, or an alcohol wash, or an ether roll just to actually measure what your Varroa levels are afterward. Let's come back after about 24 hours and take a look and see what kinds of things we'll find on the sticky sheet. If you're checking your screens after 24 hours, they usually don't have too much debris on them. And we can start looking through each of these squares to count how many mites we're seeing. So, one of the things that takes a little bit of learning when using these sticky boards is being able to decipher mites from other debris that can collect on these boards. So, sometimes you'll see little bits of wax flecks. Sometimes you'll see actual wax scales

that have fallen off of the bees' bodies before they've been able to start shaping them. Sometimes you see bits of pollen or little bits of bees' bodies from dead bees. You might also see legs and wings. And you can also expect to sometimes see wax moth cocoons, especially if you have a big wax moth infestation. So, Varroa mites, once you train your eye to be able to recognize them, you can find them fairly easily as you're looking square by square on these sheets. So, in this particular instance, over a 24 hour period, we actually caught two Varroa mites. So, there's one mite found here, and then another mite found here. So, let's actually take a closer look at Varroa mites on sticky boards and get kind of used to seeing what they look like. So, in contrast with the board on the right, which is the one that I just pulled out of the hive, this is how much debris has built up in about 24 hours. We can look at the amount of debris that builds up after about one month. You can see it's considerably more, and it would be much harder to sift through and count the mites. And we would expect that there would be several more mites on this board that's been in for a much longer period of time, compared to the one that's only been in for 24 hours. So, after you have observed the mites on that sticky sheet, you can simply throw it away, add a new one, and repeat the process over and over again, so long as you have a screened bottom board beneath your hive. And there you have it, that is the step by step procedure of how to use a sticky board in conjunction with the screened bottom board as one part of your integrated pest management approach for Varroa mites. Why it works: Mites, particularly those that are chewed/injured by bees, may fall to the bottom of the hive. If they land on a solid bottom board, they can crawl back up onto the bees, but if they fall on a screened bottom board, they may fall out of the hive entirely and some may be unable to crawl back up. With sticky boards in place, mites will stick to the boards and die. How effective is it? Screened bottom boards are minimally effective in reducing mite populations and should not be used as the sole method of Varroa control. With them, mite populations may be reduced by up to 10%, but surveys conducted by the Bee Informed Partnership report no advantage of their use. Their ability to reduce mite levels likely varies seasonally. More mites naturally fall during broodless periods. Who shouldn't use it? Screened bottom boards can be used by beekeepers of all operation, sizes, and goals, but cannot be used with top bar hives. Studies show there is no

difference in weight gain or frames of bees between colonies with screened bottom boards versus those with solid bottom boards; in other words, screened bottom boards do not negatively impact honey bee colony growth. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Cultural Methods for Varroa Management — Small Hives How it works: Colonies are kept in a hive the size of one deep hive body with only 1-2 honey supers added during a honey flow. Why it works: Small colonies do not produce a lot of brood, so mite populations in a colony with 10,000–20,000 bees are not able to grow as large they would in a colony with 40,000–50,000 bees. Small colonies also swarm more frequently (usually at least once a year), taking about 30% of the mites with them as they leave and creating a break in brood rearing in both the parent colony and the new colony. How effective is it? Cornell bee researcher Tom Seeley has shown that colonies with brood nests housed in one deep hive body have significantly lower mite population growth compared to colonies kept in four deep hive bodies. Who shouldn't use it? Beekeepers whose main goal is honey production would not benefit from using small colonies, as they produce little to no surplus honey. Beekeepers who live in residential areas and are unable to catch the swarms should not use this method. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Cultural Methods for Varroa Management — Colony Spacing How it works: Colonies are spaced apart and provided with unique landmarks. Hive entrances face in different directions. Why it works: In most bee yards, colonies are crowded together. Typical commercial yards contain anywhere between 20–50 colonies, placed on pallets, in an acre or less. This promotes drifting and robbing among colonies, with bees transferring Varroa mites among different colonies. In nature, on the other hand, colonies are spaced about half a mile apart. Having colonies spread apart reduces drifting and robbing. Spacing colonies apart, using landmarks, and changing the directions of entrances helps foragers identify their home hive. How effective is it? Colonies spaced apart have reduced Varroa mite levels, reduced Varroa mite transmission, and increased overwinter survivorship. Tom Seeley has compared overwinter survivorship between colonies crowded together (8 colonies placed side-by-side on pallets) and colonies spread apart (9 colonies placed 30–80 yards away from each other). None of the colonies received any mite treatments. In his experiment, all 8 colonies that were crowded together died by mid-December, while 5 out of 9 colonies spaced apart survived the winter.
