The five surviving colonies had low mite infestation levels the following April (0.47 mites/100 bees). Similar experiments conducted by other researchers echo these results. Apiaries with colonies spaced at least 100 yards apart have significantly lower Varroa mite transmission from drift, compared to colonies that are next to each other or even 10 yards apart. Who shouldn't use it? Beekeepers that manage hundreds or thousands of colonies may not have the space available to place colonies far apart. Similarly, backyard beekeepers may not have the available space, either. Colonies placed in agricultural land for pollination services usually need to be placed on pallets for ease of transportation.
Photo credit: Mary Kate Wheeler Back to Table of Contents

Read: Cultural Methods for Varroa Management — Brood Interruption How it works: There are a variety of ways to introduce a brood interruption (also known as a brood break) into a colony: Allowing the colony to swarm: The remaining colony experiences a brood break as it waits for a new queen to emerge, mate, and begin laying. This brood break can last several weeks, especially if there are afterswarms. On the other hand, if you capture the swarm and put it in a hive where there is drawn comb available, it will take at least 9 days for capped brood to be present (if the queen begins laying right away). If no drawn comb is available, the brood break will be longer. Performing splits: Strong colonies can be split into two smaller colonies. The colony without the original queen experiences a brood break. No new eggs will be laid for several weeks if the colony rears its own queen. In this case, there will be approximately 35 days without any capped brood present in the colony. Some beekeepers remove the queen entirely and have both colonies rear new queens. Requeening: Requeening a colony can offer a small break in the brood cycle. This may not be enough to significantly lower the mite population if the newly introduced queen is mated and begins laying in a few days. In this case, the effects on the Varroa population are maximized if the colony is requeened with hygienic or Russian stock. The brood break lasts much longer if the colony rears its own queen (allowing approximately 35 days without any capped brood), or if a queen cell is introduced (allowing approximately 20 days with no capped brood). Temporarily cage the queen: Cage the queen for the duration of a brood cycle (25 days) to cause a brood break. If the queen is released after 25 days and begins laying eggs right away, this gives the colony approximately 10 days without any capped brood present. Release the queen after this time so that egg laying can resume. Keeping the caged queen in the colony allows the workers to detect the queen pheromone and prevents them from rearing a new queen. Use a cage where workers are still able to feed the queen. Why it works: Mites require capped honey bee brood in order to reproduce. Without brood present in the colony, mite population growth momentarily ceases. Mites present on adult bees are also at risk to be chewed or fall off. Since adult mites can live for several

months, the brood break is not a long enough period for the entire mite population to die off, but it can be reduced. Brood breaks are most effective when the queen is not permitted to lay for an entire brood period (at least 24 days). If a queen lays eggs the same day the brood interruption begins, 24 days ensures that the last eggs that were laid have had time to emerge as adults before she begins laying again. Longer brood breaks are more effective at reducing mite levels than shorter brood breaks. Photo credit: Mary Kate Wheeler How effective is it? Brood interruption is mildly to moderately effective in reducing Varroa mite populations when used on its own. Studies where queens are caged inside colonies for 25 days find between 11%–24% mite mortality. One study found that mite levels before the queen was caged averaged 4.36 mites/100 bees, while after caging the queen for the duration of a brood cycle the mite levels averaged 3.24 mites/100 bees. Brood interruption can be even more effective when beekeepers exploit the broodless period to apply a chemical mite treatment. As most mite treatments only target phoretic mites, a brood break ensures that all the mites in the colony must be on the adults, providing an ideal opportunity to treat. A study published in 2016 evaluated the efficacy of the mite treatment Apiguard in combination with queen caging. Apiguard used alone killed 76% of mites in the colony and caging the queen for three weeks with no other treatment killed

40% of mites in the colony. But the combination of caging the queen and treating during the brood break killed 97% of mites in the colony. The researchers did not observe elevated rates of queen death. Similar studies with oxalic acid find Varroa mites are significantly reduced when application coincides with a brood break from caging the queen. Who shouldn't use it? Longer brood break periods may reduce the population size of the colony, which may have negative implications on honey production. Beekeepers who live in residential areas and are unable or unwilling to catch the swarms that are cast should not use swarming as their brood break method of choice. Other considerations: Brood breaks are best conducted after the honey crop is removed and before the colony begins rearing winter bees (ideally around late July in New York). Brood breaks performed before the honey flow may reduce the overall forager population, while brood breaks conducted in early autumn may interrupt the colonies' production of winter bees. Also, performing splits in late summer or early fall might result in colonies too small to overwinter successfully. Finding queens to cage can be quite time consuming and unfeasible for large-scale operations. Some large-scale operations are having success by temporarily moving colonies into cold storage facilities to naturally induce brood breaks. Lastly, although there are benefits to using this method, it must be noted that forcing the entire mite population onto adult honey bees likely presents a risk to bee health, as their feeding damages fat bodies and transmits viruses. To reduce this risk and to maximize mite death, beekeepers can apply a Varroa treatment as soon as colonies become completely broodless. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Ineffective Cultural Methods for Varroa Management Varroa mites are more likely to ☆ Key Points reproduce in drone cells. While this is due to the developmental time of drones, some people thought that the Using small celled foundation does not reduce Varroa mite levels. size of drone cells may play a role as well. Drone cells are larger than worker cells. In small cell foundation, it was thought that mites may have difficulty reproducing, developing, and moving within the cell because there is limited space. For this reason, many people believe that using small cell foundation can reduce the numbers of Varroa mites in a colony… but does it really work? Past experiments have had conflicting results, but several more thorough studies published since 2001 have found that using small cell brood comb does not reduce Varroa infestations, and that mites enter small cells and regular-sized cells at the same rate. For this reason, small cell foundation should not be included as part of your IPM strategy to combat mites. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Cultural Management Practices and Wild Honey Bee Colonies Tom Seeley has spent decades ☆ Key Points studying the wild honey bee colonies in the Arnot Forest. He and his colleagues have observed how the colonies have changed since the introduction of Varroa. Some of those observations can help us manage our colonies in healthier ways. Watch this Wild honey bee colonies living with Varroa mites have provided insights into the cultural practices that beekeepers can use to better manage mites in their own colonies. video to learn more. Video Transcript At this point, I wondered how are these wild colonies able to persist with Varroa? I mean, nobody's putting chemicals in them, helping them out. They're all on their own. Well, this was an interesting mystery. And we don't have it fully solved, but we're learning more every year. Part of the story is, of their survival, is that they have good genes. And part of their survival is that they have a good lifestyle, or a good ecology. Let's look first at their good gene side of the story. I don't have time to go through it in detail, but I'll emphasize one thing that is interesting about the genetic changes that have occurred in these wild colonies as a result of natural selection, created by the Varroa, is that the wild bees now are smaller than they used to be. Back in 1978, if you measure their head width, for example, or the space between their wings, and you compared those 1978 bees with the 20 bees we collect from the wild in 2011, the bees are markedly smaller now than they were before. Now, why would that help the bees resist Varroa? It's because that smaller body size is probably a function of the bees having a shorter development time. We're not sure about that, but that's our working, current understanding. And by shaving a day off the development time, which is what they have done, that gives the mites one day less of the 21 days of development. It takes a day off the, a day less for the mites to mature before the bee climbs out of the cell. And that ends the mite's reproduction. So that's part of the story. Genetic changes changing development time, changing body size and other traits. The other side of the story is the lifestyle, or ecology of these wild colonies. And one thing I

want to stress here is that a huge difference between how honey bees live in the wild versus how they live in our bee yards is the spacing of the colonies. We crowd colonies in our apiaries, whereas in the forest, they're widely spaced. On average, in the woods, they are a half mile apart between the colonies. And why is that so important for the bees' survival with the Varroa? It's important because when we put our colonies close together in an apiary, we're creating a situation where it's very easy for Varroa to get from one colony to the next. This can occur when worker bees drift carrying Varroa from one hive to the next. It can occur when bees rob from one colony. They can pull the Varroa out of a dying colony, for example, and bring those Varroa home with them. And it can happen also when beekeepers like ourselves move combs between colonies. Now, so Varroa can move from one colony to another in an apiary easily. And that means that in an apiary, the Varroa can be actually very virulent and very damaging to colonies because they can kill this colony, and by the time they've killed this colony, and this colony is collapsing, the Varroa, through drifting and the other mechanisms, has already moved off into the next colony. So, it doesn't kill, the Varroa doesn't kill itself if it kills its host. In the wild, it's a completely different situation, with these colonies a half a mile apart, living up in these trees in dense forest. If Varroa kills its colony, it kills itself because there's no good way for Varroa to get to another colony living in a tree that's half a mile away. And what does that mean? It means that in the wild, there's selection on Varroa itself to not be virulent, to contain its reproduction so it doesn't kill its host. So, colony spacing is a big part of the ecology that has changed the selection on the mites. And the mites have evolved their virulence. But it also, the colony spacing has another effect. It also means that there's just less drifting of the bees themselves from one colony to the next. There's probably zero drifting in the wild, whereas there's abundant drifting In an apiary. And we've measured this level of drift recently by doing a simple experiment. We set up two groups of 12 colonies, 12 colonies in each group. In one group, the colonies are crowded together like in a standard apiary. In the other, they were scattered. They weren't as widely spaced as the bee trees are in the wild. They were only 30 to 80 meters apart, or 30 to 80 yards apart. But when we measure the amount of drift of the drones between colonies in the crowded group versus the dispersed group, it was like night and day. The drones in the crowded group, if you looked at, we used genetic markers to measure this, but we found that one third of the drones going into a hive in the apiary setting, were produced from a different

colony, from one of the other hives in that apiary. One third of the drones, that's a lot of drifting, a lot of mixing, and thus, a lot of opportunities for Varroa to get from one hive to another. In the scattered situation, it was 0% drift of the drones. All of the drones going into each hive came from that hive. So, it just shows you how different it can be. And it also suggests that we beekeepers might want to think about spacing our hives out. They don't have to be a half mile apart, but if we can get them 30 yards apart with some trees and things like that in between, that can reduce the opportunities for Varroa to get around. There's another thing about colonies living in the wild that is helping them deal with Varroa, and it is that they're living in relatively small nest cavities. They're only about the size of one deep hive body. What does that mean? Why does that help? That helps because these colonies living in the wild swarm every year. And that helps them deal with Varroa because when a colony swarms, as the swarm leaves, it takes away about a third of the mites in the parent colony. So, it knocks down by one third the population of mites in a colony. But it also does more, because it creates a period of time in the colony when there's no sealed brood. And this period can be quite long. It can be several weeks long if there's after swarming going on. And when there's no sealed brood in a colony, the mites have to be out on the bees and on the combs. They can't be hiding away in the sealed cells. And when the mites are out on the bees and the combs, they're vulnerable to being groomed and chewed by the bees. And that knocks down their population as well. And we've studied this, again, with experiments. We've set up experiments. We have two groups of colonies. In one group, the colonies are living in hives managed for honey production. Four deep hive bodies. And those colonies have big brood nests and they make lots of honey, and they produce lots of mites. And then, the other treatment is colonies kept in one deep hive body. And those colonies don't make any honey, but they make lots of swarms, and they don't make many mites. And in the big colonies, it's what you would expect. The mite populations just grow exponentially and they kill the colonies. The colonies living in the small hives, the mite population stay under control and the colonies survive. So, these are some of the things that we're learning about how bees live in the wild and how we can use that, use what we're learning about how bees live in the wild to tune up our beekeeping practices if we want to keep bees without having to treat them heavily with acaricides to control the Varroa mites. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Chemical Controls for Varroa Management Overview When monitoring reveals that mite ☆ Key Points levels are at or above the treatment threshold, it is a good time to apply a chemical control. There are currently eight chemical treatments registered for Varroa control in New York State. Beekeepers in other states or countries should seek information about the treatments registered in their regions. The approved treatments in New York include a variety of chemicals that can be used under different circumstances, depending on the temperature, the presence of brood, and the presence of honey supers. Broadly, the chemicals can be broken down into two categories: synthetic chemicals (also known as hard chemicals) and natural chemicals (also known as soft There are currently eight chemical treatments registered in NYS to use for Varroa control. Become familiar with the treatments available in your state or province. Chemicals can be broken down into three classes: synthetic chemicals, essential oils, and organic acids. Each chemical has specific requirements (temperature, frames of bees, presence of honey supers, etc.) that must be fulfilled in order to use the product safely. Always monitor colonies before and after chemical treatments to evaluate the treatment's efficacy. chemicals). Natural chemicals can further be categorized as organic acids and essential oils. The organic acids and essential oils used for Varroa control are naturally occurring in plants. For instance, thymol comes from thyme plants and oxalic acid is produced in rhubarb. The concentrations in the mite treatments, however, are much higher than what naturally occurs in plants.

There are eight registered chemical treatments for Varroa in New York State: Apiguard® (active ingredient: thymol) Api Life Var® (active ingredients: thymol, eucalyptus oil, and menthol) Mite Away Quick Strips® and the similar new product Formic Pro® (active ingredient: formic acid) Oxalic acid (active ingredient: oxalic acid dihydrate) HopGuard III® (active ingredient: hops beta acids) Apivar® (active ingredient: amitraz). Note that widespread resistance to amitraz was found in the USA in 2024/2025. Apistan® (active ingredient: fluvalinate). We do not recommend using this product. CheckMite+® (active ingredient: coumaphos). We do not recommend using this product. The illustration below depicts how they are categorized by active ingredient. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Chemical Controls for Varroa Management Here, Emma provides directions on how to use many of the various chemical controls for Varroa mite management. Apivar The active ingredient in Apivar is amitraz. It has been the backbone of Varroa destructor control for over two decades but in 2019, the USDA documented amitraz resistance in New York State and other states in America. Then, in 2024/2025, nearly all mites screened by the USDA from USA-based collapsing colonies were resistant to amitraz, thus suggesting widespread resistance to this miticide, and this in turn is believed to be a major driver of the exceptionally high honey bee colony losses in the USA for 2024/2025. Signs of resistance have also been reported worldwide. Video Transcript The active ingredient and Apivar is Amitraz, which is a formamidine insecticide. The strips contain 3.33% Amitraz. The insecticide is released slowly from the strip. So, as bees touch the strip of Apivar, small amounts of insecticide transfer to their bodies. As bees move and interact within the hive, they spread the insecticide. And when it comes in contact with mites, it impairs nerve functioning in the mite, and the mite is killed. Before you apply Apivar, carefully read all instructions to ensure proper application and safety. Wear a long sleeve shirt, long pants, shoes and socks, and chemical-resistant gloves. This product is not temperature dependent. Apivar is best used in early spring before the honey flow has begun, and in autumn, after honey supers are removed. Don't use this treatment during winter or when honey supers are on. To use Apivar, first remove the strips from the pouch, and keep any unused strips in the original packaging. Hang the strips between the frames so that bees can come in. To hang the strips, insert a toothpick or a thin nail in the small hole in the top of the strip, and lay the ends of the toothpick on the frames. Make sure that you remove all honey supers that are on the hive first. Apivar cannot be used with honey supers, as residues can be found in the honey. The number of strips that you insert depends on the number of frames of bees in the hive. Use one strip for every five frames of bees, use two for every 6-10 frames of bees, use three

strips for every 11-15 frames of bees, and use four strips for 16 frames or more of bees. Do not use more than four strips in one hive, and do not place more than two strips in each brood chamber. Place the strips within the bee cluster in the brood box. And if using two strips, place the two strips apart at least two frames from each other. Leave the strips in the hive for 42 days. If, after 42 days, you find that the bee cluster has moved and the bees are no longer in contact with the strips, reposition the strips into the bee cluster, and leave them there for an additional 14 days. Do not leave the strips in for longer than 56 days. After removing the treatment, wait two weeks before adding honey supers. Don't reuse the strips, and dispose of them according to the instructions on the label. Also, don't use Apivar more than twice a year. Apistan Video Transcript The active ingredient in Apistan is tau-fluvalinate, which is a pyrethroid insecticide. The strip contains 10.25% fluvalinate. The insecticide is released slowly from the strip, and as bees touch the strip of Apistan, small amounts of insecticide transfer to their bodies. As bees move and interact within the hive, they spread the insecticide. When it comes in contact with mites, it impairs nerve functioning in the mites and the mite is killed. Before you apply Apistan, carefully read all instructions to ensure proper application and safety. Wear a long sleeve shirt, long pants, shoes and socks, and chemical-resistant gloves. Use this product when outside temperatures are warmer than 50 degrees Fahrenheit, or 10 degrees Celsius. This product is best used in early spring before the honey flow has begun, and in autumn after honey supers are removed. Don't use this treatment during winter or when honey supers are present. So, let's go through the steps of applying Apistan. First, we're going to remove Apistan strips from the pouch, and keep any unused strips in the original packaging. Remove honey supers that are on the hive. Apistan cannot be used when honey supers are on, as residues can accumulate in the honey. The strips will be hung between frames so that bees can come in contact with both sides of the strip. The bees will come in contact with the chemical and will pass it to other bees as they rub against each other in the hive. You can bend the top flaps of the strip to hang them effectively between the frames. After using this treatment, do not consume any honey or beeswax from the brood nest. The strips will begin wet, and they'll dry once they're placed inside of the hive. While

they're wet, they can kill bees that come in direct contact with them. So, to minimize these risks, this treatment is best applied during times of reduced activity. So, this could be early in the morning, in the evening, or on a cloudy day. The number of strips that you insert depends on the number of frames of bees in the hive. So, you use one strip for every five frames, or fewer, of bees. This means a nuc or a weak colony with five or fewer frames of bees would receive one strip. A colony that has 10 frames of bees in a deep hive body would receive two strips. A colony with a brood chamber spanning two deep hive bodies and 20 frames of bees would receive four strips. Hang the strips so that they're within two combs of the edge of the bee cluster. The strips have to be in contact with the brood nest bees for the entire treatment period. For colonies in one deep hive body, hang the strips in the center of the brood nest. And for colonies with two deep hive bodies, hang the strips in alternating corners of the bee cluster. Leave the strips in for 42-56 days. This translates from 6-8 weeks. Do not leave the strips in for longer than 56 days. Once the treatment has finished, honey supers can be added immediately after. Don't re-use the strips, and make sure to dispose of any waste materials according to the label. There have been cases of resistance to Apistan. To minimize resistance in your colonies, rotate this treatment with other chemical treatments, and use an integrated pest management approach that includes cultural and genetic controls as well. Make sure to monitor for mites after the treatment is over to ensure the treatment was effective. Api Guard Video Transcript The active ingredient and Apiguard is Thymol, an essential oil that's produced by thyme plants. Apiguard contains 25% thymol. The treatment comes in a gel formulation that provides a slow, controlled release of the vapors. In addition to the vapors dispersing throughout the hive, bees also pick up the gel to clean it out from the hive. And in doing so, they help spread it throughout the colony. Apiguard comes in two sizes. You can buy the single trays that we're showing in this video, or you can purchase it in a big tub that treats at least 30 colonies. When you purchase a big tub of it, you'll scoop the right amount onto foil trays that you place on the top bars. But in the single application method, no measuring is required.

Before handling Apiguard, make sure to wear safety goggles, a long sleeve shirt and pants, socks and shoes, and chemical-resistant gloves. And before applying Apiguard, remove all of your honey supers that are present. Apiguard can not be used during a honey flow. Use Apiguard in early spring or in autumn when the temperature requirements are met. So, it needs to be between 60 and 105 degrees Fahrenheit, or 16 to 41 degrees Celsius. Apply Apiguard by first opening the foil lid from the tray and peel it back. Leave one corner of the foil lid attached to the tray. Add a rim spacer or an empty super to the hives so that there is free space, at least a quarter of an inch, between the top of the tray and the inner cover. This will allow the vapors to dissipate in the hive and it will allow the bees to access the gel. Close the hive. After two weeks replace the tray with a new one. Leave the second tray in the hive for an additional two weeks. If there's still gel in the tray after that, leave the tray in the hive until it's empty. Remove the tray before putting honey supers on. If you purchase the tub of Apiguard and are measuring the dose to give your bees, be careful that you don't overdose the colony. Thymol overdoses can cause increased mortality, absconding, and an increase in defensive behavior. In the event that the colony is overdosed, remove the excess product from the colony promptly. After you're finished treating your colony, dispose of any packaging according to the label. Api Life Var Video Transcript Api Life Var is an essential oil treatment that contains 74% thymol, 16% eucalyptus oil, and 4.7% menthol. The treatment comes in the form of a tablet, and the essential oil vapors will evaporate from the tablet and dissipate throughout the colony. Before applying this treatment, wear long sleeves, long pants, shoes and socks, safety goggles, chemicalresistant gloves, and a filtering respirator. Api Life Var is also combustible, so keep it away from your smoker. This treatment cannot be used when honey supers are in place to prevent excessive residues in honey and wax. After the treatment is ended, wait 30 days before applying supers. And don't apply this treatment when bees are robbing the colony. The best time to use this treatment is in early spring and autumn, when temperature requirements are met. So, the temperature must be between 65 and 85 degrees Fahrenheit, or 18 and 30 degrees Celsius. Don't use this treatment more than two times a year.

This treatment can only be used on Langstroth colonies that contain 8 to 20 frames of bees. All colonies that fulfill this requirement receive the same treatment dose. So, each package contains two tablets. First, open the package and remove one tablet. Break it into four even-sized pieces. The tablets break really easily and are quite fragile, so be careful handling them. Place the four tablets on the top frames of the brood nest at the edges of the brood nest. Don't put the tablets directly on top of the brood nest. Close the hive and keep the tablets in there for 7 to 10 days. After this time, replace the tablets with four fresh pieces and leave them in for another 7 to 10 days. After this time, replace the tablets again with another four fresh pieces and leave them in there for 12 days. After 12 days have passed, remove the tablets and dispose of them according to the label. So, in this way, the treatment of one colony requires one and a half packages of Api Life Var and four visits to the hive. Do not reuse tablets. Hop Guard II (Now HopGuard III) HopGuard III is a next-generation, more stable, and user-friendly formulation of the same natural hop beta acids used in HopGuard II. While the active ingredient is the same, the formulation, delivery system, and performance are substantially improved in HopGuard III thus offering greater consistency, less brood stress, and less cleaner handling. Video Transcript The active ingredient and Hop Guard II is potassium salt of hops beta acids. This ingredient comes from hops, the same flowers that are used to make beer. The treatment strips contain 16% hops beta acids. The strips are covered in liquid, and it's important not to remove any liquid from the strips before putting them in the colony. When applying this treatment, wear long shirt sleeves and pants, socks and shoes, safety goggles, and waterproof gloves. Hop Guard II can be used a maximum of three times per year. It can also be used when honey supers are present. But it's less effective when brood is present. So, if you're using this treatment during the honey flow when brood is present, you may need to follow up with another treatment shortly afterward if your mite levels remain above the treatment threshold. Always monitor to check your efficacy. It is safe to consume honey from honey supers that are present during treatment application, but do not consume honey from the brood nest.

This treatment can be used on colonies that have at least five frames of bees. Apply one strip per five deep frames of bees in the brood chamber. If the brood chamber has four or fewer frames of bees, do not use Hop Guard. If the brood chamber has five to nine frames of bees, use one strip. If it has 10 full frames of bees, use two strips. Bees in single brood boxes will use a maximum of two strips, while bees in double brood boxes will use a maximum of four strips. If using two strips, place them on different frames at least four inches apart from each other. And do not place any strips in honey supers. Once the strips are in, leave them in the colony for 30 days. The bees may chew up the strips in time, but if any remain after 30 days, make sure to remove them. Hop Guard II can also be used to treat package bees. In this case, beekeepers can cut strips in half and staple three half strips from the top of the package so that they're dangling inside the package and bees can come in contact with them. Keep the bees in contact with strips for 48 hours before installing them into a hive. Three half strips can be used for both two pound and three pound packages of bees. Oxalic Acid Note that while there are no strict temperature requirements for using the fumigation method for oxalic acid, the product is most effective when used at temperatures above freezing (0°C/32°F). At temperatures below freezing, the tight clustering of the honey bees does not easily permit vapors to travel throughout the cluster and contact all the bees. Video Transcript The active ingredient in oxalic acid is oxalic acid dihydrate. And this is an organic acid that naturally occurs in some plants, like rhubarb. The oxalic acid that you purchase for mite control contains 97 percent oxalic acid dihydrate. Trace levels of oxalic acid are naturally found in honey, but at higher levels, around 400-900 parts per million, it can alter the taste of honey. The current applications of oxalic acid cannot be used with honey supers on. Oxalic acid treatments can only be applied a maximum of two times a year. Do not give a colony oxalic acid treatments more than two times a year, as it can be harmful to the colony. The efficacy of this product is not temperature dependent. This treatment is only effective when there's no brood in the colony. This could be in early spring, late fall, or winter here in the Northeast, or if you're creating a broodless period, for example, by caging the queen. Do not use in colonies that are overwintered indoors, as the product can only be applied outside. Oxalic acid is approved for treating mites in three

ways. First, it can be fumigated into a colony. Second, it can be dribbled in a colony. And third, it can be sprayed onto a package of bees. Let's first go over the fumigation method. When oxalic acid is fumigated into a colony, it begins as a solid, but it's heated up to become a gas. While you're applying the treatment, the gas is coating all the bees, phoretic mites, and the hive interior, so that everything will possess a thin film of oxalic acid crystals. With the appropriate dose, the oxalic acid film is not harmful to honey bees, but it is fatal to phoretic mites. When applying this miticide, wear a long sleeve shirt and long pants, shoes and socks, gloves, goggles, and most importantly, a half face respirator with a cartridge or particulate filter. It is very important not to breathe in the vapors, as it's very poisonous. And when inhaled, it can damage your lungs and other organs. Also, don't stand close to the hive while treatment is in progress, and take care to avoid any vapors that are released from the entrance. Do not use when honey supers are on the hive, as it can contaminate honey. After treating a colony with oxalic acid, wait 14 days before adding honey supers. Close all upper hive entrances and seal any equipment cracks with tape to prevent oxalic acid vapor from escaping the hive. If you have a screen bottom board on your hive, replace it with a solid bottom board. Make sure to follow the instructions on your oxalic acid vaporizer. In this video, we're using the Varrox vaporizer, but your vaporizer might have slightly different requirements. There are also some models that require a heat gun to use. Always follow the instructions that come with your specific device. So, let's get started. First, we're going to scoop oxalic acid into the pan of the vaporizer. The amount of oxalic acid you use depends on the configuration of your hive. Use one gram per brood chamber. If you have a colony housed in one brood box, use one gram of oxalic acid. If you have a colony housed in two brood boxes, use two grams of oxalic acid. And there will be a measuring device that comes with the oxalic acid when you purchase it. Scoop the oxalic acid into the pan and insert it fully into the hive entrance. After the vaporizer is inside, seal up the entrance with a strip of foam or a cloth so that the vapors don't escape. After the entrance is sealed, connect the vaporizer to a car battery. If you're using the Varrox vaporizer, you'll need a 12 volt, 12 amp battery. Leave it inside the hive, connected to the car battery, for two and a half minutes. During this time, the pan is heating up, causing the solid oxalic acid crystals to vaporize into a gas. And this conversion of a solid into a gas is called sublimation. So, sometimes this is referred to as the Oxalic Acid Sublimation Method. If there are still some crystals left in the pan after this time, continue

to heat for an additional half minute until all crystals have vaporized. And during this time, all the oxalic acid will sublimate, and you may see fog coming out of the entrance of your hive. Disconnect the vaporizer from the battery and keep it inside the hive for another two minutes before pulling it out, to allow the oxalic acid vapor to settle. Remove the vaporizer and completely seal the entrance with a cloth or a strip of foam. And keep the entire entrance sealed for 10 minutes. Cool the vaporizer by dipping it in a bucket of water to ensure that the oxalic acid sublimation doesn't begin occurring before it's inserted into the next hive. The great thing about using oxalic acid in late fall is that you don't need to open up the colony in cool weather and you don't need to come back to the hive to remove any strips later. So, it's very convenient. It's really important to only use oxalic acid that's been formulated for treating Varroa mites. It will specify this on the label. Other oxalic acid, or wood bleach purchased from hardware stores, can contain additives that can potentially harm bees. Using nonregistered forms of oxalic acid for mite treatment, or non-registered forms of any mite treatment for that matter, is against the law. Now, let's go over the dribble method. The dribble method of oxalic acid application requires you to dissolve oxalic acid into sugar syrup. So, dissolve 35 grams of oxalic acid dihydrate in one liter of 1-to-1 sugar syrup. This will make a 2.8 percent oxalic acid solution. You'll want to use warm water because this will completely dissolve the crystals and it won't chill the bees when you trickle it onto them. Using a syringe, trickle five milliliters of the solution directly onto the bees in each bee space in each brood box. The maximum dose for a colony is 50 milliliters, regardless of whether the bees are in a single brood box or double brood boxes. You can purchase a measuring syringe from your bee supply company when you purchase the oxalic acid. It's important to note that you shouldn't use the dribble method on cold autumn days or in the winter; any day less than 37 degrees Fahrenheit, or three degrees Celsius, as this can risk chilling the bees. In this environment, it is best to use the fumigation method instead. The last registered method for oxalic acid is the package method. The package method uses the same solution that we just discussed to spray onto a package of bees before you install them into a hive. Before you spray your package, place it in a cool, dark area for 24 hours to encourage the bees to cluster together. First, you want to spray your package with 1-to-1 sugar syrup without any oxalic acid. This will encourage the bees to engorge

themselves on syrup, so that they're not consuming a lot of oxalic acid when you give it to them later. Wait two hours after spraying them with sugar syrup. Then, you want to spray them with the oxalic acid solution. Apply three milliliters per 1000 bees, using a spray bottle. So, what does that translate to? Well, a two pound package of bees contains about 7000 bees, which requires 21 milliliters of solution. On the other hand, a three pound package of bees contains about 10,500 bees, which would require 31.5 milliliters of solution. Apply the solution evenly on both sides of the package, and then keep the package in a cool, dark place for another 72 hours before you put them in a hive. Some important things to note about oxalic acid is that it doesn't penetrate brood cappings, so it will not kill any mites that are inside the brood, only phoretic mites. In the US, oxalic acid is not registered to use when brood is present. However, in Europe, some beekeepers will use oxalic acid during spring or early summer, when brood is present in the hive. And they'll apply a treatment, wait a week for some of the brood to emerge, apply another treatment again, wait another week, and apply a third treatment. And some beekeepers in the U.S. have also experimented with this practice. But research shows that repeatedly using oxalic acid when brood is present isn't nearly as effective as using one application when brood is not present. Repeated applications during spring or summer gives an efficacy of only 37 to 73 percent, whereas applying oxalic acid to broodless colonies yields an efficacy of 82 to 99 percent. Furthermore, repeated applications of oxalic acid can be damaging to honey bee health and can cause increased winter mortality. Also, it can result in higher adult, brood, and queen mortality, and can reduce the amount of brood the queen lays for up to two months after the treatment ends. This most often occurs with the exposure to multiple applications using the dribble method, but not so much with multiple applications using the fumigation method. So, those are some considerations when using oxalic acid. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Chemical Controls for Varroa Management — Mite Away Quick Strips The active ingredient in Mite Away Quick Strips® is formic acid, an organic acid found in some plants. Formic acid is also naturally found in honey, sometimes in trace amounts and sometimes in concentrations as high as 2,000 parts per million. A Mite Away Quick Strip application increases the formic acid content in honey well below a hundred parts per million, so it does not exceed the levels that can naturally be found in honey. For this reason, it is safe to use when honey supers are present. Mite Away Quick Strips contain 46.7% formic acid. A Mite Away Quick Strip is a gel strip with a paper wrapping surrounding it to control the vapor release. The vapors are going to dissipate throughout the colony to kill mites. The product also has the ability to penetrate brood cappings to kill some mites that are reproducing in the brood. Because of its ability to use when brood and honey supers are present, it's a great option to use in summer, should you find your mite levels exceed the treatment threshold. Mite Away Quick Strips can also be used in spring and autumn when the temperature requirements are met. You want to make sure that you disturb your colony as little as possible before applying Mite Away Quick Strips. If you're inspecting or monitoring your colonies, wait at least three days before you apply the treatment. Applying the treatment right after disturbing the colony can result in increased queen loss and absconding. Formic acid can also affect queens and drones. Queen supersedure may be observed and drone eggs are sometimes removed. Drone mortality is also sometimes observed. For these reasons, we don't recommend that you use Mite Away Quick Strips to treat colonies that are being used for queen-rearing or drone-rearing. There are two application options for Mite Away Quick Strips. Option 1 consists of a seven-day treatment; it is recommended for all critical treatments as well as for under-the-cap Varroa control. Option 2 consists of a 21-day treatment; it is recommended for control of Varroa mites in the dispersal (phoretic) phase. For both options, outside temperatures must be between 50 and 85 degrees Fahrenheit, or 10 to 29 degrees Celsius, for the product to be most effective. Hot temperatures above

92 degrees Fahrenheit, or 33 degrees Celsius, can cause excessive brood mortality and queen loss. You also want to ensure that colonies have plenty of ventilation during treatment. Remove any entrance reducers in the hive. Before applying the treatment, make sure that you're wearing long pants, a long-sleeved shirt, gloves, shoes and socks, safety goggles, and a respirator with an organic vapor-removing cartridge. For the seven-day treatment, remove the strips from the plastic wrapping but do not remove the paper wrap. Place two strips on top of the brood box, staggered so that they have about two inches between strips and about four inches between the ends of the hive body. For colonies in double brood boxes, place the two strips in the same manner, but put them in between the two brood boxes. If you have honey supers on top, place the strips beneath the queen excluder. Colonies will expand their cluster within the first three days as a response to this treatment, and it's normal to observe bearding during this time. For really strong colonies, you can add an empty honey super on top of the top brood box so that they have room to expand. It's important not to open the colonies for seven days after the treatment is applied because it needs to be vaporizing properly. For the 21-day treatment, apply one strip on Day 1 across frames in the center of the brood box then replace that strip with another strip on Day 14. If the application of the second strip is delayed by unsuitable temperatures, plan to apply that second strip as soon as weather conditions permit. Follow all recommendations listed above for the seven-day treatment (exception: removing and replacing the first strip on Day 14). After treatment ends, you can remove the strips and compost them, or you can allow the bees to chew them and remove them from the hive in time. Do not reuse the strips, and dispose of any packaging according to the label. Formic Pro® is a new product created by the same company that makes Mite Away Quick Strips. While the basic application and look of the product is the same as the Quick Strips, Formic Pro has a longer shelf life and the treatment duration is a longer period of time; two strips can be placed on hives for 14 days, or one strip can be placed on hives for 10 days and replaced with a fresh strip for an additional 10 days. Read: Safety and Biosecurity of Chemical Controls Although mite treatments are designed to kill mites, some of them can also be harmful to bees and to humans. Always read the product label and use gloves, goggles, and ventilators when called for. It is a violation of federal law to use any pesticide product in a manner that is inconsistent with its labeling in the US. Too often, beekeepers ignore personal safety, putting themselves at risk for acute or chronic issues. Even natural chemical treatments, at the relatively small doses required to kill Varroa mites, can be poisonous to people. The beekeeper's safety is the number one priority. Be fully prepared when it is time to treat and train any employees, volunteers, or friends in personal protection safety when they are helping apply mite treatments. Oxalic acid vapor is particularly harmful and can be fatal if inhaled. A respirator face mask with a cartridge is required. Miticides can also be toxic to honey bees, particularly if they are not used according to the directions on the label. The risk to bee health for some chemicals is heightened if chemicals are applied when it is warmer than the upper threshold on the label or if they are applied more frequently than the maximum annual usage indicated on the label. Formic acid, Api Life Var, and Apivar can only be used a maximum of two times per year and can be harmful to honey bees if used more frequently than that.

An overview of the documented symptoms that can be observed in bees is in the table below: Documented Symptoms of Chemical Treatments Chemical Treatment Adult Mortality Brood Mortality Queen Mortality Interrupted Queen Laying Reduced Sperm Viability (Queen) Reduced Drone Sperm Viability Impaired Brood Development Apivar X Apistan X X X Apiguard X X X Api Life Var X Mite Away Quick X X X Strips Oxalic Acid X Hop Guard III No adverse impacts reported yet; more research is needed. Watch: The Controversy Surrounding Some Synthetic Chemical Treatments For the past twenty years, the main chemical treatments for Varroa mites were Apistan (active ingredient fluvalinate) and CheckMite+ (active ingredient coumaphos). Fluvalinate is among the oldest treatment options and has been used to treat Varroa mites since their introduction into the US. For several years, this treatment worked very well to control mites; however, in 1998, the first resistance to fluvalinate was documented in the US. Worried about the inability to effectively control Varroa, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency granted CheckMite+ an emergency approval. After only three years, resistance to CheckMite+ was also documented in the US. Apistan and CheckMite+ remain registered treatments for controlling Varroa mites, but they are almost never used by beekeepers as miticides (though sometimes CheckMite+ is used to control small hive beetles). At this time, the two most common treatments were unreliable, and yet Varroa mites were still posing a significant challenge to beekeepers. To make matters worse, research was beginning to uncover that fluvalinate and coumaphos sometimes had negative impacts on honey bee health. Specifically, these two chemicals can be harmful to queens and drones, interfering with their ability to reproduce. Studies showed that treatments of either chemical could lead to low birth weight of queens, high mortality rates of queens, and physical abnormalities of queens during development. Fluvalinate can interrupt a queen's ability to lay. Coumaphos can hinder the ability of a colony to rear queens, as fewer queens develop and are accepted. Coumaphos exposure can also cause low sperm counts in both queens (in their spermatheca) and in drones. As with many pesticides, fluvalinate and coumaphos are “lipophilic,” meaning they are fatsoluble. For this reason, they persist in beeswax (which is made primarily of lipids) and are now ubiquitous in commercial combs and wax foundation. Several large-scale studies have found these two miticides are the most frequently detected pesticides in beeswax. The largest survey of pesticide residues in wax examined 259 colonies across North America. The most prevalent pesticides that were present in these colonies were fluvalinate and coumaphos. 98% of colonies contained both of these miticides, and residues were present at higher levels than any other insecticide, herbicide, or fungicide. Coumaphos is the most persistent of the two chemicals, with a half-life of 115–346 days in beeswax. This means that the chemical can be present in the colony for years, well after

application. The ability of these and other miticides to remain in wax in low levels can help contribute to mite resistance. Furthermore, coumaphos is not degraded by heat. Commercially recycling contaminated beeswax to create wax foundation sheets results in contaminated foundation. This has made it difficult for beekeepers to avoid introducing low levels of coumaphos into their colonies, even those who avoid using synthetic chemical treatments. The best way for beekeepers to reduce their bees' exposure to contaminated wax is by gradually recycling out their old combs. Plastic foundation likely has lower residue levels than wax foundation, although plastic frames do still contain a thin coating of beeswax. The most recently developed synthetic chemical, amitraz, breaks down quickly in wax and honey. Residues cannot be detected after several weeks, though its breakdown chemicals can be present in honey for up to two months. Watch this video to hear about the introduction of naturally-derived chemical treatments and some considerations for using any kind of chemical treatment in your hives. Video Transcript There's a lot to know about mite treatments, as controlling Varroa is the biggest challenge that beekeepers face today. So, I'd like to give you a brief overview of some different chemicals, and some considerations to keep in mind as you're using treatments to manage Varroa. So, the first mite treatments to come on the market were synthetic chemicals. And these chemicals were developed because they're much more toxic to mites than they are to bees. For instance, fluvalinate, the active ingredient in Apistan, is 800 to 1000 times more toxic to mites than it is to bees. This means that not many bees die during treatment. So, that was a really great development. Although researchers found that there can be other negative impacts on bee health from the synthetic chemicals of fluvalinate and coumaphos. So, there's more desire to use more natural compounds in hives. And this is especially true because of concerns with residues in honey and beeswax, and with the ability of Varroa mites to develop resistance to some of the synthetic chemicals that are on the market.

So, for this reason, over 150 essential oils have been tested for Varroa mite control. And the most effective essential oils are the ones that can evaporate to produce vapors inside of the colony. And of the 150 that have been tested, only about 24 of them are able to evaporate quite readily. The next difficult thing about finding essential oils that work are that at concentrations needed to kill Varroa mites, many also kill honey bees. Unlike with synthetic chemicals, the specificity to target only mites is much lower in these natural treatments. So, for this reason, there's only a handful of essential oils that are toxic to mites, but safe for honey bees. The current registered treatments on the market include Thymol, eucalyptus oil, and menthol. It's important not to purchase your own essential oils from health food stores to make your own mite treatments because the products on the market are the right concentration and formulation to be safe for bees. They're also delivered in gels, packages, or tablets that allow them to vaporize at specific rates. Let's talk a little bit about treatment efficacy. So, the efficacy of treatments varies greatly depending on a number of environmental and colony factors. The amount of brood in your colony, for instance, affects treatment efficacy. So all treatments, except for Mite Away Quick Strips, only affect phoretic mites. Therefore, they're most effective when the colony has little to no brood. This could be during autumn, or if you're creating a broodless scenario. If you're using mite treatments when brood is present, such as during spring, or early summer, or in the middle of summer, they tend to be most effective when mites have just exceeded the economic threshold. If you have very high mite populations well above the economic threshold, they might not be brought down significantly if you're applying a treatment during this time. Treatment efficacy can also be impacted by the environmental temperature. And this is especially important for treatments that are vaporizing in the colony. The rate that a treatment vaporizes changes with temperature. So, it might occur more quickly in hot temperatures, which can pose a threat to bee health and can reduce the efficacy of the treatment because it's not present for a long enough time. On the other hand, if it vaporizes too slowly at cold temperatures, then it can also cause the product to be less effective because the mites aren't being exposed to the right concentration at the right time. For this reason, it's very important to only apply chemicals during their appropriate temperature windows. Because treatment efficacy can vary, it's always important to monitor after the treatment is finished to determine whether or not it worked. You don't want to assume that your mites are under control simply because you applied a treatment.

When you treat your colonies, it's also important not to open the colony while the treatment is in progress. So, you don't want to disturb the vaporization or anything else that's taking place during that time. It's also important to treat all the hives in an apiary at the same time. As soon as there's one colony in an apiary above the treatment threshold, all the colony should be treated because mites from highly infested colonies can easily be spread through robbing and drift. So for this reason, you want to treat on a yard-by-yard basis. With all these treatments available, beekeepers sometimes ask me, why are there still Varroa mites when we've been treating our colonies for decades? Well, there's a couple of reasons why. First, there's no treatment that kills 100 percent of mites on a colony. Even treatments with 99 percent efficacy still leave some mites present that will continue to reproduce in the colony, and perhaps spread to other colonies. The current treatment on the markets range in efficacy from 61 to 99 percent when used according to the label. So, there's always some mites that are still around. And second, not all beekeepers treat their colonies. The Bee and Farm Partnership surveys find that while most commercial beekeepers are treating their colonies, less than 50 percent of hobbyists manage Varroa mites in any way. So, any unmanaged colonies in an area can contribute mites to your colonies, even if you happen to treat them. So, until we have widespread adoption of honey bee stock that is resistant or tolerant to Varroa mites on their own, using chemical treatments when needed as part of a broader integrated pest management approach is our best strategy to keep mites at bay. So, I hope that some of these considerations help you when you're making decisions for mite management. Treating on an apiary basis is a great idea under these circumstances: 1. If the beekeeper doesn't know the mite levels of every colony in the yard but instead sampled a portion of them to understand the Varroa dynamics of the entire apiary 2. If the colonies in the yard are susceptible to drift because there are numerous hives in close proximity to each other 3. If the treatment will occur at a time of year when robbing is likely However, if robbing and drift is not a concern, and if beekeepers are aware of the mite levels in each individual colony, they can effectively control Varroa by treating on a colony basis (i.e. only treating colonies that exceed the mite treatment threshold). Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Varied Management Practices Beekeepers use a variety of chemical managements. A Cornell University survey of 60 New York State beekeepers in 2016 show that chemical controls tend to vary by operation size. Hobby beekeepers (with fewer than 50 colonies) are least likely to use chemical treatments, and when they do, they most commonly use natural chemicals. Only 3% of hobby beekeepers in the survey used synthetic chemicals. On the other hand, synthetic chemicals are much more common among commercial beekeepers; 42% reported using synthetic chemicals as part of their Varroa control strategy. Both hobby and commercial beekeepers had similar levels of Varroa mites. Some beekeepers choose not to use synthetic chemicals in an effort to reduce the potential build-up of residues in the combs or to minimize the negative impacts on bee health. Other beekeepers may choose not to use any treatments at all. If a beekeeper chooses to be chemical-free, Integrated Pest Management methods should continue to be followed. Being a successful treatment-free beekeeper requires diligence and good record keeping. Colonies should be monitored on a monthly basis, genetic stock for Varroa resistance should be introduced, and cultural methods should be used. Colonies that exceed treatment thresholds should be selectively treated or culled. Without the use of chemical treatments, colonies may need to be managed more intensely and this management is likely to be more time consuming. As we mentioned earlier in this module, it is a risk to those and other honey bee colonies, including wild ones, to practice chemical-free beekeeping without the use of any cultural treatment options and without closely monitoring mite populations. Chemical-free beekeeping is more successful in isolated areas, where colonies that can effectively manage Varroa without treatments are protected from re-introduction by robbing from outside colonies. The combination of Varroa prevalence and its role in colony losses, the importance of effectively managing mite levels, and the wide variation of beekeepers' treatment preferences paves the way for disputes. During disagreements, it is very important to be respectful of other beekeepers' opinions and to try to understand the reasoning behind their choices. Master Beekeepers have an important role to play with regard to Varroa management. They must work to educate other beekeepers on Integrated Pest Management and help others be comfortable, knowledgeable, and confident in managing their colonies effectively.

Watch these videos to hear honey bee experts Randy Oliver and Dr. Dennis vanEngelsdorp discuss the importance of mite management and the responsibility beekeepers have to their honey bees, their beekeeping community, and to nature. Randy Oliver Video Transcript Back in the day, beekeeping used to be much easier before the Varroa mite arrived. You could go in the Sears Roebuck catalog and order your hive, and it would be delivered by mail. You put the hive together, then you order your package bees, get your Starlines and Midnights, again through Sears Roebuck. They'd be delivered mail. You put your bees into the box, and that's the last thing you have to do. The bees would just take care of themselves. You go out once a year. You could take honey from the hive. And that hive would just survive for ten years, 20 years. No problem at all. No other input from the beekeeper. And I would hope someday, we get back to there, when bees evolve resistance to Varroa. But right now, that's not the case. It takes actual input to the beehive to practice bee husbandry to help them out. And the beekeeper has a responsibility to the bees that are in their care, and to the community of beekeepers, and to the feral population of bees. Taking a package of commercially-raised bee stock, which are bred for commercial production with lots of husbandry, and putting them in a hive, and then leaving them on their own is not fair to the beekeeping community, and it's not beneficial to the natural bee population because those bees won't survive. They're going to crash from the Varroa virus complex, and then they're going to flood the surrounding community with extra mites. So, all you've become then is a Varroa producer to the detriment of the beekeeping community and the surrounding bee population. So, you have a responsibility to the community, and to nature, if you're going to keep bees, to manage them, to keep them from collapsing from the Varroa mite. Dennis vanEngelsdorp Video Transcript The number one issue, I think, especially among backyard beekeepers, is Varroa mite. We consistently see, we sample a lot of colonies across the country. And we consistently see in September and October, when, that's the most critical time to get your mites under control because that's the time that you're going to produce your winter bees so they can live all year round or all winter. And so, when they're producing those winter bees, you

want that colony to be as healthy as possible so that those bees are going to live as long as they can. And we consistently see that a majority of beekeepers have mite levels in September and October that are above what we think the colonies can withstand without hurting them. And so, we think that after three mites per hundred, you need a treatment. After five mites per hundred, your colonies are already going to suffer ill effects, even if you start to treat. We also notice, especially among backyard beekeepers, that a majority of backyard beekeepers are not using a known Varroa mite control product. And I think that one of the reasons they don't is actually very altruistic. I think it's a really good reason. Some people think, "Well, I can afford, I'm a backyard beekeeper, I'm not feeding my family on this hobby. I have 10 colonies. I can afford to lose nine colonies. If one colony survives and I can breed from that survivor and then I'll save the world." And who doesn't want to save the world? That's a great thing to do. I applaud it. It's actually a fantastic idea until you think about what happened to those last nine colonies. So, we've been doing this project called the Sentinel Apiary Project across the country, especially in Maryland. And what we find is there's three, so these Sentinel Apiary projects, what we do is we go in and we get the beekeeper to sample eight colonies once a month for six months. So, it's the same colonies and we know what's happening. And we find that there are three patterns of mite development. This is Kelly's work, my PhD student. The first is, is the people who don't treat. So, they start with low mites, and the mites go through the roof, and, indeed, are well above threshold in October, and some of them start to die. The other one is what you would expect, is you have, you see that grows slowly, mite populations double every month, you see they grow slowly, August or September they treat, mites go down, and the mite levels stay low. That's what you want. That's an effective, good treatment and mite levels are down. Then we have this other third of the population that treats, mites go down. And then a month later, the mite levels are three times higher than they possibly could be based on normal mite reproduction. And so, we think this is evidence of these mite bombs in the landscape. That these colonies that are dying from mites, those bees, those last bees and mites don't say, "Oh, too bad, I'm just going to die here." They take off and they fly away. As far as two kilometers away, we found these. They blow up and they spread these mites across all the beekeepers within a three kilometer radius. So, what's happening is these people who don't treat their colonies are basically letting those mites invade their other colonies. And you're never going to breed resistance to mites that way. Like, I mean, if you

have all these mites invading, bees aren't going to be able to ever evolve resistance to that. And they're also infecting their neighbors. And so our message is: You need to have a Varroa management plan in place because it's irresponsible. We would not say that it was acceptable to breed a tick-resistant dog by letting our dogs die from ticks. That just would not be an acceptable thing. Why is it okay to do that with bees, especially if you're invading and hurting your neighbor? And I think that's a really important question that we have to ask ourselves. I still think it's very noble to be breed persistence. Don't get me wrong. And a lot of people say, "Oh, what you mean?" I think what you have to do is you have to monitor your colonies. And you measure the mites. Your colonies that have the lowest mite levels, you breed from. And the other ones, you either treat those mites, or if you're really opposed to treating, kill those bees and those mites because they're going to die anyway. It's better to do that before you spread it to everybody else. So, I think there are ways of accommodating this very important and long-term solution to our mite problem is breeding resistance. But you can't do it just by letting them die and spreading mites everywhere. That's just irresponsible for everybody. And that's one of the biggest learning points that I've had, and that has surprised me over the last period of time. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Developing Your Own Varroa Management Plan The active beekeeping season is a busy time. Beekeepers are often making splits, trying to build their colonies up to maximize forager populations for the major honey flows, adding supers, extracting honey, and preparing their colonies for winter. Without planning a Varroa management calendar upfront, it's easy to let mite management fall by the wayside and then get blindsided with high mite counts. Watch this video to see how we plan our Varroa management calendar at the Dyce Lab and to gain some tips that you can use when creating your own plan.
