Module Wrap-up: Varroa Mites Understanding Varroa mites — from their biology to their treatment — is fundamental to successful beekeeping. With this knowledge, beekeepers can better monitor their colonies and implement appropriate control measures to protect their bees from this devastating parasite. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Viruses The study of honey bee viruses is a relatively new field that has grown in recent years with advances in molecular technologies. We now know that honey bees are host to a variety of different viruses, some that don't show many symptoms, and others that can be devastating to colonies. Of all the pests, parasites, and pathogens included in this course, viruses are by far the most difficult to manage. It is important for beekeepers to be aware of the potential viruses that can infect honey bees and what symptoms to look for, should any be presented. In this module, we will explore the most well-understood honey bee viruses and the impacts they can have on colony health. Back to Table of Contents

Read: An Overview of Viruses Viruses are small infectious particles that live and reproduce inside another organism (their host). Nearly all life forms, including plants, animals, and bacteria, can be infected by different kinds of viruses, and honey bees are no exception. Apis mellifera is susceptible to at least nineteen different viruses, with new species and strains continuously discovered. These viruses can have a range of impacts on honey bee health: individual bees may have no symptoms at all, individual bees might die while the colony survives, or the entire colony could be wiped out. Viruses are the most difficult diseases for beekeepers to diagnose for a variety of reasons: 1. Infected bees are asymptomatic at low levels and only begin showing symptoms at high levels 2. Symptoms may not be evident in all life stages of a honey bee 3. Many different viruses can exhibit the same symptoms 4. Several viruses can be present in a colony at once, making it difficult to interpret symptoms and distinguish the effects of one virus over another. Furthermore, viruses cannot be viewed with a simple microscope like the spores of American foulbrood or Nosema. Without access to facilities to analyze DNA, many beekeepers may have colonies with high rates of infection without knowing it. This can translate to infections spreading without the beekeeper realizing, and colonies dying without the beekeeper understanding why.

Viruses are often in an inactive state or are asymptomatic, but under certain conditions they can be activated and become symptomatic. Some stress events, such as a bee experiencing other disease pressures (e.g., being exposed to certain pesticides or being chilled) can contribute to certain pathogens becoming “active.” At this point in time, we are aware of at least 7 viruses that are vectored by Varroa mites: deformed wing virus, Kashmir bee virus, acute bee paralysis virus, Israeli acute paralysis virus, slow bee paralysis virus, Varroa destructor virus-1, and Kakugo virus. This means that the mite can contract the virus in its own body from feeding on a honey bee and then transmit this virus to a different honey bee afterward. Often, these viruses do not show any symptoms until Varroa mites are present in the colony to exacerbate the infection. For these viruses, the best defense against high infection levels is to maintain low levels of Varroa mites for the entire year. If Varroa levels are not managed all summer long, but then a mite treatment is applied in autumn, the colony can often have low mite levels entering winter but still die from the viruses that have increased all season.

Read: Sacbrood Virus Sacbrood virus is one of the most ☆ Key Points common honey bee viruses worldwide. It was described in 1913, making it the first known honey bee virus. Sacbrood can infect brood and adults, but easily observed symptoms are only visible in brood. Once sacbrood is contracted in a larva, it fails to shed its final skin to become a pupa once the cell is capped. Instead, it remains in the larval stage, curling upward and developing Depending on the stage of the infection, sacbrood virus can be identified by the larva's curledupward position and shrunken head, by its fluid-filled sac-like appearance, or by its removable scale. Sacbrood is most common in spring or times of dearth. a “shrunken head” appearance, where its head looks smaller and pointier than normal. Over time, its skin becomes filled with fluid and turns pale-yellow and swollen. This fluid-filled “sac” appearance is the origin of the name sacbrood. Many replicates of the virus are contained beneath the skin in this fluid, enough to infect many other bees if the skin is punctured and the fluid released. Eventually, the larva's head begins to turn brown and the body dries out and becomes brown or black, turning to a flat scale on the cell floor that can be scraped out with a toothpick or small twig. The virus can remain active in this state for several weeks. Adult bees infected with sacbrood virus don't have symptoms that are easily observed, but their behaviors can be altered. Infected adults usually transition from nurse bees to foragers earlier than expected. They become poor foragers, collecting less pollen than healthy bees.

Progressive sacbrood infection. Credit: All photos from Bee Informed Partnership The virus can be transmitted from infected brood food and it is also associated with Varroa mites. Food becomes contaminated when nurse bees feed an infected larva and then move on and feed a susceptible larva. While Varroa has not yet been confirmed to vector this virus to honey bees, we do know that the mites can carry the virus. When inspecting your brood frame, look for any cells that have perforated cappings or the cappings entirely chewed off, an example that nurse bees are detecting the diseased brood. Open any perforated cappings with your hive tool and check for the characteristic “shrunken head” or sac-like larva. Sometimes, only one or two cells are affected. A brood comb with a heavy sacbrood infection appears spotty (due to hygienic behavior) and has many cells with perforations and symptomatic larvae. Sacbrood virus is most common in early spring and during periods of dearth. As with other viruses, sacbrood is primarily managed through proper nutrition and maintenance of colony vigor with a fertile queen. In mild cases of infection, bees can prevent a major outbreak by removing diseased larvae through hygienic behavior in the early stages of infection. If a colony experiences a bigger outbreak (with at least 5% of brood cells visibly infected), discard brood frames that contain many infected cells and requeen the colony (ideally with hygienic stock). Clean your hive tool and hands before working another colony.
Sacbrood virus also infects bumble bees. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Deformed Wing Virus Deformed wing virus (DWV) is the most prevalent virus in North America, and one of the most destructive to honey bees. High levels of this virus, combined with Varroa mites, are a leading cause of over winter colony mortality. Every year, the USDA-APHIS surveys find over 80% of honey bee colonies sampled across the U.S. have DWV. Cornell University's survey of over 200 colonies in 2016 found 96% of them to be infected with DWV. Because of its prevalence, this virus has recently been classified as a worldwide epidemic. ☆ Key Points Deformed wing virus is the most prevalent honey bee virus and has been declared a worldwide epidemic. The most identifiable symptom is deformed, dysfunctional wings. The virus occurs at low levels, often without symptoms when Varroa mites are not present. When mites are present, the virus can activate, increase, and ultimately kill colonies. There are at least two different strains of DWV: strain A and strain B. Strain A is the historical strain of the virus distributed worldwide, but since the mid 2000s, a new, more virulent strain, strain B, has emerged in Africa, Asia, and Europe. Until recently, we were unaware whether or not it was present in the US. In early 2017, the USDA-ARS lab screened samples that were stored in a freezer and discovered strain B (also called Varroa destructor virus-1) is indeed present in the U.S. and was likely introduced sometime around 2010. The strain has since spread across much of the nation without our realizing, from a mere 2 colonies infected in 2010 to 64% of colonies infected in 2016. There is no indication yet that strain B is more virulent than strain A in the US, but the USDA-ARS lab is continuing to investigate the virus, its spread, and how it relates to colony losses. The growth and spread of DWV coincides with the expansion of Varroa. Without Varroa mites present, this virus is transmitted inefficiently between bees and symptoms are rarely observed. But once Varroa mites become an issue in the colony, the virus can be transmitted rapidly. DWV replicates in mites just as in honey bees, increasing in the mite before it is passed to a bee. The more DWV there is present in a mite, the more likely the honey bee it is feeding on will develop deformed wings.
Credit: Bee Informed Partnership Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Deformed Wing Virus Transmission and Symptoms Although DWV is most often present asymptomatically, when it does show clinical symptoms, they are distinct and striking. Its name comes from its telltale sign: deformed, dysfunctional wings. These wings are deformed from the pupal stage onward. Pupae often acquire DWV from Varroa mites while still in the cell. Infected pupae often fail to complete development and die inside their capped cells. If they do survive the pupal stage, these infected bees are usually unable to fly or perform regular tasks and quickly die. All castes can have deformed wings. Infected adults also have a shortened, bloated, and darkened abdomens. Watch this video to see the symptoms of DWV and learn how it can impact colonies. Video Transcript The name deformed wing virus comes from its telltale sign: deformed, dysfunctional wings. Infected adults may also have shortened, bloated, and darkened abdomens, and all castes can become infected with this virus. This is what a worker bee looks like with deformed wings. And here is what a queen bee looks like that has deformed wings. Now, this virus can be passed from bee to bee, through trophallaxis and cell cleaning. And it can even be passed from the queen to her daughters through the eggs that she lays. However, transmission from these routes mostly results in low levels of deformed wing virus, usually without any symptoms being observed. The introduction of Varroa mites has changed the epidemiology of the virus. High deformed wing virus infections are almost exclusively as a result of Varroa mite transmission. Without Varroa mites present, the virus is not a major problem. But with Varroa mites present, it becomes deadly. The symptom of deformed wings occurs when the bee becomes infected with high levels of the virus as a pupa. So, it's the mites that are reproducing inside the cell that feed on the pupa and infect it. The bee will emerge as an adult with these deformed wings, She'll never fly or be able to perform regular tasks, and she'll die at an early age. Many other pupae that become infected with this virus never emerge and die inside their cells. Varroa is a very effective vector of this virus. Because deformed wing virus levels are low in colonies without mites, maintaining low levels of Varroa is the best way to maintain low levels of deformed wing virus. After you apply a mite treatment, it will take about six weeks before the virus levels are lowered in a

colony. This is because the lifespan of a worker is about six weeks long. So, the colony needs to experience a full turnover of the bee population before they're able to clear most of the virus infection. Even after Varroa is effectively controlled, colonies that were previously infected can still maintain low levels of the virus. So, while you're inspecting your colonies for disease, be on the lookout for deformed wings. If you see that symptom, monitor for mites to determine what your levels are and if it's time to treat. DWV can also infect bumble bees, carpenter bees, and orchard bees. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Black Queen Cell Virus Each year since 2009, the USDA-APHIS ☆ Key Points National Honey Bee Pests and Diseases Survey reports the national trends of honey bee viruses. Black queen cell virus has consistently been the second most prevalent virus, always found in over 80% of bee colonies that are sampled. Aptly named, when black queen cell virus Black queen cell virus is the second most prevalent virus. Despite how common it is, the virus is most often asymptomatic. This virus infects all honey bee castes, but “black cells” are only observed in queens and drones. (BQCV) infects a queen larva, the bee dies sealed inside the queen cell. After a few days, the body of the bee turns sac-like and yellow, and eventually dark brown or black. Often the cell wall also becomes dark brown or black. These symptoms are also observed in drone cells, though rarely. Queen cell with black queen cell virus. Credit: Bee Informed Partnership As with other viruses, BQCV can infect adult worker bees, but is most often asymptomatic. Infected worker pupae do not develop the characteristic black cell. Sometimes adult workers with BQCV have the symptom K-wing: their wings become disjointed (no longer

connected to one another by the hamuli) and form the shape of the letter “K.” Unlike other viruses discussed here, BQCV has no clear association with Varroa mite infestations. It sometimes co-occurs with Nosema apis, and both are strongly evident in the spring. For this reason, BQCV may particularly be a problem for queen-producing operations. Because the virus is most often asymptomatic, it is unclear how much of a risk it poses to overall colony health. Watch this video clip to see a worker bee with K-wing. Management is primarily through good nutrition and proper health, maintaining sterile and clean grafting and hive tools, and by removing any infected BQCV queen or drone cells, if observed. Queen breeders should not re-use any cell builders or mating nucs in which they have observed symptoms of BQCV. Black queen cell virus can also infect bumble bees. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Acute Bee Paralysis Virus Complex Acute bee paralysis virus (ABPV), ☆ Key Points Kashmir bee virus (KBV), and Israeli acute paralysis virus (IAPV) are closely related viruses from the same family that are best analyzed as a complex. All three viruses are distributed worldwide and are fairly common. All of these viruses are transmitted by Varroa. The The three viruses in this complex are closely related and are transmitted by Varroa. Symptoms of these viruses vary but include paralysis, hair loss, and acute death. viruses generally persist asymptomatically at low levels, but if a bee experiences high infection levels, the virus or viruses will cause characteristic symptoms and rapid death. Once they reach their critical high level, these viruses can kill colonies so quickly that a beekeeper may never notice any symptoms of paralysis in the colony at all. ▶ Acute Bee Paralysis Virus Acute bee paralysis virus was first isolated in 1963. Until the population growth and spread of Varroa through the US, ABPV was not a serious problem. Now that Varroa is nearly ubiquitous, ABPV is much more common than it was in the past. The USDA-APHIS survey finds ABPV to be present in around 15–25% of colonies in the US, where it tends to peak in late summer. This virus infects both brood and adults. When symptoms are showing, bees may darken, lose hair, tremble, and be unable to fly. Bees with symptoms of APBV die within days, and at high infection levels, just one day (hence the name “acute”). The virus accumulates in the brain and hypopharyngeal glands of the adult bee. It is likely transmitted orally, either through contact with contaminated brood or feces, or by eating infected brood. This virus can also infect bumble bees. Israeli Acute Paralysis Virus ▶

Israeli acute paralysis virus was first discovered in 2004 in Israel when beekeepers experienced high numbers of colony losses. As it was isolated just before Colony Collapse Disorder became a widespread national concern, it was a natural suspect for the die-offs in the U.S. and some parts of Europe. Some studies found IAPV in U.S. colonies, and the presence of IAPV was strongly associated with colonies that died from CCD. However, more recent studies have shown that not all colonies with IAPV experience CCD, and not all colonies with CCD have IAPV, ruling out this virus as the cause of CCD. About 10–20% of colonies sampled across the U.S. are infected with IAPV. IAPV can be present in all life stages of honey bees and usually shows no observable symptoms. Bees that suffer from Varroa mite infestations and IAPV infections experience immune suppression. When symptoms are observed, bees display shivering wings and become disoriented. They may be paralyzed or crawl slowly, and they ultimately die (often just outside the hive). Their body often turns darker and the thorax and abdomen become hairless. Colonies infected with IAPV experience declining colony growth and reproduction, and in severe infections, death. Watch this video clip of a sick bee that has become hairless and shiny. Note: Sometimes bees that get nectar dripped on them during hive inspections can appear hairless and shiny. Sick bees can be differentiated from "wet" bees because they are not sticky to the touch and are often seen "crawling" like the bee in this clip. Kashmir Bee Virus Kashmir bee virus was discovered in 1974, and today there is 10–15% incidence in U.S. honey bee colonies. KBV infects brood and adults. It is transmitted by Varroa; when virus particles are fed to bees, the bees do not experience an infection. However, if the virus particles are injected directly into the hemolymph (which is what happens when Varroa mites feed on bees), the bees can develop the infection. The virus can be extremely virulent (destructive) following Varroa transmission. Once acting virulently, KBM can kill bees at any life stage and has no clearly identifiable symptoms—the trembling and hairless progression of ABPV and ▶

IAPV does not occur with KBV. Infected bees die within three days. KBV tends to peak in autumn, later than ABPV. As with the other viruses infecting honey bees, KBV can only be managed by general considerations of nutrition and a strong queen. Most importantly, Varroa mite management is crucial for lowering viral loads. This virus can be transmitted from honey bees to bumble bees. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Chronic Bee Paralysis About 5 to 15% of colonies sampled ☆ Key Points across the U.S. have chronic bee paralysis virus (CBPV) infections. CBPV causes the same symptoms as ABPV, but bees take longer to die — often several days compared one day for There are two forms of symptoms from CBPV: one causing “hairless black syndrome” and the other causing paralysis. ABPV. Although current research suggests that Varroa mites do not act as a biological vector for CBPV because CBPV does not replicate within the mite, Varroa mites likely act as a mechanical or facilitating vector, worsening conditions that favor CBPV outbreaks. There are two forms of symptoms in adult bees. In the first syndrome, adults may turn dark and hairless (but are not paralyzed). This syndrome has been called “hairless black syndrome” in honey bees. In the other syndrome, bees are paralyzed or crawl, experience trembling wings and bodies, demonstrate K-wing, and do not darken or lose hair. Some bees develop bloated abdomens, and dysentery in and outside of the hive can be observed from the fluid buildup in their digestive tract. Both syndromes can be observed in different bees in the same colony at the same time. Colonies with high levels of CBPV often have hundreds or thousands of bees crawling on the ground in front of the hive. If many trembling bees are present in a colony, it is more likely infected with CBPV than ABPV, as most bees from ABPV die before symptoms are observable. Because of the black, shiny appearance of some of these bees, they are occasionally mistaken for robber bees from other hives (who are stripped of their hairs from fighting). In addition, the trembling, flightless bees at the colony entrance have been mistakenly believed to be exhibiting symptoms of pesticide poisoning.

Black hairless syndrome. Credit: Jennifer Tsuruda. This infection is spread by fecal-oral contact. It can also be spread through body contact, particularly in crowded colonies or colonies that are confined (e.g., during winter or transport). Back to Table of Contents

Read: Other Viruses In this module, we have only covered the main honey bee viruses that are regularly monitored and present in the US. Other viruses impact honey bee health as well, and even more viruses have been identified, but have not been well characterized and their genomes have not yet been sequenced, making it difficult to monitor their prevalence, distribution, and impact. For instance, the USDA-APHIS program is continuously monitoring for the introduction of slow bee paralysis virus (SBPV), which was discovered in England in 1974. To our knowledge, this virus is only present in Europe and Oceania. It is primarily an asymptomatic infection but can sometimes involve paralysis of the front two pairs of legs and is associated with the death of brood and adults. It is transmitted orally as well as by Varroa mites. In areas where this virus is present, viral loads peak midsummer. This virus also infects bumble bees. Additionally, one other virus is closely related to deformed wing virus (Kakugo virus). Collectively, DWV, Varroa destructor virus-1 (DWV strain B), and Kakugo virus are referred to as the Deformed Wing Virus Complex and all three are transmitted by the Varroa mite. While Kakugo virus and Varroa destructor virus-1 haven't been regularly screened for in the past, the latter will be routinely screened starting in 2018 after the discovery of its prevalence in the US. Scientists are working to create molecular screening methods to make it easier to track the prevalence and spread of these viruses.

Read: Managing Viruses There are currently no treatments that ☆ Key Points target viruses in the honey bee colony. Keeping colonies otherwise healthy and free of other stresses is the best strategy to reduce the likelihood of virus levels increasing. Healthy colonies can be achieved by ensuring adequate nutrition (which can help ensure optimum immune functioning), strong colony populations, fertile queens, and by limiting other stresses that can The only way to manage viruses is to keep colonies healthy with adequate nutrition, strong populations, and few external stressors. Maintaining low levels of Varroa mites all year long is key to reducing infections of viruses transmitted by the mite. impair immune functioning or foster infection, including but not limited to pesticide exposure, moisture, or prolonged confinement. To limit the viruses transmitted by Varroa, maintain low mite populations all year. Frames with heavy infestations of viruses that impact brood (sacbrood or Black Queen Cell Virus) can be removed from the colony to reduce the infection load. To date, it is unclear

how long wax or other equipment from a dead colony can retain live virus particles. New research in 2019 found viruses can be detected in comb (and in honey and pollen stored in comb), and they can remain virulent for several months. Research is urgently needed to determine whether stored combs from dead colonies pose a significant risk to bees that are installed on them and, if they do, to develop effective sterilization methods. Reduce the transmission to other colonies by sterilizing hive tools and changing gloves/washing hands in between working colonies that have observable symptoms. Viruses can be present on your hands and tools for the short time period it takes to open a new colony. Back to Table of Contents

Module Wrap-up: Viruses Our exploration of honey bee viruses has revealed the complexity of these pathogens and their varied effects on colony health. From seemingly harmless infections to those causing severe colony damage, we've learned to recognize key viral symptoms and understand their impacts. While these pathogens remain among the most challenging to manage, this knowledge equips beekeepers with the awareness needed to better monitor and respond to viral threats in their colonies. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Other Honey Bee Parasites Honey bee parasites are organisms that live inside or outside a honey bee host and require the host to feed and/or reproduce. Parasites benefit at the host's expense. Honey bees are susceptible to a variety of internal and external parasites, and so far in this course we have described several serious enough to require their own modules: Varroa mites, Nosema apis, and Nosema ceranae. In addition to these three parasites, honey bees are susceptible to several others. This module explores the additional parasites that impact honey bee health, and discusses methods for identifying and managing them. Back to Table of Contents

Read: History of Tracheal Mites Tracheal mites are a parasite that, as ☆ Key Points the name suggests, reside in the honey bees' trachea. The appearance of tracheal mites in the early 20th century was one of the largest honey bee disease epidemics in history, wiping out thousands of colonies each year in Europe, North America, and The appearance of tracheal mites in the 1980s caused an epidemic of colony losses. Today they are a minimal threat to colonies. The Buckfast bee stock was bred for tracheal mite resistance. elsewhere until effective controls were developed. In this section, we will describe tracheal mite infestations and how beekeepers can manage infestations in their own colonies. Tracheal mites were first noticed on the Isle of Wight, an island just off the coast of the United Kingdom in 1904. Mysteriously and rather suddenly, honey bee colonies began collapsing on the island. Over the next 14 years, 90% of the colonies died. The problem spread to the rest of Great Britain, devastating the beekeeping industry and decimating feral honey bee colonies. The mysterious disease was named “Isle of Wight Disease” until, in 1921, scientists discovered the tracheal mite was likely one of the culprits of these colony deaths, along with Nosema apis and starvation. Shortly after the mite's discovery, the United States Honey Bee Act was enacted (1922) in an effort to keep the mite out of the U.S. by preventing the importation of honey bees from Europe. Brother Adam, a beekeeping monk from the Buckfast Abbey in England, bred the Buckfast bee stock to be resistant to tracheal mites after 30 of the Abbey's 46 colonies died from the mite. This stock was adopted by many beekeepers, and is still in use today.

Buckfast bee stock Despite the Honey Bee Act, tracheal mites were introduced into the U.S. in 1983, when it is believed that infested swarms crossed the border from Mexico. The movement of packages, queens, and nucs rapidly spread the infection across the U.S. and elsewhere. Importing bees from other countries where the mite was unknowingly present also contributed to its quick spread. Tracheal mites are now present in every continent except Australia. They are also not yet present in the province of Newfoundland in Canada. While they initially devastated honey bees, tracheal mites are not a major parasite threat today. The Beltsville Bee Lab has been tracking tracheal mites in the U.S. since their introduction. Based on samples submitted by beekeepers and state inspectors, their estimated incidence has decreased from a peak of 45% of colonies infected in the mid1980s, to a mere 2% in 2015. This reduction has likely resulted from 1) the development of resistant stocks, 2) natural resistance developed by honey bees that survived infestations, and 3) effective control strategies used by beekeepers once an infestation is confirmed. Nevertheless, infestations still do occur, so beekeepers should be knowledgeable about tracheal mites' impacts, symptoms, diagnosis, and treatments. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Tracheal Mites Biology The tracheal mite, Acarapis woodi, is a ☆ Key Points very small, white mite that measures about 150 micrometers in length (a micrometer is one thousandth of a millimeter). Their effect on honey bees is referred to as “Acarine disease.” They infest adult honey bees of all castes and do not affect brood. They reside Tracheal mites infest the trachea of honey bees, impairing their ability to breathe. With breathing impaired, infested bees cannot fly and die at an earlier age. exclusively in the prothoracic trachea– the tracheae located at the very front of the thorax, just at the honey bee's “neck.” To get to these tracheae, they crawl through the spiracle at the base of the wing of 1–2 day old adult bees, usually during the night when colony activity is low. After a few days in the tracheae, they begin to reproduce, laying eggs that will develop into adults. Their offspring mate with each other and mature inside the trachea. Tracheal mites only infest young bees, identifying them based on their odor. This allows the mites to complete their entire life cycle before the adult bee dies. Before the bee dies, the tracheal mites exit this bee's body through its spiracle and looks for other young bees to infest.

Tracheal mite in honey bee trachea. Credit: Bee Informed Partnership. Inside the trachea, the mites feed on the bees' hemolymph by piercing through their tracheal walls with their sharp mouthparts. Honey bees experience reduced respiration as their breathing tubes are clogged with mites and become damaged and scarred. The bees also experience blood loss from the mites' feeding. Tracheal mite infestations tend to peak in autumn and winter in the Northeast US. When over 30% of bees in a colony are parasitized, the colony experiences a significant reduction in its adult population. As a result, the colony experiences decreased honey production and overwintering success. Colonies that survive the winter may build up slowly or die in early spring. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Tracheal Mites Symptoms Symptoms of tracheal mite infestations include the following: Adult bees crawling on the ground in front of the hive, unable to fly “K-wing” (in some cases) An inability to cluster in cool temperatures. When you open your colony on a cool autumn day, you expect to see a tight cluster of bees. With a tracheal mite infestation, you may instead see bees scattered on the frames, not in a cluster Dwindling adult population as infestation rates increase Watch this video clip of a bee in front of the hive, unable to fly. Bees that are parasitized by tracheal mites exhibit this behavior. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Diagnosing Tracheal Mites Tracheal mites can be diagnosed by ☆ Key Points microscopic examination, at home or at the Beltsville Bee Lab. With access to a dissecting microscope, diagnosing tracheal Tracheal mites can identified simply and quickly using a dissecting mites can be accomplished quickly and easily. microscope. These microscopes have low magnification, and you won't need slides. If you do not wish to purchase a microscope yourself, you can talk to your local bee club about a collective purchase. Alternatively, Cornell's Dyce Lab for Honey Bee Studies in Ithaca, New York, has a dissection microscope that you can use. Collect bees that are crawling on the ground, unable to fly, as these bees are the most likely to have tracheal mites. It is best to collect live bees, as diagnosis is difficult in bees that have died, especially if they have begun to decay. Keep collected bees in the freezer or in 70% alcohol until you are ready to dissect them. The dissection process involves removing the honey bee head and front two legs to expose the prothoracic trachea. You will be examining the trachea to look for the presence of 1) tracheal mites, and/or 2) scarring and discoloration that is caused by tracheal mites. Dissect around 20 different bees to test for tracheal mites. If you find 10-20% of the bees you dissect have tracheal mites, it is time to treat your colonies. ▶ ▶ Read: Treating Tracheal Mites There are several ways to treat and prevent tracheal mites infestations, such as by using resistant stock or employing chemical or non-chemical controls. Requeening with Resistant Stock Several stocks of honey bees are fairly resistant to tracheal mites, including New World Carniolans, Buckfast, and Russians. Using these stocks reduces the likelihood of a tracheal mite infestation developing in the first place. If you do experience an infestation, we recommend requeening your colony with a resistant stock after providing them with a treatment. Non-Chemical Control Using Grease Patties Grease patties can help clear tracheal mite infestations. These patties are made by mixing 1 part vegetable oil with 3 parts powdered sugar to form a patty. Mix the ingredients very well until it has the consistency of Play-Doh®. Place it in between two sheets of wax paper, flattening it to the thickness of a thin pancake about ten inches in diameter. Place the patty on the top bars of the frames over the brood nest (beneath the queen excluder, if you are using one). As the bees consume and remove the patty, they become covered in grease, masking their odors. This interferes with the mites' ability to detect young bees to infest. Eventually, the old mites die without reinfesting new bees. Caution is required with this treatment, however, because it can attract small hive beetles and other pests. Chemical Control Menthol (under the trade name Mite-A-Thol™) is currently the only registered treatment for tracheal mites. The menthol chips arrive in a mesh bag. Place the entire bag on top of the brood nest (beneath the queen excluder, if you are using one) to prevent bees from removing the individual crystals, and leave it ▶

there for a minimum of 28 days. The temperature must be between 60–80°F (15–27°C) in order for the product to be effective. Temperatures above 80°F can lead to adult and queen mortality. As the menthol evaporates, it enters the bees' tracheae and kills the mites inside. Wear protective eyewear and gloves when applying this treatment. Menthol cannot be used when honey supers are present. Honey supers can be added 30 days after the treatment ends. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Zombees: Honey Bees Parasitized by Phorid Flies From 2010 to 2016, the media was ☆ Key Points abuzz with stories on “zombees”— honey bees that left their hives at night and behaved strangely. Beekeepers and scientists wondered if this new ailment could explain Colony Collapse Disorder, a phenomenon where bees suddenly abandon their hive. As it turns out, zombees are not a major Phorid flies parasitize bees, altering their host's behavior so that they fly to light sources during night. Phorid fly parasitism is uncommon in the U.S. and is not a major concern for honey bee health. issue for North American beekeepers; nor are they behind Colony Collapse Disorder. Nonetheless, it's important to understand this parasite in case it does become widespread and to field any questions from beekeepers or the public that have seen the media stories. What Causes Honey Bees to Become Zombees? In 2010, researchers discovered that a species of fly, Apocephalus borealis, commonly called the phorid fly, was behind some odd behavior of honey bees This phorid fly is native to North America and historically parasitized only paper wasps and bumble bees. Recently, it jumped hosts and is now able to parasitize honey bees. The phorid fly is a small white fly, 2 mm in length, that resembles a fruit fly. When a phorid fly parasitizes a honey bee, it inserts its ovipositor into the bee’s abdomen and lays eggs. The eggs hatch and the larvae (maggots) crawl through the bee's body, feeding on it while the bee is still alive. Within a week, the bee dies from being consumed from the inside. After the bee dies, the larvae exit the bee's body; as many as 15 maggots can crawl out of one bee. They pupate outside of the bee's body, and adult flies emerge after 28 days, ready to mate and begin the cycle again.

Phorid fly laying eggs in honey bee Photo from: Core A, Runckel C, Ivers J, Quock C, Siapno T, et al. (2012). " A new threat to honey bees, the parasitic phorid fly Apocephalus borealis" Symptoms Before the bee dies, its behavior is changed by the parasite. The main symptom is that infested bees abandon their hives at night. These bees tend to be attracted to light and can be observed flying around streetlights and outdoor house lights, even during rain or cool temperatures when they don't normally fly. The bees become stranded at these light sources and die. Disoriented bees may also walk in circles, or be unable to stand without falling over. Because of these strange behaviors, honey bees parasitized by these flies have earned the colloquial name of “zombees.” It is still unknown why parasitized bees abandon their hives at night and are attracted to the light. It may be that this behavior benefits the phorid fly's reproduction in some manner, or it may be that abandoning the hive reduces the chances that the bees' nestmates also become infested. More research is needed to investigate this behavior.

All bees that become parasitized die, and research has found that up to 18% of foragers in a colony can be infested. However, while it can stress a colony, entire colonies rarely, if ever, die from the infestation. More research is needed to understand what role the phorid fly plays in modern day colony losses, if any. There are currently no treatments for phorid fly infestations. Documenting Incidences The scientists who first discovered the phorid fly's parasitism of honey bees in the U.S. launched a citizen science project in 2012 to document cases of infestation in North America. Sightings are entered on the website http://www.zombeewatch.org. Thanks to these reports, we now know that the fly parasitizes bees in many U.S. states and Canadian provinces along the west coast and in Northeast North America. The U.S. states include Maine, Vermont, New York, Pennsylvania, Virginia, North Carolina, South Dakota, California, Oregon, and Washington. While the fly is widespread, reported cases are very low, with just under 100 confirmed incidences in the U.S. as of June 2017. Back to Table of Contents

Tropilaelaps mites Throughout this module as well as the course, we have learned that there are several parasites that depend on honey bees to live and reproduce. Module Wrap-up: Other Honey Bee Parasites Beyond the major parasites like Varroa mites and Nosema species, we've now examined the broader range of internal and external parasites that can affect honey bees. Understanding how to identify and manage these additional threats adds another important layer to our knowledge of honey bee health management, helping beekeepers maintain stronger, healthier colonies. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Brood Diseases One fungal brood infection and two bacterial brood infections can pose a health risk to honey bees: chalkbrood, American foulbrood, and European foulbrood. These diseases infect and kill larvae and pupae, but do not impact adults. Chalkbrood is a fungal infection that can have minor to moderate implications on bee health. American foulbrood, on the other hand, is the most infectious and destructive honey bee bacterial infection. While foulbrood is arguably the oldest disease that beekeepers have been aware of, its prevention and management is changing due to new FDA regulations regarding antibiotics. In this module, we will describe these brood diseases and how to properly diagnose and manage them. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Chalkbrood Ascosphaera apis, commonly referred ☆ Key Points to as chalkbrood, is a fungal disease that infects honey bees in the larval stage. The fungus reproduces through spores, and larvae consume these spores in their brood food. The spores germinate in the hindgut of the larvae, and once the cell is capped, they become vegetative and the active infection begins with visible symptoms. Drone and worker larvae are infected more often than queens. The genus Ascosphaera contains many species of fungal diseases that infect bees. While honey bees are infected by Ascosphaera apis, other Chalkbrood is caused by the fungus Ascosphaera apis. Infected brood turns hard and white, resembling a piece of chalk. Fruiting bodies make the mummies develop brown or black coloration. Chalkbrood mummies can be observed in the brood cells, on the bottom board, or on the ground in front of the hive. Chalkbrood can be managed by requeening and ensuring colonies are strong and housed in dry hives. species of Ascosphaera can infect bumble bees, leaf cutting bees, and mason bees with chalkbrood. In honey bees, the vegetative fungus resembles very small white threads. As it overcomes the larva's body, the larva becomes covered and eventually comes to resemble a piece of chalk. Hard, white larvae in this form are called chalkbrood "mummies." After the larva dies, the fungus develops fruiting bodies that eventually produce spores to reproduce. These fruiting bodies first appear as brown or black spots on the chalkbrood mummy and eventually, the mummy turns completely black as it becomes covered in fruiting bodies. Mummies can be seen inside their cells in the brood frame. Depending on the fungus' life stage, the mummies can appear white and chalky in appearance (with or without black spots), or can be completely black and hardened. Mummies can be removed from the brood frame by tapping the frame against a solid surface. This action helps differentiate chalk brood from other brood diseases—tapping the frame does not easily dislodge brood with other types of infections. Chalkbrood mummies are often removed by the bees

through hygienic behavior and left on the bottom board, at the entrance of the hive, and/or on the ground. Like most fungi, the chalkbrood pathogen thrives in an environment that is cool and humid. Mummies are most often seen along the periphery of the brood nest where temperatures aren't as well-regulated. They are most common in spring, when brood may be exposed to cool temperatures, or in colonies with small populations that are unable to effectively maintain a warm brood nest. Moisture in the hive can also help promote the growth of chalkbrood. Honey bees can create a "social fever" in an effort to kill chalkbrood infections. They accomplish this by increasing the temperature of their brood nests by shivering their wings. Bees elevate the brood nest temperature just enough (around 0.9°F, or 0.5°C) to exceed the temperature for chalkbrood to develop, but within the normal developmental temperature window for bees. Social fevers can be initiated after symptoms have begun developing or before symptoms have started. It is still not known how bees identify larvae infected with chalkbrood.

Photo credit: All photos from Mary Kate Wheeler Preventing Chalkbrood The key to avoiding chalkbrood is to maintain strong colony populations (with sufficient bees to keep the brood nest warm) and eliminate moisture in the hive. Avoid making splits or nucs in early spring without enough bees to warm the brood nest. More generally, ensure that your hives are not in cool, damp places, and provide ventilation in the hive bodies. It is recommended that the two oldest brood combs in each hive body be rotated out each year to remove any existing fungal spores that may be present. Treating Chalkbrood Chalkbrood is not regarded as a detrimental disease to the colony as infections usually clear up in the summer as the temperature rises. It rarely impacts the queen, and nurse bees can usually prevent or control it with hygienic behavior. There are no registered treatments for chalkbrood control. If infections do not clear up on their own, requeening (ideally with hygienic stock) may help a colony clear up the infection. If more than 10–20% of brood cells on a single frame are infected, remove those frames and replace them with frames of drawn comb or foundation. Back to Table of Contents

Read: American Foulbrood: An Overview American foulbrood (AFB) is a bacterial ☆ Key Points infection caused by the bacterium Paenibacillus larvae. The bacterium has two states: the vegetative state (when it actively causes infection and reproduces) and the spore state (when American foulbrood is the most infectious bacterial disease, with spores that remain viable for over 40 years. it does not cause infection). The vegetative bacterium reproduces by creating many spores, which can be found in honey and bee bread, as well as on wax and woodenware. AFB spores under a microscope. Credit: Bee Informed Partnership To contract the infection, young larvae consume spores that are fed to them by nurse bees, which they have picked up from food or from feeding an infected larva. Worker, drone, and queen larvae are only susceptible within the first three days after they hatch from the egg. Furthermore, as larvae age, they are less susceptible to AFB. Only one spore is needed to infect a one-day-old larva, while more are needed in two-day-old larvae, and even more in three-day-old larvae. Beyond that age, larvae do not typically develop the infection, even if they consume spores. Once a spore is ingested by a larva of the right age, the bacterium becomes vegetative. After one day it begins replicating in the larva's midgut. The infection continues to multiply as the bacteria feeds off the larva.

Soon after the cell is sealed, the prepupa dies. The prepupa becomes a brown, mucouslike substance that lays flat on the bottom of the cell, eventually drying out into a black, brittle scale. The colony ultimately dies either because adults are no longer replaced or because there are too few of them to protect the colony against robbing. Spores can be present in the hive at any time of year and a colony can become infected whenever young larvae are present. Larvae laying flat in cell turning brown in color. Credit: Bee Informed Partnership What's the Big Deal? Although incidence is relatively low in New York State (less than 2% of colonies become infected each year) and elsewhere, the problem with this disease is that the bacteria remain alive in the spore state for over 40 years. The long-lived spore is resistant to changes in the weather, hot and cold temperatures, bactericides, and antibiotics. Colonies that are positively diagnosed need to be managed carefully and immediately to reduce the chances of the infection spreading. Most states in the U.S. and all provinces in Canada have inspection programs. with the top priority being to inspect for and control cases of American foulbrood. In New York State, colonies that are leaving the state for pollination, as well as packages and nucs for sale, must be certified as AFB-free before their departure or sale. These inspection programs have been very successful in reducing AFB incidence and spread for over a century.

Read: American Foulbrood Symptoms The early and late stages of a colony ☆ Key Points infection have different symptoms. In the early stages, you can expect to observe the following: The telltale symptoms of American foulbrood are coffee-colored larvae laying flat in their cells that rope Spotty brood pattern with sunken/concave or perforated cappings. when pulled. In some cases, the infection is associated with a foul odor. Caramel or coffee-colored prepupae. Prepupae laying flat on the lower cell wall with a mucous consistency. Prepupae stringing out into nearly inch-long "ropes" (2 cm) when pulled with a toothpick or small twig. (Note that prepupae in the very early stages of infection may not rope out.) If death occurs in the pupal stage, some pupae may have their tongues sticking out. Distinctive foul odor in some cases (though not all cases). The odor smells similar to old gym socks. It is worth noting that colonies can give off a foul odor in other circumstances, such as during infections of European foulbrood, during brood decay after prolonged colony death by any cause, and during the ripening of goldenrod honey. Ropy prepupa. Credit: Paul Cappy

Black scale. Note we are looking down the face of the frame, and scale is on the bottom of the cells. Credit: Paul Cappy Heavily infected colony. Credit: Bee Informed Partnership Many infected "molten" prepupae Concave, moist cappings and molten prepupaPerforated and concave cappings

Pupal tongues A lot of scale in stored comb In the late stages, usually after a colony has died or when the colony is nearing death, you can expect to observe the following: Dead prepupae become a thin, dark scale along the lower cell wall. In this stage, they are no longer "ropy." This scale does not pick out if you scrape it with a toothpick or small twig. Distinctive foul odor in some cases (though not all cases). Few adult bees present (toward the ultimate demise of the colony). Sunken cappings and black scale. Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Inspecting for an AFB Infection Three times a year, do a ☆ Key Points comprehensive inspection for AFB (spring, post honey harvest, and before wintering). This requires you to go through every brood frame in every Comprehensive inspections for AFB should occur three times a year. hive, looking for the symptoms described on the previous page. To make sure you don't miss any cells, shake the bees off the frames as you check them. Notice whether the brood pattern is solid or spotty, then carefully examine the frame to look for cappings that are concave or perforated. Anytime you see a cell like this, use your hive tool or a small twig or toothpick to open up the cell. If you see a larva or pupa that is the distinct caramel color, it's time to do a test. Even if only one cell is affected, test it. It's best if you catch the infection in an early stage. Watch as Paul Cappy, New York State apiculturist, demonstrates the proper technique to inspect frames for American foulbrood. Video Transcript When you're looking at a frame of brood to determine if you've got American foulbrood, you first pull it out of the brood nest and shake off all the bees. And then, you hold the top bar toward you and the bottom bar away from you. This gives you the correct position, since the individual cells have a slight upward slope. And so, from the top bar you can look down and look at the side, the lower side of the cells. And so, when you're holding it, you want to be able to rotate it in such a way that you will find the proper angle where you're actually looking down into the cell on the bottom side of the cell for the dead larva. It can be chalkbrood, Sacbrood, European, American, all of these, it can be any of those. And so, you practice by looking at the brood to start with. Unhealthy, but as you go along you'll start to pick up where cells haven't hatched out, they're sunken, or there seems to be something wrong, perforated, this type of thing. So, it's actually important to look and see the bad cells. And the good cells are always convex, they're oval. And the cells that will not hatch, they're usually sunken, or concave, and they're dark in color and can also be perforated. So, those are the kinds of cells that you're looking for. But it's very important to hold the frame, to get the right angle. So, you take a hold of the top bars and you rotate this around until you can see all the cells. There's about 2500 cells on the side of a comb.

So, when you're looking, you should be able to look with a quick glance across the comb and be able to pick out the cells that did not hatch. And one of the last things is that when you're trying to do this, it's nice to do it on a sunny day, so the sun can be at your back and you can then see the sun that will come over your shoulder and look down in the cell and make it shine into the cells so you can see the disease quite nicely. And the final point is, when you're looking for American foulbrood, make that the only thing you're going to do when you're going through the colony. Just concentrate on looking for American foulbrood on four to six combs. And just look at all your colonies in a bee yard, concentrating, just looking for disease. Do not look for other things just concentrate mainly on looking for the disease so that you can easily pick out the disease. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Tests to Diagnose an AFB Infection There are four tests that you can use to ☆ Key Points diagnose AFB. The two most reliable are the Vita AFB test kit and the laboratory test at the Beltsville Bee Lab. Additional tests, though less reliable, include the ropy test and the The two most reliable ways to diagnose AFB are to use the Vita test kit and to send samples to the Beltsville Bee Lab. Holst milk test. Label any colony that is suspected to have AFB so that you can easily find that colony again later, should an inspector need to visit it. The Vita AFB Test The Vita AFB test is a small kit available from bee equipment supply companies. They cost about $13 and are very convenient. The results are ready in about three minutes. At the Dyce Lab, we keep a couple of these test kits in our inspection tool box at all times. That way, if we see a suspicious brood cell we can take a sample right then and there. To use the kit, simply scoop out some of the suspicious brood and place it inside the small test tube with liquid in it. Shake the contents together and apply two or three droplets to the test kit. After two minutes, the results will be available. Watch this video to see how to use an AFB Vita test kit. Video Transcript The Vita AFB test kit is a really simple and convenient way to test whether or not your colony has American foulbrood. And it can be done right in your bee yard. Let's take a second to go through the steps of how to use this test. So, the test comes in this packaging and everything you need is inside of it. You'll see the expiration date in the bottom, left corner of the package, so make sure that you're always using a current test. When you open it up, the first thing you'll see are instructions. Make sure you read these so that you're actually following the protocol properly. Next, you'll also see the solution, which contains buffer and some of the antibodies and enzymes that are going to make this test useful. And the test kit itself is in this package, which we'll open a little bit later, once we're ready. You'll also see a plastic rod that we're going to use to extract the larvae

or pupae from their cells. And this plastic pipette that we can use to suck up some of the contents. So, we're in this colony that suspect might have American foulbrood, and we're going to remove at least one infected looking larva or pupa. And we're going to put it right in this buffer. You can extract more than one if you would like, but one is all that it takes to activate this test. You're then going to shake the contents together for at least 30 seconds. So next, we're going to open our package to reveal our test kit. And while we're doing this, we're going to allow our solution to sit for two minutes so that the chemical reaction can occur. So, inside the solution there are antibodies that are linked to enzymes. And if the antibodies bind to AFB bacteria, so if the bacteria is present in our sample, then the enzyme will give a color change. So, we're going to use the pipette to suck up some of the fluid from the bottle, and then we're going to apply two to three drops on this circle part of the test, right here. And then, it'll take about two minutes for the test to work. And, we're going to speed things up for you so you don't have to wait too long. You will start to see that this fluid moves across the test kit. So, in this example, we only see one line under the C, for control. There is no line under the T, for test. And this means that our colony does not have American foulbrood. If your colony does have American foulbrood, then you will see two lines: one under the T, and one under the C. Even if the line is very faint under the T, this is still a positive response. If your test kit shows that there are no lines, not a test line or a control line, then this means that the test was defective and you should use another one. And there you have it. That's how you use a Vita AFB test kit in your own bee yard. Ropy Test Before test kits and laboratory testing, many inspectors in the field commonly diagnosed AFB based on the ropy test. With the ropy test, a toothpick is inserted into the cell, the goopy contents are stirred in a circular motion once or twice, and then the toothpick is slowly lifted out. If the contents create a rope about an inch long, it is a positive diagnosis. This test isn't always reliable, however, as AFB larvae do not always rope out and the presence of ropiness depends on the time of the infection. Furthermore, European foulbrood (another bacterial disease) can also rope out, confounding the diagnosis between these two infections. Doing a quick ropy test and finding that the infected brood does rope out is a strong indicator of AFB, but a Vita test and/or a Beltsville Bee Lab test should always confirm it.

Beltsville Bee Lab Test Another option — if you live in the U.S. — is to send a sample to the Bee Lab in Beltsville, Maryland, where they process samples free of charge. The Beltsville Bee Lab tests for the presence of American foulbrood, as well as antibiotic resistance. It is important to determine whether any confirmed infections are resistant to traditional antibiotics. Information on how to submit a sample to the Beltsville Bee Lab can be found here. The results of the lab test are usually returned in two weeks. Because of this delay, it is best to use the Vita test kit while in the field and simultaneously take an additional sample to send to the Beltsville Bee Lab for diagnosis confirmation and resistance testing. If you have a positive result from the Vita test, you can follow the necessary procedures. The Holst Milk Test To conduct the Holst milk test, scoop out the ropy larva with a twig and place it in a plastic or glass tube or jar. If you are testing scale, rip out the entire bottom of the brood cell using tweezers and place it in the tube. Add a small amount of water, enough to generously cover the contents in the tube or jar. Next, add a few drops of milk (skim is preferred) or a pinch of 1% skim milk powder. Enough drops are needed to make the water begin to look cloudy. Swirl the contents together and let the mixture sit for 30 to 40 minutes. If the milk solution becomes translucent and yellow (similar to the color of apple juice), it indicates the presence of AFB. If the brood is infected with European foulbrood, the solution may also change color slightly but remain cloudy. The reaction can be sped up by placing the container in hot water (up to 165°F/74°C). This test is not always accurate and should be accompanied by a Vita test and/or a Beltsville Bee Lab test.
The Holst milk test for American foulbrood. The vial on the right contains AFB, while the vial on the left does not. Back to Table of Contents

Read: You Have a Positive AFB Result; Now What? If you receive a positive result with the ☆ Key Points Vita test kit or from the Beltsville Bee Lab, report your result to your state/provincial apiculturist. In New York State, it is the law to report all cases of AFB. Find out the laws surrounding AFB reporting and In New York State, all AFB-infected colonies must be reported to the state apiculturist and destroyed by burning with the oversight of a bee inspector. treatment in your state/province/country. First and foremost, disinfect your equipment and wash your hands thoroughly. Do not open up another colony until everything has been cleaned. Scrape off all traces of propolis and wax from your hive tool, scrub it with a stainless steel wool pad, and soak it in a bleach solution. After it's dried, the hive tool can also be inserted into a smoker with an open flame for further disinfection. Use bleach wipes or bleach-soaked paper towels to clean the bellows of your smoker and any other items that may have come in contact with spores. Change your clothes. Bee jackets and leather gloves can be washed in the washing machine, but if leather gloves appear to remain contaminated with wax or propolis after washing, it is safer to discard them in the trash. Any toothpicks or twigs that were in contact with the infected larvae should not be thrown on the ground. Instead, they can be placed inside the affected hive or can be disposed of in a sealed garbage bag. Place all used test kit materials and tubes in a sealed garbage bag. Once you have a positive diagnosis, do not remove the hive from the apiary. The hive is considered to be in quarantine. In New York State, the state apiculturist will send an inspector to visit your operation. If a sample has not yet been sent to the Beltsville Bee Lab, they will send one to verify the results and test for antibiotic resistance. The inspector will inspect all of the hives in the affected yard to determine the extent of the infection. He or she will ask questions to help determine where the disease originated. If, for example, the colony came from a nearby apiary or nuc producer, inspectors may visit those sites to determine whether that was the source of the infection. Though most bees forage no more than two miles from the hive, some bees may forage over an area five to

six miles or more in diameter, so tracking down a source of infection can be difficult. For this reason, we recommend keeping detailed records of where bees were purchased, which colonies came from swarms or building cut-outs, and where colonies have traveled. Beekeepers should also communicate with neighboring beekeepers to learn whether they are also monitoring their colonies for disease. Destroying Colonies In the state of New York, all confirmed colonies must be burned. Do not attempt to control the infection by discarding affected frames or treating with antibiotics—the entire colony must be burned with an inspector's oversight. The entrance to the colony is screened shut and the hive bodies stapled together to prevent bee escape. A hole is dug in the ground and the hive (including bees) are burned in it. After the burn is completed, the hole is covered up with enough dirt that an animal cannot uncover it. If the hole is in an agricultural field, the hive must be buried below plow depth. If the area is dry and fires are not permitted, the colonies can be buried deep in the ground on the beekeeper's property or in a landfill. Your county will issue a permit to bury it in a landfill. As with burning, the inspector must be present during the procedure. In some cases, the inspector may determine that not all the equipment has to be burned. Some outer covers, inner covers, and bottom boards that do not have deep cracks or rotten wood may be able to be scorched with a blowtorch and used again. Not all states and countries have the same protocol as New York. It is important to determine the protocol for your region. A hole is dug in the ground. Credit: Jon Ryan
Infected equipment is added and ignited. Credit: Jon Ryan Credit: Jon Ryan
Credit: Jon Ryan The hole is covered up. Credit: Jon Ryan Back to Table of Contents

Watch: The History of Antibiotics While you are not allowed to treat ☆ Key Points infected colonies with antibiotics, you can treat other uninfected colonies in the yard to reduce their likelihood of contracting the disease. Antibiotics can kill vegetative Paenibacillus larvae, but it cannot kill the spores. The While many beekeepers would treat colonies with antibiotics prophylactically in the past, this management practice is no longer recommended. three antibiotics available in New York are the following: Oxytetracycline hydrochloride (brand name: Terramycin) Tylosin (brand name: Tylan, Pharmasin, Tylomed-WS) Lincomycin (brand name: Lincomix) Historically, beekeepers applied these antibiotics prophylactically to their colonies in spring, fall, or sometimes both. This practice was especially common among commercial beekeepers, as a positive diagnosis prevents them from being certified to sell packages or nucs or transport their colonies out-of-state for pollination. An AFB diagnosis can translate to a considerable economic cost for some beekeepers. For this reason, beekeepers fed antibiotics to their colonies to reduce the chances of an outbreak occurring. Unfortunately, the overuse of tetracycline resulted in Paenibacillus larvae developing resistance to the drug, making it temporarily ineffective in preventing further outbreaks. It is not only that Paenibacillus larvae has developed resistance to tetracycline; many other bacteria have developed resistance to this antibiotic as well. Such antibiotics are used for honey bees as well as other livestock and humans. Consuming meat and other food products from animals, as well as coming in physical contact with animals that carry antibiotic-resistant bacteria, can cause antibiotic-resistant infections in humans. Once bacteria are resistant to a specific antibiotic, that antibiotic becomes ineffective at treating the infection. In serious cases, antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections in humans can be very difficult to control, putting a patient's life at risk and placing a considerable burden on the healthcare system. Escalating antibiotic resistance has been identified as one of the top health challenges for medicine, as two million people develop antibiotic-resistant infections and 23,000 die each year from these infections in the United States alone.

Watch this video to hear Paul Cappy discuss the history of antibiotic use and resistance in New York State. Video Transcript In 2001, after a five-year gap of no bee inspection, general bee inspection being done, New York State brought on many bee inspectors to start to look for American foulbrood. At that point, Beltsville was showing that about five percent of the cases of American foulbrood were resistant to Terramycin. And as time went on to 2005, the resistance level grew to 30 percent of the colonies were actually resistant to Terramycin. And, at this point, in December of 2005, Tylan was registered, and in 2006, the commercial beekeepers started using Tylan aggressively. And as a result, they actually reduced the number of bee yards that were positive with American foulbrood by 91 percent in 2006. Along came 2007, and the sideliners actually started to use Tylan. And it took them about two years, but they dropped the number of apiaries that had American foulbrood by 88 percent in that two-year period. So, there was a tremendous drop of American foulbrood during that period of time. In 2001, we had 8.6 percent, or over 400, cases of American foulbrood. And by 2009, we have 0.8 percent of cases of American foulbrood. And this was a substantial drop. But the drop was caused mainly by bee inspectors. But the other portion of the drop was really by having a new antibiotic, Tylan, that actually helped tremendously to lower the amount of foulbrood. And it's been a good tool in the toolbox ever since. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: New Antibiotic Regulations Because of increased resistance to ☆ Key Points oxytetracycline and other antibiotics in a range of human and livestock infections (including Paenibacillus larvae), the FDA now requires a veterinarian prescription or veterinary feed directive for antibiotics As a result of bacterial resistance to tetracycline, new FDA regulations require a veterinarian prescription or a veterinary feed directive to obtain antibiotics. administered to food-producing animals (animals that provide meat, eggs, milk, honey, etc.). Bee inspectors are not allowed to write prescriptions. There must be a confirmed case of AFB in order to acquire a prescription or veterinary feed directive. Should you need a prescription for antibiotics, the veterinarian will explain how to feed it to your bees. It is most often mixed with powdered sugar and dusted on the colony. To reduce the likelihood of residues in honey, the treatment must be applied at least four weeks before supers are added. These regulations came into effect across the entire U.S. in January 2017. If you are in the US, you can find a list of veterinarians at the Honey Bee Veterinarian Consortium website. There has been a lot of concern from the U.S. beekeeping community around this new regulation. In several discussions surrounding the new laws, beekeepers have admitted to performing desperate behaviors to continue using antibiotics prophylactically. Dangerously, some of these antibiotics being purchased are prepared for other livestock and the concentrations/doses altered for bees. These actions might buy beekeepers some time to continue treating their colonies prophylactically, but the risks of antibiotic misuse impact more than just the beekeeping industry. It impacts the quality of our food and the quality of life in other animals and humans. The best way to minimize risk and infection spread is for all beekeepers to report all infections, and for all infectious colonies to be destroyed. It needs to be a large-scale, community-wide effort to ensure AFB levels continue to be kept low. Watch this video to hear Chris Cripps, Doctor of Veterinary Medicine and owner of BetterBee Inc, discuss the new regulations in more detail.

Read: How Does Resistance Develop? Resistance occurs when the bacteria develop a mutation that permits them to escape the mechanism through which the antibiotic kills the bacteria. In a large bacterial population, there may be one or a few individuals that randomly develop this resistance, allowing them to survive in the presence of an antibiotic. The rest of the individuals that are susceptible to the antibiotic die during a regular treatment. Over time, the resistant organisms increase in population. The next time the antibiotic is applied, it might no longer work. An infection that used to be easy to control is now much more difficult. The misuse and overuse of antibiotics facilitate the development of this resistance. The illustration below depicts bacterial resistance developing in a population.

This image illustrates the process of antibiotic resistance development in bacterial populations through natural selection. Here's what it shows:Initial State: The diagram starts with a mixed population of bacteria — orange cells (susceptible to antibiotics) and blue cells (resistant to antibiotics), with the orange cells being the majority.Selection Process: When an antibiotic is applied, it kills most of the susceptible (orange) bacteria, while the resistant (blue) bacteria survive. Some susceptible bacteria may also survive if they didn't encounter the antibiotic.Population Recovery: Between antibiotic treatments, the surviving bacteria multiply and repopulate. However, since more resistant bacteria survived the previous treatment, the proportion of resistant (blue) bacteria increases in each generation.Repeated Cycles: With each subsequent antibiotic treatment, this selective pressure continues — more susceptible bacteria die while resistant bacteria survive and reproduce.End Result: After multiple rounds of antibiotic treatment and bacterial reproduction, the population becomes predominantly resistant (mostly blue bacteria), with only a few susceptible (orange) bacteria remaining.
