Read: Preventing AFB Infection in Your Colonies There are several potential ways to protect your colonies from AFB infection. Ten Tips for Preventing AFB Infection in Your Colonies Significantly reduce the risk of infection in your colonies by following these ten essential preventive measures. 1. Inspect colonies for AFB three times a year: spring, right after removing the honey crop, and prior to overwintering. 2. Do not purchase bees or equipment from companies or beekeepers without an inspection certificate. 3. Do not purchase or use someone else's old equipment. When you acquire more equipment, always buy it new or build it yourself. With spores persisting for at least 40 years, there could be a risk of introducing infectious agents to your colonies. 4. Reduce drift in your own apiaries. Robbing and drifting bees can spread infection. 5. Always do a thorough inspection of the brood nest before transferring equipment, frames, or bees among your hives. 6. Sterilize your hive tool and wash your hands in between visiting apiaries or working in an infected colony. 7. Do not bring your gloves, hive tools, or other equipment to someone else's apiary. If you must, sterilize them thoroughly after the visit. 8. Swarms and cutouts can carry AFB. When acquiring bees of unknown origin, keep them isolated from other colonies for a few months to allow the colony to rear a few cycles of brood. Use separate equipment and monitor the colony closely. 9. When possible, order hygienic stock bees. 10. Do not feed colonies honey purchased from the grocery store, as it can contain AFB spores.

A "Vaccine" for Preventing AFB Infection in Your Colonies A novel “vaccine” against American foulbrood has been developed for honey bees. Rather than functioning like vertebrate vaccines, it exploits transgenerational immune priming (TGIP): By feeding killed P. larvae bacteria to worker bees, which then feed it to the queen, immune signals or fragments get passed into eggs. The offspring thus inherit enhanced resistance to P. larvae. The USDA has granted this vaccine a conditional license in 2023, making it the first insect vaccine of its kind in the U.S. It offers a promising preventive tool, but it is not a panacea because it cannot eliminate spores, it must be carefully administered, and its efficacy is contingent on maternal health and proper beekeeping practices. Beekeepers should apply the AFB vaccine preventively, ideally in early spring or when introducing new queens, so that immune signals are transferred to developing eggs. For best results, beekeepers should pair vaccination with the apiary practices outlined above in the "Ten Tips for Preventing AFB Infection in Your Colonies." Note that this vaccine should not be used during active AFB outbreaks since the vaccine does not eliminate P. larvae spores. This means that infected colonies must still be destroyed under state regulations. It is also useless to use this vaccine late in the season (late fall/winter) since queens are not laying heavily by then, so immune priming won’t reach many offspring. Back to Table of Contents

Read: European Foulbrood Overview European foulbrood disease (EFB) is another bacterial infection that can impact the health of honey bee colonies. Like AFB, this disease is found worldwide. This infection is caused by the bacteria Melissococcus plutonius. It does not reproduce using spores and is not nearly as damaging and difficult to control as AFB, but the bacteria can reside in old combs for several years. In addition to Melissococcus plutonius, other bacteria are often present in the dead larvae, which cause them to decay, change color, and develop a pungent odor. As with AFB, young larvae become infected with EFB when nurse bees inadvertently feed the bacteria to them. The larvae must be less than two days old to be susceptible to infection. Once they consume the bacteria, it begins reproducing in their midgut and competes with the bee for food. If larvae receive adequate food, they may be able to overcome the infection. During times of the year where there may be fewer nurse bees or inadequate nutrition, EFB can be evident in a colony. In the Northeast, EFB typically strikes in late spring, when many nurse bees are recruited to foraging with the onset of a nectar flow, leaving behind fewer bees to feed the brood. EFB can also strike when there is a dearth and food sources are scarce. Colonies sometimes seem to be more susceptible to developing EFB when they are nutritionally stressed providing pollination to nutrient-poor crops; this is most commonly seen following blueberry or cranberry pollination. This observation is not always consistent, however; some studies find a correlation between pollination and EFB, while others do not. All castes can be infected with EFB. Within a few days of contracting the infection, the larvae die. Unlike the effect of AFB, they most often die before they have been capped. They become yellow or brown and their tracheal system can sometimes be seen beneath their skin. Their body may become contorted into a twisted coil. Eventually, they decay into a goopy puddle in the bottom of the cell. In this state, they sometimes rope out when pulled with a toothpick (usually shorter than an AFB rope; much less than an inch long). The dead larvae eventually dry up into a scale that can be easily removed with a toothpick and feels rubbery to the touch. Back to Table of Contents

Read: European Foulbrood Symptoms The early and late stages of a colony infection have different symptoms. In the early stages, you can expect to observe the following: ☆ Key Points The telltale symptom of European foulbrood is twisted brown larvae with visible tracheal systems. Spotty brood pattern Yellow or brown larvae, sometimes with a visible tracheal system Larvae twisted inside the brood cell Healthy-looking larvae in pools of contaminated yellow jelly European foulbrood can sometimes look similar to American foulbrood. Always test suspicious larvae to confirm the infection. Melted-looking larvae with a mucous consistency Larvae that "ropes" (strings out to a length of around half an inch [~1.5 cm] when pulled with a toothpick or small twig) In the late stages, usually after a colony has died or is nearing death, you can expect to observe the following symptoms: Larvae become a thin, dark scale along the lower cell wall. This scale can be picked out with a toothpick or small twig and is rubbery to the touch. Distinctive foul odor in some cases (but not all cases). The odor smells sour or fishy and differs depending on the bacterial community present in the decaying larvae. Few adult bees present (toward the final demise of the colony).
The top six photos show early stages of the infection: Larvae are twisted and beginning to change color, or appear wet and swollen. In some cases, there is a yellow jelly.
The middle three photos show the middle stage of the infection: Larvae have turned brown in color and have visible tracheal systems.

The bottom three photos show the advanced signs of infection: Larvae become a hardened scale at the bottom of the cell. Just before this stage, larvae may be brown and goopy and "rope out" when pulled with a toothpick. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Diagnosing and Treating EFB During your usual colony inspections, ☆ Key Points look out for any indications of disease. If you see any of the symptoms described here (especially twisted/discolored larvae or melted brown larvae), perform a test. In cases European foulbrood colonies do not require burning. Colonies can be requeened and/or treated with antibiotics. where symptoms overlap with AFB, testing is encouraged to accurately determine the bacterial species. European foulbrood infections can be reliably diagnosed two ways: The Vita EFB Test and the laboratory test at the Beltsville Bee lab. The Vita EFB Test The Vita EFB test works the same way as the Vita AFB test. This test kit costs about $13 and is very convenient to use. The results are ready in about three minutes. Test larvae that are in the early stages of infection (twisted or curled in appearance and white or only slightly changing color), as these larvae will be infected with Melissococcus plutonius and will test positive. EFB larvae that are melted or scale may not test positive for EFB with this test kit, as by this stage it mainly consists of secondary bacteria. Beltsville Bee Lab Test The second option, if you live in the US, is to send a sample to the bee lab in Beltsville, Maryland. The Beltsville Bee Lab processes samples free of charge. They test for the presence of European foulbrood, as well as antibiotic resistance. It is important to determine whether any confirmed infections are resistant to traditional antibiotics. Information on how to submit a sample to the Beltsville Bee Lab can be found here. The results of the lab test are usually returned in two weeks. Because of this delay, it is best to use the Vita test kit while in the field, and simultaneously take an additional sample to send to the Beltsville Bee Lab for diagnosis confirmation and resistance testing. If you have a positive result from the Vita test, you can follow the necessary procedures. How to Treat the Disease

In the US, European foulbrood does not need to be reported to the state apiculturist and colonies do not need to be burned. In some European countries, however, EFB colonies must be reported and destroyed. In many cases, a mild infection can clear up on its own through hygienic behavior of worker bees and adequate nutrition. To help a colony overcome a mild level of disease, the beekeeper can requeen it. For moderate to high level of infection, beekeepers can acquire antibiotic prescriptions from a veterinarian. EFB can be treated with oxytetracycline. The same measures taken to prevent and manage AFB apply to EFB. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Idiopathic Brood Disease Syndrome The foulbrood diseases and Parasitic Mite Syndrome can sometimes be confused for a different brood disease called idiopathic brood disease syndrome. This syndrome was first described in 1994 when a USDA researcher observed larvae of different ages that were sunken in the bottoms of their cells instead of healthy-looking larvae that are curled into “C” shapes and white in color. Some beekeepers refer to this syndrome as "snotty brood." The unhealthy larvae can adopt a variety of appearances: They can be white and sunken in their cells as we sometimes see with Parasitic Mite Syndrome, they can be twisted or yellow in appearance like we see with European foulbrood, or they can have a brown “molten” liquefied appearance similar to the symptoms of American foulbrood. However, laboratory tests confirm that it is not a bacterial infection and the liquefied larvae do not rope out. This brood disease is not caused by Varroa mite infestations and is present without mites. Idiopathic brood disease syndrome samples analyzed in the lab are often infected with viruses, but the viruses are not the same in every case. The prevalence of idiopathic brood disease is not currently documented in the U.S.

White circles indicate cells with idiopathic brood disease syndrome. Photo credit: Mary Kate Wheeler To date, scientists do not know what causes this disease; hence, the name “idiopathic,” which means “the underlying cause is unknown.” We do know, however, that this disease increases the likelihood that a colony dies. Colonies with idiopathic brood disease are three times more likely to die within 50 days than colonies without this syndrome. It is therefore important to use diagnostic tests on all discolored, twisted, or molten larvae to determine whether infections are bacterial. Perform a sugar shake, alcohol wash, or ether roll to determine if it is parasitic mite syndrome. Pull off infected larvae from their cells and inspect the cells for mites or guanine crystals. If neither of these tests are positive, the colony has idiopathic brood disease syndrome. Unfortunately, until more is known about this issue, no treatments or prevention strategies are available to help clear and prevent it. Back to Table of Contents

Module Wrap-up: Brood Diseases In this module, we've explored the three major brood diseases — chalkbrood, American foulbrood, and European foulbrood—and their varying impacts on colony health. From the relatively mild effects of fungal chalkbrood to the devastating consequences of American foulbrood, we now understand how to identify these diseases and implement appropriate management strategies. With recent changes in antibiotic regulations, this knowledge is particularly crucial for modern beekeepers to effectively protect their developing bees. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Bee Health—The Big Picture Through this course, we've identified and discussed various pests, parasites, and pathogens that can impact our bees. The details are important for keeping your colonies healthy—but Master Beekeepers should also be able to take a step back and look at the bigger picture. What is the broader status of honey bee health in the US? What have been the effects of Colony Collapse Disorder? How can the health of your colonies impact the broader environment? It is important to be able to differentiate among different honey bee health concerns when you read media stories and scientific papers and to be able to communicate accurate information to new beekeepers and the public. This module explores the grander scheme of honey bee health. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Honey Bee Colony Declines You have no doubt heard that honey ☆ Key Points bee colonies are in decline. Since 2010, the Bee Informed Partnership (BIP) has reported total annual losses ranging between approximately 30% and 45% of the total number of colonies in the U.S. every year. The pests and diseases covered in this course pose enormous challenges; pesticides have affected honey bees Honey bee colonies have been declining over the past decade in the U.S., Canada, and Europe. In the U.S., colony losses total 30 to 45% each year. 53 species of wild bees are also experiencing population declines in the Northeastern U.S. since the 1870s, and the quantity and quality (including diversity) of bee forage has declined in most areas of the U.S. Each of these issues, along with others, interact to threaten honey bee colonies even further. In light of these challenges, beekeeping requires Despite decreases in honey bee and several wild bee populations, the demand for crop pollination continues to grow. Multiple factors contribute to pollinator health declines. ever-more intensive management as beekeepers must purchase more nucs and packages, split more colonies, and manage smaller operations. They also have to spend more time and money monitoring and managing disease and pest pressures.

U.S. national colony losses from 2006 to 2020. In 2010, Bee Informed Partnership began collecting annual loss data (losses from April of one year to March of the next year) in addition to winter loss data. Credit: Bee Informed Partnership. Shared with permission. These stresses shape annual losses, but changes in the number of managed hives domestically and globally reflect economic factors as much as ecological ones. From year to year, colony numbers fluctuate based in part on the price of honey or the demand for wax, subsidies, and pollination contracts (particularly almonds). Competition from imported honey and cheap sugar and sugar substitutes also drive declines in the number of colonies in industrialized countries. Even social and political events shape the number of colonies: For example, the collapse of the Soviet Union halved the number of colonies in Eastern Europe in the 1990s. In short, the number of managed colonies in U.S. is largely driven by economic factors.

In 2006, Colony Collapse Disorder (CCD) made headlines in the U.S. Unfortunately, media stories have often tended to conflate CCD with colony deaths more generally and longterm trends in colony numbers, even though these are three very different things. Master Beekeepers should be sure not to make the same mistake. Today, many beekeepers are losing colonies for a variety of reasons; some relatively recent and others longstanding. More to the point, most colony losses in the U.S. and elsewhere are not attributable to CCD. Although CCD shook the industry and set into motion a great deal of research, it was a short-lived phenomenon and very few incidents have been confirmed since 2010. Wild bee species have also experienced population declines throughout North America, and by 2017 eight species of wild bees were officially listed as “endangered” under the U.S. Endangered Species Act. Of the 416 documented species of wild bees in the Northeastern U.S., 53 of them are currently experiencing population declines, and 35 of these species are now considered rare. Wild bees face some of the same pressures as honey bees as well as very different ones: Habitat loss, parasites, pathogens, and climate change are among the leading factors responsible for wild bee declines. At the same time, the number of pollinator-dependent crops planted in the U.S. is increasing. One oft-repeated concern is that food production might be impacted should there be too few bees to pollinate the flowering crops. Honey bees are the most common pollinator commercially used in agriculture, pollinating over 100 fruit, nut, and seed crops in the U.S. Indeed, in 2005, there were not enough honey bee colonies available in the U.S. to pollinate over a half-million acres of almonds, and colonies were imported from Australia to ensure that there would be a sufficient almond crop that year. But almonds are unique: In the last few decades, the number of acres of almond orchards in California has doubled and they are pollinated almost exclusively by honey bees. Almonds make up a disproportionate part of the pollination “demand,” affecting the “supply” of honey bee colonies and pollination contract prices. Most staple crops do not depend on insect pollination, but many of our favorite and most nutritious fruits, vegetables, and nuts/seeds do. In other words, concerns about “food production” must be specific about which crops are threatened or made more expensive by declines in honey bees and other pollinators, where those crops are, their degrees of dependence on insect pollination, and other details.

In 2015, to address rising annual losses of honey bee colonies and the decline of some wild pollinators in the U.S., President Barack Obama announced the development of a federal strategy to promote pollinator health. Each state was required to create an action plan to help improve the health of pollinators and reduce colony losses. Thanks to funding through these plans, in addition to other government, organization, and academic funding, pollinator health research and conservation is an active area of work in recent years. Taken together, thousands of studies have identified that there is not a single cause for pollinator health problems; instead, multiple overlapping factors interact and contribute to both honey bee and wild bee health problems. For honey bees, parasites, pathogens, pesticides, beekeeper management, climate, genetics, and nutrition all influence bee health. Beekeepers must therefore think about bees holistically and consider all levels of the honey bee system (the bee, the colony, the apiary, the operation, the beekeeper, the community, and the environment), along with all the inputs that can affect it (disease, environment, management, genetics, as well as social, physical, and financial factors). Thinking about bees in this big-picture way can help us, as Master Beekeepers, to identify and take action on many aspects of bee health, pollinator health, and the broader health of agricultural and natural ecosystems. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Colony Collapse Disorder In 2006, a phenomenon appeared in the U.S. (and later in Switzerland) that became known as Colony Collapse Disorder (CCD). Beekeepers found that their recently healthy-looking colonies had collapsed: there were little to no adult bees present, resulting in sudden colony death. These colonies did not exhibit the recognizable signs of death and instead had the following symptoms: ☆ Key Points Colony Collapse Disorder is a syndrome with specific symptoms. The term is not synonymous with the general “colony declines” that are observed each year. A single cause for CCD was never discovered. Instead, several factors likely contributed to CCD. A rapid decline in colony population, with the majority of the adult bees disappearing, leaving brood poorly attended and the queen with only a few young nurse bees Few or no dead bodies in or around the hive Sufficient stored food (honey and pollen) A lack of robbing by bees from neighboring colonies or pests such as wax moths or small hive beetles Levels of Varroa and Nosema that are below the treatment threshold

CCD was most frequently reported by migratory commercial beekeepers who wintered their colonies in warmer states, but also by some beekeepers who kept their hives stationary in one region. Beekeepers of all operation sizes were affected. These beekeepers experienced a range in losses from this mysterious phenomenon, from 30% of their colonies to over 90%. The scientific community has tried to determine what was behind this disorder, but to this day no single causal factor has been found. Over the winter of 2006–2007, 23% of beekeepers lost colonies to CCD. Those affected lost an average of 45% of their colonies. The condition was widespread, affecting beekeepers in 22 states. This syndrome was never observed in Canada or most of Europe. CCD was continuously reported from 2006 until about 2010 in the US. Today, CCD is not as prevalent, with only a few unconfirmed cases reported in the past few years. For instance, only 6% of beekeepers reported losing colonies to CCD over 2013–2014. That number is likely an overestimation, as some beekeepers may report that their colonies died from CCD if they don't know what the true cause was (and if they don't know the specific criteria for CCD diagnosis). Dr. Dennis vanEngelsdorp and his colleagues at the University of Maryland have been leaders in trying to determine the causes of CCD. In 2009, they conducted a comprehensive study examining nearly all known stress factors to honey bees for their

potential involvement in the disorder. They inspected and sampled colonies that exhibited CCD characteristics to compare to healthy colonies, looking for one or a few variables that would point to an underlying cause. In this study, they compared 61 variables, including body mass, protein content in bees (an indicator of nutritional stress), genetic origin of bees, bee body symmetry (an indicator of healthy development), brood pattern, Varroa mite levels, Nosema levels, chalkbrood, tracheal mites, virus levels, European foulbrood, and levels of a variety of pesticides (including fungicides, miticides, insecticides, and herbicides). No single factor was proven to be responsible for CCD. Instead, researchers found that colonies in the throes of CCD were less healthy overall. These colonies were more likely to 1) be infected with multiple viruses, at higher levels, and 2) be infected with both species of Nosema simultaneously. The pesticide levels in colonies with and without CCD were the same. These findings suggest that either colonies were collapsing because they were faced with several stressors, or they had compromised immune systems from some unknown, undiscovered cause, making them vulnerable to viruses and Nosema. Unlike a previous study that had found Israeli Acute Paralysis Virus (IAPV) to be present almost exclusively in CCD colonies, the vanEngelsdorp study (which sampled beekeeping operations more widely) did not find IAPV to be exclusive to CCD colonies. Instead, IAPV was present in both CCD and non-CCD colonies. At this point, the scientific community has come to the consensus that several factors likely contributed to CCD. Sudden, widespread colony losses are not uncommon throughout history. Indeed, there have been many instances of colonies collapsing for unknown reasons, many of which exhibit similar symptoms that are observed in CCD (sudden adult population loss, leaving behind a queen with some young bees, food, and brood). There have been 18 known documented cases of mysterious large-scale colony losses since 1869, with these syndromes given names like “disappearing disease,” “fall dwindle disease,” and “disappearing syndrome.” Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Colony Collapse Disorder Investigation Watch this video to hear Dr. Dennis vanEngelsdorp discuss his investigations into CCD. Video Transcript So, the story of colony collapse disorder, in its current, in the last 10 years, what we discovered. So, 10 years ago, I was state apiarist in Pennsylvania, and the largest beekeeper, who has given his permission for me to tell this story, the largest beekeeper in Pennsylvania, David Hackenburg, I'd seen him at the October state meeting, and he was bragging about how great his bees looked. They were fantastic. And then, he went down to Florida a month later, as he does all the time, he moved all his bees down there, and he went back a month later. And he describes getting out of the truck and it being dead silent. And as you know, if you're a beekeeper, one of the great joys is that big, loud buzz when you get of the truck, and that was gone. And so, he didn't really know what was going on. And so, he describes looking around and noticing just nothing was moving. Nothing was there. He got his hands and his knees, and looked in the entrance. And then, there was just nothing. There were no dead bees. Just everything had disappeared. And this was peculiar. There was honey on the colonies. And so, he knew something was different here. And so, he picked up a couple of these colonies and some that were just in the last stages of collapse. And he shipped them up to Pennsylvania, where I received some of these samples. And at the time, we didn't call it colony collapse disorder. We called it fall dwindle disease, because what we did was we looked through the literature, and we said, did this happened before? And what should we call it? And so, we sent out a report online to do that. And then it became really clear that we need to go to Florida and sample other colonies. And so, we did. We found that a lot of other operations were suffering this very strange condition. And that strange condition we define very, very carefully. We define it as the rapid loss of adult bees. And that's important. Rapid, as in, like, two weeks, that they really quickly, all the adult bees left. And we knew that this happened in Florida, because we saw big sheets of brood. And we know that they could not have laid all these eggs and maintained that brood with such a small cluster size. We also knew that if there were bees left, they were young bees, so just emerging bees from the brood, presumably, and the queen was there. There was enough honey stores in colonies that had completely collapsed. Those stores weren't getting robbed out. So, that was peculiar. Until we cracked

it open. And if we cracked it open, the next day they might get robbed out. So, there were these really clear set of characteristics that describe these dead colonies. And so, that's when we got on a conference call with a whole bunch of other people who had been sampling. And we coined this new term, colony collapse disorder. And so, we termed that to describe, very specifically, the set of symptoms, the rapid loss of adult bees, the queen is present, there were food stores, and, really importantly, the amount of the Varroa mite and Nosema in these colonies could not explain that loss. And that's an important distinction because Varroa can give you these symptoms in the late summer. If your strongest colonies, I mean it's famous, you know, the colonies that had the most honey supers you could go to, and suddenly there's no bees left. And that's Varroa mediated. You can find the Varroa in the brood capping. If you had done monitoring, you would have known it was coming. But in the case of CCD, this was not the case. Now, I do want to say that, in general, the new term, colony collapse disorder, really captured the public's imagination. And so suddenly, every dead colony was colony collapse disorder. This was never our intent when we came up with that phrase. That phrase was meant to be very specific to that case definition. But you really can't fight the media. And so, that's become, I think, a very common word to describe unusual losses. But that use of the word is not what we originally intended. Our original intent was to describe this very specific set of symptoms. What's really quite amazing about this is that if you look back in the literature, there's some evidence from 900 years in the current era. So. In Ireland, where they described something very, very similar. Just the other day, I have a friend who works at the National Agricultural Library. And he gave me an article from 1862, the South Carolina Farmer. And it talks about a symptom, and these beekeepers who describe exactly what we describe as CCD. And so, it seems like this condition has occurred for apparently thousands of years, and it pops up once in a while. And they called it different things at different times. But this symptom has, these symptoms, this group of symptoms, seems to be consistent over time. So, what's going on? Well, when we first did this study, we took all these samples, and we wanted to do descriptive study. So, wanted to describe what was happening. So, we map the yards where this were. And what we found was, that colonies that were sick were more likely to be close to sick colonies than colonies that weren't sick. Which just seems obvious if it's a contagious condition. And so, that suggests there was a contagious condition. We looked at Varroa and Nosema, and that didn't explain differences. We looked at viruses and we found that, in fact, the CCD colonies had much higher levels of

viruses than the non-CCDs. But It wasn't a consistent virus. At first, we thought it was just Israeli acute paralysis virus. But then with more analysis, and new tools, and a bigger data set, it was clear it wasn't just one virus. It was several viruses. And we think that it's actually those viral infections that caused the symptom of CCD. And bees are social organisms. And other social organisms, that means you don't look at a bee as an individual, you look at the colony as the super organism. And so, super organisms, these collective units of living things, have evolved a lot of different social ways of protecting themselves against damage. And one of those is that if individuals get sick, they let other individuals know, don't touch me, and then they fly away and leave the colony. You see this in termites, for instance. They don't find away, but what they do is they get a fungal infection, and as they walk out of their nest, they do something called the leper's walk, where they pound on the ground with a steady beat, saying don't touch me because I've got a fungal infection, and you'll get sick, too. And then they walk out of the colony and die. And so, some really good work out of North Carolina. Dr. Rueppell showed that they could imitate this altruistic suicide with pesticide exposure. And so, we think what happens is, is that, for some reason, these viruses have taken a hold in this colony, spread really rapidly. And so, all these bees are leaving collectively because they're sick and dying away from the colony, trying to prevent the colony from dying. But since everyone left at one time, the colony collapses. And so, we think that's the driver of those symptoms, is these heavy viral infections inducing this mass abandoning the colony. It's sort of a bad consequence of this behavior. So, we started seeing these symptoms first in the fall of 2006. Most of our samples got taken in California and Florida in the winter of 2007. And that's when we came up with the term, colony collapse disorder. We found it in lots of different operations. How widespread? I don't know. Because one of the things we do, of course, is survey. And ask people, did you have colonies die without bees? Now, we still see that symptom come up, and often people say, well that's CCD. But, of course, there's other symptoms involved. And so, Varroa can cause this, too. And so, it's a little bit leery just defining something CCD on that one symptom. Although that tends to be what happens. So, we think that these colonies are dying from the symptoms of these heavy viral infections. What we don't know is, why did they become so susceptible to these viruses? One possibility is that there were these lethal strains, and at that time, we did not have the technology that we could have differentiated that. The other, of course, is that they were exposed to other things that predisposed them to getting ill. And one of those is pesticides. We hear pesticides a lot. For the CCD samples we sampled in 2007, one of the clearest distinctions between sick

and healthy colonies was the healthy colonies have more pesticides, which is not a very easy data point to reconcile. But that clearly suggests that it wasn't pesticides that underlay these conditions. Also, the fact that we've seen these conditions occur in time, well before we started using pesticides, suggests it's not pesticides. And so, do we know the answer of what caused CCD? No. We think it's viral related, and we think it's just maybe a very highly virulent strain of the virus that's sort of wiping through the population and then spreading through time. I do think that that event, colony collapse disorder, even though we don't see very much of it all, I have not seen what I would say is a classic case of CCD in the last four years, and I looked. I've been looking pretty actively. Not so much this last year, but I've been looking, and we haven't seen it. But what it did highlight, I think, was the fact that we were losing a lot of colonies, year in and year out, and beekeepers weren't talking about it because they were sort of embarrassed. And we come from a time that, well, I did something wrong, and so we're not going to talk about it. I think this sort of opened that door, and it showed that colonies were dying from a whole host of factors. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Honey Bee Health in History Honey bee health has faced periodic ☆ Key Points problems, and the rates of annual losses as well as the number of colonies in the U.S. in general has risen and fallen over time. Recent honey bee colony losses are not unique in history. There have been several periods in the past where large-scale losses were Between April 2016 and March 2017, a observed. third of the colonies in the U.S. perished, according to the Bee Informed Partnership, the gold standard for measuring honey bee Honey bee colony numbers are influenced by economic, social, and environmental factors. colony numbers in the US. This is worrying, although it represents a slight improvement from recent years, where as many as 45% of colonies perished. More importantly, the BIP survey is a relatively recent snapshot. Information on annual losses has only been collected for seven years—before 2010–11, the surveys only covered winter losses, and before 2006–07, there were no national loss surveys at all. And some practices have changed dramatically in the last century, making comparisons unreliable. For instance, before the advent of modern beekeeping and the Langstroth hive, some beekeepers killed their strongest and weakest hives to harvest the honey. The logic was that the strongest hives usually had the most honey and that the weakest were least likely to survive the winter anyway. This makes winter loss rates seem as though they used to be much lower, when, in fact, beekeepers used to simply “take their losses” earlier, although we don't know how much this affects the numbers. In short, it is difficult, if not impossible, to make meaningful comparisons to past honey bee colony losses since methods for gathering data, counting losses, harvesting honey, and other indicators have changed over time. Lessons from the long-term trends in the number of colonies across the U.S. are also limited. The number of honey bee colonies has been monitored by the National Agriculture Statistics Service since the 1940s; earlier records are just estimates based on historical data about honey production. These statistics tell us that the number of honey bee colonies has been declining for the past 70 years: in 1947, there were 5.5 million colonies, and by 2006, there were 2.4 million—a 56% reduction. But these declines need to

▶ be understood in their economic and historical context: most colonies in the U.S. are managed as livestock and are not wild creatures. And the number of colonies today is similar to the number (estimated) a century ago; the figure from 1947 is the high point, as World War II made beekeeping more profitable and popular. A historical perspective is therefore helpful. Here, we describe some of the factors that have affected honey bee health historically or that continue to shape colony numbers in the US. Foulbrood In the late 1800s and early 1900s, a scourge of foulbrood spread across the US, seriously depressing honey production for decades (vanEngelsdorp and Meixner, 2010). The science was still being worked out: American and European foulbrood were often conflated well into the 1900s, and for a while, foulbrood was known as “New York bee disease,” to the consternation of beekeepers in the Empire State (White, 1906). Ironically, disease was spread further with the adoption of modern equipment and related practices (e.g., re-using comb in movable frame hives, year after year), as well as the growth of the industry. Efforts to prevent and treat foulbrood gave rise to new laws requiring the destruction of infected colonies, government inspection programs, and education through extension programs, which together have made foulbrood a more minor concern today. ­Beekeeping in WWI and WWII: During both world wars (1910s and 1940s), the rationing of sugar, the jump in prices of sweeteners, and the many uses of wax pushed honey prices up, making the number of beekeepers and honey bee colonies in the U.S. soar. Indeed, there were approximately 6 million colonies in the U.S. immediately following WWII, which is still the highest number of colonies ever in U.S. history. While the landscape (both agricultural and urban) was different then, these numbers are also a helpful reminder that changes in the number of honey bee colonies upward or downward generally reflect economic factors as much as or more than ecological ones. In other words,

▶ ▶ markets drive the number of honey bee colonies as much as disease, or pest pressures, or forage availability. Isle of Wight Disease In the early 1900s, bees in England perished in large numbers. The malady was traced back to, or at least named for, the Isle of Wight (an island south of England, in the English Channel), where 90% of the honey bees died, in three separate years. To this day, there is no complete agreement on the cause: the deaths are generally attributed to tracheal mites, but it has also been suggested that Nosema apis was at fault, or simply overcrowding and beekeeper mismanagement that led to starvation. Pesticides Today, there is much discussion about the insidious, chronic, and sublethal effects of new classes of pesticides. Pesticides have caused problems for honey bees since the 1870s (Johansen and Mayer, 1990), when arsenical sprays on fruit trees led to many losses. In the 1920s, aerial spraying of cotton fields killed many bees as well. In the 1950s, the insecticide Sevin was discovered to have the ability to damage colonies even one season after it was applied if it contaminated stored pollen. In 1967, it is estimated that half a million colonies were poisoned by pesticides, a significant fraction of the total number in the U.S. (Johansen and Mayer, 1990). Today, newer generations of pesticides can be used at lower dosages, and there are increasingly stringent rules about their application. However, there is still much to be learned about their possible effects on pollinators, including synergies between different agricultural inputs, particularly those initially thought to be harmless to bees (e.g., fungicides and adjuvants).

▶ Environmental Factors The quality and quantity of good bee pasture available in the U.S. has declined over the last several decades because of more intensive agriculture. This has included less cover cropping, a reduction in forage in field margins and in understories, and regional changes in agriculture (e.g., the loss of alfalfa in New York State as the dairy industry has declined). Depending on the habitat surrounding colonies and the amount of competition in the area, bees may be at a higher risk of malnutrition and may require more intensive feeding. Ironically, some invasive species such as purple loosestrife and Japanese knotweed have been a boon to honey bees, making environmental conservation programs to eradicate them less straightforward! Finally, while the effects are so far limited, climate change may soon begin to impact honey bees (it is currently only documented to affect bumble bees). Indirectly, honey bees will be most affected by changes in forage. The flowering of plants is affected generally by water availability, temperature, and photoperiod. In the Northeast, nights and days will both likely be warmer, with more frost-free days, and the weather wetter, so the spring greening will probably come earlier, with mixed effects for honey bees. Social and Economic Factors The profitability of beekeeping wanes and waxes based on many factors, including the price of honey, pollination contracts, and the cost of treatments for various pests and diseases. These factors contribute to the total number of hives in the U.S. or specific regions. Shifts in international trade in bees and the movement of bees within countries have contributed to the genetic diversity of honey bees in the US, but also inadvertently introduced and spread pests and pathogens. More broadly, major political events and social change can affect the beekeeping industry. For instance, in ▶
the early 1990s in Europe, the number of colonies declined quickly, largely due to the collapse of the Soviet Union. Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership Back to Table of Contents

Read: Tying It All Together As the primary caretaker of our colonies, we also serve as the "primary care physician" to our bees. We look for signs of unhealthy colonies, identify the set of symptoms we see, interpret those symptoms, and diagnose a problem. From there, we weigh our management options on how to restore the colony back to health, then choose the best option for the situation. ☆ Key Points Performing colony inspections, monitoring, and communicating with other beekeepers can increase your opportunity to identify issues along with your confidence to diagnose them. Follow a systematic routine for identifying abnormalities in your colonies. In this course, we presented you with different pests, parasites, and pathogens that can impact bee health. There's a lot of information to navigate: Some ailments impact adult bees, Refer to the symptom chart to help diagnose diseases. When in doubt, send a sample to the Beltsville Bee Lab or reach out to your local extension associate. while some impact brood; some are more common in the spring, while others are more common in summer and autumn; and sometimes colonies are afflicted with more than one ailment at once, as fighting one infection may make a colony more susceptible to developing another. Perhaps the most difficult aspect of diagnosing bee diseases is that many of the symptoms overlap or seem vague (spotty brood, K-wing, etc.). Diseases appear different in different cases. The photographs here may not look identical to what you're seeing in your own colonies. All of this taken together can make it difficult to feel confident in a diagnosis and choose a treatment option. To gain more experience and confidence in diagnosing bee diseases, be sure to perform regular colony inspections. If you have friends in your bee club that are experiencing issues, ask if you can observe them (but remember the guidelines about using your equipment, such as hive tools, in other bee yards). Attend workshops, conferences, and meetings that allow you to observe more case studies in specific diseases. The more

exposure you have in observing honey bee diseases, the better you will recognize them in your own colonies. Make time to inspect your colonies every 10 to 14 days. Observe the outside and entrance of the hive for dead, disoriented, or twitching bees. When you examine the brood nest, look at three or four frames of brood to get an idea of what's going on in the colony. Keep your eye out for common symptoms such as reduced adult population, spotty brood pattern, supersedure cells, and perforations in capped brood. These symptoms are common for a variety of diseases; if you observe any of these symptoms, a closer look is warranted. Carefully examine the brood cells. Look for discolored brood and larvae that aren't in the normal “C” shape. If you see perforated cappings, open them with your hive tool and examine the larvae or pupae inside. Take a look more broadly at the adults on the frame. How does the population size seem? Is it normal for that time of year? Do you see any adult bees with deformed wings, hairless bodies, or K-wing? In addition to these regular, brief colony inspections, make time in your beekeeping schedule to perform routine monitoring for the most common and most serious diseases. Monitor for Varroa mites once a month from March to October. Monitor for Nosema when you see symptoms by sending in a free sample to Beltsville or doing a spore count under a microscope. Monitor for American foulbrood three times a year (spring, post honey harvest, and pre-wintering) by looking for symptoms on every frame in the brood nest. Take advantage of tools and resources that help take the guesswork out of diagnosing diseases. The Beltsville Bee Lab provides free diagnostic services for Nosema, tracheal

mites, chalkbrood, European foulbrood, American foulbrood, and small hive beetles. In addition, you can purchase Vita test kits for AFB and EFB for quick and convenient results. Regular inspections, scheduled monitoring, and incorporation of diagnostic tools give you the best chance at finding and addressing diseases early. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Pathogen Spillover to Wild Bees Throughout this course, we've ☆ Key Points mentioned pathogens and parasites that are shared between honey bees and wild bees, such as Nosema ceranae, deformed wing virus, black Some parasites and viruses are shared among different bee species. queen cell virus, acute bee paralysis virus, sacbrood virus, and slow bee paralysis virus. Because these pathogens share some bee hosts, there is the possibility for the transmission from sick honey bees to healthy wild bees. Pathogen spillover refers to the transmission of pathogens from a reservoir population (with high infection prevalence) to a new host population. In this module, we are referring to pathogens spilling over from infected honey bee colonies to wild bee populations, and vice versa. Research has shown that honey bees can and do spread infections to the broader pollinator community. One study tested honey bees and bumble bees for disease across Great Britain and found that the prevalence of honey bee deformed wing virus and Nosema ceranae was strongly linked to the prevalence of these infections in bumble bees: Areas with many infected honey bees also contain many infected bumble bees. Infection rates were higher in honey bees, suggesting that these pathogens are “spilling over” from the honey bee population to the wild bee population. Another study from Vermont in 2019 found DWV and BQCV infections were more prevalent in bumble bees that were caught near apiaries. When honey bees in the area had high infection levels, so did nearby bumble bees. And when there were no apiaries near bumble bee communities, there were no DWV infections in bumble bees. These findings are a staggering reminder of the importance of being responsible beekeepers by maintaining healthy honey bees.

Watch: How Do Wild Bees Catch These Infections? Honey bees are kept in nearly every ☆ Key Points country that is inhabited by humans, with numerous colonies distributed throughout the landscape. They are transported to a variety of agricultural areas for crop pollination and they are also scattered in natural and urban settings as backyard beekeeping continues to increase in popularity. As viruses and Nosema are so prevalent in honey bees, and honey bee colonies Honey bees can spread diseases to wild bees by visiting the same flowers and sharing other resources. As stewards of the environment, it is critical that beekeepers maintain healthy honey bee colonies to protect wild bee communities. are so numerous and widely distributed, the risk of pathogen transmission to wild bee communities can be quite high. Many of these pathogens are picked up from flowers. Honey bees, bumble bees, and many other wild bees are generalist pollinators, meaning they collect food from many different types of flowers. Unfortunately, it also means they can deposit and pick up pathogens from a variety of flowers. Pathogens can be deposited and collected from contaminated nectar and pollen, and they can also be deposited through infected feces on plants. Simply put, if an infected honey bee visits a flower and inadvertently deposits pathogens on that flower, the next wild bee that visits may pick up that pathogen and become infected. Watch this video to hear Dr. Scott McArt, Professor of Pollinator Health at Cornell University, discuss pathogen spillover between wild and managed bees. Video Transcript So, a lot of pathogens that you have learned about in this course are not specific to honey bees. So, those pathogens can infect multiple bee species, or at least be present in multiple bee species. Sometimes we find that these pathogens, such as Nosema ceranae, can actually cause active infections in wild bee species. Other times, we find that there are bits of DNA of the Nosema ceranae in these wild bee species, but they're not necessarily causing an active infection. As you well know from 416 species here in New York of wild

bees and about 20,000 species worldwide, it's not always going to be the case that every single one of those species is going to develop an active infection from a pathogen from honey bees. But some of those bee species will develop an active infection and have negative consequences as a result of that. So we're finding out more, this is definitely an emerging field. We're finding out more and more about what types of pathogens are present in different bee species on an ecological time scale, and which pathogens are actually having a negative impact. So, it's not just, that the pathogen was found, a little bit of DNA was found, but it's actually is causing an active infection and negative impacts on bees. So, some of our current research is actually looking into the transmission biology of these pathogens. So, any time we talk about potential for parasite spillover from managed bees into wild bees, or either just transmission from wild bee to wild bee, or managed bee to managed bee, the key to controlling these, these types of interactions and trying to limit parasite spread, is understanding how transmission is actually taking place. And there's been an assumption in the literature for probably the last five or ten years or so, that transmission has been taking place at flowers. But this was largely untested up until just a year or two ago. So now, there is one study out by Pete Graystock, who is a post-doc in our lab here at Cornell, actually showing in a flight cage that particles of both know Nosema ceranae and Nosema bombi can actually be transmitted in flowers between honey bees and wild species of bumblebees, and that those can lead to active infections once they are transmitted at flowers. One of the more surprising results that we found scientifically in the past five or ten years or so, has been a surprising level of bee pathogens that we have found on flowers. So, in about 36 percent of the 200 flowers or so that we have screened for honey bee pathogens, we found detectable levels of those pathogens. So, about a third of flowers that we have screened actually have detectable levels of pathogens on them. Now, this is significant in the amount of pathogen that we're finding, the prevalence of pathogens on flowers, but it should be noted that we don't know whether those levels are actually at sufficient quantities to be causing transmission and active infections in bees. We are currently following up with many studies as you might suspect, to try and understand what predicts a transmission event. What level is actually required on flowers to result in an active infection and a bee that has this pathogen transmitted to it. That said, it's sort of staggering to me that a third of flowers out there actually do have detectable levels of bee pathogens on them.

So, as a bee interacts with a flower, it is obviously interacting quite a bit with the anthers, where it's trying to grab pollen, and also the nectary to try and grab nectar. As it's doing so, it's rubbing itself on various parts of the flowers. So, transmission could be taking place if the bee actually has pathogen particles on the surface of its body. So, just simple contact with the body surface of those bees on the flower could be transmitting pathogens. The other main venue that people have really looked into is fecal-oral contact. So, if a bee is defecating on the flowers, Nosema particles, in particular, could be being deposited on the flower surface. As the bee is lapping up nectar, or lapping up pollen, it is potentially coming into contact with some of those fecally transmitted diseases via that oral contact as well. So what you can see here is the common eastern bumblebee. So, this is Bombus impatiens, our most abundant wild bee here in New York. It's interacting with a lot of different golden rod flowers right here. And what we found is on this particular species, here's a honey bee right here, actually, interacting on another part of this flower. But what we found with, here in New York, is this particular species, Solidago altissima, what we found is that the vast majority of these flowers on Solidago have detectable levels of honey bee pathogens on them, some of which are known to be transmitted to this particular bee species, Bombus impatiens. So, one of our best studies that exists to date on the question of whether management practices and managed honey bees can be having impacts on wild bee species comes out of the United Kingdom. Where last year, so in 2016, a study was published in Nature, showing that honey bee viruses, in particular, deformed winged virus, is shared among wild bumblebee species and managed honey bees. And what they found is that, in those, in the places with a large proportion of managed honey bees and potentially bees that were not necessarily being controlled very well for Varroa, and therefore have large quantities of deformed wing virus, there was a higher proportion of bumblebees. And this was across three different bumblebee species that had higher levels of deformed wing virus. They took those results into the lab and actually did bioassays with those bumblebee species and those particular strains of deformed wing virus, and they showed that, lo and behold, that particular strain was highly virulent in those bumblebee species and caused accelerated mortality. So that, in combination with what we know about bumblebee species declining globally, I would say, is two independent data sets suggesting that viruses and other pathogens can be having impacts on bumblebee species, and here's one case example where we actually

showed a bit of cause and effect. Whether that can be extrapolated to all the other declines that might be occurring for bumblebee species, most likely not. But it would be surprising to me if that was the only isolated incident where pathogen spillover from managed honey bees to wild bees was actually having an impact on those wild bees. As someone who's keeping managed bees, just as someone who is actually keeping any managed animals, such as cows, or pigs, or anything else, the best thing that we can do to protect our wild bees is to keep healthy managed bees. So this involves actively looking for Nosema infections and treating if you do have large problems with Nosema. And probably the biggest thing you can do, and the simplest thing you can do, is what most beekeepers are concerned about, and that is Varroa management. So, as you know Varroa transmits many of the viruses, such as deformed wing virus and other virus such as Kashmir bee virus, Israeli Acute Paralysis Virus, slow bee paralysis virus, lots of different viruses. Nosema ceranae, especially, and also those viruses are known to be prevalent and causing active infections in many of the wild bee species that we look for. So, simply managing and keeping, managing for those diseases or parasites and keeping your bees healthy can potentially really help wild bees out there, in terms of minimizing pathogen spillover from your managed bees into wild bees communities. As stewards of the environment, it is critical that beekeepers actively maintain healthy honey bee colonies. It's worth remembering that if wild bee colonies become sick, they cannot receive any treatment to help them. On the other hand, beekeepers can intervene to help sick honey bee colonies. They can control Varroa mites with a variety of chemical and cultural methods to reduce viruses. They can supplement colony nutrition and requeen colonies that are struggling. And if colonies do die from disease, beekeepers can purchase more packages and nucs to replenish their stocks. Wild bees do not have these same opportunities. If they are sick, no one provides them with treatments. If they die, their populations are not replaced. Many species of wild bees are already facing declines from challenges including diseases, pesticides, climate change, and nutrition. It is our responsibility to avoid contributing additional challenges. Keeping our honey bees healthy can help ensure we are keeping our surrounding pollinator population healthy. Assignment: Course Project — Fighting the Mite in Bee Yards Throughout this course, we've explored a variety of pests, parasites, and pathogens that impact honey bee health. Of them, Varroa mites are currently the biggest challenge to the beekeeping industry. We examined the many genetic, cultural, and chemical management practices that help maintain low mite levels, and during our Varroa module discussion, you had the opportunity to read other students' views on what works and doesn't work for them. In this project, you will complete two activities related to Varroa mites. The first activity is for you to design your own mite management plan to use during the upcoming beekeeping season. The second activity is a scenario-based question that will help you prepare for your role as a Master Beekeeper. You will be invited to put yourself into the mindset of a consultant who provides advice to a "client," meaning another beekeeper who will most likely have a beekeeping operation that is VERY different from yours. Glossary Master Beekeeping Part III: Managing Pests and Diseases College of Agricultural Life and Sciences, Cornell University abdomen The abdomen is one of three main body segments of insects (which also include the head and thorax). The abdomen contains the digestive and reproductive systems. absconding Absconding is the act of an entire honey bee colony leaving the nest or hive entirely. If disease or pest levels are too high, bees may leave their current location and search out another one. This can also be triggered by hive damage, repeated bear attacks, or other environmental problems. Acarine disease Acarine disease is the name of the condition given to a honey bee colony that is highly infested with tracheal mites. active (vegetative) infection A period in an infection’s life cycle where it is proliferating. Symptoms can be present when infections are active. adaptive immunity Adaptive immunity includes the immune responses that are “learned” over time with exposure to different pathogens. The production of antibodies to respond to previouslyencountered bacteria is one function of adaptive immunity. Africanized honey bee The Africanized honey bee, colloquially called the killer bee, is a hybrid of Apis mellifera scutellata (A), and Apis mellifera mellifera (M). These bees are known for their aggressive nature and sustained defense of their hives. afterswarm An afterswarm is a second, smaller swarm that can occur a few days following a colony’s first swarm. allogrooming Allogrooming is the social behavior whereby one bee grooms another bee. . Master Beekeeping Part III: Managing Pests and Diseases College of Agricultural Life and Sciences, Cornell University altruism Altruism, biologically speaking, is animal behavior that benefits another animal at the expense of the first, in terms of survival or reproduction. Worker bees forgoing their own reproduction in order to help the queen reproduce is one of the most extreme examples of altruism in nature. See kin selection. American foulbrood American foulbrood is a highly infectious bacterial infection caused by the bacterium Paenibacillus larvae. It only infects brood. amino acid Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. They are a necessary part of bees’ (and humans’) diets, necessary to function and develop. Pollen is the source of amino acids in bee bread and royal jelly. anaphylactic shock Anaphylactic shock is an extreme, life-threatening allergic reaction. anther The anther is the part of a flower that contains pollen. apiary An apiary is a collection of one or more hives, also called a bee yard. Most backyard beekeepers have only one apiary, but commercial beekeepers may manage dozens. Apidae Apidae is a family classification of bees. It is the largest family of bees and includes honey bees, bumble bees, carpenter bees, and many others. Apis Apis is a genus classification of bees. It includes all bees that produce and store honey. Apis mellifera Apis mellifera is the scientific name for the Western honey bee. Apis is the genus and mellifera is the species. Mellifera means “bearer or maker of honey” (melli means “honey” and fera means “bearer”). arthropods (Arthropoda) Arthropoda is one of the many phyla of the animal kingdom. Honey bees are in the phylum Arthropoda, and are therefore known as arthropods. All arthropods are invertebrates and have jointed bodies and paired jointed appendages. . All rights reserved. All other copyrights, trademarks, trade names, and logos are the sole property of their respective owners.

Master Beekeeping Part III: Managing Pests and Diseases College of Agricultural Life and Sciences, Cornell University artificial queen insemination (also known as instrumental insemination) Artificial queen insemination is a method of controlled mating where semen from a drone is used to inseminate a queen. assessment See colony assessment. asymptomatic A disease that does not show any symptoms. autogrooming Autogrooming is the behavior of a bee grooming itself. bait hive A bait hive is a hive body or other box used to catch swarms. bee bread Bee bread is pollen that has been moistened by honey and honey bee glandular secretions and fermented by microorganisms such as yeast, bacteria, and fungi. Pollen in the form of bee bread is honey bees’ major source of protein, fats, and vitamins, and is an important nutrient source for the development of brood. bee space Bee space is 3/8”, which leaves enough room for bees to pass one another on opposite combs. If the space between combs is less than 3/8”, bees will likely fill it with propolis. It if is greater than 3/8”, the bees will tend to build burr comb to fill the space. bee yard See apiary. beeswax See wax. biosecurity Biosecurity is the procedures and management practices one can take to reduce the spread of pests and pathogens. brood Brood is the name given to the egg, larvae, and pupae stages of insects. . Master Beekeeping Part III: Managing Pests and Diseases College of Agricultural Life and Sciences, Cornell University brood nest The brood nest is the part of the hive where the brood is developing, distinct from the area where honey is being processed and stored. Conditions such as temperature are more important here for the healthy development of brood. brood pheromone Brood pheromone is released by larvae and indicates its sex, caste, and age. It influences development and behavior of other bees, most notably by inhibiting the development of ovaries in workers. burr comb Burr comb is comb built anywhere the beekeeper doesn’t want it, namely between frames or hive bodies. It is likely to be built in spaces with dimensions that exceed the width of bee space. candy board A candy board is a piece of hive equipment used to supplement carbohydrates to honey bee colonies during the winter. They resemble an inner cover filled with a solid candy made of sugar and water. carbohydrate Carbohydrates are the sugars in food that are a source of energy for organisms. Honey bees acquire their carbohydrates from nectar, honey, or sugar syrups. cast swarm See afterswarm. caste A caste is one form within a species that may differ from other forms in terms of anatomy, physiology, and reproduction. The three honey bee castes are queens, workers, and drones. cell builder A cell builder is a colony used to rear queens. Cell builders can be either "cell starters" or "cell finishers." A cell builder consists of a strong population with many nurse bees, pollen, and honey or sugar syrup, and can be queenright or queenless. cell finisher A cell finisher is the cell building colony used to finish queen cells when rearing queens. Nurses in the finisher colony continue to provision the queen cells with royal jelly and complete the construction of the queen cell. . All rights reserved. All other copyrights, trademarks, trade names, and logos are the sole property of their respective owners.

Master Beekeeping Part III: Managing Pests and Diseases College of Agricultural Life and Sciences, Cornell University cell starter A cell starter is the cell building colony used to start queen cells when rearing queens. Nurses in the starter colony provision the queen cells with ample royal jelly and begin building out the cell with wax. chalkbrood Chalkbrood is an infection in honey bee brood caused by the fungus Ascosphaera apis. It can affect both sealed and unsealed brood. Affected larvae often take the appearance of small white pieces of chalk and, in this stage, are referred to as "chalkbrood mummies." checkerboarding Checkerboarding is the practice of alternating frames of drawn comb with frames that are already filled in the broodnest. This provides the colony more space to fill with brood and resources and, as a result, can help prevent swarming. chromosome Chromosomes are the structures containing an organism’s genetic material in the form of DNA. class Class is a rank in the classification of life, below phylum and above order. Honey bees are members of the class Insecta (insects). cleansing flights A cleansing flight is the delicate name given to the act of leaving the hive to defecate. Bees can delay defecation for months during winter, but will leave the hive on a warm day to void their waste. Fecal staining may be evident around or on the outside of hives in winter and early spring. cluster (also winter cluster) Clustering is a thermoregulatory behavior where bees congregate on the comb to keep warm when environmental temperatures are below 64°F. Colony functions such as foraging and water collection cease when bees are clustering. cocoon A cocoon is a silky pupal casing spun by insect larvae to protect them during their pupal stage. .
