Glossary Accounts Receivable. Amounts owed to a business by its customers for products and services already delivered. In other words, outstanding invoices. Considered a current asset on the balance sheet. Accrual Accounting. An accounting method that records revenues when goods and services are produced, and expenses when production costs are incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands. Accrual Adjustments. Accounting adjustments made at the end of a financial period to go from cash accounting to accrual accounting. Accumulated Depreciation. The total depreciation expense associated with a noncurrent asset. Equivalent to the annual depreciation expense multiplied by the number of years the asset has been in service. Asset. A productive resource with economic value that a business owns and uses to generate income. Balance Sheet. A financial statement that reports business assets, liabilities, and net worth at a specific moment in time. Also called a Net Worth Statement. Book Value. The value of an asset on the balance sheet, calculated by subtracting accumulated depreciation from the original cost. Cash Accounting. An accounting method that records business transactions when cash changes hands, regardless of when the revenues and expenses were incurred. Current Assets. Cash and all other assets that a business expects to convert to cash or use up in normal business operations within 12 months. Current Liabilities. Financial obligations that must be paid within 12 months. This includes the portion of noncurrent liabilities due within 12 months. Depreciation. The reduction in value of a long-term business asset over time as it is used in normal business operations. Equipment. Tangible assets that a business uses over multiple years to produce goods or services. Examples include tools, machines, hive woodenware, vehicles, and electronic devices. Equity. The value of an ownership claim to a business. Owner equity is synonymous with net worth, and refers to the value of the owner(s)'s stake in a business. Expenses. The costs of producing and selling goods and services. Fair Market Value. The price that an asset would be expected to fetch in the marketplace, given a reasonably interested buyer and seller. Fixed Asset. A tangible asset that has an expected useful life greater than one year, and is not easily converted into cash. Sometimes called property, plant and equipment (PP&E). Income Statement. A financial statement that reports the total value of farm production, the total cost of production, and net farm income over a specified period of time. Also called a Profit and Loss Statement. Intangible Asset. A business asset that does not have physical form. Common examples include intellectual property (patents, trademarks) and public opinion (brand loyalty, goodwill). 4

Glossary (continued) Inventory. A systematic list of all the productive resources that a business owns and uses to generate income. Also refers to the process of creating such a list. Liability. A financial obligation that must be met in the future through the transfer of cash, goods, or services. Liquidity. A measure of the extent to which a business has cash on hand, or other assets that can be quickly converted to cash, in order to meet immediate and short-term financial obligations without disrupting normal business operations. Machinery. Tangible assets made up of multiple parts that use mechanical energy to produce goods or services. A subcategory of equipment. Examples include honey extractors and vehicles. Net Farm Income from Operations (NFIFO). Another name for farm profit, defined as the total value of farm production for a given year minus the total cost of production in that year. Net Worth. The difference between total assets and total liabilities equals net worth. Net worth is synonymous with owner equity, and reflects the value of the owner(s)'s stake in a business. Net Worth Statement. A financial statement that reports business assets, liabilities, and net worth at a specific moment in time. Also called a Balance Sheet. Noncurrent Asset. Any asset that has an expected useful life greater than one year. Noncurrent Liability. Any financial obligation due beyond the next 12 months. Prepaid Expense. A future expense that has been paid in advance. Common examples include insurance premiums and some taxes. Considered a current asset on the balance sheet. Profit. Farm profit is defined as the total value of farm production less the total cost of production over a specified period of time. Synonymous with Net Farm Income from Operations (NFIFO). Profit and Loss Statement. A financial statement that reports the total value of farm production, the total cost of production, and net farm income over a specified period of time. Also called an Income Statement. Real Estate Improvement. A building or other infrastructure development that is permanent in nature and adds value to the property. Examples include buildings, roads, and permanent fencing. Revenue. Income from selling goods and services. Solvency. A measure of the extent to which a business would be able to pay all of its financial obligations if it were to close and sell off all of its assets. Supplies. Items that a business consumes in the production of goods or services. Considered a current asset on the balance sheet. Tangible Asset. An asset that has physical form. Examples include both current assets (supplies, products) and noncurrent assets (equipment, buildings, land). 5

Inventory of Supplies Supplies are items that a business consumes in the production of goods or services. Supplies are different from equipment, in that supplies are consumable goods that become incorporated into the finished product. In other words, a business uses equipment, but it uses up supplies. This section divides supplies into three different categories that are common to beekeeping businesses. Beekeeping supplies (page 12). This worksheet records the value of supplies that beekeepers use to raise and maintain honey bee colonies. Feed (sugar, protein, supplements), medications (mite treatments, antibiotics), and other consumable supplies (smoker fuel, American Foulbrood test kits) should be listed in this category. Hive equipment (boxes, frames, foundation, feeders) or tools intended for use over multiple years should NOT be listed in this section (see page 22). If your operation stores gasoline, diesel fuel, or any supplies for vehicle maintenance, those items may also be listed here. Supplies for making nucs and queens (page 13). This worksheet records the value of supplies used to make nucleus colonies or queens for sale to other beekeepers. This includes boxes, frames, and foundation used to assemble nucs. Inventory of Accounts Receivable and Prepaid Expenses This section records the value of all accounts receivable and prepaid expenses. Accounts receivable refers to money that customers owe to a business for products or services that the customers have received. Accounts receivable can be thought of as outstanding invoices. Take the example of a beekeeping business that delivers ten barrels of honey to a wholesale client. Payment is not collected upon delivery, so the beekeeper invoices the client. From the moment the honey is delivered to the client, until the moment that payment is received, the value of that transaction is recorded under accounts receivable. Prepaid expenses refer to money that a business has paid for products or services that it will use at a later date. Prepaid expenses can be thought of as future business expenses that have been paid in advance. Common examples include insurance premiums and estimated taxes. When a business pays for an insurance policy before the insurance coverage begins, that payment constitutes a prepaid expense. Similarly, if a business makes quarterly payments of estimated taxes, those payments are made in advance of the actual tax liability and are therefore considered prepaid expenses. Farmers’ market booth fees are a prepaid expense if they are paid before the market season begins. Accounts receivable and prepaid expenses are considered to be business assets. As such, they are must be included in the annual inventory. The change in accounts receivable and prepaid expenses between the start and end of the year will be important for calculating business profit at the end of the financial cycle. Inventory of Equipment and Machinery This section records the value of all equipment, machinery, and vehicles owned and used by your business. These items are considered to be durable goods, and must therefore have a useful lifespan of more than one year. Hive equipment (page 24). The first worksheet in this section records the value of hive equipment, which includes all of the components that make up your permanent hives: hive bodies, inner and outer covers, bottom boards, queen excluders, frames, foundation, feeders, etc. You may include boxes and frames used in mating nucs, or for nucs that serve as replacement colonies. Do NOT list boxes, frames, or foundation used to make up nucleus colonies for sale - these items should be listed under the Inventory of Supplies for Producing Queens and Nucs (page 11). Some pieces of hive equipment, like hive bodies, may have a useful life of 10 years or more, while frames and foundation may have a shorter lifespan. In fact, replacing frames and foundation every 5 years is recommended as a best management practice to reduce the buildup of pesticides and disease-causing spores. To simplify recordkeeping and depreciation estimates, we propose using a standard of 7 years as the useful life for all items in the hive equipment category. General equipment (page 26). The second worksheet in this section records the value of all other equipment, including beekeeping, extraction, and bottling equipment. All equipment valued at $500 or more at the time of purchase should be included here. You may also list equipment valued at less than $500, if it has a projected life span of more than one year. Vehicles and machinery (page 30). The third worksheet records the value of machinery and vehicles. Machines use mechanical power to accomplish a specific task. Vehicles are a type of machinery, used for transporting people or products. There may be some overlap between the machinery and equipment categories - if an item fits into both categories, record it only once on the worksheet of your choice. Assets and Liabilities Assets Liabilities An asset is a productive resource that can be bought and sold. Companies own assets and use them to generate income. Assets can be tangible, like tractors and livestock, or intangible, like patents and trademarks. For the purposes of farm financial analysis, we separate assets into two categories that reflect their level of permanence in the business: current and non-current assets. Most businesses incur financial debts or obligations during the course of normal business operations. These obligations are known as liabilities, and they represent a claim on the value of business assets held by an outside entity. Liabilities are settled over time when the business transfers money, goods, or services that relieve its prior obligations. Liabilities are also sorted into current and noncurrent categories. Current Assets Current assets refer to resources that will be converted into cash or used up within one year. Examples include: Current Liabilities Current liabilities are obligations that the business expects to meet within one year. Examples include: • Cash • Checking and savings account balances • Feed • Supplies • Prepaid expenses • Accounts receivable • Apiary products inventory Noncurrent Assets In contrast, noncurrent assets are resources that the company expects to own for more than one year. Examples include: • Vehicles • Machinery • Equipment • Buildings • Land We also consider the inventory of honey bee colonies, as with other breeding livestock, to be a noncurrent asset. Intangible assets are also considered to be noncurrent assets. • Short-term loans • Lines of credit • Credit card balances • Accounts payable • Accrued expenses The portion of a long-term loan due within 12 months is also considered to be a current liability. Noncurrent Liabilities In contrast, noncurrent liabilities include the portion of all longterm financial obligations - including loans and mortgages - that are due beyond the next 12 months. 42

Net Worth Statement The Net Worth Statement is a record of a farm's business assets (what the business owns) and liabilities (what the business owes) at a specific moment in time. Net worth is defined as the difference between total assets and total liabilities. Owner equity is synonymous with net worth; both terms refer to the value of the business share that belongs to the owner(s). The Net Worth Statement is sometimes called a Balance Sheet, because it is structured around the accounting relationship that balances assets, liabilities, and net worth in a single equation: Assets - Liabilities = Net Worth This financial statement provides a snapshot of the farm's financial condition. Farm businesses can benefit from taking an annual financial snapshot by producing a Net Worth Statement at the beginning of each financial year, typically January 1st. Lenders may require a current Balance Sheet to evaluate a loan application. A Net Worth Statement is useful to farm managers and their lenders because it shows the overall liquidity and solvency of the business. Liquidity reflects the ability of a farm business to pay its bills on time without disrupting day-to-day operations. In accounting terminology, liquidity measures the relationship between current assets and current liabilities. In contrast, solvency refers to the relationship between total assets and total liabilities. In other words, solvency represents the ability of a business to pay off its debts in the event that the business were to shut down and sell all of its assets. Farm Profit The Income Statement summarizes the relationship between farm revenues (income from the sale of goods and services) and expenses (costs of producing and selling goods and services) over a defined period of time, usually a fiscal year. This financial statement provides information about a company's ability to generate profits. As such, it is also commonly called a Profit and Loss (P&L) Statement. For a farm business, annual profit is defined as the total value of production for a given year less the total cost of production in that year, illustrated in the following equation: Total Value of Production - Total Cost of Production = Farm Profit It is important to note that cash transactions do not always coincide with the exact moment when revenues are generated or when costs are incurred. For instance, apiary products produced in one business year may not be sold until the following year. Similarly, expenses incurred in 2017 may not be paid until 2018. Most farm businesses rely on the cash accounting method, in which they record transactions when the cash changes hands. However, the difference between total cash revenues and total cash expenses - termed Net Cash Farm Income - is not an accurate measure of farm profit: Total Cash Income - Total Cash Expense = Net Cash Farm Income In contrast to cash accounting, accrual accounting records business revenues and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands. This accounting method is better suited to calculate profit. However, farms rarely use accrual accounting in day-today operations. For farms using the cash accounting method, managers can apply accrual adjustments at the end of the financial year to calculate the total value of production and total cost of production. The following equation is analogous to the first equation on this page, with NFIFO being synonymous to farm profit: Total Adjusted Income - Total Adjusted Expense = Net Farm Income From Operations (NFIFO) The Income Statement template on pages 50 - 51 records cash farm income and cash farm expenses, which can be found on the IRS Schedule F (Profit or Loss from Farming) or Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) tax form. The template also incorporates accrual adjustments to income and expenses, based on asset and liability values recorded earlier in this handbook. 48

Homepage Video Transcript This is probably one of the most fun aspects of beekeeping. Here, we're going to take a step beyond our bee yard and talk about some of the rewards as a beekeeper, and contributions that we can make. I'm looking forward to showing you all the possibilities of business opportunities with beekeeping, whether it's honey production, pollination services, or making up packages and nucs for sale. You'll gain advice directly from experienced beekeepers and experts who've made careers producing and selling their products and services. And we'll learn how to be leaders in our community and serve as ambassadors for bees. What you'll do Identify major honey bee product and service opportunities and considerations Participate in beekeeping-related organizations that fit your specific needs while enabling you to give back to the beekeeping community (and the bees!) Explore the business considerations of turning your bees into profit opportunities Understand laws, regulations, and registration requirements impacting beekeepers Identify credible and reputable sources of information to stay current in bee research Contribute effectively to citizen science and data collection Course Description Beekeepers are in a unique position to both reap financial benefit from their hives and contribute to the health of pollinator populations as well as the greater beekeeping community. In this course, you will learn about major hive products and services, how to grow your operation, and what options to consider for beekeeping as a business. Even if you are not interested in making a profit from your bees, you'll gain a valuable appreciation for the beekeeping industry and understand how hard bees and beekeepers work. You will discover how to evaluate the quality of information sources on bees and beekeeping, enabling you to contribute to education, research, and outreach. You'll also mentor less-experienced beekeepers, participate in research activities, and raise

awareness on pollinator issues. This course will prepare you to be a leader in your beekeeping community. This is the fourth in a series of courses that equip beekeepers at both the hobby and commercial levels with the concepts, knowledge, and best management practices needed to pass the written, oral, and field components of Cornell University’s Master Beekeeper Certificate. Emma is interested in pollinator conservation and has held advisory roles for the development of the Ontario Pollinator Health Action Plan and the New York State Pollinator Protection Plan. Module Introduction: Honey Honey is a historically important food, valued by ancient populations as well as contemporary cultures around the world. Humans have consumed honey for some 10,000 years, as depicted by cave drawings of honey hunters in Spain from the Stone Age (6,000–8,000 B.C.). To this day, Indigenous honey hunters and beekeepers alike are revered for their ability to provide honey and beeswax. In this module, we will explore honey: how it is made, what it is made of, and the different ways in which beekeepers process and pack it. Back to Table of Contents

Read: From Nectar to Liquid Gold The main source of energy for a bee colony, honey is comprised of carbohydrates and eaten by the bees to provide energy for activities such as flying, fanning, and heat production, or it can be converted to fat for later use. Storing honey in the hive offers a food source during times of poor weather or a nectar dearth. ☆ Key Points Honey is the main energy source for honey bees; it is comprised mainly of fructose and glucose. Bees ripen nectar into honey by adding enzymes and lowering its level of moisture. With some exceptions (e.g., honey produced from the honeydew of aphids), honey is derived from sugary floral nectar that has been manipulated and dried by bees of the genus Apis. Bumble bees and other honey bee species within the Apidae family make variations of honey, but we will focus on what is made by Apis mellifera, the typical honey bee cultivated by beekeepers. Honey is a saturated solution of sugars — primarily fructose and glucose — along with numerous other minor components. Its composition varies by the different sources of nectar and with regard to the environmental and seasonal conditions during its production. Under the right circumstances, a colony of Apis mellifera bees produces more honey than is necessary for winter survival; indeed, it is the only bee species that produces enough to allow for harvest in North America. The beekeeper’s challenge is to manage the colony to maximize the honey production with a surplus greater than the bees’ needs for winter. ▶ Nectar Sources Influence the Classification of Honey Honey can be polyfloral (or multifloral), monofloral (or varietal), or honeydew honey. Most honey is polyfloral, from a wide variety of honey plants in bloom, with no main nectar source dominating the flavor or other characteristics. Such honey might be labeled as wildflower honey, spring honey, summer blossom honey, fall honey, or meadow honey. Monofloral honey is harvested from a distinct source of nectar. Though there are typically other plants in

bloom simultaneously, and most monofloral honey labeled as such probably includes nectar from several different plants, beekeepers identify these unique honey varieties based on the heavy-flow sources like black locust, clover, basswood, or goldenrod, to name a few of the most common wild sources here in the Northeast. Monofloral honey may also result when colonies are near large agricultural plantings of alfalfa, sunflowers, apples, oranges, strawberries, blueberries, soybeans, buckwheat, and numerous other crops. Honeydew honey, sometimes called forest honey, is a rare variety produced from the sugary excrement of sap-sucking insects such as aphids, leafhoppers, and psyllids. Honey bee on orange blossom flower. Collecting Nectar Nectar is a mix of chemically altered waterborne nutrients that are secreted into plant nectaries. Nectaries are typically located inside the blossoms, although some are extrafloral (meaning that they are found on leaves, stems, and other plant parts). The sweetness (concentration of sugar) of nectar varies, both in plant species and individuals. Honey bee foragers prefer the highest sugar content available. Pear blossom nectar, for example, is typically about 512% sugar and therefore often bypassed for other flowers that may yield as much as 60%. ▶

▶ In one foraging session, a honey bee typically gathers 25–40 mg of nectar by visiting many flowers. To gather this much nectar, she visits up to 500 flowers in a foraging session, nearly always visiting the same type of flower. On a good day, foragers embark on about ten foraging sessions. If nectar is plentiful, bees can carry loads as great as 70 mg — about 85% of their body weight! As nectar travels from a forager’s mouth to her honey stomach for temporary storage, enzymes from her hypopharyngeal and salivary glands are added. This initiates the process of the nectar becoming honey. These enzymes — namely invertase and diastase — break down the large sucrose molecules of nectar into the smaller sugars of fructose and glucose. From Nectar to Honey Upon her arrival at the hive to unload the nectar, the forager is greeted by receiver bees, who add a variety of additional enzymes to the nectar. When ripe (fully converted from nectar), most honey has less than 5% sucrose. The bees also add glucose oxidase, converting small amounts of glucose into gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide. This increases the acidity of the honey, thus lowering the pH. The nectar is passed from bee to bee, with each bee adding more enzymes (as well as the amino acid proline) to the liquid. With all of these additions, the chemical properties of the nectar change to become more like honey. Finally, after being passed along by several bees, the unripened honey is deposited in a honey cell.

Once in the cell, the unripened honey must have its moisture content reduced. Nectar receivers smear it on the walls of the honey cells, and other house bees fan their wings to circulate air throughout the hive and promote evaporation. When the water content is reduced to approximately 18%, usually after a few days of fanning and handling, the honey is fully ripened. The time devoted to the process and eventual moisture content depends on the ambient humidity and temperature, the characteristics of the nectar (in other words, the mix of flowers from which it is derived), and the colony population and its other activities. When the transformation of nectar into honey is complete, bees cap the honey cell with beeswax. The properties of honey give it a very long shelf life; indeed, it is one of the only foods with no expiration date. Specifically, the high sugar content, the low pH, and the presence of hydrogen peroxide and various enzymes make it an inhospitable environment for most bacteria and other microorganisms. Read: Medicinal Benefits of Honey Honey has been revered for centuries ☆ Key Points for its medicinal value. Ancient medical philosophers such as Hippocrates and Aristotle praised and promoted honey Honey is effective in managing coughs and wounds. for a variety of internal and external ailments and injuries. In ancient times, honey was used to “cure” everything from intestinal distress, cough, insomnia, wounds, heart palpitations, anemia, poor eyesight, gout, nervous disorders, fever, contraception, baldness, and tuberculosis. It was a major ingredient in medicines in ancient Egypt, Greece, India, China, Babylonia, and Rome, and there are references to honey's healing properties in the Bible, the Qur’an, and the Torah. Since the introduction of antibiotics in the early 1900s, the use of honey as a medicine has largely fallen by the wayside, although many websites and naturopathic doctors continue to promote honey as medicine and cure for many diseases. But few of the claims about the diseases and ailments that honey is advertised to cure have been proven scientifically. In order to be considered medicine and recommended for use in hospitals and doctors’ offices, drugs and other treatments must be rigorously tested in randomized clinical trials with a large number of human patients. Today, there are only two conditions for which honey has been scientifically shown to be medically effective: treating coughs and treating wounds. Clinical trials have shown that honey can be an effective cough suppressant in children. It works better than taking no cough suppressant and can be as effective at reducing cough frequency as dextromethorphan (the active ingredient in most over-the-counter cough suppressants). Honey helps to soothe and coat the throat, and a teaspoon and a half before bed can help children sleep longer through the night with fewer coughing episodes.

To treat wounds, honey is applied to a dressing and the dressing is placed on the wound. This accelerates skin healing and kills and prevents bacterial growth on the skin’s surface. Some companies sell prepackaged honey-coated wound dressings. Of course, not all honey is created equal. Honeys with higher peroxide concentrations exhibit stronger antibacterial effects. Honey dressings have also been shown to accelerate the healing of burns as compared to other types of wound dressings, with patients who receive honey dressings healing four to five days sooner. Some evidence suggests honey can heal postoperative wounds, pressure ulcers, and diabetic foot ulcers faster than other antiseptic treatments and with fewer adverse effects. The beneficial effects of honey as a wound dressing are primarily due to its antimicrobial activities. It helps kill bacteria at the wound site, keeping the area clean while the wound heals. Some antioxidants present at low levels in honey (particularly dark honeys) can help reduce inflammation and improve healing.

Read: Manuka Honey: The Most Antibacterial Honey In the 1980s, manuka honey was ☆ Key Points discovered to have unusually strong antibacterial effects; more so than other types of honey. Manuka honey is derived from the manuka bush native Manuka honey has exceptional antibacterial properties due to the presence of methylglyoxal (MGO). to New Zealand and Australia. Methylglyoxal (MGO) is the chemical responsible for these enhanced antibacterial effects. The higher the level of MGO, the greater the honey’s antibacterial effects. Manuka honey is primarily used as a topical ointment for wounds and burns. Some hospitals use manuka honey dressings on patients. Studies in the laboratory exposing bacteria to manuka honey in petri dishes have found that manuka honey can kill 58 different species of bacteria, including Helicobacter pylori (responsible for stomach ulcers) and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (a type of antibiotic-resistant infection sometimes found in hospitals). This laboratory research is promising, but scientists have not yet tested its use to control these particular infections in human patients. Just like other honeys, not all manuka is created the same. Some manuka honey has lesspronounced antibacterial properties. It believed that climate and soil type play a role in the level of chemicals in manuka bush flowers. In New Zealand, manuka honey is tested for its level of MGO and assigned a number called a Unique Manuka Factor (UMF). Honey with a value of at least 10 UMF is considered therapeutic; it can be marketed as “Active Manuka Honey” or “UMF Manuka Honey” and sold for a premium price. An 8-ounce jar of 10 UMF manuka honey retails for $40–$50, and an 8-ounce jar of 20 UMF manuka honey retails for $100–$200.

Photo Credit: Scott McArt Given these prices and the fact that New Zealand's manuka honey market has grown substantially over the past ten years, it is sought after by many beekeepers. Some follow the manuka honey flow across the country, flying their hives into manuka-rich areas by helicopter. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Composition of Honey Sugars comprise 98% of the solids found in honey, making it a great natural sweetener. The major sugars present in honey are fructose and glucose, while the minor sugars are sucrose and maltose. The chart below shows the typical composition of honey, based on 490 samples tested in the U.S. ☆ Key Points In addition to sugar and water, honey contains acids, vitamins, minerals, and some microorganisms. The Clostridium botulinum spores naturally present in some honey are a risk to infants. Although honey has a sweet taste, it is actually acidic. Much of the acidity is contributed by gluconic acid but other acids are naturally present in honey as well, such as formic acid, oxalic acid, acetic acid, and lactic acid. Vitamins and Minerals Honey contains trace amounts of vitamins and minerals. Darker honeys and honeydew honeys are highest in vitamins and minerals. These include Vitamins B1, B2, B3, B6, and C, along with the minerals sodium, potassium, magnesium, calcium, copper, iron, manganese, phosphorus, chlorine, and sulfur. The levels of vitamins and minerals are extremely low — only about 0.17% of honey — and make up a tiny fraction of a person's recommended daily intake. For this reason, honey should not be relied upon as a source of nutrients for the human diet. Microorganisms Most bacteria do not grow in super-saturated sugar solutions such as honey. Nonetheless, some species of bacteria and yeasts can survive in this environment. Sugar-tolerant yeast spores are often present in honey, but the low moisture content prevents their activation. Should the moisture content increase, yeast spores can activate and the yeast can multiply, putting honey at risk of fermentation. The most notable bacterium is Clostridium botulinum. While the active bacteria cannot survive in honey, its spores can. A test of over 2,000 honey samples found that 5%

contained Clostridium botulinum spores. If spores are consumed, they can become active and cause an infection of botulism. The bacteria produce a neurotoxin that can cause paralysis and death. Infants under the age of 12 months are at risk because they have not yet developed the healthy gut microbiome that outcompetes the bacteria. (Adults, on the other hand, are not affected by the spores.) For this reason, honey should never be given to infants under a year old. Many U.S. beekeepers therefore include cautionary language about feeding honey to infants on their labels. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Changes in Honey Over Time — Crystallization In time, honey can undergo some ☆ Key Points changes. Most honeys will eventually crystallize, and some ferment. Crystallization occurs when glucose precipitates out of the Crystallization water in honey. Honey is a super-saturated sugar The rate of honey crystallization solution. This means that the water has depends on the presence of absorbed more sugar than it can foreign particles, the nectar under normal circumstances. This source, and the temperature at state is not very stable, and some of which it is stored. the glucose naturally precipitates out of the water in time, forming solid crystals. This is called “crystallization.” Once a crystal forms, it is a platform for more crystals to join, meaning that once the crystallization process begins, it continues until the entire jar of honey is crystallized. Sugar crystals are also more likely to form around other foreign particles in the honey, such as granules of pollen, wax, propolis, dust, or even air bubbles. Crystallization is also more likely to occur when honey is stored in cool temperatures (typically below 68°F [20°C]), as water absorbs more sugar in warm temperatures (such as the warm temperatures in a bee hive). Above all, the floral source of the honey influences the rate of crystallization. Some honeys are notorious for crystallizing quickly, such as goldenrod, alfalfa, clover, apple, canola, raspberry, and dandelion, which can crystallize in several weeks or months. Honeys that are slower to crystallize include acacia, black locust, sage, buckwheat, orange blossom, and tupelo. These honeys may not crystallize for many months or years. Honeys with a low moisture content tend to develop finer crystals (for a texture similar to creamed honey), while honeys with a higher moisture content develop coarser crystals. The best way to liquefy or soften crystallized honey is to place it in a warm water bath (95– 104°F [35–40°C]), with the water reaching the level of honey in the jar. The heat slowly dissolves the sugar crystals to make the honey liquid again. If you sell honey, you may want to include these instructions to your customers and explain to them that crystallization is a natural process. Some customers think that crystallized honey has gone bad or has additional sugar added to it, since they are more accustomed to seeing filtered honey on grocery store shelves.

Delaying Crystallization Without Pasteurization To delay crystallization, strain the honey through a fine nylon cloth before storing or bottling it. This removes most of the foreign particles, such as flecks of wax or pollen grains, that can initiate crystallization. Crystallization does not occur below 32°F (0°C) and occurs very slowly below 50°F (10°C), so honey can be stored at cold temperatures until it is ready to sell. Crystallization can also be further delayed by allowing bees to clean extracted “wet” honey supers before the equipment is stored for winter. If extracted supers are stored wet, the honey can form crystals over the winter. When you place the supers on colonies next spring, last year’s crystals may be incorporated into this year’s crop and contribute to earlier crystallization. To allow the bees to “clean up” the wet honey on the frames, place the extracted supers on top of their hives (above the inner cover but below the outer cover) for a couple of days. Read: Changes in Honey Over Time — Fermentation The sugar-tolerant yeast spores ☆ Key Points present in honey can become active if the moisture content exceeds 18%. Honey with a moisture content above 19% will likely ferment within one year. Usually, when honey is sufficiently Under some conditions, natural yeasts can consume the sugar in honey, transforming it into alcohol and carbon dioxide. ripened and capped by bees, the moisture is low enough to prevent yeast growth. But sometimes during strong nectar flows, such as orange blossom flows in the South, bees bring in nectar so quickly and in such great quantity that they do not ripen it sufficiently before capping. This honey can have high levels of moisture and is more susceptible to fermentation. Most honey fermentation occurs when honey becomes crystallized. Water is freed when sugar crystals precipitate, leaving a jar of honey with crystallized sugar on the bottom and liquid on the top. This liquid is susceptible to yeast growth. When yeast begins to grow in honey, it consumes sugar, transforming it into carbon dioxide and alcohol in a process called fermentation. Honey in the early stages of fermentation tastes fruity but, in time, develops a yeasty, unpleasant taste. It may also look foamy or bubbly. Preventing Fermentation Without Pasteurization Before Honey Is Extracted Honey with a moisture content below 18% is safe from the risk of fermentation, while any honey with a moisture content above 18% has the potential to ferment. To reduce the risk of fermentation, only frames that are at least 80% capped should be extracted. Beekeepers can test their honey before extraction to determine the moisture content; this can be accomplished with a honey refractometer. Test small samples from a few cells on a frame to get an idea of the moisture content for the entire frame of honey. If the moisture content is below 18%, you can extract it. If it is above 18%, you must reduce the moisture level first. To do so, honey supers can be temporarily stored in a warm room with a dehumidifier or a warm fan blowing. In several days (depending on the initial level), it can be brought down to an acceptable range. Many beekeepers have drying rooms (called hot rooms) in their honey houses for this purpose, where warm, dry air (90–95°F or 32–25°C)

circulates. With this setup, 1–3% moisture can be removed in a 24-hour period. Alternatively, honey with a higher moisture content can be blended with honey of a lower moisture content to create a large batch of honey with an overall moisture content below 18%. After Honey Is Extracted Straining honey immediately after extraction with a fine mesh or nylon removes particles that can initiate crystallization. After the honey is placed Fermented honey on the frame. in bottles, barrels, or buckets, ensure these containers are airtight. A refractometer. If it is in contact with the air, moisture can accumulate on the surface of the honey, and fermentation can begin. Honey can also be stored at cool temperatures below 52°F (11°C) until it is sold. At these temperatures, yeast cannot grow. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Processing Liquid Honey After honey comes out of the extractor, ☆ Key Points it can be processed in a variety of ways. Straining, filtering, and ultra- For most backyard beekeepers, honey is consumed or sold raw. The U.S. National Honey Board defines raw filtering remove varying amounts of particles from honey, including pollen. honey as "honey as it exists in the beehive or as obtained by extraction, settling, or straining without adding heat." Today's consumers are very interested in raw honey, which is Pasteurization delays crystallization and fermentation, but it breaks down the enzymes that are naturally present in honey. convenient for small-scale beekeepers as they can extract and package it with minimal steps. These beekeepers may not process honey at all, opting to bottle it with all its pollen and propolis, along with any small bee body parts that happened to fall into it. Raw honey must be packed airtight. Nearly all raw honey eventually crystallizes. Beekeepers can remind their customers that raw honey is a superior product — the crystallization marks it as such — and that crystallized honey can be re-liquefied through slow, gentle warming. Some beekeepers process their honey by removing some of the particles that help initiate crystallization, and others even heat their honey. Below, explore how honey can be processed once it is out of the comb but before it is in the bottle. Straining Before being stored in containers, honey can be strained to remove large particles such as wax, propolis, bee body parts, dirt, wood splinters, and metal flakes from equipment. Strainers tend to be small enough to stop these products from entering the container but large enough to permit some pollen, propolis, and beeswax to flow through (200 micrometers or larger). The resulting honey is clear and attractive to consumers. A range of fabric or wire strainers are available: Cheesecloth can be used, or other metal or nylon fabric filtering bags and bucket strainers that are 200, 400, or 600 micrometers can be purchased through bee equipment supply

companies. For large-scale beekeepers, commercial honey strainers are also available for purchase through bee equipment supply companies. Honey straining through a nylon filter basket. Beekeepers may wish to filter their honey after straining it to improve the clarity even further. Filtering also prolongs the time it takes for honey to crystallize, as it removes most of the pollen grains and dust that remain in the honey after straining. Diatomaceous earth, a very fine-powdered sedimentary rock, is usually added to the honey before it passes through the filter; this process removes nearly all the particles in the honey. Honey filtered in this manner — with little to no pollen remaining — is still honey. Ultra-filtration is a different type of filtering that is rare in North America. In ultrafiltration, honey is forced through an extremely small filter (one-tenth of a micrometer). Every last particle is removed, and the final product is considered a “sweetener” — rather than honey — by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. The U.S. honey qualifications grade honey on the basis of clarity. Grade A honey (the highest score) is filtered to remove nearly all particles from honey. Grade A honey may contain trace amounts of pollen grains and other fine particles that do not affect the overall clear appearance of honey. Grade B and C honey contains more of these particles, and the honey is less clear.

Honey should contain some pollen grains. The presence of pollen grains is used to identify the source(s) of the honey. While bees collect nectar from a plant, they often incidentally collect some pollen that makes its way into the honey. This can verify that a particular honey is a specific varietal (for example, honey marketed as "orange blossom" should contain orange pollen), and it can identify the country or region from which the honey sources have come. With an estimated 91 million tons of illegal honey entering the U.S. each year, being able to identify the source of a honey based on the pollen it contains is very useful. Warming Honey that is warmed is less viscous; it flows freely from combs and through machinery, making extracting and bottling more efficient. Warming honey also prevents crystals from developing on equipment, which can contribute to crystallized honey. If honey is not heated above 105°F (40°C), it remains raw and the nutritional and medicinal values are preserved, as well as the natural aromas and flavors. Warmed to about 90°F–105°F (32–40.6°C), the equivalent of the temperature in an active hive, the honey is liquefied enough for faster extracting and bottling. At this temperature, the enzymes in honey remain intact and the honey is not permanently changed in any way. Honey can be warmed on the frame, with supers placed in hot rooms prior to extraction, or warmed at various stages of the extraction process. It may be warmed when it is passing through a sump (a temporary holding tank that receives honey from the extractor before it is pumped to other processing tanks), while it is in settling tanks, and while it is being bottled.

This heated bottling tank warms honey. Photo Credit: Betterbee Settling Commercial beekeepers who sell their honey in bulk (usually in barrels) often do not filter or bottle their own honey; instead, they remove most of the debris with settling tanks. A settling tank is a large tank that holds honey for two or three days. While the honey settles, most of the debris floats to the top. The clean honey is then piped out of the bottom of the tank into barrels, leaving most of the debris behind in the tank. Often, tanks are heated with a water jacket to aid in settling and reduce crystallization. The honey may be filtered further before bottling.

Small settling tank. Photo Credit: Betterbee Pasteurizing Pasteurization is the process of heating food to kill microorganisms. In honey, pasteurization destroys the yeasts responsible for fermentation and delays crystallization by dissolving any crystals already present. It does not, however, destroy Clostridium botulinum spores. Honey can be pasteurized by raising the temperature to 145–155°F (63–68°C) for 30 minutes, or through flash heating that brings the honey to 160°F (71°C) then immediately cools it. Most grocery store honey is pasteurized so it will remain clear and liquid. Honey that remains liquid for long periods of time is easier to handle at the table, as it pours easily.

For hobby beekeepers, pasteurization can occur in the kitchen, heating the honey in a pot on the stove. Keep a food thermometer in the honey to monitor the temperature and stir it to ensure even heating. For larger commercial beekeepers, honey-pasteurizing equipment is available through some bee equipment supply companies or food processing companies. The disadvantage of pasteurized honey is that heat breaks down the enzymes naturally present in honey, such as invertase and glucose oxidase. The higher the temperature, the faster these enzymes break down. For instance, the half-life of invertase at 176°F (80°C) is 8.6 minutes. The breakdown of glucose oxidase diminishes some of honey’s healing properties when applied to wounds; without glucose oxidase, the production of hydrogen peroxide halts. Heating at too-high temperatures can also burn the honey, causing it to caramelize, especially at the higher-end temperatures used in pasteurization. This changes the color, aroma, and flavor of the honey, thus reducing its grade and marketability. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Components and Design of a Honey House By now, students in this course are ☆ Key Points likely familiar with basic, small-scale honey extraction (while some are familiar with large-scale extraction). If beekeepers manage a few to a few A honey house should be carefully designed to maximize productivity and efficiency. dozen colonies, honey extraction can take place in their own kitchen or garage. Beekeepers who manage more than 50 colonies likely want to construct or purchase a honey house to process honey more efficiently and store honey and equipment. Let's discuss some of the main components of a honey house. ▶ General Considerations It is best for beekeepers to locate their honey house on a separate piece of land from their own home, as sharing a property can affect the retail value of the home. Keeping these buildings separate also allows beekeepers to sell each place separately if needed. The honey house should have access to electricity, water, and good drainage. Beekeepers need to maintain a clean honey house, for example, by mopping the floors. The honey house should have floor drains and a hose spigot for the convenience of hosing floors. It's also useful to have a sink for hand washing and a cupboard to store cleaning supplies. The honey house should be easily accessible by truck. Single-story honey houses on level land will need pumps to push the honey from the extractor to strainers or tanks. With a two-story honey house, extraction can take place on the top floor and bottling on the lower floor, allowing the honey to flow by gravity from the extractor to the strainer, settling tank, or bottling tank. Twostory honey houses should have truck access on both floors to eliminate the need to move equipment up and down stairs. A freight elevator will also work. Carefully plan the layout of the honey house to make it efficient and convenient. Consider the logistics of items moving into and out of the building: full supers coming into the building; empty supers going out of the

▶ building (or being stored in the building); and barrels or bottles being filled, stored, and shipped. Maximize the flow in the rooms so people are not bumping into each other and so that heavy items do not have to be moved long distances. Consider how many people will be in the rooms at one time and plan accordingly for space. Visit other beekeepers' honey houses to learn how they have been constructed, what aspects they like most about them, and what aspects they would change. This can help beekeepers design a more optimal honey house for themselves. Loading Dock The loading dock is the area where honey supers are removed from the truck and placed in the honey house (often the hot room). The beekeeper can use a forklift to easily remove supers from the truck and bring them into the honey house. If the beekeeper does not have a forklift, the loading dock should be level with the truck bed to minimize lifting. The loading dock is also the place where bottling and bee yard supplies are accepted, so it is wise to consider the height (or heights) needed for freight truck deliveries in addition to the level required for bee yard truck offloading. Many large trucks will not deliver to the honey house unless there is a forklift or loading dock available. Hot Room The hot room is where supers can be temporarily placed to be warmed and should be in close proximity to the loading dock. Its temperature is usually set to 80–100°F (26–38°C), and relative humidity is kept to 0–20%. While in the hot room, honey will become less viscous and easier to extract. If honey moisture is too high, warm air and/or a dehumidifier in this room can help to reduce water content before the supers are extracted. The hot room should contain a thermometer and a humidity gauge. ▶

▶ Beekeepers without space for a hot room can consider purchasing a honey drying machine from Dadant. These machines lower moisture content very quickly; 1–2% moisture is removed from two barrels’ worth of honey every hour. Extracting Area Once honey is warm and at the right moisture level, it can be moved into the extracting area. In this area of the honey house, honey combs are uncapped and placed in an extractor. The size of the beekeeper’s operation influences the type of extractor they use, which in turn influences the setup of the honey house. Equipment should be thoroughly researched ahead of constructing the honey house. It is also wise to plan around potential equipment upgrades, additions, and increased power needs. While hobby beekeepers tend to use heated uncapping knives and forks to remove beeswax cappings by hand, sideline beekeepers increase efficiency by using uncapping machines to do the process for them. Various versions of "sideliner uncappers" exist, but in most, the equipment calls for beekeepers to feed frames one at a time between two metal rollers with circular cutting knives on them. The circular knives slice holes in the wax cappings on both sides of the frame at once. They do not employ electricity or heat. These sideliner uncappers are resting on top of uncapping tanks to catch cappings and honey drippings. Frames are then lifted manually into the uncapper and into the extractor. Automatic electric uncappers also exist. They function by using heated, oscillating knives to cut cappings from the honey comb. Frames are loaded onto a short conveyer belt chain, which feeds the frames one by one into the uncapper. One frame at a time is guided downward between two heated, oscillating knives. The cappings and honey drippings collect in an attached cappings tank. Commercial beekeepers often purchase large pieces of equipment that form a big assembly-line system for uncapping and extracting. These systems require minimal labor to load the automatic uncapper (again, functioning by using heated, oscillating knives) and the extractor. There are even machines that can lift honey frames to feed them into the uncapper, preventing the need for the

▶ beekeeper to bend down to grab and load frames. These commercial systems have the potential to extract honey from hundreds of supers in a day. After the wax cappings are removed, the honey frames are placed in extractors. Different types of extractors will be explored later in the module. Sump In small hobby operations, honey can flow directly from the extractor into buckets. Some beekeepers may place filters over buckets to strain the honey. In larger operations, however, honey flows out of the extractor into a sump, a temporary storage tank that begins straining the honey. Sumps are placed below extractors so honey can flow into them by gravity. Any honey collected in uncapping tanks often flows to sumps as well. Sumps are often gently heated with water jackets so the honey can be strained more efficiently and wax separated from it more easily. Screened baffles help separate wax and particles out of the honey as it runs through, helping it flow through the pump without clogging it. Many sumps have floats to detect whether honey is about to overflow. Pumps connected to the sump can be automatically turned on to allow honey to drain out and prevent spills.

▶ Sump with three screened baffles for honey to pass through. Photo Credit: Betterbee Pump If a beekeeper's honey house is located on one floor, the honey will need to be pumped from the sump to the strainer — assuming the beekeeper wants to strain their honey more finely than what the sump accomplishes — or to the settling tank if they simply want to separate any remaining wax and particles by settling. All pipes must be "food grade"; i.e., rated for use with food products. Strainer or Settling Tank Large-scale operations use commercial strainers or settling tanks to further process honey. Typically when beekeepers plan to bottle and sell their own ▶

honey, they strain it first. If beekeepers sell wholesale, they often use a settling tank instead. Straining ultimately produces a higher-clarity product. If a beekeeper strains their honey through a fine mesh, a sump that removes the largest, coarsest particles ensures that the mesh does not clog quickly. A commercial-sized strainer uses a mesh made of nylon or a metal screen. This mesh is located at the bottom of a tank, submerged underneath the honey. In this way, minimal air bubbles become incorporated in the honey as it passes through the mesh. Honey is strained at a warm temperature of around 100°F (38°C) to reduce the viscosity and increase the flow through the strainer. Honey should not be strained at a higher temperature, however, because any wax will melt and pass through the mesh, making the honey cloudy when it cools to room temperature. Mesh straining bags can be replaced as needed. After passing through the strainer, honey is bottled. Beekeepers who do not finely strain their own honey use settling tanks as the last processing step before they run their honey into barrels for sale. Honey exits the pump into large tanks (often made of stainless steel) to sit for two to three days. Beekeepers who market different varietals of honey may have several separate tanks. Packing Honey Beekeepers who use barrels simply sell the barrels to other companies that bottle the honey. These barrels must be made from or coated with food-grade materials. Sideliner and commercial beekeepers who bottle their own honey often use automatic bottling machines. These machines ensure that the bottles receive a consistent and accurate volume, efficiently and with minimal spills. Labeling machines attach labels to the bottles. Small-scale beekeepers usually bottle and add labels to their honey by hand. Storage Designated areas for storage are helpful in the honey house. Beekeepers can temporarily store extracted supers before returning them to colonies, as well ▶ ▶
as barrels and packages of honey before transport or sale. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Types of Extractors Let's explore the three different types of extractors, from smallest to largest. Tangential extractor: These extractors hold between two and 16 frames at a time and can be hand cranked or electrically powered. The frames sit in a metal basket, and only one side of the frames is extracted at once. After extracting one side of the frames, the frames are flipped and the other side is extracted. Small models require the beekeeper to flip the frames by hand, but other models may rotate the metal basket inside for the beekeeper so the machine does not need to be opened again until the full extraction is finished. These extractors are usually used by small-scale beekeepers who manage fewer than 50 colonies. In the U.S., equipment of this scale is typically purchased through the bee equipment companies Maxant, Dadant, and Mann Lake. We encourage beekeepers to explore current catalogs to familiarize themselves with honey extraction products. Radial extractor: A radial extractor can hold from 10 to over 100 frames and is electrically powered. The frames are placed in the extractor like spokes in a wheel, and both sides of the frame are extracted simultaneously. These extractors are typically used by beekeepers who manage between 50 and 500 colonies. In the U.S., equipment of this scale is typically purchased through the bee equipment companies Maxant, Dadant, and Mann Lake.

Parallel radial extractor: Parallel radial extractors are radial extractors that are tipped horizontally. This allows frames to be loaded in a parallel fashion by pushing them along a ramp directly into the extractor. In this way, no lifting is required by the beekeeper. They are commonly used in large sideliner or commercial operations, for beekeepers managing hundreds or thousands of colonies. The largest extractors in the U.S. can handle 240 frames at once! These extractors are often part of a large extraction system with an automatic electric uncapper, a conveyor belt, and a powered extractor. In the U.S., these large systems can be purchased through Cowan Manufacturing or Cook & Beals.

Read: Other Honey House Considerations When thinking about honey houses, here are a few further considerations. Honey houses should be bee-proof, so no bees or wasps can enter from the outside. Any windows that may be left open should have screens. There should be a screened window in each room of the honey house with a small bee escape. Any bees that enter with the supers will be drawn to the window and find their way out. Use concrete or tile floors with drains in each room. These floors are easy to mop with water to promptly clean up honey spills. Floors should be treated with paint, acrylic, or another treatment to protect them against acid wear from honey. Honey and water conduct electricity. Electrical wires and outlets should be protected with waterproof fittings and coverings to reduce the chance of shock. Honey extracting and processing equipment should be made with stainless steel to ease cleaning and to last a long time. Iron and steel equipment can rust over time and can darken honey if they remain in contact for long periods of time. Below is a design for a sideliner-scale honey house. In this particular example, the facility is located on one floor and uses a parallel extractor.

A wax melter sits below these. Two loading docks line the left wall. In the center, a sump and pump is installed below floor level. A wax spinner is positioned in the middle right section, with a hot room beside it. An uncapping tank is situated beneath the hot room, with an extractor at the bottom right of the facility. Storage areas occupy the upper portion of the layout. Back to Table of Contents

⌃ Long description A graph showing US honey prices from 1987 to 2006. In 1987 the average price per pound hovered around 60 cents. Starting around 1994 honey prices began to rise. After a dip in 2005, the chart continues to increase and peaks in 2014 at $2.20 per pound. What Influences Honey Prices? The U.S. and international honey markets are complex, and the intricate details are not needed for the Cornell Master Beekeeper Program final exam series. One of the many factors contributing to the increased price of U.S. honey in the past 30 years is the drop in honey produced domestically. In 1987, the National Agricultural Statistics Service estimates that 3.3 million colonies produced honey in the U.S.; in 2019, this number was reduced by 15%, to 2.8 million. This is partially reflected in honey production: In 1987, 235

million pounds of honey were produced in the U.S., whereas the amount was 33% lower (157 million pounds) in 2019. At the same time, colonies that are producing honey produce less than they did in the past. In 1987, the average colony produced 71 pounds of honey; in 2019, it produced 56 pounds. The decrease in honey production is related to a variety of factors, including parasites, disease, pesticides, management practices, and shifts from honey-focused operations to pollination-focused operations. Each year, U.S. citizens are steadily increasing their honey consumption. In 2016, the average U.S. citizen consumed 1.60 pounds of honey (up from 1.20 in 2010), whether in the form of table honey, baked goods, processed foods, or candies. To fill the market’s supply for honey, the U.S. imports it from a variety of different countries; in fact, the majority of honey consumed in the U.S. is of international origin! In 2009, the U.S. produced $208 million in honey, while the value of honey imported into the U.S. from other countries was $220 million. The countries that export their honey to the U.S. change slightly each year, but the biggest in 2016 were Vietnam, Argentina, India, Brazil, Canada, and Mexico, respectively. Most imported honey is extra-light amber and light amber in color. Nearly all organic honey sold in the U.S. is imported from Brazil. The amount of honey imported and exported from the U.S., as well as the price of these honeys, also influences the changes in price of U.S. honey. Until 1995, the majority of honey imported into the U.S. was from China. China is a leader in honey production, largely due to its vast land area, the climate, and its floral diversity. For many years, China was producing a big surplus of honey and selling it to the U.S. at very low prices — lower than what they would sell it for in their own country, and lower than U.S. honey prices. Selling honey for this low price began to create an unfair competition for other honeys being sold in the U.S. To oppose this, the U.S. International Trade Commission enacted antidumping laws, preventing China from simply "dumping" their excess honey on the U.S. for low prices to gain an unfair advantage in the market. Tariffs were placed on any honey that was imported from China, and they restricted the volume of Chinese honey that was allowed to enter the U.S. With these tariffs in place, China now exports very little honey to the U.S.

Read: Selling Honey as a Sideliner or Commercial Beekeeper — Influences on Market Price The U.S. and international honey ☆ Key Points markets are complex, and the intricate details are not needed for the Cornell Master Beekeeper Program final exam series. One of the many factors contributing to the increased price of The value of honey fluctuates over time as a result of supply of and demand for domestic and imported honeys. U.S. honey in the past 30 years is the drop in honey produced domestically. In 1987, the National Agricultural Statistics Service estimates that 3.3 million colonies produced honey in the U.S.; in 2019, this number was reduced by 15%, to 2.8 million. This is partially reflected in honey production: In 1987, 235 million pounds of honey were produced in the U.S., whereas the amount was 33% lower (157 million pounds) in 2019. At the same time, colonies that are producing honey produce less than they did in the past. In 1987, the average colony produced 71 pounds of honey; in 2019, it produced 56 pounds. The decrease in honey production is related to a variety of factors, including parasites, disease, pesticides, management practices, and shifts from honey-focused operations to pollination-focused operations. Each year, U.S. citizens are steadily increasing their honey consumption. In 2016, the average U.S. citizen consumed 1.60 pounds of honey (up from 1.20 in 2010), whether in the form of table honey, baked goods, processed foods, or candies. To fill the market’s supply for honey, the U.S. imports it from a variety of different countries; in fact, the majority of honey consumed in the U.S. is of international origin! In 2009, the U.S. produced $208 million in honey, while the value of honey imported into the U.S. from other countries was $220 million. The countries that export their honey to the U.S. change slightly each year, but the biggest in 2016 were Vietnam, Argentina, India, Brazil, Canada, and Mexico, respectively. Most imported honey is extra-light amber and light amber in color. Nearly all organic honey sold in the U.S. is imported from Brazil. The amount of honey imported and exported from the U.S., as well as the price of these honeys, also influences the changes in price of U.S. honey. Until 1995, the majority of honey imported into the U.S. was from China. China is a leader in honey production, largely due to its vast land area, the climate, and its floral diversity.

For many years, China was producing a big surplus of honey and selling it to the U.S. at very low prices — lower than what they would sell it for in their own country, and lower than U.S. honey prices. Selling honey for this low price began to create an unfair competition for other honeys being sold in the U.S. To oppose this, the U.S. International Trade Commission enacted antidumping laws, preventing China from simply "dumping" their excess honey on the U.S. for low prices to gain an unfair advantage in the market. Tariffs were placed on any honey that was imported from China, and they restricted the volume of Chinese honey that was allowed to enter the U.S. With these tariffs in place, China now exports very little honey to the U.S. Bee hives placed in canola fields in Luoping, China. Read: Selling Honey as a Sideliner or Commercial Beekeeper — Honey Grades and Standards Currently, there is no official definition ☆ Key Points or standard for honey in the United States; honey is covered under the same general regulations as all other foods. However, voluntary honey grade USDA guidelines grade and classify honey based on color and clarity. standards have been developed by the USDA to designate the quality of bottled honey for sale. Beekeepers can order a grading kit to assist them in grading their honey, then label their honey for sale accordingly. The person who packages the honey determines the grade that appears on the label. This grading system is voluntary; it is not enforced or verified by the USDA. The grading system is based on points accumulated for moisture content, clarity, defects, flavor, and aroma. It does not take into account the presence of pesticides or antibiotics, nor does it consider purity (which can be reduced with the presence of added sweeteners like high-fructose corn syrup). The total score after adding points in each of these categories determines the grade of the honey. Grade A honey scores a minimum of 90 points, Grade B honey scores a minimum of 80 points, Grade C scores a minimum of 70 points, and any honey with fewer than 70 points is considered substandard. The USDA’s honey grading system was developed in 1985; it is helpful to become familiar with the criteria that it assesses.

Honey in a variety of colors and grades. Color Classifications The range of color and flavor of honeys depends on the source of the nectar gathered by the honey bees. There is a large range of variation — the National Honey Board states that there are more than 300 unique types of honey available in the U.S., each originating from a unique floral source. With colonies typically gathering nectar from a variety of sources each day, the number of potential honey blends is essentially infinite! Honey color ranges from nearly colorless to dark brown, and its flavor varies from delectably mild to distinctively bold. As a general rule, light-colored honey is milder in taste and dark-colored honey is stronger, but there are exceptions. Honey is produced in every U.S. state, but, depending on the location of the flora, certain types of honey are produced only in a few regions. The color of honey does not influence its grade, but there are specific color classifications that should be included on the label. The color designations include the following, from lightest to darkest: water white extra-white white extra-light amber light amber amber dark amber

Honey color can be classified in two ways: using the Pfund scale or using the optical density scale. The Pfund scale uses visual observations of a honey sample placed in an instrument. The honey color is matched to a specific color on a color spectrum chart that ranges from light to dark. The color chart is 140 millimeters long. The score is determined based on how many millimeters the color of the honey sample is from the beginning of the color chart. A color close to zero is water white, while a color close to 140 is dark amber. There is a bit of subjectivity to using this method; the Pfund scale is not the approved method for color classification by the USDA. Photo Credit: Betterbee More modern and precise technology involves various instruments that measure the optical density of the honey. These instruments provide a reading based on the degree of light intensity loss that occurs when a light is passed through the honey. Lower numbers, close to zero, are seen in water-white honey, whereas numbers above 3 are seen in amber honeys. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Additional Hive Products Honey is only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the products that can be harvested from the hive! Whether beekeepers are looking to produce value-added products for their businesses, or to simply have fun while developing new skills along the way, the number of products from the hive and ways to incorporate them into our lifestyles are nearly endless. In this module, we will explore the most common products harvested from the hive and evaluate the scientific evidence behind using them for medicinal purposes. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Beyond Honey Honey is far from the only hive product ☆ Key Points that is useful and valuable to humans. Following honey, the most common is beeswax, which has hundreds of uses and, although it has been superseded by synthetic materials in many applications, is still the best medium Humans utilize many products from the bee hive. The use of bee hive products in human health and medicine is called apitherapy. for candles as well as an ingredient in a range of beauty products. Wax is typically a part of honey competitions at fairs and conferences. Less-common products include the pollen pellets collected by bees, propolis, royal jelly, and bee venom. These, along with honey, are marketed for their health and medicinal benefits, collectively known as apitherapy. However, these products tend to enjoy an outsized reputation, which has paradoxically eroded many people’s faith in what these products actually are and what they can do. Master Beekeepers have a role to play in helping consumers separate the science from the myths.

Hive products clockwise from top: pollen, honey, propolis capsules, beeswax candle. The scientific research on hive products is limited for a number of reasons. There are the usual caveats about the placebo effect; the limitations of testimonials; and the necessity of large-scale, rigorous scientific studies. It is also difficult to ensure uniformity in hive products, as they vary widely based on environmental conditions and seasonality, as well as other differences among colonies. Some researchers point to the difficulty that the pharmaceutical industry would have in patenting and making profitable bee products (relative to synthesized compounds), which tends to suppress lines of research. In short, further study is needed to more conclusively prove which effects are consistent and which are not. Importantly, although some products may be beneficial for some people, they may also be dangerous: Bee venom can be lethal at high doses, and ingesting hive products may trigger allergies (although this is statistically less likely than the most common food allergies). Less dramatic but more common is the misconception that these products are natural and therefore organic or free of pesticides or other contaminants. Even if a colony is managed for pests and diseases without chemical treatments, it is exposed to whatever is being sprayed or planted in the two- to three-mile radius around the hives; there are vanishingly few places in the U.S. without any such chemicals. Collecting these materials from the hive requires attentive care, good nutrition, and careful timing — the more of these products that are harvested, the more careful management needs to be in order not to negatively impact the health of the hive. Some subspecies of Apis mellifera collect and produce more propolis, or can be bred to produce more royal jelly or collect more pollen, so a small business with these hive products would also be aided by keeping the most productive subspecies or stocks.
