Read: Rendering Beeswax When extracting honey, the beeswax cappings can be saved, cleaned, and melted into wax blocks, which can be used by the beekeeper or sold. The process of removing and processing beeswax is called rendering beeswax. Fresh wax cappings are the cleanest wax in the hive. Older wax from other parts of the hive, particularly the brood nest, is darker and filled with debris such as larval feces and cocoons. Nonetheless, with lots of processing, some beekeepers do clean it and use it. No matter the origins of the wax, rendering and filtering it is important for beauty products, competitions, and candles. It should also be processed soon after removing it from the hive: While wax moths and other pests may ruin combs, they do not go after solid blocks of wax. Removing uncapped honey/nectar and other perishable debris before they spoil also helps preserve the wax’s color and aroma. Wax is best processed in stainless-steel, aluminum, tin, enamel, or ceramic containers; iron, brass, steel, or copper may stain the wax. Care should be taken with temperature. Wax heated over 185°F (85°C) may discolor. It should never be heated directly; only with a double boiler or other indirect setup. It is highly flammable and may ignite if it gets too hot or is splattered onto an open flame. Also, wax that cools too quickly may crack, bubble, or shrink.

Read: Methods of Rendering Beeswax for Hobby Operations For beekeepers with only a few hives, ☆ Key Points wax rendering is simple and requires little equipment. The cappings are collected in a small tank (either plastic or stainless steel) and allowed to sit for a few hours, as they still contain a substantial amount of honey. The The equipment used to render beeswax depends on the operation size. Wax melts and flows freely at 143– 149°F but can discolor above 185°F. uncapping tank has a metal grid that allows the wax to remain on top and honey to drip out and gather below. Slumgum is the name for the debris filtered out of beeswax. The honey is collected out of a spout at the bottom of the tank. The wax cappings can then be gathered and rinsed or soaked in water to remove any remaining honey. From there, they can be melted using the stovetop or placed in a solar wax melter. ▶ Stovetop Melting The simplest technique to process the wax is to wrap the cappings in tightly tied cheesecloth and filter them over a stovetop in a big metal pot. The pot is filled with water and the cheesecloth with the wax is placed in the water. The water is heated on low heat and the wax melts through the cheesecloth, leaving any debris inside the cloth. The clean wax floats on the water as it hardens and can easily be removed after it has cooled. If any debris enters the water, it either sinks to the bottom of the pot or aggregates on the underside of the wax. It can be scraped off when the wax re-hardens. The remaining debris in the cheesecloth is called slumgum; it is a brown-black sludge that contains bee body parts, honey bee and wax moth cocoons, and other debris. This slumgum can be discarded or used in small pieces (or dirty filters) for lighting smokers. Slumgum may contain disease (AFB) spores and should be kept away from bees.

▶ Solar Wax Melting Many beekeepers use solar wax melters, which can be made at home or purchased from bee supply companies. Specific designs vary widely, but in general, these are shallow, sealed boxes with glass or clear plastic lids that concentrate the sun’s heat to melt the wax over several hours. The melted wax drips down a metal tray and through a filter (if one is added), collecting in a small container. Once the wax is hardened, the beekeeper can easily remove the wax blocks. Slumgum remains trapped by the filter or on the tray and can be easily scraped off and discarded. While simple and cheap, solar wax melters are inefficient in terms of the percentage of clean wax rendered from the cappings (meaning that the wax content of the remaining slumgum is high). They are also more difficult to control the heat and need to be monitored so that they do not reach temperatures high enough to discolor the wax. Left: Wax placed in a solar wax melter without the screen in place. As wax melts, it drips down the metal tray into the collection tin on the left side. Right: The melter with the solar screen in place. Methods for Large-Scale Operations In large-scale operations that routinely uncap hundreds or thousands of frames, a large amount of cappings builds up quickly in the uncapping tank ▶

and must be processed efficiently. This honey-wax slurry can be pushed along a pipe with an auger into a machine called a wax spinner or a honey/wax separator. The wax spinner is a large cylindrical device that works similarly to a washing machine on the spin cycle. The wax slurry is deposited on top of a stainless-steel spinning reel with very small perforations. The honey is flung out of the perforations as the reel spins, collecting at the base of the spinner and eventually flowing through a pipe to a sump or tank (settling tank, filtering tank, or bottling tank, depending on the operation). The wax cappings too big to fit through the perforations collect on the reel and can later be scraped off. The cappings are fairly dry after being spun. The honey/wax separator is a large centrifuge that is also very effective at separating honey from wax. The honey-wax mixture drops into the centrifuge and is flung onto the inner walls. Wax sticks to the walls and is later removed with rotary knives to drop out of the bottom of the centrifuge, where it is quite dry. The honey flows downward into an outer collection rim of the drum and is pumped to a sump, strainer, or settling tank. The wax cappings can then be transferred to a wax melting tank. The wax is slowly heated (via a water-jacket system or radiant heat) to 143–149°F (62–65°C) until it melts and flows through a series of stainless-steel filters to remove any particles. When the wax melts, any remaining honey and debris are separated from it. The wax floats above the honey and can be drained as a liquid into containers through a spout. Honey (often caramelized, darkened, and unusable after the heat) flows out a separate spout. In a few minutes, the wax begins to harden into a wax block. The wax blocks can be sold as is, or the beekeeper can further process them to create candles or other value-added products. The remaining slumgum, in large enough amounts, can be sold to a more efficient wax-rendering operation or discarded. Back to Table of Contents

Read: The Many Uses of Beeswax Beeswax has a long and storied history. ☆ Key Points Its uses were manifold: sealing envelopes, waterproofing and caulking, embalming, etc. The soaring popularity of beekeeping during WWII had much to do with the use of wax in the war effort (as well as the high price of honey). Today, beeswax has been replaced in many applications by Beeswax can be used for a variety of purposes including candles, beauty products, lubricant, food covering, and furniture polish. Over time, beeswax products can develop “bloom” that can be removed with a soft cloth. synthetic and petroleum-based waxes (such as paraffin), but it is used for a range of beauty products, including lip balms, hand creams and cold creams, makeup, and soaps. It can also be used as a furniture polish; for lubricating stuck zippers or skis; in art; or as hive foundation, crayons, cheese coatings, coatings on fruits, and more. Beeswax is often shown competitively at fairs and conferences. Different categories include wax in blocks, carved/molded artistic figures, candles, and products. Entries of wax are judged based on their cleanliness, uniformity — including an absence of cracks — and color. Sometimes aroma and artistic design are also criteria.

Wax can easily become contaminated by in-hive or environmental toxins, including agricultural pesticides and miticides in the hive. As a lipophilic (fat-loving) substance, it absorbs fat-soluble toxins (more than honey or adult bees). This includes wax purchased as comb foundation from bee supply companies. Note that the cloudy, whitish “bloom” on wax that develops over months or years is normal (and, in fact, indicates that a product is made all or in part from pure beeswax) and can be rubbed off with a soft cloth. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: The Many Uses of Beeswax — Making Candles Candles are probably the most iconic ☆ Key Points use for beeswax. Compared to candles made from paraffin and vegetable/palm waxes, pure beeswax candles burn longer and create less smoke. There are a variety of candles Pure beeswax candles burn longer and produce less smoke than paraffin and vegetable wax candles. that can be made with beeswax, such as votive candles, pillar candles, and candles poured into glass jars or molds. Here we will explore the traditional form of beeswax candles: dipped taper candles. Explore the process in this video with Ann Sill, an award-winning candlemaker for Ryan Apiaries in New York State. Video Transcript We're now going to make dipped beeswax candles, which, in my mind, are the perfect use of beeswax, and the perfect candle. So what we have here is a homemade candle melter. Read: Pollen Pollen is a high-value hive product that ☆ Key Points can be collected and sold by beekeepers. Its most common uses are Pollen is a protein-rich food. as nutritional supplements for humans, feed for bees during times of low protein availability, and supplements for other animals such as horses. It is normally sold in small pellets — the tiny, intact balls of pollen that the bees bring in on their corbiculae — but can also be added to other foods or mixed with honey. The pollen collected by bees comes from a variety of plants in a range of environmental conditions and is therefore enormously variable. Indeed, bees prefer a mixture of pollen from multiple sources to a uniform source. Even in the same place and at the same time of year, two neighboring colonies may find different sources of pollen and bring back a very different composition of pollen to the hive. Pollen is therefore difficult to characterize in definite terms, making scientific research about its medicinal effects in humans less conclusive. However, its general composition has been established as a mix of protein, carbohydrates, starches, fats, vitamins, and minerals. The table below outlines the breakdown of pollen's nutrients.

Pollen Composition Component Average Proportion Protein 23.7% Carbohydrates 27% Lipids 4.8% Vitamins and Minerals 4.6% Pollen is considered a protein-rich food. For comparison, a 3.5-ounce serving of pollen contains 24 grams of protein, while a piece of chicken of the same weight contains 27 grams of protein (mind you, no one consumes that much pollen in one sitting). It has trace amounts of the B vitamins and Vitamin A, as well as the minerals calcium, copper, iron, magnesium, manganese, potassium, and zinc. In addition, it has low levels of sodium. Pollen’s levels of Vitamins D, E, and K, however, are low or entirely lacking. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Medicinal Properties of Pollen Some people who practice alternative ☆ Key Points medicine recommend consuming honey bee pollen for treating various conditions, including gastrointestinal issues, joint pain, cancer, cancer There is no clinical evidence to suggest consuming pollen can help treat medical conditions. treatment side effects, premenstrual syndrome, aging, and as an athletic performance enhancement. The most commonly invoked benefit of pollen (whether consumed straight or in a local honey) is its potential to help relieve or reduce allergies to airborne pollen, or hay fever. The recommended dosages vary, but are usually around one to two tablespoons of pollen per day. To date, there is insufficient evidence to support using honey bee pollen for any of these conditions. Although it is rare, consuming pollen can cause serious allergic reactions in people who have pollen allergies. While most bee pollen is from insect-pollinated plants, it can contain small amounts from wind-pollinated plant as well (the variety that causes most human allergies). Several cases of anaphylactic shock have occurred from people consuming bee pollen in an effort to treat their seasonal allergies. Despite the lacking science, there is a good market for bee pollen at farmers' markets and health food stores. Beekeepers should be careful to never advertise their pollen for sale to be used as a treatment for allergies, and they should be ready to openly discuss the risk of allergic reactions to those who wish to purchase it from them for this purpose. The most common side effect of ingesting pollen is stomach upset and gastrointestinal problems. Should anyone wish to consume pollen, they should ease their way into the dosage to minimize these reactions. Start with a tiny pinch and increase the dose slowly until able to consume one or two tablespoons. Anyone who plans on consuming bee pollen should speak to a physician beforehand. Read: Harvesting Pollen Pollen can be harvested from hives ☆ Key Points using pollen traps (available from most bee equipment companies). There are various pollen traps on the market, including ones mounted beneath a hive, on top of a hive, or directly over the entrance. Each of these traps either reroute the bees through a new Pollen traps should only be engaged temporarily so as to not interfere with colony nutrition and brood rearing. Freezing pollen can preserve its nutritional content. entrance into the hive or partially block the main entrance, forcing incoming foragers to squeeze through wire mesh screens large enough to allow bees through but small enough to strip off the foragers’ pollen loads. In this way, pollen traps collect up to 70% of the pollen that comes into the hive. Pollen traps come with switches or parts that allow the trap to be engaged (allowing pollen to be trapped) or disengaged (allowing bees to enter freely and preventing pollen from being trapped). When the trap is engaged, the pollen pellets accumulate in the tray, which needs to be emptied every two days to reduce mold growth and pests, and daily if conditions are damp.

Pollen collected in the tray of a pollen trap. The amount of pollen that can be collected in a trap varies greatly and is generally between two and six pounds per colony per year. They should only be used during heavy pollen flows, as colonies require nearly all the pollen they collect during scarcer conditions. Furthermore, pollen traps should not be placed on weak colonies, as pollen is needed to grow the population, or on colonies while they receive mite treatments. Pollen traps placed on hives in pollination or adjacent to agricultural fields may collect pollen with more pesticides than those placed on hives surrounded by unmanaged natural areas. Limiting the amount of pollen coming into a hive stresses a colony and can impact brood rearing. There are no specific recommendations for how long a trap should be engaged. Cornell University suggests keeping a trap engaged for no longer than seven to ten days at a time to allow enough nutrition for the colony. If a trap is going to be activated for longer than that, beekeepers can provide the colony with a pollen substitute to help with brood rearing. As soon as pollen is collected from the tray, it should be cleaned. This is accomplished by picking out all the pieces of bee body parts and other debris by hand or sift. After cleaning the pollen, place it immediately in the freezer to retain its nutrients and kill any potential pest insect eggs that could be present. If pollen is left unfrozen and sitting at room temperature, it will lose 76% of its nutritional content after one year. Pollen can be removed from the freezer the night before it is packaged or consumed. To maintain freshness, beekeepers should only package the amount of pollen they can expect to sell fairly quickly. Encourage customers to keep the pollen in the freezer and to thaw small quantities at a time when they are ready to consume some. Some beekeepers choose to dry pollen instead, placing it in a food dehydrator until much of the moisture is removed. Drying pollen in this way can cause it to become crunchier and less

able to dissolve in other foods. The method of preserving pollen depends on the beekeeper's preferences. Debris (as shown here) should be removed from pollen before it is stored or sold. After pollen is processed in this way, it can be placed in clean glass jars for sale. Only intact pollen pellets should be in the jar, as an excess of pollen powder is generally not attractive to consumers and can affect the marketability of the product. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Propolis Propolis has long endured a bad ☆ Key Points reputation among beekeepers as the sticky stuff that gums up frames and other hive equipment. Indeed, Propolis has antibacterial and antifungal properties. beekeepers have over the centuries consciously or unconsciously selected for bees that collect and produce relatively little propolis. But propolis has an important function: It is what the bees use — a mixture of resins collected from trees and wax — to seal holes, line the interior of the hive, and entomb intruders living or dead (e.g., a “prison” for small hive beetles). New research by Dr. Marla Spivak’s team at the University of Minnesota has shown the benefits of propolis to honey bees in protecting their hives from chalkbrood and AFB, thanks to its antibacterial and antifungal properties. This stands to reason, given the origin of the resin in propolis as a plant defense of its young buds and wounds. Like pollen, the chemical composition of propolis within a hive or an apiary varies widely, depending on from which plants the bees have foraged the resins.

Propolis has properties that make it an antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory agent. It is used in alternative medicine for treating wounds and burns, sore throats, and stomach ulcers. Topical applications, including dental ones, are the most promising, but as some people may be allergic to propolis or other hive components that are mixed in, care should be taken when ingesting or topically using a propolis product. The most wellresearched avenue for propolis in human medicine is its use in oral health. In laboratory studies, propolis has been shown to kill several species of gram-positive bacteria and microorganisms common in human mouths and has therefore been incorporated in some toothpastes and oral rinses. Small clinical trials with humans, however, fail to show strong support for its use to prevent cavities or help cure oral infections. Larger and more robust clinical trials are needed before propolis can be recommended as a definitively helpful product in human medicine. Propolis can also be marketed for beekeepers to use as a stain for their hives, supplementing the natural propensity of their bees to propolize the interior and lowering demands on the bees’ immune systems. Thus, propolis can be sold fresh or powdered, in a tincture, or as an ingredient in a range of products (ointments, creams, and wood finishes) to be applied topically to humans or applied to wood. Read: Harvesting Propolis For most home uses, chips of propolis ☆ Key Points can simply be scraped off from wherever it has accumulated in the hive, although this propolis is usually mixed with wax, some wood particles, Harvesting propolis is accomplished by scraping it from the hive or by using a propolis trap. and other debris and may need to be cleaned before being used. These propolis scrapings can be soaked in warm water several times to help dislodge any debris inside. Propolis pieces sink, while other debris tends to float. Larger amounts of pure propolis can be collected with a propolis trap laid across the top bars of a hive (replacing the inner cover) at any time during the active season. These traps look like queen excluders, but the openings are smaller than bee space, meaning that the worker bees cannot fit through them and they are stimulated to fill the holes with propolis. Once removed, the trap is frozen to kill any pest insect eggs and make the propolis brittle so that it cracks off the trap when the trap is flexed or rapped sharply against another surface. If beekeepers plan to sell propolis, they should use a propolis trap for a cleaner product, rather than simply using the scrapings off various hive equipment.

Read: Preparing Propolis Some beekeepers sell dried propolis to ☆ Key Points healthcare suppliers to create propolis capsules to be consumed. These are made by grinding frozen propolis with a pestle and mortar to a fine dust. Propolis can be incorporated into capsules or tinctures for human consumption. More commonly, beekeepers produce propolis extracts to sell as a specialty item. A propolis extract is created by adding propolis to high-proof grain alcohol (not to be confused with rubbing or other kinds of alcohol that can be toxic for human consumption!) to extract and dissolve compounds from the propolis. There are many recipes online and in books, but commonly a 5–30% concentration propolis solution (by weight) is created by adding it to grain alcohol and placing it in a closed container. This solution is allowed to sit for two weeks in the dark at room temperature, until the solution has taken on the color of the propolis (often brown or red). After this time, the solution is filtered through fine filter paper to remove any chunks or debris and is bottled in small, dark glass dropper bottles. The alcohol preserves the propolis extract for over one year. On its own, a few drops of this extract can be consumed as a tincture. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Royal Jelly Royal jelly is a complex and nutritious ☆ Key Points blend of sugars, proteins, fatty acids, amino acids, vitamins, and salts. While royal jelly helps queens live an order of magnitude longer than their workersisters, its effects in humans are much less well understood and not nearly so The most common uses for royal jelly are in nutrition, cosmetics, and queen rearing. Royal jelly is the hive product that commands the highest sale price. dramatic. Still, the product commands a high price as a nutritional supplement and an ingredient in Royal jelly is harvested from queen larvae cups. cosmetics (e.g., creams and masks). Of course, beekeepers use it to rear queens by priming cells before grafting young larvae. Nutritional Supplement As a nutritional supplement, royal jelly is commonly consumed as dried powder inside capsules, or a small spoonful of fresh jelly is dissolved under the tongue. While royal jelly does display some antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties in laboratory studies (likely from the fatty acids), there are no large-scale human clinical studies that have investigated any medical benefits. Small-scale clinical studies are exploring royal jelly's ability to help regulate blood glucose in patients with diabetes. Findings are conflicting, and more robust studies are needed before recommendations can be made.

Royal jelly nutritional capsules. Cosmetics Because royal jelly consumption stimulates cellular pathways that enable queen bees to live so long, many people believe that it has anti-aging properties that also work on humans. Royal jelly is included in face masks and moisturizes with the idea that it can help skin remain youthful. No scientific studies support this notion, yet the royal jelly cosmetic industry remains huge, especially in China and other Asian countries. China produces the most royal jelly in the world, but there is also a market in the U.S. Royal Jelly is the hive product that carries the highest value; in the U.S., one ounce of royal jelly can typically be sold for around $15.

Collecting Royal Jelly Collecting royal jelly is time consuming, although its logistics make it relatively easy to combine with a queen-rearing operation. Indeed, the steps for jelly collection are largely the same as the first few steps of queen rearing, namely, creating queenless, populous colonies with lots of nurse bees, supported by protein and carbohydrate resources to create a "starter colony." One-day-old queen larvae are grafted into queen cups along cell bars and are placed in the starter colony. When the larvae are three to four days old, the cell bars are removed. The larvae are picked out with tweezers (and are either disposed of or used in animal feed), and the royal jelly is spooned out with a small spatula or sucked out with a small vacuum device. Three- or four-day-old larvae have the most royal jelly in their cups; harvesting jelly from younger or older larvae give smaller yields. Seasonality is also important: Queen rearing — and, by extension, the production of royal jelly — is easiest in the spring swarm season. Royal jelly production requires some specialized equipment over and beyond what is necessary for queen rearing, particularly items that can handle small quantities with exact measurements: an accurate scale, small storage containers, extraction tools, and a freezer. The jelly should be frozen or refrigerated immediately. When frozen, it retains its nutrients for one year. When refrigerated, it retains its nutrients for four months. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Venom Most beekeepers take measures to ☆ Key Points avoid being stung. But some beekeepers specialize in the production of bee venom for human medicine. Many studies with animals have demonstrated bee venom has anti- Bee venom injections are used to treat bee sting allergies. Venom is most commonly collected through the electroshock method. inflammatory and pain-relieving effects. This is true of extracted venom (purified and usually diluted) injected into a patient, as well as live bee stings, but not whole-body extract injections (bees crushed, blended, and clarified), which are ineffective. The clearest benefit of bee venom is, unsurprisingly, in treating bee sting allergies (immunotherapy). This is usually done by injecting patients with very low doses of venom and gradually increasing the dosage over a period of days or weeks to desensitize them, followed by maintenance injections for several years. This is expensive, complicated, and labor intensive to do correctly for individuals who suffer from life-threatening allergic reactions to bee stings, but clinical studies have found that venom injections are effective. Because of the risk of fatal allergic reactions, immunotherapy should only be conducted under the care of a physician. Aside from immunotherapy, the most thoroughly researched applications for bee venom are for rheumatoid arthritis. Because venom has been shown to have anti-inflammatory properties in animals, there is the potential that it can help with inflammatory diseases. To date, only a few small-scale clinical trials have been conducted, but these have yielded promising results. More robust large-scale clinical studies are needed to verify these results before recommendations can be made. As always, caution should be exercised when using venom. Medical professionals should oversee treatments. Allergic reactions can be fatal.

Venom extraction from a colony. Photo Credit: Timothy Ferris. Extracting Venom Since venom collection began in the 1930s, a variety of methods have been developed. Perhaps the most painstaking was by carefully squeezing several bees, one at a time, until a single drop of venom collected at their sting tips that could be gathered. Today, the most common method is to use the electroshock method. In this method, a tray-like device containing several wires placed in parallel lines over a glass plate is positioned at

the entrance of the hive. Electricity is turned on to run through the wires, which agitates any bees that leave the hive and come in contact with it. Momentarily, many bees can be stinging these wires, as alarm pheromone attracts more defenders. The bees do not lose their stinger during this process and therefore survive. With each sting they dispense a portion of their venom, which collects on a glass plate beneath the wires. The electricity is run for about 15 minutes at a time (for up to three rounds, totaling 45 minutes), and then the tray is removed and the venom is allowed to dry into crystals. The crystals are collected and are often stored in the freezer to maintain freshness. It is estimated that it takes about one million bee stings to produce one gram of dry venom. Venom collection is not very common, and there is not a large market for it in the U.S. It is currently used mainly for human medicine. In this YouTube video, Timothy Ferris, owner of Extract and Box Ltd, describes the process of venom collection. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Mead Mead is an ancient drink that is ☆ Key Points underappreciated! A simple fermented beverage with optional flavoring from fruits, spices, and even grains, a fine Mead is an alcoholic beverage made with fermented honey. mead is as good as any wine. Mead can be dry or sweet based on the brewing and bottling processes, strongly or subtly alcoholic, and sparkling or still. Its flavor is infinitely variable, based on the assortment of monofloral honeys used. Commercial meads are still relatively rare; a majority of mead lovers brew their own small batches at home. Mead making is not a quick endeavor — most require at least six months to ferment — but it is simple, and there is much room for variation once the basics have been perfected. In essence, mead is simply spoiled honey. Being hygroscopic, exposed honey attracts water from the surrounding atmosphere. When the water content of honey increases beyond 18%, it becomes susceptible to microbial growth from bacteria, fungi, yeasts, and other microorganisms. Yeasts are the primary microbes responsible for converting sugars into alcohol; however, they require nutrients as well as the proper conditions in order to do so. There are many kinds of yeasts in the environment that foragers are exposed to and bring back to colony. These yeasts are incorporated or trapped in the honey as it is ripened. When water is added to raw honey, mead is produced as the sugars present in honey are converted to alcohol by yeasts that have been activated in the honey. Since raw and minimally processed honey already contain yeast and sugars, it is thought that mead may be the oldest alcoholic beverage.

▶ Read: Making Mead — The Basics Mead making is simple — or at least it can be. Raw honey already comes prepackaged with two of the three main ingredients: honey (sugars) and yeast. To make a basic mead, beekeepers can just extract their honey and add water; it's as easy as that. However, if beekeepers want to make mead that is even more palatable, there are additional things to consider, such as honey, yeast, equipment, and good fermentation practices. Honey First, not all honey is created equal. Although every beekeeper knows honey comes from nectar, it takes time and experience to learn which flowers contribute to different honey flows and when. In central New York, the major honey flows come from clovers, black locust trees, basswood/linden trees, knotweed, goldenrod, and aster. All of these honeys produce distinctly flavored meads, provided they are treated properly throughout fermentation. Linden is a prized mead-making honey in much of Europe, as its pronounced minty flavors tend to carry through to the beverage. Goldenrod honey is a regional favorite with which to ferment, as it yields fruity and malty notes in its resulting mead. Yeast Second, not all yeasts are equal in the eyes of a mead maker. Thanks to the wine and beer industries, many strains of yeast are available that have distinct fermentation characteristics that factor into the production and, ultimately, the taste of the beverage. For instance, temperature influences the fermentation speed and final flavor profile of the mead; most yeast strains have a recommended temperature range for fermentation. In addition, the alcohol and sugar tolerance determine how much alcohol and sugar any particular strain of yeast can handle before they either stop or start fermenting. Most people use these tolerances to understand the upper alcohol limit for a particular mead recipe; for example, many beer yeasts stop fermentation after 7–10% alcohol by volume in solution. ▶

Different yeasts also vary in their “congener profiles.” Congeners are compounds other than alcohol and carbon dioxide that yeast produce during fermentation, and they can affect the flavor, mouthfeel, color, and overall complexity of any fermented beverage. Some of the most recognizable congeners are flavor compounds such as diacetyl (buttered popcorn), acetaldehyde (green apple), 4-vinyl-guaiacol (clove), and isoamyl acetate (banana). The same congener can be perceived as either desirable or a fault in the beverage, depending on personal preference. Lastly, nutrient requirement is of the utmost importance when making mead. Other than sugar, nitrogen is the most important nutrient needed for fermentation, and the right amount of nitrogen is needed to feed the yeast. Because honey is low in nitrogen-containing compounds, the mead maker must add some in a specific dose in the early stages of fermentation. Protocols detail the doses and proper times to add the nitrogen. Taking good care of the yeast requires being mindful of all of these factors. However difficult it may be to master, learning to achieve a balance with the yeast will bring the mead to new levels and audiences. ▶ Equipment Yeast (left) and yeast nutrient (right). Photo Credit: Michael Rowell

▶ Basic meads do not require much equipment; a fermenter, airlock, and mixing implement are the three main pieces of equipment necessary for a small batch of mead. However, it is helpful to have a kitchen scale, a spray bottle, and a racking cane (a tube used for siphoning liquids) as well. These items allow mead makers to better implement and record recipes, sanitize equipment, and transfer mead to another container after primary fermentation as well as to the final bottle. Procedure Honey and water are mixed together in the fermenter; in a separate bowl, yeast is activated by providing it with warm water and some nutrients. After the yeast is activated, it can be combined with the honey-water mixture and sealed with an airlock. Over the course of a few days, initial nutrients can be added according to the specific recipe the mead maker is following. After the fermentation stops and the yeast settles, the mead can be transferred to another container, where the yeast is allowed to fully settle out of the solution. After this step, the mead maker conditions and ages the mead however they choose. Additions can be made here, such as oak, spices, fruits, or clarifying agents. When the mead has been sufficiently conditioned, the bottles are filled and stored. The mead should be allowed to sit and age in the bottle for one month to one year or longer. Aging time is determined by frequent tasting; when the mead maker is satisfied with its flavor, the mead is declared "ready to drink."

▶ Mead fermenter (left), floating airlock (middle), and mixing implements (right) for making mead. Photo Credit: Michael Rowell. Mead Styles Since mead has been around for so long, it is no wonder that humans have experimented with putting almost everything imaginable into it! In most cases there are names associated with various additives or styles: cyser (apples), pyment (grapes), acerglyn (maple syrup), metheglin (herbs/spices), melomel (fruits), rhodomel (rose), braggot (barley/grains), poltorak (Polish mead made with a honey:water ratio of 2:1), bochet (caramelized honey), etc. Conversely, traditional or “show meads” are simple meads that do not feature any additives; they consist of water, honey, and yeast. In addition to the limitless possibilities for additives, there are many stylistic choices that can affect the final product. Meads can be clarified and filtered to be brilliantly clear, or they can be left unfiltered and hazy for a rustic, or saison, style. Mead can be fortified with spirits for a port style, or aged in a solera system to achieve a sherry-like flavor profile. It can be made sweet, semi-sweet, or dry, and carbonated or still. One stylistic choice that is distinctively tied to mead is aging. Short meads, much like beers, are to be consumed almost immediately after production. Most meads are similar to wines in that they can be aged past two years and grow in complexity. Mead is distinct in that

there is a category called grand meads, which are meant to be aged for 12 to 20 years before reaching peak flavor and complexity! Many meads take on more nutty, caramel, and pleasant earthy aromas in this time. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Pollination Services Bees are the main insect pollinators throughout the world, and their services are critical to our agricultural systems. Wild and managed bees are estimated to contribute $20 billion to the U.S. agricultural economy and over $217 billion worldwide. Honey bees are the most common bee species used in pollination, and colonies are rented to pollinate at least 70 crops in the U.S. While many other bee species are excellent pollinators and forage in rainy and cool weather, it is very easy and convenient to bring honey bees into a crop system. Hives can be moved on trucks and placed wherever they are needed, and each hive has around 20,000 foragers that can be immediately introduced into a field. Some other bees are also managed for pollination in the U.S., though to a lesser extent than honey bees. Bumble bees are commonly used in greenhouses, especially for tomato pollination; alfalfa leafcutter bees are used to pollinate alfalfa in western U.S.; and two species of orchard bees are used to pollinate early-flowering orchard fruits. Watch: Pollination: The Birds and the Bees Pollination facilitates the sexual reproduction of plants. When an ovule becomes fertilized by pollen, it develops into a seed to generate a new plant. Many plants rely on wind or water to transfer pollen. Some examples of wind-pollinated plants include wheat, corn, rice, oats, and barley. These plants do not produce bright, attractive, fragrant flowers because they do not need to advertise for animal visitors. When you see pollen in the air and experience pollen allergies, this is mostly from windpollinated plants. Many water weeds and pond weeds use water pollination, where pollen grains are released into the water and float on the surface until they contact a flower. Most of the flowering plants in the world, however, rely on animals to pollinate; in fact, around 90% of the world’s flowering plants require animal pollination in order to reproduce. Flowers and bees have co-evolved over billions of years. Flowers attract bees through color, light patterns, and fragrance, advertising their pollen and sugary nectar. Bees, in turn, have evolved specialized anatomy to collect pollen. This video delves into flower pollination and how honey bees transfer pollen efficiently. Video Transcript Pollination is the sexual reproduction of a plant. It's the process where pollen from the male part of the flower is transferred to the female part of the flower. And this results in fertilization, where a plant sperm fertilizes a plant's egg and gives rise to the production of a seed. The male part of a flower is collectively called the stamen, and it consists of the filament, which is long stalk, and the anther, containing the pollen grains. The female part of a flower is collectively called the pistol. It consists of the stigma, which is the receptacle that receives the pollen, the ovary, and the style, which is the stock that connects the two together. The pollen grains, which contain a plant sperm, are located on the anthers of a plant, while the egg, or ovule, is located in the ovary. During pollination, bees transfer pollen grains onto the plant's stigma, where it can grow a pollen tube that travels down the style of the plant, ultimately reaching the ovary and the ovule it contains. The sperm fertilizes the ovule, and a seed is eventually produced. After pollination, the petals fall off the flower. The seed begins to form and the plant's ovary begins to swell, turning into a fruit such as an apple, pepper, cucumber, or into a pod.

Some plant species can reproduce through self pollination or wind pollination, where they don't need bees' help to generate seeds. Corn, wheat, rice, soybeans, and sorghum are all examples of plants that do not need pollinators. The majority of flowering plants, however, need pollinating animals in order to help them transfer pollen grains to the stigmas of flowers on other plants of the same species. And without these pollinators, the plants would not be able to reproduce. Flowering plants have been evolving with bees for millions of years, and have developed specialized structures, colors, sizes, odors, and carbohydrate-rich nectar rewards to attract bees and other animals. In turn, bees have developed specialized tongues, hairs, and pollen carrying structures that enable them to collect pollen efficiently. And this evolved dependence of bees and flowers is truly one of the most remarkable and beautiful relationships on the planet. And honey bees have evolved to be excellent pollinators. The first behavior that makes them such great pollinators is their communication of food sources. Scout bees are the first to discover a pollen or nectar rich plant in bloom, and they return back to the hive to tell their sisters all about the food source, through the waggle dance, through the plant's odors that they carry back on their bodies, and by sharing small samples of nectar with them. In a short period of time, this communication can result in a plant becoming covered with bees, foraging on its nectar and pollen, and visiting nearby plants of the same species. This helps the plant by greatly enhancing the likelihood of pollination. It has a lot of helpers. Scouts are excellent at locating the most abundant and sweetest nectar sources near the hive. Next, bees' behavior to actively collect pollen, as well as their hairy bodies, helps them to transfer pollen from plant to plant. While collecting pollen, the bee's body can become dusted with it, making it really easy to transfer to the stigmas of other flowers they visit. Bees visit multiple flowers in a single foraging trip, and in this way, individual bees can help pollinate flowers before returning back to the hive. Even after a forager's trip is over and she returns back to the hive, the colony is still aiding in pollination. Studies find that flower pollination is enhanced by pollen transfer within the hive. So a bee that's recently returned from foraging will come in contact with many of her estimates in the crowded hive as she walks toward a cell to deposit her pollen. In doing, so her nest mates get dusted with small amounts of pollen. And when these bees fly out to visit flowers, they can effectively pollinate them. Lastly, honey bees display floral fidelity. This means that individual bees tend to visit the same species of flower for an entire foraging trip. If the flower species is abundant, the

same bee will continue visiting that same species throughout the entire day. This benefits the plant tremendously. It means that honey bees are transferring pollen to the same species of plant, increasing the likelihood that ovules will get fertilized. For instance, it would not be beneficial for an apple tree's reproductive success if after a bee collected its pollen, it then went to visit a dandelion. Instead, traveling from apple tree to apple tree increases its chances of reproduction. By scouting out food sources that are rich pollen nectar sources, by communicating beneficial food sources to other foragers in the hive, by trapping and passing pollen in their staticky hairs, and by being loyal to a single type of flower during a foraging trip, honey bees can optimize their own food collection while inadvertently optimizing a plant's chances for reproduction. There are a variety of animals that help plants pollinate: bees, some flies, butterflies, some wasps, some beetles, and hummingbirds. Of these, bees are the superior pollinators and very efficient at collecting pollen. While butterflies and hummingbirds are iconic pollinators, they only actively collect nectar from plants; some pollen incidentally lands on their bodies and gets transferred from plant to plant while they feed on nectar. Read: Preparing Colonies for Pollination A colony ready for pollination should ☆ Key Points have a strong population and should be growing in size. Colonies with little brood production dwindle over time and may not produce a lot of foragers to be available for pollination. Strong colonies are also good for business, as growers who can see lots At minimum, pollination colonies should contain eight frames of bees and four frames of brood. Preparing strong colonies for spring pollination begins the previous autumn. of honey bees on their flowers and who experience good crop yields of high-quality fruits and vegetables will want to continue renting colonies from a beekeeper year after year. Colonies for pollination are typically organized into two double-deep Langstroth hive bodies. If the crop tends to produce enough nectar to yield a honey crop (like oranges or blueberries), beekeepers may add supers on top. Pollination colonies should contain at least eight frames of bees and at least four frames of brood when they enter pollination; however, the contract between the beekeeper and grower may vary. Below, you will explore the requirements of a colony that is ready for pollination. Bees The eight frames of bees should contain individuals of various ages: Older bees can forage immediately on the crop. Middle-aged bees will soon transition to foraging and can receive nectar from incoming foragers and build comb for storage. Younger bees can tend to the brood and keep the colony growing. If frames of bees cannot easily be counted because it is favorable weather and most of the foragers are outside, an exiting rate of 60 bees per minute with at least one-third of returning bees carrying pollen is a good indicator of a strong colony.

Brood The four frames of brood serve two purposes: Brood emits pheromone cues to stimulate foragers to collect pollen. If colonies have little brood, some beekeepers add a strip of synthetic brood pheromone to the hive to stimulate pollen collection. The product SuperBoost® is a commercially available synthetic brood pheromone product that comes in a pouch to be placed between brood frames. Brood keeps a colony growing and replaces the cohort of bees that die. Drawn Comb Several frames of drawn comb should be available: The queen should have room to lay to prevent swarming and to continue brood production. Foragers reduce pollen collecting when the brood population decreases. There should be room for nectar and pollen storage coming into the hive. Foragers reduce food collection when they are honey- or pollen-bound. Queen A strong, fertile queen should be present in the hive: She can continue brood production, contributing to a growing colony and providing impetus for foragers to collect pollen. Weak queens may be superseded, which can reduce colony productivity and growth for a short while.

Strong queens laying lots of brood often result in strong colonies, better equipped to overcome pests and some infections. Food Stores Food stores should be in the hive: The colony should have enough honey and pollen stores to fulfill their nutrition and energy needs while it is in pollination. Colonies must not be nutritionally stressed. Thirty pounds of stored food is typically expected, but the grower and beekeeper can negotiate this amount. Hives in an almond orchard. Building strong colonies for spring or summer pollination begins in the previous autumn. Ensuring colonies have enough protein (pollen or pollen substitute) and carbohydrates (honey or syrup) to survive winter and build up quickly in the spring is important. The winter cluster should be comprised of a large number of young bees. These bees require

adequate protein and fats for their development in September and October so that they are able to raise brood in late winter. In addition to fall feeding, beekeepers who prepare their colonies for pollination often begin feeding dry sugar in January and pollen patties in February. Sugar syrup feeding begins in March. These carbohydrate and protein supplements are continuously fed until the first nectar and pollen flows occur. This intensive nutritional management ensures that colonies are active and strong, with a large forager population coinciding with crop bloom. Colonies that exit winter weak but are otherwise healthy can be merged to boost the population strength. In addition to healthy, populous colonies, hive equipment should be clean and in good condition when it is brought to someone’s farmland. Colonies should be free of any observable disease and should have Varroa mite levels below the treatment threshold for the particular time of year. Colonies should be placed in farmland as soon as some of the crop flowers are already in bloom. The presence of flowers attracts foragers to that crop. If colonies are moved into a field before the crop is in bloom, the bees look for other food sources and may not visit the crop as readily once it does bloom. Colonies are typically removed just before flowering finishes or immediately after flowering finishes. The grower should inform the beekeeper when this occurs. Colonies should be removed before any post-bloom pesticides are applied to the crop. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Renting Hives — Costs Beekeepers have historically made the ☆ Key Points majority of their profits through selling honey. In recent decades, however, there has been a shift in the beekeeping industry toward providing pollination services over honey production. In fact, many commercial beekeepers focus primarily on Pollination services have shifted to become a major source of profits for beekeepers in recent years. Hive rental rates have increased dramatically over the past few decades. pollination, selling honey and wax as a small part of their business. With hive rental rates having increased so Providing pollination services can be stressful to colonies. dramatically over the past few decades, beekeepers are able to make good money renting colonies for pollination. Furthermore, this money can be made in a short period of time, as colonies may only need to be placed in a field for two weeks or so depending on the bloom period of the crop. Cost: Stress to Colonies Multiple pollination events are stressful to honey bee colonies. Beekeepers are wise to prioritize colony health, since losing a substantial number of colonies comes at a big cost. Transporting colonies can be stressful, as bees are exposed to temperature fluctuations, vibrations, and confinement for days at a time. Maintaining the brood nest temperature can be particularly difficult for bees while in transport. During almond pollination, bees may still be clustering and trying to stay warm while moving at high speeds on a truck. During summer months, colonies may have a difficult time keeping cool, unable to leave their colonies to beard or collect water. Queen losses during transport can also occur. Once placed for pollination, bees can experience nutritional deficiencies if their diet is comprised nearly entirely of one pollen source. These nutritional deficiencies are more common in large monoculture fields and less common in farmland surrounded by natural vegetation. Beekeepers can provide pollen patties during pollination to supplement bee diet.

If the grower has rented hives from several beekeepers, a colony can become exposed to Varroa mites, foulbrood, viruses, and pests from its neighboring colonies. Hives are usually placed on pallets in or adjacent to fields, with four or six colonies in close proximity. Sharing flowers, drifting, and robbing can occur, facilitating disease spread. Colonies should be carefully inspected before and after pollination to promptly manage parasites, pathogens, and pests. In addition to potential stress from disease and pests, colonies can be exposed to many pesticides, and the number of pesticides to which they are exposed grows with increasing pollination events. Pollination contracts should clearly define which pesticides can be used during pollination and whether or not the grower will compensate any colonies lost from acute pesticide poisoning events. All pesticide poisoning events should be reported to both the state apiculturist and the appropriate state department (usually the Department of Environmental Conservation [DEC] or Department of Plant Industry). Beekeepers can find the appropriate office to call for their state by consulting this Quick Guide to Reporting a Pesticide-Related Bee Kill Incident. To circumvent nutrition stress, many beekeepers place their colonies in wildflower meadows to recover between and following pollination events. There is no scientific research that has examined how many crops a colony can tolerate pollinating in one year and still overwinter healthy and strong. Many commercial beekeepers relieve overwintering stress on bees by placing them in warm winter locations

where they can continue to fly and where they can be fed and re-queened as necessary. It is up to the beekeeper to judge the health of a colony and determine whether or not the colony should continue entering new crops for pollination. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Renting Hives — Benefits A large benefit of renting hives is the profit you'll derive from it. Determining the price to rent hives takes many factors into account. First, it must be profitable for the beekeeper. Before entering a pollination contract, beekeepers should think about how much it costs them to perform the service. The following factors should be tallied: Estimations of mileage, gas, meals, and hotel stays to move colonies to and from the crop. Price of labor if help is needed. Price of transportation if trucks are to be rented. Price of syrup and pollen patties to be fed to colonies before, during, and sometimes after pollination. The pollen from some crops, such as alfalfa and blueberry, are not very nutritious for bees, and the bees can exit these crops nutritionally stressed or with limited population growth, requiring more attention from the beekeeper. Cost of miticides or other treatments that might be necessary after exiting pollination. The beekeeper’s hourly rate and number of hours they will spend preparing, moving, and placing colonies. This last point is very important: Too often beekeepers do not include the value of their own labor in the price. To determine the minimum price for a hive rental, the value that is determined from the exercise above can be divided by the number of colonies that will be rented for pollination. This number can then be compared to average rental prices in the beekeeper’s state, and both can serve as a helpful reference for price negotiations between beekeeper and grower. The National Agriculture Statistics Service (NASS) collected hive rental data for the first time in 2016. This makes it possible to know how much beekeepers were paid to rent their hives for pollinating different crops, how many acres of each crop were pollinated, and how many colonies were rented. State-specific rental rates for a particular year can be found on the NASS website, but here we present a table summarizing hive rental information for the entire U.S. Take some time to become familiar with which crops rented the most hives and which crops paid the highest hive rental prices. Average price per colony is based on 2016 NASS data. What Influences the Price of Hive Rentals? Hive rental price is dictated in part by the necessity for honey bee pollination. For instance, almond pollination in California is completely dependent on honey bees. Orchards are so vast and separated from other natural vegetation that very few wild bees visit their flowers, and the number is not sufficient to produce an almond crop. Because almond growers are so dependent on honey bees, they are willing to pay premium dollars for them. Other crops may be surrounded by natural vegetation and thus might support a robust wild bee community. In these cases, honey bees supplement the natural pollination services already occurring, and growers may pay less for honey bee hives. Pollination rates have increased drastically over the past few decades. This is most notable with almonds. The acreage of almond orchards in California has grown significantly over the years; in 1996 there were 430,000 acres, while in 2016 there were 971,000 acres! At the same time that the demand for almond pollination services was increasing, the supply of honey bee colonies available for pollination was decreasing. Beekeepers across the U.S. have been experiencing higher colony losses than normal due to a variety of factors, including parasites, pathogens, pesticides, and management practices. The dynamics between supply and demand resulted in skyrocketing rental prices. For example, in 2004 the average cost to rent one bee hive for almonds was $54, while in 2016 the average rental price was $167! This increase in price for almond pollination also helped to drive rising prices in pollination of other crops. Additionally, the percent of agricultural land since the 1960s has increased faster than the availability of honey bee colonies; this has driven growers to pay a premium price for the limited number of colonies available. Tool: Creating a Pollination Contract Like any contract, a pollination  Download the Tool contract is a legally binding document for both the grower and the beekeeper. It outlines the expectations of both parties and includes the following information: How many hives will be rented. The rental price for each hive. You can download this example pollination services contract. Beekeepers may use this template as a starting point for their own grower negotiations and edit it to suit their needs. The date the rental fee is payable. The status of those hives upon entering the crop (number of frames of bees, brood, and amount of stored food). Any cost penalties from deviations of the minimum colony status should be clearly outlined. The dates the hives will be placed and removed. Some growers do not provide specific dates, as crop flowering can vary from year to year and it can be difficult to precisely time flowering. In these cases, the grower should carefully monitor crop bloom and provide beekeepers with a notice period (for example, 48 hours) for when the hives should be delivered and removed. The application timing of specific pesticides. Whether or not the grower assumes liability if hives are damaged or stolen while on their property. The contract should outline the compensation cost of a hive that was damaged or lost in these circumstances.

Additional agreements can be negotiated by the beekeeper and grower and outlined in the contract. For instance, if a hive has fewer frames of bees or brood than expected, a specific previously agreed-upon discounted rate can be given to the grower. On the other hand, if a colony is stronger than the minimum colony status, an increase in fee could be agreed upon. If one party does not fulfill their obligations as outlined in the pollination contract, the dispute can be settled in court. In the past, many crop pollination services were done simply with a "handshake" contract. Nothing was written on paper or signed; the parties simply shook hands in agreement. The issue with these types of contracts is that individuals can misremember specific details of what was discussed. Writing down a contract ensures both individuals think precisely about specific details. Drafts can be exchanged before the contract is signed to ensure all factors are considered before the colonies are moved. With oral handshake contracts, some details might be missing that need to be resolved later. As pollination services are a business relationship between a grower and a beekeeper, we recommend that written contracts be utilized on every occasion. Witnesses should also be present to sign the contract. It is best to begin making pollination service agreements with growers before winter so the beekeeper has sufficient time to prepare colonies to be strong and healthy for spring pollination.

Read: Preparing to Transporting Hives Transporting hives for pollination is a ☆ Key Points big endeavor that requires careful preparation and planning. While this section is written from the context of pollination services, these recommendations can be used when Beekeepers must apply for the proper permits and certifications to transport bees into and out of certain states and provinces. moving colonies for any purpose, whether tracking a honey flow, changing apiaries, or moving to a new wintering site. With travel dates approaching, the beekeeper should assess the needs of the colonies and prepare the bees for travel. It is necessary that the colonies are well populated and free of disease. Their stores should be assessed and the bees should be provided supplemental sugar feed and pollen substitute if necessary. Weak colonies should be united with strong colonies a few weeks in advance to give them enough time to organize themselves. There are numerous hive configurations that are good for transportation. Typically, most are moved in two deep hive bodies, but sometimes they are shipped in a single deep, a deep and a medium, or either of these configurations with a queen excluder and a super. Hives taller than that are seldom seen in a load for travel. More importantly, uniform hive heights make the most secure load. Allowing plenty of time to prepare colonies and being thorough improves the chance for success. The colonies should have enough time to work propolis to secure the boxes, lids, and combs before loading. This reduces comb slapping and bee crunching that can occur while taking corners on the road. The risks associated with transportation of bees for pollination require vigilant monitoring and assessment. For the collective health of honey bees and preventing the spread of contagious diseases, it is the responsibility of the apiarist to be compliant with pertinent laws. At least two weeks in advance of an interstate move, the beekeeper must apply for a Certificate of Apiary Inspection for Interstate Movement of Honey Bee Colonies and Equipment through the State Department of Agriculture of the origin state. In New York State, this is acquired by calling the NYS Apiculturist. Truck drivers must always have this certificate on hand so that they can show any police officials that they are transporting a legal load. Some states, like Florida, have an agricultural station that asks for the certificate at the border.

Though the regulations address the same purpose, there is a lack of uniformity with various requirements from state to state. In California, for instance, bees must be registered with the Department of Agriculture in the destination county. Some states like Texas require numerous permits, like the Importation Permit, Exportation Permit, Bee Removal Transportation Permit, Intrastate Travel Permit, and Certificates of Health for Queen Breeders. Maryland requires the beekeeper to show a health certificate from both the beekeeper's home state and an entry permit for Maryland in order to enter. It is the responsibility of beekeepers to know the laws of the states and obtain the required permits and certificates. To ease any inspections that may occur, hive bodies and the pallets on which they are sitting should be clean, with no mud or vegetation. Any pest insects found by border guards or police officials on hitchhiking plants or mud can considerably slow (or prevent) a beekeeper’s travel through a state. Upon arrival at the pollination site, the bees should be in prime condition for inspection and for pollination. Photo Credit: Brian Evans Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Transporting Hives — Loading the Truck Honey bees are moved on all sizes of ☆ Key Points trucks, from small pickup trucks to large semi trucks that carry just under 500 hives. Whatever the size of truck or load of colonies, the considerations for transporting honey bees remain the same. Colonies should be secured to trucks with ropes and checked on frequently; certain conditions also require providing water and traveling screens. All hive entrances must be screened to prevent bees from exiting while in transit. If the weather is hot, it is prudent to replace the hive covers with traveling screens to increase ventilation (no inner cover or outer cover is placed on top of the traveling screen). Each hive receives a strap to hold together the bottom board, hive bodies, and covers. Many beekeepers staple these hive pieces together for added security. Once each hive receives a strap, it is loaded onto a truck. Depending on how many hives a beekeeper is transporting, they can be loaded by hand (with a two-person hive carrier it is possible to hand-load heavy colonies), with a boom, or with a forklift. Some beekeepers recommend leaving the engine of the vehicle running while the bees are being loaded and unloaded; they claim the vibrations seem to either stun or calm the bees, keeping them quieter than they would be with the motor off. This clip demonstrates how hives can be loaded onto a truck using a boom. Video Transcript There is no audible dialogue in this presentation. Conversation and machinery sounds are heard in the background. Two people work together in a grassy field, using a hoist to lift hives from the field onto a flatbed truck. If possible, the hives should be arranged so the combs are oriented to the direction of travel. The hive entrances face forward or backward (towards the driver or tail lights), while the broad faces of the combs should face the sides of the truck to avoid the bee-killing “comb slap” that happens if they are loaded sideways and sudden stops occur. This may

be more difficult with big loads containing hundreds of hives but is easily accomplished with smaller loads. The hives are roped or strapped to the truck or trailer for the trip. It is always good practice to first drive a few miles, then stop to retighten the straps or ropes before proceeding into the bulk of the trip. Ropes and straps should then be checked every couple hours or about every 100 miles. With big loads, additional mesh netting is thrown over all the colonies to further reduce the chance of bees escaping. The netting should be checked so it remains taut and bee tight around the bottom. This mesh should also be hosed with water occasionally to keep bees cool. Bees normally collect water when they are hot, but they do not have access to it when they are confined to their hives on trucks. With water passing through the mesh and coming in contact with the hive entrance screens, bees are able to collect water to help with thermoregulation. These tasks should be regularly and thoroughly attended while assessing the bees' needs for water. Larger operations do better by loading palletized bee hives (four or six at a time), often with the hive entrances left open. Loaded at night when all the field bees are in the hives, these colonies are then covered with a net. Even though the bees can crawl out of their hives, the bulk remain in the hive and the net prevents most escapees. Many bees become disoriented during the loading and netting. Whether the load is large or small, loading should always be done during the night. It is good practice for a team to work together to make loading bees as quick and smooth as possible. The team must dress with fully secured clothing since the bees at night are “crawly” and find their way into poorly secured coveralls and veils that are sufficient during the day. Smokers must be used liberally and kept handy. It is best to use headlamps to keep your hands free. On a tractor-trailer flatbed, a pair of beekeepers can unfold the net over the load as the forklift operator positions the bees from front to back. Once the net covers the entire load and is tucked in all around, it can be strapped down with the load. This keeps the net from blowing and flapping, while keeping the stacks of bees solidly anchored to the truck.
Back to Table of Contents Photo Credit: Brian Evans

Read: Transporting Hives — Travel Considerations Monitoring and watering the load on ☆ Key Points the road is an important consideration. Appropriate parking is also constant challenge for a driver en route with a Some beekeepers transport bees in refrigerated vans. load of bees. A collection of “hitchhiker” honey bees typically accumulates on the outside of the load. When the truck stops during daylight hours, these disoriented bees fly about and can become a nuisance if the truck is parked too near human activity. This is a challenge for fuel stops close to a place of business. A conscientious driver is constantly on the lookout for low activity and suitable facilities to top off the fuel tanks or perform other necessary maintenance on the truck. A load of bees on a flatbed trailer or truck, even in the open air, generates a lot of concentrated heat, which is hard on bees in transit, especially on hot days in full sun. To help bees stay cool in such conditions, it is necessary for the driver to park in the shade to check the bees, observe them for a nervous clamorous buzz, and provide water as needed to cool the hives. The bees should be misted and not soaked. It is helpful to have a thermometer with a probe in the center of the load. Temperatures over 100°F indicate that the bees need assistance cooling the hives. While spraying water on the hives, the driver can generally see the bees relax. Through these experiences, a beekeeper gains a sense of how to best keep them adequately supplied and calm. It is handy to carry a container of water, a hose, and a pump to spray water on the load while parked in an isolated location. On a semi, this might be a 55-gallon barrel with an electric pump. On small loads, a garden-sized sprayer with a hand pump is adequate. However, especially with tractor-trailer loads, watering is usually done at truck stops or other facilities that can provide water and a hose near appropriate parking. Grain elevators and farm supply stores in small rural towns are often good places for watering. The driver uses such isolated locations to check tires, the tautness of the straps, and the seal of the netting that prevents bees from escaping through voids. For trips longer than 500 miles, it is generally best to have a team of drivers who can switch off while continuing to travel, sleeping en route. The beekeeper-drivers should put fuel in the vehicle before loading the bees. The vehicle should be roadworthy and current with all maintenance needs before loading. Roadside mechanical problems are

challenging, and mechanics are reluctant to assist vehicles loaded with bees. Stopping en route is best done routinely and deliberately to avoid problems. The route should be thoroughly planned, including the location where the colonies are to be unloaded. The drivers should be prepared with equipment and knowledge to handle bees in case of an unpredicted weather event, mechanical problem, or traffic accident. Coveralls, smoker, and veils should be part of the general on-board tool kit. Hauling Bees With Refrigerated Trucks Many beekeepers haul hives in refrigerated trucks (also known as “reefer trucks”). The cooler temperatures help to keep bees less active, and the load is more reliably contained than with netting on a flatbed. Closing the doors to keep bees contained is also simpler than netting a flatbed load. Watering the bees in reefers is unnecessary. While it seems that the temperature of a reefer can be set to keep the bees in a constant loose cluster, the reality is that typical refrigerated vans cannot compete with the heat generated by the colonies. Colonies can increase the temperature to the point where bees are active inside the van. The bees also need fresh air and ventilation, which is not provided with most reefers. Some beekeepers have retrofitted refrigerated vans with adjustable ventilation systems and powerful refrigerator units. Their success indicates that this technology will likely be further developed and made more available in the future. Refrigerator vans need a loading dock for forklift loading and unloading. Beekeepers and drivers using reefers need to make special plans and arrangements to load and deliver their colonies. Special Transport Considerations: Hauling Nucleus Colonies and Packages Aside from providing pollination services, beekeepers may move their colonies for a variety of other reasons (tracking nectar flows, moving to wintering sites, etc.). Beekeepers who raise queens and produce nucleus and package bees have numerous occasions to haul bees to various apiaries and customers. Many of those customers also make trips to the breeder/production farms to pick up their own colonies. All of these people need to be aware of the special needs of these bees in transit. Nucleus colonies and packages are generally less stable than established colonies of bees that have fully occupied one or two deep hive bodies. Many of these bees are subject to long trips as well, such as bringing packages from southern Georgia into central New York. In such situations, nucs are handled like full colonies (as described above), keeping a keen eye on the heat. Nucleus hives and package bees can be sprayed with cool water to relieve overheating. While in transit and well watered, they typically arrange themselves in a cluster. If they are thirsty,

they break out of the cluster into a nervous clamor. When they are misted with water, they should quiet down. Package bees can be vulnerable to cold, wind, and rain; in such conditions, they should have protective side panels strapped onto the load. If the weather is severe, the driver will need to offer some protection on the top of the package as well. Such protection can be provided with plywood or cardboard panels strapped onto the load. If the weather is warm and sunny, they can be less protected but may need to be watered. Back to Table of Contents
