Module Introduction: Confidence in Communicating About Pesticides The discussion of pesticides is so common among members of the beekeeping community that it warrants its own module. Beekeepers are frequently asked about the impacts of pesticides on bees and may not feel equipped to properly answer the question. This is further complicated by the fact that research on pesticides is vast and continues to update each day, making it difficult to stay on top of the latest findings. In this module, we will discuss the research on various pesticides and how they affect bees. We will also discuss why there exists such a strong controversy about neonicotinoid pesticides as well as what recommendations you can give the public and other beekeepers to help reduce pesticide use and exposure to bees. Back to Table of Contents

Read: An Overview of Pesticides — What’s in a Pesticide? Pesticides are an integral part of ☆ Key Points conventional agriculture. Insecticides, herbicides, and fungicides help maximize crop quantity and quality by reducing the pests and diseases that Pesticide products contain active ingredients and inert ingredients; both can impact honey bee health. cause damage. Especially in today’s world of large monoculture fields, pesticides are needed to keep out the various fungal, insect, and weed pests that can flourish in these expansive systems. While nearly all pesticide research investigates products used in agricultural areas, their use is not restricted to farms. Many pesticides are also applied to urban and suburban gardens and lawns. “Pesticide” is an umbrella term that applies to insecticides (intended to kill insects), herbicides (intended to kill weeds), fungicides (intended to kill fungi), and even miticides (intended to kill mites). Pesticide products contain many ingredients, classified as active ingredients (the ingredient that causes the pest’s death) and inert or inactive ingredients. The active ingredients must be listed on the product label. Often, it comprises a very small amount (often around 5%) of the pesticide product. The majority of our understanding of how pesticide products impact honey bee health is by studying active ingredients, and we will explore these impacts in detail over the next few pages. The remaining 95% or so of pesticide formulations are inert ingredients. In the U.S., inert ingredients are not required to be listed on pesticide labels, as pesticide manufacturers consider them “trade secrets.” They are various chemicals that help deliver the pesticide and increase the efficacy of the pesticide when applied to a plant or soil. Adjuvants are a common type of inert chemical in pesticide formulations, and their function is to improve the performance of the active ingredient. The most common adjuvants are surfactants, used in products sprayed onto plants. They help the active ingredient stay on the plant instead of quickly rolling off as droplets. Other adjuvants help the active ingredient penetrate the tissue of the pest, some reduce degradation of the active ingredient from UV light, and others help thicken the formulation to reduce pesticide drift into the environment. Little research has investigated the impact of adjuvants and other so-called inert chemicals on honey bee health. However, in recent years, some scientists are beginning to

find that not all of them are inert for bees. In 2012, researchers at Penn State University found bees that ingested organosilicone surfactants — the most frequently used adjuvant in almond orchard pesticides — experienced impaired learning. In early 2017 the team found that these same adjuvants could lead to worsened virus infections. The impact of inert ingredients on the environment is an active field in science. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Pesticides in the Environment and in the Hive Close to 1 billion pounds of pesticides ☆ Key Points are applied to U.S. agricultural lands each year. Herbicides make up most of this usage, followed by insecticides, Pesticides are common in the environment and in bee hives. and then fungicides. Pesticide applicators are required by law to report pesticide use data to the Department of Environmental Conservation. The U.S. Geological Survey compiles the data for pesticide usage each year, and that data can be viewed online through the work of the Pesticide National Synthesis Project; simply select the pesticide and year to view a map showing the areas it was used and the crops to which it was applied. Due to the sheer quantity of pesticides applied to land in the U.S., they are very common in the environment. Low levels of pesticides can be found in plants, soil, water systems, and a variety of animals. For this reason, all registered pesticides must undergo human health and environmental evaluations to determine whether they pose a risk to the environment or to people. Laboratory tests with honey bees are included as part of the environmental evaluations by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Pesticides are common in bee hives. They come into the hive on pollen and nectar from plants that were treated with pesticides, in water that was collected from contaminated puddles or guttation droplets on plants, or directly on bees’ bodies after they have been foraging in treated landscapes or walking on contaminated soil. Pesticides are even placed in the hive by beekeepers trying to manage hive pests such as Varroa mites and hive beetles. Extensive studies across the U.S. have found that there are, on average, between three and seven different pesticides in a bee hive at any given time. Of course, this varies depending on how close the hive is to pesticide-treated lands, how often it is used in pollination services, and how frequently beekeepers apply mite treatments. The science is clear that pesticides are common in bee hives, and that fact alone might be alarming to people. The real question, however, is whether they are at levels that cause harm to bees. The simple fact that they are present does not give us information as to whether they are partially responsible for the widespread colony health problems that have been experienced in recent years. To give this some context, think about your dog's flea or tick medication. Prophylactic treatment of the animal is meant to reduce the
incidence of illness that occurs when pests are left unchecked. Keeping the treatment below the threshold where the treatment itself becomes a problem is the balancing act. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Measuring Harm to Honey Bees There are a variety of ways to measure ☆ Key Points whether or not a pesticide harms honey bees; these ways can be broken down into four categories. Measuring harm to bees involves the consideration of acute, residual, and chronic toxicity, as Acute Toxicity well as sublethal and synergistic A common way to measure whether a effects. pesticide is toxic to bees is by measuring acute toxicity. Acute toxicity The LD50 is the dose of pesticide that kills half a honey bee determines the dose of a pesticide that population in a short period of is needed to kill a bee in a short time time. period (often 24 hours, but sometimes 48, 72, or 96 hours). To determine this amount, many individual bees are exposed to various doses of the active ingredient in a laboratory. Bees can be fed these active ingredients to determine the ingredient's oral toxicity, or scientists can apply small droplets to bees' bodies to determine its contact toxicity. The dose that kills 50% of the bees in this acute time period is known as the Lethal Dose 50 (or the LD50). Similarly, the concentration that kills 50% of bees in this time period is known as the Lethal Concentration 50 (or the LC50). The lower the LD50, the more toxic the pesticide. For example, a pesticide with an LD50 of 1 microgram per bee is more toxic than a pesticide that has an LD50 of 8 micrograms per bee, because it takes a much smaller dose to kill half the bees. The LD50 and LC50 values for honey bees have been determined for pesticide active ingredients. Determining these values is part of the environmental evaluations conducted by the EPA before a pesticide is registered. This information is important because it tells us whether there is a risk of bees dying when they are foraging during or shortly after pesticides have been applied. If it is determined that the pesticide poses a risk of acute toxicity to bees, there is language included on the product label that prohibits applicators from applying it during bloom, when bees are actively foraging. When beekeepers observe pesticide poisoning events shortly after a pesticide was applied or after the planting of seed-treated crops, they are observing acute toxicity of the pesticide.

The EPA classifies the acute toxicity of pesticides into "highly toxic," "moderately toxic," and "practically non-toxic" based on their LD50 values. A value of <2 micrograms/bee is considered highly toxic, a value of 2-10.99 micrograms/bee is moderately toxic, and a value of 11 or greater micrograms/bee is practically non-toxic. Below is a list of contact and oral LD50 values for various pesticides. This is only a small subset of the most commonly used pesticides in the U.S., as there are nearly a thousand active ingredients used today. There is no need to memorize any of these numbers, but students should familiarize themselves with how the data is presented. Which pesticides are highly toxic to bees, and which are practically non-toxic? Which are more toxic when consumed by bees, and which are more toxic when they are applied to a bee’s cuticle? Notice that insecticides are generally the most toxic substances to honey bees, relative to fungicides or herbicides. The LD50 values are much lower for insecticides; often it takes less than 1 microgram per bee to kill half those tested. This makes sense, as insecticides are targeted to kill insects, and honey bees are insects. In this list, the top three most toxic insecticides ordered by oral LD50 are clothianidin, imidacloprid, and thiamethoxam — all neonicotinoid insecticides. By examining acute toxicity data, we can understand which pesticides pose the greatest risk to foraging bees when they are used.
LD50 values in this table are from McArt, et al., 2017 and the references therein.

⌃ Long description This image shows a data table listing various pesticide active ingredients and their toxicity measurements for bees. The table has four columns: Pesticide Active Ingredient, Type of Pesticide, Oral LD50, and Contact LD50 (measured in microgram/bee). The pesticides are categorized into three types: insecticides, fungicides, and herbicides. The table includes 24 different pesticides, with insecticides generally showing lower LD50 values (meaning higher toxicity) compared to fungicides and herbicides. Clothianidin and Imidacloprid show the lowest oral LD50 values at 0.004 microgram/bee, while Penthiopyrad has the highest known oral LD50 at 385 microgram/bee. The contact LD50 values range from 0.003 (Spinosyn) to 312 (Penthiopyrad) microgram/bee. The table uses alternating white and light blue rows for easier reading, and the header row is displayed with a teal background. One entry (Atrazine) has an "unknown" oral LD50 value. All measurements are precisely listed to up to three decimal places where applicable. The data is organized in roughly ascending order of oral LD50 values within each pesticide type category, making it easy to compare relative toxicity levels among different pesticides. Residual Toxicity Residual toxicity is the time required to reduce the acute toxicity of a pesticide (and its residues) so that bee mortality is lowered to 25%. This means that when one in four bees that visit the flowers die, the pesticide has reached "low residual toxicity." The residual toxicity of a pesticide influences when growers are allowed to apply the pesticide to blooming plants. Pesticides with extended residual toxicity remain highly toxic on the plant for at least eight hours after application (and with some pesticides, over one week!), whereas pesticides with low residual toxicity remain highly toxic for fewer than eight hours. Most pesticides with high residual toxicity cannot be applied to blooms because

the risk to beneficial insects that visit the flowers is too high. The EPA includes language on the product label prohibiting high residual toxicity pesticides from being applied when bees are visiting the area being treated. Low residual toxicity pesticides, however, can be applied at night when bees do not visit the flowers. By morning, the pesticide no longer presents an acute risk. Chronic Toxicity Acute toxicity only captures the lethal effects within a very short time frame. However, pesticides often remain in the hive for longer than one to four days. They can be brought in with pollen and stored as bee bread. They can also accumulate in wax for days, months, or even years, depending on the pesticide. The chronic toxicity of a pesticide — the adverse effects after long-term exposure — have only been calculated for a handful of pesticides. A pesticide that causes chronic toxicity does not kill bees immediately, but it may kill bees at a later time or exhibit other negative impacts on bee health or behavior. The chronic effects of pesticides is being intensively studied at present. Sublethal Effects Health impacts other than mortality are considered “sublethal” effects. Investigating the sublethal impacts of pesticides is a fairly recent area of research and has revealed that many pesticides harm bees without killing them outright. Many sublethal impacts can affect individual bees, through impacts on learning, memory, locomotion (movement), feeding, reproduction, and foraging behavior. They also include cellular and physiological effects on bees. These may be changes in nerve transmission, changes in which genes are turned “on” or “off,” alterations to the gut microbiome, and the death of certain cells. Sublethal impacts can also be explored at the colony level. These studies investigate whether the consumption of or contact with pesticides by individuals can affect the entire colony. Some outcomes that can be measured include colony growth, overwintering survival, honey production, and brood production. Sublethal effects have been explored in fairly great detail for neonicotinoids and some miticides but remain largely unexplored for most other classes of pesticides.

An example of a sublethal impact would be a reduction in foraging behavior. Synergistic Effects Traditionally, when researchers investigate the impact of pesticides on bees, they study how a single pesticide affects bees. With our growing understanding of the multitude of pesticides with which bees come in contact at any given moment, we now know that in order to understand the overall risk posed to bees in the environment, we need to investigate how those pesticides may be interacting with one another. Two pesticides can interact synergistically, meaning they are more toxic when occurring together than the sum of both pesticide’s toxicity levels on their own. Through these next few pages, we will explore the current knowledge of insecticides, fungicides, and herbicides on honey bee health. New science is continually being published on this topic, so students are encouraged to stay up to date on the latest research if they are ever in a position to speak or write on this subject. The final exam series for the Master Beekeeping Program will only ask questions based on the information we cover in this course.

Read: An Overview of Insecticides Insecticides are generally the most ☆ Key Points toxic substances with which honey bees can come in contact. While there were some insecticides created before World War II, the development of most In general, insecticides are the most toxic pesticides to honey bees. insecticides, as well as the widespread adoption of their use, occurred after 1947. With respect to honey bee evolutionary time, this is a fairly new stress for them to face. Until the development of modern chemistry techniques that allow the detection of low levels of pesticides in bee products, beekeepers were unaware that there were often low levels of pesticides in bee hives. Now we understand that insecticides are fairly common in bee hives, and many can exhibit chronic and sublethal effects on bee health. Nearly all pesticide poisoning events reported by beekeepers are from applications of toxic insecticides. Rarely do fungicide or herbicide applications cause acute bee death. If insecticides are sprayed on plants when honey bees are actively foraging, they can come in contact with toxic doses. If insecticides have extended residual toxicity, acute bee kills can occur when bees are not present during spraying but visit flowers in the days afterward. Reducing unnecessary acute exposure of honey bees to toxic insecticides is one of the best ways to mitigate the risk of insecticide poisoning.

One outcome of the U.S. Pollinator Protection Plan addresses this exact issue. Beginning in 2017, the EPA implemented new label recommendations to reduce the risk of acute toxicity. Any pesticide that (1) exceeds the EPA’s acute risk level of concern to honey bees; (2) is applied to foliage as a liquid or dust (a formulation more dangerous to bees); and (3) is applied to crops that use bees for pollination services should include updated label language. The label will now clearly state which pesticides are toxic to bees and outline specific restrictions for applying the product. Some restrictions include the following: The pesticide cannot be applied during bloom. The pesticide can only be applied in a specific temperature window (avoiding temperatures when bees are active). The pesticide cannot be applied if bees are on site. The pesticide should be applied in a manner that reduces drift. The rate of application on a site should be below the EPA’s level of concern for bees. As a Master Beekeeper, there is no need to memorize extensive lists of insecticides, nor be a specialist in chemistry or honey bee toxicology. Instead, Master Beekeepers should feel confident in discussing pesticide issues with other beekeepers, the public, and the media, and they should be aware of the current understanding of the health impact on bees. To

help beekeepers build knowledge in this topic, we will cover the most common classes of insecticides — particularly those known to be highly toxic to honey bees — and discuss the current status of honey bee research in this field. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Insecticides There are tens of thousands of pesticide products registered in the U.S.; most of these products can be classified into the five major classes of synthetic insecticides: Organophosphates Carbamates Pyrethroids Insect Growth Regulators Neonicotinoids (covered on the next pages) ☆ Key Points Most insecticides act by impairing the nervous system in insects. All classes of insecticides vary in their risk to honey bee health. Some are practically non-toxic to bees, while others are highly toxic. There are several other classes of insecticides that are less commonly used and therefore not covered in this course. In addition to synthetic pesticides, there are also a variety of natural pesticides derived from living organisms (such as bacteria) that are used in organic farming. Their effects on bees are not well studied; in fact, very little research has investigated the sublethal impacts of insecticides other than neonicotinoids on honey bee health, despite the fact that many other insecticides are used widely in agriculture. Organophosphates Organophosphates are chemicals that inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, an important molecule needed for normal nerve functioning in insects (as well as most animals and humans). When the pesticide inhibits this enzyme, it disrupts nerve signaling and causes nerves to fire continuously. At doses high enough to cause acute toxicity, pest insects experience paralysis, twitching, and death. At low levels, it can cause sublethal impacts such as disorientation and impaired learning and memory. Organophosphates vary widely in their toxicity to honey bees. Some are practically non-toxic, while others are highly toxic. The table at the bottom of the page lists the organophosphates that are most toxic to honey bees.

Shortly after they were developed, organophosphates became widely used pesticides. Their use is declining in recent years, however, as some have been shown to be toxic to a variety of organisms (including humans), and many pests have developed resistance to some of the active ingredients. Nonetheless, some organophosphates continue to be used in conventional agriculture. The most commonly applied organophosphate in the world is chlorpyrifos. This insecticide is highly toxic to honey bees and is unfortunately commonly detected in hive products: A large-scale analysis of pollen and honey samples from North America, South America, and Europe found it in 15-20% of hives. The study also found that phosmet (another organophosphate) was commonly detected. The levels of these two organophosphates detected in pollen and honey were high enough to classify them as “posing a high risk to honey bee health.” In fact, of the 161 pesticides detected in hive products during this study, these two organophosphates posed the second- and third-highest risks to bees, respectively, after thiamethoxam (a neonicotinoid). Experimental studies have found chlorpyrifos can impair learning and memory in honey bees, and bees show an increased susceptibility to deformed wing virus and black queen cell virus following exposure to the insecticide. Furthermore, field-realistic doses of chlorpyrifos-spiked pollen fed to colonies have been shown to interfere with queen development. Other organophosphates have shown sublethal impacts on bees. For instance, methyl parathion can impair foraging behavior, and diazinon can impact learning and memory. Carbamates Carbamates act on the acetylcholinesterase enzyme in the same manner as organophosphates. High levels kill pest insects through disrupted nerve functioning. Similar acute symptoms of paralysis and sublethal symptoms of learning and memory impairment are observed as with organophosphates. Carbamates range from practically non-toxic to honey bees to highly toxic. The sublethal impacts of carbamates are not well known; only one study examined impacts on adult bees and found the carbamate carbaryl reduced bees’ lifespans and delayed the age they transitioned to become foragers.

Pyrethroids The passage of sodium through sodium channel proteins allows nerves to communicate with one another. Pyrethroids bind to these sodium channels and hold them open, causing nerves to fire repeatedly. At high doses, twitching, paralysis, and death are observed. Pyrethroid insecticides are considered broadspectrum insecticides, meaning they kill a wide variety of insects instead of selectively targeting specific pest species. For this reason, many are highly toxic to honey bees and other beneficial insects. In general, pyrethroids have low residual toxicity, so the residues dissipate quickly. At high sublethal levels, the pyrethroids esfenvalerate and permethrin have been shown to reduce honey bee locomotion and social interactions among nestmates. Low doses of deltamethrin can impair development, reduce foraging behavior, and hinder foragers’ ability to find their way home, and low doses of cyfluthrin, permethrin, cypermethrin, and tetramethrin have all been shown to impair motor functioning in bees in various studies. An experiment in 2016 exposed young adult bees to pollen contaminated with fieldrealistic levels of cyhalothrin and found that the young bees consumed less pollen (as if in an effort to avoid it). These bees experienced shorter lifespans and poor nutrition. Insect Growth Regulators Insect growth regulators (IGRs) are chemicals that disrupt the growth of immature insects using a variety of mechanisms. This makes them toxic to insects in the larval stage, but not to adults. Some IGRs work by altering juvenile hormone levels in pest larvae, which prevents these insects from developing into adults (in honey bees, juvenile hormone has several roles). Other IGRs act by altering the ability for an insect to molt or by preventing the formation of the hard outer cuticle on an insect. All these mechanisms result in eventual larval death. While IGRs do not pose a risk of acute toxicity to honey bee adults, several experiments have documented that the larval-killing effects of IGRs occur in honey bee larvae as well; these larvae die, develop malformed, or are removed by their nestmates. Those who do survive can

have altered foraging behavior and are more likely to be rejected from the colony by their nestmates. The table below lists some common insecticides that are known to be highly toxic to honey bees. Students can refer to this list in the event that they are asked by the public, growers, or other beekeepers about the risk of specific pesticide products to honey bees. Highly Toxic Insecticides to Honey Bees Organophosphates Pyrethroids Carbamates Neonicotinoids Acephate Azinphos-methyl Chlorpyrifos Diazinon Dimethoate Malathion Methidathion Naleda Oxydemeton-methyl Phosmet Cypermethrin Aldicarb Cyfluthrin Carbarylb Bifenthrin Methomyl Deltamethrin Oxamyl Esfenvalerate Fenpropathrin Cyhalothrin Permethrina Clothianidin Dinotefuran Imidacloprid Thiamethoxam a In South Carolina in 2016, Naled aerial sprays for killing mosquitos as a Zika virus prevention measure caused large-scale, widespread honey bee deaths. b Carbaryl sprays on crops in the 1960s-1980s in the U.S. caused many large-scale honey bee poisoning events. Read: A Special Class of Insecticides: Neonicotinoids Neonicotinoid insecticides were ☆ Key Points developed in the 1980s in response to an increase in pest resistance to other common pesticides on the market. They were commercially introduced in In recent years, neonicotinoids have become the most used insecticide worldwide. the 1990s, making them a fairly new class of pesticide. In a short period of time, they have now become the most-used insecticide worldwide, applied in 120 countries and on over 1,000 different crop types. Their surge in popularity was due to the fact that they are very safe for humans and are able to target and kill many different pest species. There are seven neonicotinoids commercially available: imidacloprid, thiacloprid, clothianidin, thiamethoxam, acetamiprid, nitenpyram, and dinotefuran. Neonicotinoids, like the other insecticides we have presented, interfere with the nervous system, including the insect brain. They exhibit a similar mode of action as nicotine by binding to acetylcholine receptors and overestimating nerves. At high-enough levels, they cause paralysis, twitching, and death. Humans and other animals also have these receptors in their nervous systems, but neonicotinoids bind with greater selectivity to insect receptors than mammal receptors, which makes them much less toxic to humans. Bee nerves also contain acetylcholine receptors, so they have the potential to experience the toxic effects of neonicotinoids. If exposed to high levels, bees die; at low levels, they can experience a variety of sublethal impacts. For instance, foraging is reduced, locomotion is affected, and bees become disoriented and have trouble finding their way back home. Because many acetylcholine receptors are found in the honey bee mushroom body, neonicotinoid exposure has also been shown to impair learning and memory in bees. With locomotion, orientation, learning, and memory so crucial to honey bee foraging and colony success, concerns arose that neonicotinoid exposure could be involved in widespread honey bee health challenges.

Neonicotinoids act on acetylcholine receptors throughout the bee brain, including the mushroom body (highlighted here). Neonicotinoids Are Systemic Pesticides Neonicotinoids are applied to plants in a variety of ways. They can be sprayed onto plants directly, injected into tree trunks, drenched into soils, and coated on seeds. This last method — termed “seed treatments” — is the predominant mode of neonicotinoid application. With this method, seeds (usually corn and soy) are coated in neonicotinoids and planted into the soil. As the plant grows, all its tissues take up small amounts of this pesticide. Neonicotinoids are effective pesticides because they are distributed throughout the plant’s tissues to protect the whole plant. This action classifies neonicotinoids as “systemic pesticides” because they protect the entire plant system instead of one local, isolated area. The petals, leaves, stem, and roots all take up the pesticide; in this way, the plant is protected from a variety of pests that feed on or damage different parts of the plant. Unfortunately, this also means that pollen and nectar can contain neonicotinoids, which can put pollinators at risk. In the U.S., 79–100% of corn hectares and 34–44% of soybean hectares are treated with neonicotinoids before planting. This type of pest control is a step backward from integrated pest management: Instead of applying pesticides only when treatment thresholds indicate to do so, these pesticides are applied prophylactically —

regardless of whether or not they are needed. As a result, neonicotinoids are present in the soil (where they can remain for up to a few years), water, and nearby vegetation. Neonicotinoid treated corn seeds. Exposure Bees are exposed to neonicotinoids through a variety of avenues. Often, they collect contaminated pollen and nectar from flowers. This food is brought back to the colony and fed to larvae and adults. Studies show that bees do not only collect pesticidecontaminated pollen from the crops that have been sprayed, but they also collect it from nearby wildflowers exposed to these pesticides through application drift and from soil uptake into the roots. Neonicotinoids leach from plants and treated seeds into the soil and waterways, presenting additional routes of exposure to bees and other wildlife. From these routes of exposure, bees come in contact with low levels of neonicotinoids that do not often cause acute pesticide poisoning but may exert sublethal effects, chronic effects, or no effects at all. Lastly, when treated seeds are planted in the soil, the planting machines release contaminated dust into the environment. Any bees that are foraging in close proximity to

seed planting (usually within one mile, but up to three miles) can come in contact with this dust and become exposed to high doses of neonicotinoids. Exposure through this route can cause acute pesticide poisoning. In these circumstances, beekeepers may observe their bees twitching, acting disoriented, extending their proboscises, and dying in large heaps at the entrance of their hive and nearby. Planting corn seeds releases dust that drifts in the environment. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Toxicity of Neonicotinoids Neonicotinoids range from practically ☆ Key Points non-toxic to highly toxic to honey bees. The variation of different neonicotinoids in toxicity is based on their chemical structure. Nitrocontaining neonicotinoids (imidacloprid, clothianidin, thiamethoxam, nitenpyram, and Nitro-containing neonicotinoids are more toxic to bees than are cyano-containing neonicotinoids. Neonicotinoids do pose a risk to honey bee health in some regions and under some conditions. dinotefuran) are more toxic to bees than cyano-containing neonicotinoids (acetamiprid and thiacloprid). The nitro-containing neonicotinoids have LD50 values under 2 micrograms/bee, classifying them as highly toxic. There is a high likelihood that bees die after consuming and coming in contact with neonicotinoids at these doses. On the other hand, the cyano-containing neonicotinoids have higher LD50 values that classify them as moderately toxic to practically non-toxic. The majority of studies investigating neonicotinoid toxicity have been laboratory studies. These experiments expose bees to various doses and concentrations of neonicotinoids to see if any negative impacts result. Pesticides are applied directly to the bees’ bodies or are fed to them through neonicotinoid-spiked sugar syrup or pollen. Scientists then observe what happens over a period of time. Collectively, these studies have demonstrated that low doses of neonicotinoids can cause a variety of sublethal impacts on bees, including impaired learning and memory, locomotion, feeding behavior, foraging behavior, altered gene expression, and reduced immunity. These studies are beneficial because they allow us to see exactly how the pesticides alone impact bee health, without the effects being compounded by the additional factors often experienced by bees, such as climate, diseases, or nutrition. There are several limitations to these types of studies, however. First, they only evaluate the effects at the individual level, eliminating our understanding of colony-level effects. The bees are also forced to encounter neonicotinoids, since they are contained in all the food they are given. As such, the risk from these studies does not reflect the risk to bees foraging naturally in the world around them. Lastly, there has been criticism of some

studies that expose bees to high concentrations or doses of neonicotinoids — much higher than what bees would encounter in the real world. To understand how these pesticides can impact colonies, scientists conduct field studies in which nucleus colonies or full-sized colonies are placed outside. Bees are fed fieldrealistic concentrations of neonicotinoids in sugar syrup or protein patties, or they are placed adjacent to neonicotinoid-treated crop fields. Colonies are followed for periods of time that usually range from two weeks to years. Studies of this nature explore what bees experience in the real world. They can show effects on entire colonies and for longer periods of time. If neonicotinoids are partially responsible for the widespread colony health issues documented in recent years, we would expect to see some negative effects through these types of studies. It is these studies that tend to produce the most controversy on the topic of neonicotinoids. Some field studies show negative impacts to colony health, while others do not. The results have been inconsistent and have rarely demonstrated that colonies die after being exposed. One study in particular found that while individual bees experience health issues and sometimes die, strong colonies are able to compensate for the losses of some bees and continue to grow and be productive. Of course, producing strong colonies requires a range of suitable environmental factors. Since these are not uniformly available, we again note that "all beekeeping is local," therefore field study results cannot be universally applied. With all the controversy, there has been a priority for these studies to be well designed, well replicated, and as realistic as possible to reflect the risk posed in nature. Some excellent studies have been published in recent years, and they are starting to shed some much-needed light on the subject. This video provides a summary of some of these studies. Video Transcript Studying the sublethal impacts of neonicotinoids on bees is challenging. Because there's so much natural honey bee colonies, in order for results to be statistically significant in experiments, it requires that researchers have access to many colonies, ideally close to a hundred, and lots of plots of land in the right places. These plots of land either need to be in close proximity to neonic-treated fields or really far away from neonic-treated fields. It also requires a lot of manpower because these colonies need to be regularly monitored

and outcomes need to be measured. You need teams of people to accomplish this. So, by nature, it's tricky and expensive to accomplish all of these factors. Nonetheless, there's been several studies that have investigated the impacts of neonicotinoids in the field. Five studies that were conducted before 2014 reported no negative health impacts on honey bees as a result of being placed near neonicotinoidtreated canola or sunflower seeds. These studies looked at colony mortality, brood production, colony weight, worker lifespan, various health outcomes, honey production, and foraging behavior. And these researchers didn't dose or feed their colonies neonicotinoids; they simply placed them next to small fields that were either treated or not treated, and the honey bees foraged as they may. The results from these studies raised a lot of controversy right off the bat, as these findings conflicted with what researchers were finding in the laboratory. In the lab, when we're feeding honey bees neonics, we're seeing that this can lead to impairments in learning and memory, locomotion, feeding, foraging, the expression of certain genes, and immunity. So why weren't these outcomes being observed in field studies? Part of the reason could lie in the limitations of the studies. One of the biggest limitations is that treated fields are really small. So honey bees forage two to three miles around their colonies, far beyond the application areas, meaning that there is no guarantee that a colony is going to primarily feed on that one treated plot. A two hectare research plot, for instance, encompasses only 0.025% of a honey bee's foraging area. In another one of these studies the untreated and treated canola fields were about 300 meters apart. So colonies could easily visit both fields, making it really tricky to detect differences between the two groups. Also, many of these studies only place honey bee colonies in treated fields for short periods of time, failing to capture the effects of chronic exposure to these chemicals. So, as I mentioned before, the constraints of having access to enough land in the right places and the time and manpower to measure outcomes for extended periods of time can make it challenging to study these effects in a meaningful way. Here's a summary of the field studies that were conducted up until 2015. It's easy to see where the conflicting results lie and understand why there's been so much controversy and confusion surrounding neonicotinoids. In this graph, the number of studies are found on the y-axis, whereas the outcomes are measured on the x-axis. So, these studies are looking at mortality, colony growth, brood production, honey production, foraging, overwintering, acetylcholinesterase activity in the brain, and virus infections. The blue parts of the bar represent studies that are not finding any impacts from neonicotinoids.

Whereas the red are studies that find negative impacts from neonicotinoids on these outcomes. So, right off the bat, we can see that a lot of factors have no effects. Colony growth, brood production, honey production and overwintering are all not affected in these studies by neonicotinoids. Whereas acetylcholinesterase activity and the susceptibility to developing virus infections are impacted by neonicotinoids. And in some areas there's conflicting results. Six studies find that mortality is impacted, whereas two don't. And one study finds that foraging is impacted, where another study doesn't. So it can be really hard to interpret what this means. Some scientists wanted to make sure that honey bees were, in fact, consuming these low doses of neonics, and that these studies weren't limited by the amount of land that they had access to. So, instead of placing colonies near small fields that were either treated or untreated, the scientists would spike pollen or sugar syrup with pesticides to colonies and observe what happened with the bees. There were a lot of early field studies, however, that were actually dosing colonies with high levels of neonics that were being criticized for not reflecting realistic exposure. So recent field studies are now emphasizing the use of field-realistic levels of neonics to evaluate the real world risk that these pesticides are posing on bee health. And before we dive into looking at these studies, let's take a second to talk about what doses we tend to find in hive products. Real world doses of neonicotinoids differ depending on the application method. Seed treated applications, which is what we have with corn and soy, results in levels and hive products that average around 0.8 to 3.9 parts per billion. Levels in hive products tend to be higher if neonicotinoids are applied by soil drenching. They tend to be in the realm of 12 to 131 parts per billion. And lastly, foliar sprays are associated with the highest level of neonics in hive products, often between 5 and 208 parts per billion. For this reason, a lot of foliar sprays are not allowed to be applied when flowers are actually blooming. Lastly, applications to ornamental plants are applied at higher doses than applications to agricultural plants. So this can translate to higher doses in hive products. More recent studies have done a great job to thoroughly investigate the impact of neonics on bees in the field and they're helping to clear up some of the confusion. Let's go through two that are particularly well designed, and then we'll recap what we can say when we take everything together that we've discussed so far. The first study is one that was conducted in Ontario, Canada, and published in 2017. It studied neonicotinoid exposure in 55 hives that were distributed across five apiaries, either very close to cornfields or very far away from cornfields. They sampled the bees, pollen, and nectar from the hive at various time points during this study. What the researchers found is that

honeybees near cornfields in Ontario are exposed to significantly more neonicotinoids than colonies far from cornfields. They also found neonics were present in the hive products for three to four months after corn seeds were being planted, demonstrating that there was a chronic exposure of these pesticides for most of the colonies' active foraging season. The researchers then took the average dose of neonics that they were finding in pollen and dosed colonies in a separate experiment. They found that this exposure to chronic low doses of neonics, exactly what the colonies were experiencing on Ontario, does have sublethal health impacts. The long term doses caused a significant increase in worker mortality, a decrease in hygenic behavior, and an increase in queen failure. The largest study conducted to date was done in Europe and was also published in 2017. This study was a massive undertaking. It followed a 198 colonies in 33 sites across the United Kingdom, Hungary, and Germany for two years. At each of these sites the researchers had plots that contained seed treated oil seed rape and large pots that contained untreated oil seed rape. They measured impacts on colony health during the crop flowering period, and also checked in after winter to measure the chronic effects on colony survival. And the authors found some interesting results. The biggest finding was that the effects differed depending on the country the bees were in. For instance, in the UK and in Hungary, colonies near the treated fields experienced population decreases. While in Germany, colonies in treated fields actually experienced slight population increases. Another example is that in Hungary, the negative effects of neonics persisted into the following spring. Colonies near treated fields were 24% smaller compared to colonies near control fields that received no treatments. And these effects were not seen in the other two countries. So how on earth do we interpret this? It's really easy to see where the controversy lies. It's clear that in some places at some times with some types of neonicotinoids, bee health is negatively impacted. But this relationship is not observed all the time. This makes it really easy for pesticide companies to interpret the results to say that there is no hard consensus that neonicotinoids harm bees. Researchers, on the other hand, say yes, sometimes neonics can harm bees. The take home message is that neonics can be harmful. However, whether or not a colony is affected depends on a variety of interacting factors. The first is how strong and healthy the colony was to begin with. Strong, healthy colonies may be less impacted by neonicotinoids. Colonies that are experiencing other stress factors such as disease may be more susceptible to the stress of pesticides. I already mentioned the correlations between neonicotinoids and virus levels. And studies also find interactive

effects with the neonics and Nosema infections as well. Similarly, colonies that are weak with few foragers to begin with may not be able to recuperate from the adult population losses that sometimes happen from neonicotinoid exposure. Second, how close the colony is located to an area that's treated with neonics. This varies by time and by region. Third, the dose of neonics that are present on the bees, in the pollen, in the wax and in the nectar of the hive. Low doses below sublethal impacts may not affect honey bee colonies, while higher doses can. The Xerces society has put together a table that shows the doses that cause sublethal and chronic impacts on honey bees. Depending on the neonicotinoid, it can take between 0.25 parts per billion to 12,500 parts per billion before negative impacts are observed. You can download this table at the end of the course in the downloadable resources section. So it's easy to see that in some cases, colonies are at risk of effects from neonics more so than in other cases. Studies in the field have also documented that neonics can be quite persistent in the environment. They can be found in plants and soil for several months, or even years after being applied. Neonics that have leeched from plants or seeds in the soil can even be taken up by other plants, including wildflowers that were never sprayed or treated to begin with. So, neonics and other pesticides are quite prevalent in the environment, though most often in low levels. And although we've been studying these pesticides for many years now, we're still in the early stages of understanding exactly how their presence fully impacts honey bee colonies, but we know that it is a complex and interacting thing. Bees Often Encounter Neonicotinoid Concentrations at Levels That Cause Sublethal and Chronic Effects In 2020, Cornell University published an assessment of neonicotinoid risk to pollinators, summarizing the findings of field trials from over 400 published scientific studies across North America. The report, written by Grout, et al., sheds light on how frequently bees are exposed to neonicotinoid concentrations known to cause sublethal impacts in different agricultural landscapes. The authors estimated risk by using a metric called “lowest observed effect concentration," or LOEC. The LOEC is the lowest concentration of a chemical where scientists observe sublethal or chronic effects on an organism. Scientists have determined the LOECs of different neonicotinoids for a variety of responses in honey bees, such as impacts to physiology, behavior, and reproduction. By comparing the concentrations that bees are exposed to in the environment to their respective LOECs, the report authors determined the risks that different landscapes pose.

The analysis found that honey bees are commonly exposed to neonicotinoid concentrations that can cause sublethal and chronic impacts. The most evidence exists for field crops (corn and soy). Data from 96 field crop assessments indicate that 74% of neonicotinoid exposures are at concentrations above those known to impact honey bee physiology, 58% are above those known to impact honey bee behavior, and 37% are above those known to impact honey bee reproduction. This means that the majority of exposures to neonicotinoids in corn and soy fields are risky; the usage of seed treatments are likely to impact bee physiology in three-quarters of cases, behavior in over half of cases, and reproduction in over one-third of cases. The risks for fruit crops, vegetables, and landscape management were also calculated; they are included in the table below. You’ll notice that risks are higher in vegetable crops and landscape plants but lower in fruit crops. The take-home message from this report is that honey bees are frequently exposed to concentrations of neonicotinoids that can result in sublethal and chronic impacts, though the risk varies depending on the agricultural landscape. Read: Herbicides Herbicides are the most commonly ☆ Key Points used class of pesticide in conventional agriculture. By far, the most frequently applied herbicide used throughout the world is glyphosate (the active ingredient in Roundup). Glyphosate became commercially available in 1974 In general, most herbicides do not pose a major risk to honey bee health. Herbicides can indirectly impact bees by limiting floral resources. and is a very effective weed killer. In fact, it kills all vegetation to which it is applied, so it was originally only applied to areas where growers and landowners wanted to eliminate all plants. In 1996, Roundup Ready glyphosate-tolerant crops were developed. Since then, glyphosate could be applied onto these crops; weeds are killed, but the crops are genetically engineered to be unaffected by the herbicide. Roundup Ready cotton, corn, soy, and canola became common worldwide, and as a result glyphosate use skyrocketed. In 1994, the U.S. used 124 million pounds of glyphosate. By 2014, the usage increased to reach 1.82 billion pounds! Glyphosate has been detected in air, soil, water, and food products, including honey. Concerns have arisen about the prevalence of this pesticide in the environment and in human food; in 2015, the World Health Organization classified it as a "probable human carcinogen."

Not much research has been conducted to understand the risk of herbicides to honey bees. Of all herbicides, glyphosate is the most researched, likely because of its prevalence. Overall, this herbicide is classified as practically non-toxic to honey bees. The LD50 values are greater than 100 micrograms/bee, and while glyphosate is very prevalent in the environment, levels this high are not commonly detected in bee hives. Of the very few studies that have investigated the sublethal impacts of glyphosate on bees, these studies find conflicting results. One small-scale study determined that sublethal levels of glyphosate could impair bees’ ability to return home after foraging trips, while another study found no effect on bees’ ability to forage but demonstrated that learning can be slightly impaired. The latest paper published in 2018 reported that glyphosate can alter adult bees’ beneficial gut microbiome. On the other hand, several other studies report no negative impacts of glyphosate exposure on survival or development. The actual concentrations and doses of glyphosate bees are exposed to in the field is not well documented. Glyphosate testing is not commonly done on honey bees because its analysis requires a different (and expensive) machine as compared to most other pesticides. Without more research to determine the levels that honey bees experience in the real world and more studies investigating the sublethal impacts of these realistic doses, it is too soon to say with confidence whether exposure to low levels of glyphosate in the field can cause effects at the colony level.

Most other herbicides are classified as non-toxic to honey bees as well. After glyphosate, atrazine is the second-most commonly used herbicide in the U.S., followed by metachlor. LD50 values are high for these two pesticides and, as such, they do not pose a risk to honey bee mortality. These herbicides frequently turn up in honey bee hive products. Research conducted by the NYS Beekeeper Tech Team in 2016 found these herbicides to be common at very low levels in honey bee wax; atrazine was detected in 17% of colonies sampled, while metachlor was detected in 58% of colonies. Another study conducted by Dr. Scott McArt at Cornell University found similar results: Low levels of atrazine were present in the bee bread of 20% of colonies tested. Despite their environmental prevalence and their occurrences in bee hives, these particular herbicides have not been studied with regard to their potential sublethal impacts on bee health. Some less-common herbicides are highly toxic and include language on the product label that emphasizes not to apply them when honey bees are foraging. If honey bees come in direct contact with these herbicides when wet, they can be toxic. However, after the product has dried and no longer presents a risk of residual toxicity, there is low risk to honey bee health. Indirect Effects on Bees While there is not strong evidence to suggest that exposure to herbicides directly harms bees, herbicide use can affect resource availability for honey bees and wild bees. Weeds and wildflowers surrounding agricultural, urban, suburban, and commercial land provide valuable food sources for nearly all species of bees and nesting sites for wild bees. While no study has investigated whether the increased use of specific herbicides correlates with a reduction in certain bee populations, habitat loss has been identified as a primary driver for native bee declines worldwide. Furthermore, the increased use of glyphosate is suggested to be a contributing factor to the decline in monarch butterflies, as its use is correlated with decreased milkweed abundance in agricultural fields in recent years.

Watch: Fungicides Fungicides control fungal diseases that ☆ Key Points infect a variety of vegetables, fruits, and grains. Because several fungal diseases of crops commonly occur during bloom, many fungicides can be EBI fungicides can harm bees by increasing the toxicity of other pesticides. sprayed while these plants are flowering. Bees in these crop systems can easily carry fungicides back to the hive. In fact, next to miticides applied by beekeepers to control Varroa, residues in hives are predominantly fungicides. These residues have been detected in pollen, bee bread, wax, and honey. Despite the prevalence of fungicide use in conventional agriculture, scientific research is only beginning to uncover how they may affect bees. Most fungicides are not acutely toxic to honey bees. Often, adult bees that come in contact with fungicides do not die, unless levels well exceed those normally found in landscapes. There are a few, however, that can be toxic to other life stages of honey bees. For instance, larvae fed field-realistic doses of the fungicides captan, iprodione, and ziram all fail to develop to adulthood in the laboratory. Honey bee colonies used to provide pollination services for multiple crops are at the biggest risk of exposure to fungicides, simply because they are transported from one crop to another, usually at times when fungicides have been recently applied. One study conducted in California found this exposure can affect the quality of bee bread fed to larvae. The researchers sampled bee bread from colonies that provided both almond and apple pollination in the same year, and they found that bees incorporate fungicide residues into bee bread at high enough levels to alter its composition. Specifically, the presence of fungicides kill the beneficial fungi that are naturally present in bee bread and that help in the fermentation process. The downstream effects of larvae consuming this altered bee bread has not yet been studied. Another interesting finding that deserves further research is that a positive correlation exists between the presence of fungicide residues in honey bee hives and the occurrence of colony disorders (population weakness, queen loss, and brood problems); colonies that experience these disorders tend to have more fungicide residues in their hives than healthy colonies. The exact reason why is not yet known. Watch Scott McArt — assistant professor of pollinator health in the

Department of Entomology at Cornell University — discuss how his lab has been studying fungicides for the past few years. Video Transcript My lab has been studying the impact of fungicides on bees for the last three to four years now. And most of those beekeepers were coming to us and saying, "You know, when we put our bees in to do pollination, they really seem to be impacted by pesticides." We think that the bees are getting exposed to a lot of fungicides, and that might be having some impacts on them." Okay, so the next study, along the lines of fungicides that I'll summarize is something that we did recently related to four declining species of bumblebees across the United States. So, this is a really impressive data set. Luckily, I didn't actually take the data on, I was able to borrow some data from someone. But what these researchers did is they went out to 284 sampling locations across the United States, sampled 10,000 bumblebees, and this included four species that are known to be in decline. So these are experiencing range contractions, and this includes the rusty patched bumblebee, which is now on the federal

endangered species list. So across all of those different sampling sites and all of those different bees, believe it or not, people actually dissected all 10,000 of these bees and found out whether they had Nosema bombi. It's a related pathogen to Nosema ceranae, which we find in a lot of honey bees. So, what we were able to do from this data set is we were able to say, "Okay, here's the prevalence. So how many bees are actually sick?" But because we had all of these different sampling locations across the United States, we could say, well, what are the different attributes of those locations which may have actually caused the bees to become sick and potentially caused them to be lost from sites where they used to be. So, over particular regions where we know that the bumblebees used to be, but now they no longer exist in those particular areas. So what we did is we looked at lots of different factors. We looked at things like habitat fragmentation, things like latitude, longitude, elevation, urbanization, the human population density around those areas, the type of agriculture that was actually used in those areas. And then we also used a new database where we can actually make good predictions of pesticide usage across the whole United States. And that was applicable to every single one of these sites as well. So we can get good estimates of all 456 compounds of pesticides that were potentially sprayed across these locations. So as you can imagine, this was a large analysis with a lot of data. So we used some sort of fancy statistical techniques to look at this. But what we found in the end, is that the best predictor of Nosema prevalence, how many bees were actually getting sick at these sites, was not percent agriculture, it was not neonics, it was not human population density. It turns out it was the single most used fungicide in the US, chlorothalonil. So chlorothalonil was the most predictive of whether the bees were getting Nosema in them or not. We also know that in these four declining species they have elevated levels of Nosema compared to the species that are not necessarily doing so bad. Whether that's causal or not we don't know, but we do see that pattern. So the bees are getting sick where there is a lot of this fungicide chlorothalonil sprayed and there are more sicknesses in these declining species. The next thing we looked at was what was the best predictor of range contraction. So, whether the bees were actually lost from those sites, or whether they were still present in those sites. And, low and behold, what we find after we look at all these different factors again, in terms of what's predictive of loss of the bees, those declined species from the sites, is total fungicide usage in the United States. So again, I think if we were sort of to tie all of this data together, we find with the honey bees in apple orchards and a lot of other studies looking at similar things as we did that fungicides are the main things that our bees are bringing back to their hives. This is true for honey bees, this is true for bumblebees and we

actually know for some solitary bees as well. The fungicides are the main things that they're being exposed to. In addition, now we have some data showing that fungicides may not necessarily be as benign as we think. There could be interactions with insecticides that could increase the toxicity of those insecticides, or there could be interactions with pathogens. So specifically, this Nosema pathogen that we found was at elevated levels and related to fungicide exposure. We also have data, manipulative experiment data, in the lab with honey bees. So, Jeff Pettis showed several years ago that if you expose bees to, or you feed bees pollen that contains chlorothalonil versus control pollen that does not contain chlorothalonil, those honey bees that are exposed to the chlorothalonil are more susceptible to Nosema. Why exactly that is the case, we don't know. But it's something that we're looking into and hopefully something that we're going to be able to pass on recommendations to hopefully improve this situation with risk about fungicides in the future.
