Read: Fungicides — Synergistic Effects Laboratory studies have shown that a ☆ Key Points certain class of fungicides can be quite dangerous to honey bees when found in combination with other pesticides. Entombed pollen is associated with high levels of fungicides. This class is the ergosterol biosynthesis-inhibiting (EBI) fungicides. Several studies have found that these fungicides exhibit synergistic effects when found in combination with pyrethroid insecticides, neonicotinoids, and even some Varroa miticides. The most well- studied EBI fungicide in this regard is prochloraz. This particular fungicide is not registered in the U.S., but there are several other EBI fungicides that are. Laboratory studies find prochloraz can substantially increase the toxicity of the pyrethroid insecticide deltamethrin. When both pesticides are fed to honey bees at sublethal doses, mortality is higher than when bees are fed either pesticide alone. The combination is not always fatal but can have other negative impacts on bee health as well. For example, the joint exposure of prochloraz with pyrethroids deltamethrin or difenoconazole impairs bees’ ability to regulate their body temperature. If this exposure occurs in cool climates, bees may be susceptible to hypothermia. In addition to pyrethroids, EBI fungicides increase the toxicity of miticides. Prochloraz elevates the toxicity of tau-fluvalinate (Apistan®), coumaphos (CheckMite+®), and fenpyroximate (a miticide registered for use on some crops but not for Varroa control). This effect was not seen with amitraz (Apivar®) or thymol (Apiguard® and Api Life Var®). These synergistic effects are especially concerning given the prevalence of miticides and fungicides together in honey bee hives. Lastly, EBI fungicides can also increase the toxicity of neonicotinoids. Imidacloprid and acetamiprid become especially deadly when found in combination with the EBI fungicide fenbuconazole. The neonicotinoid thiacloprid increases greatly in toxicity when bees are also exposed to the EBI fungicides prochloraz and tebuconazole. These observations are from laboratory studies but have not yet been documented in the field. For instance, one study investigated colony effects due to the combination of thiacloprid and tebuconazole and found no impacts on mortality, foraging, colony growth, brood production, or honey production. More field studies examining potential synergistic

effects are critically needed. Studying pesticide interactions is very important because it is rare for honey bees to encounter only one chemical at a time. The environment, and therefore bees’ hives, tend to test positive for several different pesticides at once. Why Do EBI Fungicides Increase the Toxicity of These Other Pesticides? When pyrethroids and neonicotinoids enter the honey bee body, they are broken down in part by an enzyme called cytochrome P450-monooxygenase. This enzyme is important for honey bees to detoxify chemicals from their bodies. EBI fungicides work by stopping the action of cytochrome P450-monooxygenase in fungi. When these fungicides enter honey bee bodies through contact or consumption, the same enzyme is inhibited in the bees' bodies! Now, when bees are exposed to pyrethroids and neonicotinoids, they are unable to break them down and clear them from their bodies. In this way, low levels of these insecticides can build up and become very toxic. Entombed Pollen In 2009, Dennis vanEngelsdorp’s lab discovered a strange phenomenon in some U.S. honey bee colonies: entombed pollen. Entombed pollen has a dark, sunken, wax and propolis capping. Often there are several cells of entombed pollen scattered among normal-looking bee bread and brood cells. When the researchers scraped off the capping to reveal what was beneath, the pollen was brick-red in color. Laboratory analyses found that every sample of entombed pollen had high levels of the fungicide chlorothalonil (on average, 40 times higher than in regular pollen!). This fungicide is commonly detected in honey bee colonies. After following these colonies over time, they discovered those with entombed pollen died at significantly higher rates than those that did not. It appears the bees' sealed off the pollen, perhaps due to the high fungicide levels, to avoid it. Entombed pollen tends to be more commonly found in older wax combs, possibly because old wax tends to accumulate more pesticide residues than younger wax.

Left photo shows a close up view of cells containing entombed pollen; middle photo shows a frame containing many affected cells; and right photo shows an entombed pollen cell with capping scraped, exposing brick red pollen. Photo credit: Bee Informed Partnership Entombed pollen is fairly common today. In spring 2017, the NYS Beekeeper Tech Team found entombed pollen in 11.5% of colonies they sampled across the state (37 out of 321 hives). This entombed pollen was a variety of colors. Beekeepers should keep toothpicks in their inspection kits to scrape off suspicious wax and propolis cappings to determine the presence of entombed pollen. If beekeepers observe many cells of entombed pollen in
their hives (5–10% of cells), it is recommended that they discard the affected frames and replace them with frames of foundation or newly drawn comb. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Reducing Bees' Exposure to Pesticides Throughout this module, we have ☆ Key Points examined how pesticides are prevalent in the environment. Low doses of some pesticides have the potential to cause sublethal impacts on honey bee health, and the interactions among pesticides common in bee hives have been largely unexplored. Acute pesticide poisoning events occur when honey bees are in areas where pesticides are being applied or are Ultimately, reducing pesticide exposure in honey bee colonies requires collaboration among beekeepers, growers, pesticide applicators, the public, and policy makers. Beekeepers can reduce miticides in their colonies by using integrated pest management. foraging on recently treated plants within the residual toxicity time period. Communicating with landowners in the area and rotating old combs Beekeepers may feel powerless when it comes to reducing pesticide are good practices to reduce pesticide exposure. exposure. They may have little control over the proximity of their apiary sites to agricultural fields, and providing pollination services may be a focal part of their beekeeping business. Losing bees from acute pesticide poisoning events is a devastating experience for everyone. While it is nearly impossible to prevent bees from being exposed to pesticides, there are several measures beekeepers can take to reduce the degree of exposure. Protecting pollinators from pesticide exposure involves beekeepers’ cooperation with a variety of groups of people, including pesticide applicators, growers, and the public. The importance of communication among these groups cannot be overstated. Combs Many pesticides and their residues (including some Varroa miticides) accumulate in wax over many years. Residues can be slow to break down, causing exposure to bees for months or even years after the pesticide was first brought into the hive. To

reduce contaminants in hives, beekeepers should rotate out two of the oldest frames from each hive body every year. If beekeepers experience a pesticide poisoning event whereby brood, nurse bees, and/or the queen is affected, it is likely that contaminated pollen was brought into the colony (because the foragers did not die immediately in the field). In these cases, beekeepers may want to promptly remove all comb with bee bread/pollen and replace it with drawn comb. Because pollen usually surrounds brood, brood may be discarded in this process. Beekeepers can make this decision based on the severity of the pesticide poisoning. In severe cases, where hundreds of bees continue to die each day and the queen does not resume egg laying after several days, it may be worth it to discard the frames, brood and all. In mild cases where only some adults and brood are affected, but the effects are not continuously observed over consecutive days, it may not be necessary. Miticides Nearly all studies that quantify pesticide levels in beeswax and pollen find that Varroa miticides are the most frequently detected and contribute the highest residue levels in hives. While most beekeepers need to apply miticides to their colonies to control Varroa, practicing integrated pest management (IPM) is the best way to minimize miticide residues. By incorporating genetic and cultural controls,

fewer pesticide applications are needed. IPM does not encourage the prophylactic use of miticides; instead, they are only applied when mites exceed a treatment threshold. Beekeepers can further aim to reduce pesticide residues by using those with short residual periods in beeswax first (essential oils, organic acids, and amitraz) and by limiting (or eliminating) their use of fluvalinate or coumaphosbased chemicals, which can remain in comb for years. Pollination It is very likely that the risk of pesticide exposure is higher for colonies that pollinate multiple crops in a single year as compared to those that pollinate no crops or only a single crop, though no studies have specifically investigated this topic. The idea is that with each new crop, bees are exposed to a new cocktail of chemicals. In 2019, the NYS Beekeeper Tech Team found higher pesticide residues in commercial colonies compared to hobbyist colonies, though it is not clear whether this is driven by pollination services, comb age, or other management practices. To reduce exposure to the multitude of pesticides bees face when pollinating a variety of crops, beekeepers may wish to be strategic about which colonies they use for pollination and how many pollination events they work. For instance, beekeepers could limit pollination service events for individual colonies. If they manage 100 colonies for pollination, 50 could be used to pollinate apples, while the other 50

could be used to pollinate squash. Of course, to determine the strategy that works best for their operation and goals, the beekeeper will want to weigh the costs and benefits of renting fewer colonies with the stress the colonies can incur and with the income they will generate through providing these services. An alternative scenario could be to specifically manage colonies for a certain purpose. Beekeepers could achieve this by keeping a group of colonies that are maintained in low-pesticide environments for honey production or for reserves (building comb or rearing queens for later use) and have another group of colonies that are used for the riskier task of pollination services. Pulling resources from the healthy colonies to use in the pollination colonies can help mitigate losses. This method of avoiding “putting all your eggs in one basket” may help reduce the overall operation’s pesticide exposure. If colonies do experience pesticide stress or die from acute poisoning events, beekeepers have a reserve of strong, healthy colonies from which they can recuperate losses. Colonies that are used for pollination should be strong and healthy, and they should receive nutritional supplements (carbohydrates and/or protein) before, during, and after, as needed. In this manner, pollen substitute and sugar syrup can provide a clean, uncontaminated food option for bees to consume. Colonies that come out of pollination can be placed in wildflower fields for the remainder of the year to have the opportunity to forage on a variety of plants with minimal pesticide exposure and recover.

Contracts Pollination service contracts are a great way to communicate expectations between beekeepers and growers. They allow beekeepers and growers to determine up front the pesticide risk to honey bees, as well as what would happen if a poisoning event were to occur. Beekeepers and growers can negotiate which pesticides can and cannot be applied to crops while bees are on site, how much notice beekeepers require before pesticide application, and how much a grower will compensate a beekeeper for pesticide poisoning events. These contracts can reduce pesticide exposure to honey bees, help form trusting relationships between growers and beekeepers, and put both parties at ease before any services are performed.

Reporting Beekeepers are encouraged to report all pesticide poisoning events to the state apiculturist as soon as they are experienced. They should take photos and videos of the bees at the entrance of the hive, as well as photos of any affected brood. Additionally, they should photograph and document the crops that are blooming in the area at the time of the event. Investigators will interview the beekeeper and sample dead or dying bees from the affected colonies for pesticide residues. These bees must be as fresh as possible and not yet experiencing any decay. Remember, many pesticide residues can break down after several days, so the quicker the beekeeper acts to report the event, the better. Beekeepers are discouraged from taking any bee samples themselves before reporting the incident. Technicians will advise them whether or not to collect their own samples to store before the investigation occurs. In addition to dead bees, the inspector may also take samples of pollen, wax, or any pesticide dust at the hive entrance.

The inspector will then explore nearby sites of possible pesticide use (such as nearby agricultural fields, ornamental gardens, utility lines, and roadside drainage ditches) in an effort to determine whether pesticides were applied illegally (i.e., not in accordance with the product label). The inspector may interview landowners and take samples of vegetation, soil, or water for pesticide analysis. Pesticide samples taken by the investigators are analyzed free of charge, but it may take several months before results are provided. Alternatively, beekeepers can send in their own samples for a fee. The Bee Informed Partnership offers this Emergency Response Kit that includes testing 16 hives for over 170 different pesticides. The cost for this kit is $1,229. The turnaround time for results is much quicker than waiting for the state government results. The U.S. used to have programs to compensate beekeepers for colony losses from pesticide poisoning events, but no such programs exist today. Unfortunately, beekeepers are the ones who bear the cost for these tragic situations, even though the incidents are nearly always beyond their control. However, there is a still a benefit to reporting pesticide kills. Records of pesticide poisoning events can help uncover trends as to which pesticides are causing the most acute harm to bees. Ontario, Canada's 2015 decision to regulate neonicotinoid seed-treated corn and soy was partially as a result of the number of acute pesticide poisoning events that were

reported after seed planting. In 2012, pesticide kills in 240 yards were reported. Investigations found 70% of dead bees tested positive for neonicotinoid residues. In 2013, a total of 340 yards were reported, with 75% of dead bees testing positive for neonicotinoids. Without these reports, there might not have been a strong enough case for the new regulations. Pesticide poisoning events are underreported in the U.S.. Some beekeepers feel that without government compensation for their losses, there is no point to starting an investigation. However, reporting losses and investigating the pesticides responsible can lead to changes in pesticide regulations. Talking to Growers In addition to drafting pollination contracts with growers, simply communicating with growers in the area can make a big impact. Beekeepers should be friendly and open with farmers and let them know where their bee hives are located. Growers and pesticide applicators cannot be expected to avoid spraying pesticides near honey bee colonies if they do not know where they are. Some states and countries have mandatory registration where beekeepers can be contacted and notified before pesticide applications, and others use an online program called FieldWatch®, where growers are able to get in touch with beekeepers prior to applying pesticides. In states and countries without such programs (like New York), it is the beekeeper's responsibility to make their colonies known. Beekeepers should provide nearby landowners with their contact information and print their contact information (in big letters) on signs near hives in high-risk areas so that they can be seen from a distance. Bringing nearby growers a jar of honey with their contact information on it is a great way for a beekeeper to start the discussion.

Generally, growers want to protect bees. They are aware of the benefits they bring ecosystems as well as the crop quality and yield improvements that result from bee pollination. Ask them what pesticides they plan on applying this year and whether any of the labels include precautionary statements for bees. Many are willing to adopt integrated pest management practices to reduce pesticide use in their fields. Others are willing to use alternative pesticides that are delivered in a formulation safer for bees or that have shorter residual toxicity periods. Developing friendly relations and regularly touching base with growers helps to facilitate these open conversations. Growers may be more likely to keep honey bees in the backs of their minds when planning for their next growing season. Moving Hives Moving colonies out of agricultural areas to accommodate pesticide applications is a contentious issue. Many beekeepers feel that having to move their colonies puts the onus of pollinator health on beekeepers instead of on growers, pesticide applicators, or landowners. Often the notification period for informing beekeepers

of a pesticide application is 48 hours. This can be a very short time period for beekeepers to pick up their colonies and move them, especially if they are in another state or province (which is sometimes the case, especially among commercial beekeepers). It can also be incredibly tricky for beekeepers to find alternative safe land on which to temporarily move their colonies. These barriers make it difficult to assume every beekeeper can move their colonies out of pesticide areas. Some beekeepers, however, may be able to move their colonies; if they are able to, they should. Moving colonies at least four miles from the area that will be treated can make a difference with regard to a pesticide poisoning event. Beekeepers should not return the colonies until at least 72 hours after the pesticide has been applied (or longer if the grower informs them of specific label language for residual toxicity for bees). Beekeepers should consider establishing “holding apiaries” for bees in advance so that they have a location to move colonies before a pesticide risk event occurs. Talking to the Public

Today the public is more aware of pollinator health than ever. Many homeowners actively plant pollinator gardens and want to do their part to help the bees. Even home and garden stores have felt the pressure from the public to sell plants that are free of certain pesticides. Home Depot, Inc., for instance, provides tags on their plants to alert customers as to which ones have been treated with neonicotinoids and plans to phase them out entirely. This is an excellent first step that demonstrates that the public cares about pollinators and has the power to drive change. Beekeepers can also inform the public where to purchase plants. Studies from Europe, the U.S., and Canada find that most plants in garden stores labeled as “bee friendly” are actually sprayed with insecticides and fungicides — the label simply means that they are a flower that bees often visit and from which they feed. Instead of purchasing these plants, beekeepers can inform people of the benefits of purchasing plants from an organic nursery. Beekeepers can even help change the public’s perspective on weeds to regard them as valuable bee forage instead of an eyesore. Through these interactions with neighbors, customers, and local gardeners, beekeepers can make a difference in whether or not the public applies pesticides to their lawns and gardens.

The European Union, a supranational political and economic union of 27 member states located primarily in Europe, implemented significant bans and restrictions on neonicotinoid pesticides due to severe risks to bees and pollinators. In 2018, it banned outdoor uses of key neonics (clothianidin, imidacloprid, and thiamethoxam) and later banned the substance thiacloprid entirely. A 2023 court ruling closed loopholes for emergency use, preventing member states from granting exemptions for banned seed treatments and reinforcing the EU's strong stance on these bee-toxic chemicals. In the USA, the New York State Senate passed, in 2023, a ban on neonicotinoids that will go in effect on January 1, 2029. According to the text of the bill, NY State will prohibit "any person to sell, offer for sale or use, or distribute within the state any corn, soybean or wheat seeds coated or treated with pesticides with the active ingredients clothianidin, imidacloprid, thiamethoxam, dinotefuran, or acetamiprid; provided, however, that the Commissioner may, by written order, temporarily suspend the provisions of this paragraph at any time based on the Commissioner's determination, after consulting with the Commissioner of Agriculture and Markets, that there is an insufficient amount of commercially available seed to adequately supply the agriculture market that has not been treated with pesticides with the active ingredients clothianidin, imidacloprid, thiamethoxam, dinotefuran or acetamiprid or the purchase of seed that complies with the requirements of this paragraph would result in undue financial hardship to agricultural producers." In this discussion, you will analyze pesticide impacts on bees and explore mitigation strategies, supporting your insights with research. Take some time to investigate this topic in beekeeping books and journals, as well as on Google Scholar and other websites. Module Introduction: Turning Bees Into Business As a beekeeper, you have by now deepened your knowledge and understanding of honey bees and explored management strategies to maximize their health and productivity. As a Master Beekeeper student, you have likely also successfully implemented much of your learning into good practice and have possibly seen an increase in colony survival. At this point, many hobby beekeepers are satisfied to sustain their colony numbers without having to purchase bees each year. They produce enough honey for their bees, for themselves, and for gifts to friends and family. Some hobbyists even produce enough to sell their honey to other local beekeepers’ operations or have ventured into small-scale honey sales of their own. Other beekeepers are ready to grow beyond the hobbyist realm and into a legitimate business where the bees and their products are paying for themselves and making a profit for the beekeeper. The transition from hobbyist to business owner requires a shift in mindset about time management, expenses, and hive/yard management. These beekeepers work for their bees as well as for themselves. In this module, we will explore the factors beekeepers can consider when growing their operation and beginning a beekeeping business. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Considerations When Growing Your Operation Growing a beekeeping operation can ☆ Key Points certainly happen organically. Many beekeepers have found themselves starting out with a couple of colonies, and within three to six years having 20 colonies or more. When growing the operation, especially for a selfsustaining business, it is important to Before starting a business, beekeepers should develop a clear goal and plan to reach it. Increasing a beekeeping operation slowly is less risky than purchasing many new colonies at once. have a firm goal in mind. It can take years for a beekeeper to develop a sense of what they would like to do with their bees to turn a profit, and that's fine. However, when the decision is made to grow, there needs to be a goal. Without a goal, a plan forward cannot be formed, and the operation may be ill- equipped to handle issues that can arise in a bad year, such as low honey and wax yields, slow population growth, inclement weather in mating season, unexpected colony losses, and particularly harsh winter and spring conditions. Identifying the main goal(s) will help beekeepers to focus their business on the facet of beekeeping that is most appealing to them. A beekeeper’s business goal is often centered around the main product or service that sets the operation apart from others. Will the beekeeper be producing bees for sale; focus on queen rearing; operate as a contract pollinator; offer bee retrieval and cutout services; produce specialty honey for a specific market; sell bulk hive products like wax and honey; or create value-added products such as soaps, balms, and mead? Choosing one or a few products is not meant to limit the operation and prevent the beekeeper from offering all of these products or services someday, but making this choice is the start of understanding how to structure the business around a central product so that it can generate enough revenue to sustain the business. This, in turn, allows the beekeeper the time and budget to expand their product lines and services as the business grows. With larger operations, time management is a critical skill to develop. Planning business and apiary tasks is best done in advance, and many beekeepers find it easiest to plan in the quieter winter months. Falling behind in management tasks one month can carry

through to the next. For instance, not getting the colonies off to a good start in the spring affects management for the summer and fall. Not managing bees for optimized health going into winter sets the beekeeper’s operation up for a difficult season in the year to come. So, although beekeeping seems to consist of discrete, year-to-year events, success each year is dependent on the year before. Beekeepers are encouraged to plan thoroughly and to schedule time points for conducting spring and autumn colony assessments, feeding, mite monitoring (and treating), honey extraction, checking inventory, equipment assembly, equipment ordering, and organizing records. Two main modes of business startup and growth exist: (1) organic/cumulative; or (2) aggressive expansion/fast track. If beekeepers are new to business ownership and relatively new to beekeeping, organic growth is the way to go, as it affords more room for error and the inevitable steep learning curve the beekeeper needs to overcome for success. Aggressive expansion is possible, but the margin for error is slim, and aggressive expansion requires ample amounts of funds as well as the realization that the business may be in debt for the first several years while startup costs are being paid off. The fasttrack pathway should only be considered by entrepreneurs who are familiar with the ins and outs of business financing and operations. It requires extensive planning and a fiveto-ten-year business model that is written down and can be reviewed by potential investors and financial institutions. These facets of the fast-track pathway are outside of the scope of this course and require extensive business coursework, training, and field
experience that can inform the process. We will instead focus on the organic growth model, where a beekeeper can learn good business practices as the business grows. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Considerations When Growing Your Operation — Record Keeping Just as keeping colony records is important for understanding and tracking the health of bees, keeping financial records is essential to understanding and tracking the health of the business. In this video, Mary Kate Wheeler, NYS Beekeeper Tech Team Agricultural Economist, discusses the financial records beekeepers should keep and offers advice on ways to make record keeping convenient. Video Transcript Keeping good financial records is super important for beekeeping businesses. A lot of beekeepers put a lot of time and energy into keeping really good production records, which help them to understand the health and productivity of their colonies, and it's just as important to keep really good financial records, because that allows you to understand the health and the viability of your beekeeping business. Good record keeping also helps beekeepers to make better decisions about growth opportunities and other management decisions in their business. And it also helps to communicate the financial position of your business to other people, like lenders, accountants, and other service providers. So, there are four different types of financial records that you're going to want to keep in your in your beekeeping business. The first two, most people are pretty familiar with, and often they do a good job of tracking these. So, these are your revenues, business revenues and expenses. Revenues reflect all of the income that your business generates through your normal operations, so, through your sales of products or services, that money coming in is the revenue of your business. And expenses, on the other hand, reflect all the costs of doing business. So, when you're purchasing supplies and materials, or when you're purchasing larger pieces of equipment that your business needs, those are all examples of expenses. And most people do a great job tracking these because it's actually required at the end of the year by the IRS when you're filing your tax return. So the difference between your business revenues and your expenses is the profit that your business earns. And that is typically calculated over a period of time. So, normally people are looking at their business profits over the course of a calendar year. And that's what gets reported to the IRS when you file your tax returns.

So, that's revenues and expenses. And the other two types of financial records are called assets and liabilities. So, assets reflects, well, assets are resources. They're productive resources that the business actually owns and uses to generate value or to generate income through the course of your operations. So, an asset, livestock is a type of asset, so your honey bees are actually an asset of your business. Supplies that you have on hand are an example of an asset. The cash balance of your checking account and your business savings account, those are assets. As well as buildings, and property, and larger pieces of equipment and machinery. So these are all different types of assets that your business is using to be productive, to produce honey or bees for sale. So, on the other hand, your liabilities are obligations, like debts or financial obligations that the business has that have to be paid in the future or have to be met in the future. So, examples would be a mortgage, loans like a vehicle loan or an operating loan. Even your credit card balance is a short term liability. And another type of liability happens if your customer pays you for a product or service that you haven't delivered yet. So that also becomes a liability because it's an obligation that your business has to meet in the future. So when we think about that relationship between assets and liabilities, we think about another accounting concept called equity. So, equity is the share of the business that actually belongs to the owner. And the relationship there is your equity is equal to the total business assets minus the liabilities. So that's like saying all of the resources that the business owns, minus all of its financial obligations. And you definitely want to see over time your equity increase in the business. So it's important to track these things consistently and to track them over time. Equity is a little bit different from profit, which we talked about, because equity is measured at a specific moment in time. We looked at profit over the course of a year, but your equity is typically measured at least annually, and it's often done on January first because that represents the ending of your last year's financial cycle and the beginning of the new cycle. So what we recommend is doing an inventory every year right around January first, where you actually go through all of the assets that your business owns, you track, you count those things and figure out their value, and then at that time you also take stock of the business liabilities, the financial obligations. And taking the difference between those two things gives you your equity at that January first date. So tracking these things over time and keeping your financial records is going to help you to make better decisions about taking advantage of opportunities and growing your business in the ways that work best for you.

So we've talked to all the different kinds of financial records you're going to want to keep, but then the next question is, "Well, how I actually track these things," right? And so there's a couple different ways to track financial records. It's important to pick a system that's going to work for you. You don't want to pick a system that's going to be difficult for you to use because then you're going to, it's going to be really easy to fall behind in your record keeping. So, some people use a really simple system, pencil and paper. You can find these accounting booklets that are structured to provide room for you to record all your business transactions, so all your purchases and sales over the course of the year. So if you want to, you can keep records that way. Some people use Excel and actually generate spreadsheets for tracking all the business transactions and assets and liabilities. And the benefit there is that Excel can do a lot of the math for you, it can actually calculate your totals at the end of the year, and it's a little bit more powerful tool for doing analysis along the way. And then a lot of folks also use QuickBooks, which is an accounting software that's very powerful, it's much more sophisticated, and it can also be used to track your transactions throughout the year. And a benefit of QuickBooks is that it can be, make it really easy to share your financial data with accountants and other service providers that are going to help you either put together your reports or do financial analysis. So I hope that helps you, gives you some things to think about in terms of what to track, how to track it, and how that investment, investing your time in record keeping is going to help you to be a better beekeeper and make better business decisions. ▶ Read: Building Your Business Business growth happens in three main phases: startup, market establishment, and stabilization. Let's explore each in detail. Startup The startup phase consists of planning the business: exploring the market for the main product, researching competition, developing the business strategy, differentiating products from competitors, and formation of the business as a legal and taxable entity. In other words, the startup phase requires a lot of research and even more decision making. It is a very daunting phase; however, there are ample resources available to the public that make starting a business an achievable dream. For starters, the U.S. Small Business Administration offers resources, staff, mentors, coursework, and workshops to those looking to start a business. The USDA offers online resources for farmers and business owners in agricultural trades. In New York State, the Department of Agriculture and Markets is committed to aiding small agriculture businesses and farms, and can offer protections and guidance to startups that are located within an "Agricultural District" (land that has been designated to be preferentially developed or maintained for agricultural use). New York also houses the organizations Groundswell (a farm/business incubator) and Cornell Cooperative Extension (CCE); both are dedicated to serving agribusinesses, especially those in the startup phase. For example, CCE in Tompkins County has partnered with local marketplaces to offer spaces to host small farm market events for farms that are not featured in established farmers' markets, which can have membership fees and practices that are high barriers of entry for startups. Beekeepers should explore business-supporting organizations and programs in their area before they start out, and they can reach out to agricultural extension personnel for resources.

In the startup phase, beekeepers should consider a growth rate that is scalable with the product. For instance, if the beekeeper is planning on gaining profits through honey sales, they should determine how much honey — and at what price — results in high-enough revenue for the beekeeper to pay themself and to purchase more equipment and bees for growth the following year. It is suggested to only add 10–30 new colonies per year for the first two or three years. This growth rate allows for recovery of colony losses, low crop yields, and growing/grooming the market share or consumer base. This also enables the beekeeper to transition into new business and yard management strategies that stem from time limitations. There are many factors that go into placing a product in the market, but one key to successful deployment is packaging that is appropriate and appealing to the demographic the beekeeper is targeting. For instance, a commercial operation may only sell honey in bulk containers to other businesses, and therefore packaging costs can be limited to containers and simple labels. However, small honey producers in a competitive marketplace, such as a farmers' market, require an edge over other competitors and need to invest in packaging that both differentiates their product and reflects their brand and values (e.g., glass jars, labels that are informative and attractive, ribbons and accessory packaging such as bundle packs and baskets). The small business must be aware of how the buyer experiences the product, as well as the

▶ quality of the product itself. For a small business, marketing is akin to telling a story and inviting the consumer into the experience. Market Establishment The second phase of business growth is market establishment. This is the experimental phase. No matter how much thought and planning goes into the startup phase, establishing a business and selling products in the market takes time. During this phase, beekeepers should seek ample feedback from consumers and businesses that are buying the product. Market events are invaluable in this sense, as they allow business owners to directly interact with consumers and solicit immediate feedback about their products. Events also allow owners to observe how consumers interact with the product and how they respond to the overall story. This phase is the best time for the business to react to customer feedback by refining packaging and storytelling, and ultimately establishing a successful and cohesive brand. This phase is both nerve wracking and rewarding. Often expenditures are on par with revenue, but mindfully investing in the business while refining the targeted market should yield steady growth in the following years. This is the time when pivoting is easiest and most frequent. Pivoting is making changes to the business model in reaction to the reality of what the business experiences in the marketplace as opposed to what was expected to happen. A business that does not react to the market, or adheres too rigidly to a plan, will have a difficult time entering the final phase in the growth cycle, or may fail outright and shut down. Stabilization The final phase of the business growth cycle is stabilization. This phase is marked by steady adoption of product into the marketplace, climbing sales, ▶

and a stable or consistent pattern of revenue on a yearly basis. An indication that the business, brand, or product is entering the stabilization phase is the occurrence of repeat customers and orders. Word-of-mouth feedback (referral sales) is another indicator. These are exciting developments for any business, especially for a new business owner; however, they do not indicate that the work is done. The stabilization phase indicates the time when the beekeeper may be able to divert some time and effort from active sales outlets (marketplaces, events, etc.) to passive sales outlets (online, storefront, etc.), as well as considering whether or not it is time to offer more product lines. It is not advisable to consider diversification of products before the stabilization of the core business. More products equals more time spent away from the bees and more processing equipment and packaging in which to invest. If your business reaches this phase, give yourself a good pat on the back — you’ve earned it! Back to Table of Contents

The saying “time is money” becomes readily apparent for owners as businesses start up. Beekeepers are compelled to increase efficiency in the bee yard to ensure all tasks are accomplished Adjusting from a hobby operation to a large-scale operation requires changes in time management and expense management. Large equipment purchases are important investments to the business, and as such they should be thoroughly researched beforehand. promptly and to make time to devote to other aspects of owning a business. The changes that accompany becoming a business owner call for beekeepers to reflect on their own Delegating tasks to other people and professionals as the business grows allows the beekeeper to focus on what they do best. personal strengths and to plan for how to address their challenges. Developing skills in time management and expense management reveals the areas of the business where the beekeeper’s skill set is most valuable; this is the area in which they can have the greatest influence. If there are skills that the beekeeper is lacking, they can delegate tasks to other people as the business grows. Professional services, such as lawyers, accountants, insurers, marketing specialists, designers, and manufacturers, may be better equipped to offset a beekeeper’s workload in these areas. Hiring help to manage office needs or processing and packaging products can be intimidating to a new business owner, but remember that a beekeeper’s skill set best serves the business in the bee yard with the bees — increasing bee health, product yield, and population growth. In this video, Mary Kate Wheeler, NYS Beekeeper Tech Team Agricultural Economist, discusses the shifts in perspectives that beekeepers must undergo in order to run a successful business. Video Transcript

Let's talk about some of the differences between being a producer and being a business manager. So, a lot of you folks, if you're taking this course, have considerable experience beekeeping and managing your hives and your apiaries. And what I want to highlight is that there's a really big change in perspective when you go from keeping bees as a hobby or as a fun activity, to actually managing a beekeeping business. So as a producer, your focus is really on the logistics of managing your apiaries and your colonies, producing really incredible products. So a lot of hobbyists are really product focused. Managing the health of your bees and keeping them healthy and happy. And a lot of the focus is kind of on the the present moment, really the experience of working with bees. So in contrast, when you move over to managing a business, you want to have more of an entrepreneurial perspective. One of the key differences is that instead of focusing so much on the products, you really have to focus on the customer, understanding the needs and the desires of your target customer, and how you can deliver your product to them in a really unique and innovative way. Because that's what's going to create a unique value and a unique position for your business. So on top of that, an entrepreneur is thinking not only about production, but also about a bunch of other complex systems that the business requires to be sustained and successful. And the entrepreneur is also thinking ahead, thinking out into the future, and not getting lost in day to day operations, but pursuing kind of a strategy and a vision to be successful in the business. So, I want to tell you guys about this great book. It's like a business advice book for small businesses that was first put out back in the 80s, it's called the E Myth. So in this case, E stands for entrepreneurial, the entrepreneurial myth. And this book is based on the premise that there's a myth in our culture in America, that sort of says anybody can start a business. If you have a technical skill or area of expertise, that is easy for you to just go into business for yourself. Forget having a boss, you can run the show, you can be in charge and be successful. But the statistics don't actually back that up because a lot of small businesses don't succeed. And a lot really struggle, and many actually fail within the first few years. So this book, The E Myth, sort of explores some of the reasons for why that happens. One of the most interesting ideas in the book is this concept of the three business personalities. And so, the three are, there's a technician, the manager, and the entrepreneur. You can think about the technician as being a doer, a tinkerer, somebody who loves to get their hands dirty. That's solving problems, getting things done, and just

loves to be immersed in their work itself. So the strength of the technician is really execution, getting things done. In terms of the manager, this is a person who's really organized, very pragmatic, practical, loves planning, thinking about systems, and creating structure and organization. So, if you're somebody that loves spreadsheets and record keeping, you might be a manager at heart. And the strength of the manager is bringing stability to the business. Helping to be sure that the business activities can be sustained over time. So the third personality, the entrepreneur, is the visionary. The big picture thinker. This person loves change, thrives in super chaotic environments, craves control, and can articulate a vision or concept that other people can rally around. And so the strength in a business setting of the entrepreneur is that this person can really drive the business forward and identify opportunities for growth. So the tricky thing, is that any business needs all three of these perspectives. And as a small business, you may just be one person in charge. Right? And so it's really important to have an awareness of your own personality and what your strengths and weaknesses are. And this framework is really helpful. Right? Because you can think about, are you more of a technician, a manager, or an entrepreneur? If you're one of these, or if you are most comfortable in one of these areas, can you build skills in another area and bring that into your business? And if not, who else can you bring in? Can you in an employee, maybe a partner or an adviser, that has a complementary perspective that can help you get all three of those perspectives in your business. So, now I want to talk a little bit about some of the business functions, core business functions, that, again, are different, or one of the major differences between beekeeping as a hobby and a fun activity, versus beekeeping as a business. So, we already talked a little bit about production, and that fits into what we call operations. So, operations is the first function of a business. And that really has to do with the logistics of how you're producing things, or products and services for your clients. And as beekeepers, you already have a lot of experience with this. So it's probably the area you're most familiar with in terms of thinking about how to plan for your operations. So, the next thing, after you're producing something in a business, you have to think about how am I going to sell this? Who are my target customers? How am I going to get the product to them? What am I going to charge? How is it going to be packaged? And that all fits into the second core business function, which is marketing. So, marketing has

a lot to do with connecting your product with your target consumer, and telling your story and communicating the value of what your product provides. Okay, so you've got your production and you get your sales, but the next question is how are you going to pay for all of this? So, how are you going to finance your production? How are you going to finance that marketing piece? And that brings us to the third function of a business, which is finance. And so that has to do with managing income and expenses, managing your cash flow so that you're never short. It has to do with projecting, budgeting, projecting your profits, and keeping track of all your financial records. So those are three core functions. On top of that, I also usually add management, sometimes as administration or even human resources. And the management function has to do with making sure all of the other functions are coordinated with each other, and it also has to do with additional business considerations. Thinking about things like legal issues, your business structure, regulatory issues, taxes, insurance, managing risk, managing people and labor in your operation. So those are all sort of comprise that fourth function, which is management. And then the final function that's critical for any business, long term, is leadership. And this function sort of encompasses all of the rest of them. So leadership requires one to step out of the day-to-day activities of the business and think about what is it that you really doing? What are your goals for the business? What's your vision? Where are you headed? And how well is your business currently meeting those goals? Is the business actually going in the right direction at the moment, or do you need to change course? And so, that leadership function is often easy to lose track of in the hustle and bustle of your day to day operations, but it's critical in terms of ensuring that the business takes you where you want to go in the end. So to wrap up, those are some of the key differences between beekeeping as a hobby and beekeeping as a business. Having the right perspective where you are thinking like an entrepreneur and focusing our customer needs. And also just keeping track of all the various business functions not just your production, but also your marketing, finance, management piece, and then trying to keep one eye on the future and on the big picture direction of your business. The necessity for record keeping and timely inspections increases exponentially as a beekeeper starts a business and their colony numbers increase. The days of being able to go into the yard only on the clearest, warmest days to accomplish tasks will be over. The

business of beekeeping requires working the bees in less-than-ideal conditions on cloudy, windy, or even cool days. Business owners need to be even more selective and conscientious beekeepers. As a hobbyist, it makes sense to spend time trying to nurse a struggling colony along for a season. It is an informative experience, and therefore time well spent. From a business standpoint, it is important to realize the threshold where this is no longer the case. It often makes more sense to cull or merge struggling colonies than it does to keep supporting them through the whole season. Culling or merging allows the beekeeper’s time to be spent on colonies that demonstrate a better chance of survival or of producing a big honey yield. Eliminating weak colonies sounds harsh, but the reality is that it reduces the chance of those sick or failing colonies affecting the other colonies in the yard. As a business owner, time is likely best spent helping the healthiest colonies maintain that health, as it translates to increased honey, wax, and bee yields. Photo Credit: Ben Rulison While the business is starting, the beekeeper is likely to experience sticker shock from purchases of large amounts of equipment or large pieces of equipment. A business plan is invaluable at this point, as it helps them to visualize how these large costs spread out over

time. What seems like a large purchase — such as 400 hive bodies, 400 supers, and 4,000 of their respective frames during a seasonal sale from an equipment manufacturer or supplier — is spread out over the course of 10 to 30 years, depending on how well the equipment is maintained. Compound this example with the fact that manufacturers tend to increase the price of goods 1–10% each year in response to inflation and market factors. One-time large purchase orders of durable goods become a prudent choice — as long as it does not exceed the growth plan for the business. There are incentives for business owners to make purchases in this manner. Business expenses are often tax deductible, and beekeepers may choose to have equipment depreciate over time, making the initial expense easier to manage in future years. Seek counsel from a certified accountant on business expenditures and financial planning. An accountant’s services can seem expensive, but they should save time (and eventually money) and provide the business with better results than if a beekeeper were to attempt to manage these details by themself. Beekeepers are also encouraged to talk to other beekeepers and visit their operations to hear their opinions on specific equipment, as they may offer invaluable advice. Overall, be prudent with purchases, and buy equipment that can grow with the operation. Equipment that increases throughput often pays for itself in the time and labor it saves compared to undersized, cheaper-priced equipment. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Deciding on Business Structure One of the more technical yet ☆ Key Points ambiguous aspects of starting a business — beekeeping or otherwise — is how the owner structures the business. The structure of the business and how it operates is largely dependent on the regulations and There are a variety of ways businesses can be registered, and beekeepers should explore each in detail to determine which method best suits their goals. laws in place wherever the beekeeper is doing business. It is important to be mindful of not only where a beekeeper physically sets up shop, but also where the products are distributed. In all cases, the business interests are always best served by being informed of local laws, customs, practices, and limitations. In the U.S. — and New York specifically — there are four main categories to register and define a business with the state and federal government: sole proprietorship, partnership, limited liability company (LLC), and corporation (Inc.). Each entity has pros and cons associated with it. The main factors to consider with each setup are the tax structure, the benefits afforded to the business, and the amount of financial and legal liability each structure/entity allows to pass through to the owner(s). The other factor to consider is the cost associated with registering the business as any one of the structures or switching between types. This information is presented purely as a helpful resource to beekeepers who are curious about growing and starting a beekeeping business; the final exam series will not ask questions about different business structure details.

▶ Sole Proprietorships Sole proprietorships are the most basic form of business structure. There is no legal distinction between the owner and the business — the owner is responsible for any taxes, litigation, and liability due to operating the business. This is often the easiest form of business to set up, with minimal paperwork, minimal fees, and minimal time to do so. However, this structure carries a large amount of risk to the business owner. If a charge comes against the business, such as a personal injury case or tax collection, assets of the owner can be seized in order to satisfy the charges against the business. Partnerships Partnerships are similar to sole proprietorships in the sense that the risks, taxes, and liabilities are all directly linked to the owners. The amount of risk can depend on how this structure is set up in the beginning. Not all partnerships are equal in the distribution of risk. Partnerships involve multiple parties (partners can be people, investors, and other business entities), and so they can require legal assistance to start. This assistance is mainly for defining the ▶

▶ ▶ roles and responsibilities of each partner, as well as the liability that each partner assumes as business is carried out. Limited Liability Companies Limited liability companies are a hybrid entity that affords similar tax and liability benefits to the owner as a corporation, while requiring slightly less paperwork and legal fees to maintain over time than a corporate structure. LLCs are able to file taxes with the federal government as a corporation. LLCs, as their name implies, offer liability protection to the owners in the event of bankruptcy or litigation against the company. If the business collapses, the owner is not responsible to pay for any business accounts or taxes that have not been personally guaranteed. The downsides of an LLC include the highest initial cost to set up, and there are additional paperwork and steps in New York to announce the formation of the business. The business is required to file a semiannual report with the state. However, maintenance costs are minimal and, over time, cheaper than incorporation. Corporation Corporation is the last of the business structures. There are three main types of corporations: S corporation, C corporation, and B corporation. The most pertinent to beekeeping are S and B corporations. S corporations are small corporate entities defined by having fewer than 100 shareholders. S corps allow all corporate income and losses to be passed through to the shareholders, who report these directly on their personal income tax returns at the income tax rate. This allows the owners to avoid corporate tax, which many see as a "double taxation." C corporations are taxed separately from their shareholders to whom they are responsible, and B corporations are similar in structure to C corps in this respect. B corps differ from C corps in the sense that they are intended to provide a public or societal good or mission, and most treat employees as shareholders. All corporate structures offer liability protection for shareholders in the case of action taken against the company, be it financial, legal, or otherwise.

▶ Corporations require rigid structure, dedication to turning a profit to benefit shareholders and are subject to filing corporate documents on a regular basis to interested parties. Corporations that fail to follow these practices are subject to action by their shareholders, such as upper management being replaced (i.e., the original owners/founders), the business being shuttered for not turning a profit or adhering to the corporate goals, or the business being dissolved to reduce shareholder burden for bankruptcy. The startup cost for an incorporation (forming a corporate entity) is less than that of an LLC, with similar protections. However, the maintenance costs increase as the corporation grows. Registering a Business Registering a business can be a daunting task, but the benefits of doing so far outweigh the risks of operating an unregistered business. Registered businesses are eligible for many tax benefits and qualify to receive resources made available by the federal and state governments that are designed to help business owners start, grow, and expand. The USDA offers many loan and grant opportunities to small business owners, as does New York State. Creditors and financial institutions are more likely to lend on favorable terms to registered businesses, and investors are more comfortable investing in a registered business. Lastly, consumers often view a registered business as being more reliable and trustworthy, paying a higher premium for products and brands that leverage this image accordingly. Read: Programs and Resources to Help Beekeepers Overview Today, more resources and programs exist to help beekeepers than ever before. Some programs help beekeepers maintain healthy colonies, while others help them mitigate risks and manage their businesses. Depending on your operation size and beekeeping goals, some of these programs might be helpful for you (even if you don’t own a beekeeping business). Others may not suit you but are nonetheless good to be aware of in the event a fellow beekeeper turns to you for support. Many of these programs are not well advertised and may not be known in bee clubs. In this course, we will present a brief overview of U.S. programs as well as programs specific to New York State to help beekeepers. Beekeepers from other regions are encouraged to check in with their state or provincial apiculturist and local extension associates to find similar resources that can help them. We will not ask questions about these programs in the Master Beekeeper Program Exam Series. We realize this information is not helpful for everyone, but it can be helpful to some. NYS Beekeeper Tech Team

Watch: Programs to Help With Colony Health New York State Beekeeper Tech Team The NYS Beekeeper Tech Team is fully funded by the state Pollinator Protection Plan to provide three years of colony health sampling to 25 beekeepers across the state. Colonies are sampled twice per year (early summer and late summer) for Varroa mites, Nosema, and pesticides. In addition, beekeepers receive counseling on best management practices and develop an annual plan to maximize colony health and productivity. Enrollment is on a first-come/first-served basis to operations based in New York State that bring in annual revenues of at least $1,000. Priority is given to commercial beekeepers as well as beekeepers who have consistently experienced unsustainable colony losses. After three years, beekeepers graduate from the program and new beekeepers are enrolled. Website: https://pollinator.cals.cornell.edu/resources/nys-beekeeper-tech-team Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Programs to Help With Your Beekeeping Business USDA Farm Service Agency Loan Programs National Program The USDA offers a variety of loan and grant programs for which beekeepers can apply to help them establish or operate their business. Some loans, such as the "Beginning Farmer and Rancher Development Loan Program” are appropriate for beekeepers that have been in business for fewer than 10 years. Loans for “Socially Disadvantaged Farmers and Ranchers” allow farmers to buy and operate family-sized farms; eligible groups include “American Indians or Alaskan Natives, Asians, Blacks or African-Americans, Native Hawaiians or other Pacific Islanders, Hispanics, and women.” Depending on the loan, it can be used to help cover costs of purchasing buildings, land, equipment, livestock, chemicals, feed, and insurance. “Emergency Loans” can help beekeepers recover from unexpected production losses as well as livestock and equipment losses from natural disasters or disease quarantine. There are a variety of these grant programs available, with more information and options found at the website below. Website: https://www.fsa.usda.gov/programs-and-services/farm-loan-programs/index NY FarmNet New York State Program NY FarmNet is a government-funded program that provides financial analysis, business planning, and psychological counseling to beekeepers struggling with their businesses. High colony losses can be devastating emotionally and financially, so FarmNet representatives offer help free of charge. In addition, NY FarmNet can help with business transitioning for beekeepers nearing retirement. NY FarmNet also offers a webinar course through eCornell on business and succession planning. Website: https://www.nyfarmnet.org In this video, Dan Welch, Extension Support Specialist for NY FarmNet, discusses how the program can help beekeepers. Video Transcript FarmNet is a program based out of Cornell that's supported by New York State to assist farm families throughout the state with business transitions, maybe from one generation

to another, looking at profitability, and assisting sometimes with some of the thornier issues that come up when you're working close together with family and friends that can sometimes lead to conflict. And if those situations aren't dealt with, that can have negative impacts on business. So we try to be a resource for those farms and help them to continue to make good business decisions so their farms are viable into the future. New York FarmNet is a 100% free and confidential service that's available to beekeepers and any other farm in New York State. We are supported through the state budget by the Department of Ag and Markets and New York State Office of Mental Health. And that enables us to go out to any farm, and we come right to the operation, so you don't have to come down to Ithaca to meet with us. One of the other services that we offer is helping individuals and families work together in developing techniques to manage some of the stress that comes along with keeping bees. I know here in New York, a lot of beekeepers have been losing a lot of their colonies, which causes both financial and mental stress, and can also stress relationships. Our family consultants are able to work with beekeepers to give them good techniques for managing that stress so that you can focus on your business and continue to grow. If you're just looking for more information, you can go to our website, which is www.nyfarmnet.org. Or you can call 1-800 number, and that number is 1-800-547-3276, and that's a number where there's always a person. If it's outside the office hours, it will go to an answering service where there's a real, live human being. And then shortly after we get that message, one of our consultants will come back to schedule a meeting with you. New York State Beekeeper Tech Team: Financial Analysis and Business Benchmarking Program New York State Program In addition to investigating a beekeeper’s colony health and management practices, the New York State Beekeeper Tech Team provides financial analysis and business benchmarking for beekeepers. Beekeepers enrolled in the program meet with an agricultural economist to develop financial statements that allow beekeepers to understand the financial position of their business, which in turn allows them to make informed business decisions. The program also offers record-keeping assistance and provides beekeepers with a report on how their businesses are doing compared to similarly sized beekeepers that are also participating in the program. Website: https://pollinator.cals.cornell.edu/nys-beekeeper-tech-team/

Module Introduction: Being a Leader in Your Community Community involvement is a natural part of keeping bees; after all, our animals of interest are themselves organized as complex social organisms. Indeed, we need to be involved with other beekeepers, as honey bees fly well beyond our property lines. Foragers travel two to three miles in each direction from their colony to collect nectar and pollen, and virgin queens can fly about eight miles in search of drones. This behavior, combined with the density of our human population, means that the territories of our apiaries often overlap. Our problems become our neighbors' problems, just as our solutions may also work for our neighbors. For the sake of healthy colonies and maintaining genetic diversity, we should offer and accept ideas from our neighboring beekeepers. Our success with honey bees also directly benefits from relationships with scientists, gardeners, farmers, the public, honey lovers, and everyone with an interest in bees. Nearly all Master Beekeeper Programs are developed with public education and community service as a core value, and Cornell’s is no exception. We encourage you to provide volunteer service in your community, in whatever way is most fulfilling to you. While our program does not require you to log volunteer hours, we do hope you step up to be an ambassador for honey bee and pollinator health. In this module, we will discuss leadership skills and explore opportunities for serving your communities. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Mentoring Being a mentor allows beekeepers to reflect on their early lessons in beekeeping and fosters their own curiosity. It forces them to slow their pace and think about what they are doing when they open a hive or purchase new equipment. Mentors who articulate what is seen, what is done, and why should remain open to comments and questions. They will discover occasional holes in their reasoning or perhaps a fact that needs to be checked, and they may be grateful for the insight. ☆ Key Points Mentoring new beekeepers is a valuable way to share knowledge and skills. Mentoring requires skills in beekeeping, teaching, and communicating. Beekeepers should review how much time they have available to mentor before committing to any mentees. There is a lot for a newcomer to the apiary to absorb. Finding the right level of exposure and appropriate tasks for an apprentice is one of the first challenges met by a mentor. You might start with a lazy conversation in lawn chairs beside some hives on a fair day for an introduction to a mentor-mentee relationship. This way, you can share personal insights and ambitions with apiculture, as well as a preliminary lesson in observing entrance behavior. Becoming familiar with bees in the air and in the hive, as they buzz about and land on people, helps newcomers understand the various sounds of bees, one of many skills required to work a colony with gentleness and composure. During one or two years of mentorship, new beekeepers gradually gain perspective into seasonality and other details of timing. It is often necessary to experience a few seasons to absorb such knowledge, just as it was for you! It may take several more seasons to be able to apply creative decision making to colony management.

As the apprentice develops a commitment to beekeeping, they will become a contributing member to the beekeeping community. Apprentice beekeepers may provide healthy pollinators for crops and natural vegetation, contribute to the local economy through their businesses, and may even educate some new beekeepers. Investing in the next generation of beekeeping through mentoring can be a very rewarding way for a beekeeper to spend their time. Being a beekeeping mentor requires a number of skills and qualities, including (1) a knowledge of the art and science of beekeeping; (2) experience in beekeeping; (3) being an effective communicator; and (4) being a patient and compassionate teacher. Master Beekeepers, by definition, fulfill the first two criteria. For some, mentoring might come naturally. Many beekeepers are happy and excited to share their knowledge, expertise, and guidance with new beekeepers. If mentoring is not for you, that is OK! Master Beekeepers can contribute to the community and beekeeping industry in a variety of ways beyond mentoring. Mentoring is a form of informal teaching through modeling methods and providing opportunities for hands-on learning. Learning through continuous dialogue is natural and effective in the apiary and honey house. The beekeeper can describe the rationale of management choices and manipulations, while the mentee can ask questions about any gaps in understanding. It is common to hear experts describe how much beginners teach

them simply by asking questions that require articulate, thoughtful answers or a little extra research. Group mentorships can also be effective in beekeeping clubs. Beginners and experts alike build their knowledge and refine their skills with a synergistic collective intelligence, seeking advice from peers in their groups. Every local beekeeping association should have a mentoring program. If yours does not, one of the first impacts you can make as a Master Beekeeper is to help start one. To find mentees, advertise your contact information on your club’s website and social media channels. Preparation Start small. If you have never mentored before, begin with one beekeeper. Decide whether you want the mentee to learn and practice on your colonies, whether you want to travel and teach with their colony, or a combination. Some mentors prefer to work with their mentees’ colonies and get an understanding of the needs of those colonies to best answer any questions they have, while others appreciate an extra hand with their own apiary chores! Mentoring goes beyond arriving at a new beekeeper’s apiary and giving them an hour to ask you questions. It is guiding them through the process of learning at an

appropriate pace. If the mentee has specific things they would like to learn, have them tell you up front so that you can work those topics into your sessions. Availability New beekeepers are excited and passionate about beekeeping. They generally have many questions and are grateful to have someone to consult for answers. From the start, you may want to set contact boundaries. Decide upon your schedule of meeting times and determine what times it is OK for your mentee to call you outside of the sessions. When you are meeting with your mentee, be approachable and patient. Foster an environment where they feel comfortable asking questions. It can take considerable time and energy to be a one-stop shop for all questions and conversations about beekeeping. Encourage your mentee to seek out other sources of information. Suggest that they join a beekeeping club if they have not already, turn to the local honey bee extension associate, sign up for introductory classes (either online or in person), subscribe to beekeeping journals, and read books. We recommend the following introductory books: "Honey Bee Biology and Beekeeping" by Dewey Caron and Lawrence John Connor "The Beekeeper’s Handbook" by Diana Sammataro and Alphonse Avitabile "Beekeeping for Dummies" by Howland Blackiston (a good introductory guide despite the title) Feedback is important — and do not forget the positive kind! Recognize your mentee when they are handling frames gently and identifying colony items correctly, and provide useful, constructive criticism if they slip up. Do this in an honest, encouraging manner. As leaders and educators, mentors should tell their mentees what they need to hear, not what they want to hear. Be compassionate when communicating advice and suggestions. Back to Table of Contents
