Watch: Community Service Master Beekeepers are valued for community services like speaking to organizations, mentoring new beekeepers, providing public education with lectures for schools and civic organizations, conducting handson workshops, and discussing current issues with the media — all activities to benefit the public good and the environment. ☆ Key Points Master Beekeepers can be leaders in their communities in many ways, including working with other beekeepers, students, researchers, the government, and the public. Beekeepers can learn how their customers benefit from having honey at their table, who plants pollinator gardens, and which farmers are finding ways to reduce their use of pesticides; in turn, they can foster ties with all who support pollinator protection efforts. The benefits extend to the beekeepers themselves as they enjoy fulfillment from service and teaching. The ever-changing world of apiculture is a rich environment for lifelong learning. There are several ways that Master Beekeepers can volunteer in their communities. Depending on their skills, comfort level, and time availability, some avenues may be more appropriate than others. We encourage beekeepers to explore the suggestions below.

▶ Speaking to Media Honey bee issues are a hot topic in media in recent years. Journalists frequently seek beekeepers to interview for TV, news, and radio segments, but unfortunately they sometimes perpetuate inaccurate information. One common example is colony collapse disorder. Although it no longer has a major effect on honey bee health in the U.S., many stories are still centered on colony collapse disorder. In reality, Varroa mites, viruses and other diseases, management practices, pesticides, and economic pressures are bigger issues facing bees today. Most of what the public learns about bees is from the media, so an informed beekeeper’s voice can make an impact on the community’s understanding of the current status of bees. If beekeepers are interested in speaking to the media, they can submit their name at their club and local university as a contact person for when those institutions receive inquiries. Contributing to Policy Discussions ▶

▶ With the increasing awareness of pollinator health declines, new policies and regulations are being developed to help mitigate bee health issues. Pollinator protection plans are being created (and continuously updated) at the state level, and now several counties and cities are developing their own strategies to help bees. During the formulation of new policies and programs, beekeepers, scientists, other pollinator stakeholders, and government legislators discuss the issues and possible solutions for better bee health. Beekeepers are often invited to speak on behalf of the beekeeping industry and voice the issues affecting beekeepers in their region. Master Beekeepers can contribute effectively to these discussions. Delivering Presentations to Schools Educating children about bees is, above all, fun! The students may grow up to be beekeepers, environmental scientists, farmers, landscape architects, or politicians; no matter what they do, the more they recognize the importance of agriculture, pollinators, and their habitats, the better. Some teachers advertise opportunities to have beekeepers give presentations and demonstrations to their students. Depending on the age of the children a beekeeper visits, they can create a simple presentation about bees and beekeeping, then combine it with a fun activity, story time, or show-and-tell with equipment and an observation hive. Beekeepers can also invite classes to take a field trip to their honey house to see the ins and outs of extracting honey. Students learn where honey comes from, how the bees make it, and how people harvest it.

▶ Photo Credit: Connor Smith Before working in schools, beekeepers should speak to the teacher about protocols regarding food (especially sweets!), bee allergies, and stings. Taking on a Leadership Role in a Bee Club Bee clubs are the heart of the hobbyist beekeeping community, with members of all experiences, ages, and lifestyles meeting together with a common goal. They are a great source of information for beekeepers, as well as friendships and partnerships that can last a long time. In this video, Shelley Stuart, former president of the Finger Lakes Beekeepers Club, discusses the dynamic community of beekeeping clubs. Video Transcript As a new beekeeper, and even as a beekeeper with a few years under your belt, I find that bee clubs can be really helpful in building a bee community. And it's not just about getting information, it's about sharing your own expertise. I was president of the Finger Lakes Bee Club for about five years, I think it was. When I started, I had two years of beekeeping under my belt, so I wasn't particularly expert in beekeeping, but I could organize a meeting. And

what I found with the beekeeping community is that everybody shares their information and experience, their microclimates, their tips, their tricks, and it really encourages a vibrant beekeeping community. When folks that are in your local area say, "This worked for me, but it may not work for you," or "I'm also up on a windy hill, and here is what I've done to successfully overwinter my bees," or "I'm seeing the goldenrod flow start now and my hive is putting on weight," or, "For the spring, I'm seeing drone cells in my hives, so it's time to make splits." And I think that information flow and sharing of information not only makes for better beekeepers in your area, but eventually, ultimately, will fill your area with better bees. And you'll see that in your own hives with the genetics because your neighbor's drones are going to be mating with your queens, and vice versa, and the stronger your greater area of bees are, then the stronger your own hives will be. Every club is different, but most meet once a month to discuss honey bee news, management practices appropriate for the current season and climate, and upcoming events in the community. Most offer mentorship opportunities to partner experienced beekeepers with new beekeepers. Here is a list of additional activities and resources provided by some clubs: Host speakers to talk about current research or specialized topics in beekeeping. Hold workshops for club members on topics such as introductory beekeeping, monitoring for Varroa mites, and wintering colonies. Share equipment and resources, including honey extractors, microscopes, Varroa mite vaporizers, and beekeeping books. Order nucs/packages or mite treatments in bulk to sell or distribute to members. Develop breeding programs to improve the genetics in the local beekeeping community. Set up booths at festivals and fairs to promote honey bees and sell honey from various club members. Hold honey judging competitions. Hold conferences (typically state- or province-wide bee clubs). Host social events like potlucks and honey tastings. Put together floats for community parades.

▶ Get involved in apicultural research. Support pollinator protection organizations. If beekeepers have the time and interest, joining the club as an officer or board member can be an effective way to influence the quality of the club and the benefits it offers its members. Clubs often need many individuals to help them run efficiently. The leadership roles are diverse, including organizing meetings, managing membership and finances, sending out and responding to emails, and managing social media. Giving Presentations With their knowledge and expertise, Master Beekeepers are in a position to help educate others through public speaking. Presenting at clubs, workshops, and bee conferences (such as the annual Eastern Apicultural Society or American Beekeeping Federation conferences) can allow them to share valuable information with other beekeepers from different regions or experience levels. Beekeepers who wish to give talks should choose topics that are important to them, on which they feel confident speaking, and that are interesting or valuable to others. Later in this module, we will discuss how to prepare and deliver an effective presentation. Presentations are not restricted to beekeeping organizations but could also be beneficial to gardening clubs, agricultural organizations, horticultural societies, ornithology associations, golf clubs, and nature groups. Writing Articles The written word can reach a much larger audience than a presentation with a limited audience. Consider submitting something to American Bee Journal or Bee Culture, newsletters for regional or state beekeeping clubs, or the local paper. If beekeepers have ideas for articles, they should reach out to magazine or newspaper editors to pitch them. Volunteering at Universities ▶ ▶

Universities are the hubs for honey bee research and extension. These institutions often have lots of projects underway and are grateful for all the volunteer help they can get. The Dyce Lab, for instance, could not effectively function without help from volunteers! There are many volunteer opportunities maintaining research and extension colonies, supporting scientific experiments, teaching workshops, responding to beekeeper inquiries through email or phone, creating handouts and educational materials, and managing social media. If beekeepers want to be on the cutting edge of research or extension, they can contact their nearest academic institution to see what opportunities are available and where they will best fit in. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Participating in Research Pollinator health research has grown in recent years, and one of the most impactful ways that Master Beekeepers can give back to the community is through participating in the research. While scientists are aware of the factors impacting honey bee health, we have yet to understand their relative importance and develop solutions. To investigate the real-world situations of honey bees, institutions are turning to beekeepers to help provide data. Beekeepers do not have to be trained in scientific research to participate. ☆ Key Points Citizen science projects harness the efforts of many people to collect data on the health of honey bees and other pollinators. Many universities and institutions regularly seek out beekeepers to participate in pollinator health projects. Responding to Bee Informed Partnership’s annual colony loss survey provides invaluable data for understanding honey bee health problems. There are two major ways that beekeepers can take part in research: participating in citizen science and responding to beekeeper surveys. While beekeepers must devote some time to collecting samples or filling out surveys, the benefits are numerous, as the data can provide insight into a variety of questions: How many colonies were lost in the area last winter? What were the main causes of mortality? What are the disease levels and pesticide risks in the area? When are nearby colonies swarming? Answers to such questions can allow beekeepers to make more informed management decisions in their own bee yards.

▶ Citizen Science Citizen science is scientific research conducted in part by non-scientists. The process usually involves citizens collecting and submitting scientific data and, as such, can foster collaborative efforts between beekeepers and scientists. Citizen science allows for the study of bees in a variety of environments where they are normally found or managed. Unlike strictly controlled scientific experiments, this encompasses the real-world variations encountered by bees. Citizen science is a good approach for understanding trends that are widely distributed across a state or country because many volunteers can gather much more information in a short period of time than a few scientists could. There are several ongoing citizen science projects on honey bees and other pollinators in the U.S. New York Bee Wellness The nonprofit organization New York Bee Wellness collects data on swarm dates, mite counts, and virus levels to post on virtual interactive maps. Beekeepers simply enter their swarm and mite information online but must send in samples of bees at four time points across the year to determine virus levels.

Bumble Bee Watch Bumble Bee Watch is a citizen science project tracking North America’s bumble bee populations. Citizens photograph bumble bees, identify the species, and upload the photos to a website where experts verify their identifications. In this way, bumble bee abundance and diversity can be tracked continuously across the U.S. and Canada, particularly for rare or endangered species such as the rusty-patched bumble bee. National USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) Survey The National APHIS Survey is a government program that surveys beekeepers' colonies for parasites, pathogens, and pesticides. It also actively monitors the presence or absence of invasive threats to honey bee health (such as the Tropilaelaps parasite and slow bee paralysis virus). This program is conducted through the state apiculturist and state inspectors, who select different beekeepers each year to participate. Cornell University Projects Each year, the Dyce Lab recruits beekeepers to participate in various research projects. In 2015 and 2019, beekeepers and growers participated in an apple pollination pesticide study. Every year since 2016, the lab samples colonies of approximately 25 beekeepers participating in the NYS Beekeeper Tech Team for Varroa, Nosema, and pesticides to understand these threats as well as beekeepers’ management practices. The projects for each summer are determined the previous winter and spring and are advertised on the Pollinator Network website and the Dyce Lab Facebook page. Beekeepers from New York that are interested in participating in Cornell University research are encouraged to check these avenues regularly. Surveys At this point, all information about colony losses across the country are from voluntary beekeeper survey data. Beekeeper observations about colony losses and management practices are critical, as they are often cited by scientists and media to provide an overview of the status of honey bees. These data can even be helpful in persuading grant reviewers and legislators to provide ▶

research funding for projects about bees. The more data that is gathered, the more complete the picture is for honey bee health and the beekeeping industry. New York Bee Wellness One survey that is specific to New York is released each year by New York Bee Wellness; it asks participants about their colony losses, winter management practices, and suspected causes of colony deaths. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Delivering Effective Presentations If beekeepers plan to give talks to bee ☆ Key Points clubs, conferences, schools, or other venues, it is important to work toward delivering effective presentations. Being an effective presenter is not a quality with which people are born but a skill that can be developed and continuously improved. The final exam A good presentation includes simple slides, compelling information, and effective communication. It is helpful to develop an outline prior to creating a presentation. series of the Cornell University Master Beekeeping Program requires students to give a 15-minute presentation on a topic in beekeeping. Students will be graded on this presentation. The considerations that we present here will be important for beekeepers to use when they are preparing their presentations for their final exam, as well as when they are giving presentations to the community as Master Beekeepers. An effective speaker can accomplish the following: Present compelling information in a logical order.

▶ Use effective visuals. Speak clearly and convey enthusiasm. Let’s explore each in more detail. Present Compelling Information in a Logical Order An effective presentation, like a good story, needs to be easy for the audience to follow. The audience should be able to identify the key points and understand how it relates back to the original question or purpose. Once the audience gets lost, it is hard for them to maintain their focus on the rest of the talk. An audience can quickly fall behind if the information is presented at a level that is above their comprehension. To avoid this, learn who your audience is ahead of time. If an audience consists of beginner beekeepers, assume they do not know anything about bees or beekeeping when you create your presentation; define and explain everything. If the audience has a few years of beekeeping experience, do a quick recap of the prerequisite knowledge they should have before you dive into your topic. For instance, if you are going to give a presentation on the impacts of neonicotinoids on honey bee health, start by simply introducing what neonicotinoids are. While most people in the audience may already have a general idea of this pesticide, there might be some who have heard of neonicotinoids but do not actually know what they are. Bring everyone to the same level of understanding early in the presentation, then build up to new information together. It's important to remind beekeepers that once they have a few years of experience, they have gained specialized knowledge that others do not yet have. Start simple. Before you create your accompanying presentation slides, develop an outline of your presentation. This keeps the presentation logical and to the point. A presentation outline includes the following information: Description of the audience. Presentation title. Introduction section: Introduce the specific question or purpose to be addressed in the presentation. Identify any information the audience needs

to know before getting to the body of the talk; this ensures everyone has the same level of understanding from the beginning. Some presenters like to also include a brief overview of the presentation in the introduction so the audience has a preview of what is to come. The length of the introduction depends on the length of the talk. For a 15-minute talk, aim to give a four-minute introduction. For a one-hour talk, aim to give a 10minute introduction. The body of the talk: This is the main focus of the talk. In this section, list the important points to cover and identify the sources of information that are included to support the key points. Information should be presented with a logical flow, using smooth transitions to get from one main point to the next. Keep information interesting and supportive of your main question or purpose. Try not to stray into tangents or focus on irrelevant material. Think about personal experiences to share during the main body of the talk. By nature, people like stories and can connect easily with a speaker who shares an anecdote related to the topic. For a 15-minute talk, aim to spend about nine minutes on the body. For a one-hour talk, aim to spend about 45 minutes on the body. Conclusion: Repeat the main findings and overall take-home message of the talk. Clearly identify how this information applies to the audience and what they can do (if anything) after hearing the presentation. For a 15minute talk, a two-minute conclusion should suffice. For a one-hour talk, a five-minute conclusion is ideal. Creating this outline will help speakers stay focused and organized. It works to ensure that the information presented is relevant to the main topic and presented thoughtfully. Use Effective Visuals Effective visuals are a great accompaniment to a presentation; after all, a picture is worth a thousand words. Include many photos and visuals in the presentation, and reduce text to only include a few keywords. Any words that the audience may not be familiar with should also be shown as text to make them more comprehensible and memorable; e.g., "superorganism," ▶

"neonicotinoids," "queen pheromone," and "waggle dance." Use large font in colors that are complementary to the rest of the presentation's color scheme. Having little to no text on slides directs the audience’s attention to what the speaker is saying, rather than tempting them to concentrate on the slides. It also prevents the speaker from relying on looking at the slides too much. Instead, the speaker can look at the audience, make eye contact with individuals, and engage them. Make sure to always include photo credits for photos that are not your own. Not sure how many slides to create for your presentation? Anticipate spending 30 seconds to one minute on each slide. Slides with more elaborate illustrations or diagrams take longer. Speak Clearly and Convey Enthusiasm An effective presentation engages the audience from the beginning. Get their attention with some sort of hook; maybe a thoughtful question posed to the audience, a relevant humorous anecdote, or a powerful photo. The speaker’s voice should be clear and projected so that the person in the last row can hear them. Slow down when speaking. Nervous speakers tend to ▶

speak very quickly; while this is normal, it unfortunately makes it more difficult for the audience to understand them and keep up with the information. The speaker can slow down by taking advantage of natural pauses. Blank air can feel a bit strange to the speaker, but it is helpful to have a few seconds of silence in between main points to allow the audience a moment of reflection. This is also an ideal time for the speaker to take a sip of water or gather their thoughts for how they are going to transition to the next slide. Conveying enthusiasm is the easiest way to interest an audience in a topic. Excitement is contagious. Enthusiastic speakers are not monotone; instead, their voices naturally vary in tempo along with rises and falls in pitch. Some speakers find ways to further engage their audience and keep them focused on the presentation. Posing a question or two to the audience during the presentation can make them feel more like they are participating in a discussion rather than simply watching someone talk. Lastly, always rehearse presentations before they are delivered. Practicing helps speakers stay within their time limit, transition seamlessly between points, and remain on track. It can also reduce your anxiety if you are nervous about public speaking. Practice in front of friends or family that can give constructive feedback, or by yourself, to become familiar with the content and be confident in your delivery. Steve Jobs, the late cofounder of Apple and world-renowned public speaker, rehearsed every one of his presentations for hours before giving them to the public. An Example of an Effective Presentation An example of an effective presentation is this 15-minute TED talk by Dr. Marla Spivak. Note how she uses many of the suggestions we discussed on this page. She engages the audience from the start by showing a captivating photo that illustrates the importance of bees. She uses effective visuals without relying on text on a slide. All the text is limited to a few keywords. Marla speaks clearly and slowly, and she makes use of natural pauses. She tells a few stories and personal anecdotes to which the audience can relate. Her four main points on why bees are declining are clearly stated: diseases and parasites, pesticides, monocultures, and flowerless landscapes. In her conclusion, she recaps the issues harming bees, explains
to the audience why this issue matters, and gives examples of what they can do to help. This is a very effective presentation. Back to Table of Contents

Module Introduction: Keeping Up With Science By studying to be a Master Beekeeper, you are already motivated to learn best beekeeping practices and to understand the biology of the honey bee. After this course is over, you will want to stay up to date as new information becomes available on topics such as disease, nutrition, behavior, and the condition of the local environment where your bees live. Being familiar with current science findings can benefit your management practices and will better inform your discussions with others in the beekeeping community. Furthermore, any educational work that you do as a Master Beekeeper is facilitated if you are prepared to answer questions about and discuss new findings. You can learn about recent science advances without a science degree. In this module, we will look at some ways to find, comprehend, and evaluate science. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Where to Find New Information There are two main reasons to look for bee science information. Beekeepers either browse to learn what is new or hunt for information on a specific topic. In both cases, there are three avenues that beekeepers can explore when seeking new information about bees and beekeeping. Popular Science Articles Popular science articles appear in newspapers, news sites, and journals. These pieces highlight research without delving into too much detail. The authors are science writers who generally quote an expert or experts to support the information they present. Primary Literature Primary literature, in the form of academic journal articles, is where scientific discoveries first appear in print. Authors of the primary literature are the researchers who did the work. The results and methodology necessary to repeat the study appear in a primary research paper. Primary literature can be challenging to read because it is written for other scientists, not laypeople. Even scientists from different disciplines may have difficulty following a primary literature paper outside of their own field of study. However, beekeepers can certainly gain confidence in reading these articles with practice. Reviews Reviews are summaries of multiple primary research papers dealing with the topic of interest — they are not the original research. Reviews are also published in academic journals and are reputable sources of information. Scientific reviews are typically written for the “generalist scientist"; anyone who has taken general science courses in college is likely able to understand a review, even if they are not experts on the topic being discussed. A good review is an efficient way to find much of the available information on a topic. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Popular Science Articles “Did you see that article claiming 75% of all flying insects in Europe are dead?!” ☆ Key Points Critically reading popular science articles takes practice. This is the type of exchange beekeepers may engage in with their friends. In order to be an informed participant in a conversation about a trending topic in honey bee science, beekeepers have to find the popular Media articles often sensationalize scientific findings. Some popular science journals and magazines are more reputable than others. sources and read them, then dig deeper: Locate the original research cited within those articles, get copies of the original papers, and evaluate them. Browsing the internet for bee science news requires more scrutiny for authenticity than running a specialized academic search on a specific topic. It is important to look past the headlines and think critically while reading the article. Often, popular science articles are deliberately sensationalized in order to increase readership; for example, the headline in Newsweek on this topic is “Flying Insect Numbers Fall By 75%, Threatening 'Ecological Armageddon.'" Most would agree that this title is sensationalized! The actual work is frequently fairly pedestrian and far less earth shaking than the headlines make it out to be. We learn this by going to the primary literature sources and evaluating them directly. The primary avenue of most beekeepers for learning about new findings in bee science is through popular science, as their easy-to-read style and incorporation of photos and videos makes them fun and engaging to consume. They are also frequently distributed through email and posted on social media sites. Popular reviews are the easiest to understand because they were written for a lay audience; however, not all science writers do justice to the research papers about which they write. Readers need to look at the original work as well for a deeper understanding. Let's examine how to perform a popular science news search.

▶ Searching for Reputable Popular Science Articles To receive new articles without having to regularly search for them, beekeepers can customize their interests in Google News. After they enter a few key words under "Your Interests," the search engine pulls up related articles each time they sign in to check Google News. This feature lists every type of article available on the subjects they chose, so it is a necessity to be able to evaluate the sources. Searching within Google News is more effective at pulling up news stories than if beekeepers were to broadly search in Google. Before wasting time reading a poor source, scan the journals and newspapers that published various versions of the story and select those whose coverage is likely to be the best. Some of the most trustworthy news sites that use evidenced-based reporting are Nature News, National Geographic, Smithsonian, New Scientist, The Atlantic, Live Science, The Guardian, BBC, The Scientist, Science News, and Discover. The reasons why they are good sources include: These publications focus on science, not politics. The articles are written for the intelligent layperson. Data are presented, not merely opinions. Methodology is explained so readers can broadly understand how the study was conducted. The news articles do not make grand, sweeping conclusions based on the one primary literature study they are reporting. Information about the authors of the study, their institutions, and the journal in which the study was published is included in the news article.

▶ It is a good idea to browse at least two of the articles on a topic, as this helps readers find and ignore biased reporting. It is also useful to see how various stakeholders present the same basic facts. But what if readers do not know which news source is best? They can spend a few minutes each time they do a search investigating one or two of the unknown journals or newspapers that come up in their results, allowing them to move faster through the list of options they have the next time they do a search. Beekeepers may find that certain news sites are not real organizations or that they have a specific agenda. Searching for news organizations on Wikipedia or the business- and organization-reviewing website Sitejabber can help beekeepers navigate which news outlets are trustworthy. Absorbing the Main Points When reading news articles, extract information about the researchers, the institution where the work was performed, the method of how they conducted the study, and the major findings of the study. Let's use the news article we introduced at the top of this page that covers the massive insect die-off in Europe. We will start by reading the article in The Scientist, which was published on October 18, 2017; it is titled "Germany sees drastic decrease in insects." Follow the link and read the article. Try jotting down some key points, and then compare them to our list below. Key Points From the Article in The Scientist: 1. The research is published in PLoS ONE. This is an open-access journal, meaning the public is able to read the primary paper since this journal does not require a paid subscription to access it. 2. The authors are experts. They include plant ecologists from the Netherlands and some colleagues from the Entomological Society in Krefeld, Germany, who have been collecting data on flying insect biomass for two decades. 3. Researchers sampled 63 protected nature areas throughout Germany over 27 years and found a 76% decrease of flying insect mass. 4. The methodology is described. Here, the technique used to collect insects consisted of deploying “malaise traps," specialized mesh tents that direct flying insects toward a chamber with collection bottles filled with alcohol.

They are transparent about the data collection: 37 of the locations were only sampled once, and 26 locations at least twice, with many years in between. All of the sampling sites are lowlands regions amid agricultural lands and human-populated areas. 5. The major finding was that after 20 years, the scientists began to see a drastic decrease in insects of about 80%, so they re-sampled certain locations to ensure that their information was accurate. The trend continued, and by midsummer the decline had reached 82%. 6. The reasons behind the decline are not fully understood. Weather and temperature patterns, plant inventories, and the type of preserve were all examined for associations, but no factor alone could explain the disappearance of the flying insects. Climate change could not explain the results either. 7. At the end of this paper, the original citation in PLoS ONE is given, so readers can pull up the primary research article. If readers are not scientists, it might be best to continue to evaluate the work by reading more of the popular science articles rather than heading straight to the research paper in PLoS ONE. Each one should have a different synopsis to help readers absorb the key findings. If, for example, we compare the article in The Scientist with another one reporting the same study in Science Daily, we see that some points are omitted, while new ones appear. The article in Science Daily was published on October 19, 2017; it is titled "Three-quarters of the total insect population lost in protected nature reserves." Follow the link and read the article. Additional Key Points From the Article in Science Daily: 1. The article provides information on previous work in this field: Previous research has shown an overall pattern of decline in insect diversity and abundance but has focused on single species or taxonomic groups, whereas this study looked at overall insect biomass over an extended period of 27 years. 2. There is further extrapolation into the reasons behind the insect decline: The authors believe large-scale factors are involved in this loss. After reading several articles from reputable news sites, beekeepers may wish to read the original scientific article. One reason to go to PLoS ONE to read the

article would be to look at the actual data as well as how the authors presented and interpreted their findings. Readers can also find all the other articles that have been referenced in the study to provide additional sources of information on the topic. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Obtaining Reputable Scientific Articles The insect die-off paper is easily ☆ Key Points obtained online through open access to the journal PLoS ONE. Open-access journals like this one make a profit by charging the authors a fee to publish within it. Research that was publicly funded is also available for free on While most scientific journals require subscriptions, beekeepers can access many for free. Authentic, high-quality papers are found in peer-reviewed journals. PubMed when the term “open access[filter]” is included in the search bar. Beekeepers can also search within the search engine Google Scholar to find articles of interest. By searching these three avenues — within open-access journals, the PubMed database, or Google Scholar — beekeepers are able to locate and download many scientific articles at no charge. Review articles published in peer-reviewed scientific journals can also be searched in this exact same manner. However, most research papers are in journals that require a subscription to access, or readers must physically be in a university library that owns a subscription in order to read the paper. If beekeepers want to read a paper that is behind a journal paywall, their local public library may be able to assist them through interlibrary loan. Alternatively, they can try to contact the authors, who are usually willing to send them a PDF copy of their paper. Determining Authenticity Once beekeepers have obtained the scientific paper, they are ready to begin reading! When combing through the pages, critique the quality and rigor of the work, as well as the content of the paper. An important feature of reputable journals is that each research article has been read by at least two experts in the field and comments have been returned to the authors for

improvement of the paper before it is published. Through this method, known as peer review, inferior or incomplete work is culled, and readers who are not experts can trust that the published research represents the highest standards and best experimental approach available. Journals can be verified as peer reviewed by visiting their website and reading about the publication. For instance, we can establish that PLoS ONE is peer reviewed by visiting the “About” section on their website, where there is detailed information about their peerreview process, giving us confidence that we have an authentic source. Be aware that there are hundreds of “desktop publishers” of science journals with impressive-sounding names that publish insufficiently peer-reviewed and inferior work. When in doubt, search the web for information about the source. When reading articles, be on guard against sources that are attempting to persuade readers, promote products or institutions, or sell products. The funding source for the research should be outlined in the paper. The researchers should declare any conflicts of interest for their work (or if there are none). Scientific articles should be unbiased and present information based on evidence. Lastly, do not trust a source that does not identify the authors or provenance of the work. Read: Developing Skills in Reading Scientific Articles — Understanding Layout Scientific papers are organized in a ☆ Key Points very stylized way. These papers are written for science colleagues, not for the general public, and therefore may be difficult for a layperson to follow. Articles are organized in a precise way that helps readers navigate content. Readers can avoid getting bogged down in technical details by focusing on the way science papers are organized into sections. The sections of a research paper include, in this precise order1: 1. Abstract: A brief summary of the topic, the approach, and key findings. The abstract is always freely available, even to those who do not own a subscription to the journal. By reading the abstract, a beekeeper can quickly identify the take-home message, and they can determine if they want to continue reading the rest of the article. 2. Introduction: Relevant background information on the topic is summarized with citations (references) to key studies that led up to the current work. The introduction usually concludes with a statement of purpose, or hypothesis, for the paper. 3. Materials and Methods: Techniques used in the experiment are described in detail in the Methods section. All special materials are referenced, and information on where they were obtained is given. Any detailed method that has been described elsewhere may be referenced with a citation to the original description. Any reader should be able to repeat the entire experiment based on the methods stated here. It is important that all studies and experiments be repeatable by other scientists. 4. Results: Major findings are presented in the form of tables, graphs, mathematical analyses (if appropriate), and photographs. Each graphic includes a descriptive legend, and all findings of the study are detailed without interpretation. Results that are statistically significant are mentioned here. In scientific papers, the word “significant” has a very precise definition. Every time this word is mentioned, it means that the results are very unlikely to be found by chance (usually less than a 5% chance). Authors most often present significant findings by reporting a “p-value.” A p-value less than 0.05 is considered significant — there is less than a 5% chance the same outcome would be observed by random chance. In experimental studies, a statistically

significant result gives scientists confidence that the outcomes they measure are a response to the treatment they provided. 5. Discussion: The major findings presented in the results are interpreted. The authors contextualize their work with reference to previously published studies. In this section, authors speculate on the significance of their findings. If there are any limitations to the study, they are often outlined here. This section usually closes with a brief set of conclusions drawn from the study and a suggestion for future investigation of the topic. 6. Citations (also known as References or Bibliography): Any paper or papers that were cited in the article or detail techniques used by the authors is listed in the Citations. This makes it possible for readers to locate these articles in the event that they wish to read them. 1 Some journals put the Materials and Methods section at the end of the paper. Interpreting Papers Interpreting papers does not come naturally to anyone; it is truly a skill that requires practice. For beekeepers just being introduced to reading primary science articles, it is helpful to pause and reflect on what they have just read as they go through an article. This can help them think critically throughout the article and gauge whether or not they are able to logically follow the content. With particularly dense articles, it is normal to require reading the paper several times to fully digest all the information. Be patient with yourself. Scientific papers often use a lot of jargon. Write down any words that you do not recognize so you can look them up afterward. It is not necessary to fully understand the statistical analyses of a paper in order to learn the major findings and the take-home message. Here are some examples of reflection questions beekeepers can ask as they read a paper. Practicing reading scientific articles in this manner helps to strengthen skills in critical thinking:

Interpreting Scientific Papers After reading this section... ...Try to answer these questions. What are the specific questions being tested? Introduction Why are the authors interested in testing these questions? What is the extent of background knowledge pertaining to this topic? How are the authors specifically testing this question? Methods What outcomes are they measuring (e.g., colony survival, honey production, virus levels)? Do the results help answer the specific questions they tested? Results Are any of the results significant? What are the figures and tables in a paper describing? How might I interpret these results? How did the authors interpret these findings? Discussion Did the paper reference any other articles that support or dispute their findings? Do I agree with the author's interpretation? Are there any limitations to this study? What are the follow-up questions to research in this field?
Abstract Back to Table of Contents In rereading the abstract after I have finished the paper, does it make clear sense to me? Would I be able to provide a similar summary after reading the paper?

Watch: Developing Skills in Reading Scientific Articles In the following video, Courtesy Assistant Professor and fourth-generation beekeeper Dr. Christina Wahl takes us through reading and interpreting a scientific article. The article she will use as an example is the PLoS One article on insect declines that we have been following throughout this module. After viewing the video, download the paper and read through it. Reflect on whether or not you are able to understand the main points in the article and interpret the tables and figures. Video Transcript We're going to be looking at the science paper that you've already been reading about in this module from PLoS ONE, and that paper is titled "More than 75 percent decline over 27 years in total flying insect biomass in protected areas." This paper was written by quite a number of people all working in Europe on the phenomenon of how many insects are flying near the ground over periods of time in Germany. How do we approach a science paper? This is the research paper, this is the primary literature that we have on the topic here. You want to read it differently than a book because it's written for professionals, it's not written for the average person on the street. So it's going be difficult to comprehend, especially if you try to start at the beginning and plod through it like you would a newspaper article. So I'm going to suggest how to go about reading this. The first thing to do is to look at the abstract. In a very short amount of text, sometimes 150 to 250 words, the entire study is summarized. And from the abstract that you read on this paper, you're going to see that it's an observational study, it's not a controlled experiment, it doesn't test a hypothesis, it's making notes about the natural environment in a controlled and disciplined way. The bottom line in the abstract here is that as much as 82 percent of flying insect biomass was lost over a period of 27 years in Europe. The average loss was 76 percent, but a midsummer decline of up to 82 percent was seen. So, that's what our abstract's telling us. Now, the introduction is the next section of the paper, and normally that gives you the background of the study, why it was worth doing, what other people have found in the past, and sort of concludes with a little here's where we're going with this. We're going to skip over that for now. And then we get to materials and methods, which is the next section of a literature paper, primary literature paper. And here I take a little time and take a quick look. So there's the

data section, and it describes how the biomass data was acquired. Now, biomass is weight of biology, so what they did was collect insects, dry them according to a specific protocol, and then weigh that biomass to see how much there was, again, over time in different locations. Then they described what their locations were, they talk about how they collected the insects, they show photos of the type of traps they used, and they also have some table data on how the experiments were set up. So we're going to look at one table and a couple of figures out of this paper in some detail and try and get a sense for you of how to evaluate these things as best you can. And don't feel bad if you don't understand them because even the experts in other fields that try to read a paper in this category may have trouble. So in table one, it's an overview of malaise trap sample sizes. Now, the malaise trap is the kind of device they use to collect the insects. and I notice, reading the columns from left to right, that they have a column of years, the next column is the number of locations they collected from in those years, the next column over is the number of locations that have been set sample previously in those years. A lot of zeros there. They didn't realize until the last ten years or so that this was going to be important data; they were collecting it for some other reason. They said at some point, "Oh my gosh, there are fewer and fewer insects here," so then they turned it into a real study. The number of samples is in the next column, and that varies from a low of 4 to a high of 348 in 2014 here. Then comes the mean exposure time, which is simply a list of numbers. 146.6, 228.5, what does that mean? To find out, you have to go to the table legend, where you learn that it's exposure time in days. And then finally, you have the standard deviation of exposure time. If you don't understand descriptive statistics or basic statistics, there are very good short explanations online, Wikipedia and so forth have these. But for this purpose the standard deviation is the range plus and minus around the mean that gives you the range within which half your data is going to be found. So if the value is, say, 13 then that means subtract 13 and add 13 to the mean and you get the range for all the data. The next couple of tables deal with some fairly sophisticated statistics that would take us quite a bit of time and effort to wade into, and for now, let's just don't. And we'll go to figure two. Figure two is the temporal distribution of insect biomass. So when I look at a graph, I hope when you look at graphs the first thing you do is you look at the x-axis, that horizontal axis which gives you the independent variable. This is the information that's going to change no matter what else happens. Something like time, a for instance, which is on the x-axis and both halves of this figure. The upper half A is in years and the lower half B is in months.

The y-axis is the dependent variable, that's the variable that's changing according to whatever is happening on the x-axis. And in both of the cases A and B here, we see that the y-axis is biomass, which is measured in grams per day. Okay, so real quickly then, if we look at a part A on this figure we see that between 1990 and 2010 there is a trend line that's going downhill for biomass. So biomass is being lost on a steady basis over that period of time. In part B we see that, in terms of an annual change in biomass, from March is the first month here, December is the last month on this graph. We see a kind of increase and then a decrease, which is what you expect in a temperate climate like Germany where we don't see too many things flying around in January, but in June and July things are very busy. So, lots of bugs flying around in the middle of the summer, not so many in November. And that is consistent throughout the whole study, all 27 years. But what we see in the color coded part of this graph is that the earlier years are in the darker blue and the later years, like 2016, is in orange. And so, from that you can see that the curve is dampening, meaning that the height of the season when there should be the most biomass, June, July and August, is much diminished compared to years past. So, while the overall cycle of biomass change is still there, the amount of change has been reduced quite a bit. There's much less biomass in figure two. Now, figures three and four present versions of that data in different ways, trying to pull a little more information out of the same data set that was collected. And you should look at those and see if you can understand what they're trying to show you and how it differs from the other figures, but I'm going to go right ahead here to figure five, which is titled "Marginal effects of temporal changes and considered co-variants on insect biomass." Now, you'll remember that we went over a lot of complicated statistics earlier. Those statistics were designed to evaluate the possible correlative factors that might have influenced the decline in biomass. So it could have been has it been climate change, temperature changing over time, has it been a decrease in tree cover in the areas that were examined, could it be the amount of herbs growing on the ground? Whatever it was, they had all these different variables to look at and they came up with different ways of testing those. And the result is, one way of looking at it, is presented here in figure five, where the x-axis is the zero line in the middle and the y-axis shows you the contribution to insect biomass development, which is either positive above the zero or negative below the zero. And if you look across the graph you'll see that temperature has a positive effect on biomass, which doesn't surprise me because sure, in June and July temperatures are warm, lots of insects are flying. So temperature has a positive correlation with insect biomass.

Another one that's positive is the amount of nitrogen, probably increasing the amount of plant matter, and that makes insects happy. And arable land. If there's more arable land, there's more bugs. That's fine, too. But all of them hover around zero, more closely than the unknown bar over there on the left, which you'll see is extremely negative. How so, why is that extreme? Look at the double hash bar in the middle of that column and you'll see that the scale is so much larger that they had a kind of collapse to fit it here. What that's telling us is that unknown factors are the most strongly correlated with the change in insect biomass. They don't know why the insect biomass was declining, and their statistics didn't fish anything out, either. So we don't need to go back and understand all those statistics. Let's go on to the discussion now. And in reading the discussion, what I generally do is I read the first sentences of each paragraph, which in a well written paper should pretty much tell you what the content of that paragraph is, and if I find that the paper is very readable and I don't have to struggle too hard with it, I'll actually read the whole discussion more carefully. When you do that with this paper you will find that, indeed, what we just concluded from those two figures we looked at is what they concluded from the whole project. That they've seen this extreme decline in biomass, but that they weren't able to correlate it with any of the variables expected that might account for it. And what they propose is that some of the variables that they didn't look at could influence this. And they didn't look at pesticide use, the increasing amount of monoculture in the area. They didn't look at herbicides, or fertilizers, or any other kind of human activity in the area. Because they were working with nature preserves and forested land, they didn't think there would be a problem with that in those regions, but now they're considering maybe there is some drift over of effect and they should go back and do that analysis. They also mentioned in the discussion that there has only been one other study that looks at the decline of insect biomass, and it wasn't anywhere near as extensive as this one, but there was also another study done with vertebrates, animals with backbones, that shows there's been a large decline in biomass among vertebrates. So I would at this point say, "Wow, I want to read more." I could go to the bibliography and find those other studies, the other one on insects and the one on vertebrates, that have also been shown to decline over time and go to those papers and read them. And that's what the bibliography is for. So, in summary then, what you want to do with a primary research paper is read the abstract, skim over the methods to get a gist of some sense of what was going on there. Then look at the figures in more detail. Read a little bit of the discussion. If it seems like an accessible paper, read the whole thing. And by all means, go back, as we reviewed earlier

in module, and find a good popular review that was written by an expert or as a result of an interview with somebody who could help interpret the paper for the lay person. And as you probably can tell, what we found in popular reviews was very good as far as getting just about all the information we needed out of this paper in PLoS ONE. Back to Table of Contents

Read: Distinguishing Science From Pseudoscience The scientific method is the process by ☆ Key Points which scientists conduct experiments. This method relies on a series of steps: Fallacious arguments are mistakes in reasoning. 1. Scientists make observations of the natural world around them. 2. They formulate hypotheses to explain these observations. 3. They test these hypotheses by gathering data and/or conducting experiments. The risk of fallacious argument is low in a peer-reviewed journal of good repute. The term "pseudoscience" refers to work based on fallacious arguments. 4. They refine, alter, expand, or reject their hypotheses over time through continuous data collection. 5. They develop a scientific theory — a A scientific theory is a wellfounded explanation based on evidence. repeatedly tested explanation of the natural world based on extensive scientific evidence. Note that this definition is substantially different from the common vernacular use of the word “theory,” which simply means a speculative guess. One of the chief reasons that scientists around the world rely on the use of the scientific method is that a properly designed experiment avoids fallacious arguments, or mistakes in reasoning, and its findings help move our collective understanding toward the truth. Good science is published in peer-reviewed journals and stands the test of time; it is referenced and repeatable by others. There is much fake science online, and some is perpetuated in the beekeeping industry through the promotion of certain apitherapy products. Be critical (in the sense of critical thinking; not mean or disparaging) about conclusions drawn by peers conversing at bee clubs, in online blogs, and in popular science articles that appear at first glance to be quite scientific. Pseudoscience involves beliefs or statements that claim to be scientific and factual but in reality contain fallacies in their arguments. Always examine the evidence behind claims to distinguish between scientific fact and fiction.

It is important to be able to recognize a fallacious argument. Perhaps beekeepers will be better able to recognize a fallacy by considering a few examples. Example 1: “My spring honey is dandelion honey because dandelions are blooming when the bees are foraging.” In this example, there is insufficient evidence to infer a causal link between dandelion bloom and the type of honey that bees are producing. It is possible that there are other plants in bloom that are contributing to the honey. Example 2: “I lost 200 hives as a result of the local farmer’s increased use of pesticides.” In this example, there is no evidence provided to show a link between the pesticides and those hive deaths. They do not provide any evidence that the farmer’s pesticide usage has increased. The beekeeper speculates that this is the cause, but there are other causes that should also be investigated. Example 3: “Neonicotinoids must be killing my bees because I have Varroa mites under control.” In this example, these arguments are presented as though there are only two competing explanations, when, in fact, there are more than two. The bees could be dying for other reasons, or a combination of reasons, such as disease or poor nutrition. Back to Table of Contents

Watch: Exploring Your Curiosity: How to Design Your Own Study Beekeepers are a wide range of people ☆ Key Points with diverse backgrounds, opinions, lifestyles, and personalities. However, if there is one trait that beekeepers share, it is curiosity. Beekeepers by nature tend to be curious about bees and the inner workings of the colony, the enticing products they produce, their role in the surrounding Beekeepers are able (and encouraged!) to test questions in their own bee yards. Controlled experimental studies test questions by comparing treatment groups to control groups. ecosystem, and what factors and management practices can make a colony either flourish or perish. Beekeepers may find it quite In these experiments, all factors other than the treatment remain constant. empowering to learn what works best for their bees through simple experiments, and they do not have to be scientists to begin testing their questions in their own bee yards.

One component of the Master Beekeeper final exam series is to deliver a 15-minute presentation on a research topic. Beekeepers have two options: Option 1: They can select a topic from a list provided by the facilitator to thoroughly research online, through books, journals, or other avenues. Option 2: They can conduct their own research experiment or study on which to present. The research projects we introduce in this course are controlled experimental projects. The projects are considered “experimental” because the beekeeper is manipulating one group (i.e., applying a "treatment" to one group) of colonies and recording the resulting effects. The projects are considered “controlled” because all other aspects remain the same for colonies, except for what the beekeeper wishes to test. In addition, there is a "control group"; this group does not receive a treatment and serves as a benchmark. Controlled experimental studies are different from observational studies, where researchers do not control any variables but instead simply observe and collect data on how colonies behave in the natural world. Even if students do not choose to conduct their own research project for their final exam, understanding the basic steps of these projects

can allow them to test questions they may have in the future. Beekeepers need a minimum of two colonies to perform controlled experiments, but the power in the accuracy of results is much improved if more colonies are tested as there is a lot of natural variation in honey bee colonies; no two are identical! The Questions That Can Be Tested Are Limitless There are infinite opportunities when it comes to conducting research projects. Beekeepers can choose to investigate questions that are relevant to their own operation, goals, or business. Some examples of questions that beekeepers may be interested in testing with a controlled experiment include: Which bee stock performs better in my region with regard to Varroa mite levels? Does using a honey excluder reduce honey production? Does applying pollen patties to my colonies in February boost the colony population in time for apple pollination in May? Does the combination of breaking the brood cycle plus applying a mite treatment reduce Varroa levels more so than applying a mite treatment alone? Does wrapping colonies for winter improve overwintering success compared to colonies that are not wrapped? Do my colonies experience more disease and lower brood production after they come out of blueberry pollination? Each of these questions can be tested quite simply in the bee yard, yet the results can help beekeepers make meaningful decisions that can affect the amount of time or money they spend on a specific practice. For instance, beekeepers may find that they do not need to spend money on winter wraps every year, or that the time investment of breaking the brood cycle is worthwhile to reduce mite levels. Let’s go through a hypothetical example to see how a beekeeper could test a question in their bee yard, then we will summarize the main considerations to take into account for any experiment. The question we will investigate is the first example in this list: "Which bee stock performs better in my region with regard to Varroa mite levels?" Video Transcript Let's go through an example of a beekeeper designing and conducting his own experiment so that you can see how to set out and test your own beekeeping questions. A beekeeper, let's call him Matt, has been spending lots of time and money treating his bees for Varroa mites in recent years. But despite his efforts, he continues to lose colonies every

year from high infestations. He's been reading a lot about different bee stocks for mite resistance, but he doesn't know which ones will work best in his operation. And he's heard some mixed reviews from other beekeepers who've tried them. Matt is most interested in two stocks, Varroa sensitive hygenic bees and Russian bees, and he has 12 colonies that he can use in his experiment. The specific questions he wants to set out to test are as follows. First, which bee stock requires the fewest mite treatments? And second, which bee stock experiences the greatest overwintering success? The outcomes that he is going to measure to test these questions are the number of mite treatments needed in the season and survival the following spring. The first thing Matt needs to do is divide up his colonies into three groups. One group will test the Varroa sensitive hygenic bees, the next group will test the Russian bees, and the third group will be his current bee stock. The current bee stock is considered his control group. This group is the normal, or usual, state for his operation and it doesn't receive a treatment. In this case, a Varroa-resistant stock. Having this control group will allow him to see whether the Varroa-resistant stocks are better than what he's currently using. His 12 colonies can be divided up equally so that there's four colonies in the Varroa sensitive hygenic group, 4 in the Russian group, and 4 in the control group. Matt gets on the phone and he calls up some reputable queen breeders and orders 4 Varroa sensitive hygenic queens, 4 Russian queens, and 4 queens from his current supplier. He wants to requeen all 12 of his colonies to treat them identically throughout the experiment. The act of requeening, regardless of the stock, may influence Varroa mite levels, so to be sure that the response that we're seeing is from the actual genetic stock and not from the act of requeening in general, Matt will requeen all of his colonies. Each colony is numbered so that he can easily keep track of them in his notebook. Before the experiment begins, he considers all other factors that might skew his results and he figures out ways to address them ahead of time. For instance, Matt knows that Varroa populations can also be influenced by bee drift, and he doesn't want this to confound his results. So he separates the groups of colonies from each other by placing them in three separate nearby apiaries. And he adds unique labels on the front of each hive to minimize drift. He makes sure that the apiaries are close enough, though, so that colonies are still able to experience the same climate and the same access to food sources. The population strength of bees can also influence Varroa. If any of his colonies are particularly weak to begin with, he'll first equalize them by swapping frames of bees and

brood so that they all start out the experiment with a roughly equal population. He also monitors his colonies for Varroa mites before the experiment begins to ensure that they are all starting with roughly equal mite numbers. If needed, he treats his colonies to bring them all below the treatment threshold for the start of the experiment. In late May his queens arrive. He marks them all with different colors for each group to keep track of them, and he requeens all of his colonies. The experiment has officially begun. Throughout the season, Matt takes monthly Varroa mite samples as he normally does in his beekeeping operation. If colonies are above the treatment threshold, he treats on an apiary basis, again, as he normally does in his operation. Each group is managed identically for Varroa. He keeps records on how many treatments each group receives. Occasionally, he spots the queens and ensures that they're the same ones that he introduced. In all other respects besides the genetic stock and Varroa treatments, Matt manages all his colonies identically. For instance, if they need feeding, he feeds them all. When it's time to winter, he winters them all in the same manner. After he winters his colonies, he observes which ones survived over winter, and he records survivorship for each hive. Matt has done a fantastic job controlling all factors in his experiment. Now it's spring and Matt has collected data on which colonies survived, and it's time to take a look at his results. Here are his data in his record book. Mite levels are recorded in number of mites per 100 bees. The way that he's organized his notebooks show us his mite levels and whether or not he needed to treat throughout the months of July and October. The first column are his 12 colonies The first four are the Varroa sensitive hygenic colonies, followed by the next four, which are his Russian colonies, followed by the last four, which are his control colonies. In July, he monitors them all, but it turns out that both the Varroa sensitive hygenic colonies and Russian colonies are all below the treatment threshold. He does not need to apply a treatment to that group. However, in his control group, there are a few colonies that are above the treatment threshold, so he needs to apply a treatment to these. In August, we see the same trend. He doesn't need to treat his Varroa sensitive hygenic group or his Russian group, but he does need to treat his control group. In September, it's the first time he needs to treat his Varroa sensitive hygenic group. He has at least one colony that's above the treatment threshold. He does not need to treat the last two groups. In October, he doesn't need to treat his Varroa sensitive hygenic group at his low mite levels, but he does need to treat his Russian group for the first time. There's at least one colony that's above the treatment threshold. And he also needs to

treat his control group for a third time because, again, there's high mites in at least one colony. The final column is denoting survival over winter. It says Yes if that colony is alive in the spring and No if that colony isn't. At this point scientists perform statistical analyses to determine whether there are significant differences among groups. Statistics helps you determine the probability of finding the same results by pure chance. If there's a very low probability, usually less than 5 percent, of finding the same results by chance, but it's highly suggestive that the findings were a result of the treatment. In this example, the statistics find that the likelihood of winter survival or number of mite treatments needed is actually really low by pure chance, then it's likely to be related to the genetic stock that Matt tested. It's important to note that master beekeepers do not need to be statisticians, and performing statistics goes well beyond the requirements for this course and the final exams. If you're familiar with stats and like to formally test your data, please do so. But in this example we're just going to base it on his notebook observations. So, by looking at the data, we can see that the Varroa sensitive hygenic stock had the best overall winter survival. All four out of four colonies survived. The Russian stock group had the next best survival. Three and four colonies made it until spring. The control group did the poorest, with only one of the four colonies surviving. As for the number of mite treatments that were needed, both the Russian stock and Varroa sensitive hygenic stock were tied. Each required only one treatment throughout the beekeeping season. On the other hand, the control group required three treatments. This information is incredibly useful for Matt. He now has info about which stocks work best in his operation conditions and under his management practices. Although it's only one beekeeping season's worth of data and it's not looking at very many colonies, it still gives them the confidence to order Varroa sensitive hygenic queens for his operation next year to see how they continue to perform. This experiment suggests that he might save time and money on mite treatments, and he might experience greater overwinter survival. After watching this example, you can see the steps and considerations that are required for performing a controlled experiment. The steps are similar regardless of the question that is asked. Step 1: Determine the question to ask and the outcomes to test (e.g., honey production, overwintering survival, frames of brood)

Step 2: Organize colonies into groups. For a controlled experiment, there must be a control group that does not receive a “treatment.” Step 3: Control for all factors other than the treatment. Ensure colonies begin with the same population and access to resources, and manage colonies in an identical manner throughout the experiment. Step 4: Record measurements. Step 5: Interpret results. Scientists use statistics to help find meaningful differences in the data; however, it is not necessary to do this for the Master Beekeeper Program. Take some time to think about how you could set up and test the other five examples provided near the top of the page. What types of questions could you imagine wanting to find answers to in your bee yard? Begin to gain confidence in thinking scientifically about testing your questions. Back to Table of Contents

Assignment: Final Project Throughout this course, we’ve explored the products beekeepers can harvest from their colonies, how they can grow their operations, and how they can serve as a go-to source for the latest information about honey bees. For this assignment, you can choose to complete one of two options. Option 1: Growing Your Operation In this project, you will investigate the time, expenses, and potential income involved in growing your beekeeping operation. The number of colonies you plan for is up to you. For example, if you currently manage five colonies, you might plan the requirements and commitments of managing 30 colonies; whereas if you currently manage 100 colonies, you might plan for managing 300 colonies. This project focuses on pricing basic equipment and consumable items; there is no need to include costs of buildings, utilities, insurance, labor, land, or transportation. Pricing for items can be found from beekeeping equipment supply company websites and catalogs. Time management will be estimated for one month (the template uses August, but you may choose a different month if you wish) and should include only core beekeeping tasks (e.g., inspections, feeding, treatments, honey handling). Time for business activities and transportation is not required. If any students are seriously interested in growing their operation, this exercise may serve as a starting point for taking that next step. If you are unsure how much a specific item costs, reach out to your facilitator for assistance. You may complete the provided template or create your own in Word, Excel, or a similar program. Use the downloadable document to: Price out the equipment and supply costs required for expansion. Estimate your time investment for managing a larger operation. Estimate the income your expanded operation could realistically generate. Include at least one income source from the list below: Honey sales (bulk or retail) Nucleus colonies (nucs)

Queens or packages Pollination services Beeswax or value-added hive products (candles, lip balm, propolis, etc.) For each income source chosen for your expanded operation, report: Production per colony (per season) Total production for your planned operation Price per unit (cite a realistic source) Total estimated income Instructions for Option 1: Download the document for "Growing Your Operation." Download the rubric for "Growing Your Operation." Option 2: Analyzing a Scientific Paper In this project, you will find a peer-reviewed scientific article online about bees. You will read it and interpret it by answering the questions in the downloadable document. Responses can be given in point form or full sentences. Do not copy and paste responses directly from the article; you are being evaluated on your ability to demonstrate you can understand, interpret, and communicate scientific research. Not sure where to start looking for peer-reviewed articles? Many scientific journals offer free access to the public: PLoS One Ecology and Evolution Scientific Reports Nature Apidologie (some articles are free, while others are not) You are discouraged from purchasing articles for this project. If you are having trouble finding a freely accessible article, reach out to your facilitator, who may be able to access that article and send it to you! Please note that articles from Bee Culture magazine and American Bee Journal are not peer reviewed. Please attach a PDF of or a URL link to your chosen scientific article when you upload your assignment so your course facilitator has access to it. Instructions for Option 2:

Download the document for "Analyzing a Scientific Paper." Download the rubric for "Analyzing a Scientific Paper." Your project will graded as "Complete" or "Incomplete." All questions must be answered sufficiently for this project to be marked "Complete." A grade of "Complete" is required for you to pass the course. Your facilitator will provide feedback for your submission and is available to answer questions as you work on your project. If you receive a grade of "Incomplete," you can resubmit your project after incorporating the feedback from the facilitator. Mentoring Schedule for a First-Year Mentee Visit Number Date Activities & Topics to Discuss 1 End of April • Assess the mentee’s apiary site and ensure they have the proper equipment to get started. • Learn the mentee's beekeeping goals. • Discuss additional information resources for them to explore. 2 Mid May • Demonstrate how to light a smoker. • Help install the mentee’s nuc or package with them and feed syrup, explaining the hows and whys as you go along. • Discuss what to do if you get stung and how to reduce the likelihood of stings. 3 End of May • Inspect the colony together. • Demonstrate how to use the hive tool and hold frames carefully. • Discuss and identify the following items/topics: wax construction, the three castes, brood stages, food stores, and basic aspects of honey bee social behavior. • Have the mentee practice identifying eggs. 4 Mid June • Inspect the colony together. • Discuss Varroa mites and monitor for mites. Many beekeepers do not start to consider Varroa until the second year, believing young colonies will not accumulate high mite levels. This is not the case; many first-year colonies will develop high Varroa levels. Discuss treatment options, if needed. 5 Early July • Inspect the colony together. • Discuss colony population growth and add a second deep hive body, if needed. • Discuss how to identify a colony preparing to swarm or a colony that has swarmed. Note that it is unlikely at this time (being a young colony in the month of July) that the mentee will observe signs indicating swarming. 6 End of July • Inspect the colony together. • Discuss nectar flows in the region. • Discuss how to inspect the brood pattern to evaluate the queen and colony health. 7 Early August • Have the mentee lead the colony inspection while you observe. • Evaluate honey stores in preparation for winter. • Discuss pests and diseases that can affect bees and the symptoms to look for. • Discuss colony thermoregulation and provide additional ventilation if needed. 8 Mid August • Discuss the honey harvest! Whether they have a super of honey or not, invite them to join your honey extraction endeavors. 9 Early • Have the mentee lead the colony inspection while you observe. September • Ask them to demonstrate the skills they have developed so far: finding eggs, differentiating different types of food stores and brood stages, scraping burr comb, gently moving and replacing frames and hive bodies, etc. • Observe the mentee monitoring for mites; discuss treatment options if necessary. 10 Mid • Have the mentee lead the colony inspection while you observe. September • Ensure the colony is ready for winter: begin feeding heavy syrup and pollen patties, if needed; merge weak colonies or those with failing queens. • Advise your mentee which wintering equipment to purchase. 11 Mid October • Have the mentee lead the colony inspection while you observe. • Ensure the colony is still on track for wintering successfully. • Have the mentee monitor for mites. Discuss treatment options if necessary. 12 Mid • Winterize the colony together. November • Provide information (or a beekeeping calendar) to your mentee regarding winter inspections, maintenance, and feeding. Be available for questions they may have during winter.
